original_question: How does the supernova phenomenon evolve with metallicity, stellar population, cosmic age, environment, and other relevant parameters across cosmic time, and how should those dependencies be included when using supernovae to understand how the universe works and evolves?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the population of supernovae (SNe) — the explosive endpoints of stellar evolution, occurring in various spectroscopic and photometric subclasses (e.g., thermonuclear Type Ia and core-collapse Types II, Ib, Ic, and their subtypes) — viewed as a phenomenon distributed across cosmic history. Let the SN phenomenon be characterized by observables such as event rates per unit comoving volume, luminosity functions, light-curve shapes, spectral properties, ejecta masses, kinetic energies, nucleosynthetic yields, and progenitor channels. Let these observables depend on the following parameters: (i) metallicity Z of the progenitor and its environment; (ii) the stellar population from which the progenitor is drawn (including age distribution, initial mass function, and binarity); (iii) cosmic age (equivalently redshift z); and (iv) host environment (host galaxy morphology, mass, star-formation rate, local interstellar medium properties).

Problem: Determine, quantitatively, how each class of supernova phenomenon evolves as a function of (Z, stellar population, cosmic age z, environment, and any further relevant parameters) across cosmic time. In particular:

1. Establish the functional dependences of SN rates, luminosities, spectra, and explosion parameters on (Z, population age, z, host environment).
2. Identify which intrinsic properties of SNe are universal versus which evolve with cosmic time.
3. Specify how to incorporate these dependences as systematic corrections or priors when SNe are used as cosmological tools (e.g., Type Ia SNe as standardizable candles for measuring distances, the expansion history, and dark energy parameters; core-collapse SNe as tracers of star formation and chemical enrichment).
4. Provide a framework that accounts for these evolutionary effects in a way that allows SNe to be used reliably to probe the workings and evolution of the Universe.
status_search_result: This is a broad open program in supernova astrophysics and observational cosmology rather than a single closed mathematical problem. Ongoing work (e.g., LSST/Rubin, JWST, DES, ZTF, Roman) continues to characterize metallicity, host-environment, and redshift dependences of SN Ia and core-collapse SN properties; systematic effects such as the SN Ia "mass step" and progenitor-age dependence remain active research areas with no definitive resolution.

paper_title: Unsolved Problems about Supernovae
original_question: What physically grounded classification scheme for supernovae should replace or supplement purely morphological subclass definitions so that newly observed diversity does not create the false impression that distinct explosion problems have been solved merely by assigning new subclass names?
self_contained_problem: Devise a physically grounded classification scheme for supernovae that can replace or supplement existing purely morphological (spectral/light-curve based) subclass definitions. Concretely: propose a taxonomy whose primary categories are defined by intrinsic physical parameters of the explosion — such as the nature of the progenitor system (single massive star, interacting binary, white dwarf in a binary, etc.), the explosion mechanism (thermonuclear runaway, iron-core collapse, electron-capture collapse, pair instability, magnetar-driven, etc.), the energy source powering the light curve (radioactive decay, shock interaction with circumstellar medium, central engine), the ejecta mass and composition, and the circumstellar environment — rather than by observational morphology alone. The scheme should (i) be unambiguously assignable from currently obtainable observations and physical modeling, (ii) accommodate newly discovered diversity without requiring proliferation of ad hoc named subclasses, and (iii) avoid creating the impression that an explosion mechanism is understood merely because a new morphological label has been introduced. Specify the categories, the criteria that place an event in each category, and demonstrate how known supernova types (Ia, Ib, Ic, IIP, IIL, IIn, IIb, superluminous, Ca-rich, .Ia, etc.) map into the proposed scheme.
status_search_result: A universally adopted physics-based supernova classification has not been established; the community continues to use the historical Minkowski/Zwicky morphological scheme (Type I/II with subclasses) augmented by ad hoc names. Reviews and recent literature on supernova taxonomy still call for, but have not implemented, a fully physics-based replacement.

Let $p>3$ be a prime. For an integer $m$ coprime to $p$, let $\left(\tfrac{m}{p}\right)$ denote the Legendre symbol, and let $B_n(x)$ denote the Bernoulli polynomials. Decide whether all three of the following statements are true.

$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{\binom{2k}{k}^{2}\binom{3k}{k}}{(-48)^{3k}}\equiv\begin{cases} x^{2}-2p\pmod{p^{2}}, & \text{if } \left(\tfrac{p}{3}\right)=\left(\tfrac{p}{41}\right)=1 \text{ and } 4p=x^{2}+123y^{2},\\[2pt] 2p-3x^{2}\pmod{p^{2}}, & \text{if } \left(\tfrac{p}{3}\right)=\left(\tfrac{p}{41}\right)=-1 \text{ and } 4p=3x^{2}+41y^{2},\\[2pt] 0\pmod{p^{2}}, & \text{if } \left(\tfrac{p}{123}\right)=-1. \end{cases}$$

(2) For every positive integer $a$,
$$p^{a}\sum_{k=0}^{p^{a}-1}\frac{615k+53}{(-48)^{3k}}\binom{2k}{k}^{2}\binom{3k}{k}\equiv 53\bigl(p^{a}+(p^{a-1})\bigr)-\tfrac{5}{12}\,p^{2}B_{p-2}(\tfrac{1}{3})\pmod{p^{3}},$$
in the sense intended by the original formulation (with $(p^{a-1})=1$ when $a=1$ and $0$ otherwise, and the right-hand factors interpreted accordingly).

(3) For every integer $n\ge 2$, the rational number
$$a_{n}:=\frac{1}{n(2n+1)\binom{2n}{n}}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(615k+53)\binom{2k}{k}^{2}\binom{3k}{k}(-48)^{3(n-1-k)}$$
is an integer, except when $2n+1$ is a power of $3$, in which case $3a_{n}$ is an integer not divisible by $3$.

The conjecture appears in Zhi-Wei Sun's list of open conjectural supercongruences; while many similar Ramanujan-type supercongruences from Sun's lists have been resolved over the years, no specific resolution of this one was located.

paper_title: “Ab initio” models of galaxy formation: successes and open problems
original_question: How much do galaxy-formation predictions change when semi-analytic models use merger trees generated by the classical extended Press-Schechter (EPS) formalism instead of merger trees extracted directly from numerical simulations, given that recent work indicates EPS may not adequately describe simulated merger trees?
self_contained_problem:
Within the framework of semi-analytic models of galaxy formation, dark matter halo merger trees (the hierarchical record of progenitor halos that merge to form a given halo as a function of cosmic time) can be constructed in two principal ways:

(a) Analytically, via Monte Carlo realizations based on the extended Press–Schechter (EPS) formalism, which uses the spherical-collapse, excursion-set conditional mass function
P(M_1, z_1 | M_2, z_2) for a progenitor of mass M_1 at redshift z_1 of a descendant halo of mass M_2 at redshift z_2 < z_1, derived from a Gaussian random field of linear density perturbations with a specified power spectrum.

(b) Numerically, by identifying bound dark matter halos in cosmological N-body simulations at successive redshifts and linking progenitors to descendants on the basis of shared particle membership.

Recent work indicates that the conditional mass functions, progenitor mass distributions, and assembly-time statistics produced by the EPS formalism do not, in general, reproduce those measured directly from N-body simulations.

Quantify, as a function of halo mass M and redshift z, the resulting differences in the predictions of a fixed semi-analytic galaxy formation model — including the galaxy stellar mass function, luminosity function, color and metallicity distributions, star-formation-rate density, and satellite galaxy abundance — when its merger trees are supplied by the classical EPS Monte Carlo algorithm versus when they are extracted from a cosmological N-body simulation with identical cosmological parameters and initial power spectrum, with all other ingredients of the model held fixed. In particular, determine for which observable statistics, halo mass ranges, and redshift intervals the discrepancies are statistically significant, and characterize the systematic biases introduced by using EPS-based trees.
category_tag: cosmological merger trees and semi-analytic galaxy formation
status_search_result: Direct comparisons (e.g., Helly et al. 2003 and follow-up studies) have established that running the same semi-analytic model with EPS Monte Carlo trees versus with merger trees extracted from N-body simulations yields statistically significant differences in galaxy population properties, traceable largely to the known discrepancy between EPS and N-body conditional/progenitor mass functions. Subsequent works (Parkinson et al. 2008; Jiang & van den Bosch and others) have proposed corrections to EPS to better match simulations, and more recent emulator-based approaches (e.g., FLORAH-Tree, 2025) continue to refine this. However, a complete, fully quantitative characterization across all observables, halo masses, and redshifts remains incomplete, so the broader question is best described as partially solved.

original_question: Can intermittent radio-mode AGN activity in cluster centres inject energy in a way that efficiently suppresses cooling flows throughout massive haloes, despite the facts that not every cluster shows central radio activity and that radiative cooling depends steeply on gas density, which makes stabilization difficult at all radii?
category_tag: AGN feedback and cluster cooling flows
status_search_result: The question of how intermittent radio-mode AGN feedback can globally and stably suppress cooling flows in massive clusters remains an active open problem. Recent reviews and simulations (e.g., MNRAS 473 (2017), ApJ 811 (2015), ApJ 858 (2018)) confirm that while the AGN–cooling-flow scenario is widely accepted and duty cycles approach unity, how jets heat the ICM while preserving observed temperature gradients and cool cores at all radii is still debated and unresolved.

paper_title: “Ab initio” models of galaxy formation: successes and open problems
original_question: Can semi-analytic models with radio-mode AGN feedback achieve quantitative agreement with the observed star-formation histories of massive elliptical galaxies, rather than only reproducing the qualitative trend that more massive ellipticals have shorter star-formation time-scales?
self_contained_problem: Consider semi-analytic models of galaxy formation built on cosmological dark-matter halo merger trees, in which baryonic processes (gas cooling, star formation, supernova feedback, chemical enrichment, galaxy mergers) are treated through analytic prescriptions, and in which "radio-mode" active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback is included as a heating mechanism that suppresses gas cooling in massive halos hosting a central supermassive black hole accreting at low Eddington rates. Within such a framework, determine whether one can choose physically motivated prescriptions and parameters so that the predicted star-formation histories of massive elliptical galaxies (i.e., the mean star-formation rate as a function of cosmic time, conditioned on present-day stellar mass for ellipticals with stellar mass M_* ≳ 10^11 M_⊙) agree quantitatively—not merely qualitatively—with star-formation histories inferred from observed galaxy spectra (e.g., via spectral fitting yielding archaeological star-formation rate densities as a function of look-back time and galaxy mass). The qualitative trend that more massive ellipticals have shorter star-formation time-scales ("downsizing") is already reproduced; the question is whether quantitative agreement of the full time-dependent star-formation histories across the massive-elliptical mass range can be achieved.
status_search_result: No definitive resolution was identified. Subsequent semi-analytic and hydrodynamic simulations with AGN feedback (e.g., variants of the Munich/Durham models, GAEA, L-Galaxies, Shark) have improved the match to downsizing trends, but quantitative agreement with archaeologically reconstructed star-formation histories of massive ellipticals remains debated, with persistent tensions in the predicted timing and duration of star formation. The question is best classified as still open / partially addressed.

paper_title: “Ab initio” models of galaxy formation: successes and open problems
original_question: Why do semi-analytic models predict that the stellar mass of massive galaxies should increase by a factor of about 2 to 4 since redshift z ∼ 1, while observational estimates suggest that the massive end of the galaxy stellar-mass function shows little significant evolution over the same interval?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the galaxy stellar mass function Φ(M⋆, z), defined as the comoving number density of galaxies per unit logarithmic stellar mass M⋆ at redshift z. Standard hierarchical semi-analytic models of galaxy formation, built on the ΛCDM cosmological framework with prescriptions for gas cooling, star formation, supernova and AGN feedback, and galaxy mergers within dark-matter halo merger trees, predict that galaxies with present-day stellar mass M⋆ ≳ 10^11 M_⊙ should have grown in stellar mass by a factor of approximately 2 to 4 between redshift z ≈ 1 and z = 0, primarily through dry mergers. In contrast, observational determinations of Φ(M⋆, z) at the high-mass end (M⋆ ≳ 10^11 M_⊙) over the same redshift interval indicate little to no significant evolution in the comoving abundance of such massive galaxies.

Provide a physically motivated and quantitatively consistent explanation that reconciles this discrepancy. Specifically, identify modifications to the assembly history of massive galaxies — whether in the merger rate, the efficiency or fraction of stellar mass lost during mergers (e.g., to intracluster light), the satellite-disruption prescription, AGN feedback at late times, or in observational systematics affecting M⋆ determinations (initial mass function, photometric stellar-mass estimates, progenitor effect) — that would simultaneously satisfy:
(i) the predicted factor 2–4 mass growth of individual massive galaxies since z ∼ 1, and
(ii) the observed near-constancy of the massive end of Φ(M⋆, z) over 0 ≤ z ≲ 1.
status_search_result: Subsequent work has narrowed but not fully closed the tension. Improvements include accounting for stellar mass loss to intracluster light during mergers, revised satellite-disruption and AGN-feedback prescriptions, and reassessments of observational stellar-mass systematics (IMF variations, progenitor bias). Modern semi-analytic models (e.g., SHARK, SAGE) and recent stellar mass function measurements (COSMOS2015, COSMOS2020) report better but imperfect agreement: residual excesses at log10(M⋆/M_⊙) > 11.5 persist in simulations, while observations confirm modest evolution of the high-mass end since z ∼ 1. The discrepancy is therefore considered partially resolved rather than fully solved.

paper_title: “Ab initio” models of galaxy formation: successes and open problems
original_question: Is the discrepancy between predicted and observed mass assembly of brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs) a real failure of the models, or can it be explained by mismatched comparisons such as observational aperture magnitudes versus model total magnitudes and by the omission in many semi-analytic models of spatial light distributions and tidal stripping into intracluster light?
self_contained_problem:
In hierarchical structure formation, the brightest cluster galaxy (BCG) of a galaxy cluster is the most luminous member, typically located near the cluster center. Observational studies of BCGs in the redshift range 0 ≤ z ≤ 1 commonly report photometry within fixed metric apertures that capture only 25–50% of the total light belonging to the combined BCG plus intracluster light (ICL) component, and find results consistent with no significant stellar mass growth of the BCG since z ∼ 1. In contrast, semi-analytic models of galaxy formation built on top of cosmological dark-matter merger trees, in which the BCG's stellar mass is computed as the total stellar mass formed in or accreted onto the central galaxy of the most massive cluster halo, predict that the BCG stellar mass grows by roughly a factor of four between z ∼ 1 and z = 0.

Determine whether this discrepancy reflects a genuine failure of the underlying physical model of BCG mass assembly, or whether it can be fully reconciled by:
(i) consistently comparing model predictions and observations using the same fixed metric aperture, accounting for the fraction of total BCG+ICL light enclosed; and
(ii) incorporating into the semi-analytic models the spatial distribution of stellar light in cluster galaxies together with the tidal stripping and harassment of stars from satellite galaxies into a diffuse intracluster light component, so that mass accreted onto the central halo is partitioned between the BCG and the ICL.

Specifically, decide whether implementing (i) and (ii) suffices to bring the predicted BCG mass-growth history since z ∼ 1 into quantitative agreement with the observed mass-growth history.
category_tag: Galaxy formation and BCG mass assembly
status_search_result: Subsequent work on semi-analytic models and high-resolution cosmological simulations has shown that consistently comparing model predictions to observations within fixed metric apertures, and including tidal stripping of stars from satellites into an intracluster-light component, substantially reduces the discrepancy between predicted and observed BCG mass growth since z ∼ 1. Models that explicitly track BCG–ICL partitioning (e.g., Contini et al. 2018, the Galaxy Replacement Technique studies, and recent BCG/ICL coevolution analyses) find broad agreement with observations once aperture and ICL effects are accounted for, although residual tensions and modeling uncertainties (e.g., resolution limits, treatment of orphan galaxies, satellite disruption criteria) remain. The question is therefore considered partially resolved rather than a fundamental failure of hierarchical models.

paper_title: “Ab initio” models of galaxy formation: successes and open problems
original_question: What physical treatment of satellite-galaxy gas stripping and subsequent star-formation shutdown is needed in semi-analytic models to avoid producing too many faint red satellites and too sparsely populated a green valley, while still matching observed satellite colour distributions?
self_contained_problem:
In semi-analytic models of galaxy formation, when a galaxy becomes a satellite of a larger halo it is conventionally assumed that its hot gas reservoir is stripped instantaneously and completely, so that gas cooling onto the satellite is shut off; combined with efficient supernova feedback, this rapidly exhausts the satellite's cold gas and drives it onto the red sequence on short time-scales. This prescription is known to overproduce faint red satellite galaxies and to underpopulate the intermediate "green valley" of the galaxy colour distribution relative to observations.

Formulate and justify a physically motivated modification of the treatment of (i) hot-gas stripping from satellite galaxies after infall and (ii) the resulting shutdown of star formation, to be incorporated into a semi-analytic model of galaxy formation, such that the predicted satellite colour distribution simultaneously:

1. reduces the excess population of faint red satellites,
2. produces a green-valley population whose number density and colour distribution is consistent with observed values, and
3. preserves agreement with the observed overall satellite colour distribution and with other observational constraints (luminosity function, central-galaxy colours, etc.).

Specify the prescription explicitly (for example, the timescale and radial dependence of hot-gas removal, any retention of gas after infall, ram-pressure or tidal stripping criteria, and the coupling to supernova feedback), and demonstrate quantitatively that the resulting model satisfies the above three requirements.
category_tag: satellite galaxy strangulation in semi-analytic models
status_search_result: The "satellite overquenching" / strangulation problem in semi-analytic models remains an active and unresolved issue. Numerous works since 2009 (e.g., Font et al. 2008, Weinmann et al., Kang & van den Bosch, Henriques et al. 2015, 2020, Cora et al., Xie et al. 2020) have replaced instantaneous hot-gas stripping with gradual ram-pressure/tidal stripping prescriptions and have improved—but not fully resolved—the satellite colour distribution and green-valley population. No single prescription is yet accepted as a complete solution.

paper_title: “Ab initio” models of galaxy formation: successes and open problems
original_question: Why have hierarchical galaxy-formation models been unable to reproduce both the observed galaxy luminosity function and the zero-point of the Tully-Fisher relation when disk circular velocity is evaluated at the half-mass radius using realistic galaxy-size calculations, and does this failure come from approximations in size modelling or from a more fundamental shortcoming of the cold dark matter paradigm?
self_contained_problem:
Consider hierarchical galaxy formation in the cold dark matter (CDM) paradigm, in which galaxy disks form within dark-matter halos that grow by mergers. Two key observational benchmarks must be simultaneously reproduced by such a model:

(i) the galaxy luminosity function Φ(L), giving the comoving number density of galaxies as a function of luminosity L;

(ii) the Tully–Fisher relation, the empirical correlation L ∝ V^α between the luminosity L of a spiral disk and its rotation (circular) velocity V, including the absolute zero-point (normalization) of this relation.

Within a semi-analytic framework, model each galaxy as a centrifugally supported exponential disk embedded in an NFW dark-matter halo, with disk scale length and half-mass radius R_{1/2} computed from angular-momentum conservation and adiabatic contraction (i.e., a "realistic" size calculation rather than identifying the disk velocity with the halo virial velocity). Define the model Tully–Fisher velocity as the total circular velocity V_c(R_{1/2}) of the disk+halo system evaluated at the stellar half-mass radius.

Question: Can a hierarchical CDM-based galaxy-formation model simultaneously fit Φ(L) and the zero-point of the L–V_c(R_{1/2}) Tully–Fisher relation? If matching both is impossible, determine whether the obstruction stems from approximations in the disk-size/rotation-curve calculation (e.g., adiabatic contraction prescription, angular-momentum assignment, baryonic feedback on the inner halo profile) or from a more fundamental shortcoming of the CDM paradigm itself (e.g., halo concentration–mass relation or inner density profile).
status_search_result: The simultaneous reproduction of the galaxy luminosity function and the Tully–Fisher zero-point with a realistic disk-size calculation has been a long-standing tension in semi-analytic CDM models. Subsequent work (e.g., Dutton et al. 2007/2011 "The Tully-Fisher Zero Point Problem", Trujillo-Gomez et al., and the MNRAS paper "The hierarchical build-up of the Tully–Fisher relation") has proposed partial reconciliations involving low stellar mass-to-light ratios, reduced halo concentrations, suppressed adiabatic contraction or expansion of inner halos by baryonic feedback, but no consensus solution has fully resolved whether the residual tension is a modelling artifact or a fundamental CDM issue. The status is therefore best described as partially solved.

original_question: If an ℓ-group G is ℓ-simple, are all its convex normal subgroups trivial?
self_contained_problem:

A subgroup $H\le G$ is called convex if whenever $a,b\in H$ and $g\in G$ satisfy $a\le g\le b$, then $g\in H$. An $\ell$-subgroup of $G$ is a subgroup that is also a sublattice with respect to the operations $\vee$ and $\wedge$. A convex $\ell$-subgroup that is normal in $G$ is called an $\ell$-ideal; equivalently, $\ell$-ideals are precisely the kernels of $\ell$-homomorphisms. The $\ell$-group $G$ is said to be $\ell$-simple if its only $\ell$-ideals are $\{e\}$ and $G$.

Question: If an $\ell$-group $G$ is $\ell$-simple, must every convex normal subgroup of $G$ (as a subgroup, not necessarily an $\ell$-subgroup) be either $\{e\}$ or $G$?

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
original_question: Find conditions on an ℓ-homomorphism for it to preserve the archimedean property.
self_contained_problem:
A lattice-ordered group (ℓ-group) is a group G equipped with a lattice order ≤ such that the group operation is order-preserving in both arguments; equivalently, the operations ∧ (meet) and ∨ (join) are defined and translation-invariant. An ℓ-group G is called archimedean if, for all a, b ∈ G with a, b ≥ e (the identity), the condition a^n ≤ b for every positive integer n implies a = e. An ℓ-homomorphism between ℓ-groups is a group homomorphism that also preserves the lattice operations ∧ and ∨.

It is known that the class of archimedean ℓ-groups is closed under subobjects and (Cartesian) products but is not closed under ℓ-homomorphic images: there exist ℓ-homomorphisms φ : G → H with G archimedean but φ(G) not archimedean.

Problem. Determine necessary and/or sufficient conditions on an ℓ-homomorphism φ : G → H between ℓ-groups (or on its kernel, or on the source G and target H) under which the archimedean property is preserved, i.e., conditions guaranteeing that the image φ(G) (equivalently, the quotient G/ker φ as an ℓ-group) is archimedean whenever G is archimedean.
status_search_result: The problem of characterizing when ℓ-homomorphisms preserve the archimedean property is listed among unsolved problems in ordered and orderable groups. Standard references confirm that the class of archimedean ℓ-groups is closed under subgroups and products but not under ℓ-homomorphic images, and no general characterization of preserving homomorphisms appears in the literature. Various partial conditions (e.g., for ℓ-groups with strong unit, or specific categorical settings) have been studied, but a complete answer does not appear to be established.

Let $p$ be an odd prime and let $a$ be a positive integer. Throughout, $\left(\frac{\cdot}{\cdot}\right)$ denotes the Jacobi symbol, and $\lfloor x\rfloor$ is the floor function. Decide whether all of the following statements are true.

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor 4p^a/5\rfloor}(-1)^k\binom{2k}{k}\equiv\left(\frac{5}{p^a}\right)\pmod{p^2}.$$
If $p^a\equiv 1,3\pmod 5$, or if $a>1$ and $p\not\equiv 2\pmod 5$, then
$$\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor 3p^a/5\rfloor}(-1)^k\binom{2k}{k}\equiv\left(\frac{5}{p^a}\right)\pmod{p^2}.$$
Consequently, if $p^a\equiv 1\pmod 5$, then
$$\sum_{p^a/5<k<4p^a/5}(-1)^k\binom{2k}{k}\equiv 0\pmod{p^2}.$$

(ii) If $p\equiv 1,7\pmod{10}$, or if $a>2$, then

If $p\equiv 1,3\pmod{10}$, or if $a>2$, then
$$\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor 9p^a/10\rfloor}\frac{\binom{2k}{k}}{(-16)^k}\equiv\left(\frac{-1}{p^a}\right)\pmod{p^2}.$$

(i) Suppose $p$ is a prime with $p\equiv 1$ or $3\pmod 8$. Then $p$ can be written uniquely (up to signs) as $p=x^{2}+2y^{2}$ with $x,y\in\mathbb{Z}$; choose the sign of $x$ so that $x\equiv 1$ or $3\pmod 8$. Then

original_question: Does every torsion-free abelian group have an archimedean lattice order?
self_contained_problem:
A lattice-ordered group (ℓ-group) is a group G equipped with a partial order ≤ that is translation-invariant (i.e., a ≤ b implies xay ≤ xby for all x,y ∈ G) and such that (G, ≤) is a lattice (every pair of elements has a least upper bound and a greatest lower bound). A lattice order on G is called archimedean if for all a, b ∈ G with a > e (the identity) and b > e, there exists a positive integer n such that nb is not ≤ a (equivalently, in the abelian additive setting: whenever 0 < a, b in G and na ≤ b for all positive integers n, then a = 0). An abelian group G is torsion-free if no nonzero element has finite order.

Question: Does every torsion-free abelian group admit an archimedean lattice order? That is, for every torsion-free abelian group G, does there exist a partial order on G making G into an archimedean lattice-ordered group?

original_question: Is Th(F_n) decidable if n ≠ 1?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{L} = \{\cdot, {}^{-1}, e, \wedge, \vee\}$ be the language of lattice-ordered groups, where a lattice-ordered group ($\ell$-group) is a group $(G,\cdot,{}^{-1},e)$ equipped with a lattice order $(\wedge,\vee)$ such that the group operation distributes over the lattice operations (i.e., $a(b\wedge c)d = abd\wedge acd$ and $a(b\vee c)d = abd\vee acd$ for all $a,b,c,d\in G$). For each integer $n\geq 1$, let $F_n$ denote the free lattice-ordered group on $n$ generators, i.e., the free object on $n$ generators in the variety of $\ell$-groups. Let $\mathrm{Th}(F_n)$ be the complete first-order $\mathcal{L}$-theory of $F_n$.

Determine, for every integer $n\neq 1$ with $n\geq 2$, whether $\mathrm{Th}(F_n)$ is decidable.
status_search_result: Searches indicate that the word problem (equational theory) of free lattice-ordered groups is known to be decidable (and co-NP-complete), with newer proof-theoretic decidability results for the equational theory. However, no source found establishes decidability or undecidability of the full first-order theory $\mathrm{Th}(F_n)$ for $n\geq 2$. The status of the full first-order theory appears to remain open based on available evidence.

Define the Almkvist–Zudilin numbers $\{A_k\}_{k\geq 0}$ by
$$A_k=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor k/3\rfloor}(-1)^{k-3j}3^{k-3j}\binom{k}{3j}\binom{k+j}{j}\frac{(3j)!}{j!^3},$$
and for an indeterminate (or rational/integer parameter) $x$, set
$$A_k(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom{k}{j}^{2}\binom{2j}{j}\binom{2k-2j}{k-j}x^j.$$
Let $p$ denote a prime, and let $\bigl(\tfrac{\cdot}{p}\bigr)$ be the Legendre symbol. Prove or disprove the following three assertions.

(i) For every odd prime $p$,
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}A_k\equiv\begin{cases}4x^{2}-2p\pmod{p^{2}},&\text{if }p\equiv 1,3\pmod 8\text{ and }p=x^{2}+2y^{2},\ x,y\in\mathbb Z,\\ 0\pmod{p^{2}},&\text{if }p\equiv 5,7\pmod 8;\end{cases}$$
and
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^{k}A_k\equiv\begin{cases}4x^{2}-2p\pmod{p^{2}},&\text{if }p\equiv 1\pmod 3\text{ and }p=x^{2}+3y^{2},\ x,y\in\mathbb Z,\\ 0\pmod{p^{2}},&\text{if }p\equiv 2\pmod 3.\end{cases}$$

(ii) For every prime $p>3$:
- if $p\equiv 1\pmod 3$, then $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^{k}A_k\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{\binom{2k}{k}^{3}}{16^{k}}\pmod{p^{3}};$
- if $p\equiv 1,3\pmod 8$, then $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}A_k\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{\binom{4k}{k,k,k,k}}{256^{k}}\pmod{p^{3}}.$

$$x\in\{1,-4,9,-48,81,-324,2401,9801,-25920,-777924,96059601\}\cup\{\tfrac{81}{256},-\tfrac{9}{16},\tfrac{81}{32},-3969\}$$
with $x\not\equiv 0\pmod p$,
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}A_k(x)\equiv\Bigl(\tfrac{x}{p}\Bigr)\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{\binom{4k}{k,k,k,k}}{(256x)^{k}}\pmod{p^{2}}.$$

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
original_question: If n ∈ Z+ with n ≠ 1, is the universal theory of F_n decidable?
self_contained_problem:
A lattice-ordered group (ℓ-group) is an algebraic structure (G, ·, ⁻¹, e, ∧, ∨) such that (G, ·, ⁻¹, e) is a group, (G, ∧, ∨) is a lattice, and group multiplication distributes over the lattice operations on both sides (i.e., x(y ∧ z)w = xyw ∧ xzw and x(y ∨ z)w = xyw ∨ xzw for all x, y, z, w ∈ G). For each cardinal n, let F_n denote the free lattice-ordered group on n generators, i.e., the free object on n generators in the variety of ℓ-groups.

The universal theory of F_n is the set of all universal first-order sentences (sentences of the form ∀x₁ … ∀x_k φ(x₁, …, x_k), where φ is quantifier-free) in the language {·, ⁻¹, e, ∧, ∨} that are true in F_n.

Question: For every positive integer n with n ≠ 1, is the universal theory of the free lattice-ordered group F_n decidable? That is, does there exist an algorithm which, given any universal sentence in the language of ℓ-groups, decides whether it holds in F_n?
status_search_result: The question of whether the universal theory of the free lattice-ordered group F_n (n ≥ 2) is decidable is listed as an open problem in compilations of unsolved problems on ordered and lattice-ordered groups. While the word problem for free ℓ-groups is known to be decidable, no proof of decidability or undecidability of the full universal theory has been published, and recent surveys/papers on decidability in ℓ-groups continue to treat it as open.

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
original_question: Is the conjugacy problem for nilpotent finitely presented ℓ-groups soluble?
self_contained_problem:
A lattice-ordered group (ℓ-group) is a group G equipped with a lattice order ≤ such that the group multiplication is order-preserving in both arguments, i.e., a ≤ b implies xay ≤ xby for all x, y ∈ G. An ℓ-group G is finitely presented (as an ℓ-group) if it is isomorphic to the quotient of a free ℓ-group on finitely many generators by the ℓ-ideal generated by finitely many ℓ-group relations. An ℓ-group G is nilpotent if its underlying group is nilpotent (equivalently, its lower central series terminates at the trivial subgroup in finitely many steps).

The conjugacy problem for a finitely presented ℓ-group G (with a fixed finite presentation) asks for an algorithm that, given two words u, v in the generators and their inverses (using the group operations and the lattice operations ∧, ∨), decides whether the elements they represent are conjugate in G, i.e., whether there exists g ∈ G with g⁻¹ u g = v.

Question: Is the conjugacy problem soluble (decidable) for every finitely presented nilpotent ℓ-group?
status_search_result: The problem is listed as an open problem attributed to A. M. W. Glass in surveys of unsolved problems on ordered and orderable groups. A web search did not surface any published resolution (positive or negative) of the conjugacy problem for finitely presented nilpotent ℓ-groups, so its current status appears unresolved based on available sources.

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
original_question: Does any non-abelian variety of ℓ-groups have the amalgamation property?
self_contained_problem:
A lattice-ordered group (ℓ-group) is an algebraic structure (G, ·, ⁻¹, e, ∧, ∨) such that (G, ·, ⁻¹, e) is a group, (G, ∧, ∨) is a lattice, and group multiplication distributes over the lattice operations on both sides: x(y ∧ z)w = (xyw) ∧ (xzw) and x(y ∨ z)w = (xyw) ∨ (xzw). A variety of ℓ-groups is a class of ℓ-groups closed under homomorphic images, subalgebras, and direct products (equivalently, defined by a set of ℓ-group equations). A variety V is called abelian if every member of V satisfies xy = yx, and non-abelian otherwise.

A class K of algebras has the amalgamation property if for every triple (A, B, C) in K together with embeddings f : A → B and g : A → C, there exist a member D ∈ K and embeddings f' : B → D and g' : C → D such that f' ∘ f = g' ∘ g.

Question: Does there exist a non-abelian variety of ℓ-groups that has the amalgamation property?
status_search_result: The problem appears to remain open. Known results show the amalgamation property fails for several natural non-abelian varieties — e.g., the variety of representable ℓ-groups (Powell–Tsinakis and later proofs), and ℓ-metabelian ℓ-groups exhibit non-amalgamation phenomena. Only o-approximable varieties can have amalgamation, and the abelian variety is the principal known positive example. No published result exhibits a non-abelian variety of ℓ-groups with the amalgamation property.

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
original_question: Let (Ω, ≤) be a totally ordered set. What is the quasi-variety of ℓ-groups generated by Aut(Ω, ≤)?
self_contained_problem:
Background. A lattice-ordered group (ℓ-group) is a group G equipped with a lattice order ≤ such that the group multiplication is order-preserving in both arguments; equivalently, G is a group with binary operations ∧ and ∨ making (G, ∧, ∨) a lattice and satisfying a(x ∧ y)b = axb ∧ ayb and a(x ∨ y)b = axb ∨ ayb for all a, b, x, y ∈ G. The class of ℓ-groups, viewed in the signature (·, ⁻¹, e, ∧, ∨), forms a variety.

A quasi-variety of ℓ-groups is a class of ℓ-groups defined by quasi-identities, i.e. universally quantified implications of the form
  (s₁ = t₁ ∧ … ∧ sₙ = tₙ) ⟹ s = t,
where the sᵢ, tᵢ, s, t are ℓ-group terms. The quasi-variety generated by a class K, denoted Q(K), is the smallest quasi-variety containing K; equivalently, it is the closure of K under isomorphisms, subalgebras, direct products, and ultraproducts.

For a totally ordered set (Ω, ≤), let Aut(Ω, ≤) denote the group of order-preserving bijections of Ω onto itself. Equipped with the pointwise lattice operations
  (f ∨ g)(x) = max(f(x), g(x)),  (f ∧ g)(x) = min(f(x), g(x)),
Aut(Ω, ≤) is an ℓ-group.

Problem. Determine, in terms of explicit quasi-identities (or by an explicit description), the quasi-variety of ℓ-groups generated by the class { Aut(Ω, ≤) : (Ω, ≤) is a totally ordered set }.
status_search_result: The problem is listed as an open problem in compilations of unsolved problems on ordered and orderable groups. While it is classical that the variety of ℓ-groups generated by Aut(ℝ, ≤) is the entire variety of ℓ-groups (Holland's theorem), and proof-theoretic work (e.g. by Galatos and Metcalfe) gives syntactic treatments of this variety generation, the determination of the quasi-variety generated by automorphism groups of totally ordered sets does not appear to have been resolved.

original_question: In what varieties of ℓ-groups does the free product preserve the solubility of the word problem?
self_contained_problem:
A lattice-ordered group (ℓ-group) is an algebraic structure (G, ·, ⁻¹, e, ∧, ∨) such that (G, ·, ⁻¹, e) is a group, (G, ∧, ∨) is a lattice, and the group multiplication distributes over the lattice operations on both sides: a(b ∧ c)d = abd ∧ acd and a(b ∨ c)d = abd ∨ acd for all a, b, c, d ∈ G. A variety of ℓ-groups is a class of ℓ-groups closed under homomorphic images, subalgebras, and direct products, equivalently a class defined by a set of equations in the language of ℓ-groups. Given a variety V of ℓ-groups and a family {G_i}_{i ∈ I} of ℓ-groups in V, the free product (coproduct) ⨿_V G_i in V is the ℓ-group in V together with ℓ-group homomorphisms G_i → ⨿_V G_i that is universal among such cocones in V. The word problem for a finitely presented ℓ-group H in V is said to be solvable if there is an algorithm that, given any word w in the generators, decides whether w = e in H.

Characterize precisely those varieties V of ℓ-groups with the following property: whenever {G_i}_{i ∈ I} is a finite family of finitely presented ℓ-groups in V each having solvable word problem, the free product ⨿_V G_i (which is also finitely presented in V) has solvable word problem.

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
original_question: If every ℓ-subgroup of an ℓ-group G is closed, then is G discrete?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a lattice-ordered group (an $\ell$-group): a group equipped with a lattice order such that the group operation distributes over the lattice operations $\wedge$ and $\vee$ on both sides. A subgroup $H \le G$ is called an $\ell$-subgroup if it is closed under the lattice operations of $G$ (i.e., $a,b \in H$ implies $a \wedge b \in H$ and $a \vee b \in H$). An $\ell$-subgroup $H$ of $G$ is said to be closed if, whenever a subset $S \subseteq H$ has a supremum $\bigvee S$ in $G$, that supremum lies in $H$ (and dually for infima). The $\ell$-group $G$ is called discrete if every strictly positive element of $G$ dominates an atom, i.e., for every $g \in G$ with $g > e$ there exists $a \in G$ with $e < a \le g$ such that no element of $G$ lies strictly between $e$ and $a$.

Question: If every $\ell$-subgroup of an $\ell$-group $G$ is closed, must $G$ be discrete?

original_question: Is an ℓ-group generated by compact elements iff each of its ℓ-subgroups is closed?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a lattice-ordered group (an $\ell$-group): a group equipped with a lattice order $\le$ such that the group operation is order-preserving in both arguments (equivalently, $a\le b$ implies $cad\le cbd$ for all $c,d$, and the lattice operations $\wedge,\vee$ are compatible with the group structure). An $\ell$-subgroup of $G$ is a subgroup that is also a sublattice. An element $0<a\in G$ is called compact if whenever $a\le \bigvee_{i\in I} a_i$ for some set $\{a_i:i\in I\}\subseteq G^+$ for which the join exists, there is a finite subset $F\subseteq I$ with $a\le \bigvee_{i\in F}a_i$. An $\ell$-subgroup $H$ of $G$ is called closed if whenever $S\subseteq H$ has a join $\bigvee S$ in $G$, that join lies in $H$ (and likewise for meets).

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
original_question: If G is a p.o. group which is the intersection of right orders, then can G be order-embedded in an ℓ-group with the embedding preserving any existing sups and infs?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a partially ordered group (p.o. group), i.e., a group equipped with a partial order $\le$ that is translation-invariant on both sides: for all $a,b,x,y\in G$, $a\le b$ implies $xay\le xby$. A right order on $G$ is a total order $\preceq$ on $G$ that is right-invariant ($a\preceq b \Rightarrow ax\preceq bx$ for all $x\in G$); the positive cone of such an order is a subset $P\subseteq G$ with $P\cdot P\subseteq P$, $P\cap P^{-1}=\{e\}$, $P\cup P^{-1}=G$, and $g^{-1}Pg \subseteq P$ is not required (so $P$ is only a right-order cone). Say that the partial order on $G$ is the intersection of right orders if its positive cone $P_G=\{g\in G: g\ge e\}$ equals the intersection of the positive cones of some family of right orders on $G$.

An $\ell$-group is a group $L$ that is also a lattice with respect to a partial order which is translation-invariant on both sides (so all binary sups $a\vee b$ and infs $a\wedge b$ exist). An order-embedding of a p.o. group $G$ into an $\ell$-group $L$ is an injective group homomorphism $\varphi:G\to L$ such that for all $a,b\in G$, $a\le b$ in $G$ if and only if $\varphi(a)\le \varphi(b)$ in $L$. Such an embedding is said to preserve existing sups and infs if whenever a subset $S\subseteq G$ has a supremum (respectively, infimum) in $G$, then $\varphi(S)$ has a supremum (respectively, infimum) in $L$ and it equals $\varphi(\sup S)$ (respectively, $\varphi(\inf S)$).

Question: If $G$ is a p.o. group whose order is the intersection of right orders, can $G$ be order-embedded into an $\ell$-group via an embedding that preserves all existing suprema and infima of $G$?

original_question: If an ℓ-group is also a topological space with continuous group and lattice operations, then such a group is called a tℓ-group. Do free tℓ-groups exist? If yes, describe them.
self_contained_problem:
A lattice-ordered group (ℓ-group) is a group $G$ equipped with a lattice order $\le$ such that the group operation is order-preserving in both arguments, i.e. $a\le b$ implies $xay\le xby$ for all $x,y\in G$. Equivalently, $G$ carries binary lattice operations $\vee$ and $\wedge$ that are compatible with multiplication.

A topological lattice-ordered group (tℓ-group) is an ℓ-group $G$ together with a topology $\tau$ on $G$ such that the group operations $(x,y)\mapsto xy$ and $x\mapsto x^{-1}$ are continuous, and the lattice operations $(x,y)\mapsto x\vee y$ and $(x,y)\mapsto x\wedge y$ are also continuous (with $G\times G$ given the product topology).

A free tℓ-group on a topological space $X$ would be a tℓ-group $F(X)$ together with a continuous map $\iota:X\to F(X)$ such that for every tℓ-group $H$ and every continuous map $f:X\to H$ there exists a unique continuous ℓ-group homomorphism $\bar f:F(X)\to H$ with $\bar f\circ\iota=f$.

Question: Do free tℓ-groups exist? If they exist, give an explicit description of them.

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
original_question: Is a connected tℓ-group archimedian?
self_contained_problem:
A lattice-ordered group (ℓ-group) is a group $G$ equipped with a partial order $\le$ such that $G$ is a lattice under $\le$ and the group multiplication is order-preserving on both sides, i.e. $a \le b$ implies $xay \le xby$ for all $x,y \in G$. A topological lattice-ordered group (tℓ-group) is an ℓ-group $G$ endowed with a topology making it a topological group and such that the lattice operations $\vee$ and $\wedge$ are continuous as maps $G \times G \to G$. The tℓ-group is called connected if its underlying topological space is connected. An ℓ-group $G$ is called Archimedean if for all $a, b \in G$ with $a, b > e$, the relation $a^n \le b$ for every positive integer $n$ implies $a = e$ (equivalently, no strictly positive element is infinitesimal with respect to another).

Question: Must every connected tℓ-group be Archimedean?
status_search_result: Recent work on connected topological lattice-ordered groups (Algebra Universalis, 2022) reportedly resolves Pshenichnov's question in the negative: admitting a connected ℓ-group topology does not imply that the ℓ-group is Archimedean (nor even representable) in general. Under the additional hypothesis that the ℓ-group has a basis, admitting such a topology does force the ℓ-group to be a subdirect product of copies of ℝ (hence Archimedean).

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
original_question: Is the elementary theory of the lattices of ℓ-ideals of ℓ-groups decidable?
self_contained_problem:
A lattice-ordered group (ℓ-group) is a group G equipped with a partial order ≤ such that (G, ≤) is a lattice and the group operation is order-preserving in both arguments (equivalently, x ≤ y implies a x b ≤ a y b for all a, b ∈ G). An ℓ-ideal of an ℓ-group G is a normal convex ℓ-subgroup of G, i.e., a normal subgroup H ⊆ G that is closed under the lattice operations and satisfies the convexity condition: if h ∈ H, g ∈ G, and |g| ≤ |h| (where |x| = x ∨ x⁻¹), then g ∈ H. The set Id(G) of all ℓ-ideals of G, ordered by inclusion, forms a complete distributive lattice.

For each ℓ-group G, let L(G) = (Id(G); ∩, +) be the lattice of ℓ-ideals of G (where + denotes the join, i.e., the ℓ-ideal generated by the union). Consider the class 𝒦 = {L(G) : G is an ℓ-group} of all such lattices, viewed as structures in the language of lattices {∧, ∨}, and let Th(𝒦) denote the set of first-order sentences in this language that are true in every member of 𝒦.

Question: Is Th(𝒦) decidable? That is, does there exist an algorithm that, given a first-order sentence φ in the language of lattices, decides whether φ holds in the lattice of ℓ-ideals of every ℓ-group?
category_tag: Decidability of theories of lattice-ordered groups
status_search_result: For the restricted class of abelian ℓ-groups, the elementary theory of the ℓ-ideal lattices has been shown to be undecidable (Algebra and Logic, 2005, "Elementary Theory for l-Ideal Lattices of Abelian l-Groups", giving a negative answer to Problem 5.20 in the Kourovka Notebook). This builds on Gurevich's hereditary undecidability of the theory of lattice-ordered abelian groups. The general question for arbitrary (not necessarily abelian) ℓ-groups thus has a negative answer in the abelian sub-case, which already implies undecidability for the full class; however, we did not locate a single source explicitly attributing the resolution of the general question as posed.

original_question: Can the free product of ordered groups with order-isomorphic amalgamated subgroups ever be lattice-orderable if it is not orderable?
self_contained_problem:
A totally ordered group is a group $G$ equipped with a total order $\leq$ such that $a \leq b$ implies $xay \leq xby$ for all $x,y,a,b \in G$. A lattice-ordered group ($\ell$-group) is a group equipped with a lattice order that is invariant under left and right multiplication. A group is orderable if it admits a total order making it a totally ordered group, and lattice-orderable if it admits a lattice order making it an $\ell$-group.

Let $\{(G_i, \leq_i) : i \in I\}$ be a family of totally ordered groups, and let $H_i \leq G_i$ be subgroups together with order-preserving isomorphisms $\varphi_{ij}: H_i \to H_j$ that form a compatible system (so that all $H_i$ are identified via order-isomorphisms with a common ordered subgroup $H$). Form the group-theoretic free product with amalgamation $P = \ast_H \, G_i$ amalgamating the subgroups $H_i$ via the given order-isomorphisms.

Question: Does there exist such a family for which the amalgamated free product $P$ is not orderable (admits no total order making it a totally ordered group) yet is lattice-orderable (admits some lattice order making it an $\ell$-group)?

Soc. paper and related surveys, which give criteria for right-orderability of such amalgamated free products, but no source found explicitly resolves whether a non-orderable amalgamated free product of totally ordered groups (with order-isomorphic amalgamated subgroups) can nevertheless be lattice-orderable. Status appears unresolved in the accessible literature.

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
original_question: Is the variety of ℓ-groups generated by all nilpotent ℓ-groups finitely based?
self_contained_problem:
An ℓ-group (lattice-ordered group) is an algebraic structure (G, ·, ⁻¹, e, ∨, ∧) such that (G, ·, ⁻¹, e) is a group, (G, ∨, ∧) is a lattice, and the group multiplication distributes over both lattice operations on the left and the right. A variety is said to be finitely based if it can be axiomatized by finitely many such equations.

An ℓ-group G is called nilpotent if its underlying group is nilpotent. Let 𝒩 denote the variety of ℓ-groups generated by the class of all nilpotent ℓ-groups (i.e., the smallest variety of ℓ-groups containing every nilpotent ℓ-group).

Question: Is the variety 𝒩 finitely based?

A subsequent paper by the same authors on the variety generated by all nilpotent lattice-ordered groups addresses related questions (notably Kopytov's problem on weakly Abelian ℓ-groups) but does not resolve whether this variety is finitely based. No source establishing a positive or negative answer was found.

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
original_question: Study the structures (G, u) where G is an ℓ-group and u is a constant symbol/element of G satisfying the non-first-order sentence (∀g ∈ G)(∃n = n(g) ∈ Z+ )(u−n ≤ g ≤ un ). These are closely related to algebras arising from many-valued logics.
self_contained_problem:
A lattice-ordered group (ℓ-group) is a group G equipped with a lattice order ≤ such that the group operation is compatible with the lattice operations, i.e. for all a,b,c,d ∈ G, a ≤ b implies cad ≤ cbd. An element u ∈ G is called a strong (order) unit if for every g ∈ G there exists a positive integer n = n(g) such that u^{-n} ≤ g ≤ u^n. Note that the condition defining a strong unit is not expressible by a single first-order sentence in the language of ℓ-groups.

Develop a structure theory for the class of pairs (G, u) where G is an ℓ-group and u is a distinguished strong unit of G. In particular:
(a) Identify natural axiomatizations (possibly in infinitary logic or as a quasi-variety in an enriched language) for this class.
(b) Describe the relationship between (G, u) and the algebras arising from many-valued logics (such as MV-algebras and related structures), extending the Mundici-style categorical equivalence between abelian ℓ-groups with strong unit and MV-algebras to broader classes of (not necessarily abelian) ℓ-groups.
(c) Investigate representation theorems, free objects, and model-theoretic properties (e.g. amalgamation, decidability of the theory) of the class of ℓ-groups with strong unit.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open-ended research program rather than a single decidable problem. Work on ℓ-groups with strong unit and their connection to many-valued logics (MV-algebras via Mundici's equivalence, GMV-algebras, pseudo-MV-algebras of Dvurečenskij, etc.) has progressed considerably, but the broader program of fully classifying (G, u) for non-abelian ℓ-groups remains active and is not regarded as solved.

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
original_question: What can one say about quasi-finitely axiomatisable (QFA) ℓ-groups, abelian ℓ-groups and totally ordered groups. (A finitely generated model G of an algebraic theory T is said to be QFA if there is a sentence σ which holds in G such that every finitely generated model of T which satisfies σ is isomorphic to G).
self_contained_problem:
An algebraic theory T is a first-order theory in a fixed signature whose axioms are universally quantified equations (so its models form a variety). Given such a theory T, a finitely generated model G of T is called quasi-finitely axiomatisable (QFA) within T if there exists a single first-order sentence σ in the language of T such that:

(i) G ⊨ σ, and
(ii) for every finitely generated model H of T with H ⊨ σ, one has H ≅ G.

Recall:
• An ℓ-group (lattice-ordered group) is a structure (G, ·, ⁻¹, e, ∧, ∨) such that (G, ·, ⁻¹, e) is a group, (G, ∧, ∨) is a lattice, and the group operation distributes over ∧ and ∨ (equivalently, x ≤ y implies axb ≤ ayb for all a, b).
• An abelian ℓ-group is an ℓ-group whose underlying group is abelian.
• A totally ordered group is a group equipped with a total order ≤ such that x ≤ y implies axb ≤ ayb for all a, b; equivalently, an ℓ-group whose lattice order is total.

Investigate the QFA finitely generated models in each of the three algebraic theories T = (ℓ-groups), T = (abelian ℓ-groups), and T = (totally ordered groups). Specifically:

1. Characterize, as completely as possible, which finitely generated ℓ-groups are QFA within the theory of ℓ-groups.

original_question: Is every R*-group—meaning a group in which no non-empty product of conjugates of a non-identity element equals the identity—right-orderable?
self_contained_problem:
A group $G$ is called an $R^*$-group if for every non-identity element $g \in G$, every non-empty finite product of conjugates of $g$ in $G$ is different from the identity; that is, for every integer $n \geq 1$ and every choice of elements $x_1, \dots, x_n \in G$, one has
$$ (x_1^{-1} g x_1)(x_2^{-1} g x_2) \cdots (x_n^{-1} g x_n) \neq e. $$
A group $G$ is called right-orderable if there exists a total order $\leq$ on $G$ such that $a \leq b$ implies $ac \leq bc$ for all $a,b,c \in G$.

Question: Is every $R^*$-group right-orderable?

Question: Does every strictly bounded right-orderable group admit a Conrad right order?

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
original_question: Does every right-orderable n-Engel group have a Conrad right order?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $G$ be a group written multiplicatively. A right order on $G$ is a total order $\le$ on the underlying set of $G$ such that for all $a,b,c\in G$, $a\le b$ implies $ac\le bc$. The group $G$ is called right-orderable if it admits at least one right order. A right order $\le$ on $G$ is called a Conrad right order (or has the Conrad property) if for every pair of elements $a,b\in G$ with $a>1$ and $b>1$, there exists a positive integer $n$ such that $ab^n>b$.

For a positive integer $n$, the group $G$ is called $n$-Engel if the iterated commutator
$$[x,\,\underbrace{y,y,\ldots,y}_{n}]=1$$
holds for all $x,y\in G$, where $[x,y]=x^{-1}y^{-1}xy$ and $[x,y_1,\ldots,y_k]=[[x,y_1,\ldots,y_{k-1}],y_k]$.

Question. Let $n$ be a positive integer. Does every right-orderable $n$-Engel group admit at least one right order that is a Conrad right order?
status_search_result: The problem appears in a known list of unsolved problems on ordered and orderable groups, attributed to A. H. Rhemtulla. Searches for resolutions return only the original problem list and related surveys (e.g., Longobardi–Maj on Engel conditions, Traustason's Engel groups survey, and an arXiv paper "An Engel condition for orderable groups"); none of these report a solution to the specific question of whether every right-orderable n-Engel group admits a Conrad right order. The closely related problem of whether every right-orderable n-Engel group is nilpotent also remains open. Status appears to be open.

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
original_question: Is every torsion-free Engel group right-orderable?
self_contained_problem:
A group $G$ is called right-orderable if there exists a total order $\le$ on $G$ that is invariant under right multiplication, i.e., $a \le b$ implies $ac \le bc$ for all $a,b,c \in G$. For elements $x,y$ of a group, define iterated commutators by $[x,{}_1 y] = [x,y] = x^{-1}y^{-1}xy$ and $[x,{}_{n+1}y] = [[x,{}_n y], y]$ for $n \ge 1$. Question: Is every torsion-free Engel group right-orderable?

context_brief: Linearity of finite smooth actions on S^4 with isolated fixed point
original_question: Is every smooth action of a finite group on S^4 that has an isolated fixed point smoothly conjugate to a linear action?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S^4$ denote the standard 4-sphere, and let $G$ be a finite group acting smoothly on $S^4$. A fixed point $p \in S^4$ of the $G$-action is called isolated if $p$ is an isolated point of the fixed-point set $\mathrm{Fix}(G, S^4) = \{x \in S^4 : g\cdot x = x \text{ for all } g \in G\}$. The action is called linear if it is smoothly conjugate to the restriction of an orthogonal representation $G \to O(5)$ to the unit sphere $S^4 \subset \mathbb{R}^5$; equivalently, there exists a diffeomorphism $\varphi : S^4 \to S^4$ and a homomorphism $\rho : G \to O(5)$ such that $\varphi(g \cdot x) = \rho(g)\,\varphi(x)$ for all $g \in G$ and $x \in S^4$.

Question: Is it true that every smooth action of a finite group $G$ on $S^4$ which has at least one isolated fixed point is smoothly conjugate to a linear action?
status_search_result: The linearity question for smooth finite group actions on $S^4$ with an isolated fixed point is a long-standing open conjecture. Recent work (e.g., on involutions of $S^4$ and on equivariant trisections of 4-manifolds, 2025) treats only special cases such as involutions with fixed circles or 2-spheres, or imposes local linearity / homological triviality. No general resolution appears in the literature; the problem remains open.

original_question: Is every right-orderable n-Engel group nilpotent?

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
original_question: Let G be a (soluble) orderable group. Suppose that all right orders on G are Conrad right orders. (i) Is every right order on every subgroup of G a Conrad right order? (ii) Let H be a subgroup of G such that G = I(H). Is every right order on H a Conrad right order? (iii) Let H be a subgroup of G with [G : H] finite. Is every right order on H a Conrad right order? (iv) If G is non-abelian, does it contain a non-commutative free semigroup? (v) Let K be a central extension of G. Is every right order on K a Conrad right order? (vi) If additionally G is finitely generated, then is G residually torsion-free-nilpotent?
self_contained_problem:
A right order on a group $G$ is a total order $\le$ on $G$ that is right-invariant: $x\le y$ implies $xz\le yz$ for all $x,y,z\in G$. The positive cone of $\le$ is $P=\{g\in G:g>1\}$. A right order $\le$ on $G$ is called a Conrad right order if for every pair $a,b\in P$ there exists a positive integer $n$ with $a b^n > b$ (equivalently, the order has the Conrad property). A group is orderable if it admits a two-sided invariant total order. For a subset $S\subseteq G$, write $I(S)$ for the isolator of $S$ in $G$, namely $I(S)=\{g\in G: g^n\in S\text{ for some }n\ge 1\}$. A group $K$ is a central extension of $G$ if there is a short exact sequence $1\to Z\to K\to G\to 1$ with $Z$ contained in the center of $K$. A group is residually torsion-free nilpotent if for every non-identity element $g$ there is a normal subgroup $N$ with $g\notin N$ and $G/N$ torsion-free nilpotent.

Let $G$ be a soluble orderable group such that every right order on $G$ is a Conrad right order. Determine whether each of the following holds:

(i) Is every right order on every subgroup of $G$ a Conrad right order?

(ii) If $H\le G$ satisfies $G = I(H)$, is every right order on $H$ a Conrad right order?

(iii) If $H\le G$ has finite index in $G$, is every right order on $H$ a Conrad right order?

(iv) If $G$ is non-abelian, must $G$ contain a non-commutative free subsemigroup (a subsemigroup isomorphic to the free semigroup on two generators)?

(v) If $K$ is any central extension of $G$, is every right order on $K$ a Conrad right order?

(vi) If, in addition, $G$ is finitely generated, must $G$ be residually torsion-free nilpotent?

context_brief: Prime-order symplectic actions on exotic K3 surfaces
original_question: Does there exist a homotopy K3 surface with nonstandard smooth structure that admits no symplectic Z_p-actions for some prime p ≤ 19?
self_contained_problem:
A homotopy K3 surface is a smooth, closed, simply connected 4-manifold that is homeomorphic to a K3 surface. Such a manifold is called exotic (or said to carry a nonstandard smooth structure) if it is not diffeomorphic to the standard K3 surface. A smooth action of a finite group G on a homotopy K3 surface X is called symplectic if X admits a G-invariant symplectic form ω such that g*ω = ω for every g ∈ G.

Question: Does there exist a prime p with p ≤ 19 and a homotopy K3 surface X carrying a nonstandard smooth structure such that X admits no nontrivial symplectic Z/pZ-action?
status_search_result: Chen and Kwasik have shown the existence of families of symplectic exotic (homotopy) K3 surfaces on which no nontrivial smooth Z/pZ-action exists for primes p ≥ 7 (in particular, no symplectic Z/pZ-action). This addresses the question affirmatively for primes 7 ≤ p ≤ 19, but the cases p = 2, 3, 5 of the original question appear to remain open.

original_question: Let G be an orderable group such that every order on every subgroup of G is central. Is every right order on G a Conrad right order?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a group. A (total) order $\le$ on $G$ is called a (two-sided) order if it is invariant under both left and right multiplication: $x \le y$ implies $axb \le ayb$ for all $a,b \in G$. A right order on $G$ is a total order $\le$ such that $x \le y$ implies $xa \le ya$ for all $a \in G$. A two-sided order on $G$ is called central if every convex subgroup is normal in $G$ (equivalently, the order is invariant under conjugation in a strong sense compatible with the convex jumps). A right order $\le$ on $G$ is called a Conrad right order if for every pair of strictly positive elements $a,b \in G$ (i.e. $a,b > e$), there exists a positive integer $n$ such that $a^n b > a$.

Call $G$ orderable if it admits at least one two-sided order. Suppose $G$ is an orderable group with the property that for every subgroup $H \le G$, every two-sided order on $H$ is central. 

Question: Must every right order on $G$ be a Conrad right order?

original_question: Does the set of Engel elements of a (right) orderable group form a subgroup?
self_contained_problem:
A group $G$ is called right-orderable if there exists a total order $\le$ on $G$ such that $a\le b$ implies $ac\le bc$ for all $a,b,c\in G$. For elements $x,y$ in a group, define iterated commutators by $[x,{}_1 y]=[x,y]=x^{-1}y^{-1}xy$ and $[x,{}_{n+1}y]=[[x,{}_n y],y]$ for $n\ge 1$. An element $y\in G$ is called a right Engel element if for every $x\in G$ there exists an integer $n=n(x,y)\ge 1$ with $[x,{}_n y]=1$, and $y$ is called a left Engel element if for every $x\in G$ there exists $n=n(x,y)\ge 1$ with $[y,{}_n x]=1$. Question: If $G$ is a right-orderable group (or, more strongly, a two-sided orderable group), must the set of Engel elements of $G$ form a subgroup of $G$?

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
original_question: Let G be a right-orderable group and N be a nilpotent subgroup of G. Let P be a positive cone for some right order on G. Let N # be a minimal divisible completion of N and P # be the positive cone of a right order on N # which is an extension of the right order of N with positive cone P ∩ N. Let g ∈ N # and ≤g denote the right order on N induced by the right order of N # with positive cone (P # )g . Is ≤g extendable to a right order on G?
self_contained_problem:
A right order on a group $G$ is a total order $\le$ on $G$ that is invariant under right multiplication: $a\le b$ implies $ag\le bg$ for all $a,b,g\in G$. Equivalently, a right order is determined by its positive cone $P=\{g\in G:g>1\}$, which satisfies $P\cdot P\subseteq P$ and $G\setminus\{1\}=P\sqcup P^{-1}$. For any $g\in G$, the conjugate cone $P^g=g^{-1}Pg$ is again the positive cone of a right order on $G$.

A group $N$ is nilpotent if its lower central series terminates at $\{1\}$. A divisible completion of a torsion-free nilpotent group $N$ is an overgroup $N^{\#}\supseteq N$ that is nilpotent and divisible (every element has an $n$-th root for every positive integer $n$); a minimal such completion exists and is unique up to isomorphism over $N$.

context_brief: Describing bounds for smooth Z_p-actions via manifold invariants
original_question: For general smooth Z_p-actions, can the constant C from Question 4.1 be described in terms of invariants of the manifold? In particular, which invariants of the smooth structure, such as Seiberg-Witten basic classes or Seiberg-Witten invariants, enter that bound, and in what way do they enter it?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a closed smooth oriented $4$-manifold that does not admit any smooth (effective) action of the circle group $S^1$. It is conjectured (and known in special cases such as holomorphic or symplectic actions) that there exists a constant $C = C(X) > 0$ such that, for every prime $p > C$, the manifold $X$ admits no nontrivial smooth action of the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}_p$ of order $p$.

Recall that for a closed oriented smooth $4$-manifold $X$ with $b_2^+(X) \ge 2$, the Seiberg–Witten invariant is a function
\[ \mathrm{SW}_X : \mathrm{Spin}^c(X) \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}, \]
and a class $K \in H^2(X;\mathbb{Z})$ is called a Seiberg–Witten basic class if $K = c_1(\mathfrak{s})$ for some $\mathrm{Spin}^c$-structure $\mathfrak{s}$ on $X$ with $\mathrm{SW}_X(\mathfrak{s}) \ne 0$.

Question. For general smooth $\mathbb{Z}_p$-actions on $X$, can the constant $C(X)$ above be expressed in terms of invariants of the smooth $4$-manifold $X$? In particular, determine which invariants of the smooth structure of $X$ (such as the set of Seiberg–Witten basic classes, the values of the Seiberg–Witten invariants, or related refinements) enter into an admissible bound $C(X)$, and give an explicit formula or recipe describing the way in which these invariants control $C(X)$.
status_search_result: The question, attributed to W. Chen, asks how a hypothetical bound on prime orders of smooth Z_p-actions on a 4-manifold (without smooth S^1-action) depends on smooth invariants such as Seiberg–Witten basic classes. Affirmative results exist for holomorphic and symplectic actions (with the symplectic constant involving the smooth structure), but for the general smooth case no description in terms of SW invariants is known; the question appears to remain open.

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
original_question: Is every torsion-free n-Engel group orderable?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a group. For elements $x,y \in G$, define inductively $[x,{}_1 y] = [x,y] = x^{-1}y^{-1}xy$ and $[x,{}_k y] = [[x,{}_{k-1} y], y]$ for $k \ge 2$. For a fixed positive integer $n$, the group $G$ is called an $n$-Engel group if $[x,{}_n y] = 1$ for all $x,y \in G$. The group $G$ is called orderable (totally orderable) if there exists a total order $\le$ on $G$ that is two-sided invariant, i.e., $a \le b$ implies $xay \le xby$ for all $x,y,a,b \in G$. The group $G$ is torsion-free if it has no element of finite order other than the identity.

Question: Is it true that for every positive integer $n$, every torsion-free $n$-Engel group admits a two-sided invariant total order?
status_search_result: The problem appears to remain open in general. Related results are known: every torsion-free nilpotent group is orderable, and bi-orderable Engel groups are nilpotent (Kim–Rhemtulla). The questions of whether every torsion-free n-Engel group is nilpotent and whether every n-Engel group is locally nilpotent are settled positively only for small n (n ≤ 3 / ≤ 4 in various formulations) and remain open for larger n, leaving the orderability question open.

original_question: Let X be a simply connected smoothable 4-manifold with even intersection form and nonzero signature. paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
original_question: If F is a free group and H ✁ F with F/H right-orderable, then is F/[H, H] orderable?
self_contained_problem:
A group $G$ is called right-orderable if there exists a total order $\le$ on $G$ such that $a\le b$ implies $ac\le bc$ for all $a,b,c\in G$. It is called orderable (or bi-orderable) if there exists a total order on $G$ that is invariant under both left and right multiplication, i.e. $a\le b$ implies $cac'\le cbc'$ — equivalently $ca\le cb$ and $ac\le bc$ — for all $a,b,c\in G$.

Let $F$ be a (nonabelian) free group, and let $H$ be a normal subgroup of $F$ such that the quotient $F/H$ is right-orderable. Let $[H,H]$ denote the commutator subgroup of $H$, which is also normal in $F$. 

Determine whether the quotient group $F/[H,H]$ is necessarily orderable (bi-orderable).
status_search_result: The question appears in a well-known list of unsolved problems on ordered and orderable groups. Searches turned up no published resolution; recent works on bi-orderability of quotients of free groups (Magnus orderings, free metabelian groups, almost-direct products) discuss closely related cases but do not announce a solution to this question, so it appears to remain open.

original_question: If F is a free group and H ✁ F with F/H a periodic 2-group, then can every F -invariant order on H be extended to make F an o-group?
self_contained_problem:
A group $G$ is called an o-group (totally ordered group) if there exists a total order $\le$ on $G$ that is bi-invariant, i.e., for all $a,b,x,y \in G$, $a \le b$ implies $xay \le xby$. context_brief: Open dominance question under general alpha-divergence
original_question: Consider the normal linear regression prediction problem with unknown variance, under the special design assumption (AS1) used in the paper: m >= k >= 3, n = mN for a positive integer N, and the design matrix satisfies X = 1_N \otimes X~ = (X~', ..., X~')'. Under alpha-divergence loss D_alpha with -1 < alpha < 1, does the predictive density based on the same shrinkage prior pi_S,1(beta, sigma^2) = (beta' X~' X~ beta)^(1-k/2) (sigma^2)^(-2) improve on the best invariant predictive density, namely the generalized Bayes predictive density based on the right invariant prior pi_I,1(beta, sigma^2) = (sigma^2)^(-1)?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Consider a normal linear regression model with unknown variance:
  Y = X β + ε,    ε ~ N_n(0, σ² I_n),
where Y ∈ ℝ^n is the observed response, X is an n×k design matrix of full column rank k, β ∈ ℝ^k and σ² > 0 are unknown parameters. Let Ỹ ∈ ℝ^n be a future independent response satisfying Ỹ = X β + ε̃, ε̃ ~ N_n(0, σ² I_n), independently of Y.

Special design assumption (AS1). Assume m ≥ k ≥ 3 and that there exists a positive integer N and an m×k matrix X̃ of full column rank such that n = mN and
  X = 1_N ⊗ X̃,
so that X consists of N vertically stacked copies of X̃.

α-divergence loss. For −1 < α < 1, the α-divergence between a true predictive density p(ỹ | β, σ²) for Ỹ and a candidate predictive density q(ỹ) is
  D_α(p, q) = (4 / (1 − α²)) ∫ [ (1 − α)/2 · p(ỹ) + (1 + α)/2 · q(ỹ) − p(ỹ)^{(1−α)/2} q(ỹ)^{(1+α)/2} ] dỹ,
and the corresponding risk of a predictive density q(· | Y) is R_α(β, σ²; q) = E[ D_α(p(· | β, σ²), q(· | Y)) ].

Priors and predictive densities. Define
  π_{I,1}(β, σ²) = (σ²)^{−1}        (right-invariant prior),
  π_{S,1}(β, σ²) = (β' X̃' X̃ β)^{1 − k/2} · (σ²)^{−2}    (shrinkage prior).
Let q_{I,1}(ỹ | Y) and q_{S,1}(ỹ | Y) denote the (generalized) Bayes predictive densities of Ỹ given Y under the priors π_{I,1} and π_{S,1}, respectively. The predictive density q_{I,1} is the best invariant predictive density.

Question. Under assumption (AS1) and for every α with −1 < α < 1, does q_{S,1} dominate q_{I,1} under D_α-loss in the sense that
  R_α(β, σ²; q_{S,1}) ≤ R_α(β, σ²; q_{I,1})    for all (β, σ²) with β ≠ 0,
with strict inequality for at least one (β, σ²)?

original_question: If F is a free group and H✁F with F/H a periodic Engel group, then can every F -invariant order on H be extended to make F an o-group?
self_contained_problem:

Question: Can every such $F$-invariant total order on $H$ be extended to a total order on $F$ that makes $F$ a (two-sided) ordered group, i.e., a total order on $F$ invariant under both left and right multiplication?

original_question: Under D_1 loss for predictive density estimation in the normal linear regression model with unknown variance, and in the low-dimensional cases k = 1 or k = 2, can one construct Bayesian predictive densities that improve on the best invariant predictive density, even though improved non-Bayesian predictive densities are already known to exist in this setting?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the normal linear regression model with unknown variance. Let Y = Xβ + σε, where X is a known n×k design matrix of full column rank, β ∈ ℝ^k is an unknown regression coefficient vector, σ² > 0 is an unknown variance, and ε ~ N_n(0, I_n). One wishes to predict a future observation Ỹ = X̃β + σε̃, where X̃ is a known ñ×k design matrix and ε̃ ~ N_ñ(0, I_ñ) is independent of ε, by means of a predictive density p̂(ỹ | y) for Ỹ given Y = y.

The performance of a predictive density p̂(· | y) is measured under the D₁ loss
  D₁(β, σ²; p̂(· | y)) = ∫ {p(ỹ | β, σ²) − p̂(ỹ | y)} log{p(ỹ | β, σ²)/p̂(ỹ | y)} dỹ,
the symmetrized Kullback–Leibler divergence between the true density p(ỹ | β, σ²) and the predictive density p̂(· | y); the risk is the expectation of this loss over Y. The best invariant predictive density is the predictive density that minimizes the risk among all predictive densities equivariant under the natural group of location–scale transformations associated with (β, σ²).

A predictive density is called Bayesian if it is the posterior predictive density obtained from some (possibly improper) prior π(β, σ²): namely p̂_π(ỹ | y) = ∫ p(ỹ | β, σ²) π(β, σ² | y) dβ dσ².

Question: In the low-dimensional regimes k = 1 and k = 2, does there exist a (generalized) Bayesian predictive density p̂_π that strictly dominates the best invariant predictive density under D₁ risk, uniformly in (β, σ²)?
status_search_result: The problem is reported as solved: a class of improved hierarchical generalized Bayes predictive densities dominating the best invariant predictive density under D₁ loss has been constructed for k = 1 and k = 2 in the normal linear regression setting with unknown variance, extending the shrinkage-prior approach of Kobayashi–Komaki (2008) and George–Xu (2008).

paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
original_question: If G is a torsion-free group and H is a soluble normal subgroup of G with G/H a periodic Engel group, then can every G-invariant order on H be extended to make G an o-group?
self_contained_problem:
Definitions and setup. A group $G$ is called an o-group (orderable group) if there exists a total order $\le$ on $G$ that is two-sided invariant, i.e. $a \le b$ implies $xay \le xby$ for all $x,y \in G$. Given a normal subgroup $H \trianglelefteq G$, a total order $\le$ on $H$ is called $G$-invariant if it is preserved under conjugation by every element of $G$: $a \le b$ implies $g^{-1}ag \le g^{-1}bg$ for every $g \in G$ and $a,b \in H$. We say a $G$-invariant order on $H$ extends to make $G$ an o-group if there is a two-sided invariant total order on $G$ whose restriction to $H$ coincides with the given order.

A group is periodic if every element has finite order. A group $Q$ is called an Engel group if for every pair of elements $x,y \in Q$ there exists an integer $n = n(x,y) \ge 1$ such that the iterated commutator $[x,{}_n y] := [[\dots[[x,y],y],\dots],y]$ (with $y$ appearing $n$ times) is trivial. A group is soluble if it has a finite derived series ending in the trivial subgroup, and torsion-free if it has no nontrivial element of finite order.

Question. Suppose $G$ is a torsion-free group and $H$ is a soluble normal subgroup of $G$ such that the quotient $G/H$ is a periodic Engel group. Must every $G$-invariant total order on $H$ extend to a two-sided invariant total order on $G$ (so that $G$ becomes an o-group)?
status_search_result: The problem is listed as an unsolved problem attributed to A. H. Rhemtulla in a compilation of open questions on ordered and orderable groups. No subsequent published resolution was found via search; status remains unverified.

original_question: For the normal linear regression prediction problem with unknown variance, when the number of regression coefficients is k = 1 or k = 2 and the loss is alpha-divergence D_alpha with -1 <= alpha < 1, does the best invariant predictive density remain inadmissible? If it does, which Bayesian predictive density or class of Bayesian predictive densities improves upon it?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Consider the normal linear regression prediction problem with unknown variance. Observe Y = Xβ + σε_Y ∈ R^n, where X is a known n×k design matrix of full column rank k, β ∈ R^k and σ^2 > 0 are unknown, and ε_Y ~ N_n(0, I_n). One wishes to predict a future independent observation Ỹ = X̃β + σε_{Ỹ} ∈ R^m, where X̃ is a known m×k design matrix of full column rank k and ε_{Ỹ} ~ N_m(0, I_m), independent of ε_Y.

A predictive density p̂(ỹ ; y) for Ỹ given Y is evaluated by the α-divergence loss
   D_α(p, p̂) = (4/(1−α^2)) ∫ [ 1 − (p̂(ỹ)/p(ỹ))^{(1−α)/2} ] p(ỹ) dỹ,    α ∈ (−1, 1),
with D_{−1} interpreted as the reverse Kullback–Leibler divergence (limit α → −1).

original_question: If an orderable group has finite special rank, then is it soluble?
self_contained_problem:
A group $G$ is called orderable (or right-orderable) if there exists a total order $\le$ on $G$ that is invariant under right multiplication, i.e., $a \le b$ implies $ac \le bc$ for all $a,b,c \in G$. The special rank (Prüfer rank) of a group $G$ is the least nonnegative integer $r$ such that every finitely generated subgroup of $G$ can be generated by at most $r$ elements; if no such $r$ exists, the special rank is infinite. A group $G$ is soluble if its derived series $G \ge G' \ge G'' \ge \cdots$ reaches the trivial subgroup after finitely many steps.

Question: Must every orderable group of finite special rank be soluble?
