paper_title: Open Problems in Universal Induction & Intelligence
original_question: Does treating the agent's actions themselves as universally distributed random variables and then conditioning the universal semimeasure on those actions lead to a meaningful alternative formulation of the generalized universal prior used in AIXI?
self_contained_problem:
Setting. Consider a reinforcement-learning style agent interacting with an environment in discrete cycles. At cycle k the agent outputs an action a_k from a finite alphabet A and then receives a percept o_k from a finite alphabet O. Histories are finite sequences h_{<k} = a_1 o_1 a_2 o_2 ... a_{k-1} o_{k-1}. An environment is modeled as a lower-semicomputable chronological conditional semimeasure ν: given any sequence of actions a_{1:k}, ν(o_{1:k} | a_{1:k}) is a semimeasure on percept sequences (i.e. nonnegative with ∑_{o_{1:k}} ν(o_{1:k} | a_{1:k}) ≤ 1, and chronological in that ν(o_{1:k} | a_{1:k}) does not depend on a_{k+1:∞}).

Let M denote the class of all such lower-semicomputable chronological conditional semimeasures. The standard generalized universal mixture is
  ξ(o_{1:k} | a_{1:k}) = ∑_{ν ∈ M} 2^{-K(ν)} ν(o_{1:k} | a_{1:k}),
where K(ν) is the Kolmogorov complexity (prefix code length) of ν. This ξ is the universal prior used to define the AIXI agent, whose policy at history h_{<k} maximizes the expected ξ-discounted reward extracted from percepts.

Alternative construction. Instead of conditioning on actions, treat the actions themselves as universally distributed random variables. Concretely, regard a joint history a_1 o_1 a_2 o_2 ... as a single sequence over the alphabet A ∪ O and let M̃ be the universal (lower-semicomputable) semimeasure on such joint sequences. Define an alternative universal prior ξ̃ over percepts given actions by conditioning M̃ on the realized actions:
  ξ̃(o_{1:k} | a_{1:k}) := M̃(a_1 o_1 ... a_k o_k) / M̃(a_1, a_1 o_1 a_2, ..., a_{1:k}),
or, more precisely, by an appropriate conditional version of the universal semimeasure on joint action–percept sequences.

Question. Does this alternative construction—treating the agent's actions as universally distributed random variables and then conditioning the universal semimeasure on those actions—yield a well-defined and meaningfully different formulation of the generalized universal prior, in the sense that:
(1) ξ̃ is a chronological conditional semimeasure on percepts given actions;
(2) ξ̃ is not equivalent (up to a multiplicative constant) to the standard mixture ξ defined above; and
(3) the resulting AIXI-style agent (with ξ replaced by ξ̃) has properties such as universality, optimality, or self-consistency that are at least as desirable as those of standard AIXI?

Determine whether such a construction provides a viable alternative definition of the generalized universal prior for AIXI and characterize how its induced agent compares to the standard one.
category_tag: Universal AI and algorithmic information theory
status_search_result: A web search returns surveys and recent work on AIXI, generalized universal priors, and chronological conditional semimeasures (e.g., computability of AIXI, embedded versions, value under ignorance), but no source establishes an affirmative or negative resolution of whether treating actions as universally distributed random variables and conditioning the universal semimeasure on them yields a meaningful alternative generalized universal prior. The question appears to remain open.

original_question: Let T: C[0,1] -> C[0,1] be a bounded linear operator, and let X be a separable Banach space that does not contain a copy of c_0. Assume T fixes a copy of X, meaning that there is a subspace of C[0,1] isomorphic to X on which T acts as an isomorphic embedding. Must T then fix a copy of C[0,1]? Equivalently, must the dual operator T^* have non-separable range?
self_contained_problem:
Let $C[0,1]$ denote the Banach space of real-valued continuous functions on $[0,1]$ with the supremum norm. We say that a bounded linear operator $T : C[0,1] \to C[0,1]$ fixes a copy of a Banach space $Z$ if there exists a closed subspace $Y \subseteq C[0,1]$ such that $Y$ is isomorphic to $Z$ and the restriction $T|_Y : Y \to C[0,1]$ is an isomorphic embedding (i.e. bounded below).

It is known (Rosenthal) that if the dual operator $T^* : C[0,1]^* \to C[0,1]^*$ has non-separable range, then $T$ fixes a copy of $C[0,1]$.

Question: Let $X$ be a separable Banach space which does not contain an isomorphic copy of $c_0$, and let $T : C[0,1] \to C[0,1]$ be a bounded linear operator that fixes a copy of $X$. Must $T$ fix a copy of $C[0,1]$? Equivalently, must $T^*$ have non-separable range?
status_search_result: The problem is a long-standing question of H. P. Rosenthal regarding fixing properties of operators on C[0,1]. Partial results exist: Rosenthal proved that if T* has non-separable range, T fixes a copy of C[0,1]; subsequent work (e.g., on operators preserving copies of asymptotic ℓ₁ spaces) establishes further special cases. No complete solution to the general problem was found in the search.

paper_title: Open Problems in Universal Induction & Intelligence
original_question: What algebraic properties and deeper structural principles characterize AIXI, and can they be distilled into an axiomatic characterization that separates essential assumptions from technical details and thereby guides proofs about the model?
self_contained_problem:
Background. Let $\mathcal{X}$ be a finite observation alphabet and $\mathcal{Y}$ a finite action alphabet. Let $\mathcal{M}$ be the class of all lower semicomputable chronological semimeasures over interaction sequences in $(\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{X})^\infty$. Define the universal a priori semimeasure
$$\xi(x_{1:n}\,\|\,y_{1:n})\;=\;\sum_{\nu\in\mathcal{M}} 2^{-K(\nu)}\,\nu(x_{1:n}\,\|\,y_{1:n}),$$
where $K(\nu)$ denotes the prefix Kolmogorov complexity of the program describing $\nu$. Fix a bounded reward function extracted from observations, a discount sequence $(\gamma_t)_{t\ge 1}$ with $\Gamma_t=\sum_{k\ge t}\gamma_k<\infty$, and a finite or effective horizon $m$. The AIXI agent is the policy
$$y_t^{*} \;=\; \arg\max_{y_t}\sum_{x_t}\cdots\max_{y_{t+m}}\sum_{x_{t+m}} \Bigl(\sum_{k=t}^{t+m}\gamma_k\,r_k\Bigr)\,\xi(x_{t:t+m}\,\|\,y_{1:t+m}).$$

Problem. Identify and formalize the algebraic and structural properties that characterize AIXI as a mathematical object. Concretely:

(a) Determine the algebraic structure (e.g., monoidal, lattice-theoretic, categorical, or operator-algebraic) carried by the family of expectimax operators
$$T_t^{\nu}[V](h_{<t}) \;=\; \max_{y_t}\sum_{x_t}\nu(x_t\,\|\,h_{<t}y_t)\bigl(\gamma_t r_t + V(h_{<t}y_t x_t)\bigr)$$
acting on bounded value functions, and the way these operators compose under mixtures $\nu\mapsto\xi$.

(b) Provide a finite list of axioms — phrased purely in terms of policies, environment classes, value functionals, and a universality/dominance property — such that any agent satisfying those axioms is provably equivalent to AIXI (up to a precisely specified equivalence, such as equality of induced action sequences on all histories, or pointwise equality of value functions on $\mathcal{M}$).

(c) Show that the axiomatic characterization in (b) cleanly separates the essential assumptions (universality of $\xi$, Bayes-optimality with respect to $\xi$, sequential decision structure) from technical choices (specific reference universal Turing machine, specific horizon scheme, choice of reward bound), and demonstrate its utility by re-deriving at least one nontrivial known result about AIXI (for instance, a self-optimization, dominance, or value-convergence theorem) directly from the axioms.

original_question: A distortable Banach space is called boundedly distortable when it is lambda-distortable for some lambda > 1 but not for every lambda > 1. Does there exist a boundedly distortable Banach space?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $(X,\|\cdot\|)$ be an infinite-dimensional Banach space. For $\lambda>1$, the space $X$ is called $\lambda$-distortable if there exists an equivalent norm $|||\cdot|||$ on $X$ such that, for every infinite-dimensional closed subspace $Y\subseteq X$,
$$\sup\Big\{\frac{|||y|||}{|||z|||}\;:\; y,z\in Y,\ \|y\|=\|z\|=1\Big\}\;\ge\;\lambda.$$
The space $X$ is called distortable if it is $\lambda$-distortable for some $\lambda>1$, and arbitrarily distortable if it is $\lambda$-distortable for every $\lambda>1$. A distortable Banach space that is not arbitrarily distortable is called boundedly distortable.

Question. Does there exist a boundedly distortable Banach space? Equivalently, does there exist an infinite-dimensional Banach space $X$ that is $\lambda_0$-distortable for some $\lambda_0>1$ but fails to be $\lambda$-distortable for some $\lambda>1$?
status_search_result: The bounded distortion problem is widely cited as a long-standing open question in Banach space geometry. Tsirelson's space T is a natural candidate, known to be (2−ε)-distortable for every ε>0, but it is not known whether T is arbitrarily distortable. No known example of a boundedly distortable Banach space has been published; surveys of open problems continue to list this question as unresolved.

paper_title: Open Problems in Universal Induction & Intelligence
original_question: To what extent is AIXI essentially independent of its defining parameters—such as the observation space, action space, planning horizon, and choice of universal machine—so that the model is unique up to inessential variation rather than genuinely parameter dependent?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Fix a finite observation space $\mathcal{O}$, a finite action space $\mathcal{A}$, a planning horizon $m \in \mathbb{N}$, and a universal (prefix) Turing machine $U$. For a policy $\pi:(\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{O})^{*}\to\mathcal{A}$ acting in interaction with an environment $q$ (a computable chronological semimeasure), define the AIXI agent by
$$
\pi^{*}_{U,m,\mathcal{O},\mathcal{A}}(\ae_{<k})\;=\;\arg\max_{a_{k}\in\mathcal{A}}\sum_{o_{k}\in\mathcal{O}}\cdots\max_{a_{m}\in\mathcal{A}}\sum_{o_{m}\in\mathcal{O}}\Big(r_{k}+\cdots+r_{m}\Big)\sum_{q:U(q,a_{1:m})=o_{1:m}}2^{-\ell(q)},
$$
where $r_{i}$ denotes the reward component of $o_{i}$ and the inner sum is the Solomonoff-style universal mixture induced by $U$.

Question. Prove or disprove that the AIXI agent is essentially independent of its defining parameters in the following sense: for any two choices $(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{A},m,U)$ and $(\mathcal{O}',\mathcal{A}',m',U')$ (within natural compatibility constraints, e.g. encodings between the observation/action alphabets and bounded differences in horizon and universal machine), the induced agents $\pi^{*}_{U,m,\mathcal{O},\mathcal{A}}$ and $\pi^{*}_{U',m',\mathcal{O}',\mathcal{A}'}$ agree up to an inessential, suitably quantified variation (for instance, differing on at most finitely many histories, or producing asymptotically equivalent behaviour and value). In particular, determine whether AIXI is unique up to such inessential variation, or exhibit explicit choices of parameters yielding genuinely inequivalent agents.
status_search_result: Subsequent work (notably by Leike and Hutter, "Bad Universal Priors and Notions of Optimality", 2015) has shown that AIXI is genuinely sensitive to the choice of universal Turing machine: no nontrivial, non-subjective optimality results hold, and AIXI must be regarded as a relative (UTM-dependent) theory. This provides a negative answer for the universal-machine parameter, while parameter independence with respect to observation/action spaces and horizon (via discounting) has been addressed only partially. A complete characterization of inessential vs. essential parameter dependence remains unresolved.

original_question: Is Tsirelson's space T, or its dual, boundedly distortable rather than arbitrarily distortable?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X, \|\cdot\|)$ be an infinite-dimensional Banach space. For $\lambda > 1$, $X$ is said to be $\lambda$-distortable if there exists an equivalent norm $|\cdot|$ on $X$ such that for every infinite-dimensional closed subspace $Y \subseteq X$,
$$\sup\left\{ \frac{|y|}{|z|} : y, z \in Y,\ \|y\| = \|z\| = 1 \right\} \geq \lambda.$$
$X$ is called distortable if it is $\lambda$-distortable for some $\lambda > 1$, arbitrarily distortable if it is $\lambda$-distortable for every $\lambda > 1$, and boundedly distortable if it is distortable but not arbitrarily distortable.

Tsirelson's space $T$ is the completion of $c_{00}$ under the implicitly defined norm
$$\|x\| = \max\left\{ \|x\|_{\infty},\ \tfrac{1}{2} \sup \sum_{i=1}^{n} \|E_i x\| \right\},$$
where the supremum is taken over all admissible sequences $E_1 < E_2 < \cdots < E_n$ of finite subsets of $\mathbb{N}$, that is, sequences with $n \leq \min E_1$ and $\max E_i < \min E_{i+1}$. Here $E_i x$ denotes the restriction of $x$ to the coordinates in $E_i$. It is known that $T$ is $(2-\varepsilon)$-distortable for every $\varepsilon > 0$.

Determine whether Tsirelson's space $T$, or its dual $T^*$, is boundedly distortable (equivalently, prove or disprove that $T$ or $T^*$ fails to be arbitrarily distortable).
status_search_result: Tsirelson's space $T$ is known to be distortable, in fact $(2-\varepsilon)$-distortable for every $\varepsilon>0$, but whether $T$ (or its dual) is arbitrarily distortable, equivalently whether it is merely boundedly distortable, remains an open problem in Banach space theory. Available references and surveys on distortion in mixed Tsirelson spaces continue to list this as unresolved.

paper_title: Open Problems in Universal Induction & Intelligence
original_question: How does the intelligence order relation compare, both theoretically and on restricted problem classes, to conventional IQ tests and other intelligence or performance measures, and does narrowing the order relation to specific classes of environments reveal principled connections between apparently different domain-specific performance metrics?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Consider reinforcement-learning style agents interacting with computable environments. An environment $\mu$ is a computable measure assigning probabilities to observation–reward sequences given the agent's actions, with rewards bounded so that the total expected reward is finite. For an agent $\pi$ and environment $\mu$, let $V_\mu^\pi$ denote the expected total (discounted or bounded) reward obtained by $\pi$ in $\mu$. Define the intelligence order relation (IOR) on agents by
$$ \pi_1 \succeq \pi_2 \iff \forall \mu \in E,\ V_\mu^{\pi_1} \geq V_\mu^{\pi_2}, $$
where $E$ is a chosen class of computable environments. The universal intelligence measure on a single agent is
$$ \Upsilon(\pi) = \sum_{\mu \in E} 2^{-K(\mu)} V_\mu^\pi, $$
where $K(\mu)$ is the prefix Kolmogorov complexity of $\mu$.

Problem. 
(a) Establish a precise theoretical comparison between the IOR (and the associated measure $\Upsilon$) and conventional human IQ tests, as well as other proposed performance-based measures of machine intelligence: identify formal correspondences, monotonicity relations, or impossibility results relating these measures.
(b) Investigate whether the IOR, defined over the full class of computable environments, is too coarse or too general to discriminate meaningfully among practical agents. 
(c) For natural restricted subclasses $E' \subseteq E$ (for example, finite Markov decision processes, bandit problems, sequence-prediction tasks, or game-playing environments), define the restricted IOR $\succeq_{E'}$ and the restricted measure $\Upsilon_{E'}$, and determine whether these restricted relations coincide with, refine, or are equivalent to the standard performance metrics used within each such class. Specifically, exhibit principled mathematical connections (or prove their absence) between $\succeq_{E'}$ and the canonical domain-specific performance metric for each restricted class.
status_search_result: Search results show that the Legg–Hutter universal intelligence measure and intelligence order relation remain active research topics, with later approximations (e.g., AIQ) and surveys discussing comparisons with IQ tests and domain-specific benchmarks, but no comprehensive theoretical comparison of the IOR (and its restrictions to specific environment classes) to conventional IQ tests and other performance metrics has been established. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Give a purely combinatorial proof that every real-valued uniformly continuous map on the unit sphere of c_0 is oscillation stable, where oscillation stable means that for every epsilon > 0 there is an infinite-dimensional subspace Y such that the oscillation of the map on the unit sphere of Y is at most epsilon, and do so without using ultrafilters.
self_contained_problem:
Let $c_0$ denote the Banach space of real sequences converging to $0$, equipped with the supremum norm, and let $S_{c_0} = \{x \in c_0 : \|x\|_\infty = 1\}$ be its unit sphere. For an infinite-dimensional closed linear subspace $Y \subseteq c_0$, let $S_Y = \{y \in Y : \|y\|_\infty = 1\}$. A function $f : S_{c_0} \to \mathbb{R}$ is called oscillation stable if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists an infinite-dimensional closed linear subspace $Y \subseteq c_0$ such that
$$\sup_{x,y \in S_Y} |f(x) - f(y)| \leq \varepsilon.$$
It is known (Gowers' theorem) that every uniformly continuous function $f : S_{c_0} \to \mathbb{R}$ is oscillation stable, but the standard proofs proceed via methods of topological dynamics on the Stone–Čech compactification $\beta\mathbb{N}$, in particular using ultrafilters.

Provide a purely combinatorial proof of the following statement, avoiding any use of ultrafilters or of the topological dynamics of $\beta\mathbb{N}$: every uniformly continuous map $f : S_{c_0} \to \mathbb{R}$ is oscillation stable.
status_search_result: Several purely combinatorial, ultrafilter-free proofs of Gowers' c_0 oscillation stability theorem now exist. Christian Rosendal published a paper titled "A purely combinatorial proof of Gowers' theorem," and finite/combinatorial versions have been developed by Ojeda-Aristizabal and others, with primitive recursive bounds obtained for the finite version. More recently, a proof via the Carlson–Simpson dual Ramsey theorem has been given. These collectively provide combinatorial proofs as requested.

original_question: Let X be a separable Banach space with the property that every separable Banach space is Lipschitz isomorphic to a subset of X. Must X contain a copy of c_0?
self_contained_problem:
Aharoni's theorem states that every separable metric space admits a bi-Lipschitz embedding into the Banach space $c_0$ of real sequences converging to $0$ (equipped with the supremum norm). In particular, every separable Banach space is Lipschitz isomorphic to a subset of $c_0$.

Recall that for metric spaces $(M,d_M)$ and $(N,d_N)$, a map $f:M\to N$ is a Lipschitz isomorphism onto its image if there exist constants $0<a\le b<\infty$ such that $a\,d_M(x,y)\le d_N(f(x),f(y))\le b\,d_M(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in M$. A Banach space $X$ is said to "contain a copy of $c_0$" if there exists a closed linear subspace of $X$ that is linearly isomorphic to $c_0$.

Question (converse Aharoni problem): Let $X$ be a separable Banach space with the property that every separable Banach space is Lipschitz isomorphic to a subset of $X$. Must $X$ contain a (linear) copy of $c_0$?
status_search_result: The converse Aharoni problem appears to remain open. Recent surveys and papers on the nonlinear geometry of Banach spaces (e.g., Godefroy's short course and works on Lipschitz-free spaces, 2013–2024) continue to list it as an open question: it is not known whether a separable Banach space that contains bi-Lipschitz copies of all separable Banach spaces (equivalently, of $c_0$) must contain a linear isomorphic copy of $c_0$. Partial results are known, e.g., a Banach space Lipschitz isomorphic to $c_0$ itself is linearly isomorphic to $c_0$ (Godefroy–Kalton–Lancien-type results), but the general converse remains unresolved.

paper_title: Open Problems in Universal Induction & Intelligence
original_question: Once a computable version of the intelligence order relation is available, what experimental behavior does it exhibit across different problem spaces, does it correlate with human IQ test scores, and in restricted domains such as classification or sequence prediction does it rank algorithms in a way that agrees with standard performance measures and observed real-world performance?
self_contained_problem:
Background. Let $\mathcal{A}$ be the class of agents (computable policies) interacting with computable environments $\mu$ from a class $\mathcal{E}$ over an interaction history of observations, actions, and rewards $r_t \in [0,1]$. For an agent $\pi$ and environment $\mu$, let
$$V^{\pi}_{\mu} := \mathbb{E}^{\pi}_{\mu}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{\infty} \gamma_t\, r_tight]$$
be the expected discounted total reward, with a fixed summable discount sequence $(\gamma_t)$. The \emph{intelligence order relation} (IOR) on $\mathcal{A}$ is defined by
$$\pi_1 \succeq \pi_2 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad  orall\, \mu \in \mathcal{E}: \ V^{\pi_1}_{\mu} \ \ge \ V^{\pi_2}_{\mu},$$
or, in a quantitative version, by a weighted aggregate $\Upsilon(\pi) := \sum_{\mu \in \mathcal{E}} 2^{-K(\mu)} V^{\pi}_{\mu}$, where $K(\mu)$ is the prefix Kolmogorov complexity of $\mu$.

Since $\Upsilon$ and the unrestricted IOR are not computable, fix a computable approximation $\widetilde{\Upsilon}$ (for instance, by replacing $\mathcal{E}$ with a finite class of time- and space-bounded environments and replacing $K$ with a bounded-resource version) and the induced relation $\widetilde{\succeq}$.

Problems. Carry out the following investigation of $\widetilde{\Upsilon}$ and $\widetilde{\succeq}$:

(1) Implementation and behavior. Implement $\widetilde{\Upsilon}$ as an algorithm and characterize, theoretically and empirically, how the induced ranking of agents in $\mathcal{A}$ depends on the choice of bounded environment class, the resource bounds, and the reference universal Turing machine. Determine the qualitative behavior of $\widetilde{\succeq}$ across distinct families of problem spaces.

(2) Human correlation. When $\widetilde{\Upsilon}$ is administered to human subjects (treating the human as the agent on the same family of bounded environments used in standard inductive intelligence tests), determine whether the resulting scores correlate significantly with scores on standard human IQ tests.

(3) Restricted domains. Restrict $\widetilde{\Upsilon}$ and $\widetilde{\succeq}$ to (a) supervised classification problems and (b) sequence prediction problems, and determine whether the ranking of standard algorithms (e.g., decision trees, $k$-NN, neural networks for (a); Markov, CTW, LSTM, and Solomonoff-style predictors for (b)) under $\widetilde{\succeq}$ agrees with the ranking induced by standard performance measures (classification accuracy, log-loss, regret, etc.) and with observed real-world performance.

Provide either a positive resolution (with quantified correlations and agreement statements) or a negative resolution (with an explicit construction of a computable IOR approximation whose rankings systematically disagree with these external benchmarks).
status_search_result: The question is an empirical research program about computable approximations of the universal intelligence order relation (Legg–Hutter style). No comprehensive experimental evaluation correlating such a measure with human IQ across problem spaces, nor a definitive comparison with standard classification/sequence-prediction rankings, appears in the literature; partial efforts (e.g., Hernández-Orallo's anytime universal intelligence tests, the C-Test, and limited algorithmic IQ studies) exist but do not resolve the broader program. Status remains open.

original_question: Does every infinite-dimensional Banach space have an infinite-dimensional quotient with a Schauder basis?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be an infinite-dimensional Banach space over the field of real or complex numbers. A sequence $(e_n)_{n\geq 1}$ in a Banach space $Y$ is called a Schauder basis of $Y$ if every $y\in Y$ admits a unique representation $y=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n e_n$ as a norm-convergent series with scalar coefficients $a_n$. A quotient of $X$ is a Banach space of the form $X/M$, where $M$ is a closed linear subspace of $X$, equipped with the usual quotient norm.

Determine whether the following holds: every infinite-dimensional Banach space $X$ admits a closed subspace $M\subseteq X$ such that the quotient space $X/M$ is infinite-dimensional and possesses a Schauder basis.
category_tag: Banach space quotients and Schauder bases
status_search_result: The "quotient problem" of Banach and Pełczyński — whether every infinite-dimensional Banach space has an infinite-dimensional quotient with a Schauder basis — is widely cited as a long-standing open problem in Banach space theory. Partial results exist (e.g., for spaces of density less than the Baire category number, and via biorthogonal-system techniques of Argyros–Dodos–Kanellopoulos and Finet–Godefroy), but no full solution has been reported.

paper_title: Open questions regarding the arrow of time
context_brief: Second Law, coarse-graining, and temporal presupposition
original_question: In statistical thermodynamics, can the Second Law and the arrow of time be explained without presupposing a direction of time through the very notion of evolution or through time-asymmetric preparation and observation procedures? More specifically, if entropy is defined through probabilities over coarse-grained macrostates built from definite microscopic classical states, what principled justification can be given for the required coarse-graining and ensemble measure without smuggling in a pre-existing temporal asymmetry via state preparation, incomplete observability, or external observers?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a classical statistical-mechanical system whose microstates are points x of a phase space (Γ, μ) endowed with a Hamiltonian flow φ_t : Γ → Γ preserving the Liouville measure μ. Fix a partition (or fuzzy partition) of Γ into macrostates {M_α}, and define the Boltzmann/Gibbs entropy of a microstate x via S(x) = k log μ(M_{α(x)}), or, more generally, of a probability measure ρ on Γ via S(ρ) = −k ∫ ρ log ρ dμ relative to a coarse-graining map.

The Second Law, in this framework, asserts that for typical initial data S is non-decreasing along the flow φ_t for t > 0.

Provide a derivation of the Second Law and of the thermodynamic arrow of time that satisfies all of the following constraints simultaneously:

(a) The notion of "evolution" used in the derivation must not itself presuppose a preferred direction of time; in particular, the underlying microscopic dynamics φ_t is time-reversal invariant, and the argument may not be phrased in a way that distinguishes t → +∞ from t → −∞ by fiat.

(b) The choice of coarse-graining {M_α} (or of the reference measure used to define S) must be justified from intrinsic structural features of the system (Hamiltonian, observables, symmetries), not by appeal to an experimenter's preparation procedure, to "incomplete observability," or to an external observer who selects macrovariables.

(c) The probability measure (ensemble) used as the initial condition must be justified without invoking a time-asymmetric act of preparation, i.e., without postulating a low-entropy initial macrostate as an unexplained boundary condition imposed at one temporal end.

Either exhibit such a derivation, together with a precise statement of the resulting Second Law as a theorem about (Γ, μ, φ_t, {M_α}), or prove that no derivation meeting (a)–(c) can exist within classical Hamiltonian statistical mechanics.
category_tag: arrow of time and Second Law foundations
status_search_result: The problem is a foundational question in the philosophy and mathematical physics of statistical mechanics. It remains an active area of debate without consensus: standard derivations (Boltzmann's H-theorem, Lanford's theorem, typicality approaches, the Past Hypothesis) all rely on either time-asymmetric assumptions about initial conditions or on observer/coarse-graining choices, which is precisely what the question rules out. No widely accepted derivation satisfying all three constraints has been established.

original_question: Does every infinite-dimensional Banach space have a non-trivial infinite-dimensional separable quotient?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be an infinite-dimensional Banach space over the real or complex field. A quotient of $X$ is a Banach space of the form $X/M$, where $M$ is a closed linear subspace of $X$. Such a quotient is called non-trivial and infinite-dimensional separable if $X/M$ is infinite-dimensional and contains a countable dense subset.

Question: Does every infinite-dimensional Banach space $X$ admit a closed subspace $M \subseteq X$ such that the quotient Banach space $X/M$ is both infinite-dimensional and separable?
status_search_result: The separable quotient problem, posed by Banach and Mazur, remains open in general as of recent surveys. Affirmative answers are known in many special cases (reflexive spaces, weakly compactly generated spaces, dual spaces, spaces with large or small density character), but the general question for arbitrary infinite-dimensional Banach spaces is still unresolved.

paper_title: Open questions regarding the arrow of time
context_brief: Cosmological origin of the thermodynamic arrow
original_question: What is the cosmological origin of the universal thermodynamic arrow of time? In particular, should the present arrow be explained by a special low-entropy condition at the big bang, by a Boltzmann-style giant fluctuation in an eternal universe, or by some other mechanism; and if the low-entropy condition is tied to the big bang, how can one understand the consequences for oscillating-universe models, where the thermodynamic arrow would otherwise have to reverse direction?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a universe modeled as a Hamiltonian (time-symmetric) dynamical system whose macrostates carry a coarse-grained Boltzmann entropy S, and which exhibits a universal thermodynamic arrow of time, i.e., a monotone increase of S throughout the observable epoch. Three candidate cosmological explanations are to be analyzed:

(a) Special initial condition hypothesis: the universe began in a macrostate of extraordinarily low entropy at an initial singularity ("big bang"), and the observed arrow follows from the subsequent monotone relaxation toward equilibrium.

(b) Boltzmann fluctuation hypothesis: the universe is eternal and typically near equilibrium, and the present low-entropy macrostate is a giant statistical fluctuation.

(c) Some alternative dynamical or structural mechanism not of the above two forms.

The problem is to determine which of (a), (b), or (c) correctly accounts for the cosmological origin of the thermodynamic arrow of time, addressing in particular:

(i) The "Boltzmann brain" objection to (b): show whether, under (b), typical observers with present-like memories would more probably arise as small local fluctuations than as products of a much-lower-entropy past, and whether this renders (b) self-refuting.

(ii) Under (a), analyze the implications for an oscillating-universe cosmology in which the scale factor undergoes successive expansions and contractions: determine whether the thermodynamic arrow must reverse during a contracting phase, and whether such a reversal is consistent with the requirement that opposite thermodynamic arrows cannot coexist in causally connected regions.

Provide a precise mechanism (initial condition, dynamical law, or selection principle) that explains the universality and direction of the thermodynamic arrow consistent with the observed cosmological data and with time-symmetric microscopic dynamics.
category_tag: arrow of time and cosmological initial conditions
status_search_result: The cosmological origin of the thermodynamic arrow of time remains an open foundational problem. Proposals include Penrose's Weyl Curvature Hypothesis (low-entropy big bang), Boltzmann fluctuation scenarios (widely criticized via Boltzmann-brain arguments), Carroll–Chen-style eternal inflation models, and Barbour et al.'s Janus-point/two-arrow proposals, but no consensus solution exists.

context_brief: long Schauder bases and biorthogonal systems
original_question: Given an infinite-dimensional Banach space X, what is the greatest possible order type of a Schauder basis carried by a quotient of X? In particular, must every non-separable Banach space have an uncountable biorthogonal system?
self_contained_problem:
Let X be an infinite-dimensional Banach space. A Schauder basis of a Banach space Y is a (possibly transfinite) sequence (e_α)_{α<κ} of vectors in Y, indexed by an ordinal κ, such that every y ∈ Y has a unique representation as a norm-convergent (in an appropriate transfinite sense) series y = Σ_{α<κ} c_α e_α with scalars c_α. The order type of such a basis is the ordinal κ. A biorthogonal system in Y is a family {(y_i, y_i^*)}_{i∈I} ⊂ Y × Y^* with y_i^*(y_j) = δ_{ij}.

(a) Determine, for an arbitrary infinite-dimensional Banach space X, the supremum (in the sense of ordinal order type) of the lengths of Schauder bases that can be carried by quotient spaces of X. In particular, characterize this supremum in terms of the structure of X.

(b) Decide whether every non-separable Banach space admits an uncountable biorthogonal system {(x_i, x_i^*)}_{i∈I} ⊂ X × X^* with |I| ≥ ℵ_1.
category_tag: Non-separable Banach spaces and biorthogonal systems
status_search_result: The question whether every non-separable Banach space admits an uncountable biorthogonal system is a long-standing open problem (first explicitly raised by Davis and Johnson) and is known to be sensitive to set-theoretic axioms. Partial positive results exist under additional assumptions (e.g., under the P-ideal dichotomy, every non-separable Asplund space of suitable density admits one), but the general ZFC question, as well as the broader question on the longest Schauder basis carried by a quotient of a given Banach space, remains open.

paper_title: Open questions regarding the arrow of time
context_brief: Time direction from stochasticity and quantum events
original_question: Does stochastic or quantum indeterminism itself define a genuine direction of time, and if so in what form? More concretely, when observed quantum facts arise irreversibly in measurement-like events, should this be understood as a fundamental collapse law, as events outside dynamical law, as a mere increase of information in the Copenhagen sense, as the result of hidden variables, or as branching into Everett worlds; and can any of these interpretations explain the temporal asymmetry without using the same asymmetry they are meant to explain?
category_tag: arrow of time and quantum measurement
status_search_result: No mathematical or physical consensus has been reached on whether quantum or stochastic indeterminism defines a fundamental arrow of time, or on which interpretation of measurement explains temporal asymmetry without circularity. Reviews and recent work on the arrow of time and quantum foundations continue to treat this as an open foundational problem.

original_question: Assume the P-ideal dichotomy, namely that for every P-ideal I of countable subsets of some index set S either there is an uncountable T subset of S whose countable subsets all belong to I, or S can be decomposed into countably many pieces with no infinite subset in I. Under that assumption, are the following equivalent: (1) every non-separable Banach space has an uncountable biorthogonal system, and (2) b = aleph_2?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let S be a set. An ideal I on S is a P-ideal of countable subsets of S if I ⊆ [S]^{≤ω}, I is closed under finite changes and finite unions, and for every countable family {A_n : n ∈ ω} ⊆ I there exists A ∈ I such that A_n \ A is finite for every n.

The P-ideal dichotomy (PID) is the assertion: for every set S and every P-ideal I of countable subsets of S, at least one of the following holds:
 (a) there exists an uncountable T ⊆ S such that every countable subset of T belongs to I;
 (b) S can be written as a countable union S = ⋃_{n∈ω} S_n such that, for each n, no infinite subset of S_n belongs to I.

The bounding number b is the least cardinality of a family F ⊆ ω^ω such that no single g ∈ ω^ω eventually dominates every f ∈ F (i.e., no g satisfies f(n) ≤ g(n) for all sufficiently large n, for all f ∈ F).

A biorthogonal system in a Banach space X is a family {(x_α, x_α^*) : α ∈ Γ} ⊆ X × X^* with x_α^*(x_β) = δ_{αβ}. A Banach space is non-separable if it has no countable dense subset.

Question. Assume PID. Are the following two assertions equivalent?
 (1) Every non-separable Banach space admits an uncountable biorthogonal system.
 (2) b = ℵ_2.
status_search_result: Work of Brech and Todorcevic on biorthogonality in Banach spaces under the P-ideal dichotomy establishes the analogous equivalence for the restricted class of non-separable Asplund spaces (under PID, every non-separable Asplund space has an uncountable biorthogonal system iff b = ω_2), and proves partial results for general non-separable Banach spaces (e.g. existence of uncountable biorthogonal systems in non-separable spaces of density < b with weak*-sequentially compact dual unit ball). No source found resolves the equivalence for all non-separable Banach spaces, so the problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open questions regarding the arrow of time
original_question: Why do electromagnetic absorbers, and more generally physical absorptive processes, pick out only one temporal direction? In the case of retarded versus advanced Maxwell fields, if absorbers and thermalization can account for retarded shadows and the absence of incoming high-frequency radiation, what explains the fact that all absorbers absorb in the same time direction rather than admitting the time-reversed alternative with advanced correlations?
self_contained_problem:
Consider classical electrodynamics in Minkowski spacetime, where the source-free Maxwell equations are time-reversal invariant and the inhomogeneous Maxwell equations admit two equally valid Green's-function solutions: the retarded field $F^{\mathrm{ret}}$ (built from past sources) and the advanced field $F^{\mathrm{adv}}$ (built from future absorbers). Empirically, radiation in our universe is described by retarded fields: charges produce outgoing waves and shadows lie on the past-light-cone side of opaque bodies, while the time-reversed scenario — coherent incoming high-frequency radiation correlated so as to converge on emitters — does not occur.

A standard partial explanation invokes absorbers (including the matter content of the early universe) together with thermalization: an absorber in a low-entropy state with many available microstates effectively damps outgoing radiation and breaks the symmetry between $F^{\mathrm{ret}}$ and $F^{\mathrm{adv}}$. However, every individual absorber, whether on Earth, in stars, or in the cosmological plasma, absorbs in the same temporal direction.

Provide a derivation, within a precisely formulated dynamical and statistical-mechanical framework (e.g., a coupled field-plus-matter Hamiltonian system with an explicit choice of initial/final macroscopic constraints), of the following:

1. State sufficient conditions on initial data, boundary conditions, or constraints on phase-space measures under which all absorbers in the universe absorb in a single common temporal direction, rather than some absorbing toward the future and others toward the past, or all absorbing toward the past with advanced field correlations.

2. Determine whether this universal alignment of absorption directions can be deduced from a low-entropy past condition (a Past Hypothesis) on the joint matter+radiation state alone, or whether an independent posited absence of advanced correlations is required.

3. Quantify, in a suitable measure on initial conditions, the relative likelihood of (a) configurations with universal retarded absorption, (b) configurations with universal advanced absorption, and (c) mixed configurations, and reconcile this with the claim that absence of advanced correlations is generic while a special low-entropy past condition is not.
category_tag: arrow of time and electromagnetic absorbers
status_search_result: The question of why all absorbers select the same temporal direction (the electromagnetic arrow of time and its relation to the thermodynamic and cosmological arrows) remains an open foundational problem. Discussions in the philosophy-of-physics and foundations literature (Price, Zeh, Rovelli, Wallace, and others) continue to debate whether the absorber-based explanation reduces to a Past Hypothesis or requires an independent assumption about absence of advanced correlations; no consensus derivation exists.

original_question: A support set in a Banach space X is a nonempty convex set C such that every point x of C is a support point, meaning there is a functional f on X with f(x) equal to the infimum of f over C and strictly less than the supremum of f over C. Which Banach spaces admit support sets, and do all non-separable Banach spaces have support sets?
self_contained_problem:
Let X be a (real or complex) Banach space, and let X* denote its topological dual. A nonempty convex subset C ⊆ X is called a support set if every point x ∈ C is a support point of C, that is, for every x ∈ C there exists a continuous linear functional f ∈ X* such that
    f(x) = inf{ f(y) : y ∈ C }   and   inf{ f(y) : y ∈ C } < sup{ f(y) : y ∈ C }.

Characterize the Banach spaces X that admit a support set. In particular, decide whether every non-separable Banach space admits a support set.
status_search_result: The question is known to be independent of ZFC. Koszmider constructed (consistently with ZFC) a non-separable Banach space of the form C(K) with no uncountable semibiorthogonal sequence, hence with no support set, giving a consistent negative answer. Conversely, under various set-theoretic assumptions (e.g., consistent statements forcing every non-separable Banach space to have an uncountable biorthogonal system), every non-separable Banach space admits a support set. Thus the question whether all non-separable Banach spaces have support sets is undecidable in ZFC; the broader characterization problem remains open.

paper_title: Open questions regarding the arrow of time
context_brief: Precise nature of the low-entropy initial condition
original_question: What is the precise physical content of the low-entropy initial condition that gives rise to the arrow of time? Since different Zwanzig projections and relevance concepts can be useful for defining macroscopic entropy in different situations, which aspect of the universe’s initial state is the real, objective low-entropy property that underwrites temporal asymmetry rather than merely reflecting a convenient coarse-graining choice?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a classical Hamiltonian system with phase space $\Gamma$, Liouville measure $\mu$, and Hamiltonian flow $\phi_t:\Gamma	o\Gamma$ preserving $\mu$. A coarse-graining (Zwanzig projection) is specified by a partition $\mathcal{P}=\{C_\alpha\}$ of $\Gamma$ into measurable cells, or equivalently by a projection $P_{\mathcal{P}}$ on $L^1(\Gamma,\mu)$ that averages a probability density $ho$ over each cell. The associated Boltzmann/coarse-grained entropy of a state $ho$ is
$$S_{\mathcal{P}}(ho)\;=\;-\!\int_\Gamma (P_{\mathcal{P}}ho)\,\log(P_{\mathcal{P}}ho)\,d\mu,$$
and for a microstate $x\in\Gamma$ one sets $S_{\mathcal{P}}(x)=\log\mu(C_{\alpha(x)})$ where $C_{\alpha(x)}$ is the cell containing $x$.

Different choices of $\mathcal{P}$ (different "relevance concepts") yield different entropy functions, and a state that is low-entropy with respect to one projection can be high-entropy with respect to another. Suppose the universe is modeled by such a system and that at an initial time $t_0$ its microstate $x_0$ (or initial density $ho_0$) gives rise to a thermodynamic arrow of time, in the sense that for a broad class of physically natural projections $\mathcal{P}$ the function $t\mapsto S_{\mathcal{P}}(\phi_t x_0)$ is nondecreasing on $[t_0,\infty)$.

Problem. Identify a projection-independent property $\mathcal{L}(x_0)$ of the initial microstate (or initial density) such that:
(i) $\mathcal{L}$ is defined intrinsically from $(\Gamma,\mu,\phi_t)$ without reference to any particular partition $\mathcal{P}$;
(ii) whenever $\mathcal{L}(x_0)$ holds, $S_{\mathcal{P}}(\phi_t x_0)$ is nondecreasing for every projection $\mathcal{P}$ in a specified broad class;
(iii) conversely, if a thermodynamic arrow of time exists at $x_0$ with respect to that class of projections, then $\mathcal{L}(x_0)$ holds.

In other words, give a precise, coarse-graining-invariant characterization of "low-entropy initial condition" that underwrites temporal asymmetry, or prove that no such projection-independent characterization exists.
status_search_result: The foundational question of identifying a projection-independent, objective low-entropy property of the universe's initial state (the "Past Hypothesis") remains an active topic of debate in the foundations of statistical mechanics and cosmology, with no consensus characterization. Proposals such as Penrose's Weyl Curvature Hypothesis address gravitational degrees of freedom but are not established as a complete coarse-graining-invariant answer.

original_question: Does every Banach space of density greater than aleph_1 have a support set?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a real Banach space. A subset $S \subseteq X$ is called a support set if $S$ is convex and every point of $S$ is a support point of $S$, i.e., for every $x \in S$ there exists a continuous linear functional $f \in X^*$ with $f \not\equiv 0$ on $S$ such that $f(x) = \inf f(S)$. The density character of $X$, denoted $\operatorname{dens}(X)$, is the smallest cardinality of a dense subset of $X$.

Question: Does every Banach space $X$ with $\operatorname{dens}(X) > \aleph_1$ contain a support set?
status_search_result: The problem, attributed to Todorcevic, asks whether every Banach space of density greater than ℵ₁ admits a support set (a convex set in which every point is a support point). It is known that every C(K) space of density > ℵ₁ admits a support set, but the general Banach space case appears to remain open as of recent surveys on Banach spaces and Ramsey theory.

paper_title: Open questions regarding the arrow of time
context_brief: Initial homogeneity and the Weyl tensor condition
original_question: Is the relevant low-entropy condition of the early universe best understood as primordial homogeneity, as Penrose’s vanishing-Weyl-tensor condition on past singularities, or as some closely related condition; and if the Weyl condition cannot be explained by absorptive matter in the way electromagnetic retardation can, must it instead be taken as the law-like ingredient that establishes the causal asymmetry of the universe by excluding future-relevant initial correlations?
self_contained_problem:
In general relativistic cosmology, the thermodynamic arrow of time is widely attributed to a very low-entropy initial state of the universe. One proposal identifies this initial low-entropy condition with the spatial homogeneity of the early universe; a sharper formulation, due to Penrose, postulates that the Weyl curvature tensor vanishes on all past (initial) singularities, while no analogous restriction is imposed on future singularities.

(a) Determine whether the appropriate "special" low-entropy condition characterizing the early universe is best formulated as (i) primordial spatial homogeneity, (ii) Penrose's vanishing-Weyl-tensor condition on all past singularities, or (iii) some closely related geometric/statistical condition, and give a precise mathematical statement of the chosen condition together with a justification that it captures the required low-entropy property.

(b) In the analogy with electromagnetism, the use of purely retarded radiation (excluding incoming free fields) can be derived from the presence of a sufficient distribution of absorbing matter (the Sommerfeld/Wheeler–Feynman absorber argument). Decide whether the Weyl curvature condition in (a) admits an analogous derivation from a dynamical mechanism (e.g.\ from properties of matter fields in general relativity), or whether instead it must be imposed as an independent law-like postulate. In the latter case, show that this postulate is necessary and sufficient to establish the causal asymmetry of the universe in the sense of excluding initial correlations that would be relevant to the future evolution.

original_question: Does every Banach space X of density greater than the continuum c have an infinite unconditional basic sequence? If not in full generality, does adding hypotheses such as reflexivity change the answer?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a (real or complex) Banach space. The density of $X$ is the smallest cardinality of a norm-dense subset of $X$. A sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ of nonzero vectors in $X$ is called an unconditional basic sequence if it is a Schauder basis of its closed linear span $\overline{\mathrm{span}}\{x_n:n\in\mathbb{N}\}$ and, in addition, there exists a constant $C\geq 1$ such that for every finitely supported sequence of scalars $(a_n)$ and every choice of signs $\varepsilon_n\in\{-1,+1\}$,
$$\Big\|\sum_n \varepsilon_n a_n x_n\Big\|\leq C\,\Big\|\sum_n a_n x_n\Big\|.$$
Let $\mathfrak{c}=2^{\aleph_0}$ denote the cardinality of the continuum.

(a) Determine whether every Banach space $X$ whose density is strictly greater than $\mathfrak{c}$ contains an infinite unconditional basic sequence.

(b) If the answer to (a) is negative in general, determine whether the conclusion holds under the additional assumption that $X$ is reflexive.

status_search_result: The question of whether every Banach space of density greater than the continuum contains an infinite unconditional basic sequence appears to remain open in ZFC. original_question: For a given prime p, does there exist a field F and an F-division algebra of degree p that is not cyclic? Equivalently, can one construct a prime-degree division algebra whose maximal Galois subfield is not cyclic over its center?
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be a prime number. Recall that a central simple algebra $A$ over a field $F$ is called a division algebra if every nonzero element of $A$ is invertible, and that the degree of $A$ is $\sqrt{\dim_F A}$. Such an algebra $A$ of degree $p$ is called cyclic if it contains a maximal subfield $K \supset F$ with $[K:F]=p$ such that $K/F$ is a cyclic Galois extension; equivalently, $A \cong (K/F,\sigma,a)$ for some generator $\sigma$ of $\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$ and some $a \in F^\times$. By a classical theorem of Wedderburn, every division algebra of degree $2$ or $3$ over any field is cyclic.

Problem: For each prime $p \geq 5$, exhibit a field $F$ together with an explicit central division algebra $D$ over $F$ of degree $p$ such that $D$ is not cyclic, i.e., $D$ contains no maximal subfield that is a cyclic Galois extension of $F$ of degree $p$.
status_search_result: For primes $p=2,3$ all degree-$p$ division algebras are cyclic (Wedderburn). For primes $p\ge 5$ the question of constructing a non-cyclic division algebra of degree $p$ has long been a central open problem. A 2020 preprint by E. Matzri (arXiv:2009.05772, "Non cyclic division algebras of prime degree") claims to produce examples of non-cyclic division algebras of prime degree as primary components of generic crossed products. The status of this result and its acceptance in the community is not clearly verified, so the problem can be considered at most partially solved.

paper_title: Open questions regarding the arrow of time
context_brief: Black holes, singularities, and information loss
original_question: In the quantum-gravitational treatment of black holes, should one impose a time-symmetric Weyl-tensor condition on all spacelike singularities, and would doing so eliminate genuine black-hole interiors, horizons, or information loss? Because the black-hole interior is causally inaccessible and quantum gravity no longer sharply distinguishes past from future singularities, the unresolved issue is whether a symmetric singularity condition is the correct way to understand black-hole entropy and avoid the information-loss paradox.
self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. In a Lorentzian 4-manifold (M,g) modelling a spacetime in a quantum-gravitational regime, let C_{abcd} denote the Weyl conformal curvature tensor of g. A "Weyl curvature condition" at a spacelike singularity Σ ⊂ ∂M is the requirement that, in a suitable limit toward Σ, an appropriate scalar invariant of the Weyl tensor (e.g. C_{abcd}C^{abcd} relative to the Ricci scalar squared, or a similar measure of Weyl anisotropy) vanishes, so that Σ is conformally regular. The classical Weyl curvature hypothesis imposes this only on initial (past) spacelike singularities, thereby providing a low-entropy past boundary condition while permitting generic high-Weyl future singularities inside black holes.

Consider instead the time-symmetric Weyl curvature condition: require that C_{abcd} satisfies the same vanishing/regularity condition on every spacelike singularity of M, both past and future, on the grounds that in quantum gravity past and future singularities cannot be sharply distinguished and that the interior of a black hole is causally inaccessible to external observers.

Problems.
(a) Determine whether the time-symmetric Weyl curvature condition is mathematically consistent with the known classical and semiclassical observational constraints on cosmological and astrophysical spacetimes (in particular, with the existence of the observed CMB low-entropy initial state and with the exterior geometry of astrophysical black holes).

(b) Determine whether imposing this time-symmetric condition forces, at the level of the allowed quantum-gravitational spacetimes, the absence of genuine event horizons and trapped black-hole interiors — i.e. whether all apparent black-hole-like regions must be replaced by horizonless, information-preserving configurations.

(c) Decide whether such a condition provides a consistent statistical-mechanical account of black-hole entropy (e.g. reproducing the Bekenstein–Hawking area law as a coarse-grained entropy) while avoiding any genuine information-loss paradox in the global evolution.

State and prove (or disprove) the precise theorems answering (a), (b), and (c) within a chosen rigorous framework for semiclassical or quantum gravity.
category_tag: Weyl curvature hypothesis and black-hole information
status_search_result: The question concerns a foundational proposal in quantum gravity: whether a time-symmetric Weyl curvature condition on all spacelike singularities is consistent and whether it eliminates horizons and information loss. No definitive resolution exists; the black-hole information paradox and the status of the Weyl curvature hypothesis remain active open problems, with ongoing work on island formulas, firewalls, and Penrose's CCC, but no rigorous theorem settling the time-symmetric variant proposed here.

original_question: If an F-division algebra has prime period, must it be a crossed product? In other words, for each prime p, is every central division algebra whose Brauer class has order p necessarily obtained from a Galois crossed-product construction?
self_contained_problem:
Let $F$ be a field and let $D$ be a finite-dimensional central division algebra over $F$. Recall that $D$ represents a class $[D]$ in the Brauer group $\mathrm{Br}(F)$, and the period (or exponent) of $D$ is the order of $[D]$ in $\mathrm{Br}(F)$. The algebra $D$ is called a crossed product if it contains a maximal subfield $K \subset D$ such that $K/F$ is a Galois extension; equivalently, $D$ arises from the standard crossed-product construction associated with some finite Galois extension $K/F$ and a 2-cocycle in $H^2(\mathrm{Gal}(K/F), K^\times)$.

Question: Is it true that for every prime $p$, every central division algebra $D$ over an arbitrary field $F$ whose period equals $p$ is a crossed product?

While Amitsur (1972) constructed noncrossed product division algebras of composite period, no noncrossed products of prime period have been found, and no proof of the crossed-product property in prime period is known. Surveys on open problems in central simple algebras list it explicitly as unresolved.

paper_title: Open questions regarding the arrow of time
context_brief: Emergence of time in Wheeler-DeWitt quantum gravity
original_question: How do physical time and its arrow emerge in quantum gravity when the fundamental Wheeler-DeWitt equation has no external time parameter? More specifically, if the quantum-gravitational wave functional satisfies HΨ = 0 and there is no external variable t with respect to which a time direction can be defined, under what assumptions and through what mechanism can one recover an effective physical time and a corresponding arrow of time from intrinsic variables and semiclassical structure?
self_contained_problem:
Consider canonical quantum gravity in the Wheeler–DeWitt formulation. Let configuration space be superspace, the space of Riemannian 3-metrics h_{ab} on a spatial slice (together with non-gravitational matter fields φ), modulo spatial diffeomorphisms. A physical state is described by a wave functional Ψ[h_{ab}, φ] satisfying the Wheeler–DeWitt constraint

   H Ψ[h_{ab}, φ] = 0,

where H is the Hamiltonian constraint operator (a hyperbolic second-order functional differential operator on superspace whose kinetic term involves the DeWitt supermetric, which has indefinite signature with one negative direction associated with the local scale of h_{ab}). Because Ψ has no explicit dependence on any external parameter t, the equation contains no a priori notion of time evolution and no a priori arrow of time.

Problem. Formulate precise assumptions on (i) the structure of Ψ (for example, a WKB/semiclassical ansatz Ψ ≈ C[h] exp(i S[h]/ℏ) χ[h, φ] with respect to a suitable expansion parameter, such as an inverse power of the Planck mass), (ii) boundary conditions on Ψ in superspace (for instance, conditions imposed in the limit of vanishing three-volume), and (iii) the decomposition of degrees of freedom into "heavy/geometric" and "light/matter" sectors, under which one can:

(a) derive an effective Schrödinger-type equation iℏ ∂_τ χ = H_matter χ for the light sector, where τ is an intrinsic parameter constructed from the heavy variables (e.g. along integral curves of ∇S on superspace), so that τ plays the role of a physical, emergent time;

(b) identify a mechanism — for example, a low-entropy/simplicity condition on Ψ at the boundary corresponding to small three-volume together with decoherence between semiclassical branches — that singles out a preferred direction along τ, thereby producing an arrow of time correlated with the growth of suitable entropy functionals.

State explicitly the minimal set of assumptions on H, on Ψ, and on the boundary behaviour in superspace, and exhibit the construction of τ and of the asymmetry of correlations along τ that yields both an effective physical time and its arrow from a fundamentally timeless equation HΨ = 0.
category_tag: Quantum gravity and emergence of time
status_search_result: The problem of recovering time and its arrow from the timeless Wheeler–DeWitt equation is a long-standing foundational question. Semiclassical (Born–Oppenheimer/WKB) derivations of an effective Schrödinger equation are well known and partially address (a), but no consensus exists on a fully rigorous mechanism producing the arrow of time; the question is generally regarded as open and actively discussed in reviews on the problem of time and quantum cosmology.

context_brief: Initial conditions for partial Schrödinger waves
original_question: Can the global intrinsic dynamics of the Wheeler-DeWitt framework determine the initial conditions of the partial Schrödinger waves that appear in the semiclassical WKB regime? Since the WKB approximation yields approximately autonomous matter-wave evolution along quasi-classical geometries but does not by itself justify an ensemble of trajectories, the unresolved problem is how the full, timeless quantum state fixes the initial data for the branch-dependent partial waves observed as evolving quasi-classical worlds.
self_contained_problem:
Consider canonical quantum gravity coupled to matter, in which physical states $|\Psi\rangle$ are annihilated by the Hamiltonian constraint, yielding the timeless Wheeler–DeWitt equation
$$\hat{\mathcal{H}}\,\Psi[h_{ij},\phi] = 0,$$
where $h_{ij}$ denotes a spatial 3-metric on a closed 3-manifold and $\phi$ collectively denotes matter fields. In a semiclassical (WKB) regime far from a putative initial singularity, one expands
$$\Psi[h,\phi] \approx \sum_{\alpha} A_{\alpha}[h]\, e^{i S_{\alpha}[h]/\hbar}\, \chi_{\alpha}[h,\phi],$$
where each phase $S_\alpha$ satisfies the gravitational Hamilton–Jacobi equation, defining a congruence of quasi-classical 4-geometries, and the matter wave functional $\chi_\alpha[h,\phi]$ obeys, to leading order in $\hbar$, an effective Schrödinger equation
$$i\hbar\, \nabla S_\alpha \cdot \delta_{h}\chi_\alpha = \hat{H}_{\text{matter}}[h,\phi]\,\chi_\alpha$$
along the integral curves of $\nabla S_\alpha$. Each $\chi_\alpha$ is a "partial Schrödinger wave" associated with one branch of the global superposition.

Problem: Determine whether the intrinsic global dynamics encoded by the Wheeler–DeWitt equation, together with any natural boundary condition on $\Psi$ at small 3-geometries (the "big-bang" boundary of superspace), uniquely fixes the initial data $\chi_\alpha[h_0,\phi]$ for every partial Schrödinger wave $\chi_\alpha$ on a hypersurface of constant $S_\alpha$ in the WKB region. Equivalently, give a derivation that selects, from the timeless quantum state $\Psi$, a canonical assignment of initial conditions for each branch-dependent matter wave $\chi_\alpha$, or prove that no such derivation exists within the framework, so that additional postulates beyond the Wheeler–DeWitt dynamics are required.
status_search_result: No published derivation appears to extract canonical initial data for the branch-dependent partial Schrödinger waves of the WKB expansion directly from the timeless Wheeler–DeWitt state. Standard references on the Wheeler–DeWitt equation and its semiclassical (WKB) limit treat such initial conditions as additional input (e.g., via Hartle–Hawking or tunneling proposals), and the issue of justifying an ensemble of WKB branches and their matter initial states remains a recognized foundational problem in quantum cosmology.

original_question: If a field F has cohomological dimension at most 2, is every central simple F-algebra a crossed product?
self_contained_problem:
Let $F$ be a field. The cohomological dimension of $F$, denoted $\mathrm{cd}(F)$, is the smallest non-negative integer $n$ (or $\infty$) such that $H^i(\mathrm{Gal}(F^{\mathrm{sep}}/F), M) = 0$ for every $i > n$ and every finite discrete torsion $\mathrm{Gal}(F^{\mathrm{sep}}/F)$-module $M$ whose order is invertible in $F$ (equivalently, the cohomological dimension of the absolute Galois group of $F$, in the sense of Serre, when $F$ is perfect; otherwise one uses the standard extension to the imperfect case).

A central simple $F$-algebra is a finite-dimensional associative $F$-algebra $A$ with center exactly $F$ and no two-sided ideals other than $0$ and $A$. By Wedderburn's theorem, $A \cong M_n(D)$ for a unique (up to isomorphism) central division $F$-algebra $D$, and $\dim_F A$ is a perfect square; write $\dim_F A = d^2$ and call $d$ the degree of $A$.

A central simple $F$-algebra $A$ of degree $d$ is called a crossed product if it contains a (commutative) maximal subfield $K \supseteq F$ with $[K:F] = d$ such that $K/F$ is a Galois extension. Equivalently, $A$ is Brauer equivalent to a cocycle algebra $(K/F, G, c)$ for some finite Galois extension $K/F$ with Galois group $G$ and some 2-cocycle $c \in Z^2(G, K^{\times})$, with $[K:F] = \deg(A)$.

Question: If $F$ is a field with $\mathrm{cd}(F) \le 2$, is every central simple $F$-algebra a crossed product?
category_tag: central simple algebras and crossed products
status_search_result: The question is listed as an open problem in surveys on central simple algebras. All known examples of non-crossed product central simple algebras are constructed over fields of cohomological dimension at least 3, and no resolution (positive or negative) appears to be known for fields of cohomological dimension at most 2.

context_brief: Negative scale factor and pre-big-bang interpretation
original_question: In loop quantum cosmology, what physical meaning, if any, should be assigned to negative values of the scale factor a after continuing the Wheeler-DeWitt dynamics through a = 0, and how can that continuation be reconciled with the thermodynamic arrow? If negative a is interpreted as a pre-big-bang phase, one must explain how WKB time could continue through a = 0 and how a low-entropy state at a = 0 could have been preceded by an even lower-entropy state at a < 0 without forcing a reversal of the thermodynamic arrow in an oscillating-universe picture.
self_contained_problem:
In the Wheeler–DeWitt formulation of quantum cosmology for a homogeneous and isotropic universe with scale factor a, the wavefunction Ψ(a, φ) (with φ a matter field) is governed by a hyperbolic-type constraint equation that admits, in suitable regimes, a WKB form Ψ ≈ A(a, φ) exp(iS(a, φ)/ℏ) from which a notion of classical "WKB time" emerges via the gradient of S. The classical configuration variable a is taken to be nonnegative, but the Wheeler–DeWitt equation is naturally defined for all real a, and one may attempt to extend solutions and the dynamics through a = 0 to negative values of a.

Loop quantum cosmology refines this picture by replacing the differential operator in a by a difference operator on a discrete lattice in a (or in volume), and the resulting quantum dynamics is also formally defined for negative values of a.

Address the following questions in this setting:

(a) Determine whether negative values of the scale factor a admit a consistent physical interpretation after extending the (Wheeler–DeWitt or loop quantum cosmology) dynamics through a = 0, and in particular whether they can represent a "pre-big-bang" epoch.

(b) Establish whether, and in what precise sense, the WKB time function S can be continued through the locus a = 0 so as to provide a classical-time interpretation on both sides.

(c) In an oscillating-universe interpretation in which a < 0 is identified with a pre-big-bang phase, decide whether it is possible to have a low-entropy state at a = 0 preceded by an even lower-entropy state at a < 0 without forcing a reversal of the thermodynamic arrow of time, and reconcile this with the second law of thermodynamics.

Provide a precise mathematical and physical resolution, or demonstrate that no consistent extension is possible.

self_contained_problem:

A subfield $K \subseteq A$ containing $F$ is called a maximal subfield of $A$ if $[K:F] = n$; equivalently, $K$ is its own centralizer in $A$. If $K/F$ is separable, let $\widetilde{K}/F$ denote the Galois closure of $K$ inside a fixed separable closure of $F$, and call $\mathrm{Gal}(\widetilde{K}/F)$ a splitting group of $A$ arising from a maximal subfield.

(a) Determine, as a function of $F$ and $A$, the finite groups of smallest order that can occur as $\mathrm{Gal}(\widetilde{K}/F)$ where $K$ ranges over separable maximal subfields of $A$.

(b) In particular, decide whether for every field $F$ and every central $F$-division algebra $A$ of degree $n$, there exists a separable maximal subfield $K \subseteq A$ such that $\mathrm{Gal}(\widetilde{K}/F) \cong A_n$, the alternating group on $n$ letters.

original_question: Is every division algebra split by an abelian Galois extension of its center, and for specific ground fields can one bound the degree of such an abelian splitting field?
self_contained_problem:
Let $D$ be a finite-dimensional central division algebra over a field $F$ (so $F$ is the center of $D$ and $\dim_F D = n^2$ for some integer $n \geq 1$, called the degree of $D$). A field extension $K/F$ is called a splitting field of $D$ if $D \otimes_F K \cong M_n(K)$, the algebra of $n \times n$ matrices over $K$. The extension $K/F$ is called an abelian Galois extension if it is Galois with abelian Galois group $\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$.

(a) Does every finite-dimensional central division algebra $D$ over an arbitrary field $F$ admit a splitting field $K$ such that $K/F$ is a finite abelian Galois extension?

(b) For specific classes of ground fields $F$ (for instance global fields, local fields, or fields of given cohomological dimension), determine sharp bounds on the minimal degree $[K:F]$ of an abelian Galois splitting field $K$ of $D$ in terms of the degree $n$ of $D$ (and other invariants of $F$).
category_tag: central simple algebras and splitting fields

Partial results exist (e.g., lower bounds on the order of abelian splitting groups by Tignol–Amitsur, and results for division algebras of prime degree), but no general resolution is known.

original_question: For semidirect products G = C_p semidirect C_m with m prime to p, when does every G-crossed product over F descend to a crossed product for a smaller or more abelian group G'? In particular, is every division algebra of prime degree p that is split by C_p semidirect C_m necessarily cyclic, and are all quasi-symbols cyclic?
self_contained_problem:
Let $F$ be a field and let $p$ be a prime number. For a finite group $G$, write $G \Rightarrow_F G'$ to mean that every $G$-crossed product central simple $F$-algebra is also a $G'$-crossed product (i.e., is split by some Galois extension of $F$ with group $G'$).

Recall that a central simple $F$-algebra $A$ is a $G$-crossed product if $A$ contains a maximal subfield $K$ that is Galois over $F$ with $\mathrm{Gal}(K/F) \cong G$. A division algebra of degree $p$ is called cyclic if it is a $C_p$-crossed product. Following standard usage, a division algebra $A$ of prime degree $p$ over $F$ is called a quasi-symbol if there exist a cyclic extension $L/F$ of degree $m$ prime to $p$ with $L \subseteq F(\zeta_p)$ (where $\zeta_p$ is a primitive $p$-th root of unity) such that $A \otimes_F L$ is a symbol algebra, equivalently $A$ is split by a Galois extension of $F$ whose group is a semidirect product $C_p \rtimes C_m$ with $C_p$ normal.

Let $m$ be a positive integer prime to $p$, and let $G = C_p \rtimes C_m$ be a semidirect product (with $C_p$ normal).

(a) Determine whether $C_p \rtimes C_m \Rightarrow_F C_p \times C_m$ for every field $F$ (of suitable characteristic). Equivalently, decide whether every division algebra of prime degree $p$ over $F$ that is split by some Galois extension of $F$ with group $C_p \rtimes C_m$ is necessarily cyclic.

(b) Decide whether every quasi-symbol is a cyclic algebra.
status_search_result: The questions of whether $C_p \rtimes C_m \Rightarrow_F C_p \times C_m$ and whether every quasi-symbol is cyclic appear in standard problem lists on central simple algebras and remain open. Subsequent literature on descent and on non-cyclic division algebras of prime degree continues to discuss these as outstanding problems, with no resolution found in available sources.

original_question: For a field F and positive integer n, is the n-torsion subgroup nBr(F) generated by Brauer classes of cyclic algebras of degree dividing n?
self_contained_problem:
Let $F$ be a field and let $n$ be a positive integer. The Brauer group $\mathrm{Br}(F)$ is the group of equivalence classes of finite-dimensional central simple $F$-algebras under Brauer equivalence (where $A \sim B$ iff $M_r(A) \cong M_s(B)$ for some positive integers $r,s$), with multiplication induced by tensor product over $F$. Let ${}_n\mathrm{Br}(F) := \{[A] \in \mathrm{Br}(F) : n\cdot[A] = 0\}$ denote the $n$-torsion subgroup. A central simple $F$-algebra $A$ of degree $m$ (so $\dim_F A = m^2$) is called cyclic if it contains a maximal subfield $K \subset A$ with $K/F$ a cyclic Galois extension of degree $m$; equivalently, $A$ is isomorphic to a cyclic algebra $(K/F,\sigma,a)$ for some generator $\sigma$ of $\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$ and some $a \in F^\times$.

Question: Is ${}_n\mathrm{Br}(F)$ generated, as an abelian group, by Brauer classes $[A]$ of cyclic $F$-algebras $A$ whose degree divides $n$?
status_search_result: The problem is classical and goes back to Albert (1936). By the Merkurjev–Suslin theorem, when $n$ is invertible in $F$ and $F$ contains a primitive $n$-th root of unity, ${}_n\mathrm{Br}(F)$ is generated by classes of cyclic algebras of degree $n$. Without the root-of-unity hypothesis the question is open in general, although affirmative answers are known in various special cases (e.g. small torsion, certain types of fields). The general problem remains open.

original_question: When char F is not 7 and F does not contain a primitive seventh root of unity, is the 7-torsion subgroup 7Br(F) generated by cyclic algebras of degree 7?
self_contained_problem:
Let $F$ be a field of characteristic different from $7$ that does not contain a primitive seventh root of unity. Let $\mathrm{Br}(F)$ denote the Brauer group of $F$, and let ${}_{7}\mathrm{Br}(F)$ denote its $7$-torsion subgroup, i.e. the subgroup of classes $[A] \in \mathrm{Br}(F)$ satisfying $7\cdot[A]=0$. A cyclic algebra of degree $7$ over $F$ is a central simple $F$-algebra of the form $(E/F,\sigma,b)$, where $E/F$ is a cyclic Galois field extension of degree $7$, $\sigma$ is a generator of $\mathrm{Gal}(E/F)$, and $b\in F^{\times}$; equivalently, it is the $F$-algebra generated by $E$ and an element $u$ subject to $u^{7}=b$ and $ux = \sigma(x)u$ for $x\in E$.

Determine whether ${}_{7}\mathrm{Br}(F)$ is generated, as an abelian group, by the Brauer classes of cyclic $F$-algebras of degree $7$.
category_tag: Brauer groups and central simple algebras
status_search_result: The question is listed as an open problem in surveys on central simple algebras, where it is noted as the smallest open prime-degree case (the analogous statements for primes 2, 3, 5 are known via Merkurjev–Suslin / Rost-type results, while degree 7 without a primitive 7th root of unity remains unresolved). No subsequent resolution was found in the literature.

original_question: More weakly than asking for cyclic generators, is every class in the n-torsion subgroup nBr(F) representable by a central simple algebra of degree n?
self_contained_problem:
Let $F$ be a field and let $n\ge 2$ be an integer. Recall that the Brauer group $\mathrm{Br}(F)$ is the group of equivalence classes of finite-dimensional central simple $F$-algebras under the relation $A\sim B$ iff $M_r(A)\cong M_s(B)$ for some positive integers $r,s$, with multiplication induced by tensor product over $F$. For a central simple $F$-algebra $A$, the degree of $A$ is $\deg(A)=\sqrt{\dim_F A}$. Let
$${}_n\mathrm{Br}(F)=\{[A]\in\mathrm{Br}(F):n\cdot[A]=0\}$$
denote the $n$-torsion subgroup of $\mathrm{Br}(F)$.

Question: Is every element of ${}_n\mathrm{Br}(F)$ represented by (equivalently, is ${}_n\mathrm{Br}(F)$ generated as an abelian group by Brauer classes of) central simple $F$-algebras of degree $n$?
category_tag: Brauer groups and central simple algebras
status_search_result: The question is a weakening of the classical cyclicity problem (Albert) and of the question whether ${}_n\mathrm{Br}(F)$ is generated by cyclic algebras of degree $n$. By Merkurjev–Suslin, when $n$ is invertible in $F$ and $F$ contains a primitive $n$th root of unity, ${}_n\mathrm{Br}(F)$ is generated by cyclic algebras (hence by degree-$n$ algebras). In general, however, the problem of whether ${}_n\mathrm{Br}(F)$ is generated by degree-$n$ central simple algebras over an arbitrary field appears to remain open, with no evidence of a resolution.

original_question: Fix a prime p and integers r <= s. Assuming p^r Br(F) is generated by cyclic algebras, what is the minimal number l_F(p^r, p^s) such that every central simple F-algebra of degree p^s and period dividing p^r is Brauer-equivalent to a tensor product of that many cyclic algebras of degree p^r?
self_contained_problem:
Let $F$ be a field and let $p$ be a prime number. Let $\mathrm{Br}(F)$ denote the Brauer group of $F$, and for an integer $n\ge 1$, let ${}_n\mathrm{Br}(F)$ denote the $n$-torsion subgroup of $\mathrm{Br}(F)$. Recall that a central simple $F$-algebra $C$ of degree $n$ is called cyclic if it contains a strictly maximal subfield that is a cyclic Galois extension of $F$ of degree $n$; equivalently, $C\cong (E/F,\sigma,a)$ for some cyclic Galois extension $E/F$ of degree $n$, generator $\sigma$ of $\mathrm{Gal}(E/F)$, and $a\in F^\times$.

Fix integers $1\le r\le s$, and assume that ${}_{p^r}\mathrm{Br}(F)$ is generated (as an abelian group) by Brauer classes of cyclic $F$-algebras of degree $p^r$. For every central simple $F$-algebra $A$ of degree $p^s$ whose Brauer class lies in ${}_{p^r}\mathrm{Br}(F)$ (i.e.\ has period dividing $p^r$), define
$$\ell(A)=\min\Bigl\{m\ge 0 : [A]=\sum_{i=1}^m [C_i] \text{ in }\mathrm{Br}(F),\text{ with each }C_i\text{ a cyclic }F\text{-algebra of degree }p^r\Bigr\},$$
and set
$$\ell_F(p^r,p^s)=\sup_A \ell(A),$$
the supremum being taken over all such $A$.

Determine $\ell_F(p^r,p^s)$.
status_search_result: The problem of computing the symbol length $\ell_F(p^r,p^s)$ for central simple algebras of degree $p^s$ and period dividing $p^r$, under the assumption that the $p^r$-torsion of the Brauer group is generated by cyclic algebras, is a well-known open problem. Subsequent work has provided partial bounds in special situations (e.g., function fields of $p$-adic curves, positive characteristic), but no general formula is known.
