original_question: When the target algebra a is an associative bialgebra, use the comultiplication on a to define and analyze multi-orbit evaluation representations of the equivariant map algebra M(X, a)^Gamma, and determine their structure and role in the representation theory.
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a scheme of finite type over an algebraically closed field $k$ of characteristic zero, let $\mathfrak{a}$ be a finite-dimensional associative $k$-algebra, and let $\Gamma$ be a finite group acting on $X$ by automorphisms of schemes and on $\mathfrak{a}$ by $k$-algebra automorphisms. The equivariant map algebra is
$$M(X,\mathfrak{a})^\Gamma = \{\,\alpha\colon X \to \mathfrak{a} \mid \alpha \text{ is a regular morphism and } \alpha(\gamma\cdot x) = \gamma\cdot\alpha(x)\ \forall\gamma\in\Gamma,\ x\in X\,\},$$
viewed as an associative algebra under pointwise multiplication.

For a finite set $\mathbf{x} = \{x_1,\dots,x_n\}$ of $\Gamma$-orbits in the rational points of $X$, with chosen representatives, evaluation gives an algebra homomorphism
$$\mathrm{ev}_{\mathbf{x}}\colon M(X,\mathfrak{a})^\Gamma \longrightarrow \mathfrak{a}^{\Gamma_{x_1}}\otimes\cdots\otimes \mathfrak{a}^{\Gamma_{x_n}},$$
where $\Gamma_{x_i}$ is the stabilizer of $x_i$.

Now assume in addition that $\mathfrak{a}$ carries the structure of an associative bialgebra, with coproduct $\Delta\colon \mathfrak{a}\to \mathfrak{a}\otimes \mathfrak{a}$ compatible with the $\Gamma$-action. paper_title: Banach spaces and Ramsey Theory: some open problems
original_question: Let X be a reflexive Banach space such that all normalized weakly null sequences in X generate, up to equivalence, a unique spreading model; equivalently, |SP_w(X)/∼| = 1, where SP_w(X) denotes the class of spreading models generated by normalized weakly null sequences in X. Must that unique spreading model be equivalent to the standard unit vector basis of c_0 or of ℓ_p for some 1 ≤ p < ∞?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be an infinite-dimensional reflexive Banach space. Recall that, given a normalized basic sequence $(x_n)$ in $X$, a Banach space with a basis $(e_n)$ is called a spreading model of $(x_n)$ if there exists a null sequence $\varepsilon_n \downarrow 0$ such that for every $n \le k_1 < k_2 < \cdots < k_n$ and every choice of scalars $a_1,\dots,a_n$ with $|a_i| \le 1$,
$$\Big|\,\big\|\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_{k_i}\big\| - \big\|\sum_{i=1}^n a_i e_i\big\|\,\Big| < \varepsilon_n.$$
By a standard Ramsey-theoretic argument, every normalized weakly null sequence in $X$ has a subsequence that generates a spreading model. Let $\mathrm{SP}_w(X)$ denote the class of all spreading models generated by normalized weakly null sequences in $X$, and let $\sim$ denote the equivalence relation of equivalence of basic sequences (i.e., $(e_n) \sim (f_n)$ iff there exist $C_1,C_2 > 0$ such that $C_1\|\sum a_i e_i\| \le \|\sum a_i f_i\| \le C_2\|\sum a_i e_i\|$ for all finitely supported scalar sequences $(a_i)$).

Suppose $|\mathrm{SP}_w(X)/{\sim}| = 1$, i.e., all normalized weakly null sequences in $X$ generate, up to equivalence, a unique spreading model. Must this unique spreading model be equivalent to the standard unit vector basis of $c_0$ or of $\ell_p$ for some $1 \le p < \infty$?
status_search_result: The problem (without the additional hypothesis of uniformity in the constants) appears to remain open. It is classical that if the unique spreading model is generated uniformly, then it must be equivalent to the unit vector basis of $c_0$ or $\ell_p$, $1 \le p < \infty$. Recent work by Argyros, Motakis, and collaborators has constructed reflexive Banach spaces with various unique-spreading-model and unique-asymptotic-model properties, but a definitive resolution of the non-uniform reflexive case has not been located.

original_question: For an equivariant map Lie algebra M = M(X, g)^Gamma, compute higher extension groups between finite-dimensional modules, not just Ext^1, and explain how those higher Ext groups and the global dimension of the finite-dimensional module category depend on the geometry of the scheme X.
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be an affine scheme of finite type over $\mathbb{C}$ and let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a finite-dimensional reductive Lie algebra over $\mathbb{C}$. Let $\Gamma$ be a finite group acting on $X$ by scheme automorphisms and on $\mathfrak{g}$ by Lie algebra automorphisms. Define the equivariant map algebra
$$M = M(X,\mathfrak{g})^{\Gamma} = \{\,f\colon X\to\mathfrak{g}\ \text{regular}\ :\ f(\gamma\cdot x)=\gamma\cdot f(x)\ \text{for all}\ \gamma\in\Gamma,\ x\in X\,\},$$
viewed as a Lie algebra under pointwise bracket. Let $\mathcal{F}(M)$ denote the category of finite-dimensional $M$-modules.

(a) For arbitrary finite-dimensional simple (or, more generally, finite-dimensional) $M$-modules $V$ and $W$, compute the higher extension groups
$$\operatorname{Ext}^{n}_{\mathcal{F}(M)}(V,W) \quad\text{for all}\ n\ge 1,$$
expressing them in terms of the geometry of $X$, the action of $\Gamma$, and the structure of $\mathfrak{g}$.

(b) Determine the global dimension of the category $\mathcal{F}(M)$ and describe explicitly how it depends on the geometric invariants of the scheme $X$ (such as its dimension, its singularities, and the fixed-point structure of the $\Gamma$-action).
status_search_result: First Ext groups between finite-dimensional simple modules of equivariant map algebras have been computed (Neher–Savage, and extended by Kodera and others to twisted current algebras), and block decompositions of the finite-dimensional module category are known. However, a general computation of higher Ext^n groups (n ≥ 2) and a determination of the global dimension of the category of finite-dimensional modules in terms of the geometry of X does not appear in the literature, so the problem appears to remain largely open.

paper_title: Banach spaces and Ramsey Theory: some open problems
original_question: Let X be a reflexive Banach space with at most countably many equivalence classes of spreading models generated by normalized weakly null sequences; that is, |SP_w(X)/∼| ≤ ℵ_0. Does X contain a normalized weakly null sequence generating a spreading model equivalent to the standard unit vector basis of c_0 or of ℓ_p for some 1 ≤ p < ∞?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. Let $X$ be an infinite-dimensional Banach space. A normalized sequence $(x_n)$ in $X$ is said to generate a spreading model with basis $(e_n)$ if there exists a null sequence $(\varepsilon_n)$ of positive reals such that, for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, every choice of scalars $a_1,\ldots,a_k$ with $|a_i| \le 1$, and every $k \le n_1 < n_2 < \cdots < n_k$,
$$\Big| \,\big\| \sum_{i=1}^{k} a_i x_{n_i} \big\| - \big\| \sum_{i=1}^{k} a_i e_i \big\| \,\Big| < \varepsilon_k .$$
Two spreading models $(e_n)$ and $(\tilde e_n)$ are equivalent if the map $e_n \mapsto \tilde e_n$ extends to an isomorphism between their closed linear spans. Let $SP_w(X)$ denote the set of all spreading models generated by normalized weakly null sequences in $X$, and let $SP_w(X)/{\sim}$ denote its set of equivalence classes under the above equivalence relation.

Question. Suppose $X$ is a reflexive Banach space such that $|SP_w(X)/{\sim}| \le \aleph_0$, i.e., there are at most countably many equivalence classes of spreading models of $X$ generated by normalized weakly null sequences. Must $X$ contain a normalized weakly null sequence whose generated spreading model is equivalent to the standard unit vector basis of $c_0$, or to the standard unit vector basis of $\ell_p$ for some $1 \le p < \infty$?
status_search_result: The "countable spreading models problem" of Dilworth, Odell, and Sari is listed as an open problem in the Banach space theory literature. Recent papers in the program (e.g., on asymptotic models, lattice structures of spreading models, and unique $\ell_1$ spreading models) build around this question but do not announce a resolution. No source found announces a solution as of 2026.

original_question: Extend the theory of global and local Weyl modules from current and loop algebras to more arbitrary equivariant map Lie algebras. In particular, determine lengths, dimensions, and characters of local Weyl modules in that general setting, and decide whether a suitable form of BGG reciprocity also holds for general EMAs.
self_contained_problem:
Let k be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, let X be a scheme of finite type over k with coordinate ring A, let g be a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over k, and let Γ be a group acting on both X and g by automorphisms. The equivariant map algebra is

   M(X,g)^Γ = (g ⊗_k A)^Γ = { x ∈ g ⊗_k A : (γ·x) = x for all γ ∈ Γ },

with Lie bracket induced from g. Assume that with respect to a chosen triangular decomposition (or weight grading) one has well-defined notions of global Weyl modules W(λ) and local Weyl modules W_loc(λ) attached to dominant integral weights λ, generalizing the construction known for current algebras g ⊗ k[t] and loop algebras g ⊗ k[t,t^{-1}].

Address the following:

(a) For an arbitrary equivariant map algebra M(X,g)^Γ as above (in particular, beyond the cases where g is simple, X is affine of finite type, and Γ is abelian acting freely on X), determine the length, the dimension, and the graded (or weighted) character of each local Weyl module W_loc(λ).

(b) Formulate and decide a suitable analog of BGG reciprocity in this setting: namely, identify a category of M(X,g)^Γ-modules possessing a notion of standard (Weyl) modules Δ(λ) and simple/costandard modules L(μ), and determine whether the multiplicities [P(μ) : Δ(λ)] of standard modules in projective covers (or their analogs) coincide with the multiplicities [Δ(λ) : L(μ)] of simples in standard modules, in the form

   [P(μ) : Δ(λ)] = [Δ(λ) : L(μ)],

generalizing the BGG reciprocity established for current algebras and certain map algebras.
category_tag: Weyl modules for equivariant map algebras
status_search_result: Significant progress has been made: local Weyl modules for equivariant map algebras with free abelian group actions were studied (Feigin–Loktev type results, arXiv:1103.5766), and global Weyl modules for equivariant map algebras were developed (arXiv:1303.4437, IMRN 2015). Extensions to equivariant map Lie superalgebras appeared recently (arXiv:2511.01631), and BGG reciprocity has been established for current algebras (arXiv:1307.1440). However, a fully general theory for arbitrary equivariant map algebras (general schemes/groups, complete length/dimension/character results, and a fully general BGG reciprocity) does not appear to be completely settled, so the program is partially solved.

paper_title: Banach spaces and Ramsey Theory: some open problems
original_question: Suppose a Banach space X has a normalized block homogeneous Schauder basis, meaning that every normalized block sequence of the basis spans a subspace isomorphic to X. Must X be isomorphic to c_0 or to ℓ_p for some 1 ≤ p < ∞?
self_contained_problem:
Let X be an infinite-dimensional Banach space with a normalized Schauder basis (x_n). Recall that a block sequence of (x_n) is a sequence (v_n) of nonzero vectors of the form v_n = sum_{k=p_n+1}^{p_{n+1}} a_k x_k, where p_1 < p_2 < ... is a strictly increasing sequence of nonnegative integers and (a_k) is a scalar sequence; it is normalized if ||v_n|| = 1 for every n. Say that the basis (x_n) is block homogeneous if for every normalized block sequence (v_n) of (x_n), the closed linear span [v_n : n ∈ ℕ] is isomorphic (as a Banach space) to X.

Suppose X is a Banach space admitting a normalized block homogeneous Schauder basis. Must X be isomorphic to c_0 or to ℓ_p for some 1 ≤ p < ∞?
status_search_result: The classical theorem of Zippin characterizes perfectly homogeneous bases (where every normalized block sequence is equivalent to the basis) as those equivalent to the unit vector basis of c_0 or ℓ_p. The block homogeneous version, requiring only isomorphism of the spanned subspace to X (rather than equivalence of bases), is a weaker hypothesis and is listed as an open problem in surveys on Banach spaces and Ramsey theory; no resolution was located in the search.

original_question: Develop the theory of possibly infinite-dimensional representations of equivariant map Lie algebras beyond the finite-dimensional case. In particular, define and study analogues of category O, the category of integrable highest weight representations, the category of quasifinite representations with finite-dimensional weight spaces, and related representation-theoretic frameworks for general EMAs.
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a scheme (or algebraic variety) over an algebraically closed field $k$ of characteristic zero, let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over $k$, and let $\Gamma$ be a finite group acting on $X$ by scheme automorphisms and on $\mathfrak{g}$ by Lie algebra automorphisms. The associated equivariant map (Lie) algebra is
$$M(X,\mathfrak{g})^{\Gamma} \;=\; \{f \in \mathfrak{g}\otimes_k \mathcal{O}(X) : (\gamma\cdot f)(\gamma\cdot x) = \gamma \cdot f(x)\text{ for all }\gamma\in\Gamma,\;x\in X\},$$
endowed with the pointwise Lie bracket. Special cases include current algebras $\mathfrak{g}\otimes k[t]$, loop algebras $\mathfrak{g}\otimes k[t,t^{-1}]$, multiloop algebras, and twisted versions thereof.

Most existing representation-theoretic results for such algebras concern the category of finite-dimensional representations. Develop a representation theory for $M(X,\mathfrak{g})^{\Gamma}$ that goes beyond the finite-dimensional setting. Concretely:

(a) Define and study an analogue of the Bernstein–Gelfand–Gelfand category $\mathcal{O}$ for general equivariant map algebras $M(X,\mathfrak{g})^{\Gamma}$, including a suitable triangular decomposition, a class of weights, and proofs of basic structural properties (composition series, characters, duality, block decomposition).

(b) Define and classify the integrable highest weight representations of $M(X,\mathfrak{g})^{\Gamma}$, identifying the appropriate notion of dominant integral weight in this generality.

(c) Define the category of quasifinite representations of $M(X,\mathfrak{g})^{\Gamma}$ — those graded representations all of whose weight spaces are finite-dimensional — and classify the irreducible objects.

In each case, give an intrinsic description of the irreducible objects, characters, and extension/block structure that specializes to known results when $M(X,\mathfrak{g})^{\Gamma}$ is an (untwisted or twisted) affine Kac–Moody algebra, a current algebra, or a (twisted) multiloop algebra.
status_search_result: Web search indicates that representation theory of equivariant map algebras has so far focused predominantly on finite-dimensional representations and Weyl modules; no general theory of category O, integrable highest weight, or quasifinite representations for arbitrary equivariant map Lie algebras appears to have been developed. Partial progress exists for special cases (affine Kac–Moody algebras, current and (twisted) loop algebras), but the program for general EMAs remains open.

paper_title: Banach spaces and Ramsey Theory: some open problems
original_question: If X is a separable non-Hilbertian Banach space, does there exist a sequence (X_n) of subspaces of X that are pairwise non-isomorphic?
self_contained_problem: Let $X$ be a separable infinite-dimensional Banach space over the real or complex numbers, and assume that $X$ is not isomorphic to a Hilbert space. Does there necessarily exist a sequence $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ of (closed, infinite-dimensional) subspaces of $X$ such that $X_n$ and $X_m$ are not isomorphic as Banach spaces whenever $n\neq m$?
status_search_result: The question is widely cited as an open problem of Godefroy. Stronger conjectures (every non-Hilbertian separable Banach space is ergodic, hence has continuum many pairwise non-isomorphic subspaces) are also open, with substantial partial progress (e.g., for asymptotically Hilbertian spaces, Orlicz sequence spaces, and the result of Cuellar Carrera that non-ergodic spaces must be near-Hilbert). Even Johnson's weaker question of whether there is a separable Banach space with exactly two non-isomorphic subspaces is reportedly open.

original_question: For a semisimple-target equivariant map Lie algebra M and a general M-module V, describe the cohomology and homology of M in greater generality: determine H^1(M, V), understand the special case H^1(M, M_ad) related to derivations, and determine the groups H_*(M, V), including how perfectness and representation-theoretic structure are reflected in these invariants.
self_contained_problem:
Let k be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. Let X be an affine scheme of finite type over k with coordinate ring A, let g be a finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra over k, and let Γ be a finite group acting on X (equivalently on A by k-algebra automorphisms) and on g by Lie algebra automorphisms. The associated equivariant map algebra is

   M = M(X, g)^Γ = (g ⊗_k A)^Γ,

the fixed-point subalgebra of g ⊗_k A under the diagonal Γ-action, with Lie bracket [x⊗a, y⊗b] = [x,y] ⊗ ab.

Let V be an arbitrary M-module (not necessarily finite dimensional). Investigate the Chevalley–Eilenberg cohomology and homology of M with coefficients in V:

(1) Give an explicit description of the first cohomology group H^1(M, V) for a general M-module V.

(2) In the special case V = M_ad (the adjoint module), describe H^1(M, M_ad) = Der_k(M)/IDer(M), the outer derivation algebra of M.

(3) Determine the homology groups H_*(M, V) for general V, and in particular describe H_0(M, M_ad) = M/[M,M] and explain how the perfectness of M and the representation-theoretic structure of g and of A as a Γ-module are reflected in these (co)homological invariants.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open problem in the Neher–Savage survey of equivariant map algebras (2013). A search for subsequent work did not reveal a complete general description of H^1(M,V), H^1(M,M_ad), or H_*(M,V) for arbitrary modules V over a general semisimple-target equivariant map algebra; partial results exist for derivations and for H_0(M,M_ad) (perfectness criteria) in the untwisted and multiloop cases, but the general question appears to remain open.

paper_title: Banach spaces and Ramsey Theory: some open problems
original_question: Let X be a separable Banach space that fails type 2−ε, or fails co-type 2+ε, for some ε > 0. Must X contain continuum many pairwise non-isomorphic subspaces?
self_contained_problem:
Recall that an infinite-dimensional Banach space X is said to have type p (for 1 ≤ p ≤ 2) if there is a constant T < ∞ such that for every finite sequence x_1, …, x_n in X,

  E ‖∑_{i=1}^n ε_i x_i‖ ≤ T (∑_{i=1}^n ‖x_i‖^p)^{1/p},

where the expectation is over independent ±1-valued Rademacher variables ε_i. Dually, X has cotype q (for 2 ≤ q ≤ ∞) if there is a constant C < ∞ such that

  (∑_{i=1}^n ‖x_i‖^q)^{1/q} ≤ C · E ‖∑_{i=1}^n ε_i x_i‖.

Two Banach spaces are isomorphic if there is a bounded linear bijection between them with bounded inverse.

Question: Let X be an infinite-dimensional separable Banach space. Suppose that there exists ε > 0 such that X fails to have type 2 − ε, or alternatively fails to have cotype 2 + ε. Must X contain continuum many pairwise non-isomorphic (closed, infinite-dimensional) subspaces?
status_search_result: Web search did not yield a definitive resolution of this specific problem. Related results are known: any Banach space without a minimal subspace contains continuum many non-isomorphic subspaces, and there is a broader conjecture that any Banach space not containing an isomorphic copy of ℓ2 contains continuum many non-isomorphic subspaces. The specific question about spaces failing type 2−ε or cotype 2+ε does not appear to have a clearly documented resolution in the sources found.

original_question: For a perfect equivariant map Lie algebra (g tensor A)^Gamma, determine its central extensions, preferably the universal central extension, and decide in broad generality whether the natural comparison formula uce((g tensor A)^Gamma) is isomorphic to the Gamma-fixed subalgebra of uce(g tensor A).
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a field $k$ of characteristic $0$, let $A$ be a unital commutative associative $k$-algebra, and let $\Gamma$ be a finite group acting by Lie algebra automorphisms on $\mathfrak{g}$ and by algebra automorphisms on $A$. Let $\Gamma$ act diagonally on the tensor product Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}\otimes A$ (i.e. $\gamma\cdot(x\otimes a)=(\gamma\cdot x)\otimes(\gamma\cdot a)$), and consider the equivariant map algebra
$$M=(\mathfrak{g}\otimes A)^{\Gamma}=\{u\in\mathfrak{g}\otimes A:\gamma\cdot u=u\text{ for all }\gamma\in\Gamma\}.$$
For a perfect Lie algebra $L$ (i.e. $L=[L,L]$), let $\operatorname{uce}(L)\to L$ denote its universal central extension.

Assume $M$ is perfect. 

(a) Describe the central extensions of $M$, and in particular determine the universal central extension $\operatorname{uce}(M)=\operatorname{uce}((\mathfrak{g}\otimes A)^{\Gamma})$ explicitly.

(b) The action of $\Gamma$ on $\mathfrak{g}\otimes A$ lifts uniquely to an action of $\Gamma$ on $\operatorname{uce}(\mathfrak{g}\otimes A)$. Determine, in broad generality (i.e. for as wide a class of triples $(\mathfrak{g},A,\Gamma)$ as possible), whether the natural comparison map yields an isomorphism
$$\operatorname{uce}\bigl((\mathfrak{g}\otimes A)^{\Gamma}\bigr)\;\cong\;\bigl(\operatorname{uce}(\mathfrak{g}\otimes A)\bigr)^{\Gamma},$$
and identify hypotheses on $\mathfrak{g}$, $A$, and $\Gamma$ under which this holds or fails.
category_tag: Universal central extensions of equivariant map algebras
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open direction in a survey of equivariant map algebras, where the untwisted case $\operatorname{uce}(\mathfrak{g}\otimes A)$ is known (Kassel, and others) and the comparison isomorphism for the $\Gamma$-fixed subalgebra is the goal. Subsequent work by Neher and collaborators (e.g. on extended affine Lie algebras and on universal central extensions of direct limits of Lie superalgebras) has established the desired isomorphism in significant special cases (multiloop algebras, certain twisted forms), but a fully general result for arbitrary equivariant map algebras has not been verified from the available sources. The problem appears partially solved.

paper_title: Banach spaces and Ramsey Theory: some open problems
original_question: Is every complemented subspace of C[0,1] isomorphic to a space C(K) for some closed subset K of [0,1]?
self_contained_problem:
Let $C[0,1]$ denote the Banach space of real-valued continuous functions on the unit interval $[0,1]$, equipped with the supremum norm. A closed subspace $X$ of a Banach space $Y$ is called complemented in $Y$ if there exists a bounded linear projection $P:Y\to Y$ with range $X$. For a compact Hausdorff space $K$, let $C(K)$ denote the Banach space of real-valued continuous functions on $K$ with the supremum norm.

Question: Is it true that every complemented (infinite-dimensional, closed) subspace of $C[0,1]$ is linearly isomorphic to $C(K)$ for some closed subset $K$ of $[0,1]$?
status_search_result: The general complemented subspace problem for C(K)-spaces was answered negatively by Plebanek and Salguero-Alarcón (2021/2023), who constructed a 1-complemented subspace of a C(K)-space that is not isomorphic to any C(K)-space; however, their counterexample is non-separable. The separable version, in particular the question for complemented subspaces of C[0,1], is reported in subsequent literature (e.g., de Hevia–Tradacete 2025) as still open.

original_question: For population-based metaheuristic algorithms in which multiple search agents form multiple interacting Markov chains, can one develop a mathematical theory that proves convergence and characterizes the rate of convergence for these algorithms, rather than only for the limited few metaheuristics that have already been analyzed mathematically?
self_contained_problem:
A population-based metaheuristic optimization algorithm is an iterative stochastic search procedure that maintains, at each step t = 0, 1, 2, ..., a population X_t = (X_t^{(1)}, ..., X_t^{(N)}) of N search agents in a (possibly continuous) search space S, with the joint sequence {X_t}_{t≥0} forming a Markov chain on S^N whose transition kernel encodes the algorithm's selection, variation, and interaction rules. Examples include genetic algorithms, particle swarm optimization, ant colony optimization, differential evolution, firefly algorithms, cuckoo search, and similar schemes; in each case the individual agent trajectories are not independent Markov chains but interact through the population update rule.

Develop a general mathematical framework for such interacting-Markov-chain population metaheuristics that:

(1) Establishes sufficient conditions on the transition kernel under which the algorithm converges, in a precise probabilistic sense (e.g., almost-sure convergence, convergence in probability, or convergence in distribution of best-so-far value), to the global optimum of a given objective function f : S → ℝ.

(2) Provides quantitative estimates of the rate of convergence — for instance, bounds on P(f(X_t^{best}) - f^* > ε) as a function of t, N, and characteristics of f and of the kernel — applicable broadly to the class of population-based metaheuristics rather than to any single specific algorithm.

The problem is to formulate and prove such a unified convergence and convergence-rate theory for the entire class of population-based metaheuristics with interacting agents.
status_search_result: Partial progress exists: unified frameworks and Markov-chain-based asymptotic convergence analyses for population-based metaheuristics have been proposed (e.g., Harris-chain analyses of single-step metaheuristics and state-transition-matrix approaches), and runtime/convergence-rate results exist for specific algorithms such as genetic algorithms and certain evolutionary strategies. However, a fully general theory yielding quantitative convergence rates uniformly across population-based metaheuristics with interacting Markov chains has not been established; the question remains an active open research direction.

paper_title: Banach spaces and Ramsey Theory: some open problems
original_question: Let T: C[0,1] → C[0,1] be a bounded linear operator, and let X be a separable Banach space that does not contain a copy of c_0. If T fixes a copy of X, must T fix a copy of C[0,1]? Equivalently, must the dual operator T* have non-separable range?
self_contained_problem:
Let $C[0,1]$ denote the Banach space of real-valued continuous functions on the unit interval $[0,1]$, equipped with the supremum norm. Recall that a bounded linear operator $T : E \to F$ between Banach spaces is said to "fix a copy" of a Banach space $X$ if there exists a closed subspace $Y \subseteq E$ that is linearly isomorphic to $X$ and such that the restriction $T|_Y : Y \to T(Y)$ is an isomorphism onto its image. Let $c_0$ denote the Banach space of real sequences converging to zero, with the supremum norm.

Question: Suppose $T : C[0,1] \to C[0,1]$ is a bounded linear operator and $X$ is a separable Banach space that does not contain an isomorphic copy of $c_0$. If $T$ fixes a copy of $X$, must $T$ fix a copy of $C[0,1]$? Equivalently, must the dual operator $T^* : C[0,1]^* \to C[0,1]^*$ have non-separable range?

The classical direction (if T* has non-separable range, then T fixes a copy of C[0,1]) is a 1972 theorem of Rosenthal. original_question: For metaheuristic algorithms, is there an optimal way to balance local intensification, which focuses the search in promising local regions, and global diversification, which explores the search space more broadly? If such an optimal balance exists, how can it be achieved, and if it does not exist, what is the best achievable trade-off?
self_contained_problem:
A metaheuristic algorithm for solving a global optimization problem $\min_{x\in\Omega} f(x)$ (with $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and $f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$) is an iterative stochastic search procedure that, at each step, generates candidate solutions using two complementary mechanisms:

(i) Local intensification (exploitation): operations that concentrate the search in a neighborhood of currently promising candidates, in order to refine them.

(ii) Global diversification (exploration): operations that spread the search broadly over $\Omega$, in order to discover previously unexplored regions and avoid premature convergence to local minima.

Let a metaheuristic be parameterized by a control $\alpha\in[0,1]$ (or, more generally, by a schedule $\alpha_t$ over iterations $t=1,2,\dots,T$) that quantifies the relative weight given to intensification versus diversification, where $\alpha=0$ corresponds to pure diversification and $\alpha=1$ to pure intensification. Let $\mathcal{F}$ denote a class of objective functions $f$, and let $E_f[\alpha,T]$ denote the expected optimality gap after $T$ iterations of the metaheuristic with control $\alpha$ on objective $f$.

Address the following:

(a) Does there exist, for a sufficiently general class $\mathcal{F}$, an optimal value $\alpha^\star$ (or optimal schedule $\{\alpha_t^\star\}$) that minimizes $\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}} E_f[\alpha,T]$, providing a universally optimal trade-off between local intensification and global diversification?

(b) If such an optimal balance exists, give a constructive characterization of $\alpha^\star$ (or of $\{\alpha_t^\star\}$) and a method by which a metaheuristic algorithm can attain it.

(c) If no such universally optimal balance exists, determine the best achievable trade-off: identify tight bounds on $\inf_{\alpha}\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}} E_f[\alpha,T]$ and exhibit strategies (possibly adaptive in $f$ or $t$) that attain these bounds.
status_search_result: The question of an optimal exploration–exploitation trade-off in general-purpose metaheuristics is widely regarded as a long-standing open problem. No-Free-Lunch theorems (Wolpert–Macready) imply that no universally optimal balance can exist over all objective functions, but for restricted function classes the question of optimal or near-optimal schedules remains open and is the subject of ongoing research in adaptive and hyper-heuristic methods.

paper_title: Banach spaces and Ramsey Theory: some open problems
original_question: Does there exist an infinite-dimensional Banach space that is boundedly distortable, meaning distortable for some λ > 1 but not arbitrarily distortable for all λ > 1?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X, \|\cdot\|)$ be an infinite-dimensional Banach space. For $\lambda > 1$, $X$ is said to be $\lambda$-distortable if there exists an equivalent norm $|\cdot|$ on $X$ such that for every infinite-dimensional closed subspace $Y \subseteq X$,
$$\sup\left\{ \frac{|y|}{|z|} : y, z \in Y,\ \|y\| = \|z\| = 1 \right\} \geq \lambda.$$
$X$ is called distortable if it is $\lambda$-distortable for some $\lambda > 1$, and arbitrarily distortable if it is $\lambda$-distortable for every $\lambda > 1$. A distortable Banach space that is not arbitrarily distortable is called boundedly distortable.

Question: Does there exist a boundedly distortable infinite-dimensional Banach space?
status_search_result: The bounded distortion problem remains open. Tsirelson's space is a candidate (it is (2−ε)-distortable for every ε > 0, but not known to be arbitrarily distortable). Recent surveys on open problems in Banach space geometry continue to list the existence of a boundedly distortable Banach space as unresolved, and no construction is known.

original_question: Why does a balanced combination of randomization and a deterministic component lead to a much more efficient metaheuristic algorithm than a purely deterministic algorithm or a purely random algorithm?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the class of iterative search algorithms for global optimization of an objective function f : X → R on a (possibly large, discrete or continuous) search space X. Such an algorithm produces a sequence of candidate solutions x_1, x_2, ... by repeatedly applying an update rule that may depend on (i) deterministic information derived from previously evaluated points (e.g. gradients, finite differences, or rules exploiting current best solutions), and (ii) random perturbations drawn from some probability distribution. Three idealized regimes can be distinguished: (a) a purely deterministic algorithm, in which the update rule is a deterministic function of the history; (b) a purely random algorithm, in which each new candidate is drawn independently from a fixed distribution on X without using past evaluations; and (c) a hybrid metaheuristic, in which each update is a balanced mixture of a deterministic exploitation component and a stochastic exploration component.

Provide a rigorous theoretical explanation, supported by quantitative bounds, of the following empirical observation: across broad classes of objective functions f (for instance, multimodal functions on bounded domains satisfying mild regularity assumptions), a suitably balanced hybrid algorithm of type (c) converges to a global optimum (or to an ε-approximate global optimum) substantially faster, in terms of expected number of function evaluations, than any algorithm of type (a) or type (b).

More precisely, formulate and prove a theorem of the following form: identify a class F of objective functions and a family H of hybrid algorithms parametrized by a randomization level p ∈ [0,1] (with p = 0 corresponding to purely deterministic and p = 1 to purely random search) such that the expected hitting time T_p(f, ε) to reach an ε-approximate optimum satisfies

   inf_{p ∈ (0,1)} sup_{f ∈ F} E[T_p(f, ε)]  ≪  min{ sup_{f ∈ F} E[T_0(f, ε)],  sup_{f ∈ F} E[T_1(f, ε)] },

and characterize the optimal balance p* and the mechanism by which the interplay between deterministic exploitation and stochastic exploration produces this efficiency gain.
status_search_result: The question is a foundational open problem in the theory of metaheuristics: a general, rigorous theoretical explanation of why hybrid randomized–deterministic metaheuristics outperform purely deterministic or purely random search remains unresolved. Partial results exist in special settings (e.g., No Free Lunch theorems, runtime analysis of specific evolutionary algorithms, simulated annealing convergence theory), but no general theorem covering broad function classes is established.

paper_title: Banach spaces and Ramsey Theory: some open problems
original_question: Is Tsirelson’s space T, or its dual, boundedly distortable rather than arbitrarily distortable?
self_contained_problem:
Tsirelson's space $T$ is the completion of $c_{00}$ (the space of finitely supported real sequences) under the implicitly defined norm
$$\|x\| = \max\Big\{\|x\|_\infty,\; \tfrac{1}{2}\sup\sum_{i=1}^k \|E_i x\|\Big\},$$
where the inner supremum is taken over all choices of integers $k$ and finite subsets $E_1<E_2<\cdots<E_k$ of $\mathbb{N}$ with $k\le \min E_1$, and $E_i x$ denotes the restriction of $x$ to the coordinates in $E_i$. Let $T^*$ denote its dual.

For an infinite-dimensional Banach space $(X,\|\cdot\|)$ and $\lambda>1$, say that $X$ is $\lambda$-distortable if there exists an equivalent norm $|||\cdot|||$ on $X$ such that for every infinite-dimensional closed subspace $Y\subseteq X$,
$$\sup\Big\{\frac{|||y|||}{|||z|||} : y,z\in Y,\ \|y\|=\|z\|=1\Big\}\ge \lambda.$$
Say that $X$ is arbitrarily distortable if it is $\lambda$-distortable for every $\lambda>1$, and that $X$ is boundedly distortable if there exists $\lambda_0>1$ such that $X$ is $\lambda$-distortable for every $1<\lambda<\lambda_0$ but $X$ is not arbitrarily distortable (equivalently, $X$ is distortable but not arbitrarily distortable).

Question: Is Tsirelson's space $T$ (or its dual $T^*$) boundedly distortable, rather than arbitrarily distortable?
status_search_result: The problem appears to remain open. Tsirelson's space $T$ is known to be $(2-\varepsilon)$-distortable for every $\varepsilon>0$, but whether $T$ or $T^*$ is arbitrarily distortable (versus only boundedly distortable) is not resolved in the literature surveyed. While Schlumprecht constructed an arbitrarily distortable Banach space, this construction does not settle the question for Tsirelson's space itself.

original_question: How can one measure or test whether a metaheuristic algorithm has achieved a proper balance among its interacting search components?
self_contained_problem:
A metaheuristic optimization algorithm is an iterative stochastic procedure that searches a (typically large, discrete or continuous) solution space $\mathcal{S}$ for an approximate optimizer of an objective function $f:\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{R}$. Such algorithms are typically built from several interacting search components, most notably:

- an exploration (diversification) component, which generates candidate solutions far from the current population so as to broadly sample $\mathcal{S}$;
- an exploitation (intensification) component, which refines promising candidate solutions in a local neighborhood so as to improve objective values;
- and possibly additional components governing selection pressure, memory, randomization, parameter adaptation, etc.

The algorithm's overall performance is widely believed to depend on a suitable balance between these components: too much exploration prevents convergence, while too much exploitation causes premature stagnation in local optima.

Problem. Formulate a quantitative, algorithm-independent framework for measuring the balance among the interacting search components of a metaheuristic algorithm during its execution on a given problem instance. Specifically:

(a) Define a measurable quantity (or family of quantities) $B(t)$, computable from the trajectory of populations $\{P_t\}_{t\ge 0}$ produced by the algorithm and from the objective function $f$, that captures the relative contributions of exploration and exploitation (and any other components) at iteration $t$.

(b) Provide a statistical test, with explicit null hypothesis and rejection criterion, that decides whether a given run (or ensemble of runs) of the algorithm has reached a "proper" balance among its components, in a sense made precise by the framework.

(c) Show that the proposed measure and test are consistent in the following sense: on benchmark families of objective functions where ground-truth optimal balance can be characterized (for example, via theoretical convergence-rate analysis on convex quadratics, on needle-in-a-haystack functions, or on no-free-lunch style ensembles), the measure correctly identifies imbalance and the test has controlled type-I and type-II error rates.
status_search_result: The question of how to quantitatively measure exploration–exploitation balance in metaheuristics remains an active open research topic. Several diversity-based metrics (e.g., population diversity measures, the exploration/exploitation percentage of Morales-Castañeda et al., 2020) have been proposed, but no universally accepted measure or formal statistical test exists, and recent surveys continue to list this as an open problem.

paper_title: Banach spaces and Ramsey Theory: some open problems
original_question: Let X be a separable Banach space such that every separable Banach space is Lipschitz isomorphic to a subset of X. Must X contain a copy of c_0?
self_contained_problem:
Let $c_0$ denote the Banach space of real sequences converging to zero, equipped with the supremum norm. Recall that a map $f:(M,d_M)\to(N,d_N)$ between metric spaces is a Lipschitz isomorphism onto its image if there exist constants $0<a\le b<\infty$ such that $a\,d_M(x,y)\le d_N(f(x),f(y))\le b\,d_M(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in M$. By Aharoni's theorem, every separable metric space is Lipschitz isomorphic to a subset of $c_0$.

Suppose $X$ is a separable Banach space with the property that every separable Banach space is Lipschitz isomorphic to a subset of $X$. Must $X$ contain a closed linear subspace that is linearly isomorphic to $c_0$?
status_search_result: The converse Aharoni problem is listed as open in surveys on the nonlinear geometry of Banach spaces (e.g., Godefroy–Kalton-style surveys and the Castro Urdiales 2014 problem list). No published resolution was located; partial results are known (e.g., subspaces of $c_0$ are stable under Lipschitz isomorphism), but the general question remains unresolved.

original_question: How can one prove that the use of memory can significantly increase the search efficiency of a metaheuristic algorithm, and under what conditions does such an efficiency gain hold?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a metaheuristic search algorithm A that explores a finite or compact search space X in order to optimize an objective function f : X → R. A memoryless variant A_0 generates each candidate solution using only the current state (Markovian dynamics), while a memory-based variant A_M maintains an internal record of previously visited states, evaluated objective values, or other historical information, and uses this record when generating new candidates. Define the search efficiency of an algorithm as the expected number of objective function evaluations required to reach a solution within a prescribed tolerance ε of the global optimum of f, possibly weighted by a desired success probability.

Provide a rigorous mathematical proof that incorporating memory can significantly increase the search efficiency of such a metaheuristic algorithm. Specifically:

1. Formulate a precise model of memory within the framework of stochastic search algorithms, including how the memory is updated and how it is used to bias the generation of new candidate solutions.

2. Identify explicit conditions on the objective function f, the search space X, and the structure of the memory under which the memory-based algorithm A_M is provably more efficient than its memoryless counterpart A_0 — for example, by exhibiting a strict separation in the expected hitting time, the convergence rate, or the sample complexity required to achieve a given approximation ratio.

3. Determine, conversely, conditions under which memory does not yield an asymptotic efficiency gain, thereby characterizing the regime in which the use of memory is provably beneficial.
status_search_result: A general rigorous theory characterizing when memory provably improves the efficiency of metaheuristic algorithms remains an open problem. While specific results exist for particular algorithms (e.g., tabu search, ant colony optimization, runtime analysis of evolutionary algorithms with archives), no universally accepted theorem identifying necessary and sufficient conditions for a memory-induced efficiency gain in metaheuristics is established in the literature.

paper_title: Banach spaces and Ramsey Theory: some open problems
original_question: Does every infinite-dimensional Banach space X have an infinite-dimensional quotient that has a Schauder basis?
self_contained_problem:
Let X be an infinite-dimensional (real or complex) Banach space. A sequence (e_n)_{n=1}^∞ in a Banach space Y is called a Schauder basis of Y if every y ∈ Y has a unique norm-convergent expansion y = Σ_{n=1}^∞ a_n e_n with scalar coefficients a_n. A quotient of X is a Banach space of the form X/M, where M ⊂ X is a closed linear subspace, equipped with the quotient norm.

Question: Does every infinite-dimensional Banach space X admit a closed subspace M ⊂ X such that the quotient space X/M is infinite-dimensional and possesses a Schauder basis?

original_question: Do No-Free-Lunch theorems hold for multiobjective optimization, given that they have been proved for single-objective optimization on finite search domains and do not hold for continuous infinite domains, and if they do hold or do not hold for multiobjective optimization, what implications would that have for algorithm development?
self_contained_problem:
Background. The No-Free-Lunch (NFL) theorems for optimization assert, roughly, that when performance is averaged uniformly over all objective functions f : X → Y with X and Y finite, every pair of (non-revisiting) black-box search algorithms has identical average performance under any performance measure depending only on the sequence of observed objective values. NFL theorems are known to hold in this finite single-objective setting and are known to fail in general for continuous infinite search domains.

Now consider the multiobjective setting. Let X be a finite search space and let Y₁, …, Y_k be finite totally ordered value sets (k ≥ 2). A multiobjective problem is a function F : X → Y₁ × ⋯ × Y_k. A black-box multiobjective algorithm A produces, for each F, a sequence of distinct query points x₁, x₂, … ∈ X chosen adaptively based on previously observed vector values F(x₁), …, F(x_{i−1}). Fix a performance measure φ depending only on the sequence of observed value vectors (for example, hypervolume of the dominated region after m steps, or time to first hit the Pareto-optimal set).

Question. Determine whether the following analogue of the NFL theorem holds:

For every pair of black-box multiobjective algorithms A and B, and every such performance measure φ and horizon m,
   Σ_{F : X → Y₁×⋯×Y_k} φ(A, F, m) = Σ_{F : X → Y₁×⋯×Y_k} φ(B, F, m).

If the equality holds, identify the precise hypotheses on the class of problems, on the algorithms, and on φ under which it holds, and describe the implications for the design and comparison of multiobjective optimization algorithms. If the equality fails, characterize natural sub-classes of multiobjective problems (for example, those defined by a fixed Pareto front, by closure under permutation of X, or by a fixed shape of Pareto front) on which an NFL-type identity does or does not hold, and describe the consequences for algorithm development.
status_search_result: The question has been substantially addressed. Corne and Knowles (2003) showed "free leftovers" can exist for multiobjective optimization in the presence of an archiver, indicating NFL does not always hold in the standard multiobjective formulation. Conversely, Service (2010) proved an NFL theorem for multi-objective optimization showing that, with appropriate definitions, the classical NFL identity does extend: NFL holds over the set of multiobjective problems sharing a fixed Pareto front, and more generally over classes structurally closed under permutation. Thus the problem is partially solved: precise hypotheses under which NFL holds or fails for multiobjective optimization have been identified, although a unified picture and full implications for algorithm design continue to be discussed.

original_question: Can one develop a formal theoretical analysis and an agreed set of measures for comparing the performance of different metaheuristic algorithms, beyond commonly used empirical measures such as absolute objective value and number of function evaluations?
self_contained_problem:
A metaheuristic algorithm is a (typically stochastic) iterative procedure A that, given an optimization problem instance P = (f, X) with objective f : X → ℝ on a search space X, produces a sequence of candidate solutions x_1, x_2, … ∈ X aiming to approximate min_{x∈X} f(x). Common empirical measures used to compare two such algorithms A and B on a benchmark family of instances are: (i) the absolute best objective value reached after a fixed budget, and (ii) the number of objective-function evaluations needed to reach a prescribed accuracy.

Develop a formal theoretical framework for comparing the performance of metaheuristic algorithms that goes beyond these empirical measures. Specifically:

1. Propose a mathematically rigorous definition of "performance" of a metaheuristic A on a class C of optimization problems, taking into account stochasticity (e.g., expectations and tail bounds over the algorithm's random choices), convergence rate, solution quality, robustness, and computational cost.

2. Define an agreed set of comparison measures M_1, …, M_k (functionals on pairs (A, C)) such that: (a) each M_i is well-defined and computable or estimable; (b) the measures collectively induce a meaningful preorder on metaheuristic algorithms relative to a problem class; (c) the framework is consistent with no-free-lunch–type results, in the sense that universal dominance across all problem classes is precluded but class-relative dominance is captured.

3. Prove that within this framework one can derive non-trivial theoretical comparison theorems between standard metaheuristics (for example, simulated annealing, genetic algorithms, particle swarm optimization, differential evolution) on identifiable problem classes.

Provide either such a framework with proofs, or a rigorous argument that no such framework satisfying (1)–(3) can exist.

paper_title: Banach spaces and Ramsey Theory: some open problems
original_question: For a given infinite-dimensional Banach space X, what is the greatest possible length of a Schauder basis that a quotient of X can have?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be an infinite-dimensional Banach space. Recall that for an ordinal $\gamma$, a transfinite Schauder basis of length $\gamma$ for a Banach space $Y$ is a family $(y_\alpha)_{\alpha<\gamma}$ in $Y$ such that every $y\in Y$ admits a unique expansion $y=\sum_{\alpha<\gamma} a_\alpha y_\alpha$ converging in the natural transfinite sense, with the partial-sum projections uniformly bounded by some constant $C\ge 1$.

Determine, as a function of $X$, the supremum of the ordinals $\gamma$ such that some quotient of $X$ admits a transfinite Schauder basis of length $\gamma$. In particular, characterize this supremum for general infinite-dimensional Banach spaces $X$, and decide whether it can always be attained.
category_tag: Banach space quotients and transfinite bases
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open question in a list of open problems on Banach spaces and Ramsey theory. No subsequent published resolution was found in the available search results; standard references discuss transfinite bases but do not address the maximal length attainable in quotients of an arbitrary infinite-dimensional Banach space.

original_question: For the infinite-dimensional Hamiltonian with short-range or finite-range interaction considered in the paper, namely a system of the form H = sum_{j in Z^d} omega_j I_j + epsilon sum_{<i,j>} f_{i,j}(I_i, I_j; phi_i, phi_j), where the perturbation is short range or finite range and the frequencies are weakly correlated, KAM tori are constructed when the initial actions are strongly localized or even decay weaker than exponentially. Does there also exist an infinite-dimensional KAM torus when the initial actions decay only polynomially, in the sense that the action profile satisfies epsilon_j = I_j^0 approximately |j|^{-M} for some sufficiently large M > 0?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the infinite-dimensional Hamiltonian system on the lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ given, in action–angle variables $(I_j,\phi_j)_{j\in\mathbb{Z}^d}$, by
$$H \;=\; \sum_{j\in\mathbb{Z}^d} \omega_j\, I_j \;+\; \varepsilon \sum_{\langle i,j\rangle} f_{i,j}(I_i,I_j;\phi_i,\phi_j),$$
with symplectic form $\sum_j dI_j\wedge d\phi_j$, where:
- the frequencies $(\omega_j)_{j\in\mathbb{Z}^d}$ are weakly correlated (e.g. independent and identically distributed in a fixed bounded interval, or otherwise satisfy standard Diophantine-type non-resonance conditions almost surely);
- the perturbation is of short range or finite range, in the sense that the sum runs over pairs $\langle i,j\rangle$ of nearby lattice sites and each $f_{i,j}$ is a real-analytic function of the listed variables;
- $\varepsilon>0$ is sufficiently small.

By an infinite-dimensional KAM torus we mean an invariant torus of the perturbed flow, parametrised by all angle variables $(\phi_j)_{j\in\mathbb{Z}^d}\in\mathbb{T}^{\mathbb{Z}^d}$, on which the dynamics is conjugate to a linear flow with Diophantine-type frequency vector close to $(\omega_j)$, and which is obtained as a small perturbation of the unperturbed torus $\{I_j = I_j^0\}_{j\in\mathbb{Z}^d}$ for a prescribed initial action profile $(I_j^0)_{j\in\mathbb{Z}^d}$.

Existence of such tori is known when the initial actions $I_j^0$ are strongly localized (e.g. exponentially decaying) and even for slower decay of the form $I_j^0 \sim \exp\!\big(-(\log|j|)^{1+\alpha}\big)$ for some $\alpha>0$.

Question: Does there exist an infinite-dimensional KAM torus of the above Hamiltonian system whose initial action profile decays only polynomially, i.e. satisfying
$$I_j^0 \;\asymp\; |j|^{-M}, \qquad |j|\to\infty,$$
for some sufficiently large constant $M>0$?
status_search_result: Recent literature on infinite-dimensional/full-dimensional KAM tori (e.g. work of Bourgain, Pöschel, Cong, Cong–Mi–Shi–Wu, Cong–Yuan, and 2024–2025 preprints on 1D NLS and Klein–Gordon equations) has progressively weakened the required decay rate of the initial actions, but the best results to date only reach sub-exponential decay of the form $I_j^0 \sim \exp(-(\log|j|)^\sigma)$ with $\sigma>2$ (or analogous). The case of purely polynomial decay $I_j^0\asymp|j|^{-M}$ continues to be cited as an open problem attributed to Kuksin and Bourgain, with no published construction or proof of obstruction located.

paper_title: Banach spaces and Ramsey Theory: some open problems
original_question: Assume the P-ideal dichotomy, namely that for every P-ideal I of countable subsets of some set S, either there is an uncountable set T ⊆ S such that every countable subset of T belongs to I, or S can be decomposed into countably many pieces with no infinite subset in I. Under this assumption, are the following equivalent: (1) every non-separable Banach space has an uncountable biorthogonal system; and (2) b = ℵ_2, where b is the minimum cardinality of an unbounded family in N^N under eventual domination?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{N}^{\mathbb{N}}$ be ordered by eventual dominance: $f \le^* g$ iff $f(n) \le g(n)$ for all but finitely many $n$. Define $\mathfrak{b}$ to be the minimum cardinality of a subset of $\mathbb{N}^{\mathbb{N}}$ that is unbounded with respect to $\le^*$.

A family $\mathcal{I}$ of countable subsets of a set $S$ is called a P-ideal if it is closed under taking subsets and finite unions, and for every countable family $\{A_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\} \subseteq \mathcal{I}$ there exists $A \in \mathcal{I}$ with $A_n \setminus A$ finite for all $n$.

The P-ideal dichotomy (PID) is the statement: For every P-ideal $\mathcal{I}$ of countable subsets of any set $S$, either
(a) there is an uncountable $T \subseteq S$ such that every countable subset of $T$ belongs to $\mathcal{I}$, or
(b) $S$ can be written as a countable union $S = \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} S_n$ such that no infinite subset of any $S_n$ belongs to $\mathcal{I}$.

A biorthogonal system in a Banach space $X$ is a family $\{(x_\alpha, x^*_\alpha) : \alpha \in \Lambda\} \subseteq X \times X^*$ with $x^*_\alpha(x_\beta) = \delta_{\alpha\beta}$. A Banach space is non-separable if it has no countable dense subset.

Assume PID. Are the following statements equivalent?
(1) Every non-separable Banach space admits an uncountable biorthogonal system.
(2) $\mathfrak{b} = \aleph_2$.
status_search_result: Brech and Todorcevic established that, under PID, the equivalence with $\mathfrak{b} = \aleph_2$ holds when "non-separable Banach space" is restricted to non-separable Asplund spaces (and more generally to spaces with weak*-sequentially compact dual ball, of density $<\mathfrak{b}$). The full equivalence for all non-separable Banach spaces under PID does not appear to have been established in the literature, so the problem in its original generality appears partially solved.

context_brief: Pure point spectrum with non-short-range nonlinearity
original_question: Consider a Hamiltonian system whose linearized operator, for example -Delta_f + v, has pure point spectrum, with part of that pure point spectrum dense in some finite interval. If the nonlinear part of the Hamiltonian is not short range, as in Hamiltonian partial differential equations posed on the whole space, do KAM tori still exist for that system?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an infinite-dimensional Hamiltonian system on a Hilbert phase space whose linearized operator at an equilibrium is of the form L = -Δ_f + v (a Laplace-type operator plus a potential, posed on an unbounded spatial domain such as the whole Euclidean space ℝ^d). Assume that:

(i) L has pure point spectrum {λ_n}_{n≥1} consisting of nonzero real eigenvalues, and at least part of this spectrum is dense in some finite interval [a,b] ⊂ ℝ (for instance, the eigenvalues may include all rationals in [1,2]);

(ii) the Hamiltonian has the form H = ⟨Lu,u⟩/2 + P(u), where the nonlinear part P is not of short range — that is, when expanded in the eigenbasis {φ_n} of L, the coefficients of P do not decay rapidly with respect to the distance |n - m| of the indices involved (as is typical for nonlinear Hamiltonian PDEs posed on the whole space).

Question: Does such a Hamiltonian system possess KAM tori? Equivalently, do there exist small-amplitude quasi-periodic-in-time solutions, supported on finite-dimensional invariant tori in phase space, that persist under the non-short-range nonlinear perturbation P, despite the dense distribution of normal frequencies λ_n in a finite interval?
status_search_result: Existing infinite-dimensional KAM results typically assume either spectral separation/non-resonance conditions on the normal frequencies or short-range (rapidly decaying off-diagonal) structure of the nonlinearity. Results for Hamiltonian PDEs on the whole space with eigenvalues densely distributed in a finite interval and non-short-range nonlinearities do not appear in the literature; recent surveys and papers (2022–2024) on KAM for NLS/wave equations continue to treat short-range or tame-modulus nonlinearities, suggesting the problem remains open.

paper_title: Banach spaces and Ramsey Theory: some open problems
original_question: A support set in a Banach space X is a nonempty convex set C such that every point x in C is a support point, meaning there is a functional f on X with f(x) = inf{f(y) : y ∈ C} < sup{f(y) : y ∈ C}. Which Banach spaces admit support sets? In particular, does every non-separable Banach space admit a support set?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a (real) Banach space and let $X^*$ denote its topological dual. A nonempty convex subset $C \subseteq X$ is called a support set if for every $x \in C$ there exists a continuous linear functional $f \in X^*$ (depending on $x$) such that
$$f(x) = \inf\{f(y) : y \in C\} < \sup\{f(y) : y \in C\}.$$
(That is, every point of $C$ is a proper support point of $C$.)

Characterize the class of Banach spaces $X$ that admit a support set. In particular, decide whether every non-separable Banach space admits a support set.
status_search_result: Rolewicz's problem has been studied extensively, with positive results in many non-separable cases (e.g., spaces with a Markushevich basis of length ω₁, C(K) when K carries a non-separable regular measure, and characterization via semibiorthogonal sequences of length ω₁), but the general problem—whether every non-separable Banach space admits a support set—remains open. A weaker form (density > ℵ₁) is also discussed as still open.

original_question: Consider a Hamiltonian system whose linearized operator, for example -Delta_f + v, has continuous spectrum containing an interval. Can such a system admit any KAM tori, even in the case where the Hamiltonian itself may still have short-range interactions?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an infinite-dimensional Hamiltonian system on a lattice (for example, a Hamiltonian network of oscillators with short-range coupling) whose equations of motion can be linearized about an equilibrium. Suppose the linearized operator — concretely, an operator of the form $L = -\Delta_f + v$, where $\Delta_f$ is a (possibly weighted) discrete Laplacian on the lattice and $v$ is a multiplication (potential) operator — has spectrum that contains a non-degenerate interval of continuous spectrum (i.e., the spectrum is not pure point and includes an absolutely continuous or singular continuous component filling some interval $[\beta,\beta+1]$).

Question: Under these hypotheses, can the full nonlinear Hamiltonian system support any KAM tori, that is, invariant tori carrying quasi-periodic motion with Diophantine frequency vectors that persist under the nonlinear perturbation? Address this in particular for Hamiltonians with short-range interactions, where the standard KAM machinery for quasi-periodic breathers relies on pure point spectrum of the linearization. Either construct such KAM tori in the presence of an interval of continuous spectrum, or prove a general non-existence (obstruction) theorem showing that an interval of continuous spectrum in the linearization precludes the existence of KAM tori.
status_search_result: The literature on quasi-periodic breathers in Hamiltonian lattices consistently treats pure point spectrum of the linearized operator as essential for KAM constructions, and identifies continuous spectrum as an obstruction; recent works (e.g., on granular chains and coupled map lattices) still operate under pure-point or finite-multiplicity assumptions, and no general theorem either constructing KAM tori under an interval of continuous spectrum or proving their non-existence in this setting has been located. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Banach spaces and Ramsey Theory: some open problems
original_question: Does every Banach space of density strictly greater than ℵ_1 have a support set?
self_contained_problem:
A subset $S$ of a Banach space $X$ is called a support set if $S$ is convex, bounded, nonempty, and every point of $S$ is a (proper) support point of $S$, i.e., for every $x \in S$ there exists a continuous linear functional $f \in X^*$ with $f$ not constant on $S$ and $f(x) = \sup_{y \in S} f(y)$. The density (character) of $X$, denoted $\mathrm{dens}(X)$, is the least cardinality of a dense subset of $X$.

Question: Does every Banach space $X$ with $\mathrm{dens}(X) > \aleph_1$ contain a support set?
status_search_result: The problem, posed by Todorcevic, asks whether Banach spaces of density above ℵ₁ must have a support set. Related works (Todorcevic on biorthogonal systems via Baire category methods, and consistency results on unconditional basic sequences in spaces of high density by Lopez-Abad/Todorcevic) address adjacent questions but do not appear to resolve this one. No source found announcing a solution; it appears to remain open.

original_question: A planar billiard table Y is called integrable when the set of invariant circles of its billiard map has nonempty interior. Must every such integrable billiard table be an ellipse?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a planar billiard table, that is, a strictly convex bounded domain Y ⊂ ℝ² with sufficiently smooth boundary, together with its billiard map T defined on the space of inward-pointing unit tangent vectors based on ∂Y, where T sends a chord to the chord obtained by reflecting elastically off ∂Y (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection). An invariant circle of T is a homotopically nontrivial T-invariant continuous closed curve in the phase cylinder. Call the billiard table Y integrable if the union of all invariant circles of T has nonempty interior in the phase space.

Prove or disprove: every integrable planar billiard table Y is bounded by an ellipse.
status_search_result: The classical Birkhoff conjecture remains open. Significant partial results exist: Kaloshin–Sorrentino (Annals of Math., 2018) proved a local version (small integrable perturbations of an ellipse must be ellipses); Bialy, Mironov, Glutsyuk and others have settled the polynomial/algebraic version on surfaces of constant curvature. The general conjecture is still unresolved as of 2025.

paper_title: Banach spaces and Ramsey Theory: some open problems
original_question: Does every Banach space X of density greater than the continuum c contain an infinite unconditional basic sequence? Does the answer change if one imposes additional assumptions such as reflexivity?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathfrak{c}=2^{\aleph_0}$ denote the cardinality of the continuum. The density character $\mathrm{dens}(X)$ of a Banach space $X$ is the least cardinality of a norm-dense subset of $X$. A sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ in a Banach space is called an unconditional basic sequence if there exists a constant $C\ge 1$ such that, for every finitely supported scalar sequence $(a_n)$ and every choice of signs $(\varepsilon_n)\in\{-1,+1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$, one has
$$\Big\|\sum_n \varepsilon_n a_n x_n\Big\| \le C\Big\|\sum_n a_n x_n\Big\|.$$
(Equivalently, $(x_n)$ is a Schauder basic sequence whose basis is unconditional.)

(a) Does every Banach space $X$ with $\mathrm{dens}(X)>\mathfrak{c}$ contain an infinite unconditional basic sequence?

(b) If the answer to (a) is negative in general, does it become positive under the additional hypothesis that $X$ is reflexive (or under analogous structural assumptions)?
category_tag: Nonseparable Banach spaces and unconditional sequences
status_search_result: Partial results exist but the problem appears still open in full generality. Lopez-Abad and Todorcevic (2008, "Unconditional basic sequences in spaces of large density") proved, among other things, that every Banach space of density at least a sufficiently large cardinal (e.g., a weakly compact cardinal, or under suitable axioms density $\aleph_\omega$) contains an infinite unconditional basic sequence. Earlier, Ketonen and others addressed the case of very large densities. However, no published resolution is found settling the case of density just above $\mathfrak{c}$, and the reflexive variant likewise appears unresolved.

original_question: If Y is a smooth convex billiard table and the billiard flow on Y is an integrable Hamiltonian system with two degrees of freedom, must Y be an ellipse?
self_contained_problem:
Let Y ⊂ ℝ² be a smooth, strictly convex billiard table, i.e., a planar domain bounded by a smooth strictly convex closed curve ∂Y. Consider the billiard flow inside Y, defined by the motion of a point particle traveling along straight lines in the interior of Y and reflecting elastically (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection) upon hitting ∂Y. This flow can be regarded as a Hamiltonian system with two degrees of freedom on the unit tangent bundle, and its dynamics is encoded by the billiard map on the annulus of inward-pointing unit vectors based on ∂Y. The system is called (Liouville) integrable if there exists a smooth first integral, independent of the energy on an open dense set, that is invariant under the billiard map (equivalently, the phase space is foliated by invariant curves on which the dynamics is conjugate to a rotation, away from a set of measure zero).

Prove or disprove: if the billiard flow inside such a smooth, strictly convex domain Y is integrable, then ∂Y must be an ellipse.
status_search_result: The general Birkhoff conjecture (that integrable smooth convex billiards must be ellipses) remains open as of 2025. Significant partial results exist: Avila–De Simoi–Kaloshin and Kaloshin–Sorrentino established local versions for perturbations of ellipses; Bialy–Mironov solved the polynomially integrable case; and a 2025 result strengthens local spectral uniqueness for almost every ellipse. None of these resolves the full conjecture.

paper_title: Banach spaces and Ramsey Theory: some open problems
original_question: Does every Banach space of density greater than c, and does every reflexive Banach space of density greater than ℵ_1, contain an infinite sub-symmetric basic sequence?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathfrak{c}$ denote the cardinality of the continuum. Recall that an infinite sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ in a Banach space $X$ is called a basic sequence if it is a Schauder basis of its closed linear span, and it is called sub-symmetric if it is unconditional and equivalent to each of its infinite subsequences (equivalently, there is a constant $C\geq 1$ such that for every strictly increasing sequence of indices $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ and every choice of scalars $(a_k)$, $C^{-1}\bigl\|\sum_k a_k x_k\bigr\|\leq \bigl\|\sum_k a_k x_{n_k}\bigr\|\leq C\bigl\|\sum_k a_k x_k\bigr\|$, with unconditionality of $(x_n)$). The density of a Banach space $X$ is the smallest cardinality of a norm-dense subset of $X$.

Answer the following two questions:

(a) Does every Banach space of density strictly greater than $\mathfrak{c}$ contain an infinite sub-symmetric basic sequence?

(b) Does every reflexive Banach space of density strictly greater than $\aleph_1$ contain an infinite sub-symmetric basic sequence?
category_tag: Non-separable Banach spaces and basic sequences

original_question: Given a closed convex curve gamma, let G(gamma, l) denote the outer curve produced by the string or gardener construction with string length l > |gamma|. If this construction is transitive in the sense that for ellipses one has G(G(gamma_1, l_1), l_2) = G(gamma_1, l_3) for a unique l_3, are ellipses the only closed convex curves that satisfy this transitivity property?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\gamma\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ be a smooth closed convex curve with perimeter $|\gamma|$. For each real number $\ell>|\gamma|$, the string (gardener's) construction associates to $\gamma$ a closed convex curve $G(\gamma,\ell)$ defined as follows: wrap a closed inextensible loop of length $\ell$ around $\gamma$, pull it taut at a point $P$ outside $\gamma$, and let $P$ trace out a curve as it moves around $\gamma$ keeping the loop taut. The resulting locus is $G(\gamma,\ell)$; it is a closed convex curve containing $\gamma$ in its interior, and $\gamma$ is a caustic of the billiard inside $G(\gamma,\ell)$.

When $\gamma$ is an ellipse, the integrability of the billiard inside an ellipse implies the following transitivity property: for any $\ell_1>|\gamma|$ and any $\ell_2>|G(\gamma,\ell_1)|$, there exists a unique $\ell_3>|\gamma|$ such that
$$G igl(G(\gamma,\ell_1),\,\ell_2 igr)=G(\gamma,\ell_3).$$

Problem. Prove or disprove: ellipses are the only smooth closed convex curves $\gamma$ for which this transitivity property of the string construction holds.
status_search_result: The transitivity (nesting) property of the string construction is known to hold for ellipses by integrability of elliptic billiards, and Poritsky (1950) showed ellipses are the only curves with the related "string property" / Poritsky property in the plane. However, the specific characterization stated as Problem 1b — that ellipses are the only closed convex curves for which the string construction is transitive in this two-step sense — does not appear to have been resolved; recent work on curves with the Poritsky property (e.g., Glutsyuk 2022) addresses related rigidity questions but does not settle this exact problem. Status appears open.

paper_title: Banach spaces and Ramsey Theory: some open problems
original_question: Does there exist a non-separable Tsirelson-like Banach space, that is, a non-separable analogue of the classical Tsirelson construction based on a suitable non-separable analogue of the Schreier family?
self_contained_problem:
The classical Tsirelson space $T$ is constructed as follows. Let $(e_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be the unit-vector basis of $c_{00}(\mathbb{N})$. The Schreier family is
$$\mathcal{S} = \{F\subseteq\mathbb{N} : F \text{ is finite and } |F|\le \min F\}\cup\{\emptyset\}.$$
Two finite subsets $E,F\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ are admissible if $E<F$ (i.e.\ $\max E<\min F$); a sequence $E_1<E_2<\cdots<E_k$ of finite subsets is admissible if there exists $F=\{n_1<\cdots<n_k\}\in\mathcal{S}$ with $n_i\le \min E_i$ for all $i$. The norm $\|\cdot\|_T$ on $c_{00}(\mathbb{N})$ is the unique norm satisfying the implicit equation
$$\|x\| = \max\Bigl(\|x\|_\infty,\; \tfrac{1}{2}\sup\sum_{i=1}^k \|E_ix\|\Bigr),$$
where the sup is over all admissible sequences $E_1<\cdots<E_k$, and $T$ is the completion of $(c_{00}(\mathbb{N}),\|\cdot\|_T)$. The space $T$ is reflexive and contains no isomorphic copy of any $\ell_p$ ($1\le p<\infty$) or $c_0$.

Question. Does there exist a non-separable Banach space $X$ produced by an analogous construction—based on a non-separable analogue of the Schreier family $\mathcal{S}$ defined on an uncountable index set $\Gamma$, together with a corresponding admissibility relation on finite subsets of $\Gamma$—such that $X$ is non-separable, has a long (uncountable) Schauder-type basis $(e_\gamma)_{\gamma\in\Gamma}$, and shares the essential structural feature of the Tsirelson space that no subspace is isomorphic to $c_0$ or to any $\ell_p$ for $1\le p<\infty$?
status_search_result: Subsequent work by C. Brech, J. Lopez-Abad and S. Todorcevic developed non-separable analogues of the Schreier family on uncountable index sets (below the first Mahlo cardinal) using tree-based combinatorial methods, enabling Tsirelson-like constructions in the non-separable setting. This was advertised in tutorials such as Brech's at Winter School 2017 and used in related constructions (e.g., a non-separable Banach space without a subsymmetric basic sequence by Lopez-Abad and Todorcevic). The problem appears to have been at least partially answered affirmatively, although a fully canonical "non-separable Tsirelson space" with all of the classical properties is not unambiguously fixed in the literature.

original_question: Construct a strictly convex C^1-smooth billiard table with positive entropy, and also construct a convex C^2-smooth billiard table with positive entropy.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a bounded planar domain whose boundary $\partial\Omega$ is a simple closed curve. The billiard flow inside $\Omega$ is defined by the free motion of a point particle that reflects elastically (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection) at $\partial\Omega$. The associated billiard map $T$ acts on the set of unit inward-pointing tangent vectors based on $\partial\Omega$, sending an outgoing reflection to the next reflection. The metric (Kolmogorov–Sinai) entropy $h_\mu(T)$ is defined with respect to the natural invariant measure $d\mu = \sin\varphi\, d\varphi\, ds$, where $s$ is arclength on $\partial\Omega$ and $\varphi \in (0,\pi)$ is the angle of reflection.

Recall: $\Omega$ is called convex if it equals the intersection of a family of half-planes; it is called strictly convex if its boundary contains no line segment. The boundary regularity refers to the regularity of an arclength parametrization of $\partial\Omega$.

(a) Construct a strictly convex billiard table $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ with $C^1$-smooth boundary such that the billiard map $T$ has positive metric entropy.

(b) Construct a convex billiard table $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ with $C^2$-smooth boundary such that the billiard map $T$ has positive metric entropy.
status_search_result: Part (b), in the topological entropy sense, has been substantially advanced: it has been shown that there is a $C^2$-open and dense set of smooth strictly convex bodies whose billiard maps possess a nontrivial hyperbolic basic set, and consequently positive topological entropy. This provides the existence of $C^2$ (in fact $C^\infty$) strictly convex examples with positive topological entropy, although explicit constructions and the metric-entropy version remain less clear. Part (a), constructing a strictly convex $C^1$-smooth example with positive entropy, does not appear to have been resolved in the literature found.

paper_title: Banach spaces and Ramsey Theory: some open problems
original_question: Is there a compact hereditary family F of finite subsets of ω_1 that contains every singleton and has the property that every finite subset of ω_1 contains a member of F of at least half its size?
self_contained_problem:
A family F of finite subsets of ω₁ is called:
• hereditary if A ∈ F and B ⊆ A imply B ∈ F;
• compact if, identifying each finite set with its characteristic function in {0,1}^{ω₁}, the set F is closed in the product topology of {0,1}^{ω₁}.

Question: Does there exist a compact hereditary family F of finite subsets of ω₁ such that
(i) every singleton {α} (α < ω₁) belongs to F, and
(ii) for every finite subset s ⊆ ω₁ there exists t ∈ F with t ⊆ s and |t| ≥ |s|/2?
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not turn up a published resolution of this question. It is listed as an open problem attributed to D. H. Fremlin in surveys on Banach spaces and Ramsey theory, and no solution (positive or negative) was located in the available sources.

original_question: Let Phi be the phase space of a piecewise smooth billiard table Y, let P be the set of periodic points in Phi, and let P_n be the set of periodic points of period n. Is it always true that mu(P) = 0, equivalently that mu(P_n) = 0 for every n >= 2?
self_contained_problem:
Let $Y \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a piecewise smooth billiard table, i.e. a domain whose boundary is a finite union of smooth hypersurfaces meeting transversally, in which a point particle moves along straight lines and reflects elastically (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection) upon hitting the smooth part of the boundary. Let $\Phi$ denote the phase space of the associated billiard map, consisting of unit vectors based at boundary points and pointing inward, equipped with the canonical invariant Liouville measure $\mu$ (normalized to be finite). For an integer $n \geq 2$, let $P_n \subset \Phi$ be the set of periodic points of period $n$ for the billiard map, and let
$$P = \bigsqcup_{n=2}^{\infty} P_n$$
be the set of all periodic points. Note that $\mu(P) = \sum_{n=2}^{\infty} \mu(P_n)$, so $\mu(P) = 0$ if and only if $\mu(P_n) = 0$ for every $n \geq 2$.

Prove or disprove:
(i) $\mu(P) = 0$;
(ii) $\mu(P_n) = 0$ for every integer $n \geq 2$.
status_search_result: Ivrii's conjecture (1978) remains open in general for smooth/piecewise smooth billiards. It is established in several special cases: real-analytic convex boundaries, period-3 (triangular) orbits for piecewise smooth planar billiards, and period-4 (quadrilateral) orbits for planar billiards with piecewise C^4 boundary (Glutsyuk–Kudryashov). Recent work has proven the conjecture for generic complex algebraic billiards of degree d ≥ 2 for all periods, and in some cases for outer and symplectic billiards. Counterexamples exist in the broader class of projective billiards. The general non-analytic case remains unresolved.
