original_question: Let the width of a group(respectively, a monoid) H with respect to a generating set X mean the supremum over h ∈ H of the least length of a group word(respectively, a monoid word) in elements of X expressing h. A group(or monoid) is said to have finite width if its width with respect to every generating set is finite. (A common finite bound for these widths is not required.) Do there exist groups G having finite width as groups, but not as monoids? This is Question 9 in(G. M. Bergman, Bull. London Math. Soc., 38(2006), 429–440).
self_contained_problem:
For an algebraic structure H (a group or a monoid) and a subset X of H that generates H (as a group or as a monoid, respectively), define the width of H with respect to X to be

  w(H,X) = sup_{h ∈ H} min{ ℓ : h can be expressed as a word of length ℓ in elements of X },

where, in the group case, words are group words (allowing inverses of elements of X) and, in the monoid case, words are monoid words (no inverses, only products of elements of X). Note that w(H,X) ∈ {0,1,2,…} ∪ {∞}.

Say that H has finite width as a group (respectively, as a monoid) if for every subset X ⊆ H that generates H as a group (respectively, as a monoid), the width w(H,X) is finite. (No common finite upper bound on these widths over all generating sets X is required.)

Question: Does there exist a group G that has finite width as a group but does not have finite width as a monoid? Equivalently, does there exist a group G such that, for every generating set X of G as a group, every element of G is a group word of bounded length in X, yet there exists a monoid generating set Y of G for which the lengths of shortest monoid words in Y representing elements of G are unbounded?
status_search_result: The problem is Question 9 of Bergman's 2006 paper on generating infinite symmetric groups, restated in the 2026 Kourovka Notebook as a new problem. No published resolution was located in the search; the question appears to remain open.

paper_title: Some open questions in TDDFT: Clues from Lattice Models and Kadanoff-Baym Dynamics
context_brief: Rigorous density mapping for lattice TDDFT
original_question: Can density-based TDDFT on a lattice be given a fully rigorous Runge-Gross-type foundation, or otherwise characterized well enough to know when the density-potential mapping is unique and when heuristic use of lattice TDDFT is reliable? The problem is specific to lattice Hamiltonians because the usual reductio-ad-absurdum proof fails, examples contradict uniqueness of the correspondence between densities and potentials, and known v0-representability conditions are complete only in limited cases such as one particle on a one-dimensional lattice or special Hubbard dimers.
self_contained_problem:
Setting. Let $\Lambda$ be a finite connected lattice (e.g., a one-dimensional chain with $L$ sites) and consider $N$ interacting fermions on $\Lambda$ described by a Hamiltonian of the form
$$H(t)=\sum_{i,j\in\Lambda} T_{ij}\,c_i^\dagger c_j+\sum_{i\in\Lambda} v_i(t)\,n_i+W,$$
where $T_{ij}$ is a fixed (possibly complex) hopping matrix, $n_i=c_i^\dagger c_i$, $W$ is a fixed two-body interaction (e.g. Hubbard $U\sum_i n_{i\uparrow}n_{i\downarrow}$), and $v(t)=\{v_i(t)\}_{i\in\Lambda}$ is a time-dependent on-site scalar potential. Given an initial state $|\Psi_0\rangle$, the time evolution $i\partial_t|\Psi(t)\rangle=H(t)|\Psi(t)\rangle$ produces site-occupation densities $n_i(t)=\langle\Psi(t)|n_i|\Psi(t)\rangle$.

Definitions. A density trajectory $\{n_i(t)\}$ is called $v_0$-representable (with respect to $|\Psi_0\rangle$) if there exists a real on-site potential $v(t)$ such that the evolution under $H(t)$ starting from $|\Psi_0\rangle$ reproduces $n_i(t)$. Define the partial sums $S_k(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\dot n_i(t)$ (current conservation).

Known facts to be subsumed. (i) For $N=1$ on a one-dimensional lattice, $|S_k(t)|\le 2\sqrt{n_k(t)\,n_{k+1}(t)}$ for all $k$ and $t$ is necessary and sufficient for $v_0$-representability. (ii) For $N>1$ this inequality is only necessary. (iii) For the Hubbard dimer the exact density is $v_0$-representable. (iv) Explicit examples on lattices show that, in general, the map $v\mapsto n$ need not be injective.

Problem. Formulate and prove a rigorous Runge–Gross-type theorem for density-based time-dependent density functional theory on lattices: give necessary and sufficient conditions on the initial state $|\Psi_0\rangle$, the hopping $T_{ij}$, the interaction $W$, and the density trajectory $\{n_i(t)\}$ under which (a) the density trajectory is $v_0$-representable, and (b) the potential $v(t)$ that produces it from $|\Psi_0\rangle$ is unique up to a spatially constant gauge. Equivalently, characterize precisely the class of lattice Hamiltonians, initial states, and densities for which the density-to-potential mapping is well-defined and one-to-one.
status_search_result: Subsequent work has established rigorous lattice TDDFT formulations with sufficient conditions for v-representability and uniqueness (e.g., Farzanehpour & Tokatly: "Time-dependent density functional theory on a lattice" and follow-ups), showing existence/uniqueness for densities evolving from a ground state on connected lattices under regularity conditions. However, complete necessary-and-sufficient v0-representability conditions for general $N>1$ with interactions remain only partially known, and pathological non-uniqueness examples persist, so a full Runge–Gross analogue on the lattice is not fully resolved.

paper_title: Some open questions in TDDFT: Clues from Lattice Models and Kadanoff-Baym Dynamics
original_question: What are the physical regimes and corrective principles for Kadanoff-Baym dynamics combined with many-body perturbation theory when conserving approximations still show fundamental failures, such as breakdown at strong interaction, artificial correlation-induced damping, questionable steady states in extended systems, and violations of positivity in two-particle correlation functions? The setting is the nonequilibrium Green's-function approach, where the Kadanoff-Baym equations use a self-energy from approximations such as second Born, GW, or T-matrix, which conserve macroscopic quantities but do not guarantee all physically required properties.
status_search_result: The question concerns long-standing open issues in NEGF/Kadanoff–Baym dynamics with conserving many-body approximations. Subsequent literature (Stefanucci–van Leeuwen and collaborators, work on the Generalized Kadanoff–Baym Ansatz, time-linear schemes, and positivity-preserving approximations) has clarified some aspects—e.g. artificial damping is now broadly attributed to self-consistency in Φ-derivable schemes, and partial fixes (HF-GKBA, T-matrix improvements) exist—but a complete principled resolution covering strong coupling, steady-state physicality, and positivity remains unresolved. Status is best described as open / partially understood.

original_question: Suppose that G is a finite group, and A1, A2, A3 are subsets of G such that the multiplication map A1 × A2 × A3 → G is bijective. Must the subgroup ⟨A2 ⟩ generated by A2 have order divisible by the cardinality |A2 |? This is Question 8 in(G. M. Bergman, J. Iranian Math. Soc., 1(2020), 157–161). It is known(ibid.) that the corresponding statement is true for the subgroups ⟨A1 ⟩ and ⟨A3 ⟩. Moreover, |A2 | will at least divide the order of the least subgroup containing A2 and closed under conjugation by members of A1, and similarly of the least subgroup containing A2 and closed under conjugation by members of A3.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite group, and let $A_1, A_2, A_3$ be subsets of $G$ such that the multiplication map
$$A_1 \times A_2 \times A_3 \to G,\qquad (a_1,a_2,a_3)\mapsto a_1 a_2 a_3,$$
is a bijection (so in particular $|A_1|\,|A_2|\,|A_3| = |G|$). Let $\langle A_2\rangle$ denote the subgroup of $G$ generated by $A_2$.

Must $|A_2|$ divide $|\langle A_2\rangle|$?

(It is known that the analogous statement holds for $\langle A_1\rangle$ and for $\langle A_3\rangle$, and that $|A_2|$ divides the order of the smallest subgroup of $G$ that contains $A_2$ and is closed under conjugation by all elements of $A_1$, and similarly with $A_1$ replaced by $A_3$. The question is whether closure under conjugation can be removed for the middle factor.)

original_question: Suppose that S and M are groups of finite Morley rank, S is an infinite group, and M is a non-trivial connected group definably and faithfully acting on S. This action is said to be irreducible if M does not leave invariant any definable non-trivial proper subgroup of S. Prove that if S is a simple group such that every proper definable subgroup of S is nilpotent, and the action of M on S is irreducible, then this action is equivalent to the action of S on itself by conjugation.
self_contained_problem:
Work in the category of groups of finite Morley rank (i.e., groups whose first-order theory has finite Morley rank), and let "definable" mean definable in the pure group language with parameters.

Let $S$ be an infinite group of finite Morley rank, and let $M$ be a non-trivial connected group of finite Morley rank. Suppose $M$ acts on $S$ definably and faithfully (so the action $M\times S\to S$ is a definable group action and the kernel of $M\to \mathrm{Aut}(S)$ is trivial). Call this action irreducible if there is no definable subgroup $N$ of $S$ with $1\neq N\neq S$ that is invariant under the action of $M$.

Two definable faithful actions of connected groups $M_1,M_2$ on $S$ are called equivalent if there exists a definable group isomorphism $\varphi: M_1\to M_2$ and a definable group automorphism $\psi$ of $S$ such that $\psi(m\cdot s) = \varphi(m)\cdot \psi(s)$ for all $m\in M_1$, $s\in S$.

Assume in addition that:
(i) $S$ is a simple group, and
(ii) every proper definable subgroup of $S$ is nilpotent.

Prove that if the action of $M$ on $S$ is irreducible, then this action is equivalent to the action of $S$ on itself by inner automorphisms (conjugation).
status_search_result: The problem appears as a new entry in the Kourovka Notebook list of unsolved problems in group theory. It concerns simple "bad-like" groups of finite Morley rank (every proper definable subgroup nilpotent), whose existence and structure remain a longstanding open question; recent literature (e.g., results that simple groups of Morley rank 4 and 5 must be bad with all proper definable connected subgroups nilpotent) does not resolve the irreducibility/conjugation-action statement asked here. No published solution was located.

paper_title: Some open questions in TDDFT: Clues from Lattice Models and Kadanoff-Baym Dynamics
context_brief: Positive double occupancy in response approximations
original_question: How can TDDFT linear-response approximations for the Hubbard lattice be improved so that short-range correlations are treated correctly and the local double occupancy dR = <nR up nR down>, computed from the density response function, remains physically positive? In the paper's 3D homogeneous Hubbard model tests, both RPA and ALDA can produce negative double occupancies even though double occupancy is manifestly positive, showing that ALDA inherits a short-range correlation failure known from continuum electron-gas response calculations.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the 3D homogeneous single-band Hubbard model on a cubic lattice with sites $R$, on-site repulsion $U>0$, hopping $t$, and uniform average density $n$. For each site $R$ let $n_{R\sigma}=c^\dagger_{R\sigma}c_{R\sigma}$ be the number operator for spin $\sigma\in\{\uparrow,\downarrow\}$, and define the local double occupancy
$$d_R=\langle n_{R\uparrow}\,n_{R\downarrow}angle.$$
By construction $0\le d_R\le \min(\langle n_{R\uparrow}angle,\langle n_{R\downarrow}angle)$, so $d_R\ge 0$. In time-dependent density-functional theory (TDDFT) on this lattice, the density-density response function $\chi(R,R';\omega)$ in a chosen approximation (for example the random-phase approximation (RPA), which uses only the Hartree kernel, or the adiabatic local-density approximation (ALDA), which adds an exchange-correlation kernel $f_{xc}^{	ext{ALDA}}(n)=\partial^2 e_{xc}^{	ext{hom}}(n)/\partial n^2$ taken from the homogeneous reference system) determines, via the fluctuation–dissipation theorem,
$$d_R \;=\; 	frac{1}{4}\langle n_Rangle^2 \;-\;  rac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^\infty d\omega\; \mathrm{Im}\,\chi_{\sigma\sigma}(R,R;\omega) \;+\; (	ext{spin-resolved corrections}),$$
or an equivalent expression giving $d_R$ from the on-site pair correlation function built out of $\chi$.

Problem. Construct an exchange-correlation kernel $f_{xc}(R,R';\omega)$ for the lattice TDDFT linear-response equations, going beyond RPA and ALDA, with the following properties:
(i) it is computable from local/semilocal lattice quantities (or from a controlled non-adiabatic, spatially nonlocal extension thereof);
(ii) when used to compute the density response function $\chi$ of the 3D homogeneous Hubbard model, the resulting on-site double occupancy $d_R$ satisfies $d_R\ge 0$ for all densities $n\in[0,2]$ and all $U/t\ge 0$;
(iii) it correctly captures the short-range correlation behavior of the on-site pair correlation function $g(R,R)$, in particular avoiding the spurious negativity of $d_R$ produced by ALDA (which inherits the short-range failure of the continuum electron-gas ALDA response).

Either exhibit such a kernel and prove that $d_R\ge 0$ holds within the resulting approximation, or prove that no kernel of a specified class (e.g. adiabatic and local in the lattice density) can guarantee $d_R\ge 0$ uniformly in $(n,U/t)$.
category_tag: TDDFT linear response on Hubbard lattices
status_search_result: The problem of constructing an xc kernel that enforces positivity of the on-site double occupancy and correctly treats short-range correlations is identified as an open shortcoming of ALDA in lattice TDDFT, mirroring a long-standing failure of ALDA in continuum electron-gas response calculations. No general resolution appears in the literature; standard fixes (e.g. nonlocal/frequency-dependent kernels) remain partial.

paper_title: Some open questions in TDDFT: Clues from Lattice Models and Kadanoff-Baym Dynamics
original_question: How should exchange-correlation kernels for Hubbard lattice TDDFT account for qualitative features of the ALDA kernel that have no known continuum analogue, including a sign that changes with density and interaction strength, and a singularity at half filling for sufficiently large interaction U caused by the discontinuity of vxc at the Mott-Hubbard metal-insulator transition? The paper expects these features to persist when nonlocal and nonadiabatic effects are added, so a complete theory must explain how they affect density response beyond the local adiabatic limit.
self_contained_problem:
Consider lattice time-dependent density-functional theory (TDDFT) applied to the single-band Hubbard model

  H = -t ∑_{⟨i,j⟩,σ} (c†_{iσ} c_{jσ} + h.c.) + U ∑_i n_{i↑} n_{i↓} + ∑_i v_i(τ) n_i,

with site density n_i(τ) and on-site interaction U > 0. Within a Kohn–Sham mapping to a non-interacting lattice system, define the exchange-correlation (XC) potential v_xc[n] and the adiabatic local-density-approximation (ALDA) XC kernel

  f^{ALDA}_{xc}(n) = ∂ v^{hom}_{xc}(n)/∂ n,

where v^{hom}_{xc}(n) is the XC potential of the homogeneous Hubbard model at uniform density n, computed (e.g.) from Bethe-ansatz in 1D or from dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) in higher dimensions.

Two qualitative features of f^{ALDA}_{xc} are observed that have no known counterpart in continuum XC kernels:

(i) Sign change: f^{ALDA}_{xc}(n;U) changes sign as a function of band filling n ∈ (0,2) and interaction strength U.

(ii) Singularity at half filling: for sufficiently large U (specifically U > U_c^{Mott} in dimension d ≥ 2, and for all U > 0 in d = 1), v^{hom}_{xc}(n) has a discontinuity at n = 1 associated with the Mott–Hubbard metal-insulator transition, inducing a Dirac-delta–like singularity in f^{ALDA}_{xc} at n = 1.

Develop a theory of the (in general nonlocal and nonadiabatic) lattice XC kernel f_{xc}[n](i,j;ω) for the Hubbard model that:

(a) reproduces the sign-change behavior of f^{ALDA}_{xc} as a function of (n,U) in the local adiabatic limit,

(b) accounts for the half-filling singularity tied to the discontinuity of v_{xc} at the Mott transition,

(c) shows that these two qualitative features survive (in an appropriate sense to be made precise) the inclusion of nonlocality in (i,j) and frequency dependence in ω, and

(d) describes quantitatively their imprint on the interacting density response function χ(i,j;ω) of the Hubbard model beyond the ALDA.

Provide either an explicit construction of such an f_{xc} (e.g., from DMFT charge susceptibilities) together with a proof/argument that properties (a)–(c) hold and a calculation establishing (d), or else a rigorous demonstration that one of these features is artifactual and disappears when nonlocal/nonadiabatic corrections are included.
status_search_result: Subsequent work has constructed nonadiabatic XC kernels for the Hubbard model via DMFT charge susceptibilities and studied the Hubbard dimer exactly, confirming strong frequency dependence and features tied to Mott physics. However, no general theory has been established that fully characterizes how the ALDA sign change and the half-filling delta-like singularity propagate into the full nonlocal, nonadiabatic kernel and the density response. The question therefore appears still open as of the latest available literature.

original_question: Prove that a simple group of finite Morley rank without involutions cannot act definably, faithfully, and irreducibly on a connected group other than on itself acting by conjugation.
self_contained_problem:
Work in the setting of groups of finite Morley rank, i.e., infinite groups whose first‑order theory (in the language of groups, possibly enriched by definable predicates) has finite Morley rank, with all subgroups, homomorphisms, and actions considered are definable.

A group G of finite Morley rank is called connected if it has no proper definable subgroup of finite index. An action of a group H on a group N (both of finite Morley rank) is said to be:
 • definable, if the map H × N → N giving the action is definable;
 • faithful, if only the identity of H acts trivially on N;
 • irreducible, if N is connected and contains no proper non‑trivial definable connected H‑invariant subgroup.

A group G of finite Morley rank is simple if it is infinite and has no proper non‑trivial definable normal subgroup. Recall that every simple group of finite Morley rank acts on itself by conjugation, giving a definable, faithful, irreducible action of G on G.

Prove the following: Let G be a simple group of finite Morley rank that contains no involution (i.e., no element of order 2). Suppose N is a connected group of finite Morley rank, not isomorphic (as a G‑group) to G acting on itself by conjugation, and suppose G acts definably, faithfully, and irreducibly on N. Show that this is impossible; that is, no such action of G on a connected group N other than (G, conjugation) exists.

original_question: Prove that a simple(that is, without proper non-trivial connected normal subgroups) algebraic group M over an algebraically closed field cannot act definably, faithfully, and irreducibly on a simple group of finite Morley rank other than M/Z(M).
self_contained_problem: Let $M$ be a simple algebraic group over an algebraically closed field, where "simple" means that $M$ has no proper non-trivial connected normal (algebraic) subgroup. Let $Z(M)$ denote the center of $M$. Suppose $N$ is a simple group of finite Morley rank, and suppose $M$ acts on $N$ definably, faithfully, and irreducibly (i.e., the action is by definable automorphisms, the kernel is trivial, and $N$ admits no proper non-trivial $M$-invariant definable normal subgroup). Prove that such an action forces $N \cong M/Z(M)$; equivalently, prove that no such action exists when $N \not\cong M/Z(M)$.
status_search_result: The problem appears in the Kourovka Notebook as a newly posed problem. original_question: Is the(standard, restricted) wreath product G ≀ H of two finitely generated Hopfian groups Hopfian? The same question where G is assumed to be abelian or nilpotent is equivalent to Kaplansky’s direct finiteness conjecture; see(H. Bradford, F. Fournier-Facio, Math. Z., 308, no. 4(2024), Paper no. 58).
self_contained_problem:
Recall that a group $K$ is called Hopfian if every surjective homomorphism $K \to K$ is an isomorphism. Given two groups $G$ and $H$, the (standard, restricted) wreath product $G \wr H$ is the semidirect product $\big(\bigoplus_{h \in H} G\big) \rtimes H$, where $H$ acts on the direct sum $\bigoplus_{h \in H} G$ by permuting the coordinates via left multiplication on the index set.

Determine whether the following statement is true: for every pair of finitely generated Hopfian groups $G$ and $H$, the wreath product $G \wr H$ is Hopfian.
status_search_result: The question is open. Bradford and Fournier-Facio (Math. Z. 308 (2024), no. 58) showed that the special case where $G$ is abelian (equivalently nilpotent) is equivalent to Kaplansky's stable/direct finiteness conjecture, which itself remains open in general. No proof or counterexample for the full question with arbitrary finitely generated Hopfian $G,H$ is known.

original_question: A graph is called a cograph if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to a path with 4 vertices. A graph is said to be chordal if it has no induced cycles with n vertices for every n ⩾ 4. For a finite group G, the enhanced power graph E(G) is the graph with vertex set G and edges {x, y} for all x ̸= y ∈ G such that ⟨x, y⟩ is cyclic. (a) For a given integer n ⩾ 4, determine the set of all finite nonabelian simple groups G such that E(G) has no induced cycles with n vertices. (b) Determine the set of all finite nonabelian simple groups G such that E(G) is chordal. In(Preprint, 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.18073) we proved that if the enhanced power graph of a given finite group is a cograph, then it is also chordal. Also the finite nonabelian simple groups whose enhanced power graph is a cograph are described, and additional information is obtained on finite nonabelian simple groups whose enhanced power graph has no induced cycles with 4 vertices.
self_contained_problem:
For a finite group $G$, define the enhanced power graph $\mathcal{E}(G)$ as the simple graph with vertex set $G$ in which two distinct elements $x, y \in G$ are adjacent if and only if the subgroup $\langle x, y \rangle$ is cyclic. A simple graph is called chordal if it contains no induced cycle on $n$ vertices for any $n \geq 4$.

(a) For each fixed integer $n \geq 4$, determine the set of all finite nonabelian simple groups $G$ such that $\mathcal{E}(G)$ has no induced cycle on $n$ vertices.

(b) Determine the set of all finite nonabelian simple groups $G$ such that $\mathcal{E}(G)$ is chordal.
category_tag: Enhanced power graphs of finite groups
status_search_result: The problem is posed as a new problem in the 2026 Kourovka Notebook. A 2025 preprint by the same proposers classifies finite nonabelian simple groups whose enhanced power graph is a cograph and shows the cograph property implies chordality, but the full classifications requested in (a) and (b) remain open.

original_question: For a finite group G, the power graph P(G) is the graph with vertex set G and edges {x, y} for all x ̸= y ∈ G such that either x ∈ ⟨y⟩ or y ∈ ⟨x⟩. Is it true that, for every finite group G, if P(G) is a cograph, then P(G) is chordal? Cf. 21.23. This holds if every element of G has prime power order(D. Bubboloni, F. Fumagalli, C. E. Praeger, Preprint, 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.18073) and if G is a nonabelian simple group(J. Cameron, P. Manna, R. Mehatari, J. Algebra, 591(2022), 59–74; J. Brachter, E. Kaja, J. Algebr. Comb., 58(2023), 1095–1124).
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite group. The power graph $P(G)$ is the simple graph with vertex set $G$ in which two distinct vertices $x$ and $y$ are adjacent if and only if $x \in \langle y \rangle$ or $y \in \langle x \rangle$ (that is, one is a power of the other in $G$).

A simple graph $\Gamma$ is called a cograph if it contains no induced path on four vertices ($P_4$-free). It is called chordal if it contains no induced cycle of length $\ge 4$.

Prove or disprove: for every finite group $G$, if $P(G)$ is a cograph, then $P(G)$ is chordal.

Algebra 591 (2022); Brachter–Kaja, J. Algebraic Combin. 58 (2023)). The general conjecture for arbitrary finite groups appears to remain open.

original_question: (T. Breuer, R. M. Guralnick). Let G be a finite simple group and let p1, p2 be any(not necessarily distinct) prime divisors of |G|. Then can we always find Sylow pi-subgroups Hi such that G = ⟨H1, H2 ⟩?
self_contained_problem: Let $G$ be a finite non-abelian simple group, and let $p_1, p_2$ be (not necessarily distinct) prime divisors of $|G|$. Determine whether there always exist a Sylow $p_1$-subgroup $H_1$ and a Sylow $p_2$-subgroup $H_2$ of $G$ such that $G = \langle H_1, H_2 \rangle$.
category_tag: Generation of finite simple groups by Sylow subgroups
status_search_result: The conjecture has been confirmed in significant special cases: Breuer and Guralnick (and subsequent work) established that every finite non-abelian simple group $G$ is generated by a Sylow 2-subgroup together with a Sylow $r$-subgroup for any prime $r$ dividing $|G|$, and the statement is known for alternating and sporadic groups. The full statement for arbitrary pairs of (odd) primes $p_1, p_2$ remains a conjecture and is not settled in general.

original_question: (F. Lisi, L. Sabatini). Let G be a non-trivial finite group and let p1,..., pk be the distinct prime divisors of |G|. For each i, let Hi be a Sylow pi-subgroup of G. Is it true that there exists an element x ∈ G such that for all i the subgroup Hi ∩ Hix is inclusion-minimal in {Hi ∩ Hig: g ∈ G}?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a non-trivial finite group, and let $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_k$ be the distinct prime divisors of $|G|$. For each $i \in \{1,\dots,k\}$, fix a Sylow $p_i$-subgroup $H_i$ of $G$. For $g \in G$, write $H_i^g = g^{-1} H_i g$. Consider, for each $i$, the family of subgroups
$$\mathcal{F}_i = \{\, H_i \cap H_i^g : g \in G \,\},$$
partially ordered by inclusion; call a member of $\mathcal{F}_i$ inclusion-minimal if it does not properly contain any other member of $\mathcal{F}_i$.

Determine whether there always exists a single element $x \in G$ such that, simultaneously for every $i \in \{1,\dots,k\}$, the subgroup $H_i \cap H_i^x$ is inclusion-minimal in $\mathcal{F}_i$.
category_tag: Sylow subgroup intersections in finite groups
status_search_result: The Lisi–Sabatini conjecture has been verified in several classes: metanilpotent groups of odd order, sufficiently large symmetric and alternating groups, and (in a 2025 preprint using a probabilistic approach) all non-alternating finite simple groups. A complete resolution for arbitrary finite groups does not appear to have been established, so the problem is partially solved.

original_question: (M. Larsen, A. Shalev, P. H. Tiep). A permutation on a set Ω is called a derangement if it has no fixed points in Ω. Let G be a finite simple transitive permutation group. Is it true that every element in G is the product of two derangements?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite simple group acting transitively and faithfully on a set $\Omega$ with $|\Omega| \geq 2$. An element $g \in G$ is called a derangement (with respect to this action) if it has no fixed points on $\Omega$, i.e., $g \cdot \omega \neq \omega$ for every $\omega \in \Omega$. Let $\Delta(G) \subseteq G$ denote the set of all derangements in $G$ for the given action.

Determine whether every element of $G$ can be written as a product of two derangements; equivalently, decide whether
$$G = \Delta(G) \cdot \Delta(G) = \{xy : x,y \in \Delta(G)\}$$
holds for every finite simple transitive permutation group $G$.
category_tag: Derangements in finite simple permutation groups
status_search_result: Larsen, Shalev, and Tiep proved that for sufficiently large finite simple transitive permutation groups $G$, one has $G = \Delta(G)^2$, and the result holds for all alternating groups $A_n$ ($n \geq 5$). Subsequent work (e.g., Burness–Fawcett, 2024, arXiv:2409.01043) establishes the property for further classes (such as finite simple primitive groups with soluble point stabilisers) and shows generation by two conjugate derangements, but the full conjecture for all finite simple transitive groups remains open.

original_question: Let G be a finite simple transitive permutation group, and let δ(G) be the proportion of derangements in G. Is it true that δ(G) ⩾ 89/325? Note that δ(G) = 89/325 for the action of the Tits group G = 2 F4(2)′ on the cosets of a maximal parabolic subgroup of the form 22.[28 ].S3(Forum Math. Sigma, 13(2025), paper no. e98, 62 pp.).
self_contained_problem:
A permutation group $G$ acting on a finite set $\Omega$ is called transitive if for all $\alpha,\beta\in\Omega$ there exists $g\in G$ with $g\cdot\alpha=\beta$. An element $g\in G$ is a derangement (with respect to the action on $\Omega$) if it fixes no point of $\Omega$, that is, $g\cdot\alpha\neq\alpha$ for every $\alpha\in\Omega$. Define
$$\delta(G)\;=\;\frac{|\{g\in G : g\text{ is a derangement}\}|}{|G|},$$
the proportion of derangements in $G$.

It is known that for the Tits group $G={}^2F_4(2)'$ acting on the cosets of a maximal parabolic subgroup of structure $2^2.[2^8].S_3$, one has $\delta(G)=89/325$.

Prove or disprove: for every finite simple group $G$ realised as a transitive permutation group on a finite set,
$$\delta(G)\;\geq\;\frac{89}{325}.$$
category_tag: Derangements in finite simple permutation groups
status_search_result: A 2024/2025 paper (Forum Math. Sigma 13 (2025), paper e98) establishes the bound δ(G) ≥ 89/325 for all finite simple primitive groups with soluble point stabilisers, and shows the bound is tight (attained by the Tits group action on cosets of a maximal parabolic 2².[2^8].S₃). The general conjecture for all finite simple transitive permutation groups (without the solubility-of-stabiliser hypothesis) remains open.

original_question: Let G ⩽ Sym(Ω) be a finite primitive permutation group with a regular suborbit(that is, G has a trivial 2-point stabiliser). Then is it true that for all α, β ∈ Ω, there exists γ ∈ Ω such that the 2-point stabilisers Gα,γ and Gβ,γ are both trivial?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega$ be a finite set and let $G \leq \mathrm{Sym}(\Omega)$ be a primitive permutation group on $\Omega$. For points $\alpha, \beta \in \Omega$, write $G_\alpha = \{g \in G : \alpha^g = \alpha\}$ for the point stabiliser of $\alpha$, and $G_{\alpha,\beta} = G_\alpha \cap G_\beta$ for the 2-point stabiliser. A suborbit of $G$ is an orbit of a point stabiliser $G_\alpha$ on $\Omega$; such a suborbit is called regular if it has size $|G_\alpha|$, equivalently if there exist points $\alpha, \delta \in \Omega$ with $G_{\alpha,\delta} = 1$.

Suppose that $G$ has a regular suborbit. Determine whether the following statement is necessarily true: for all $\alpha, \beta \in \Omega$, there exists $\gamma \in \Omega$ such that both 2-point stabilisers $G_{\alpha,\gamma}$ and $G_{\beta,\gamma}$ are trivial.

original_question: (Well-known question). A discrete group G is said to have the Haagerup property(also known as Gromov’s a-T-menability property) if there exists a metrically proper isometric action of G on a(possibly infinite-dimensional) Hilbert space. Are all 1-relator groups Haagerup groups?
self_contained_problem:
A discrete group $G$ is said to have the Haagerup property (equivalently, Gromov's a-T-menability) if there exists a metrically proper isometric action of $G$ on a (possibly infinite-dimensional) real Hilbert space; equivalently, $G$ admits a proper conditionally negative-definite function. A 1-relator group is a group admitting a presentation $\langle x_1, \dots, x_n \mid r \rangle$ with a single defining relator $r$, a word in the free group on the generators.

Question: Does every 1-relator group have the Haagerup property?
status_search_result: The question of whether all 1-relator groups have the Haagerup property is a well-known open problem in geometric group theory. Standard references on the Haagerup property and recent work on its stability under various constructions (graph products, free/amalgamated products over finite subgroups) do not settle the case of arbitrary 1-relator groups, and no proof or counterexample appears in the literature found.

original_question: Conjecture: If N is a finite soluble group, then any regular subgroup in the holomorph Hol(N) of N is also soluble.
self_contained_problem:
Let $N$ be a finite group, and let $\mathrm{Hol}(N) = N \rtimes \mathrm{Aut}(N)$ denote its holomorph, viewed as a permutation group acting on the set $N$ via the regular action of $N$ together with the natural action of $\mathrm{Aut}(N)$. A subgroup $G \le \mathrm{Hol}(N)$ is called regular if it acts regularly on $N$ (transitively and with trivial point stabilisers); equivalently, $|G| = |N|$ and $G$ acts transitively on $N$.

Prove or disprove: if $N$ is a finite soluble group, then every regular subgroup $G$ of $\mathrm{Hol}(N)$ is soluble.
category_tag: Holomorphs of finite groups / regular subgroups
status_search_result: Recent work (2019–2023) investigates this conjecture in the context of Hopf–Galois theory and skew braces. Partial results classify possible insoluble transitive subgroups with soluble point stabilisers in Hol(N) for N finite soluble, showing strong constraints (composition factors isomorphic to PSL(2,7) of order 168, etc.), but no full proof or counterexample has appeared. The conjecture remains open.

original_question: Is the following problem decidable, and if so, what is its complexity? Given a finite group G, is there a finite group H such that the derived subgroup of H is isomorphic to G?
self_contained_problem:
A finite group $G$ is called a commutator group if there exists a finite group $H$ such that the derived subgroup $[H,H]$ is isomorphic to $G$. Consider the decision problem: given a finite group $G$ (specified, for instance, by its multiplication table), determine whether $G$ is isomorphic to the derived subgroup of some finite group $H$.

(a) Is this decision problem decidable?

(b) If it is decidable, what is its computational complexity?

original_question: Does an analogue of Dunwoody’s theorem hold for totally disconnected locally compact groups, that is, must a tdlc group of rational discrete cohomological dimension at most 1 be topologically isomorphic to the fundamental group of a graph of profinite groups?
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a totally disconnected locally compact (tdlc) topological group. Following the rational discrete cohomology theory of tdlc groups, define the rational discrete cohomological dimension cd_Q(G) to be the projective dimension of the trivial rational discrete G-module Q in the abelian category of rational discrete G-modules (i.e., Q-vector space G-modules whose stabilizers of every vector are open subgroups). A graph of profinite groups is a graph of groups in the sense of Bass–Serre theory whose vertex and edge groups are profinite groups and whose edge inclusions are continuous open embeddings; its fundamental group carries a natural tdlc topology making vertex groups open and compact.

Question: Must every tdlc group G with cd_Q(G) ≤ 1 be topologically isomorphic to the fundamental group of a graph of profinite groups?

(This is a topological-group analogue of Dunwoody's theorem, which asserts that a discrete group of cohomological dimension at most 1 over a ring R is the fundamental group of a graph of groups with finite vertex stabilizers of orders invertible in R.)
status_search_result: A 2022 work by Castellano, Marchionna, and Weigel establishes the conclusion under additional hypotheses: every compactly generated, unimodular (or 𝒞𝒪-bounded) tdlc group of rational discrete cohomological dimension at most 1 is topologically isomorphic to the fundamental group of a finite graph of profinite groups, and the class of fundamental groups of finite graphs of profinite groups coincides with the class of compactly presented tdlc groups of rational discrete cohomological dimension at most 1. The full question without compact generation/unimodularity assumptions does not appear to be settled.

original_question: (Well-known problem). A group G is a unique product group if, for any nonempty finite subsets A, B of G, there exists an element of G which can be written uniquely as ab with a ∈ A and b ∈ B. A group G is locally invariant orderable if G admits a partial order < such that for all g, h ∈ G with h ̸= 1, we have either gh > g or gh−1 > g. Does there exist a unique product group which is not locally invariant orderable?
self_contained_problem:
Definitions. Let $G$ be a group with identity element $1$.

(i) $G$ is called a *unique product group* if for every pair of nonempty finite subsets $A, B \subseteq G$, there exists at least one element $x \in G$ that has a unique representation in the form $x = ab$ with $a \in A$ and $b \in B$.

(ii) $G$ is called *locally invariant orderable* if there exists a strict partial order $<$ on $G$ such that for every $g \in G$ and every $h \in G \setminus \{1\}$, at least one of the inequalities $gh > g$ or $gh^{-1} > g$ holds.

Question. Does there exist a group $G$ that is a unique product group but is not locally invariant orderable?

original_question: Let G be a finite group, w a multilinear commutator group-word, and p a prime. Suppose that p divides the order |xy| whenever x is a w-value of p′-order in G and y is a w-value in G of order divisible by p. Is it true that then the verbal subgroup w(G) must be p-nilpotent? Without the assumption that w be multilinear, the answer is negative. An affirmative answer has been obtained in several special cases(J. Algebra, 609(2022), 926–936). Y. Contreras Rojas,
self_contained_problem:
A group-word $w = w(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ is called a multilinear commutator word (or outer commutator word) if it is obtained from the variables $x_1, \dots, x_n$ (each occurring exactly once) by nested commutators; for example, $w = [x_1, x_2]$, $w = [[x_1,x_2],[x_3,x_4]]$, and the lower-central and derived words are of this form. For a group $G$, a $w$-value in $G$ is an element of the form $w(g_1,\dots,g_n)^{\pm 1}$ with $g_i \in G$, and the verbal subgroup $w(G)$ is the subgroup generated by all $w$-values. For a prime $p$, an element has $p'$-order if its order is finite and coprime to $p$; a finite group $H$ is $p$-nilpotent if it has a normal Hall $p'$-subgroup.

Let $G$ be a finite group, let $w$ be a multilinear commutator word, and let $p$ be a prime. Suppose that for every $w$-value $x \in G$ of $p'$-order and every $w$-value $y \in G$ whose order is divisible by $p$, the order $|xy|$ is divisible by $p$. Must the verbal subgroup $w(G)$ be $p$-nilpotent?
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem in the Kourovka Notebook collection. Algebra 609 (2022), 926–936, and arXiv:2105.14474). No general resolution covering all multilinear commutator words appears in the literature, so the problem is partially solved.

original_question: Kropholler’s hierarchy(see 15.45) is closed under finite extensions, that is, (Hα F)F ⊆ Hα F for every α (P. Kropholler, J. Pure Appl. Algebra, 90(1993), 55–67). Let a hierarchy of tdlc groups HK be defined analogously to Kropholler’s hierarchy in 15.45, with K being the class of profinite groups and with the cell stabilisers of the admissible action required to be open. Is it true that HK is closed under profinite extensions, that is, (Hα K)K ⊆ Hα K for every α?
self_contained_problem:
Kropholler's hierarchy of discrete groups is defined as follows. Let F denote the class of finite groups. Set H_0 F = F. For an ordinal α > 0, define H_α F to be the class of all groups G that admit a cellular admissible action on a finite-dimensional contractible CW-complex such that every cell stabiliser belongs to ⋃_{β<α} H_β F (an action is admissible if the setwise stabiliser of any cell fixes that cell pointwise). Set HF = ⋃_α H_α F. For a class X of groups and a class Y of groups, write XY for the class of groups G having a normal subgroup N ∈ X with G/N ∈ Y. It is a theorem of Kropholler that HF is closed under finite extensions in the strong sense that (H_α F)F ⊆ H_α F for every ordinal α.

Now let K denote the class of profinite groups, and define an analogous hierarchy in the category of totally disconnected locally compact (tdlc) groups: set H_0 K = K, and for α > 0 let H_α K be the class of tdlc groups G admitting a cellular admissible action on a finite-dimensional contractible CW-complex in which every cell stabiliser is open in G and belongs to ⋃_{β<α} H_β K.

Question: Is it true that for every ordinal α one has (H_α K) K ⊆ H_α K, i.e., that H_α K is closed under extensions by profinite groups?

original_question: By definition, a constructible totally disconnected, locally compact(tdlc) group is the result of a sequence of profinite extensions and ascending HNN-extensions starting from the trivial group. As in the discrete case, soluble constructible tdlc groups have type F P∞ (G. C. Cook, I. Castellano, J. Algebra, 543(2020), 54–97). Are soluble tdlc groups of type F P∞ constructible?
self_contained_problem:
A topological group $G$ is called totally disconnected, locally compact (tdlc) if it is Hausdorff, locally compact, and its connected component of the identity is trivial. Define the class of constructible tdlc groups to be the smallest class $\mathcal{C}$ of tdlc groups such that:
(i) the trivial group lies in $\mathcal{C}$;
(ii) if $N$ is a compact open normal subgroup of a tdlc group $G$ and $G/N \in \mathcal{C}$, then $G \in \mathcal{C}$ (closure under profinite extensions);
(iii) $\mathcal{C}$ is closed under ascending HNN-extensions of tdlc groups (i.e. if $H \in \mathcal{C}$ and $\varphi : H \to H$ is a continuous, injective, open endomorphism with image a compact open subgroup, then the resulting ascending HNN-extension lies in $\mathcal{C}$).

A tdlc group $G$ is said to be of type $FP_\infty$ (in the rational discrete module category over $G$) if the trivial rational discrete $G$-module $\mathbb{Q}$ admits a resolution by finitely generated projective rational discrete $G$-modules.

A tdlc group $G$ is called soluble if it admits a finite descending series of closed normal subgroups
$$G = G_0 \trianglerighteq G_1 \trianglerighteq \cdots \trianglerighteq G_n = \{1\}$$
with each successive quotient $G_i/G_{i+1}$ abelian.

It is known that every soluble constructible tdlc group is of type $FP_\infty$.

Question: Is every soluble tdlc group of type $FP_\infty$ constructible?
status_search_result: The question is posed as a recent problem in the area of homological finiteness conditions for tdlc groups, building on work of Castellano and Corob Cook establishing one direction (constructible soluble tdlc groups are $FP_\infty$). Recent surveys and workshop reports on homological aspects of tdlc groups discuss the analogue of the Baumslag–Bieri–Strebel program but do not record a converse for general soluble tdlc groups, so the converse appears to remain open.

original_question: (S. Harper, C. Donoven). The spread of a group G is the greatest nonnegative integer k such that for all nontrivial elements x1,..., xk ∈ G there exists y ∈ G such that ⟨x1, y⟩ = · · · = ⟨xk, y⟩ = G, or is ∞ in case there is no such maximum. Does there exist a group with spread equal to 1? Such a group must be infinite if it exists(T. C. Burness, R. M. Guralnick, S. Harper, Ann. Math., 193(2021), 619–687).
self_contained_problem:
For a group $G$, define the spread $s(G)$ to be the greatest nonnegative integer $k$ such that for every choice of nontrivial elements $x_1, \dots, x_k \in G$ there exists $y \in G$ with
$$\langle x_1, y\rangle = \langle x_2, y\rangle = \cdots = \langle x_k, y\rangle = G,$$
or $s(G) = \infty$ if no such maximum exists (and $s(G) = 0$ if no such $y$ exists even for $k=1$ for some nontrivial $x_1$). It is known that no finite group $G$ satisfies $s(G) = 1$, so any group with spread exactly $1$ must be infinite. Determine whether there exists a (necessarily infinite) group $G$ with $s(G) = 1$.
status_search_result: The question of whether any group has spread exactly equal to 1 (necessarily infinite, since no finite group has spread 1) is posed by Donoven and Harper and is reported as open in subsequent literature on the spread of infinite groups (Harper's constructions yield infinite groups with finite positive spread but do not produce spread equal to 1).

original_question: It is known that there exist residually finite, locally finite, characteristically simple groups with finitely many orbits under automorphisms(A. B. Apps, J. Algebra, 81(1983), 320–339). Are there any locally finite, characteristically simple groups with finitely many orbits under automorphisms that are not residually finite?
self_contained_problem:
A group $G$ is called locally finite if every finitely generated subgroup of $G$ is finite. It is called characteristically simple if it has no proper nontrivial subgroup invariant under all automorphisms of $G$. It is said to have finitely many orbits under automorphisms if the natural action of $\mathrm{Aut}(G)$ on $G$ has only finitely many orbits. Finally, $G$ is residually finite if for every nonidentity element $g \in G$ there exists a normal subgroup $N \trianglelefteq G$ of finite index in $G$ with $g \notin N$.

It is known that there exist residually finite, locally finite, characteristically simple groups having only finitely many orbits under their automorphism group. Determine whether there exists a locally finite, characteristically simple group with only finitely many orbits under its automorphism group that is not residually finite.

original_question: A group is said to be self-similar if it admits a faithful state-closed representation by automorphisms of a regular one-rooted m-tree for some m. original_question: Let Wn = A5 ≀· · ·≀A5 be the n-times iterated permutational wreath product of A5 in its natural action(so Wn acts on 5n points), and let W = lim Wn be the inverse ←− limit(infinite iterated wreath product of A5). Does W contain a finitely generated dense subgroup of subexponential growth?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A_5$ denote the alternating group on five letters, acting naturally on the set $\{1,2,3,4,5\}$. For each integer $n\ge 1$, define the $n$-times iterated permutational wreath product
$$W_n \;=\; \underbrace{A_5 \wr A_5 \wr \cdots \wr A_5}_{n\text{ copies}},$$
taken with respect to the natural action, so that $W_n$ acts faithfully on the set of $5^n$ leaves of the rooted $5$-regular tree of depth $n$. The natural projections $W_{n+1}\twoheadrightarrow W_n$ obtained by truncating the tree form an inverse system; let
$$W \;=\; \varprojlim_{n} W_n$$
be the resulting profinite group (the infinite iterated permutational wreath product of $A_5$), endowed with its profinite topology. Recall that a finitely generated group $G$ with finite generating set $S$ has subexponential growth if $\lim_{r\to\infty} |B_S(r)|^{1/r} = 1$, where $B_S(r)$ is the ball of radius $r$ in the word metric.

Question: Does $W$ contain a finitely generated dense subgroup of subexponential growth?

original_question: (Well-known problem). Does there exist a finitely presented(infinite) simple group of finite cohomological dimension greater than 2?

original_question: A quasimorphism on a group G is a function f: G → R such that the quantity sup |f(g) + f(h) − f(gh)| is finite. A quasimorphism is homogeneous if it restricts to g,h a homomorphism on every cyclic subgroup of G. Let G be a group admitting an unbounded homogeneous quasimorphism G → R that is not a homomorphism. Must G contain a non-abelian free subgroup?
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a group. A function f: G → ℝ is called a quasimorphism if 
   D(f) := sup_{g,h ∈ G} |f(g) + f(h) − f(gh)| < ∞.
A quasimorphism f is called homogeneous if its restriction to every cyclic subgroup of G is a homomorphism, equivalently, f(g^n) = n·f(g) for all g ∈ G and all n ∈ ℤ.

Suppose that G admits a homogeneous quasimorphism f: G → ℝ that is unbounded and is not a group homomorphism. Must G contain a non-abelian free subgroup?
category_tag: Quasimorphisms and bounded cohomology of groups

original_question: An isometric action of a group G on a metric space S is called acylindrical if for every ε > 0 there exist R, N > 0 such that for every two points x, y with d(x, y) ⩾ R, there are at most N elements g ∈ G satisfying d(x, gx) ⩽ ε and d(y, gy) ⩽ ε. A group is said to be acylindrically hyperbolic if it is not virtually cyclic and admits an acylindrical action on a hyperbolic space with unbounded orbits. Is the automorphism group of a finitely generated acylindrically hyperbolic group also acylindrically hyperbolic?
self_contained_problem:
Definitions. An isometric action of a group $G$ on a metric space $(S,d)$ is called acylindrical if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exist constants $R, N > 0$ such that for any two points $x, y \in S$ with $d(x,y) \geq R$, the number of elements $g \in G$ satisfying simultaneously $d(x, gx) \leq \varepsilon$ and $d(y, gy) \leq \varepsilon$ is at most $N$. A group $G$ is called acylindrically hyperbolic if $G$ is not virtually cyclic and $G$ admits an acylindrical isometric action on a (Gromov-)hyperbolic metric space with unbounded orbits.

Question. Let $G$ be a finitely generated acylindrically hyperbolic group. Is the automorphism group $\operatorname{Aut}(G)$ also acylindrically hyperbolic?
status_search_result: The general question appears to remain open. Significant partial results are known: Genevois (2021) proved that the automorphism group of any infinitely-ended finitely generated group is acylindrically hyperbolic; analogous results hold for Aut(F_n) (n≥2), for automorphism groups of one-ended hyperbolic groups, and for relatively hyperbolic groups (with a finite collection of finitely generated proper peripheral subgroups). However, no source confirms a full positive (or negative) answer for arbitrary finitely generated acylindrically hyperbolic groups.

original_question: Does every finite 3-group T have a nontrivial characteristic subgroup C such that if T is a Sylow 3-subgroup of a finite group G, then T ∩ G′ = T ∩ H ′, where H = NG(C)? Such a characteristic subgroup is known to exist in p-groups for p ⩾ 5(G. Glauberman, Math. Z., 117(1970), 46–56), and for p = 3 there are two characteristic subgroups K1, K2 such that T ∩ G′ = (T ∩ H1′)(S ∩ H2′), where Hi = NG(Ki) (G. Glauberman, J. Algebra, 648(2024), 62–86). The group S4 shows that no such characteristic subgroups can be found in some Sylow 2-subgroups.
self_contained_problem:
Let $T$ be a finite 3-group. Does there exist a nontrivial characteristic subgroup $C$ of $T$ with the following property: whenever $G$ is a finite group having $T$ as a Sylow 3-subgroup, and $H = N_G(C)$ denotes the normalizer of $C$ in $G$, one has
$$T \cap G' = T \cap H',$$
where $G'$ and $H'$ denote the derived subgroups of $G$ and $H$, respectively?

Background context: For every prime $p \geq 5$ such a nontrivial characteristic subgroup is known to exist in any finite $p$-group $T$. For $p = 3$ it is known that there exist two nontrivial characteristic subgroups $K_1, K_2$ of $T$ such that, with $H_i = N_G(K_i)$,
$$T \cap G' = (T \cap H_1')(T \cap H_2').$$
The symmetric group $S_4$ shows that the analogous statement can fail for $p = 2$ in some Sylow 2-subgroups. The question asks whether, for $p = 3$, a single characteristic subgroup suffices.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as a new problem in the 2026 edition of the Kourovka Notebook (a standard repository of unsolved problems in group theory). The cited 2024 Glauberman paper provides only a two-subgroup factorization for $p=3$, leaving the single-characteristic-subgroup version open. No published resolution was found.

original_question: Let p be a prime, and P a finite p-group. (a) Suppose that P has an abelian subgroup of order pn. For which n does P necessarily have a normal abelian subgroup of order pn? (b) Suppose that P has an elementary abelian subgroup of order pn. For which n does P necessarily have a normal elementary abelian subgroup of order pn? It is easy to see that for p = 2, the answer to(b) is “yes” only for n = 1. The answer to both questions is “yes” for n < (p + 2)/2(G. G. Glauberman, J. Algebra, 319, no. 2(2008), 800–805), as well as for n ⩽ 5 when p ̸= 2(M. Konvisser, D. Jonah, J. Algebra, 34(1975), 309–330). The answer to both questions is “no” for n ⩾ (p+9)/2 when p ⩾ 5(for p ⩾ 7 due to G. Glauberman, Contemp. Math., 524(2010), 61–65; for p = 3, 5 due to Ya. G. Berkovich, J. Algebra, 248, no. 2(2002), 472–553). Thus, the only open cases for p ⩾ 5 are n = 6 for p = 5, and n = (p + 3)/2, (p + 5)/2, (p + 7)/2 for p > 5.
self_contained_problem:
Let p be an odd prime with p ≥ 5, and let P be a finite p-group. Determine, for the values of n listed below, whether each of the following implications holds for every such P:

(a) If P contains an abelian subgroup of order p^n, then P contains a normal abelian subgroup of order p^n.

(b) If P contains an elementary abelian subgroup of order p^n (i.e., an abelian subgroup of exponent p), then P contains a normal elementary abelian subgroup of order p^n.

The cases to resolve are:
- p = 5 and n = 6;
- p > 5 and n ∈ {(p+3)/2, (p+5)/2, (p+7)/2}.

(It is known that the answer is "yes" whenever n < (p+2)/2 or n ≤ 5 with p ≠ 2, and "no" whenever n ≥ (p+9)/2 with p ≥ 5; the problem asks to settle the remaining values of n above.)

original_question: Let L be a finite non-abelian simple group, and let D be a conjugacy class of involutions in L. Consider the complete graph Γ with vertex set D. Define an equivalence relation ∼ (graph coloring) on the set of edges as follows: (a, b) ∼ (c, d) if and only if |ab| = |cd|. An automorphism of the coloured graph Γ is a permutation τ ∈ SD such that(a, b) ∼ (aτ, bτ) for every edge(a, b). Is it true that the automorphism group of Γ is a subgroup of Aut(L)?
self_contained_problem: Let $L$ be a finite non-abelian simple group, and let $D$ be a conjugacy class of involutions in $L$. Form the complete graph $\Gamma$ with vertex set $D$, and colour its edges by the following equivalence relation: for edges $(a,b)$ and $(c,d)$, declare $(a,b)\sim(c,d)$ if and only if the orders of the products satisfy $|ab|=|cd|$. An automorphism of the edge-coloured graph $\Gamma$ is a permutation $\tau\in\mathrm{Sym}(D)$ such that $(a,b)\sim(a^{\tau},b^{\tau})$ for every edge $(a,b)$; equivalently, $|ab|=|a^{\tau}b^{\tau}|$ for all $a,b\in D$. The group $L$ acts on $D$ by conjugation, and this action extends to an action of $\mathrm{Aut}(L)$ on $D$ by colour-preserving permutations, giving a natural embedding of $\mathrm{Aut}(L)/C_{\mathrm{Aut}(L)}(D)$ into the automorphism group $\mathrm{Aut}(\Gamma)$ of the coloured graph. Determine whether $\mathrm{Aut}(\Gamma)$ always equals (is contained in) the image of $\mathrm{Aut}(L)$; that is, decide whether for every finite non-abelian simple group $L$ and every conjugacy class $D$ of involutions of $L$, the automorphism group of the coloured complete graph $\Gamma$ described above is a subgroup of $\mathrm{Aut}(L)$.

Is it true that for every finite simple group G we have Aut(Γ) = Aut2(Γ) ∩ Autp(Γ), where {2, p} are the two minimal prime divisors of |G|?

  Aut_t(Γ) = { τ ∈ Sym(D) : for all a, b ∈ D with |ab| = t, one has |a^τ · b^τ| = t },

i.e. the set of permutations of D that preserve the edge relation "|ab| = t". Let

  Aut(Γ) = ⋂_{t ≥ 1} Aut_t(Γ),

the group of all permutations of D preserving the edge labels of Γ. Let 2 and p denote the two smallest prime divisors of |G| (so p is the smallest odd prime dividing |G|). Decide whether the equality

original_question: Let G be a finite soluble group with triality, which means that G admits a group of automorphisms S isomorphic to the symmetric group of degree 3 given by the presentation S = ⟨σ, ρ | σ 2 = ρ3 = 1; σρσ = ρ2 ⟩ such that m · mρ · mρ = 1 for all m in the set of commutators M(G):= {[g, σ] | g ∈ G}. Suppose in addition that G = [G, S], the group G is generated by d elements of M(G) and their images under S, and xn = 1 for all x ∈ M(G). Is it true that the Fitting height of G is bounded in terms of d and n? An affirmative answer would provide a reduction of the analogue of the Restricted Burnside Problem for Moufang loops to the nilpotent case.
self_contained_problem:
Let $S = \langle \sigma, \rho \mid \sigma^2 = \rho^3 = 1,\ \sigma\rho\sigma = \rho^2 \rangle$ denote the symmetric group of degree 3. A finite group $G$ is said to be a group with triality if $S$ acts on $G$ by automorphisms in such a way that 
$$m \cdot m^{\rho} \cdot m^{\rho^2} = 1$$
for every element $m$ of the set
$$M(G) := \{[g,\sigma] : g \in G\} = \{g^{-1} g^{\sigma} : g \in G\}.$$
Assume that:
1. $G$ is finite and soluble;
2. $G$ is a group with triality with respect to $S$ as above;
3. $G = [G,S]$;
4. $G$ is generated by $d$ elements of $M(G)$ together with all of their images under the action of $S$;
5. there is a positive integer $n$ such that $x^n = 1$ for every $x \in M(G)$.

The Fitting height (nilpotent length) $h(G)$ of $G$ is the smallest integer $h$ such that the iterated Fitting series
$$1 = F_0(G) \le F_1(G) \le \cdots \le F_h(G) = G$$
reaches $G$, where $F_{i+1}(G)/F_i(G) = F(G/F_i(G))$ is the Fitting subgroup of $G/F_i(G)$.

Question: Must $h(G)$ be bounded by a function depending only on $d$ and $n$?

original_question: Let q be a power of a prime p, and let mn(q) be the maximum p-length of p-solvable subgroups of GL(n, q). Is it true that lim mn(q)/ log2 n = 1? İ. Güloğlu n→∞
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be a prime and let $q$ be a power of $p$. Recall that a finite group $G$ is called $p$-solvable if it admits a normal series whose factors are either $p$-groups or $p'$-groups (groups of order coprime to $p$); the $p$-length $\ell_p(G)$ is the minimum number of $p$-group factors that appear in such a series. For each integer $n \geq 1$, define
$$m_n(q) = \max\{\ell_p(H) : H \leq \mathrm{GL}(n,q),\ H \text{ is } p\text{-solvable}\},$$
where $\mathrm{GL}(n,q)$ is the group of invertible $n \times n$ matrices over the finite field with $q$ elements. Determine whether
$$\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{m_n(q)}{\log_2 n} = 1.$$

original_question: Let ℓ(X) denote the composition length of a finite group X. Let A be a finite nilpotent group acting by automorphisms on a finite soluble group G. Let c(G, A) be the number of trivial A-modules in a given A-composition series of G. (Note that c(G, A) = ℓ(CG(A)) if(|A|, |G|) = 1.) Conjecture: there are absolute constants C1 and C2 such that the Fitting height of G is at most C1 ℓ(A) + C2 c(G, A). İ. Güloǧlu
self_contained_problem:
For a finite group $X$, let $\ell(X)$ denote its composition length (the number of factors in any composition series of $X$). Let $A$ be a finite nilpotent group acting by automorphisms on a finite soluble group $G$. An $A$-composition series of $G$ is a chain $1 = G_0 \triangleleft G_1 \triangleleft \cdots \triangleleft G_n = G$ of $A$-invariant subgroups of $G$ such that each factor $G_{i+1}/G_i$ admits no proper nontrivial $A$-invariant subgroup; each such factor is regarded as an $A$-module (in the generalized sense). Define $c(G, A)$ to be the number of factors $G_{i+1}/G_i$ in such a series on which $A$ acts trivially. (When $\gcd(|A|, |G|) = 1$, this number coincides with $\ell(C_G(A))$, the composition length of the fixed-point subgroup.) Let $h(G)$ denote the Fitting height (Fitting length) of $G$, i.e. the length of the shortest normal series of $G$ with nilpotent factors.

Prove or disprove: there exist absolute constants $C_1$ and $C_2$ such that for every finite nilpotent group $A$ acting by automorphisms on every finite soluble group $G$,
$$h(G) \le C_1\, \ell(A) + C_2\, c(G, A).$$
category_tag: Fitting height of soluble groups under coprime/nilpotent action
status_search_result: The conjecture appears as a recently proposed problem attributed to İ. Güloğlu. Related work by Ercan, Güloğlu and collaborators has established Fitting-height bounds in special cases (e.g., good actions, coprime/odd-order settings, and cases where $A$ is cyclic), but no general proof of the stated linear bound $h(G) \le C_1 \ell(A) + C_2 c(G,A)$ for arbitrary finite nilpotent $A$ acting on a finite soluble $G$ is found in the literature. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Let X be a non-empty class of finite groups of odd order closed under taking subgroups, homomorphic images, and extensions. Let H be an X-maximal subgroup of a finite group G, and N a normal subgroup of G. Must H ∩ N be an X-maximal subgroup of N?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathfrak{X}$ be a non-empty class of finite groups of odd order that is closed under taking subgroups, homomorphic images, and group extensions (i.e., if $1 \to A \to B \to C \to 1$ is exact with $A, C \in \mathfrak{X}$, then $B \in \mathfrak{X}$). For a finite group $G$, call a subgroup $K \le G$ an $\mathfrak{X}$-maximal subgroup of $G$ if $K \in \mathfrak{X}$ and $K$ is maximal (with respect to inclusion) among subgroups of $G$ that belong to $\mathfrak{X}$.

Let $G$ be a finite group, let $H$ be an $\mathfrak{X}$-maximal subgroup of $G$, and let $N$ be a normal subgroup of $G$. Determine whether $H \cap N$ is necessarily an $\mathfrak{X}$-maximal subgroup of $N$.

original_question: We say that a product XY = {xy | x ∈ X, y ∈ Y } of two subsets X, Y of a group G is direct if for every z ∈ XY there are unique x ∈ X, y ∈ Y such that z = xy. Is there an infinite group G such that every subset A ⊆ G satisfies the following property: all the maximal subsets B for which the product AB is direct have the same cardinality? Note that for checking the property for a given infinite group G, it suffices to consider only those subsets A ⊆ G for which |A| = |G \ A|. Indeed, the property is equivalent to A−1 A ∩ BB −1 = {1} and A−1 AB = G, and these imply |G| = |A||B|, since G is infinite. Now, if |A| < |G \ A|, then |A| < |G|, and so |B| = |G|; and if |A| > |G \ A|, then A−1 A = G, and so |B| = 1, for all B satisfying the property.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a group. For subsets $X, Y \subseteq G$, define their product $XY = \{xy : x \in X,\ y \in Y\}$, and say the product $XY$ is direct if for every $z \in XY$ there exist unique $x \in X$ and $y \in Y$ with $z = xy$ (equivalently, $X^{-1}X \cap YY^{-1} = \{1\}$). For a subset $A \subseteq G$, call a subset $B \subseteq G$ an $A$-complement if $AB$ is direct and $B$ is maximal (with respect to inclusion) among subsets with this property.

Question: Does there exist an infinite group $G$ with the property that for every subset $A \subseteq G$, all maximal $A$-complements $B \subseteq G$ have the same cardinality?

(Equivalently, for an infinite $G$, the condition that $AB$ is direct and $B$ is maximal is equivalent to $A^{-1}A \cap BB^{-1} = \{1\}$ together with $A^{-1}AB = G$, which forces $|G| = |A|\cdot|B|$. Hence the property only needs to be checked for those $A$ with $|A| = |G \setminus A|$.)

original_question: For a finite group G, let χ1(G) denote the totality of the degrees of all irreducible complex characters of G with allowance for their multiplicities. Suppose that H is a finite group with χ1(H) = χ1(G). a) If G is an almost simple group, must H be isomorphic to G? b) If G is a quasisimple group, must H be isomorphic to G? This is true if G is a simple group(see 11.8(a) in Archive).
self_contained_problem:
For a finite group $G$, let $\chi_1(G)$ denote the multiset of degrees of all irreducible complex characters of $G$, counted with their multiplicities (equivalently, $\chi_1(G)$ records, for each positive integer $d$, the number of irreducible complex characters of $G$ of degree $d$). Recall that a finite group $G$ is called:
- almost simple if there exists a non-abelian finite simple group $S$ such that $S \trianglelefteq G \le \mathrm{Aut}(S)$ (equivalently, $G$ has a unique minimal normal subgroup, which is non-abelian simple);
- quasisimple if $G$ is perfect (i.e., $G = [G,G]$) and $G/Z(G)$ is non-abelian simple.

Let $H$ be a finite group with $\chi_1(H) = \chi_1(G)$ (equality of multisets of irreducible character degrees).

(a) If $G$ is almost simple, must $H \cong G$?

(b) If $G$ is quasisimple, must $H \cong G$?
status_search_result: The problem is listed as a new entry in recent updates of the Kourovka Notebook of unsolved problems in group theory. The analogous statement for non-abelian simple groups is known to hold (resolving the corresponding earlier Kourovka question 11.8(a) by work on alternating, sporadic, and Lie-type simple groups), and partial results characterize many quasisimple classical groups by their complex group algebras, but the full almost-simple and quasisimple cases as posed appear to remain open.

original_question: Let G be a finite group, Z(p) the localization at p, and Fp the field of p elements. Let X be the class of Fp G-modules obtained by reduction of simple QG-modules. Is it true that Z(p) G is semiperfect if and only if each projective indecomposable Fp G-module can be written as an N-linear combination of modules in X inside the Grothendieck group of Fp G? The “only if” direction is proved, and the affirmative answer is obtained if p does not divide |G| (D. Johnston, D. Rumynin, J. Algebra, 687, no. 1(2026), 776–791).
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite group and $p$ a prime. Denote by $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ the localization of $\mathbb{Z}$ at the prime ideal $(p)$, and by $\mathbb{F}_p$ the field with $p$ elements. Consider the group rings $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}G$, $\mathbb{Q}G$, and $\mathbb{F}_p G$.

For every simple $\mathbb{Q}G$-module $V$, choose a $G$-invariant $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$-lattice $L\subseteq V$ (such a lattice exists, and although it is not unique, the resulting class of $\mathbb{F}_p G$-modules is well-defined up to the relations used below). Let $\mathcal{X}$ denote the class of all $\mathbb{F}_p G$-modules of the form $L/pL$ obtained in this way (the "reductions modulo $p$" of simple $\mathbb{Q}G$-modules).

Recall that a ring $R$ is called semiperfect if $R/J(R)$ is semisimple and idempotents lift modulo the Jacobson radical $J(R)$. Let $K_0(\mathbb{F}_p G)$ denote the Grothendieck group of finitely generated $\mathbb{F}_p G$-modules with respect to short exact sequences.

Question: Is it true that $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}G$ is semiperfect if and only if every projective indecomposable $\mathbb{F}_p G$-module can be expressed as an $\mathbb{N}$-linear combination of classes of modules from $\mathcal{X}$ inside $K_0(\mathbb{F}_p G)$?

It is known that the "only if" direction holds, and that the equivalence holds when $p\nmid |G|$. Determine whether the equivalence holds in general.

original_question: For a fixed(finitely generated free)-by-cyclic group G = Fn ⋊ Z, is there an algorithm that, given a finite subset S of G, finds a finite presentation for the subgroup H = ⟨S⟩? Cf. 4.8 in Archive.
self_contained_problem:
Let $n\ge 2$ and let $F_n$ denote the free group of rank $n$. Fix an automorphism $\varphi\in\mathrm{Aut}(F_n)$ and form the (finitely generated free)-by-cyclic group
$$G \;=\; F_n\rtimes_\varphi \mathbb{Z},$$
i.e.\ the semidirect product in which a chosen generator of $\mathbb{Z}$ acts on $F_n$ via $\varphi$. The group $G$ is given by an explicit finite presentation.

Decide whether there exists an algorithm with the following specification: the input is a finite subset $S\subseteq G$ (each element given as a word in the generators of $G$), and the output is a finite presentation $\langle X\mid R\rangle$ of the subgroup $H=\langle S\rangle\le G$ generated by $S$. In particular, the algorithm must produce finite generating and relator sets describing $H$ as an abstract group.

original_question: In non-commutative, group-based cryptography, what class of group is the most appropriate platform group for building cryptographic schemes?
status_search_result: The question of identifying the "most appropriate" platform group for non-commutative group-based cryptography is widely regarded as an overarching open problem in the field. original_question: Is the uniform subgroup membership problem decidable for(finitely generated free)-by-cyclic groups? That is, for a fixed group G = Fn ⋊ Z, is there an algorithm that, given elements w, h1,..., hk ∈ G, decides whether or not w belongs to the subgroup H = ⟨h1,..., hk ⟩?
self_contained_problem:
Let $n \geq 2$ and let $F_n$ be the free group of rank $n$. A (finitely generated free)-by-cyclic group is a semidirect product $G = F_n \rtimes_\varphi \mathbb{Z}$, where $\varphi \in \mathrm{Aut}(F_n)$ specifies the action of the generator of $\mathbb{Z}$ on $F_n$ by conjugation.

The uniform subgroup membership problem for a fixed group $G$ is the following decision problem: given as input a finite list of elements $w, h_1, \ldots, h_k \in G$ (each represented as a word in a fixed finite generating set of $G$), decide whether $w \in \langle h_1, \ldots, h_k \rangle$, the subgroup of $G$ generated by $h_1, \ldots, h_k$.

Question: Is the uniform subgroup membership problem decidable for every (finitely generated free)-by-cyclic group $G = F_n \rtimes \mathbb{Z}$? Equivalently, does there exist, for each such $G$, an algorithm which on input $(w, h_1, \ldots, h_k)$ correctly decides whether $w$ belongs to $\langle h_1, \ldots, h_k \rangle$?
status_search_result: The problem appears as a new entry in the 2026 Kourovka Notebook of unsolved problems in group theory, which lists open problems. Decidability of the subgroup membership problem for free-by-cyclic groups in general is not established in the literature; only partial decidability results exist for special subclasses (e.g. certain one-relator or surface-related cases), while membership in various related families of groups is known to be undecidable. No source claims a full positive or negative resolution for arbitrary $F_n \rtimes \mathbb{Z}$.

original_question: (E. Zelmanov). Let F be a field of characteristic p > 0, and let Γ be the principal congruence subgroup of Aut(F [x1,..., xn ]) consisting of all automorphisms that send each variable xi to xi modulo terms of higher degree. Then Γ is a residuallyp group. Does Γ satisfy a pro-p identity?
self_contained_problem:
Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$, and let $F[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ be the polynomial ring in $n$ commuting variables over $F$. Let $\mathrm{Aut}(F[x_1,\dots,x_n])$ denote its group of $F$-algebra automorphisms, and let $\Gamma$ be the principal congruence subgroup consisting of all automorphisms $\varphi$ such that, for every $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$, $\varphi(x_i) \equiv x_i$ modulo terms of degree $\ge 2$ (i.e.\ $\varphi(x_i)-x_i$ lies in the square of the augmentation ideal $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$). It is known that $\Gamma$ is a residually-$p$ group, so it has a pro-$p$ completion $\widehat{\Gamma}_p$. Recall that a pro-$p$ group $G$ is said to satisfy a pro-$p$ identity if there exists a nontrivial element $w$ in the free pro-$p$ group $F_k$ on some finite number $k$ of generators such that $w$ vanishes under every continuous homomorphism $F_k\to G$. 

Question: Does $\Gamma$ satisfy a pro-$p$ identity (equivalently, does its pro-$p$ completion satisfy a pro-$p$ identity)?

paper_title: Aspects of Nonabelian Group Based Cryptography: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: For non-commutative cryptographic schemes based on groups, should the underlying platform group be finite or infinite?
self_contained_problem:
In non-commutative (group-based) cryptography, a platform group $G$ is a (typically non-abelian) group used to instantiate cryptographic primitives such as key-exchange protocols (e.g., the Anshel–Anshel–Goldfeld protocol or the Ko–Lee/Diffie–Hellman-type conjugacy protocol), digital signatures, and authentication schemes. Such a platform group is required to admit (i) an efficiently computable normal form or a solvable word problem so that elements can be represented and compared efficiently, (ii) an efficient method to sample elements from a distribution that produces hard instances of the underlying algorithmic problem (e.g., the conjugacy search problem, the simultaneous conjugacy search problem, or the decomposition problem), and (iii) no known efficient (probabilistic polynomial-time) algorithm solving the underlying hard problem on a noticeable fraction of instances.

Determine whether, for the purposes of building secure non-commutative cryptographic schemes meeting the above requirements, the platform group $G$ should be taken to be finite or infinite. Specifically, decide which of the following holds:

(a) There exists a family of finite non-abelian groups $\{G_n\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$, with $|G_n|$ growing at most exponentially in a security parameter $n$, on which a chosen group-based hard problem (such as the conjugacy search problem) is provably or empirically intractable, yielding cryptographic schemes with security at least comparable to those built on infinite platform groups; or

(b) Any family of finite non-abelian platform groups admits a subexponential-time attack against the standard group-based hard problems, so that secure non-commutative group-based cryptography essentially requires infinite platform groups (such as braid groups, polycyclic groups, Thompson's group $F$, free metabelian groups, or right-angled Artin groups).

Provide either a construction establishing (a) or a reduction/attack establishing (b).
status_search_result: The question of whether platform groups in non-commutative group-based cryptography should be finite or infinite remains a guiding open design question in the field. Most proposed platform groups (braid groups, polycyclic groups, Thompson's group, Grigorchuk-type groups) are infinite and finitely generated, but proposals based on finite non-abelian groups (e.g., matrix groups over finite rings, finite p-groups) also exist. No consensus or definitive theorem settles which class is preferable, and the issue is still discussed in surveys on non-commutative cryptography.

original_question: How can one prove that a chosen group platform is secure for non-commutative cryptographic constructions such as public-key exchange protocols, digital-signature schemes, and authentication schemes?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finitely generated non-abelian (non-commutative) group, equipped with an efficient encoding of elements and efficient algorithms for the group operations (multiplication and inversion). Such a $G$ is called a platform group for a cryptographic scheme when the security of the scheme is reduced to the computational hardness of one or more problems formulated in $G$ (for example, the conjugacy search problem, the word problem with restricted presentations, the simultaneous conjugacy search problem, the decomposition problem, or a learning-with-errors analogue over $G$).

Consider three classes of non-commutative cryptographic constructions built over such a platform group $G$:
(a) public-key exchange protocols (e.g., Anshel–Anshel–Goldfeld type or Ko–Lee type protocols),
(b) digital-signature schemes,
(c) identification/authentication schemes.

Develop a general methodology, together with explicit criteria on $G$ (such as growth, complexity of the word and conjugacy problems, distortion of subgroups, generic-case versus average-case complexity, distributional properties of random elements, and resistance to known attacks such as length-based attacks, linear-algebra attacks, and quantum attacks), under which one can give a rigorous reduction proving that schemes in classes (a)–(c) over $G$ are provably secure in a standard cryptographic model (e.g., IND-CPA, IND-CCA, EUF-CMA, or zero-knowledge soundness). Equivalently: identify a specific finitely presented non-abelian group $G$ together with a hard computational problem $P$ over $G$ whose average-case hardness can be established, and exhibit protocols for (a), (b), (c) whose security is provably reducible to $P$.
status_search_result: The question of identifying non-commutative platform groups together with average-case hard problems on which provably secure key exchange, signature, and authentication schemes can be based remains an active and open research area. Subsequent surveys (e.g., the polycyclic-group survey by Kahrobaei and collaborators) and ongoing projects such as the CCNY CAISS "Provable Cryptography from Non-Commutative Groups" continue to list this as a core open problem; while candidate platforms (braid groups, polycyclic groups, Grigorchuk groups, extra-special groups, matrix groups) have been proposed and partial security reductions exist, no general methodology or fully provably secure scheme has been established.

original_question: Is it true that if a normal subgroup A of a Sylow p-subgroup of a p-soluble finite group G has exponent pe, then the normal closure of A in G has(p, e)-bounded(or even e-bounded) p-length?
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be a prime and let $G$ be a finite $p$-soluble group, i.e., a finite group all of whose composition factors are either $p$-groups or $p'$-groups. Recall that the $p$-length $\ell_p(G)$ of $G$ is the number of $p$-factors in a shortest normal series of $G$ whose factors are either $p$-groups or $p'$-groups. Suppose that $P$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$ and that $A \trianglelefteq P$ is a normal subgroup of $P$ of exponent dividing $p^{e}$ (so every element of $A$ has order at most $p^{e}$). Let $A^{G} = \langle A^{g} : g \in G\rangle$ denote the normal closure of $A$ in $G$.

Determine whether the $p$-length $\ell_p(A^{G})$ of the normal closure $A^{G}$ is bounded above by a function depending only on $p$ and $e$ (a $(p,e)$-bounded quantity). More strongly, decide whether $\ell_p(A^{G})$ can be bounded above by a function of $e$ alone, independent of $p$ and of $G$.
