paper_title: Open Questions in GRB Physics
original_question: Are massive-star gamma-ray bursts reliable tracers of the star-formation history of the universe across cosmic time, especially at high redshift?
self_contained_problem:
Long-duration gamma-ray bursts (LGRBs) are believed to arise from the collapse of certain massive stars. Let R_GRB(z) denote the comoving rate density of long-duration GRBs as a function of redshift z, and let ψ_*(z) denote the cosmic star-formation rate density. A naive "tracer" hypothesis posits that there exist a redshift-independent constant k > 0 such that R_GRB(z) = k · ψ_*(z) for all z (after correction for instrumental selection effects, beaming, and luminosity function).

Determine whether massive-star (long-duration) GRBs are reliable tracers of the cosmic star-formation history in this sense across all cosmic epochs, particularly at high redshift (z ≳ 3). Specifically:

(a) Decide whether the proportionality R_GRB(z) ∝ ψ_*(z) holds, or whether an additional redshift-dependent factor f(z) (for example arising from a metallicity threshold, an evolving initial mass function, evolving luminosity function, or evolving beaming/jet properties) is required so that R_GRB(z) = k · f(z) · ψ_*(z).

(b) If such a factor f(z) is required, characterize its functional form and identify the dominant physical mechanism (metallicity bias, IMF evolution, luminosity-function evolution, beaming-angle evolution, or a combination) responsible for the deviation.

(c) Assess whether, after correcting for any such bias, GRB-derived measurements of ψ_*(z) at high redshift are consistent with independent determinations from galaxy surveys.
category_tag: Gamma-ray bursts and cosmic star formation history
status_search_result: Substantial evidence accumulated since 2014 indicates that long GRBs are biased tracers of star formation, with metallicity dependence widely identified as a leading cause; however, the precise form of the bias and whether additional evolving properties (luminosity function, beaming, IMF) are needed remains an active area of investigation, with recent (2024–2025) studies arguing that no single evolving property suffices and a combination is required. The question is therefore partially solved: a bias is established, but its full quantitative characterization, especially at high redshift, is still under study.

original_question: Let Γ be a graph of diameter d. For i ∈ {1, 2,..., d}, let Γi be the graph on the same vertex set as Γ with vertices u, w adjacent in Γi if and only if dΓ (u, w) = i. Does there exist a Q-polynomial distance-regular graph Γ of diameter 3 such that Γ2 and Γ3 are strongly regular? A. A. Makhnëv
self_contained_problem:
Let Γ be a finite connected simple graph of diameter d, and let d_Γ(·,·) denote the graph distance in Γ. For each i ∈ {1, 2, …, d} define Γ_i to be the graph on the same vertex set as Γ in which two distinct vertices u, w are adjacent if and only if d_Γ(u, w) = i.

Recall that Γ is called distance-regular if for all i ∈ {0,1,…,d} and all vertices u, w with d_Γ(u, w) = i, the numbers
  c_i = |{x : d_Γ(u, x) = i−1, d_Γ(x, w) = 1}|,
  a_i = |{x : d_Γ(u, x) = i, d_Γ(x, w) = 1}|,
  b_i = |{x : d_Γ(u, x) = i+1, d_Γ(x, w) = 1}|
depend only on i (not on the particular pair u, w). A distance-regular graph of diameter d is Q-polynomial (with respect to some ordering E_0, E_1, …, E_d of its primitive idempotents) if there exist scalars such that, in the Bose–Mesner algebra under entrywise multiplication, E_1 ∘ E_j is a linear combination of E_{j−1}, E_j, E_{j+1} for each j, equivalently if the dual eigenvalue sequence makes the dual intersection numbers tridiagonal.

A graph on v vertices is strongly regular with parameters (v, k, λ, μ) if it is k-regular, every two adjacent vertices have exactly λ common neighbours, and every two non-adjacent vertices have exactly μ common neighbours.

Question: Does there exist a Q-polynomial distance-regular graph Γ of diameter 3 such that both Γ_2 and Γ_3 are strongly regular?
status_search_result: Recent work by Makhnev, Nirova and collaborators studies the inverse problem of finding distance-regular graphs of diameter 3 such that Γ_2 and Γ_3 are strongly regular, producing infinite families of admissible intersection arrays but no construction of an actual Q-polynomial example. The problem appears in the new problems list of the 2026 Kourovka Notebook, indicating it remains open.

original_question: (W. Willems). Conjecture: The sum of squares of the degrees of the irreducible p-Brauer characters of a finite group G is at least the p′-part of |G|. This is known to be true for p = 2(G. Malle, Adv. Math., 380(2021), Paper no. 107609, 15 pp.).
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite group and $p$ a prime. Let $\mathrm{IBr}_p(G)$ denote the set of irreducible $p$-Brauer characters of $G$, and let $|G|_{p'}$ denote the $p'$-part of $|G|$ (i.e., the largest divisor of $|G|$ coprime to $p$). Prove or disprove that
$$\sum_{\varphi \in \mathrm{IBr}_p(G)} \varphi(1)^2 \;\ge\; |G|_{p'}$$
holds for every finite group $G$ and every prime $p$.
status_search_result: The conjecture remains open in general. It is known to hold for p = 2 (Malle, Adv. Math. 380 (2021), 107609), and earlier results of Willems established it for p-solvable groups (groups with a p-complement). Tong-Viet has reduced the conjecture to a statement about quasi-simple groups, and partial verifications exist for certain families of quasi-simple groups at odd primes, but no full proof is known.

paper_title: Open Questions in GRB Physics
original_question: Do massive-star gamma-ray bursts preferentially occur in low-metallicity environments, and is such a metallicity bias needed to explain the observed high-redshift GRB event rate?
self_contained_problem:
Long-duration gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are believed to arise from the core collapse of certain massive stars (the "collapsar" channel). Let f(Z, z) denote the fraction of cosmic star formation at redshift z that occurs in environments with gas-phase metallicity below Z, and let R_GRB(z) denote the comoving rate density of long GRBs as a function of redshift z. Assume that the comoving cosmic star formation rate density ψ(z) and the metallicity distribution of star formation as a function of redshift are known from independent observations.

(a) Determine whether long GRB progenitors are preferentially produced in low-metallicity environments; that is, decide whether there exists a metallicity threshold Z_c (with 12 + log(O/H) of order 8.4–8.7) and a bias function b(Z) such that
   R_GRB(z) ∝ ∫ b(Z) dψ/dZ (Z, z) dZ,
with b(Z) strongly suppressed for Z > Z_c, and quantify Z_c and the form of b.

(b) Determine whether such a metallicity bias is necessary (as opposed to, e.g., a redshift-dependent GRB luminosity function) in order to reconcile the observed long-GRB event rate at high redshift (z ≳ 4) with the cosmic star formation history ψ(z).
status_search_result: Multiple observational studies since 2014 (e.g., Vergani et al. 2014, Perley et al. 2015, Graham et al.) provide evidence that long GRBs are metallicity-biased tracers of star formation, with a preference for hosts having 12+log(O/H) ≲ 8.4–8.7, supporting a moderate metallicity bias. However, a 2023/2024 SHOALS-based study found a surprising lack of evolution in the high-metallicity tail of GRB host galaxies out to z≈2.5, complicating the simple low-metallicity-bias picture. Whether the bias alone (rather than an evolving GRB luminosity function) is required to explain the high-z GRB rate remains debated, so the question is partially resolved but not definitively settled.

paper_title: Open Questions in GRB Physics
original_question: Does the luminosity function of gamma-ray bursts evolve with redshift or cosmic time, so that bursts at higher redshift are systematically more luminous than those nearby?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the population of long-duration gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), modeled as point sources with isotropic-equivalent peak luminosities L distributed according to a (possibly redshift-dependent) luminosity function Φ(L, z), where z denotes cosmological redshift. Define the comoving GRB rate density ρ(z) and assume an observed sample is drawn from the joint distribution determined by Φ(L, z), ρ(z), and the survey selection function (flux-limited detection in a given energy band).

The question is whether Φ(L, z) genuinely depends on z in a non-separable or shape-changing way, in particular whether a "luminosity evolution" of the form Φ(L, z) = Φ_0(L / g(z)) / g(z) with a monotonically increasing function g(z) (for example a power law g(z) = (1+z)^δ with δ > 0) is required by the data, so that GRBs at higher redshift are systematically intrinsically more luminous than those at low redshift. Equivalently: can the observed redshift–luminosity distribution of GRBs be explained by a non-evolving luminosity function combined with a comoving rate density tracing cosmic star formation, or does consistency with observations require evolution of the luminosity function itself with cosmic time?

Determine whether such redshift evolution of the GRB luminosity function exists, and if so, characterize its functional form (e.g., the exponent δ in a (1+z)^δ parameterization).
status_search_result: Multiple statistical analyses of Swift and HETE-2 GRB samples report evidence that a non-evolving luminosity function is disfavored, with luminosity evolution roughly of the form L ∝ (1+z)^δ with δ ≈ 1.4–2.5 providing better fits, and recent (2025) work on Type II GRBs again excluding the no-evolution model. However, degeneracies between luminosity evolution and density evolution remain, and the precise form of evolution is not uniquely determined, so the question is partially resolved rather than definitively settled.

original_question: (M. Herzog, J. Schönheim). Let G be a group and let k ⩾ 2. self_contained_problem: Let $G$ be a group and let $k \geq 2$ be an integer. Suppose $H_1, \ldots, H_k$ are subgroups of $G$ and $g_1, \ldots, g_k$ are elements of $G$ such that the left cosets $g_1 H_1, \ldots, g_k H_k$ form a partition of $G$ (i.e., their union equals $G$ and they are pairwise disjoint). status_search_result: The Herzog–Schönheim conjecture (1974) remains open in general. paper_title: Open Questions in GRB Physics
original_question: Can high-redshift gamma-ray bursts be used to probe the reionization history of the universe through their near-infrared afterglow spectra, thereby constraining how and when cosmic reionization occurred?
self_contained_problem:
Cosmic reionization is the epoch during which the largely neutral intergalactic medium (IGM) of hydrogen, formed after recombination, became ionized by the first luminous sources. The history of reionization is encoded in the redshift evolution of the volume-averaged neutral hydrogen fraction x_HI(z) of the IGM.

Long gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) at high redshift produce bright, power-law near-infrared afterglows that act as background light sources whose spectra carry imprinted absorption features from intervening gas, including a redshifted Lyman-alpha damping wing whose shape depends on x_HI(z) along the line of sight, as well as metal absorption lines from the host galaxy and intergalactic absorbers.

Question: Determine whether observations of near-infrared afterglow spectra of high-redshift (z ≳ 6) gamma-ray bursts can be used to recover the reionization history of the universe — that is, to provide quantitative constraints on the function x_HI(z) and on the timing and duration of reionization. Specifically, establish (a) under what assumptions the Lyman-alpha damping-wing profile in such afterglow spectra can be cleanly decomposed into a contribution from the GRB host galaxy and a contribution from the IGM so as to yield a measurement of x_HI at the burst redshift, and (b) what statistical sample size and redshift coverage of high-z GRB afterglows would be required to constrain the global reionization history at a chosen precision.
status_search_result: The methodology is established and partially demonstrated in practice: high-S/N afterglow spectroscopy of individual high-z GRBs (e.g., GRB 050904, GRB 130606A at z≈5.91) has been used to decompose the Lyman-alpha damping wing into host and IGM contributions and to place constraints on the IGM neutral fraction. However, a full reconstruction of the reionization history requires a statistical sample of tens of GRBs at z>7–8, which does not yet exist; future missions such as THESEUS are designed to provide it. Thus the question is partially answered in principle and observationally, but not fully resolved.

paper_title: Open Questions in GRB Physics
original_question: Do gamma-ray bursts at very high redshift arise from progenitors different from those of lower-redshift bursts, for example from an earlier stellar population that forms more massive stars and perhaps powers more energetic events?
self_contained_problem:
A gamma-ray burst (GRB) is a brief, intense flash of gamma radiation observed at cosmological distances, generally believed to be produced by a relativistic jet launched during the catastrophic collapse of a massive star (long-duration GRBs) or the merger of compact objects (short-duration GRBs). Each GRB has a measured cosmological redshift z, and the population of observed bursts spans a wide range of z, from low redshift (z ≲ 1) up to z ≳ 8.

Population III stars are a hypothesized first generation of stars formed from primordial (essentially metal-free) gas in the early universe; theoretical models suggest they may have a top-heavy initial mass function and reach significantly larger masses than typical present-day massive stars, potentially producing more energetic explosive events.

Question: Do gamma-ray bursts originating at very high redshift (e.g., z ≳ 6) arise from a class of progenitor systems that is intrinsically different from the progenitors of gamma-ray bursts observed at lower redshift? In particular, do high-redshift GRBs originate from an earlier stellar population (such as Population III or its immediate descendants) consisting of more massive stars, and does this produce systematic differences (for example higher isotropic-equivalent energies, longer intrinsic durations, or different luminosity functions) in the high-redshift GRB population compared with the low-redshift one?
status_search_result: The question of whether high-redshift GRBs arise from a distinct progenitor population (such as Population III stars) remains an open observational and theoretical question. Recent reviews and studies continue to discuss possible signatures (higher energetics, longer durations) of Pop III GRBs but no definitive observational identification has been made; current samples of z>6 GRBs are too small to robustly distinguish progenitor populations.

original_question: The Gruenberg–Kegel graph(or the prime graph) GK(G) of a finite group G is a labelled graph with vertex set consisting of all prime divisors of the order of G in which different vertices p and q are adjacent if and only if G contains an element of order pq. Let GK(G) denote the abstract graph obtained from GK(G) by removing all labels. A finite group G is said to be recognizable by the isomorphism type of its Gruenberg–Kegel graph if there are no finite groups H not isomorphic to G with GK(H) isomorphic to GK(G). Are there infinitely many(pairwise non-isomorphic) finite groups which are recognizable by the isomorphism type of the Gruenberg–Kegel graph?
self_contained_problem:
For a finite group $G$, the Gruenberg–Kegel graph (or prime graph) $\mathrm{GK}(G)$ is the labelled graph whose vertex set is the set of prime divisors of $|G|$, where two distinct vertices $p$ and $q$ are joined by an edge if and only if $G$ contains an element of order $pq$. Let $\widetilde{\mathrm{GK}}(G)$ denote the underlying abstract (unlabelled) graph obtained from $\mathrm{GK}(G)$ by forgetting the prime labels on the vertices. A finite group $G$ is said to be recognizable by the isomorphism type of its Gruenberg–Kegel graph if there is no finite group $H$ with $H \not\cong G$ such that $\widetilde{\mathrm{GK}}(H)$ is isomorphic (as an abstract graph) to $\widetilde{\mathrm{GK}}(G)$.

Question: Do there exist infinitely many pairwise non-isomorphic finite groups that are recognizable by the isomorphism type of their Gruenberg–Kegel graph?

original_question: Is there an almost simple but not simple group which is recognizable by the isomorphism type of its Gruenberg–Kegel graph? Note that if a group G is recognizable by the isomorphism type of its Gruenberg– Kegel graph, then G is recognizable by its Gruenberg–Kegel graph, and therefore G is almost simple(P. J. Cameron, N. V. Maslova, J. Algebra, 607(2022), 186–213).
self_contained_problem:
For a finite group $G$, the Gruenberg–Kegel graph (or prime graph) $\Gamma(G)$ is the simple undirected graph whose vertex set is the set $\pi(G)$ of prime divisors of the order $|G|$, and in which two distinct primes $p$ and $q$ are joined by an edge if and only if $G$ contains an element of order $pq$.

A finite group $G$ is said to be recognizable by its Gruenberg–Kegel graph if every finite group $H$ with $\Gamma(H) = \Gamma(G)$ (equality of labeled graphs on the prime vertex set) satisfies $H \cong G$.

A finite group $G$ is said to be recognizable by the isomorphism type of its Gruenberg–Kegel graph if every finite group $H$ such that $\Gamma(H)$ is isomorphic to $\Gamma(G)$ as an abstract (unlabeled) graph satisfies $H \cong G$.

A finite group $G$ is called almost simple if there exists a non-abelian finite simple group $S$ such that $S \trianglelefteq G \le \mathrm{Aut}(S)$.

It is known that any finite group recognizable by the isomorphism type of its Gruenberg–Kegel graph is almost simple.

Question: Does there exist a finite almost simple group that is not simple and is recognizable by the isomorphism type of its Gruenberg–Kegel graph?
status_search_result: A 2025 preprint on characterization of groups by the isomorphism type of the Gruenberg–Kegel graph explicitly lists this as an open problem ("Problem 2"). Known results establish that groups recognizable in this sense must be almost simple, and the recognized examples investigated so far (e.g., certain exceptional groups of Lie type such as ${}^2E_6(2)$ and $E_8(q)$) are all simple. No almost simple non-simple example has been exhibited.

paper_title: Polar Broad Absorption Line Quasars: An Open Question
original_question: What fraction of broad absorption line (BAL) quasars are genuinely "polar", in the sense that they contain relativistic jets oriented close to our line of sight, and how does the incidence of such line-of-sight jets in BAL quasars compare with that in non-BAL quasars when the classification is based on very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) measurements of brightness temperature, repeated imaging, and apparent transverse jet motions rather than on two-epoch radio flux-density variability alone?
self_contained_problem:
A broad absorption line (BAL) quasar is a quasar whose ultraviolet spectrum exhibits broad blueshifted absorption troughs attributable to outflowing gas. Such a quasar is called "polar" if it harbors a relativistic jet whose axis is oriented close to the observer's line of sight. Two diagnostics commonly used to identify line-of-sight relativistic jets are: (i) two-epoch radio flux-density variability, and (ii) very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) measurements that directly probe parsec-scale jet structure via brightness temperature, repeated imaging, and apparent transverse component motions.

Determine the following:
1. What fraction of BAL quasars are genuinely polar, i.e., contain a relativistic jet oriented close to the line of sight, when polarity is established using VLBI brightness-temperature measurements, repeated VLBI imaging, and apparent transverse jet motions (rather than two-epoch radio flux-density variability alone)?
2. How does the incidence of line-of-sight relativistic jets among BAL quasars, determined by these VLBI-based criteria, compare with the corresponding incidence among non-BAL ("normal") quasars?
status_search_result: Subsequent VLBI surveys of radio-loud BAL quasars (e.g., Bruni et al. 2013, Cao Hong & Frey 2015, Hayashi et al.) have constrained parsec-scale structures and brightness temperatures, finding that compact BAL quasars are not preferentially oriented along the jet axis but include sources at a range of inclinations, with a small but non-negligible polar component. Statistical studies of BAL fraction versus radio orientation indicators (Bruni et al. 2022) report a possible BAL-fraction increase at the lowest orientation angles consistent with a population of polar BAL quasars. A precise, definitive polar fraction for BAL versus non-BAL quasars from VLBI brightness-temperature and proper-motion measurements has not been firmly established, so the question is partially addressed but not fully resolved.

original_question: Is it true that a periodic group containing an involution is locally finite if the centralizer of every element of even order is locally finite?
self_contained_problem:

Determine whether the following statement is true: Every periodic group $G$ that contains an involution and has the property that the centralizer $C_G(g)$ is locally finite for every element $g \in G$ of even order is itself locally finite.

Status appears unresolved based on available sources.

original_question: (M. Tărnăuceanu). Is it true that for every positive rational number r there exists a finite group G such that | Aut(G)|/|G| = r? A similar question is answered in the positive for graphs, monoids, partial groups, and posets(R. Molinier, Preprint, 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21059). It is also known that the set {| Aut(G)|/|G| | G is a finite abelian group} is dense in [0, +∞) (M. Tărnăuceanu, Elemente Math. (2025), https://ems.press/journals/ em/articles/14298544).
self_contained_problem:
For a finite group $G$, let $\operatorname{Aut}(G)$ denote its automorphism group. Determine whether the following statement holds: for every positive rational number $r \in \mathbb{Q}_{>0}$, there exists a finite group $G$ such that
$$\frac{|\operatorname{Aut}(G)|}{|G|} = r.$$
Equivalently, is the set $\left\{\dfrac{|\operatorname{Aut}(G)|}{|G|} : G \text{ is a finite group}\right\}$ equal to $\mathbb{Q}_{>0}$?
status_search_result: The problem appears as a newly posed question in the 2026 edition of a well-known problem collection in group theory. Related results are known: the analogous statement for graphs, monoids, partial groups, and posets has been proven (Molinier, 2025), and the set of ratios |Aut(G)|/|G| for finite abelian G is known to be dense in [0,∞) (Tărnăuceanu, 2025). However, no resolution for the full finite-group case has been found in the literature.

original_question: Let w be a multilinear commutator word, and assume that G is a group where the set of w-values is covered by finitely many cyclic subgroups. Is it true that the verbal subgroup w(G) is finite-by-cyclic? This is true for lower central words(G. Cutolo, C. Nicotera, J. Algebra, 324, no. 7(2010), 1616–1624).
self_contained_problem:
A multilinear commutator word (or outer commutator word) is a word obtained from a sequence of distinct variables by nested commutation; equivalently, it is defined recursively by setting w = x for a single variable, and given multilinear commutator words u(x_1,...,x_s) and v(x_{s+1},...,x_{s+t}) on disjoint sets of variables, declaring w(x_1,...,x_{s+t}) = [u(x_1,...,x_s), v(x_{s+1},...,x_{s+t})] to be a multilinear commutator word. Examples include the lower central words γ_k and the derived words δ_k.

For a group G and a word w(x_1,...,x_n), the set of w-values in G is G_w = { w(g_1,...,g_n) : g_i ∈ G }, and the verbal subgroup w(G) is the subgroup of G generated by G_w.

A group H is called finite-by-cyclic if H has a finite normal subgroup N such that H/N is cyclic.

Question: Let w be an arbitrary multilinear commutator word, and let G be a group such that the set of w-values G_w is contained in the union of finitely many cyclic subgroups of G. Must the verbal subgroup w(G) be finite-by-cyclic?

(It is known that the answer is affirmative when w is a lower central word γ_k.)
category_tag: Verbal subgroups and word values in groups
status_search_result: The question, posed for general multilinear commutator words, generalizes a 2010 theorem of Cutolo and Nicotera handling lower central words. Subsequent work by Detomi, Morigi, and Shumyatsky and others has studied related coverings of w-values (countable coverings, periodic subgroups, BFC-type conditions, ranks), but no source located confirms a positive resolution for arbitrary multilinear commutator words under coverings by finitely many cyclic subgroups. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Suppose that A and G are finite groups such that A acts coprimely on G by automorphisms. Let C = CG(A) be the fixed-point subgroup, and let C ′ denote its derived subgroup. Is it true that the number of A-invariant irreducible characters χ of G whose restriction χC is never zero is exactly |C/C ′ |? This would follow if one could show that χC is never zero if and only if the Glauberman–Isaacs correspondent χ∗ of χ is linear.
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ and $G$ be finite groups of coprime order such that $A$ acts on $G$ by automorphisms. Denote by $C = C_G(A)$ the subgroup of fixed points of $A$ in $G$, and by $C'$ the derived subgroup of $C$. By the Glauberman–Isaacs correspondence, there is a canonical bijection $\chi \mapsto \chi^*$ between the set $\operatorname{Irr}_A(G)$ of $A$-invariant irreducible complex characters of $G$ and the set $\operatorname{Irr}(C)$ of irreducible complex characters of $C$.

For $\chi \in \operatorname{Irr}_A(G)$, write $\chi_C$ for the restriction of $\chi$ to $C$, and say that $\chi_C$ is "never zero" if $\chi(c) \neq 0$ for every $c \in C$.

(a) Prove or disprove: the number of characters $\chi \in \operatorname{Irr}_A(G)$ such that $\chi_C$ is never zero equals $|C : C'|$.

(b) Prove or disprove the following stronger statement, which would imply (a): for $\chi \in \operatorname{Irr}_A(G)$, the restriction $\chi_C$ is never zero if and only if the Glauberman–Isaacs correspondent $\chi^* \in \operatorname{Irr}(C)$ is a linear character.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as a new entry in the 2026 edition of the Kourovka Notebook of unsolved problems in group theory. A web search located related work on the Glauberman–Isaacs correspondence and on vanishing/non-vanishing of restricted characters under coprime action, but no published proof or counterexample to the stated equivalence or counting statement was found. The problem appears to be currently open.

original_question: Which finite almost simple groups are the automorphism groups of regular polytopes of rank 3? In other words, which finite almost simple groups are generated by three involutions two of which commute? This question has been answered for finite simple groups; see 7.30 in Archive. Ya.
self_contained_problem:
A finite group $G$ is called almost simple if there exists a non-abelian finite simple group $S$ such that $S \trianglelefteq G \leq \mathrm{Aut}(S)$ (identifying $S$ with its group of inner automorphisms). An abstract regular polytope of rank $3$ has automorphism group generated by three involutions $\rho_0, \rho_1, \rho_2$ such that $\rho_0$ and $\rho_2$ commute (the "string C-condition" in rank 3 reduces to this commuting relation together with the intersection condition on the parabolic subgroups $\langle \rho_0,\rho_1\rangle$ and $\langle \rho_1,\rho_2\rangle$).

Equivalently, classify all finite almost simple groups $G$ that can be generated by three involutions $a, b, c \in G$ with $ac = ca$, and that arise as the full automorphism group of some abstract regular polytope of rank $3$.

Problem: Determine explicitly which finite almost simple groups are the automorphism groups of abstract regular polytopes of rank $3$.
category_tag: Almost simple groups and regular polytopes
status_search_result: The analogous question for finite simple groups has been answered. For finite almost simple groups, the problem has been resolved for several specific infinite families (e.g. PSL(2,q) and PGL(2,q), groups of type PGL(3,q), Suzuki and Ree groups), and an "atlas" of small almost simple groups has been compiled, but a complete classification across all finite almost simple groups does not appear in the literature. The status is therefore best described as partially solved.

original_question: Let V be a variety generated by a finite group, and let f(n)p be the order of the free group in V on n generators. Is it true that the sequence n log f(n) has a limit as n → ∞, and this limit is an integer?

$$\frac{\log\log f(n)}{n}$$
necessarily converges as $n \to \infty$, and, when it does, whether the limit is always an integer.

original_question: (V. V. Uspenskii). A Hausdorff topological group G is called minimal if it does not admit a strictly coarser Hausdorff group topology. A topological group is called Raikov complete if its two-sided uniform structure is complete. It is known that a finite direct product of Raikov complete minimal topological groups is again minimal. Is it true that an arbitrary Cartesian product of Raikov complete minimal topological groups remains minimal? It is known that an arbitrary Cartesian product of centre-free minimal topological groups is minimal(M. Megrelishvili, Topology Appl., 62, no. 1(1995), 1–19).
self_contained_problem:
A Hausdorff topological group $(G,	au)$ is called minimal if there is no Hausdorff group topology $	au'$ on $G$ with $	au' \subsetneq 	au$. The two-sided (Roelcke) uniformity on a topological group $G$ is the supremum of its left and right uniformities; $G$ is called Raikov complete if it is complete with respect to this two-sided uniformity. It is known that:

(a) any finite direct product of Raikov complete minimal Hausdorff topological groups, equipped with the product topology, is again a minimal topological group;
(b) any (possibly infinite) Cartesian product of centre-free minimal Hausdorff topological groups is minimal.

Question: Is it true that for an arbitrary family $\{G_i\}_{i \in I}$ of Raikov complete minimal Hausdorff topological groups, the Cartesian product $\prod_{i \in I} G_i$ endowed with the product topology is also a minimal topological group?

original_question: For a group word w(x1,..., xn) on n letters, define e0(x1,..., xn) = x1 and ek+1(x1,..., xn) = w(ek(x1,..., xn),..., xn) for all k ∈ N. A group G is said to satisfy the Engel type iterated identity w if for all x1,..., xn ∈ G there exists m ∈ N such that em(x1,..., xn) = 1. Conjecture: For every non-trivial word w, if a finitely generated branch group G(see 15.12) satisfies the iterated identity w, then G is a torsion group. This is true in the case of the commutator word w = [x1, x2 ] (G. Fernández- Alcober, M. Noce, G. Tracey, J. Algebra, 554(2020), 54–77).
self_contained_problem:
Let $w(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ be a group word on $n$ letters. For a group $G$, define iterates $e_0,e_1,\dots\colon G^n\to G$ by
$$e_0(x_1,\dots,x_n)=x_1, \qquad e_{k+1}(x_1,\dots,x_n)=w\bigl(e_k(x_1,\dots,x_n),\,x_2,\dots,x_n\bigr) \quad (k\ge 0).$$
The group $G$ is said to satisfy the Engel-type iterated identity $w$ if for every $x_1,\dots,x_n\in G$ there exists $m=m(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in\mathbb N$ such that $e_m(x_1,\dots,x_n)=1$.

Recall that a group $G$ acting faithfully on an infinite spherically homogeneous rooted tree $T$ is called a branch group if it acts transitively on each level of $T$ and, for every $n\ge 0$, the rigid level stabilizer (the direct product of the rigid stabilizers of all vertices at level $n$) has finite index in $G$.

Prove or disprove: for every non-trivial word $w$, if a finitely generated branch group $G$ satisfies the Engel-type iterated identity $w$, then $G$ is a torsion group.

(It is known that this holds for the commutator word $w(x_1,x_2)=[x_1,x_2]$.)

Algebra 554 (2020), 54–77, with related work on Engel elements in weakly branch groups). No reference verifying the full conjecture for arbitrary non-trivial words could be found, so the general case appears to remain open.

original_question: (D. Segal). A group word w is said to be concise in a class C of groups if for every group G in C such that the set Gw of word values of w in G is finite, the verbal subgroup w(G) = ⟨Gw ⟩ is also finite(see also Archive 2.45). Is every word concise in the class of residually finite groups? See(D. Segal, Words. Notes on verbal width in groups, Cambridge Univ. Press, 2009) for a partial solution.
self_contained_problem:
A group word is an element $w = w(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ of the free group $F_n$ on free generators $x_1, \ldots, x_n$. For a group $G$, the set of $w$-values in $G$ is
$$G_w = \{\, w(g_1, \ldots, g_n)^{\pm 1} : g_1, \ldots, g_n \in G \,\},$$
and the verbal subgroup of $G$ corresponding to $w$ is $w(G) = \langle G_w \rangle$.

A word $w$ is said to be concise in a class $\mathcal{C}$ of groups if, for every group $G \in \mathcal{C}$ with $G_w$ finite, the verbal subgroup $w(G)$ is also finite.

A group $G$ is residually finite if for every nontrivial $g \in G$ there exists a normal subgroup $N \trianglelefteq G$ of finite index with $g \notin N$.

Question: Is every group word $w$ concise in the class of residually finite groups? That is, must $w(G)$ be finite whenever $G$ is residually finite and $G_w$ is finite?
category_tag: Conciseness of words in residually finite groups
status_search_result: The general question of whether every word is concise in the class of residually finite groups remains open. Partial results exist for various families (e.g., Engel-type words, multilinear commutator words, generalizations of Engel words), and an active ERC/Horizon project ("GroupConciseness") and recent papers (2018–2025) continue to address the conjecture, but no full solution or counterexample is known.

original_question: A first order formula φ(x) in the group language with one free variable is said to be concise in a class C of groups if for every group G in C such that the set Gφ of elements in G satisfying φ is finite, the subgroup φ(G) generated by Gφ is also finite(cf. 21.105 and Archive 2.45). Is every formula with one free variable concise in the class of residually finite groups?
self_contained_problem:
Work in the first-order language of groups (one binary operation, one unary operation for inverse, and a constant for the identity). Let φ(x) be a first-order formula in this language with a single free variable x. For any group G, write
  G_φ = { g ∈ G : G ⊨ φ(g) },
and let φ(G) denote the subgroup of G generated by G_φ.

Given a class C of groups, the formula φ(x) is said to be concise in C if for every group G ∈ C the finiteness of G_φ implies the finiteness of φ(G).

A group G is called residually finite if for every nonidentity element g ∈ G there exists a finite group F and a homomorphism π : G → F with π(g) ≠ 1.

Question: Is every first-order formula φ(x) (in the group language, with one free variable) concise in the class of residually finite groups?
category_tag: Concise formulae in residually finite groups
status_search_result: A 2025 paper "Conciseness of first-order formulae" by establishes several partial positive results (e.g., every formula is concise in the class of abelian groups; every existential formula is concise in torsion-free locally nilpotent of class 2 groups; certain weakly rational and negative atomic combinations are concise in residually finite groups), but explicitly does not resolve the general question for residually finite groups, leaving it open.

Suppose that the countable group G can be partitioned into countably many dense subsets (with respect to its topology). Must G contain an expansive sequence of pairwise disjoint finite subsets?

original_question: For a finite group G let Cod(G) denote the set of irreducible character codegrees of G(see 20.78). Define σ(G) = max{|π(m)|: m ∈ Cod(G)}, where π(m) denotes the set of prime divisors of an integer m. It is proved that there exists a constant k such that |π(G)| ⩽ k · σ(G) for every finite group G(Y. Yang, G. Qian, J. Algebra, 478(2017), 215–219), but the estimate provided for k is very crude. Can the constant k be taken as 4?
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a finite group. For an irreducible complex character χ of G, define its codegree by cod(χ) = |G : ker(χ)| / χ(1), and let Cod(G) = { cod(χ) : χ ∈ Irr(G) }. For a positive integer m, let π(m) denote the set of prime divisors of m, and write π(G) = π(|G|). Define
   σ(G) = max{ |π(m)| : m ∈ Cod(G) }.
It is known that there is an absolute constant k such that |π(G)| ≤ k · σ(G) for every finite group G. Determine whether one may take k = 4; that is, does the inequality
   |π(G)| ≤ 4 · σ(G)
hold for every finite group G?
status_search_result: Searches reveal active recent research on character codegrees of finite groups (including work by Qian and collaborators), but no source establishes the optimal constant k = 4 in the inequality |π(G)| ≤ k · σ(G). The Yang–Qian result (J. Algebra 478, 2017) gives only a crude k, and no later paper found resolves whether k = 4 suffices. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Conjecture: The derived length of a finite solvable group G does not exceed |Cod(G)| − 1. The Fitting height of G is known to be at most min{|Cod(G)|−1, |Cod(G)|/2+1} (G. Qian, Y. Zeng, J. Group Theory, to appear).
self_contained_problem:
For a finite group $G$, let $\mathrm{Irr}(G)$ denote the set of complex irreducible characters of $G$. For $\chi \in \mathrm{Irr}(G)$, define the codegree of $\chi$ by
$$\mathrm{cod}(\chi) = \frac{[G:\ker\chi]}{\chi(1)},$$
and set
$$\mathrm{Cod}(G) = \{\mathrm{cod}(\chi) : \chi \in \mathrm{Irr}(G)\}.$$
Let $G$ be a finite solvable group, and let $dl(G)$ denote its derived length, i.e., the smallest non-negative integer $n$ such that the $n$-th term $G^{(n)}$ of the derived series is trivial.

Prove or disprove the following: for every finite solvable group $G$,
$$dl(G) \le |\mathrm{Cod}(G)| - 1.$$
category_tag: character codegrees of finite solvable groups
status_search_result: Recent literature on character codegrees treats the bound $dl(G) \le |\mathrm{Cod}(G)|-1$ for solvable groups as an open conjecture. Partial results bound the Fitting height by $\min\{|\mathrm{Cod}(G)|-1, |\mathrm{Cod}(G)|/2+1\}$ (Qian–Zeng), and related codegree analogues of Huppert's conjectures are actively studied, but no general proof of the derived-length bound has been published.

original_question: Let S be a nonabelian finite simple group, and x a nonidentity automorphism of S. Let α(x) be the smallest number of conjugates of x in G = ⟨x, Inn S⟩ that generate G. The values of α(x) had been studied in(R. Guralnick, J. Saxl, J. Algebra, 268, no. 2(2003), 519–571). (a) (R. Guralnick, J. Saxl). Conjecture: If S is an exceptional group of Lie type, then α(x) ⩽ 5 for every nonidentity automorphism x of S. (b) For each exceptional group S of Lie type, find the largest value of α(x).
self_contained_problem:
Let $S$ be a nonabelian finite simple group and let $x$ be a nonidentity automorphism of $S$. Identify $S$ with the inner automorphism group $\operatorname{Inn} S$ and set $G = \langle x, \operatorname{Inn} S\rangle$, an almost simple group with socle $S$. Define
$$\alpha(x) = \min\{\, k \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0} : \text{there exist } g_1,\ldots,g_k \in G \text{ with } \langle x^{g_1},\ldots,x^{g_k}\rangle = G \,\}.$$

Restrict attention to the case in which $S$ is an exceptional group of Lie type (i.e. $S$ is one of $G_2(q)$, $F_4(q)$, $E_6(q)$, ${}^2E_6(q)$, $E_7(q)$, $E_8(q)$, ${}^2B_2(q)$, ${}^2G_2(q)$, ${}^3D_4(q)$, or ${}^2F_4(q)$, in their simple versions).

(a) Prove or disprove: for every nonidentity automorphism $x$ of $S$, $\alpha(x) \leq 5$.

(b) For each exceptional simple group $S$ of Lie type, determine the exact value of $\max_{x} \alpha(x)$, where the maximum is taken over all nonidentity automorphisms $x$ of $S$.
category_tag: Generation of finite simple groups by conjugates
status_search_result: The Guralnick–Saxl conjecture on the bound α(x) ≤ 5 for exceptional groups of Lie type, and the determination of the exact maximum of α(x) for each such group, appear to remain open. Recent activity (e.g. work on sporadic socle cases settling α ≤ 4 with Fischer-group exceptions, and ongoing studies of generation by regular unipotent elements in groups of Lie type from 2024–2025) treats related cases and partial results, but no source verifying the conjecture in full or computing the maximum α(x) for all exceptional types was found.

original_question: Let S be a finite simple nonabelian group that is not isomorphic to any group 2B2(q). A nonidentity automorphism x of S is called a τ-automorphism if every two conjugates of x in ⟨x, Inn(S)⟩ generate a subgroup of order not divisible by 3. If S admits a τ-automorphism, we call S a τ-group. (a) List all τ-groups up to isomorphism. (b) Do τ-automorphisms of odd order exist?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S$ be a finite nonabelian simple group, and assume that $S$ is not isomorphic to any Suzuki group $\,^{2}B_{2}(q)$. Identify $S$ with its group of inner automorphisms $\operatorname{Inn}(S) \le \operatorname{Aut}(S)$. A nonidentity automorphism $x \in \operatorname{Aut}(S)$ is called a $\tau$-automorphism of $S$ if for every two conjugates $x_1, x_2$ of $x$ in the subgroup $\langle x, \operatorname{Inn}(S) \rangle \le \operatorname{Aut}(S)$, the order of the subgroup $\langle x_1, x_2 \rangle$ is not divisible by $3$. A finite nonabelian simple group $S$ (not isomorphic to any $\,^{2}B_{2}(q)$) is called a $\tau$-group if it admits at least one $\tau$-automorphism.

(a) Determine, up to isomorphism, all $\tau$-groups $S$.

(b) Decide whether there exists a $\tau$-group $S$ that admits a $\tau$-automorphism of odd order.

original_question: A nonempty class X of finite groups is said to be complete if X is closed under taking subgroups, homomorphic images, and extensions. The symmetric boundary of a complete class X other than the class of all finite groups is defined as the largest integer n such that Sn ∈ X. Every positive integer n ̸= 3 coincides with the symmetric boundary of some complete class. It is proved(mod CFSG, D. O. Revin, Algebra i Analiz, 37, no. 1(2025), 141–176(Russian)) that, for every complete class X, there exists a nonnegative integer m with the following property: for every finite group G and each conjugacy class D of G, if every m elements of D generate a subgroup belonging to X, then ⟨D⟩ ∈ X. The smallest such m is called the Baer–Suzuki width of X denoted by BS(X). It is also proved(mod CFSG, ibid.) that, for a complete class X of symmetric boundary n, the value of BS(X) is at least n and is bounded above in terms of n. For every positive integer n ̸= 3, let f+ (n) and f− (n) be respectively the maximum and the minimum of BS(X), where X runs over all complete classes of symmetric boundary n. (a) Find f+ (n) for n = 4, 5, 6. It is known that f+ (1) = 2, f+ (2) = 3, and f+ (n) = 2(n − 1) for n ⩾ 7. (b) Is it true that f− (n) = n for all n ̸= 3? This is known to be true for n = 1, 2, 4.
self_contained_problem:
Call a nonempty class X of finite groups complete if it is closed under taking subgroups, homomorphic images, and extensions. For a complete class X different from the class of all finite groups, define its symmetric boundary to be the largest integer n such that the symmetric group S_n belongs to X. (Every positive integer n ≠ 3 arises as the symmetric boundary of some complete class.) 

Assume the following result: for every complete class X there exists a smallest nonnegative integer m, denoted BS(X) and called the Baer–Suzuki width of X, with the property that, for every finite group G and every conjugacy class D of G, if every m-element subset of D generates a subgroup belonging to X, then the subgroup ⟨D⟩ generated by D belongs to X. Assume further that, for any complete class X with symmetric boundary n, one has BS(X) ≥ n and BS(X) is bounded above by a function of n.

For each positive integer n ≠ 3, let
   f_+(n) = max { BS(X) : X is a complete class of symmetric boundary n },
   f_−(n) = min { BS(X) : X is a complete class of symmetric boundary n }.

It is known that f_+(1) = 2, f_+(2) = 3, and f_+(n) = 2(n − 1) for all n ≥ 7, and that f_−(n) = n for n = 1, 2, 4.

(a) Determine the values of f_+(n) for n = 4, 5, 6.
(b) Decide whether f_−(n) = n holds for every positive integer n ≠ 3.

original_question: Let G be a finite group and p be a prime. Let Ψp,G be the class function of G which vanishes on all p-singular elements of G and whose value at each p-regular element x of G is the number of p-elements of CG(x). (a) Is it true that Ψp,G is a character of G? (b) If yes, can Ψp,G be afforded by a projective RG-module, where R is a complete discrete valuation ring of characteristic zero such that the field of fractions of R is a splitting field for G and its subgroups, and the residue field R/J(R) is a splitting field of characteristic p for G and its subgroups? It is known that Ψp,G is a character when G ≅ Sn for any positive integer n and any prime p(T. Scharf, J. Algebra, 139, no. 2(1991), 446–457).
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite group and let $p$ be a prime number. An element of $G$ is called a $p$-element if its order is a power of $p$, and a $p$-regular element if its order is coprime to $p$; otherwise it is called $p$-singular. For each $x \in G$, let $C_G(x)$ denote the centralizer of $x$ in $G$. Define the class function $\Psi_{p,G}: G \to \mathbb{Z}$ by
$$\Psi_{p,G}(x) = \begin{cases} \#\{y \in C_G(x) : y \text{ is a } p\text{-element}\}, & \text{if } x \text{ is } p\text{-regular},\\ 0, & \text{if } x \text{ is } p\text{-singular}.\end{cases}$$

(a) Is $\Psi_{p,G}$ a character of $G$ (i.e., the character of some finite-dimensional complex representation of $G$)?

(b) Assuming the answer to (a) is yes, let $R$ be a complete discrete valuation ring of characteristic zero whose field of fractions $K$ is a splitting field for $G$ and all its subgroups, and whose residue field $R/J(R)$ has characteristic $p$ and is a splitting field for $G$ and all its subgroups. Can $\Psi_{p,G}$ be afforded by a projective $RG$-module?

(It is known that $\Psi_{p,G}$ is a character whenever $G$ is isomorphic to a symmetric group $S_n$, for every positive integer $n$ and every prime $p$.)

original_question: A finite group G is called weakly ab-maximal if |H: [H, H]| ⩽ |G: [G, G]| for all H ⩽ G. Do weakly ab-maximal groups have bounded derived length? It is known that weakly ab-maximal groups are direct products of weakly abmaximal p-groups(F. Lisi, L. Sabatini, J. Group Theory, 27(2024), 1203–1217).
self_contained_problem:
Call a finite group $G$ weakly ab-maximal if for every subgroup $H \le G$ one has
$$|H:[H,H]| \;\le\; |G:[G,G]|,$$
where $[X,X]$ denotes the commutator subgroup of $X$. (It is known that every weakly ab-maximal finite group is a direct product of weakly ab-maximal $p$-groups.)

Question: Does there exist a constant $d$ (independent of $G$) such that every weakly ab-maximal finite group $G$ has derived length at most $d$? Equivalently, is the derived length of weakly ab-maximal finite groups bounded?
status_search_result: The problem is posed as a new question in the 2026 Kourovka Notebook of unsolved problems in group theory. Related work by Lisi–Sabatini (J. Group Theory 27 (2024)) establishes the direct product decomposition into p-group factors, and a subsequent arXiv preprint (2502.05821) constructs extremal ab-maximal p-groups answering related questions of González-Sánchez–Klopsch and Lisi–Sabatini, but no source found resolves the boundedness of the derived length for weakly ab-maximal groups. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Let C1,..., Cn be(left or right) cosets of a finite group G such that U:= C1 ∪ · · · ∪ Cn is not G. Is it always true that |G \ U | ⩾ |G|/2n? Affirmative answers are known in some special cases(B. Sambale, M. Tărnăuceanu, J. Algebraic Combin., 55(2022), 979–987).
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite group and let $C_1, C_2, \ldots, C_n$ be cosets of subgroups of $G$ (each $C_i$ is a left or right coset $g_iH_i$ for some subgroup $H_i \le G$ and some $g_i \in G$). Set
$$U := C_1 \cup C_2 \cup \cdots \cup C_n,$$
and assume $U \neq G$. Determine whether the inequality
$$|G \setminus U| \;\ge\; \frac{|G|}{2^n}$$
necessarily holds for every such configuration.

paper_title: A modified star formation law as a solution to open problems in galaxy evolution
context_brief: Galaxy-scale star-formation law in semi-analytic models
original_question: What galaxy-scale star-formation law should semi-analytic galaxy-formation models use so that they can reproduce observed galaxy populations across stellar mass, redshift, clustering, specific star-formation rate, and gas content? In this setting, semi-analytic models follow galaxy formation on dark-matter merger trees and include gas cooling, star formation, feedback, and merging. Standard prescriptions often use a Kennicutt-Schmidt-like law in which the star-formation rate is roughly proportional to cold gas mass, inversely proportional to a galactic-disk timescale, and cut off below a sharp low-gas-density threshold. The unresolved problem is to determine whether a successful law should remove the sharp cold-gas threshold, depend more strongly on host halo mass, have weak or no dependence on cosmic time, depend on molecular rather than total cold gas, and/or use a lower high-redshift normalization, while remaining physically plausible and observationally successful.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a semi-analytic model of galaxy formation built on cosmological dark-matter merger trees, in which each galaxy is followed through gas cooling from a hot halo, star formation in a cold gas reservoir, stellar and active-galactic-nucleus feedback, mergers, and environmental effects. Let M_cold denote the cold gas mass of a galaxy, t_disk a characteristic galactic-disk dynamical (or rotation) timescale, M_halo the host dark-matter halo mass, z the cosmological redshift, and M_H2 the molecular hydrogen mass within the cold gas. A standard Kennicutt–Schmidt-like prescription sets the star-formation rate to

    SFR = α · max(M_cold − M_crit, 0) / t_disk,

for a constant efficiency α and a sharp cold-gas surface-density threshold M_crit below which star formation is switched off.

Determine a galaxy-scale star-formation law SFR = F(M_cold, M_H2, M_halo, t_disk, z) such that, when inserted into an otherwise standard semi-analytic model, the resulting model galaxy population simultaneously reproduces observational constraints on:
  (i) the stellar mass function and its evolution with redshift,
  (ii) galaxy clustering as a function of stellar mass,
  (iii) the distribution of specific star-formation rates (sSFR = SFR / M_star) at low and high redshift, and
  (iv) cold gas (HI and H_2) contents of galaxies as a function of stellar mass.

In particular, decide which of the following modifications, individually or in combination, are necessary for such a law F:
  (a) removing the sharp threshold M_crit,
  (b) introducing an explicit dependence on host halo mass M_halo,
  (c) eliminating or strongly weakening the explicit dependence on cosmic time/redshift z beyond that carried by t_disk and the gas content,
  (d) replacing M_cold by the molecular gas mass M_H2 as the relevant fuel,
  (e) lowering the overall normalization of F at high redshift relative to the locally calibrated Kennicutt–Schmidt value,
while keeping F physically motivated and consistent with resolved observations of star-forming regions.
status_search_result: The question of the correct effective star-formation law to use in semi-analytic galaxy formation models remains an active and unresolved area. Subsequent semi-analytic and hydrodynamical works (e.g., Lagos et al., Somerville et al., Henriques et al., Croton et al. 2016) have explored H_2-based and modified laws, but no single prescription is universally accepted as simultaneously matching all of stellar mass functions, clustering, sSFR distributions, and gas contents across redshift. Hence the problem is best characterized as still open.

original_question: A group is boundedly acyclic if its bounded cohomology with trivial real coefficients vanishes in all positive degrees. Is every branch group boundedly acyclic?
self_contained_problem:
A group $G$ is called boundedly acyclic if its bounded cohomology with trivial real coefficients vanishes in all positive degrees, that is, $H_b^n(G;\mathbb{R}) = 0$ for every $n \geq 1$.

Recall that a branch group is a group $G$ acting faithfully and level-transitively by automorphisms on an infinite spherically homogeneous rooted tree $T$ such that, for every level $n \geq 0$, the rigid level stabilizer $\mathrm{Rist}_G(n)$ — defined as the direct product over all vertices $v$ at level $n$ of the rigid vertex stabilizers $\mathrm{Rist}_G(v) = \{g \in G : g \text{ fixes every vertex of } T \text{ not lying below } v\}$ — has finite index in $G$.

Question: Is every branch group boundedly acyclic?

Recent literature on bounded acyclicity (e.g., works on binate groups, lamplighters, and Thompson-like groups) provides many new examples of boundedly acyclic groups, but no source located identifies branch groups in general as boundedly acyclic or refutes this. The problem appears to be open.

original_question: (a) Does there exist a finitely generated simple group that is of exponential growth but not of uniformly exponential growth? (b) Does there exist a finitely generated hereditarily just-infinite group that is of exponential growth but not of uniformly exponential growth?
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a finitely generated group with finite generating set S, and let B_S(n) denote the set of elements of G expressible as words of length at most n in S ∪ S^{-1}. The exponential growth rate of G with respect to S is

  ω(G,S) := lim_{n→∞} |B_S(n)|^{1/n} ≥ 1.

The group G is said to have exponential growth if ω(G,S) > 1 for some (equivalently, every) finite generating set S, and to have uniformly exponential growth if

  ω(G) := inf { ω(G,S) : S a finite generating set of G } > 1.

Recall that a group is simple if it has no proper nontrivial normal subgroups, and that an infinite group G is just-infinite if every proper quotient of G is finite; G is hereditarily just-infinite if every finite-index subgroup of G is just-infinite.

Questions:
(a) Does there exist a finitely generated simple group that has exponential growth but does not have uniformly exponential growth?
(b) Does there exist a finitely generated hereditarily just-infinite group that has exponential growth but does not have uniformly exponential growth?
status_search_result: Wilson (2004) constructed finitely generated groups of exponential but non-uniformly exponential growth, and later examples include branch groups of this type. However, no construction is known to produce such groups that are simple, or hereditarily just-infinite. The literature on uniform exponential growth (Breuillard, Mann, Osin, Wilson, and others) does not record a resolution to either part, so both questions appear to remain open.

paper_title: A modified star formation law as a solution to open problems in galaxy evolution
context_brief: Low-mass stellar mass function without compensating failures
original_question: How can semi-analytic galaxy-formation models reproduce the low-mass end of the stellar mass function without creating other failures, such as too little star formation in low-mass galaxies at z = 0, too many red low-mass galaxies, excessive stellar mass functions at redshifts 0.8 to 2.5, overly high galaxy auto-correlation functions, physically hard-to-motivate supernova feedback efficiencies, or a dramatic overprediction of the cold gas content of galaxies? The open task is to find a physically motivated combination of star-formation, supernova-feedback, gas-cooling, and gas-heating or gas-expulsion prescriptions that resolves these linked constraints together.
status_search_result: This is a long-standing open problem in semi-analytic galaxy formation modeling. Subsequent works (e.g., Henriques et al. 2013, 2015, 2020 for the Munich/L-Galaxies model; Lu et al. 2014; Hirschmann et al. 2016; Cora et al. 2018 SAG; Croton et al. 2016 SAGE; Lagos et al. 2018 Shark) have made progress by introducing delayed/non-instantaneous reincorporation of ejected gas, environmental quenching, modified star-formation laws based on H_2, and AGN feedback variants, alleviating some tensions (notably the high-z stellar mass function and red-fraction problems). However, no single prescription set has been demonstrated to resolve all the listed constraints simultaneously while keeping supernova feedback within physical energy budgets and matching cold-gas contents; tensions in low-mass passive fractions, cold-gas content, and clustering of low-mass galaxies persist in current models.

paper_title: A modified star formation law as a solution to open problems in galaxy evolution
context_brief: Baryonic recipes versus cosmology in galaxy clustering
original_question: When semi-analytic galaxy-formation models fail to match observed galaxy two-point auto-correlation functions, is the mismatch primarily caused by the baryonic recipes used to assign stellar masses and galaxy properties, or by the underlying cosmology of the dark-matter simulation? The issue is nontrivial because galaxy positions are tied to haloes and subhaloes, while stellar-mass selection and clustering predictions can change substantially when the star-formation law changes, and similar clustering matches can be obtained with different cosmological parameters depending on the baryonic recipes.
self_contained_problem:
Consider semi-analytic models (SAMs) of galaxy formation built on top of a cosmological dark-matter N-body simulation. In such a model, halos and subhalos are identified in the simulation (which is fully specified by a set of cosmological parameters, e.g. Ωm, Ωb, σ8, ns, h), and a system of "baryonic recipes" (prescriptions for gas cooling, star formation, supernova and AGN feedback, mergers, etc., parametrized by a star-formation law and associated efficiencies) is applied to populate these halos and subhalos with galaxies of given stellar mass M⋆ and other properties.

For a stellar-mass-selected sample of model galaxies, one computes the projected two-point auto-correlation function w_p(r_p), or equivalently the real-space ξ(r), which can be compared directly with the same statistic measured for observed galaxy samples (e.g., from large redshift surveys).

Let C denote the choice of cosmological parameters and B the choice of baryonic recipes (including the form of the star-formation law). It is empirically observed that there exist pairs (C, B) ≠ (C′, B′) producing comparably good fits to the observed correlation function of stellar-mass-selected galaxies, so the two ingredients are degenerate.

Problem. Determine, in a quantitatively rigorous way, whether the persistent mismatch between SAM predictions and observed galaxy two-point auto-correlation functions for stellar-mass-selected samples is primarily attributable to:
  (a) deficiencies in the baryonic recipes B (in particular, the adopted star-formation law and the resulting stellar-mass assignments), or
  (b) the cosmological parameters C of the underlying dark-matter simulation,
or to a coupled combination of (a) and (b). Equivalently, characterize and break the degeneracy between B and C in the prediction of stellar-mass-selected galaxy clustering, and identify which component must be modified to simultaneously match observed correlation functions across stellar-mass bins and redshifts.
status_search_result: The question of disentangling baryonic-recipe effects from cosmological-parameter effects in semi-analytic predictions of galaxy clustering remains an active research topic. Subsequent works (e.g., on subhalo abundance matching, emulator-based SAM calibration, and joint clustering+lensing analyses) have constrained the degeneracy but have not definitively resolved which component dominates the mismatch in stellar-mass-selected auto-correlation functions; the issue is still considered open.

original_question: (A. Thom). Is there any group which is not isomorphic to the quotient of a residually finite group by an amenable normal subgroup?
self_contained_problem:
A group $G$ is called residually finite if for every non-identity element $g \in G$ there exists a finite group $F$ and a homomorphism $\varphi: G \to F$ such that $\varphi(g) \neq 1$. A group $A$ is called amenable if there exists a finitely additive, left-translation-invariant probability measure defined on all subsets of $A$.

Determine whether there exists a group $Q$ that is not isomorphic to $R/N$ for any residually finite group $R$ and any amenable normal subgroup $N \trianglelefteq R$. Equivalently, is every group a quotient of some residually finite group by an amenable normal subgroup?
status_search_result: The question, attributed to A. Thom, appears in a recent collection of new open problems in group theory (Kourovka Notebook). A search did not turn up any published resolution; the question relates to extensions/quotients involving sofic-like properties (since residually-finite-by-amenable groups are sofic), and no example of a group failing to be such a quotient is known. The status appears to be open.

paper_title: A modified star formation law as a solution to open problems in galaxy evolution
original_question: Is it necessary and physically justified for the star-formation efficiency in semi-analytic galaxy-formation models to have weak or no dependence on cosmic time? In the model family considered here, removing the usual time dependence of the star-formation rate may improve some observables, but it is unclear whether that modification is required and what physical mechanism, such as a time-dependent conversion of atomic to molecular gas, would produce the opposite time scaling from standard assumptions.
self_contained_problem:
In semi-analytic models of galaxy formation, the star-formation rate (SFR) of a galaxy is commonly parameterized as a function of its cold-gas mass M_cold, halo (or galaxy) mass M, and cosmic time t, typically in the form

  SFR(M_cold, M, t) = (M_cold / τ(M, t)),

where the characteristic time scale τ(M, t) explicitly depends on cosmic time t (for instance via the dynamical time of the host halo, which scales with the Hubble time). Consider the modified family of models in which τ is taken to be independent of cosmic time, so that

  SFR(M_cold, M) = M_cold / τ(M),

with τ(M) calibrated to reproduce simultaneously: (i) the observed stellar-mass function at z = 0 and at high redshift, (ii) the observed specific star-formation rate (SSFR = SFR / M_star) versus stellar mass M_star relation across redshifts 0 ≲ z ≲ 4, and (iii) the cold-gas-to-stellar mass ratios of galaxies as a function of M_star and z.

Address the following:

1. Determine whether removing the cosmic-time dependence of τ is strictly necessary in order to reproduce these three sets of observables, in the sense that no parameterization τ(M, t) with non-trivial t-dependence (consistent with standard halo dynamical-time scalings) can simultaneously fit (i)–(iii) within observational uncertainties.

2. Identify a physical mechanism — for example, a metallicity- and density-dependent conversion efficiency of atomic hydrogen (HI) to molecular hydrogen (H_2), with H_2 acting as the immediate fuel for star formation — that yields an effective τ whose cosmic-time scaling is opposite to that of the halo dynamical time (i.e., τ does not decrease with increasing redshift as t_dyn ∝ (1+z)^(-3/2) would suggest, but is instead approximately constant or increasing toward higher z). Derive, from such a mechanism, the predicted functional form of τ(M, t) and check whether it is consistent with the calibration required by (i)–(iii).
status_search_result: The question concerns whether the star-formation efficiency in semi-analytic galaxy-formation models must be cosmic-time independent and what physical mechanism (e.g., metallicity-dependent HI-to-H2 conversion) could justify the required time scaling. Subsequent work in galaxy-formation modeling (e.g., H2-based star-formation laws following Krumholz & Dekel and others, and later semi-analytic models by Lu, Somerville, Henriques, and collaborators) has explored time-(in)dependent efficiencies, but no definitive consensus has been reached that uniquely identifies the necessity of the modification or the responsible physical mechanism. The status is therefore best described as unknown / unresolved within the modeling community.

original_question: A pro-p group is(relatively) strictly finitely presented if it is the pro-p completion of a group that is finitely presented(respectively, finitely presented in some finitely-based variety of groups). A pro-p group is finitely axiomatizable if it is determined up to isomorphism by a single sentence in the first-order language of group theory. (a) Does there exist a(relatively) strictly finitely presented pro-p group that is not finitely axiomatizable in the class of all pro-p groups? (b) In particular, is every finitely generated free pro-p group finitely axiomatizable? See(A. Nies, K. Tent, D. Segal, Proc. London Math. Soc. (3), 123(2021), 597– 635; D. Segal, Preprint, 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.04816).
self_contained_problem:
Work in the first-order language of group theory (with signature consisting of multiplication, inversion, and the identity element).

Definitions.
- A pro-p group is the inverse limit of a system of finite p-groups; equivalently, a profinite group in which every open normal subgroup has index a power of p.
- The pro-p completion of an abstract group G is the inverse limit of the finite p-group quotients of G.
- A variety of groups is the class of all groups satisfying a given set of group identities (laws). A variety is finitely based if it can be defined by finitely many such identities.
- A pro-p group P is called strictly finitely presented if there exists a finitely presented abstract group G whose pro-p completion is isomorphic to P.
- A pro-p group P is called relatively strictly finitely presented if there exists an abstract group G that is finitely presented in some finitely based variety of groups, and whose pro-p completion is isomorphic to P.
- A pro-p group P is finitely axiomatizable in the class of all pro-p groups if there exists a single first-order sentence φ in the language of groups such that, for every pro-p group Q, one has Q ≅ P if and only if Q ⊨ φ.

Questions.
(a) Does there exist a (relatively) strictly finitely presented pro-p group that is not finitely axiomatizable in the class of all pro-p groups?
(b) In particular, is every finitely generated free pro-p group finitely axiomatizable in the class of all pro-p groups?

original_question: Let p be a prime number. A group Γ is called p-Jordan if there exist constants J and e such that any finite subgroup G ⊂ Γ contains a normal abelian subgroup of order coprime to p and of index at most J · |G(p) |e. (For example by the results of Brauer–Feit and Larsen–Pink, for any field K of characteristic p the group GLn(K) is p-Jordan with e = 3.) Let the p-Jordan exponent e(Γ) of the group Γ be the infimum of all constants e for which the above bound holds for some constant J = J(e). a) Is it true that this infimum is always attained? b) Is it true that e(Γ) ⩽ 3 for any p-Jordan group Γ?
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be a prime number. For a finite group $G$, denote by $|G(p)|$ the order of a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$ (equivalently, the largest power of $p$ dividing $|G|$). A group $\Gamma$ is called $p$-Jordan if there exist constants $J \ge 1$ and $e \ge 0$ such that every finite subgroup $G \subset \Gamma$ contains a normal abelian subgroup $A \trianglelefteq G$ whose order is coprime to $p$ and whose index satisfies
$$[G : A] \le J \cdot |G(p)|^{e}.$$
(By the theorems of Brauer–Feit and Larsen–Pink, for any field $K$ of characteristic $p$ the group $\mathrm{GL}_n(K)$ is $p$-Jordan with $e = 3$.) Define the $p$-Jordan exponent of $\Gamma$ by
$$e(\Gamma) := \inf\{ e \ge 0 : \text{there exists } J = J(e) \text{ such that the bound above holds for all finite } G \subset \Gamma \}.$$

(a) Is the infimum $e(\Gamma)$ always attained, i.e., is there always a constant $J$ such that the bound $[G:A] \le J \cdot |G(p)|^{e(\Gamma)}$ holds for every finite subgroup $G \subset \Gamma$?

(b) Is it true that $e(\Gamma) \le 3$ for every $p$-Jordan group $\Gamma$?

paper_title: Open problems in local discrete holomorphic dynamics
original_question: Let f be a holomorphic local dynamical system fixing a point p on a complex manifold M, and let K_f = ⋂_{k≥0} f^{-k}(U) be its stable set in a sufficiently small neighborhood U of p. What is the local topological structure of the germ of K_f at p? In particular, must K_f have non-empty interior, be locally connected at p, have K_f \ {p} connected, or impose specific homological or cohomological structure on U \ K_f near p?
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a complex manifold and let $f\colon M\to M$ be a holomorphic local dynamical system fixing a point $p\in M$; that is, $f$ is a holomorphic map defined in some open neighborhood of $p$ with $f(p)=p$. For a sufficiently small open neighborhood $U$ of $p$, define the stable set of $f$ at $p$ by
$$K_f \;=\; \bigcap_{k\ge 0} f^{-k}(U) \;=\; \{\, q\in U : f^j(q)\in U\text{ for all } j\ge 0\,\}.$$
Determine the local topological structure of the germ of $K_f$ at $p$. In particular, address each of the following:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Must $K_f$ have non-empty interior?
\item Is $K_f$ locally connected at $p$?
\item Is $K_f\setminus\{p\}$ connected?
\item What is the topological (homological, cohomological) structure of $U\setminus K_f$ in arbitrarily small neighborhoods of $p$?
\end{enumerate}
Provide either general answers valid for all such $f$, or a classification according to the local invariants of $f$ at $p$ (e.g., the spectrum of $df_p$).
status_search_result: The question concerning the topological structure of the local stable set $K_f$ for holomorphic local dynamical systems is a broad foundational question in local discrete holomorphic dynamics. Surveys by Abate and subsequent works (e.g., Reppekus 2023) treat partial results in specific regimes (hyperbolic, parabolic, elliptic, one-resonant cases) but no general answer is known; the question remains open in full generality.

paper_title: Open problems in local discrete holomorphic dynamics
original_question: For a holomorphic local dynamical system f with stable set K_f, what is the dynamical structure of the induced global system (K_f, f)? More specifically, how do orbits in K_f behave asymptotically near the fixed point, can they converge or exhibit chaotic behavior, can there be dense orbits, and what proper forward-invariant subsets of K_f can occur together with their internal dynamics?
self_contained_problem:
Let f: (C^n, p) → (C^n, p) be a holomorphic local dynamical system, i.e., f is a germ of a holomorphic self-map of C^n fixing the point p (so f(p) = p). Define the stable set of f at p to be
   K_f := { z ∈ U : f^k(z) is defined for all k ≥ 0 and f^k(z) → p as k → ∞ },
where U is a neighborhood of p on which iterates of f are defined as long as they stay in U. The pair (K_f, f) is then a (global) discrete dynamical system.

Investigate the dynamical structure of (K_f, f). In particular, address the following:

(a) Describe the asymptotic behavior of orbits {f^k(z)}_{k≥0} for z ∈ K_f. Under what conditions on f (e.g., on the spectrum of df_p, resonances, formal/analytic normal forms) do all orbits in K_f converge to p, and under what conditions can they exhibit chaotic behavior?

(b) Can the system (K_f, f) admit a dense orbit? Characterize the local dynamical systems for which topological transitivity (existence of a dense forward orbit) on K_f occurs.

(c) Classify the proper, forward f-invariant subsets S ⊂ K_f that can arise (e.g., stable manifolds, parabolic basins, Siegel-type domains, attracting petals, invariant analytic sets), and describe the internal dynamics of f restricted to each such S.
status_search_result: This is a broad guiding question in local discrete holomorphic dynamics in several complex variables. While many partial results exist in specific regimes (hyperbolic, attracting, parabolic Fatou-flower-type, Siegel/Bryuno, semi-attracting cases) due to work by Abate, Bracci, Hakim, Écalle, Rivi, and others, no complete description of the dynamics on the stable set K_f is known in general; the question is regarded as a long-standing open program rather than a single solved theorem.

original_question: Let w be a group word, and G a profinite group. Is it true that the cardinality of the set of w-values in G is either finite or at least continuum? An affirmative answer is known for several important words; see(E. Detomi, B. Klopsch, P. Shumyatsky, J. London Math. Soc. (2), 102(2020), 977–993).
self_contained_problem:
A profinite group is a topological group that is isomorphic to an inverse limit of finite groups; equivalently, a compact, Hausdorff, totally disconnected topological group. A group word is an element $w = w(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ of the free group on countably many generators $x_1, x_2, \dots$. For a group $G$, the set of $w$-values in $G$ is
$$G_w = \{\, w(g_1, \dots, g_n) : g_1, \dots, g_n \in G \,\}.$$

Question: Let $w$ be a group word and let $G$ be a profinite group. Is it true that the cardinality $|G_w|$ is either finite or at least $2^{\aleph_0}$ (the cardinality of the continuum)?
status_search_result: The question is the "strong conciseness" problem for profinite groups. It has been confirmed for several important classes of words — most notably for multilinear commutator words and for power words $x^q$ in the class of all profinite groups (Detomi–Klopsch–Shumyatsky, J. London Math. Soc. 102 (2020), 977–993), and for all words in nilpotent profinite groups. Subsequent work (e.g., Detomi–Klopsch–Shumyatsky, Math. Nachr. 2023; "On profinite groups admitting a word with only few values", arXiv:2401.15707) has extended the list of words for which it is known. The general case for an arbitrary word in an arbitrary profinite group remains open.

original_question: Is it true that the extension of the A. Agrachev–R. Gamkrelidze construction of groups from pre-Lie rings in(J. Soviet Math., 17(1981), 1650–1675) suggested in Definition 66 of(A. Smoktunowicz, J. Pure Appl. Algebra, 229, no. 12(2025), 108128) produces groups from pre-Lie rings? If this extended construction does give a group, then it also gives a brace, and so an affirmative answer to this question would have consequences for the theory of set-theoretic solutions of the Yang–Baxter equation and for the theory of braces.
self_contained_problem:
Background. A (left) pre-Lie ring is an abelian group $(A,+)$ equipped with a biadditive operation $\cdot:A\times A\to A$ satisfying the left pre-Lie identity
$$ (a\cdot b)\cdot c - a\cdot(b\cdot c) \;=\; (b\cdot a)\cdot c - b\cdot(a\cdot c)\qquad(a,b,c\in A). $$
The commutator $[a,b]:=a\cdot b-b\cdot a$ then turns $A$ into a Lie ring.

A (left) brace is an abelian group $(B,+)$ together with a second binary operation $\circ$ such that $(B,\circ)$ is a group and
$$ a\circ(b+c)+a \;=\; a\circ b+a\circ c\qquad(a,b,c\in B). $$
Braces provide non-degenerate involutive set-theoretic solutions of the Yang–Baxter equation.

The classical Agrachev–Gamkrelidze construction associates to a pre-Lie ring $A$ in which a suitable formal exponential/Magnus-type series converges (e.g. $A$ nilpotent, or a complete filtered $\mathbb Q$-pre-Lie algebra) a group structure $\circ$ on $A$ given by
$$ a\circ b \;=\; a+b+\Omega(a,b), $$
where $\Omega$ is a universal series of iterated pre-Lie products built from the pre-Lie operation, recovering on the Lie quotient the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula. Together with the additive structure this yields a brace $(A,+,\circ)$.

Extended construction. Replace the convergence/nilpotence requirement by a purely formal definition: for an arbitrary (not necessarily nilpotent, not necessarily $\mathbb Q$-divisible) pre-Lie ring $A$, define a partial binary operation $\circ$ on $A$ (where defined) by the same universal expression as in the Agrachev–Gamkrelidze formula, interpreted in $A$ via the pre-Lie product alone, with the symmetric brace-style identities used to extend it to all of $A$.

Question. Does this extended construction always produce a group? Equivalently: for every pre-Lie ring $A$, is the operation $\circ$ defined as above a well-defined associative operation on $A$ admitting two-sided inverses and the additive identity as neutral element, so that $(A,+,\circ)$ is a brace (and hence yields a set-theoretic solution of the Yang–Baxter equation)?
status_search_result: The question appears as a newly proposed problem in the 2026 update of a well-known problem collection on unsolved questions in group theory and related algebraic structures. Web searches return Smoktunowicz's recent works on the passage between braces and pre-Lie rings but no result establishing or refuting that the extended Agrachev–Gamkrelidze-type construction yields a group from an arbitrary pre-Lie ring; the problem is recorded as new and open.
