paper_title: Open problems in local discrete holomorphic dynamics
original_question: For holomorphic local dynamical systems at a fixed point in an n-dimensional complex manifold, find a class F of normal forms, preferably small, such that every system is locally conjugate to a possibly unique element of F under holomorphic, smooth, C^k, or topological conjugacy. In other words, can one classify these systems by explicit normal forms within each regularity category?
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be an $n$-dimensional complex manifold and let $p \in M$. A holomorphic local dynamical system at $p$ is a germ at $p$ of a holomorphic self-map $f : (M,p) \to (M,p)$ fixing $p$. After choosing local holomorphic coordinates centered at $p$, this is a germ $f : (\mathbb{C}^n, O) \to (\mathbb{C}^n, O)$ with $f(O)=O$.

Two such germs $f$ and $g$ are said to be:
- holomorphically locally conjugate if there exists a germ of biholomorphism $\varphi : (\mathbb{C}^n, O) \to (\mathbb{C}^n, O)$ with $\varphi \circ f = g \circ \varphi$;
- smoothly (resp. $C^k$, resp. topologically) locally conjugate if such a $\varphi$ exists as a germ of $C^\infty$ (resp. $C^k$, resp. continuous) local homeomorphism with $C^\infty$ (resp. $C^k$, resp. continuous) inverse.

Problem. For each of the four regularity categories (holomorphic, smooth, $C^k$, topological), exhibit a class $\mathcal{F}$ of holomorphic local dynamical systems at $O \in \mathbb{C}^n$, as small as possible, such that every holomorphic local dynamical system at $O \in \mathbb{C}^n$ is locally conjugate (in the chosen regularity) to at least one — and ideally to a unique — element of $\mathcal{F}$. In other words, produce a complete list of normal forms classifying all such germs up to holomorphic, smooth, $C^k$, or topological local conjugacy.
category_tag: Local holomorphic dynamics and normal forms
status_search_result: The classification of holomorphic local dynamical systems at a fixed point in $\mathbb{C}^n$ via normal forms is a long-standing open program. While many partial results exist (Poincaré–Dulac, Brjuno, Yoccoz, Écalle–Voronin in dimension 1; partial results for tangent-to-identity and semi-attracting cases in higher dimensions), no complete normal-form classification is known in any of the four regularity categories, and the problem is generally regarded as open.

original_question: A group G is said to be virtually special if G has a finite-index subgroup isomorphic to the fundamental group of a special complex(in the sense of F. Haglund, D. T. Wise, Geom. Funct. Anal., 17, no. 5(2008), 1551–1620; cf 20.60.) A group G is called a CAT(0) group if it acts properly discontinuously and cocompactly by isometries on a CAT(0) metric space. a) Is every CAT(0) free-by-cyclic group virtually special? b) A weaker question: does every CAT(0) free-by-cyclic group virtually embed into a right-angled Artin group?
self_contained_problem:
Definitions.

(1) A nonpositively curved cube complex X is called special (in the sense of Haglund–Wise) if its hyperplanes satisfy: each hyperplane is two-sided, no hyperplane self-intersects, no hyperplane self-osculates, and no two hyperplanes inter-osculate.

(2) A group G is called virtually special if G contains a finite-index subgroup isomorphic to the fundamental group of a compact special cube complex. Equivalently, G has a finite-index subgroup that embeds into a right-angled Artin group.

(3) A right-angled Artin group on a finite simplicial graph Γ with vertex set V and edge set E is A(Γ) = ⟨V | [v,w] = 1 for {v,w} ∈ E⟩.

(4) A group G is a CAT(0) group if there exists a CAT(0) geodesic metric space on which G acts properly discontinuously and cocompactly by isometries.

(5) A group G is free-by-cyclic if there is a short exact sequence 1 → F → G → Z → 1 with F a finitely generated free group; equivalently G ≅ F ⋊_φ Z for some automorphism φ of F.

Problem. Let G be a CAT(0) free-by-cyclic group.

(a) Must G be virtually special?

(b) (Weaker form.) Must G virtually embed in a right-angled Artin group, i.e., must G contain a finite-index subgroup isomorphic to a subgroup of some right-angled Artin group A(Γ)?

status_search_result: The question appears open in general. Known partial results: hyperbolic free-by-cyclic groups with irreducible monodromy act freely and cocompactly on CAT(0) cube complexes (Hagen–Wise) and are virtually special; tubular free-by-cyclic groups (Button) act freely on CAT(0) cube complexes, with virtual specialness established in tree cases. No source found resolving the question in full generality, including non-hyperbolic, non-tubular CAT(0) free-by-cyclic groups.

Let Fm be a free group of rank m and let ϕ ∈ Aut(Fm) be a polynomially growing automorphism of maximal degree m − 1, which means that for some(equivalently, any) free basis {x1,..., xm } of Fm, the sequence maxi |ϕn(xi)| grows at the rate of nm−1, where |g| denotes the minimal length of g in the xi and their inverses. a) Is the free-by-cyclic group Fm ⋊ϕ Z virtually special? b) In particular, are the Hydra groups Gm = Fm ⋊ Z = ⟨a1,..., am, t | t−1 a1 t = a1, t−1 ai t = ai ai−1 for all i > 1⟩ virtually special?

$$G_m=\langle a_1,\dots,a_m,t \mid t^{-1}a_1 t = a_1,\ t^{-1}a_i t = a_i a_{i-1}\ \text{for all } i>1\rangle$$
virtually special?

original_question: For holomorphic local dynamical systems at the origin of C^n, determine normal forms and complete invariants for the weaker equivalence relation of formal conjugacy, where maps are compared up to invertible formal power-series changes of coordinates rather than convergent holomorphic ones.
self_contained_problem:
Let f and g be germs at the origin of holomorphic self-maps of C^n fixing the origin (i.e., holomorphic local dynamical systems at O ∈ C^n). Two such germs f and g are said to be formally conjugate if there exists an invertible formal power-series change of coordinates h ∈ C[[z_1,...,z_n]]^n with h(0)=0 and dh(0) invertible such that h ∘ f = g ∘ h as formal power series. (This relation is weaker than holomorphic conjugacy, where h is required to be a convergent power series.)

Provide a classification of holomorphic local dynamical systems at O ∈ C^n up to formal conjugacy: exhibit explicit formal normal forms (canonical representatives in each formal-conjugacy class) and a complete set of invariants distinguishing the formal-conjugacy classes.

status_search_result: A general classification of holomorphic local dynamical systems at the origin of C^n up to formal conjugacy, including complete normal forms and invariants in arbitrary dimension, has not been achieved. paper_title: Open problems in local discrete holomorphic dynamics
original_question: Find natural families of one-variable elliptic holomorphic germs of the form f_{λ,a}(z)=λz+z^2 g_a(z), parametrized by a in some parameter space M, for which holomorphic linearizability is equivalent exactly to the Brjuno condition on the multiplier λ. In particular, is every elliptic polynomial, or even every elliptic cubic polynomial, holomorphically linearizable if and only if its multiplier is a Brjuno number?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C},0)$ denote the set of holomorphic germs $f:(\mathbb{C},0)\to(\mathbb{C},0)$. A germ $f(z)=\lambda z+O(z^2)$ with $|\lambda|=1$ and $\lambda$ not a root of unity is called elliptic (or irrationally indifferent). Such a germ is said to be holomorphically linearizable at $0$ if there exists a holomorphic germ $\varphi:(\mathbb{C},0)\to(\mathbb{C},0)$ with $\varphi'(0)\neq 0$ such that $\varphi^{-1}\circ f\circ\varphi(z)=\lambda z$. Writing $\lambda=e^{2\pi i\alpha}$ with $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$, and letting $(p_n/q_n)_{n\geq 0}$ be the continued fraction convergents of $\alpha$, the number $\lambda$ (equivalently $\alpha$) is said to satisfy the Brjuno condition if 
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{\log q_{n+1}}{q_n}<\infty.$$

(a) Find natural families $\{f_{\lambda,a}(z)=\lambda z+z^2 g_a(z)\}_{a\in M}\subset\mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C},0)$ of elliptic germs, parametrized by $a$ ranging over a parameter space $M$ (with $g_a$ holomorphic in a fixed neighborhood of $0$), such that for every $a\in M$ the germ $f_{\lambda,a}$ is holomorphically linearizable at $0$ if and only if $\lambda$ satisfies the Brjuno condition.

(b) In particular, decide the following: Is it true that every elliptic polynomial $P(z)=\lambda z+a_2 z^2+\cdots+a_d z^d$ (with $|\lambda|=1$, $\lambda$ not a root of unity, $d\geq 2$, $a_d\neq 0$) is holomorphically linearizable at $0$ if and only if $\lambda$ satisfies the Brjuno condition? In particular, is this true for every elliptic cubic polynomial $P(z)=\lambda z+a_2 z^2+a_3 z^3$ (with $a_3\neq 0$)?
status_search_result: The necessity of the Brjuno condition for holomorphic linearizability is known (by Yoccoz) for the quadratic family $z\mapsto\lambda z+z^2$, and sufficiency (Brjuno–Rüssmann) holds in general. Whether the Brjuno condition is necessary for linearizability of polynomials of degree $\geq 3$, and in particular for elliptic cubic polynomials, is reported in recent surveys as still open (Douady's conjecture). No proof of necessity in degree $\geq 3$ nor a counterexample appears in the literature.

original_question: (N. Brady). Do there exist finitely presented subgroups of right-angled Artin groups whose Dehn functions are super-exponential, or sub-exponential but not polynomial? Such subgroups are known to exist in general CAT(0) groups, whereas the only Dehn functions currently realized for subgroups of right-angled Artin groups are exponential and polynomial of arbitrary degree.
self_contained_problem:
A right-angled Artin group is a group given, for some finite simplicial graph $\Gamma$ with vertex set $V(\Gamma)$ and edge set $E(\Gamma)$, by the presentation
$$A_\Gamma = \langle\, V(\Gamma) \mid [v,w] = 1 \text{ for all } \{v,w\} \in E(\Gamma)\,\rangle.$$
For a finitely presented group $G = \langle X \mid R\rangle$, the Dehn function $\delta_G : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is defined by
$$\delta_G(n) = \max\{\operatorname{Area}(w) : w \text{ a null-homotopic word in } X^{\pm 1} \text{ with } |w| \le n\},$$
where $\operatorname{Area}(w)$ is the minimal $N$ such that $w$ can be written in the free group on $X$ as a product of $N$ conjugates of elements of $R^{\pm 1}$. The growth type of $\delta_G$ (up to the standard equivalence of functions $f \simeq g$ given by mutual domination after affine reparameterization) is a quasi-isometry invariant of $G$.

A function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is called:
- polynomial if $f(n) \simeq n^d$ for some integer $d \ge 1$;
- exponential if $f(n) \simeq 2^n$;
- super-exponential if $f(n)$ grows strictly faster than every function of the form $n \mapsto 2^n$ (e.g.\ $2^{2^n}$, $n!$, etc.);
- sub-exponential but not polynomial if $f(n)$ is bounded above by every function of exponential type up to equivalence, yet is not equivalent to any polynomial $n^d$ (e.g.\ $n^{\log n}$).

Question: Does there exist a finite simplicial graph $\Gamma$ and a finitely presented subgroup $H \le A_\Gamma$ of the corresponding right-angled Artin group whose Dehn function $\delta_H$ is either super-exponential, or sub-exponential but not polynomial?

However, no examples with super-exponential or with sub-exponential non-polynomial Dehn functions are known among finitely presented subgroups of RAAGs, and the problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Let G be a right-angled Artin group. Is the stable commutator length scl(g) a rational number for every g ∈ [G, G]? For free groups this is true by Calegari’s Rationality Theorem. (See 18.40 for the definition of scl(g).)
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Gamma$ be a finite simple graph with vertex set $V$ and edge set $E$. The right-angled Artin group on $\Gamma$ is the group
$$G = \langle V \mid [v,w] = 1 	ext{ for all } \{v,w\}\in Eangle.$$
For an element $g$ in the commutator subgroup $[G,G]$, the commutator length $\mathrm{cl}(g)$ is the least integer $n\ge 0$ such that $g$ can be written as a product of $n$ commutators in $G$. The stable commutator length is
$$\mathrm{scl}(g) = \lim_{n	o\infty}  rac{\mathrm{cl}(g^n)}{n},$$
which exists in $[0,\infty)$ by subadditivity. (For free groups it is a theorem of Calegari that $\mathrm{scl}(g)\in\mathbb{Q}$ for every $g\in [F,F]$.)

Question: Is it true that for every right-angled Artin group $G$ (i.e., for every finite simple defining graph $\Gamma$) and every $g\in [G,G]$, the stable commutator length $\mathrm{scl}(g)$ is a rational number?
status_search_result: The question of whether scl is rational on the commutator subgroup of every right-angled Artin group appears to remain open. Recent work of Chen and Heuer (2020) on scl in RAAGs and Coxeter groups establishes spectral gaps and shows every rational $q\ge 1$ is realized as scl of some integral chain in a RAAG, and proves that computing scl in RAAGs is NP-hard, but does not establish (nor refute) rationality of scl for all elements of $[G,G]$ in an arbitrary RAAG.

original_question: Let B be the Brjuno function on irrational angles and let r(θ) denote the infimum of the radii of convergence of linearizations for injective holomorphic germs on the unit disk with multiplier e^{2πiθ}. Does the function log r(θ) + B(θ) extend from irrational θ to all of [0,1) as a 1/2-Hölder continuous function?
self_contained_problem:
For an irrational number $\theta\in[0,1)$ with continued fraction expansion $\theta=[a_1,a_2,\dots]$, let $p_n/q_n$ denote the $n$-th convergent. The Brjuno function is defined by
$$B(\theta)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\beta_{n-1}(\theta)\,\log\frac{1}{\|q_n\theta\|},$$
where $\beta_{-1}=1$ and $\beta_{n-1}=\prod_{k=1}^{n}\{G^{k}(\theta)\}$ with $G$ the Gauss map (equivalently, the standard Yoccoz Brjuno sum), so that the set of Brjuno numbers is exactly $\{\theta : B(\theta)<\infty\}$.

For an irrational $\theta\in[0,1)$, let
$$r(\theta)=\inf\{\rho(f):f\in\mathcal{S}_\theta\},$$
where $\mathcal{S}_\theta$ is the family of injective (univalent) holomorphic germs $f:(\mathbb{D},0)\to(\mathbb{C},0)$ with $f'(0)=e^{2\pi i\theta}$, and $\rho(f)$ is the radius of convergence of the unique formal linearization $h(z)=z+\cdots$ of $f$ (i.e.\ $h^{-1}\circ f\circ h(z)=e^{2\pi i\theta}z$). By Yoccoz's theorem, $r(\theta)>0$ if and only if $\theta$ is a Brjuno number, and the function $\theta\mapsto\log r(\theta)+B(\theta)$ is bounded on the set of Brjuno numbers.

Question: Does the function $\theta\mapsto \log r(\theta)+B(\theta)$, defined on the set of Brjuno numbers in $[0,1)$, extend to a function on $[0,1)$ that is Hölder continuous with exponent $1/2$?
status_search_result: The 1/2-Hölder regularity of $\log r + B$ remains a conjecture in the general univalent-germ setting. Partial progress exists: for the quadratic family, continuous extension is known and 1/2-Hölder regularity has been proved for high-type irrationals; related Hölder regularity results have been obtained for variants of the Brjuno function (e.g., $(0,\nu)$-Brjuno functions, $k$-Brjuno and Wilton functions). The full conjecture for $\log r + B$ as stated has not been verified in the literature found.

paper_title: Open problems in local discrete holomorphic dynamics
original_question: For one-variable elliptic holomorphic germs with a Cremer fixed point at the origin, are two topological invariants sufficient for complete topological classification: the multiplier f'(0) and the homeomorphism class of the stable set germ K_f at the origin? Equivalently, do those two data completely determine the topological local conjugacy class of a Cremer point?
self_contained_problem:
Let $f \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C}, 0)$ be a germ of holomorphic self-map of $(\mathbb{C}, 0)$ fixing the origin, with multiplier $\lambda := f'(0)$ of the form $\lambda = e^{2\pi i \alpha}$ with $\alpha \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}$, and assume the origin is a Cremer point of $f$ (i.e., $f$ is not holomorphically linearizable at $0$). Define the (local) stable set (filled Julia set germ) of $f$ at $0$ as
$$K_f := \{\, z \in U : f^{\circ n}(z) \in U \text{ for all } n \ge 0 \,\}$$
considered as a germ at $0$, where $U$ is a sufficiently small neighborhood of $0$ on which $f$ is defined.

Two such germs $f, g$ are said to be topologically locally conjugate at $0$ if there exist neighborhoods $U_f, U_g$ of $0$ and a germ of homeomorphism $h : (U_f, 0) \to (U_g, 0)$ with $h \circ f = g \circ h$ near $0$.

Question: Is it true that two elliptic holomorphic germs $f, g \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C}, 0)$ each having a Cremer point at the origin are topologically locally conjugate at $0$ if and only if
(i) $f'(0) = g'(0)$, and
(ii) the germs $(K_f, 0)$ and $(K_g, 0)$ are homeomorphic?

Equivalently, do the multiplier $f'(0)$ and the homeomorphism class of the stable set germ $K_f$ at $0$ form a complete set of topological invariants for the local topological dynamics at a Cremer fixed point?
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not surface any published resolution of this classification question. Recent work on hedgehogs and neutral germs (e.g., Stony Brook IMS preprints) continues to investigate the local topology near Cremer points but does not announce a complete topological classification by multiplier and stable-set germ. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Two groups G1 and G2 are said to be commensurable if there exist finiteindex subgroups H1 ⩽ G1 and H2 ⩽ G2(not necessarily of the same index) such that H1 ∼= H2. Let A[F4 ] and A[H4 ] denote the Artin groups of spherical types F4 and H4, respectively. Are these two groups commensurable? This is the most difficult case in the classification of Artin groups of spherical type up to commensurability.
self_contained_problem:
Two groups G₁ and G₂ are called commensurable if there exist finite-index subgroups H₁ ≤ G₁ and H₂ ≤ G₂ (the indices need not be equal) such that H₁ ≅ H₂.

For a Coxeter graph Γ of spherical type with vertex set S = {s₁, …, sₙ} and edge labels m(sᵢ, sⱼ) ∈ {2, 3, 4, …} (with m(sᵢ, sⱼ) = 2 meaning no edge), the associated Artin group A[Γ] is defined by the presentation
   A[Γ] = ⟨ s₁, …, sₙ | sᵢsⱼsᵢ… = sⱼsᵢsⱼ… (each side of length m(sᵢ, sⱼ)) for all i ≠ j with m(sᵢ, sⱼ) < ∞ ⟩.

Let A[F₄] denote the Artin group whose Coxeter graph is the linear diagram on four vertices s₁ — s₂ =⁴ s₃ — s₄ (i.e., m(s₁,s₂) = m(s₃,s₄) = 3, m(s₂,s₃) = 4, and all other off-diagonal labels equal 2). Let A[H₄] denote the Artin group whose Coxeter graph is the linear diagram on four vertices t₁ =⁵ t₂ — t₃ — t₄ (i.e., m(t₁,t₂) = 5, m(t₂,t₃) = m(t₃,t₄) = 3, and all other off-diagonal labels equal 2).

Question: Are the Artin groups A[F₄] and A[H₄] commensurable?
status_search_result: Cumplido and Paris reduced the classification of Artin groups of spherical type up to commensurability to six undecided pairs, including (F₄, H₄). Soroko (2021) resolved (F₄, D₄) and (H₄, D₄) by showing those pairs are not commensurable, but the case (F₄, H₄) remains unresolved in the literature available through 2026.

original_question: If two Artin groups of spherical type are quasi-isometric, must they be commensurable? (This is not true for right-angled Artin groups.)
self_contained_problem:
Let $W$ be a finite Coxeter group with Coxeter system $(W,S)$ and Coxeter matrix $(m_{st})_{s,t\in S}$, where $m_{ss}=1$ and $m_{st}=m_{ts}\in\{2,3,\dots,\infty\}$ for $s\neq t$. The associated Artin group of spherical type is
$$A = \bigl\langle S \,\bigm|\, \underbrace{sts\cdots}_{m_{st}\text{ factors}} = \underbrace{tst\cdots}_{m_{st}\text{ factors}} \text{ for all } s\neq t \text{ with } m_{st}<\infty \bigr\rangle,$$
where $W$ is required to be finite (so the Coxeter diagram is a disjoint union of diagrams of types $A_n$, $B_n$, $D_n$, $E_6$, $E_7$, $E_8$, $F_4$, $G_2$, $H_3$, $H_4$, or $I_2(p)$).

Two finitely generated groups $G_1$ and $G_2$ are quasi-isometric if, equipped with word metrics from finite generating sets, there exist a map $f:G_1\to G_2$ and constants $K\geq 1$, $C\geq 0$ such that
$$\tfrac{1}{K} d(x,y) - C \le d(f(x),f(y)) \le K\, d(x,y) + C \quad\text{for all } x,y\in G_1,$$
and every point of $G_2$ lies within distance $C$ of $f(G_1)$. Two groups are commensurable if they contain isomorphic finite-index subgroups.

Question: If $A$ and $A'$ are two Artin groups of spherical type that are quasi-isometric as finitely generated groups, must $A$ and $A'$ be commensurable?
status_search_result: Recent work (Cumplido–Paris, 2019 and follow-ups through 2024) classifies spherical-type Artin groups up to commensurability almost completely, with a few exceptional pairs (e.g. (F4,D4), (H4,D4), (F4,H4), (E6,D6), (E7,D7), (E8,D8)) recently resolved to be non-commensurable. However, the quasi-isometric classification of spherical-type Artin groups, and in particular whether QI implies commensurability for them, does not appear to be established in the literature; the analogous question for RAAGs is known to fail in general. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open problems in local discrete holomorphic dynamics
original_question: Given two one-variable germs tangent to the identity, is there an effective decision procedure for determining whether they are holomorphically locally conjugate, despite the impracticality of explicitly computing the full Écalle-Voronin functional invariants in general?
self_contained_problem:
Let f, g : (C,0) → (C,0) be two holomorphic germs of one complex variable that are tangent to the identity at the origin, i.e. each admits a power-series expansion of the form

   f(z) = z + a_{k+1} z^{k+1} + a_{k+2} z^{k+2} + ⋯,    a_{k+1} ≠ 0,
   g(z) = z + b_{m+1} z^{m+1} + b_{m+2} z^{m+2} + ⋯,    b_{m+1} ≠ 0,

with k, m ≥ 1. Two such germs f and g are said to be holomorphically locally conjugate if there exists a holomorphic germ φ : (C,0) → (C,0) with φ(0) = 0 and φ'(0) ≠ 0 such that φ ∘ f = g ∘ φ in some neighborhood of 0.

It is classically known (Écalle–Voronin–Martinet–Ramis) that the holomorphic conjugacy class of a tangent-to-identity germ is determined by a complete set of functional invariants — the Écalle–Voronin moduli (or equivalently the horn maps) — but these invariants are in general transcendental and not effectively computable from the Taylor coefficients of the germ.

Question: Does there exist an effective (algorithmic) decision procedure that, given as input the Taylor coefficients (or any finitely presented description) of two tangent-to-identity holomorphic germs f and g, decides in finitely many steps whether f and g are holomorphically locally conjugate?
status_search_result: While the Écalle–Voronin–Martinet–Ramis theory provides complete functional invariants (horn maps) for the analytic classification of tangent-to-identity germs, these invariants are transcendental and not directly extractable from Taylor coefficients. Recent literature (e.g., works on horn maps and on residues/conjugacies for parabolic germs in finite regularity, 2023) continues to study these invariants but does not provide an effective decision algorithm for analytic conjugacy from formal data. No source found announces a solution to the effective-conjugacy problem; it appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open problems in local discrete holomorphic dynamics
original_question: Given two one-variable parabolic germs, is there an effective decision procedure for determining whether they are holomorphically locally conjugate, taking into account the multiplier, parabolic multiplicity, iterative residue, and the usually intractable functional invariants that complete the holomorphic classification?
self_contained_problem:
Let f and g be two parabolic germs of one-variable holomorphic diffeomorphisms fixing the origin, that is, f, g ∈ C{z} with f(0)=g(0)=0 and f'(0), g'(0) roots of unity (so that some iterate has the form z + a z^{k+1} + ...). Their holomorphic local classification is given by the multiplier f'(0), the parabolic multiplicity (equivalently, the integer k), the iterative residue, and the Écalle–Voronin functional invariants (the equivalence class of the horn maps).

Problem: Devise an effective decision procedure (an algorithm taking finite descriptions of f and g as input, e.g. truncated power series with computable coefficients, plus oracle access where appropriate) that decides whether f and g are holomorphically locally conjugate at 0 — i.e., whether there exists a germ h of holomorphic diffeomorphism with h(0)=0 and h ∘ f = g ∘ h. The procedure must take into account the multiplier, the parabolic multiplicity, the iterative residue, and the (in general intractable) functional Écalle–Voronin invariants, and produce a definitive yes/no answer.
status_search_result: The classification of one-dimensional parabolic germs via multiplier, parabolic multiplicity, iterative residue, and Écalle–Voronin functional invariants (horn maps) is classical and complete. However, the Écalle–Voronin invariants are functional and generally intractable; resurgent methods (Écalle, and recent work by Dudko–Sauzin) express them as convergent numerical series, but no general effective decision algorithm for conjugacy is known. The question of an effective conjugacy-decision procedure remains open.

original_question: Let f be a non-invertible dominant holomorphic germ in End(C^n, O), and let c_∞(f)=lim_{k→∞} c(f^k)^{1/k} be its asymptotic attraction rate, where c(f) is the order of f. Must c_∞(f) always be an algebraic integer of degree at most n? More precisely, do there exist integers a_0, ..., a_{n-1} with c_∞^n + a_{n-1} c_∞^{n-1} + ... + a_0 = 0, and does there also exist δ in (0,1] such that δ c_∞^k ≤ c(f^k) ≤ c_∞^k for all k≥1?
self_contained_problem:
Let $f:(\mathbb{C}^n,O)\to(\mathbb{C}^n,O)$ be a holomorphic germ fixing the origin, written as a convergent power series with no constant term. Assume $f$ is dominant (its Jacobian determinant does not vanish identically) and non-invertible (so $f$ is not a biholomorphism near $O$). Define the order of $f$ at $O$ by
$$c(f)=\min\{|\alpha|:\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^n,\ \text{the coefficient of }z^\alpha\text{ in some component of }f\text{ is nonzero}\},$$
i.e. the smallest degree appearing in the Taylor expansion of $f$ at $O$. The asymptotic attraction rate of $f$ is
$$c_\infty(f)=\lim_{k\to\infty} c(f^k)^{1/k},$$
where $f^k$ denotes the $k$-fold composition; this limit exists by submultiplicativity.

Prove or disprove the following two statements:

(a) The number $c_\infty(f)$ is an algebraic integer of degree at most $n$; equivalently, there exist integers $a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_{n-1}\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that
$$c_\infty(f)^n + a_{n-1}\,c_\infty(f)^{n-1} + \cdots + a_1\,c_\infty(f) + a_0 = 0.$$

(b) There exists a constant $\delta\in(0,1]$ such that
$$\delta\,c_\infty(f)^k \le c(f^k) \le c_\infty(f)^k\qquad\text{for all integers }k\ge 1.$$
status_search_result: In dimension n=2, the case of dominant superattracting germs has been treated: Favre–Jonsson (arXiv:1209.3450) show that the sequence c(f^k) eventually satisfies an integral linear recursion of order at most two, which yields the algebraic-integer property and the two-sided bounds in that setting. For general n and general dominant non-invertible germs, the questions appear to remain open.

paper_title: Open problems in local discrete holomorphic dynamics
original_question: For a non-invertible dominant germ f in End(C^n, O), does the sequence of orders of its iterates, {c(f^k)}_{k∈N}, eventually satisfy a linear recurrence relation with integer coefficients?
self_contained_problem:
Let $f:(\mathbb{C}^n,O)\to(\mathbb{C}^n,O)$ be a holomorphic germ fixing the origin, and assume $f$ is non-invertible (i.e. $df_O$ is not invertible) and dominant (i.e. $\det df \not\equiv 0$ as a germ). For a holomorphic germ $g:(\mathbb{C}^n,O)\to(\mathbb{C}^n,O)$, define its order $c(g)$ to be the largest integer $c\ge 1$ such that every component of $g$ (in some, equivalently any, system of local coordinates centered at $O$) belongs to $\mathfrak{m}^c$, where $\mathfrak{m}$ is the maximal ideal of the local ring of germs at $O$. Equivalently, $c(g)$ is the minimum over the components $g_j$ of the order of vanishing of $g_j$ at $O$.

Consider the sequence $\{c(f^k)\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ of orders of the iterates $f^k=f\circ\cdots\circ f$ ($k$ times).

Question: Does there exist an integer $K\ge 1$, an integer $r\ge 1$, and integers $a_1,\dots,a_r\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that
$$c(f^{k+r}) = a_1\, c(f^{k+r-1}) + a_2\, c(f^{k+r-2}) + \cdots + a_r\, c(f^k) \qquad \text{for all } k\ge K\,?$$

In other words, is it true that for every non-invertible dominant germ $f\in\operatorname{End}(\mathbb{C}^n,O)$, the sequence of orders of its iterates eventually satisfies a linear recurrence relation with integer coefficients?
status_search_result: In dimension $n=2$ (for superattracting dominant germs), the analogous sequence of attraction rates is known to eventually satisfy an integral linear recursion of order at most two, established by Favre and Jonsson and extended in subsequent work (e.g., Gignac–Ruggiero, "Growth of attraction rates for iterates of a superattracting germ in dimension two", 2012). For general $n\ge 3$ and arbitrary non-invertible dominant germs, no proof or counterexample appears to be available, so the problem is partially solved (settled in dimension two, open in higher dimensions).

original_question: Does a group need to have a subnormal abelian series if every countable subgroup of it has such a series?
self_contained_problem:
A subnormal series of a group $G$ is a finite chain of subgroups
$$\{e\} = G_0 \trianglelefteq G_1 \trianglelefteq \cdots \trianglelefteq G_n = G$$
such that each $G_i$ is normal in $G_{i+1}$. The series is called abelian (or solvable) if every factor $G_{i+1}/G_i$ is abelian; equivalently, $G$ is solvable.

Question: Suppose $G$ is a group with the property that every countable subgroup of $G$ admits a subnormal abelian series (i.e., is solvable). Must $G$ itself admit a subnormal abelian series (i.e., be solvable)?

paper_title: Open problems in local discrete holomorphic dynamics
original_question: Let f be a superattracting germ in End(C^n, O), and let H be the first nonzero homogeneous term in its expansion. If H is degenerate, meaning H(v)=0 for some nonzero v, and if the postcritical set of f is an analytic cone near the origin, must f nevertheless be holomorphically locally conjugate to H?
self_contained_problem:
Let $f \in \operatorname{End}(\mathbb{C}^n, O)$ be a holomorphic germ fixing the origin, with Taylor expansion at $O$ written as $f = H + H_{\nu+1} + H_{\nu+2} + \cdots$, where each $H_k$ is a homogeneous polynomial map of degree $k$ from $\mathbb{C}^n$ to $\mathbb{C}^n$ and $H = H_\nu$ is the first nonzero homogeneous term, with $\nu \ge 2$ (so that $f$ is superattracting at $O$). Say that $H$ is degenerate if there exists a nonzero vector $v \in \mathbb{C}^n$ with $H(v) = 0$. The critical set $\operatorname{Crit}(f)$ is the analytic hypersurface where the Jacobian determinant of $f$ vanishes, and the postcritical set is $\operatorname{PC}(f) = \bigcup_{k \ge 1} f^k(\operatorname{Crit}(f))$, viewed as a germ at $O$. Assume:

(i) $H$ is degenerate;
(ii) the germ of $\operatorname{PC}(f)$ at $O$ is an analytic cone (i.e. invariant under the dilations $z \mapsto \lambda z$ for $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}^*$, as a germ at $O$).

Question: Must $f$ then be holomorphically locally conjugate, near $O$, to its leading homogeneous term $H$? That is, does there exist a local biholomorphism $\varphi$ of $(\mathbb{C}^n, O)$ such that $\varphi^{-1} \circ f \circ \varphi = H$ as germs at $O$?
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open problem on the classification of degenerate superattracting germs in several complex variables. Known results (e.g., Böttcher-type theorems by Buff–Epstein–Koch and related work) establish that in the non-degenerate case, the analytic-cone condition on the postcritical set characterizes holomorphic conjugacy to the leading homogeneous term, but the degenerate case appears to remain unresolved in the literature, and no published proof or counterexample was located.

paper_title: Open problems in local discrete holomorphic dynamics
original_question: Let f be a superattracting germ in End(C^n, O) with first nonzero homogeneous term H, and suppose the postcritical set of f is a topological cone near the origin. Under what additional conditions is f topologically locally conjugate to H? In particular, is the answer always yes when H is non-degenerate?
self_contained_problem:
Let $f \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C}^n, O)$ be a holomorphic germ fixing the origin, written as $f(z) = H(z) + \text{(higher-order terms)}$, where $H$ is the first nonzero homogeneous term of $f$ at the origin. Assume that $f$ is superattracting at $O$, i.e., the differential $df_O$ vanishes (so $\deg H \geq 2$). Recall that the critical set of $f$ is $\mathrm{Crit}(f) = \{z : \det df_z = 0\}$, and the postcritical set is $\mathrm{PC}(f) = \bigcup_{k \geq 1} f^k(\mathrm{Crit}(f))$. The homogeneous map $H$ is called non-degenerate if $H^{-1}(O) = \{O\}$.

A subset $S \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ containing $O$ is a topological cone near $O$ if there exist a neighborhood $U$ of $O$, a topological space $L$, and a homeomorphism $\Phi: U \to (L \times [0,1))/(L \times \{0\})$ sending $O$ to the cone point and sending $S \cap U$ onto a sub-cone of the form $(K \times [0,1))/(K \times \{0\})$ for some $K \subset L$.

Suppose that the postcritical set of $f$ is a topological cone near the origin. 

(a) Determine sufficient additional conditions under which $f$ is topologically locally conjugate to $H$ at $O$ (i.e., there exists a germ of homeomorphism $\varphi$ at $O$ with $\varphi(O) = O$ such that $\varphi \circ f = H \circ \varphi$).

(b) In particular, decide whether such a topological local conjugacy between $f$ and $H$ always exists whenever $H$ is non-degenerate.
status_search_result: A targeted search for a topological-cone criterion implying topological local conjugacy of a superattracting germ in $\mathbb{C}^n$ to its leading homogeneous term did not return any resolution. Surveys on local discrete holomorphic dynamics list this as an open problem, and follow-up work (e.g., on attraction rates of superattracting germs in dimension two) addresses related but distinct questions. No published proof or counterexample resolving the criterion was located.

original_question: For a finite group G, let the type of G be the function on positive integers whose value at n is the number of solutions of the equation xn = 1 in G. a) Is it true that a group having the same type as a group with trivial solvable radical must also have trivial solvable radical? Note that there are solvable and nonsolvable groups with the same type(see 12.37). b) Is it true that a group having the same type as an almost simple group must be isomorphic to it? This is true for a group having the same type as a simple group, as follows from the affirmative answer to 12.39(in Archive).
self_contained_problem:
For a finite group $G$, define the type of $G$ to be the function $t_G:\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\to\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ given by
$$t_G(n) = |\{x\in G : x^n = 1\}|.$$
Two finite groups $G$ and $H$ are said to have the same type if $t_G(n) = t_H(n)$ for every positive integer $n$. Recall that the solvable radical of a finite group is its largest solvable normal subgroup, and a finite group is called almost simple if it has a non-abelian simple normal subgroup $S$ such that $S \le G \le \mathrm{Aut}(S)$.

Answer the following questions.

(a) Suppose $G$ and $H$ are finite groups of the same type. If $G$ has trivial solvable radical, must $H$ also have trivial solvable radical?

(b) Suppose $G$ is a finite group having the same type as a finite almost simple group $A$. Must $G$ be isomorphic to $A$?

original_question: Let f and g be superattracting germs in End(C^n, O) of the same order. Is local topological or holomorphic conjugacy between f and g completely determined by the corresponding conjugacy type of their postcritical sets? Equivalently, does a local homeomorphism or biholomorphism sending PCrit(f) onto PCrit(g) suffice, together with equality of order, to characterize local conjugacy?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C}^n,O)$ denote the set of germs at the origin of holomorphic self-maps $f:(\mathbb{C}^n,O)\to(\mathbb{C}^n,O)$ fixing $O$. Such a germ $f$ is said to be superattracting at $O$ if its differential $df_O$ vanishes. The order $c(f)$ of a superattracting germ $f$ at $O$ is the smallest integer $k\ge 2$ such that some homogeneous component of $f$ of degree $k$ in its Taylor expansion at $O$ is non-zero. The critical set of $f$ is $\mathrm{Crit}(f)=\{z:\det df_z=0\}$, and the postcritical set is
$$\mathrm{PCrit}(f)=\bigcup_{k\ge 1} f^k(\mathrm{Crit}(f)),$$
considered as a germ at $O$.

Two germs $f,g\in\mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C}^n,O)$ are locally topologically (respectively, holomorphically) conjugate if there exists a germ at $O$ of a homeomorphism (respectively, biholomorphism) $\varphi:(\mathbb{C}^n,O)\to(\mathbb{C}^n,O)$ such that $\varphi\circ f=g\circ\varphi$. The germs of postcritical sets $\mathrm{PCrit}(f)$ and $\mathrm{PCrit}(g)$ are said to be topologically (respectively, holomorphically) conjugate if there is a germ of a homeomorphism (respectively, biholomorphism) at $O$ sending $\mathrm{PCrit}(f)$ onto $\mathrm{PCrit}(g)$.

Question: Let $f,g\in\mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C}^n,O)$ be superattracting germs with $c(f)=c(g)$. Is it true that $f$ and $g$ are locally topologically (respectively, holomorphically) conjugate if and only if their postcritical sets $\mathrm{PCrit}(f)$ and $\mathrm{PCrit}(g)$ are topologically (respectively, holomorphically) conjugate as germs at $O$?

The critical set of $f$ is $C(f)=\{\det Df=0\}$, and the generalized critical set is $C^\infty(f)=\bigcup_{n\ge 0} f^{-n}(C(f))$. The germ $f$ is called rigid if:
(i) $C^\infty(f)$ (as a germ at $0$) is contained in a normal-crossing divisor $D=\bigcup_i D_i$ with smooth irreducible components;
(ii) $f^{-1}(D)\subseteq D$ as germs at $0$.

Two such germs $f_1,f_2$ are birationally-dynamically equivalent if there exists a germ of bimeromorphic map $\pi:(X_1,E_1)\dashrightarrow(X_2,E_2)$ between modifications above $(\mathbb{C}^3,0)$ conjugating the lifts of $f_1$ and $f_2$.

Problem: Provide a complete classification (i.e. exhibit a list of holomorphic normal forms, or a complete set of invariants) for all such 3-dimensional non-invertible dominant rigid holomorphic germs up to birational-dynamical equivalence.

original_question: For a non-invertible dominant germ f in End(C^3, O), under what conditions does there exist a modification π: M̃ → C^3 based at the origin, a point p in the exceptional fiber π^{-1}(O), and a holomorphic germ f̃ in End(M̃, p) that is rigid or at least weakly rigid and satisfies π ◦ f̃ = f ◦ π?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C}^n,O)$ denote the set of holomorphic germs $f:(\mathbb{C}^n,O)\to(\mathbb{C}^n,O)$ fixing the origin. A germ $f\in\mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C}^n,O)$ is called dominant if its Jacobian determinant does not vanish identically, and non-invertible if $df_O$ is not invertible. A modification based at $O$ is a proper holomorphic map $\pi:\widetilde{M}\to\mathbb{C}^n$ from a smooth complex manifold $\widetilde{M}$ such that $\pi$ is a biholomorphism outside the exceptional fiber $E=\pi^{-1}(O)$, which is a connected divisor with simple normal crossings. 

For a germ $\widetilde{f}\in\mathrm{End}(\widetilde{M},p)$ at a point $p\in E$, denote by $C(\widetilde{f}^k)$ the critical set of the $k$-th iterate $\widetilde{f}^k$, and define the generalized critical set as the (germ at $p$ of the) union $C^\infty(\widetilde{f})=\bigcup_{k\ge 1} C(\widetilde{f}^k)$. The germ $\widetilde{f}$ is called rigid if $C^\infty(\widetilde{f})$ is (the germ of) a divisor with simple normal crossings at $p$ and is totally invariant, i.e. $\widetilde{f}^{-1}(C^\infty(\widetilde{f}))=C^\infty(\widetilde{f})$ as germs at $p$. It is called weakly rigid if $C^\infty(\widetilde{f})$ has simple normal crossings at $p$ (without requiring total invariance).

Problem. Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on a non-invertible dominant germ $f\in\mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C}^3,O)$ ensuring that there exist a modification $\pi:\widetilde{M}\to\mathbb{C}^3$ based at $O$, a point $p\in E=\pi^{-1}(O)$, and a holomorphic germ $\widetilde{f}\in\mathrm{End}(\widetilde{M},p)$ which is rigid (or at least weakly rigid) and which lifts $f$ in the sense that $\pi\circ\widetilde{f}=f\circ\pi$ as germs.
status_search_result: The two-dimensional analogue (rigidification of dominant superattracting germs in $\mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C}^2,O)$) has been established by Favre–Jonsson and Ruggiero using valuative techniques, but in dimension three the problem appears to remain open: searches turn up no general rigidification theorem for non-invertible dominant germs in $\mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C}^3,O)$, and known work in higher dimension only addresses partial cases (e.g. attracting rigid germs, principal resonances). No source claims a full solution.

original_question: Let G be a hyperbolic group which is virtually compact special in the sense of Haglund–Wise. Suppose that the set of second Betti numbers of the finite-index subgroups of G is bounded. Must G be virtually either a free group or a surface group?
self_contained_problem:

$$\sup\{\,b_2(H) : H \le G \text{ has finite index}\,\} < \infty.$$

original_question: For a germ tangent to the identity in C^n, describe its stable set in terms of characteristic directions, directors, indices, and any additional necessary invariants. In particular, determine how those data control which points converge to the origin, including phenomena not captured merely by convergence tangent to a characteristic direction.
self_contained_problem:
Let f : (C^n, 0) → (C^n, 0) be a holomorphic germ tangent to the identity, i.e., f(z) = z + P_{k+1}(z) + P_{k+2}(z) + ⋯ where each P_j is a vector of homogeneous polynomials of degree j and P_{k+1} ≢ 0 (so k ≥ 1 is the order of f − id). The stable set of f is

   Stab(f) = { z ∈ (C^n, 0) : f^m(z) is defined for all m ≥ 0 and f^m(z) → 0 as m → ∞ }.

A characteristic direction of f is a point [v] ∈ P^{n−1}(C) such that P_{k+1}(v) = λ v for some λ ∈ C; it is non-degenerate if λ ≠ 0, and degenerate if λ = 0. Associated to a non-degenerate characteristic direction [v] one has its directors (the eigenvalues, suitably normalized, of an associated linear endomorphism of T_{[v]} P^{n−1}), and one can attach further holomorphic invariants such as residual indices along invariant subvarieties.

Problem. Give a complete description of Stab(f) in terms of the characteristic directions of f, their directors, the residual indices along the associated invariant data, and any additional holomorphic invariants required. In particular, characterize which orbits converge to 0, and account for trajectories converging to 0 whose behavior is not captured by convergence tangent to a single characteristic direction (e.g., orbits attracted along degenerate directions or arising from invariant subvarieties without tangent direction at 0).
status_search_result: The problem of giving a full description of the stable set of a germ tangent to the identity in C^n in terms of characteristic directions, directors, indices, and further invariants remains open in general. In dimension 2, results of Écalle, Hakim, Abate, and others give parabolic curves at non-degenerate characteristic directions; recent work (Lopez-Hernanz–Raissy–Ribón–Sanz Sánchez–Vivas, Mongodi–Ruggiero, 2021–2023) extends this and constructs parabolic manifolds and invariant curves in further situations, but in dimension n ≥ 3 examples are known of isolated germs whose only characteristic directions (even after blow-ups) are degenerate, showing no complete description is yet available.

original_question: Let G be a torsion-free group of type F∞ of infinite cohomological dimension. Must G contain a copy of Thompson’s group F?
self_contained_problem:
Recall that a group $G$ is said to be of type $F_\infty$ if it admits a classifying space $K(G,1)$ with finitely many cells in each dimension (equivalently, $G$ has an Eilenberg–MacLane space with finite skeleta). The cohomological dimension of $G$, denoted $\mathrm{cd}(G)$, is the supremum of integers $n$ such that there exists a $\mathbb{Z}G$-module $M$ with $H^n(G,M)\neq 0$. Thompson's group $F$ is the group of orientation-preserving piecewise-linear homeomorphisms of the unit interval $[0,1]$ whose breakpoints lie in the dyadic rationals $\mathbb{Z}[1/2]$ and whose slopes are integer powers of $2$; it is known to be torsion-free, of type $F_\infty$, and of infinite cohomological dimension.

Question: Let $G$ be a torsion-free group of type $F_\infty$ with $\mathrm{cd}(G)=\infty$. Must $G$ contain an isomorphic copy of Thompson's group $F$ as a subgroup?

status_search_result: The problem appears in the 2026 Kourovka Notebook list of new open problems in group theory. Web searches reveal expository works on why Thompson's group F is torsion-free, of type F∞, and of infinite cohomological dimension, but no result claiming a proof or counterexample to the embedding question. The problem appears to be open.

original_question: Let G = G1*_H G2 be a free pro-p product of coherent pro-p groups with polycyclic amalgamation. Is G coherent? For abstract groups this is known to be true. A group is said to be coherent if each of its finitely generated subgroups is finitely presented, and in the question coherency is used in the pro-p sense.
self_contained_problem:
A pro-$p$ group is called coherent if every finitely generated closed subgroup of it is finitely presented as a pro-$p$ group. A pro-$p$ group is polycyclic if it admits a finite subnormal series with procyclic factors.

Let $G_1$ and $G_2$ be coherent pro-$p$ groups, and let $H$ be a polycyclic pro-$p$ group that is a closed subgroup of both $G_1$ and $G_2$. Form the free pro-$p$ product with amalgamation
$$G = G_1 \amalg_H G_2$$
in the category of pro-$p$ groups.

Is $G$ necessarily coherent (in the pro-$p$ sense)?

(Note: the analogous statement for abstract groups — that the amalgamated free product of two coherent groups over a polycyclic subgroup is coherent — is known to hold.)

original_question: (Well-known problem). Is Thompson’s group F automatic?
self_contained_problem:
Thompson's group $F$ is the group with the infinite presentation
$$F = \langle x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots \mid x_i^{-1} x_n x_i = x_{n+1} \text{ for all } i < n \rangle,$$
which is finitely generated by $x_0, x_1$ (and admits a finite presentation on these two generators).

A finitely generated group $G$ with finite generating set $A$ is called automatic if there exists a regular language $L \subseteq A^*$ of words mapping onto $G$ such that:
(i) the evaluation map $L \to G$ is surjective, and
(ii) for each $a \in A \cup \{1\}$, the "fellow-traveler" set
$$L_a = \{(u,v) \in L \times L : \overline{u}\,a = \overline{v}\text{ in }G\}$$
is recognized by a synchronous two-tape finite automaton (equivalently, the paths in the Cayley graph of $G$ corresponding to $u$ and $v$ stay within a uniformly bounded distance of each other at all times).

Determine whether Thompson's group $F$ is automatic in this sense.
status_search_result: The question of whether Thompson's group $F$ is automatic in the classical sense remains open. Weaker or related properties have been established: $F$ is known to be 1-counter graph automatic (Burillo–Cleary–Taback / Elder–Taback, arXiv:1501.04313) and autostackable (Corwin et al.), and admits a bounded regular convergent prefix-rewriting system. However, classical automaticity has not been resolved and continues to be listed as a well-known open problem on Thompson's group problem lists.

paper_title: Open problems in local discrete holomorphic dynamics
original_question: Consider the geodesic field G = g_1(z) v ∂/∂z + (ν−1) g_2(z) v^2 ∂/∂v arising from a homogeneous vector field in dimension two. What is the local dynamical behavior of G near an irregular singularity (ζ_0, 0), where the vanishing orders satisfy μ_1(ζ_0) > μ_2(ζ_0) + 1?
self_contained_problem:
Let $Q$ be a holomorphic homogeneous vector field of degree $\nu \geq 2$ on $\mathbb{C}^2$. After blowing up the origin and working in standard coordinates $(z,v)$ on the exceptional divisor (where points of the exceptional divisor correspond to $v=0$), the dynamics of $Q$ is conjugate to that of the associated geodesic field
$$G \;=\; g_1(z)\, v\, \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \;+\; (\nu-1)\, g_2(z)\, v^{2}\, \frac{\partial}{\partial v},$$
where $g_1, g_2$ are holomorphic functions on a neighborhood of a point $\zeta_0 \in \mathbb{C}$ with $g_1(\zeta_0)=g_2(\zeta_0)=0$. For $j=1,2$, let $\mu_j(\zeta_0)$ denote the order of vanishing of $g_j$ at $\zeta_0$. The point $(\zeta_0,0)$ is called a singularity of $G$, and is said to be irregular when $\mu_1(\zeta_0) > \mu_2(\zeta_0)+1$.

Problem: Describe completely the local dynamical behavior of $G$ near such an irregular singularity $(\zeta_0,0)$ in the case $\mu_1(\zeta_0) > \mu_2(\zeta_0)+1$. In particular, classify the integral curves of $G$ accumulating at $(\zeta_0,0)$, the formal and holomorphic normal forms of $G$ near this singularity, and the recurrence behavior of nearby geodesics of the associated meromorphic connection.
category_tag: Local holomorphic dynamics of homogeneous vector fields
status_search_result: Abate's surveys and subsequent work on Poincaré–Bendixson theorems for meromorphic connections explicitly state that, to complete the description of the dynamics of homogeneous vector fields in $\mathbb{C}^2$, the behavior near irregular singularities of the geodesic field still needs to be understood. No comprehensive classification of the local dynamics in the regime $\mu_1(\zeta_0) > \mu_2(\zeta_0)+1$ appears in the literature, indicating the problem remains open.

paper_title: Open problems in local discrete holomorphic dynamics
original_question: Let λ⃗=(λ_1,...,λ_n) be eigenvalues for a diagonalizable differential, and suppose the Brjuno-type series Σ_{k≥0} 2^{-k} log(1/Ω_{λ⃗}(2^{k+1})) diverges. Does there then exist a formally linearizable germ f in End(C^n, O) with those eigenvalues that fails to be holomorphically linearizable?
self_contained_problem:
For a vector $\vec\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)\in\mathbb{C}^n$, define for each integer $m\ge 2$
$$\Omega_{\vec\lambda}(m)=\min\Big\{\,\big|\lambda^{Q}-\lambda_j\big|\;:\;Q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^n,\;2\le |Q|\le m,\;1\le j\le n,\;\lambda^Q-\lambda_j\ne 0\,\Big\},$$
where $\lambda^Q=\lambda_1^{q_1}\cdots\lambda_n^{q_n}$ and $|Q|=q_1+\cdots+q_n$. Let $\mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C}^n,O)$ denote the set of germs at the origin of holomorphic self-maps $f:(\mathbb{C}^n,O)\to(\mathbb{C}^n,O)$. Such a germ $f$ with diagonalizable differential $df_O$ having eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ is called *formally linearizable* if there is a formal power series tangent to the identity conjugating $f$ to the linear map $\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$, and *holomorphically linearizable* if such a conjugation can be taken convergent.

Suppose that
$$\sum_{k\ge 0}\frac{1}{2^{k}}\log\frac{1}{\Omega_{\vec\lambda}(2^{k+1})}=+\infty.$$
Does there necessarily exist a germ $f\in\mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C}^n,O)$ whose differential at the origin is diagonalizable with eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$, such that $f$ is formally linearizable but not holomorphically linearizable?
status_search_result: Surveys on small divisors in discrete local holomorphic dynamics indicate that, in several variables, the necessity of the Brjuno-type condition for holomorphic linearizability remains unresolved; Yoccoz's necessity result covers only the one-dimensional case. No published proof of the multivariable necessity has been located.

original_question: (M. Brin, M. Sapir). Conjecture: Every subgroup of Thompson’s group F is either elementary amenable or else contains a subgroup isomorphic to F.

original_question: (M. Bridson). Is Thompson’s group F quasi-isometric(a) to F × Z? (b) to F × F?
self_contained_problem:
Let F denote Thompson's group, that is, the group of orientation-preserving piecewise linear homeomorphisms of the closed unit interval [0,1] which are differentiable except at finitely many dyadic rational points and on each interval of differentiability have slope a power of 2. A quasi-isometry between two finitely generated groups (equipped with word metrics with respect to finite generating sets) is a map f: G → H such that there exist constants K ≥ 1, C ≥ 0 with (1/K)d(x,y) − C ≤ d(f(x), f(y)) ≤ K d(x,y) + C for all x, y ∈ G, and such that every point of H lies within distance C of the image of f. Determine:

(a) Is F quasi-isometric to the direct product F × ℤ?

(b) Is F quasi-isometric to the direct product F × F?

paper_title: Open problems in local discrete holomorphic dynamics
original_question: Given eigenvalues λ⃗=(λ_1,...,λ_n), construct families {f_{λ⃗,a}}_{a∈M} of formally linearizable germs in End(C^n, O) with diagonal differential diag(λ_1,...,λ_n) such that holomorphic linearizability holds exactly when λ⃗ satisfies the several-variable Brjuno condition (8). In particular, for n=2 and nonresonant (λ_1,λ_2), is every germ of the form f(z)=(λ_1 z_1, λ_2 z_2)+Q(z) with Q quadratic homogeneous holomorphically linearizable if and only if (λ_1,λ_2) satisfies (8)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $n\ge 2$ and let $\vec\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)\in(\mathbb C^*)^n$ be nonresonant, i.e. $\lambda^Q:=\lambda_1^{q_1}\cdots\lambda_n^{q_n}\ne \lambda_j$ for every $j\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ and every $Q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)\in\mathbb N^n$ with $|Q|=q_1+\cdots+q_n\ge 2$. Recall that a holomorphic germ $f\in\mathrm{End}(\mathbb C^n,O)$ with $df_O=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$ is always formally linearizable in the nonresonant case, and is said to be holomorphically linearizable if there exists a local biholomorphism $\varphi$ fixing $O$ with $\varphi^{-1}\circ f\circ\varphi(z)=(\lambda_1z_1,\dots,\lambda_nz_n)$.

For $k\ge 2$ set
$$\omega_{\vec\lambda}(k)=\min\Big\{\,\big|\lambda^Q-\lambda_j\big|\;:\;2\le|Q|\le k,\;1\le j\le n\,\Big\}.$$
The several-variable Brjuno condition is
$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^k}\log\frac{1}{\omega_{\vec\lambda}(2^{k+1})}<+\infty. \qquad(\ast)$$

(a) For each $\vec\lambda$ as above, construct a holomorphic family $\{f_{\vec\lambda,a}\}_{a\in M}\subset\mathrm{End}(\mathbb C^n,O)$ (with $M$ a complex manifold) of formally linearizable germs with diagonal differential $\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$ such that every $f_{\vec\lambda,a}$ is holomorphically linearizable if and only if $\vec\lambda$ satisfies $(\ast)$.

(b) In the special case $n=2$ with $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)$ nonresonant, decide whether every germ of the form
$$f(z_1,z_2)=(\lambda_1 z_1,\lambda_2 z_2)+Q(z_1,z_2),$$
with $Q$ a $\mathbb C^2$-valued homogeneous polynomial of degree $2$, is holomorphically linearizable if and only if $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)$ satisfies $(\ast)$.

status_search_result: Searches surface surveys on small divisors in discrete local holomorphic dynamics (e.g. Raissy's recent survey, 2023) which still list the construction of families detecting the multidimensional Brjuno condition, and in particular the sharpness question for quadratic perturbations of a diagonal nonresonant linear map in $\mathbb C^2$, as an open problem. In one variable, Yoccoz's theorem establishes the analogous quadratic-polynomial characterization, but no analogous several-variable result appears to have been proved.

paper_title: Structure and dynamics of reentrant nematics: Any open questions after almost 40 years?
context_brief: Microscopic mechanisms of reentrant nematic behavior
original_question: Across liquid-crystal systems that show a reentrant nematic (RN) phase—a nematic phase that appears again at lower temperature after a smectic phase—what microscopic mechanisms cause reentrancy in the different classes of systems, and how can those mechanisms be experimentally identified and distinguished, given that reentrancy is not caused by a single mechanism but by many?
self_contained_problem:
A liquid crystal exhibits a reentrant nematic (RN) phase if, upon lowering the temperature at fixed pressure (or varying another thermodynamic control parameter such as composition or pressure at fixed temperature), the system passes through the sequence isotropic → nematic (N) → smectic (Sm) → nematic (RN), so that orientationally ordered but positionally disordered nematic order reappears below a more ordered smectic phase. Empirically, reentrant nematic behavior is observed in several distinct classes of mesogenic systems, including (a) strongly polar rod-like molecules with a terminal cyano (or similarly polar) group that form bilayer (partial-bilayer) smectic phases, (b) mixtures of polar and nonpolar mesogens, (c) single-component nonpolar mesogens, and (d) systems under applied pressure.

Problem. For each class of liquid crystal systems known to exhibit a reentrant nematic phase, identify the microscopic mechanism (formulated in terms of the intermolecular interaction potential and the resulting statistical-mechanical model — e.g. antiferroelectric dipolar pairing and frustrated dimer formation à la Berker–Walker, monomer–dimer steric/induced-force competition, packing/steric entropy effects, or other) that is responsible for the reappearance of nematic order below the smectic phase. Furthermore, propose experimental signatures (structural, thermodynamic, and dynamical — for instance X-ray structure factors, dielectric response, NMR order parameters, self-diffusion anisotropy, or rheological response) that uniquely identify each mechanism and that allow one to discriminate between the competing mechanisms in a given material, taking into account that reentrancy is not produced by a single universal mechanism but by several distinct ones depending on the details of the intermolecular potential.
status_search_result: Reviews and recent literature on reentrant nematic liquid crystals indicate that no single microscopic mechanism explains reentrancy across all systems: frustrated antiferroelectric dimerization (Berker–Walker), monomer–dimer competition, and steric/packing effects each apply to different classes, and the identification of which mechanism operates in a given system — particularly in non-dimer-forming and nonpolar single-component mesogens — remains unresolved. Experimental discriminators are still under active investigation.

original_question: (Well-known problem). A classifying space for a group G is a connected CW complex with fundamental group G and all higher homotopy groups trivial. A group is of type Fn if it has a classifying space with finite n-skeleton. For example, type F1 is equivalent to finite generation, and type F2 is equivalent to finite presentability. Type F∞ means type Fn for all n. For n ⩾ 3, does every group of type Fn−1 embed as a subgroup of a group of type Fn? Or even in a group of type F∞?
self_contained_problem:
Definitions. A classifying space for a group $G$ is a connected CW complex with fundamental group $G$ whose higher homotopy groups all vanish. A group $G$ is said to be of type $F_n$ (for a positive integer $n$) if it admits a classifying space with finitely many cells in dimensions $\le n$ (equivalently, with finite $n$-skeleton). Type $F_1$ coincides with finite generation, and type $F_2$ coincides with finite presentability. A group is of type $F_\infty$ if it is of type $F_n$ for every $n \ge 1$.

Question. Fix an integer $n \ge 3$. Does every group of type $F_{n-1}$ embed as a subgroup of some group of type $F_n$? More strongly, does every group of type $F_{n-1}$ embed as a subgroup of some group of type $F_\infty$?
status_search_result: The problem is described as a well-known open question on finiteness properties in geometric/combinatorial group theory. A direct web search did not surface a published resolution. Standard references on finiteness properties (e.g., constructions of Bestvina–Brady) provide groups of type $F_{n-1}$ but not $F_n$, but the question of whether every type $F_{n-1}$ group embeds into a type $F_n$ (or $F_\infty$) group does not appear to have been settled.

original_question: (V. M. Kopytov, N. Ya. Medvedev). A subgroup H of a right-orderable group G is said to be right-relatively convex if it is convex under some right ordering on G. Is the lattice of right-relatively convex subgroups of a right-orderable group always a sublattice of the lattice of its subgroups?
self_contained_problem: Let $G$ be a right-orderable group; that is, there exists a total order $\le$ on $G$ that is invariant under right multiplication ($x \le y \Rightarrow xg \le yg$ for all $g \in G$). A subgroup $H \le G$ is called right-relatively convex if there exists some right-invariant total order $\le$ on $G$ with respect to which $H$ is convex (i.e., whenever $a \le b \le c$ with $a, c \in H$, also $b \in H$). Let $\mathcal{C}(G)$ denote the set of all right-relatively convex subgroups of $G$, and let $\mathcal{L}(G)$ denote the lattice of all subgroups of $G$, with meet given by intersection and join by the subgroup generated by the union. Determine whether $\mathcal{C}(G)$, with the partial order given by inclusion, is always a sublattice of $\mathcal{L}(G)$. Equivalently: is it true that for every right-orderable group $G$ and any $H_1, H_2 \in \mathcal{C}(G)$, both $H_1 \cap H_2$ and $\langle H_1 \cup H_2 \rangle$ belong to $\mathcal{C}(G)$?
status_search_result: The question is recorded as a problem in the Kourovka Notebook (attributed to Kopytov and Medvedev). Antolín, Dicks and Šunić (2015) studied the analogous notion of left-relatively convex subgroups and showed that intersections of such subgroups are again left-relatively convex, but the corresponding join question (and hence the sublattice property) remains a research problem with no known general resolution. No publication found resolving the right-orderable case in full generality.

paper_title: Structure and dynamics of reentrant nematics: Any open questions after almost 40 years?
context_brief: Structural and dynamical distinction between N and RN phases
original_question: For a liquid-crystal material that has both a conventional nematic (N) phase at higher temperature and a reentrant nematic (RN) phase at lower temperature, are the N and RN phases structurally or dynamically distinct, and if so what measurable structural and dynamical observables distinguish them?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a thermotropic liquid-crystal material whose equilibrium phase sequence on cooling at fixed pressure passes through a conventional nematic (N) phase, then a smectic (S) phase, and then, at still lower temperatures, a second nematic-like phase known as the reentrant nematic (RN). In both N and RN phases the molecules possess long-range orientational order along a common director but no long-range positional order, and the two phases are not separated by any symmetry-breaking transition (they belong to the same symmetry class).

(a) Determine whether the N and RN phases are genuinely distinct thermodynamic states, i.e., whether there exist intrinsic structural order parameters (such as the orientational order parameter S = ⟨P₂(cosθ)⟩, the molecular pair correlation function g(r), short-range smectic-like density modulations, or the width of the orientational distribution function) whose values differ in a measurable, non-trivial way between the high-temperature N phase and the low-temperature RN phase.

(b) Determine whether the two phases are dynamically distinct, i.e., whether single-molecule and collective dynamical observables — in particular the anisotropic translational self-diffusion tensor (D∥ along the director and D⊥ perpendicular to it), rotational/reorientational correlation times, and the relative contribution of collective transport modes to mass transport — take values in the RN phase that differ qualitatively from those in the N phase at comparable orientational order.

(c) Identify which of these structural and dynamical observables can serve as quantitative experimental or simulational signatures distinguishing N from RN, and characterize the predicted direction and magnitude of the difference (for instance, whether D∥ in RN is enhanced relative to N despite stronger orientational order).
status_search_result: Simulation and some experimental work indicate that N and RN phases, while sharing the same symmetry, can be distinguished primarily by dynamical observables: molecular dynamics simulations predict an order-of-magnitude enhancement of translational self-diffusion along the director in the RN phase, dominated by a collective transport mode, and tied to a narrowed orientational distribution. Structural differences are subtle (slightly higher orientational order, modified short-range correlations). However, experimental results conflict — some NMR/diffusion measurements report no diffusion enhancement and find N and RN dynamically similar — so the question of robust, universal structural/dynamical distinguishers remains only partially resolved.

paper_title: Structure and dynamics of reentrant nematics: Any open questions after almost 40 years?
context_brief: Nematic order across the SA-RN transition
original_question: How does the nematic orientational order parameter Q change when a liquid crystal crosses from a smectic-A (SA) phase, in which molecules organize in layers, into a reentrant nematic (RN) phase, and can experiments resolve whether Q increases sharply, changes only subtly, or shows no enhancement?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a thermotropic liquid crystal that, upon cooling at fixed pressure (or upon varying composition in a binary mixture), exhibits the phase sequence

  Nematic (N)  →  Smectic-A (S_A)  →  Reentrant Nematic (RN),

where the nematic phases possess long-range orientational order (described by the uniaxial scalar nematic order parameter Q = ⟨P_2(cos θ)⟩, with θ the angle between a molecular long axis and the nematic director) but no long-range translational order, and the smectic-A phase additionally has one-dimensional density modulation along the director (molecules organized in layers).

Determine the behavior of the nematic orientational order parameter Q as the system crosses the S_A → RN phase boundary. Specifically:

(a) Does Q increase discontinuously (jump) at the S_A–RN transition, change only by a small continuous amount, or remain effectively unchanged compared with its value in the adjacent S_A phase?

(b) Provide a theoretical prediction (e.g. via a Landau free energy with coupled nematic order parameter Q and smectic density-wave amplitude ψ) for the sign and magnitude of ΔQ across the transition, and identify experimental observables (e.g. optical birefringence, magnetic/diamagnetic anisotropy, NMR splittings, X-ray determinations of ⟨P_2⟩) capable of resolving this change.

original_question: (V. M. Kopytov, N. Ya. Medvedev). Is it true that the lattice of rightrelatively convex subgroups of a right-orderable group is distributive if and only if it is a chain?
self_contained_problem:
A group $G$ is called right-orderable if there exists a total order $\le$ on $G$ that is invariant under right multiplication, i.e., $a\le b$ implies $ag\le bg$ for all $a,b,g\in G$. A subgroup $H\le G$ is said to be right-relatively convex in $G$ if there exists a right-invariant total order $\le$ on $G$ such that $H$ is convex with respect to $\le$ (meaning whenever $a,b\in H$ and $g\in G$ satisfy $a\le g\le b$, then $g\in H$). The collection of all right-relatively convex subgroups of $G$, partially ordered by inclusion, forms a lattice $\mathcal{L}(G)$.

Prove or disprove: for every right-orderable group $G$, the lattice $\mathcal{L}(G)$ of right-relatively convex subgroups of $G$ is distributive if and only if it is a chain (i.e., totally ordered by inclusion).
status_search_result: The question is a recently posed problem in the Kourovka Notebook attributed to V. M. Kopytov and N. Ya. Medvedev. No published resolution was located in the search; surveys and books on right-ordered groups discuss right-relatively convex subgroups but do not record a proof or counterexample to this characterization. The problem appears to be open.

original_question: (V. M. Kopytov, N. Ya. Medvedev). Are there order automorphisms of Dlab groups that are not inner automorphisms?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(G,\le)$ be a right-ordered group, i.e. a group $G$ equipped with a total order $\le$ such that $a\le b$ implies $ac\le bc$ for all $a,b,c\in G$. An order automorphism of $(G,\le)$ is a group automorphism $\varphi:G\to G$ such that $a\le b$ if and only if $\varphi(a)\le\varphi(b)$. An inner automorphism is a map of the form $x\mapsto gxg^{-1}$ for some $g\in G$.

A Dlab group is a right-ordered group obtained by Dlab's construction: given a totally ordered set $\Omega$ and a subgroup $H$ of the group $A(\Omega)$ of order-preserving bijections of $\Omega$ that acts on $\Omega$ in such a way that for every $\alpha\in\Omega$ the stabilizer subgroup $H_\alpha=\{h\in H:h(\alpha)=\alpha\}$ is convex in $H$ for the right order induced by a fixed point $\alpha_0\in\Omega$ (i.e., the right order on $H$ defined by $h>1$ iff $h(\alpha_0)>\alpha_0$, extended via Dlab's lexicographic refinement using $\Omega$); equivalently, a right-ordered group whose right order arises from its faithful action on a totally ordered set in this canonical way.

Question: Does there exist a Dlab group $(G,\le)$ admitting an order automorphism that is not an inner automorphism of $G$?

paper_title: Structure and dynamics of reentrant nematics: Any open questions after almost 40 years?
context_brief: Frustration mechanism in bilayer smectic reentrancy
original_question: In liquid crystals whose smectic-A phase is a bilayer or partial-bilayer phase formed by antiparallel dipolar molecular pairs or dimers, is increasing frustration of the dipolar or dimer network really the microscopic mechanism that breaks the smectic layering and produces the reentrant nematic phase at lower temperature?
self_contained_problem:
Consider thermotropic liquid crystals that, on cooling from the isotropic phase, exhibit the following sequence of equilibrium phases: an isotropic phase, a nematic phase N (orientational order only), a smectic-A phase S_A in which the constituent rod-like molecules are arranged in fluid layers, and, upon further cooling, a reentrant nematic phase N_re (the smectic layering disappears and a nematic phase reappears at lower temperature). Restrict attention to compounds and mixtures whose smectic-A phase is of bilayer or partial-bilayer type (S_{A2} or S_{Ad}), in which strongly polar molecules associate into antiparallel dipolar pairs (dimers) so that the layer spacing is between one and two molecular lengths.

A widely invoked microscopic explanation, often called the frustrated spin-gas picture, asserts that the antiparallel dipolar pairing produces a frustrated network of dipolar interactions whose frustration grows as temperature decreases; at sufficiently low temperature this frustration breaks the dimers and destroys the smectic layering, producing the reentrant nematic phase.

Question: Determine whether increasing frustration of the dipolar/dimer network is in fact the microscopic mechanism responsible for the destruction of the bilayer (or partial-bilayer) smectic-A layering and for the appearance of the reentrant nematic phase in such liquid crystals. That is, prove or disprove that frustration of the dipolar/dimer interactions is the underlying cause of reentrant nematic behavior in liquid crystals possessing a bilayer smectic-A phase.
status_search_result: The frustrated spin-gas theory of Berker and collaborators (early 1980s) provides a successful phenomenological account of reentrant nematic and multiply reentrant sequences in bilayer smectic-A liquid crystals, but competing scenarios (e.g. competition between short-range positional order and long-range antiferroelectric order, permeation/librational fluctuations) have also been proposed. No definitive microscopic verification establishing dipolar/dimer frustration as the unique mechanism has been reported, and the question is generally treated as still open.

paper_title: Structure and dynamics of reentrant nematics: Any open questions after almost 40 years?
context_brief: Mechanism of reentrancy without dimer formation
original_question: For liquid crystals that exhibit reentrant nematic phases without forming dimers—for example single-component, terminal-nonpolar molecules whose smectic layer thickness equals the molecular length—what experimental microscopic mechanism drives the loss of smectic layering and the return to a nematic phase?
self_contained_problem:
Consider thermotropic liquid crystals composed of single-component, terminal-nonpolar rod-like molecules that exhibit a reentrant nematic phase, i.e. on cooling display the phase sequence isotropic → nematic → smectic-A → nematic (reentrant) (possibly continuing to lower-temperature phases). Suppose that X-ray diffraction in the smectic-A phase shows that the smectic layer spacing equals the average molecular length, so that antiparallel association into bilayer dimers does not occur. In such systems the classical frustrated-spacing/dimer mechanism (competition between monomer length and antiparallel-dimer length characteristic of strongly polar cyano- or nitro-terminated mesogens) cannot be invoked.

Identify and characterize, on the basis of direct experimental microscopic evidence, the molecular-scale mechanism that destabilizes the smectic-A layered order on cooling and drives the reappearance of the uniaxial nematic phase. The answer must specify which microscopic degrees of freedom (e.g. conformational/chain-flexibility changes, density or packing fluctuations, transverse dipolar correlations, intermolecular tilt or biaxial fluctuations, etc.) are responsible for the loss of layering, and must be supported by experimental observables (such as scattering, NMR, dielectric, or calorimetric measurements) rather than purely by lattice or mean-field theoretical models.
status_search_result: The microscopic mechanism driving reentrancy in non-dimer-forming (terminal-nonpolar, single-component) liquid crystals remains an outstanding open question. Theoretical proposals exist (e.g., Dowell's lattice theory based on chain flexibility, and more recent suggestions of repulsive-interaction-driven reentrancy that would apply to both polar and nonpolar systems), but no direct experimental microscopic mechanism has been established and the question is still listed as an open problem in recent reviews.

original_question: Let G be an extension of a normal elementary abelian subgroup A by an elementary abelian group B ≅ G/A such that A contains an element a with C_B(a) = 1. Is it true that the rank of the subgroup Z(⟨a, B⟩) ∩ (⟨a, B⟩)′ is at most the rank of B?
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be a prime. Let $G$ be a finite group that is an extension of a normal elementary abelian $p$-subgroup $A$ by an elementary abelian $p$-group $B \cong G/A$ (so $A \trianglelefteq G$, every nontrivial element of $A$ has order $p$, and $G/A$ is elementary abelian of exponent $p$). Suppose there exists an element $a \in A$ whose centralizer in $B$ is trivial, i.e. $C_B(a) = 1$ (where $B$ acts on $A$ via the natural conjugation action induced by the extension, after fixing a set-theoretic lift $B \hookrightarrow G$).

Consider the subgroup $H = \langle a, B \rangle \le G$, its center $Z(H)$, and its derived subgroup $H' = [H,H]$. The rank of a finite abelian $p$-group is the minimal number of generators (equivalently, $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}$ of its socle/quotient by $p$th powers when elementary abelian).

Question: Is it always true that
$$\operatorname{rank}\bigl(Z(H) \cap H'\bigr) \le \operatorname{rank}(B)\,?$$
status_search_result: The problem appears as a newly posed question in the 2026 update of the Kourovka Notebook of unsolved problems in group theory. A targeted web search did not surface any published solution or partial result addressing this specific rank inequality, so it is presented as open.

original_question: Let M be a connected Riemannian manifold isometrically immersed in Euclidean (n+1)-space E^(n+1). The immersion is of finite type when its position vector can be written as a finite sum x = c + x1 + ... + xk of E^(n+1)-valued Laplace eigenmaps satisfying Delta xi = lambda_i xi. Classify all finite type hypersurfaces in E^(n+1); in particular, classify all finite type surfaces in E^3.
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a connected Riemannian manifold of dimension $n$ isometrically immersed as a hypersurface in Euclidean space $\mathbb{E}^{n+1}$ via an immersion $x : M \to \mathbb{E}^{n+1}$. Let $\Delta$ denote the Laplace-Beltrami operator of the induced metric on $M$, acting componentwise on $\mathbb{E}^{n+1}$-valued maps. The immersion $x$ is said to be of finite type if the position vector field admits a finite decomposition
$$x = c + x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_k,$$
where $c \in \mathbb{E}^{n+1}$ is a constant vector and each $x_i : M \to \mathbb{E}^{n+1}$ is a non-constant smooth map satisfying $\Delta x_i = \lambda_i\, x_i$ for some real eigenvalue $\lambda_i$, with the $\lambda_i$ pairwise distinct.

Problem: Classify all finite type hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{E}^{n+1}$. In particular, classify all finite type surfaces in $\mathbb{E}^3$ (i.e., the case $n = 2$).
status_search_result: The classification of finite type hypersurfaces in Euclidean space, and especially finite type surfaces in E^3, is a long-standing problem posed by B.-Y. Chen. The only known finite type surfaces in E^3 are open pieces of planes, round spheres, and circular cylinders (the minimal surfaces and the 1- and 2-type known examples), and proving these are the only ones remains open. Numerous partial results exist under additional curvature or symmetry hypotheses.
