paper_title: Structure and dynamics of reentrant nematics: Any open questions after almost 40 years?
context_brief: Robustness of simulated RN phases to orientational fluctuations
original_question: In simulations or model systems where reentrant nematic behavior appears for parallel hard-core ellipsoids with fixed molecular long-axis directions and a square-well attraction, does the reentrant nematic phase survive when orientational fluctuations and rotational dynamics of the molecules are included?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a three-dimensional fluid of identical uniaxial molecules modeled as hard-core prolate ellipsoids of revolution with semi-axes a = b < c, interacting pairwise through (i) the hard-core ellipsoidal exclusion and (ii) an isotropic square-well attraction of depth -ε for center-to-center separations r in (σ, λσ] (and 0 for r > λσ), where σ is the contact distance for the given orientations and λ > 1 is a fixed range parameter. In the restricted "parallel" version of the model, the long axes of all molecules are constrained to point along a single fixed direction n̂; for this restricted model it is known (from simulation and theory) that, in a suitable region of the (temperature, density) phase diagram, the system exhibits a reentrant nematic (RN) phase, in which upon isobaric cooling the system passes through the sequence isotropic → nematic → smectic-A → reentrant nematic, and the phase diagram contains two tricritical points along the nematic–smectic boundary.

Now relax the parallel constraint: allow each molecule's long axis to be a free unit vector ûᵢ ∈ S² subject to standard rotational dynamics (or, equivalently, full orientational degrees of freedom in equilibrium statistical mechanics), keeping the same hard ellipsoidal cores and the same isotropic square-well attractive potential between centers.

Question: Does the reentrant nematic phase persist in this fully orientationally fluctuating model? That is, does there exist a choice of the parameters (aspect ratio c/a, well range λ, and a non-empty open region of pressure or chemical potential) for which the equilibrium phase diagram still contains a reentrant nematic phase appearing below the smectic-A phase upon cooling, or do orientational fluctuations destroy reentrancy in this class of single-site square-well ellipsoid models?
status_search_result: No definitive resolution was located. The question of whether reentrant nematic behavior in single-site hard-ellipsoid plus isotropic square-well models survives the inclusion of full orientational fluctuations appears to remain an open modeling question in the soft-matter liquid-crystal literature, with most explicit demonstrations of RN in such minimal models still relying on the frozen-orientation (parallel ellipsoid) approximation.

paper_title: Structure and dynamics of reentrant nematics: Any open questions after almost 40 years?
context_brief: Experimental status of enhanced RN self-diffusivity
original_question: Do reentrant nematic phases in single-component, nonpolar molecular liquid crystals exhibit the very large self-diffusivity along the nematic director n that simulations predicted for confined reentrant nematics, and can experiments establish translational diffusion—not another relaxation mechanism—as the cause of the observed dynamical signatures?
self_contained_problem:
A liquid crystal exhibiting a reentrant nematic (RN) phase is one in which, upon isobaric cooling from the isotropic (I) phase, the system passes through a nematic (N) phase, then a smectic-A (S_A) phase, and on further cooling re-enters a nematic phase, denoted RN. In a uniaxial nematic phase, let n̂ denote the director and let D_∥ denote the molecular self-diffusion coefficient measured along n̂.

Computer simulations of confined model RN phases predict that, upon entering the RN phase, D_∥ increases by approximately an order of magnitude relative to the values found in the I, N, and S_A phases, and that this enhancement is due to a collective translational transport mode along n̂ rather than to any other (e.g. rotational or fluctuation-driven) relaxation mechanism.

Question: Does an analogous order-of-magnitude enhancement of D_∥ occur in the reentrant nematic phase of bulk, single-component, nonpolar thermotropic liquid crystals (i.e., systems composed of a single nonpolar molecular species, with no solvent and no dipolar association)? Specifically:

(a) Establish, by experiment on such single-component nonpolar materials, whether D_∥ in the RN phase is significantly larger than D_∥ in the surrounding I, N, and S_A phases.

(b) Demonstrate experimentally that the dynamical signature responsible for the observed behavior is genuine translational self-diffusion along n̂, and not some other relaxation mechanism contributing to the measured response.
status_search_result: Subsequent experimental work reports a maximum in self-diffusivity upon entering a reentrant nematic phase, with diffusivity rising by roughly an order of magnitude in the RN phase before decreasing in Arrhenius fashion (Mazza et al., "Diffusivity Maximum in a Reentrant Nematic Phase," 2012). However, a separate study of anisotropic self-diffusion across N, S_A, and RN phases found the temperature dependence of translational diffusion in the two nematic phases to be uniform within experimental error, indicating residual disagreement between simulation predictions and experiment. Whether translational diffusion (rather than another relaxation mechanism) is unambiguously responsible in single-component, nonpolar systems is therefore not fully settled.

context_brief: Compact finite type surfaces in E^3
original_question: Among compact surfaces immersed in Euclidean 3-space E^3, are the ordinary spheres the only compact surfaces whose immersion is of finite type, meaning that the position vector splits into finitely many Laplace eigensections?
self_contained_problem:
Let $x \colon M \to \mathbb{E}^3$ be an isometric immersion of a compact (without boundary) smooth surface $M$ into Euclidean 3-space, and let $\Delta$ denote the Laplace–Beltrami operator of the induced Riemannian metric on $M$, acting componentwise on $\mathbb{E}^3$-valued functions. The immersion $x$ is said to be of finite type if the position vector field admits a finite spectral decomposition
$$x = x_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{k} x_i,$$
where $x_0 \in \mathbb{E}^3$ is constant and $x_1, \dots, x_k$ are non-constant $\mathbb{E}^3$-valued smooth maps on $M$ satisfying $\Delta x_i = \lambda_i x_i$ for pairwise distinct real eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k$.

Prove or disprove: the only compact surfaces of finite type immersed in $\mathbb{E}^3$ are the ordinary round spheres (i.e., the only such immersions are, up to translation, parametrizations of standard round 2-spheres).
status_search_result: B.-Y. Chen's conjecture asserting that ordinary spheres are the only compact finite type surfaces in E^3 is widely cited as still open. Subsequent works (e.g., Stamatakis–Al-Zoubi and others on ruled surfaces, surfaces of revolution, spiral surfaces, tubes, and quadrics) verify the conjecture only in special classes; no general proof or counterexample appears in the literature.

original_question: In Euclidean 3-space E^3, are the only finite type surfaces minimal surfaces together with open portions of spheres and circular cylinders?
self_contained_problem:
Let $x: M \to \mathbb{E}^3$ be an isometric immersion of a connected smooth surface $M$ into Euclidean 3-space, with induced Laplace–Beltrami operator $\Delta$ acting on smooth $\mathbb{E}^3$-valued functions componentwise. The immersion $x$ (and the surface $M$) is said to be of finite type if the position vector field $x$ admits a decomposition
$$x = x_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{k} x_i,$$
where $x_0 \in \mathbb{E}^3$ is a constant vector and $x_1, \dots, x_k$ are non-constant $\mathbb{E}^3$-valued maps satisfying $\Delta x_i = \lambda_i x_i$ for some real numbers $\lambda_i$, with $k$ finite. Recall that a surface in $\mathbb{E}^3$ is minimal if its mean curvature vanishes identically.

Prove or disprove: every surface of finite type in $\mathbb{E}^3$ is either an open portion of a minimal surface, an open portion of a round sphere, or an open portion of a circular cylinder.
status_search_result: The classification of finite type surfaces in Euclidean 3-space (Chen's conjecture) remains an open problem. Up to the present, the only known finite Chen-type surfaces in E^3 are open portions of spheres, circular cylinders, and minimal surfaces, and partial results have been obtained for special classes (ruled, tubes, spiral, factorable, surfaces of revolution), but no complete proof or counterexample is known.

paper_title: Some open problems on cycles
original_question: Let f(n) denote the maximum number of edges in a graph on n vertices in which no two cycles have the same length. Is it true that lim_{n→∞} (f(n) - n)/√n = √2.4?
self_contained_problem:
For an integer $n\ge 1$, let $f(n)$ denote the maximum number of edges in a simple graph on $n$ vertices in which no two cycles have the same length. Determine whether
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{f(n)-n}{\sqrt{n}}=\sqrt{2.4}.$$
In particular, prove or disprove that this limit exists and equals $\sqrt{2.4}$.
category_tag: Extremal graph theory: distinct cycle lengths
status_search_result: The problem, originating with Erdős and refined as a conjecture by Lai, remains open. The best known lower bounds give liminf (f(n)−n)/√n ≥ √(2 + 2562/6911) ≈ √2.371, while no matching upper bound is known. Recent literature (e.g., 2025 work on limits of cycles) still discusses the conjectured value √2.4 as unresolved.

original_question: A hypersurface immersion is of 2-type when it is of finite type with exactly two distinct Laplace eigenvalues in its spectral decomposition. Study and classify 2-type hypersurfaces in a hypersphere of E^(n+2); in particular, classify 2-type hypersurfaces of S^4 in E^5.
self_contained_problem:
Let $x: M^n \to \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ be an isometric immersion of a closed (compact, without boundary) smooth $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold $M$ into Euclidean space $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$, and assume that the image lies in a hypersphere $S^{n+1} \subset \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ (so $x$ realizes $M$ as a hypersurface of $S^{n+1}$). Let $\Delta$ denote the Laplace–Beltrami operator of the induced metric on $M$, acting on $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$-valued functions componentwise. Then the position vector admits a spectral decomposition
$$x = x_0 + \sum_{i \in I} x_i, \qquad \Delta x_i = \lambda_i x_i,$$
where $x_0$ is a constant vector in $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$, the $\lambda_i$ are distinct nonzero real numbers, and the $x_i: M \to \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ are nonzero smooth maps. The immersion (or the hypersurface $M$) is said to be of $k$-type if the index set $I$ has exactly $k$ elements, i.e., the spectral decomposition involves exactly $k$ distinct nonzero Laplace eigenvalues. In particular, $M$ is of 2-type if $|I| = 2$.

(a) Classify all 2-type hypersurfaces of a hypersphere $S^{n+1} \subset \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ for general $n \ge 2$.

(b) In particular, classify all 2-type hypersurfaces of the standard 4-sphere $S^4 \subset \mathbb{E}^5$ (i.e., the case $n = 3$).

Partial results are known under additional hypotheses (e.g., constant mean curvature, or at most two distinct principal curvatures, leading to products of spheres), and local rigidity theorems have been established, but a complete classification—even in the specific case of 2-type hypersurfaces of $S^4 \subset \mathbb{E}^5$—does not appear in the literature, and the problem is still listed as open in recent surveys on Riemannian submanifolds and finite-type theory.

original_question: Classify finite type hypersurfaces of a hypersphere in E^(n+2). Here finite type means that the position vector of the immersed hypersurface is a finite sum of Laplace eigenmaps.
self_contained_problem:
Let $S^{n+1}(r) \subset \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ denote the round hypersphere of radius $r$ in Euclidean space, and let $x : M^n \hookrightarrow S^{n+1}(r) \subset \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ be an isometric immersion of a connected $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold as a hypersurface of this hypersphere. Identify $x$ with its $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$-valued position vector field on $M$, and let $\Delta$ denote the Laplace–Beltrami operator of the induced metric on $M$ (acting componentwise on $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$-valued functions).

The immersion $x$ is said to be of finite type if there exists a decomposition
$$x = x_0 + x_{t_1} + x_{t_2} + \cdots + x_{t_k},$$
where $x_0 \in \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ is a constant vector, $k$ is a positive integer, and each $x_{t_i}$ is a non-constant $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$-valued smooth map on $M$ satisfying
$$\Delta x_{t_i} = \lambda_{t_i} x_{t_i}$$
for some real eigenvalue $\lambda_{t_i}$, with the $\lambda_{t_i}$ pairwise distinct. The smallest such integer $k$ is called the type number of the immersion.

Problem: Classify, up to congruence in $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$, all finite type hypersurfaces $M^n$ of the hypersphere $S^{n+1}(r) \subset \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$.
status_search_result: The general classification problem remains open. Only partial results are known: Takahashi's theorem fully characterizes 1-type (minimal) cases; for 2-type, Chen and others showed such hypersurfaces have constant mean and scalar curvatures, and partial classifications exist for low dimensions and special classes (e.g., quadric hypersurfaces of finite type by Chen–Dillen–Song, 1992). No complete classification of finite type hypersurfaces in a hypersphere has been published.

original_question: A hypersurface M of S^(n+1) is called a Dupin hypersurface when the multiplicities of its principal curvatures are constant and each principal curvature is constant along its principal directions. Let $S^{n+1}$ denote the unit sphere in Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^{n+2}$, and let $M\subset S^{n+1}$ be a smooth hypersurface. Recall that:

(a) $M$ is called a Dupin hypersurface if the multiplicities of the principal curvatures of $M$ are constant on $M$ and each principal curvature is constant along the leaves of its corresponding principal foliation.

(b) $M$ is called isoparametric if all principal curvatures of $M$ are constant on $M$.

(c) Viewing the inclusion $x:M\hookrightarrow S^{n+1}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n+2}$ as an $\mathbb{R}^{n+2}$-valued map and letting $\Delta$ denote the Laplace–Beltrami operator of the induced metric on $M$, the hypersurface $M$ is said to be of finite type if $x$ admits a finite spectral decomposition
$$x = x_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{k} x_i,\qquad \Delta x_i = \lambda_i\, x_i,$$
where $x_0\in\mathbb{R}^{n+2}$ is a constant vector, $x_1,\dots,x_k$ are non-constant $\mathbb{R}^{n+2}$-valued eigenfunctions of $\Delta$ with pairwise distinct eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k\in\mathbb{R}$, and $k$ is finite.

(1) Characterize precisely those Dupin hypersurfaces $M\subset S^{n+1}$ which are of finite type.

(2) Determine necessary and sufficient conditions under which a finite type Dupin hypersurface $M\subset S^{n+1}$ must be isoparametric.

original_question: Let G be a simple Eulerian graph, meaning every vertex of G has even degree. Let cd(G) denote the smallest number of edge-disjoint circuits whose union is the entire edge set E(G). Is it always true that cd(G) ≤ |V(G)|/2 for every simple Eulerian graph G?
self_contained_problem:
A graph G = (V(G), E(G)) is called simple if it has no loops or multiple edges, and Eulerian if every vertex has even degree. A circuit (cycle) in G is a connected subgraph in which every vertex has degree 2. Define cd(G) to be the minimum number k such that E(G) can be partitioned into k pairwise edge-disjoint circuits C_1, ..., C_k with E(G) = E(C_1) ∪ ... ∪ E(C_k).

Prove or disprove: for every simple Eulerian graph G,
   cd(G) ≤ |V(G)| / 2.
status_search_result: Hajós' conjecture (1968) on cycle decompositions of Eulerian graphs remains open in general. It has been verified for restricted classes such as planar graphs, projective graphs, graphs of maximum degree at most 4, graphs of pathwidth at most 6, and small graphs (up to 12 vertices). Recent work (Girão, Granet, Kühn, Osthus) establishes an approximate version for dense graphs, but the full conjecture is still unresolved.

original_question: Do there exist 2-type surfaces lying fully in an even-dimensional hypersphere of a Euclidean space? In particular, do there exist mass-symmetric 2-type surfaces lying fully in an even-dimensional hypersphere?
self_contained_problem:
Let $x: M \to \mathbb{E}^m$ be an isometric immersion of a compact surface $M$ into Euclidean $m$-space. The immersion is said to be of finite type if its position vector admits a finite spectral decomposition
$$x = x_0 + x_{t_1} + x_{t_2} + \cdots + x_{t_k},$$
where $x_0$ is a constant vector and $\Delta x_{t_i} = \lambda_{t_i} x_{t_i}$ for distinct eigenvalues $\lambda_{t_i}$ of the Laplace operator $\Delta$ of $M$. The immersion is of 2-type if $k = 2$, that is,
$$x = x_0 + x_p + x_q, \qquad \Delta x_p = \lambda_p x_p, \quad \Delta x_q = \lambda_q x_q, \quad \lambda_p \neq \lambda_q.$$
The surface lies fully in $\mathbb{E}^m$ if its image is not contained in any affine hyperplane, and lies fully in a hypersphere $S^{m-1} \subset \mathbb{E}^m$ if it lies in $S^{m-1}$ but not in any totally geodesic hypersphere of $S^{m-1}$. A 2-type surface contained in a hypersphere centered at $x_0$ is called mass-symmetric (with respect to that hypersphere) if the constant vector $x_0$ in its spectral decomposition coincides with the center of the hypersphere.

Determine whether the following hold:
(a) Does there exist a 2-type surface that lies fully in an even-dimensional hypersphere $S^{2n} \subset \mathbb{E}^{2n+1}$ for some $n \geq 1$?
(b) Does there exist a mass-symmetric 2-type surface that lies fully in an even-dimensional hypersphere $S^{2n}$?
status_search_result: The problem of whether 2-type (in particular mass-symmetric 2-type) surfaces can lie fully in an even-dimensional hypersphere is a long-standing question of B.-Y. Chen. Known partial results (Barros–Chen, Garay, and others) show that compact stationary or Chen-type mass-symmetric 2-type surfaces lie fully in $S^3$, $S^5$ or $S^7$, and that no mass-symmetric 2-type surface lies fully in $S^4$. No general resolution for arbitrary even-dimensional spheres was found in the available literature, so the problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Suppose a k-type immersion x : M -> E^m has spectral decomposition x = c + x1 + ... + xk, and for each i the subspace Ei is spanned by the values x_i(p) as p ranges over M. The immersion is called linearly independent when E1, ..., Ek are linearly independent. Study and classify linearly independent 2-type immersions.
self_contained_problem:
Let $x : M \to \mathbb{E}^m$ be an isometric immersion of a (connected) Riemannian manifold $M$ into Euclidean $m$-space, and let $\Delta$ denote the Laplace–Beltrami operator of $M$. The immersion $x$ is said to be of finite type $k$ if its position vector admits a spectral decomposition
$$ x = c + x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_k, $$
where $c \in \mathbb{E}^m$ is a constant vector and $x_1,\dots,x_k : M \to \mathbb{E}^m$ are non-constant smooth maps satisfying $\Delta x_i = \lambda_i x_i$ for pairwise distinct real eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k$. For each $i \in \{1,\dots,k\}$, let $E_i \subseteq \mathbb{E}^m$ denote the linear subspace spanned by $\{x_i(p) : p \in M\}$. The immersion $x$ (and the submanifold $M$) is called linearly independent if the subspaces $E_1, \dots, E_k$ are linearly independent, i.e. $\dim(E_1 + \cdots + E_k) = \dim E_1 + \cdots + \dim E_k$.

Problem: Study and classify all linearly independent 2-type isometric immersions $x : M \to \mathbb{E}^m$, i.e. give a complete geometric classification of submanifolds $M$ of Euclidean space that are of 2-type and whose two associated spectral subspaces $E_1$ and $E_2$ are linearly independent.
status_search_result: Partial classification results exist for linearly independent 2-type submanifolds of Euclidean space (e.g., results characterizing such hypersurfaces and spherical submanifolds, and showing in various settings that linear independence forces the immersion to lie in a product of two spheres or related configurations). However, a complete general classification of all linearly independent 2-type immersions does not appear to be available, so the problem remains open in full generality.

original_question: Let G be a simple connected graph on n vertices. Can the edge set of G always be decomposed into at most (n + 1)/2 paths?
self_contained_problem: Let $G$ be a simple connected graph on $n$ vertices. A path decomposition of $G$ is a collection $\{P_1, P_2, \dots, P_k\}$ of edge-disjoint paths in $G$ whose edge sets partition $E(G)$. Prove or disprove: the edge set of every simple connected graph $G$ on $n$ vertices admits a path decomposition into at most $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ paths.
status_search_result: Gallai's path decomposition conjecture remains open in general. Substantial partial progress exists: it has been verified for graphs with maximum degree at most 5, for graphs of treewidth at most 3, for 2-degenerate graphs (with one exception), and recently (2025) for block graphs. No proof for arbitrary connected graphs is known.

original_question: Using the same notion of linearly independent immersion, study and classify linearly independent submanifolds of codimension 2.
self_contained_problem:
Let $x:M^n\to\mathbb{E}^m$ be an isometric immersion of a connected Riemannian $n$-manifold into Euclidean $m$-space, and let $\Delta$ denote the Laplace–Beltrami operator of the induced metric on $M$. Assume $x$ is of finite type $k$, i.e., the position vector admits a finite spectral decomposition
$$x = x_0 + x_{t_1} + x_{t_2} + \cdots + x_{t_k},$$
where $x_0\in\mathbb{E}^m$ is a constant vector and $x_{t_1},\ldots,x_{t_k}:M\to\mathbb{E}^m$ are non-constant smooth maps satisfying $\Delta x_{t_i}=\lambda_{t_i}x_{t_i}$ for pairwise distinct real eigenvalues $\lambda_{t_1},\ldots,\lambda_{t_k}$. For each $p\in M$, let
$$E_i(p) := \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{R}}\{x_{t_i}(p)\}\subset\mathbb{E}^m,\qquad i=1,\ldots,k.$$
The immersion $x$ (equivalently, the submanifold $M$) is called \emph{linearly independent} if for every $p\in M$ the one-dimensional subspaces $E_1(p),\ldots,E_k(p)$ are linearly independent in $\mathbb{E}^m$.

Problem. Study and classify all linearly independent submanifolds $M^n\subset\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ of codimension $2$.
status_search_result: No definitive resolution was located. The classification of linearly independent finite-type submanifolds is known in the hypersurface case (codimension 1) and partial results exist for spherical and small-type cases, but a complete classification in codimension 2 does not appear in the searched literature, and the problem seems to remain open.

original_question: A 2-type immersion is called null when one of its two Laplace eigenvalues is zero; equivalently, a non-null 2-type immersion has two nonzero eigenvalues. If an n-dimensional submanifold of Euclidean (n+2)-space is non-null 2-type and has constant mean curvature, must it be spherical?
self_contained_problem:
Let $x: M^n \to \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ be an isometric immersion of a connected $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold into Euclidean $(n+2)$-space. Let $\Delta$ denote the Laplace–Beltrami operator of $M^n$ acting componentwise on $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$-valued maps. The immersion $x$ is said to be of finite type if the position vector admits a finite spectral decomposition
$$x = x_0 + x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_k,$$
where $x_0 \in \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ is a constant vector and $x_1, \dots, x_k$ are non-constant $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$-valued maps satisfying $\Delta x_i = \lambda_i x_i$ for real numbers $\lambda_i$. The immersion is of $2$-type when exactly two such non-constant components $x_1, x_2$ appear, with eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \lambda_2$. A $2$-type immersion is called null if one of $\lambda_1, \lambda_2$ equals zero, and non-null otherwise (equivalently, $\lambda_1 \lambda_2 \neq 0$). The mean curvature function of $M^n$ is the norm of the mean curvature vector $H$, and $M^n$ is said to have constant mean curvature when $\|H\|$ is constant on $M^n$. The submanifold $M^n$ is called spherical if $x(M^n)$ lies in some round hypersphere of $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$.

Question: Must every $n$-dimensional non-null $2$-type submanifold of $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ with constant mean curvature be spherical?
status_search_result: Searches turn up Chen's surveys on Riemannian submanifolds and finite-type theory in which this question is repeatedly listed as an open problem; no published result resolving the codimension-2 case in full generality was found. Partial results exist (e.g., for hypersurfaces, for surfaces, and under additional curvature/Chen-type assumptions), but the general statement appears to remain unresolved.

original_question: A null 2-type submanifold is one whose mean curvature vector H satisfies Delta H = lambda H for some nonzero real constant lambda. Study and classify null 2-type submanifolds. In particular, classify all null 2-type surfaces in 4-dimensional Euclidean space and in 4-dimensional pseudo-Euclidean spaces.
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be an isometrically immersed submanifold of a (pseudo-)Euclidean space $\mathbb{E}^m_s$, and let $H$ denote its mean curvature vector field. Let $\Delta$ be the Laplace–Beltrami operator of the induced metric on $M$, acting componentwise on vector-valued functions. The submanifold $M$ is called null 2-type if its position vector admits a spectral decomposition into exactly two non-constant components, one harmonic and one an eigenfunction of $\Delta$ with non-zero eigenvalue; equivalently, $M$ is non-minimal and its mean curvature vector satisfies
$$\Delta H = \lambda H$$
for some non-zero real constant $\lambda$.

(a) Develop a structure theory for null 2-type submanifolds in (pseudo-)Euclidean spaces.

(b) Give a complete classification of all null 2-type surfaces in the Euclidean 4-space $\mathbb{E}^4$.

(c) Give a complete classification of all null 2-type surfaces in the pseudo-Euclidean 4-spaces $\mathbb{E}^4_s$ for $s = 1, 2$ (i.e., in Minkowski 4-space and in the neutral pseudo-Euclidean 4-space).
status_search_result: Partial results exist (e.g., classification of null 2-type surfaces in $\mathbb{E}^3$ as open portions of circular cylinders, results on null 2-type hypersurfaces with additional curvature conditions, and on 2-type surfaces with parallel mean curvature vector), but no complete classification of null 2-type surfaces in Euclidean 4-space or in 4-dimensional pseudo-Euclidean spaces appears in the literature surveyed.

original_question: An isometric immersion x : M -> E^m is biharmonic when Delta^2 x = 0, equivalently Delta H = 0 for the mean curvature vector H. Other than minimal submanifolds, which submanifolds of Euclidean space E^m are biharmonic?
self_contained_problem:
Let $x : M \to \mathbb{E}^m$ be an isometric immersion of a (smooth, connected) Riemannian manifold $M$ into Euclidean $m$-space $\mathbb{E}^m$. Let $\Delta$ denote the Laplace–Beltrami operator of the induced metric on $M$, acting componentwise on $\mathbb{E}^m$-valued maps, and let $H$ denote the mean curvature vector field of the immersion. The immersion is called biharmonic if
$$\Delta^2 x \equiv 0,$$
which is equivalent to $\Delta H \equiv 0$. The immersion is called minimal if $H \equiv 0$; every minimal submanifold is therefore biharmonic.

Problem. Determine all biharmonic submanifolds of $\mathbb{E}^m$ that are not minimal. Equivalently, decide whether every biharmonic submanifold of $\mathbb{E}^m$ must be minimal, and if not, classify the non-minimal biharmonic submanifolds.
status_search_result: This is Chen's biharmonic conjecture (1991), which asserts that every biharmonic submanifold of Euclidean space is minimal. It remains open in general. Confirmed cases include: surfaces in $\mathbb{E}^m$ (Chen, Jiang, ~1987), hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{E}^4$ (Hasanis–Vlachos, 1995), hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{E}^5$ (Koiso–Umehara/Fu–Hong–Zhan, 2020/2021), and hypersurfaces with at most three distinct principal curvatures (Fu). Higher-codimension and higher-dimensional cases (including surfaces $M^2 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{E}^4$ in full generality and hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{E}^n$ for $n \geq 6$) remain unresolved.

original_question: Are the only biharmonic submanifolds of Euclidean spaces the minimal ones?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\phi:M^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ be an isometric immersion of a Riemannian manifold into Euclidean $m$-space, and let $\Delta$ denote the (rough/Laplace–Beltrami) Laplacian acting on $\mathbb{R}^m$-valued functions on $M$ (componentwise). The submanifold $M$ is called biharmonic if its position vector field $\phi$ satisfies $\Delta^2 \phi = 0$, equivalently $\Delta H = 0$, where $H$ is the mean curvature vector field of $M$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$. The submanifold is called minimal if $H \equiv 0$.

Prove or disprove: every biharmonic submanifold $M^n$ of a Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^m$ is minimal.
status_search_result: Chen's biharmonic conjecture for submanifolds of Euclidean space remains open in general. It is verified in several special cases—surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^3$ (Chen, Jiang), hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{R}^4$ (Hasanis–Vlachos, 1995), and hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{R}^5$ (Fu–Hong–Zhan, 2021)—as well as under various curvature or boundedness hypotheses. Recent surveys (2024–2025) confirm the general conjecture, including the case of surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^4$, is still unresolved.

original_question: Is every biharmonic hypersurface of a Euclidean space minimal?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ denote Euclidean $(n+1)$-space with its standard flat metric, and let $M^n \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ be an isometrically immersed smooth hypersurface with mean curvature vector field $\mathbf{H}$. Write $\Delta$ for the (rough/Laplace–Beltrami) Laplacian acting on $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$-valued maps via the induced metric on $M$. The immersion $\mathbf{x}: M^n \to \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is called biharmonic if $\Delta^2 \mathbf{x} = 0$, equivalently $\Delta \mathbf{H} = 0$, and minimal if $\mathbf{H} \equiv 0$.

Prove or disprove the following statement: every biharmonic hypersurface $M^n$ of $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ (for all $n \ge 1$) is minimal.
status_search_result: Chen's biharmonic conjecture for hypersurfaces in Euclidean space remains open in full generality. It is known to hold for surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^3$ (Chen, Jiang, 1987), for hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{R}^4$ (Hasanis–Vlachos, 1995), for hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{R}^5$ (Fu–Hong–Zhan, 2021), and for hypersurfaces with at most three distinct principal curvatures in arbitrary dimension. No proof or counterexample is known in general dimensions.

original_question: Is every complete biharmonic submanifold of a Euclidean space minimal?
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a smooth submanifold of Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$ via an isometric immersion $\phi: M \to \mathbb{R}^n$, and assume that $M$ is complete with respect to the induced Riemannian metric. The immersion $\phi$ is called biharmonic if it satisfies $\Delta^2 \phi = 0$, where $\Delta$ denotes the (componentwise) Laplace–Beltrami operator on $M$ associated with the induced metric. Equivalently, by Beltrami's formula $\Delta \phi = -n\, \mathbf{H}$, where $\mathbf{H}$ is the mean curvature vector field of the immersion, biharmonicity is equivalent to $\Delta \mathbf{H} = 0$. The submanifold $M$ is called minimal if $\mathbf{H} \equiv 0$.

Question: Must every complete biharmonic submanifold of a Euclidean space necessarily be minimal?
status_search_result: Chen's biharmonic conjecture (and its global/complete version) remains open in general. Partial results are known: it has been confirmed for properly immersed complete biharmonic submanifolds in Euclidean spaces (Akutagawa–Maeta), for hypersurfaces in low dimensions (including $\mathbb{R}^4$ and recently $\mathbb{R}^5$), and under various curvature or finiteness assumptions, but the full conjecture for arbitrary complete biharmonic submanifolds is still unresolved.

original_question: In recovery problems with noisy data, why do semidefinite-programming relaxations of maximum-likelihood estimators often remain tight beyond the exact-recovery regime? More concretely, when noise is large enough that the maximum-likelihood estimator cannot exactly recover the ground truth, under what structural or probabilistic conditions does the SDP relaxation still return a solution that lies in the original nonconvex model class, or equivalently matches the lower-rank quasi-maximum-likelihood solution instead of requiring a rounding step?
self_contained_problem:
Consider statistical recovery problems of the following form. A ground-truth object $x_0$ lies in a nonconvex set $\mathcal{M}$ (for example, the set of phase vectors $\{z\in\mathbb{C}^n:|z_i|=1\}$, the orthogonal group $O(d)$, or a discrete partition class). One observes a noisy datum $Y$ obtained from $x_0$ through a known statistical model, and considers the maximum-likelihood estimator
$$\hat{x}_{\mathrm{MLE}} \in \arg\max_{x\in\mathcal{M}} \, \ell(x;Y),$$
where $\ell(\cdot;Y)$ is a quadratic (or otherwise lift-able) log-likelihood. By writing $\ell(x;Y) = \langle C(Y), xx^{\!*}\rangle$ and lifting the variable to $X = xx^{\!*}$, one obtains the standard semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxation
$$\hat{X}_{\mathrm{SDP}} \in \arg\max_{X\succeq 0,\ X\in\mathcal{C}} \, \langle C(Y), X\rangle,$$
where $\mathcal{C}$ encodes linear constraints (e.g., diagonal entries equal to $1$, or block-orthogonality constraints) that are satisfied by every lift $xx^{\!*}$ with $x\in\mathcal{M}$.

The SDP relaxation is said to be tight if any optimizer $\hat{X}_{\mathrm{SDP}}$ has the rank that lifts of elements of $\mathcal{M}$ have (e.g., rank $1$ in the phase case), so that $\hat{X}_{\mathrm{SDP}} = \hat{x}\,\hat{x}^{\!*}$ for some $\hat{x}\in\mathcal{M}$.

Empirically, in many such problems (angular synchronization, multireference alignment, global registration, $\mathbb{Z}/2$ synchronization, community detection, camera-motion estimation, $k$-means clustering, etc.) the SDP relaxation remains tight with high probability in noise regimes where exact recovery is information-theoretically impossible, i.e., where $\hat{x}_{\mathrm{MLE}} \neq x_0$. In particular, $\hat{X}_{\mathrm{SDP}}$ coincides with the lifted MLE rather than producing a higher-rank optimizer that would require rounding.

Problem. Provide a unified theoretical explanation, with provable sufficient conditions, for the following rank-recovery phenomenon: identify general structural and probabilistic hypotheses on the model class $\mathcal{M}$, the constraint set $\mathcal{C}$, and the noise distribution generating $Y$, under which, with high probability, every optimizer of the SDP relaxation has the form $\hat{x}\,\hat{x}^{\!*}$ for some $\hat{x}\in\mathcal{M}$ (equivalently, equals the lifted MLE), throughout a noise regime that strictly extends the exact-recovery regime where $\hat{x}_{\mathrm{MLE}} = x_0$.
status_search_result: The general phenomenon remains an open problem with no unified theory. However, problem-specific progress has been made: tightness of the SDP relaxation beyond the exact-recovery regime has been established for angular synchronization (Bandeira–Boumal–Singer, 2014/2017), for $\mathbb{Z}/2$ synchronization and stochastic block models, for k-means clustering (Iguchi–Mixon and others, 2015+), and for related QCQPs. A general unifying explanation across all such recovery problems has not been established.

original_question: Let d > 1, n > 2, and m >= d + 1. Let A in R^(d x m) be a point cloud whose m columns are random points in R^d with i.i.d. uniform coordinates in [0,1]^d, and let O_1, ..., O_n be orthogonal transformations in R^d. Suppose the observed data are matrices A_i = O_i A + sigma eta_i in R^(d x m), where each eta_i has i.i.d. standard Gaussian entries. Form the generalized orthogonal Procrustes quasi-maximum-likelihood problem of maximizing Tr(CX) over block matrices X with X >= 0, X_ii = I_(d x d), and rank(X) <= d, and its semidefinite relaxation obtained by dropping the rank constraint. Does there exist a threshold sigma* > 0 such that whenever sigma < sigma*, with high probability the SDP relaxation has rank d and therefore exactly matches the quasi-maximum-likelihood solution?
self_contained_problem:
Fix integers d > 1, n > 2, and m ≥ d + 1, and a noise level σ > 0. Let A ∈ ℝ^{d×m} be a random point cloud whose entries are i.i.d. uniform on [0,1], and let O_1, …, O_n ∈ O(d) be arbitrary orthogonal d×d matrices (O_i O_i^T = I_d). The observations are

   A_i = O_i A + σ η_i,   i = 1, …, n,

where the η_i ∈ ℝ^{d×m} have i.i.d. standard Gaussian entries, mutually independent. The (quasi) maximum-likelihood estimator of (O_1, …, O_n) (up to a global orthogonal transformation) can be cast as the rank-constrained program

   maximize  Tr(C X)
   subject to  X ⪰ 0,  X_{ii} = I_d for i = 1, …, n,  rank(X) ≤ d,

where X is an nd × nd block matrix with d×d blocks X_{ij}, and C is the nd × nd block matrix whose (i,j) block equals A_i A_j^T. Its semidefinite programming relaxation is obtained by dropping the rank constraint:

   maximize  Tr(C X)
   subject to  X ⪰ 0,  X_{ii} = I_d for i = 1, …, n.   (*)

Question: Does there exist a constant σ* > 0 (possibly depending on d, n, m) such that for all σ < σ*, with high probability (over A and the η_i) every optimal solution of (*) has rank exactly d, and hence (*) recovers the quasi-maximum-likelihood solution?
status_search_result: The conjecture, posed by Bandeira, Khoo, and Singer in 2014, asks for a noise threshold below which the SDP relaxation of the generalized orthogonal Procrustes problem is tight (rank d). Subsequent work, in particular Ling's "Near-optimal bounds for generalized orthogonal Procrustes problem via generalized power method" (2022/2023) and follow-ups including the adversarial setting (SIMAX 2025), establishes sufficient signal-to-noise conditions under which the SDP relaxation is tight and matches the MLE, nearly matching information-theoretic limits up to a factor of d and a log term. These works substantially advance, but do not fully close, the original conjecture's regime; thus the problem is partially solved.

original_question:
For the modified focusing nonlinear Schrodinger equation on R^d, with d = 2 in the no-group-velocity-dispersion case or d = 3 in the anomalous-group-velocity-dispersion case,

 i partial_t v + Delta v + (1 + f(epsilon^r |v|^2)) |v|^2 v = 0,

where f models high-intensity corrections such as a cubic-quintic or saturated nonlinearity, can one rigorously prove the oscillatory dynamics reported in experiments and numerics, in which a solution focuses, then defocuses, then refocuses, in an almost periodic or recurrent way rather than simply collapsing once?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the modified focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation on $\mathbb{R}^d$,
$$ i\,\partial_t v + \Delta v + \bigl(1 + f(\varepsilon^r |v|^2)\bigr)|v|^2 v = 0, \qquad t>0,\ x \in \mathbb{R}^d, $$
where $\varepsilon>0$ and $r>0$ are fixed parameters, and $f:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ is a smooth saturation-type correction modeling high-intensity effects (for instance the cubic–quintic correction $f(s)=-s$ or a saturated correction such as $f(s)=-s/(1+s)$), with $f(0)=0$ and $f$ chosen so that the total nonlinearity $(1+f(\varepsilon^r|v|^2))|v|^2 v$ prevents finite-time blow-up. The dimension is taken to be $d=2$ (the no-group-velocity-dispersion case) or $d=3$ (the anomalous-group-velocity-dispersion case).

Physical experiments and numerical simulations indicate that for suitable initial data $v(0,\cdot) \in H^1(\mathbb{R}^d)$ whose unmodified cubic dynamics would lead to focusing/blow-up, the solution $v(t,\cdot)$ of the modified equation does not simply concentrate once but rather undergoes an oscillatory cycle: it focuses toward a high-amplitude state, then defocuses, then refocuses, and so on, in an almost-periodic or recurrent fashion.

Problem: Prove rigorously that there exist a class of nontrivial initial data and an admissible nonlinearity $f$ for which the corresponding global solution $v$ exhibits this oscillatory focus–defocus–refocus dynamics (in a precise, quantitative sense such as recurrence of the $L^\infty$ or $H^1$ norm to within a fixed factor of repeated peak values, or almost-periodicity of a suitable concentration profile), as opposed to monotone dispersion or single-event focusing.
status_search_result: Recent rigorous work on the cubic–quintic NLS in $\mathbb{R}^3$ and saturated NLS focuses on global well-posedness, orbital stability of solitary waves, and scattering beyond virial thresholds. None of these results establishes the experimentally and numerically observed almost-periodic focus/defocus/refocus oscillations rigorously; such oscillatory dynamics are still only observed numerically and remain unproven.

original_question:
Fix d in {2, 3}, let v_0 in H^1(R^d) be initial data for the cubic focusing NLS that produce a finite-time blow-up solution v at time T > 0, and let v_epsilon be the solution of the regularized equation

 i partial_t v + Delta v + (1 + f(epsilon^r |v|^2)) |v|^2 v = 0

with the same initial data. What is the limiting behavior of v_epsilon(t) as epsilon tends to 0 for times t > T, that is, after the blow-up time of the unregularized cubic NLS has already passed?
self_contained_problem:
Fix the spatial dimension $d \in \{2,3\}$. Consider the focusing cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation
$$ i\partial_t v + \Delta v + |v|^2 v = 0, \qquad t>0,\ x\in\mathbb{R}^d, \tag{1}$$
with initial datum $v_0 \in H^1(\mathbb{R}^d)$ chosen so that the resulting solution $v$ blows up in finite time $T>0$ in $H^1(\mathbb{R}^d)$.

Let $f:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ be a fixed smooth saturating function with $f(0)=0$, $f(s)\to -1$ as $s\to\infty$ (so that $1+f(\varepsilon^r|v|^2)\to 1$ pointwise as $\varepsilon\to 0$ for each fixed $v$, and $1+f(\varepsilon^r|v|^2)$ remains bounded for all $v$), and let $r>0$ be a fixed exponent. For each $\varepsilon>0$ let $v_\varepsilon$ be the global-in-time solution of the regularized equation
$$ i\partial_t v_\varepsilon + \Delta v_\varepsilon + \bigl(1 + f(\varepsilon^r |v_\varepsilon|^2)\bigr)|v_\varepsilon|^2 v_\varepsilon = 0, \qquad t>0,\ x\in\mathbb{R}^d, \tag{2}$$
with the same initial datum $v_\varepsilon(0,\cdot)=v_0$. (When $d=2$ this corresponds to the no-GVD setting; when $d=3$ to the anomalous-GVD setting.)

Determine the limiting behavior of $v_\varepsilon(t,\cdot)$ as $\varepsilon\to 0^+$ for times $t>T$, i.e., describe in what sense (and to what limit, if any) $v_\varepsilon(t)$ converges after the blow-up time $T$ of the unregularized cubic NLS (1).
status_search_result: A web search did not surface any work that resolves the post-blow-up ($t>T$) behavior of the saturation-regularized focusing cubic NLS solutions $v_\varepsilon$ as $\varepsilon\to 0$ in dimensions $d=2,3$. Related work treats blow-up itself or cubic-quintic/saturated NLS approximations up to and near the blow-up time, but the post-blow-up limit appears not to have been characterized. Status thus appears open.

original_question:
Consider the ionization-coupled variants of the focusing cubic NLS used for laser filamentation, namely the fixed-frame system

 i(partial_t + c_g partial_z)u + epsilon(Delta_perp + alpha_1 partial_z^2)u + epsilon(|u|^2 - rho)u = -i epsilon c(alpha_4 |u|^{2K-2}u + alpha_5 rho u),
 partial_t rho = epsilon alpha_4 |u|^{2K} + epsilon alpha_5 rho |u|^2,

and the moving-frame version

 i partial_tau v + (Delta_perp + alpha_1 partial_z^2)v + (|v|^2 - rho_tilde)v = -i c(alpha_4 |v|^{2K-2}v + alpha_5 rho_tilde v),
 -c_g partial_z rho_tilde = epsilon alpha_4 |v|^{2K} + epsilon alpha_5 rho_tilde |v|^2,

where the paper prescribes the boundary condition lim_{z -> +infinity} (nabla_perp)^l rho_tilde(tau, X_perp, z) = 0 for all l >= 0. Can one prove that solutions of these ionization models are global in dimensions 2 and 3, so that ionization really prevents finite-time collapse?
self_contained_problem:
Let $d\in\{2,3\}$ and write the spatial variable as $(X_\perp,z)\in\mathbb{R}^{d-1}\times\mathbb{R}$, where $\nabla_\perp$ and $\Delta_\perp$ denote the gradient and Laplacian in the transverse variable $X_\perp$. Fix real parameters $\varepsilon>0$, $c_g\in\mathbb{R}$, $c>0$, $\alpha_1\in\mathbb{R}$, $\alpha_4\ge 0$, $\alpha_5\ge 0$ and an integer $K\ge 2$. Consider the following two coupled systems for a complex-valued envelope and a nonnegative scalar density.

Fixed-frame system, for $u=u(t,X_\perp,z)\in\mathbb{C}$ and $\rho=\rho(t,X_\perp,z)\ge 0$:
$$ i(\partial_t + c_g\partial_z)u + \varepsilon(\Delta_\perp + \alpha_1\partial_z^2)u + \varepsilon(|u|^2-\rho)u = -i\varepsilon c\bigl(\alpha_4|u|^{2K-2}u + \alpha_5\rho u\bigr), $$
$$ \partial_t\rho = \varepsilon\alpha_4|u|^{2K} + \varepsilon\alpha_5\rho|u|^2, $$
with initial data $u|_{t=0}=u_0\in H^s(\mathbb{R}^d)$ for $s$ large enough and $\rho|_{t=0}=0$.

Moving-frame system, for $v=v(\tau,X_\perp,z)\in\mathbb{C}$ and $\tilde\rho=\tilde\rho(\tau,X_\perp,z)\ge 0$:
$$ i\partial_\tau v + (\Delta_\perp+\alpha_1\partial_z^2)v + (|v|^2-\tilde\rho)v = -ic\bigl(\alpha_4|v|^{2K-2}v + \alpha_5\tilde\rho v\bigr), $$
$$ -c_g\partial_z\tilde\rho = \varepsilon\alpha_4|v|^{2K} + \varepsilon\alpha_5\tilde\rho|v|^2, $$
together with the boundary condition
$$ \lim_{z\to+\infty}(\nabla_\perp)^l\tilde\rho(\tau,X_\perp,z)=0,\qquad\forall l\ge 0. $$

Prove or disprove: for every sufficiently smooth, decaying initial datum, the Cauchy problem for each of the two systems above admits a unique global-in-time solution (i.e., no finite-time blow-up of $\|u(t)\|_{H^1}$ or of $\|v(\tau)\|_{H^1}$ occurs) in spatial dimensions $d=2$ and $d=3$. In other words, does the inclusion of the ionization terms governed by $\alpha_4$ and $\alpha_5$ rule out the finite-time collapse known to occur for the standard focusing cubic NLS?
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open question concerning ionization-coupled focusing cubic NLS variants used in laser filamentation modeling. A web search did not surface a published global existence proof in dimensions 2 and 3 for these specific systems; standard focusing cubic NLS in these dimensions admits finite-time blow-up, and whether the ionization coupling prevents collapse appears unresolved.

original_question:
For the modified focusing cubic NLS

 i P_2(epsilon nabla) partial_t v + Delta v + |v|^2 v = 0,

assume that the positive self-adjoint operator P_2(epsilon nabla) gives only partial off-axis regularization, meaning it controls derivatives only in some distinguished directions rather than the full H^1 norm. Can one develop both the local and the global well-posedness theory in that partial off-axis case, and in particular decide whether this partial off-axis dependence is enough to prevent finite-time breakdown of solutions that would blow up for the standard focusing cubic NLS?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the modified focusing cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation
   i P(ε∇) ∂_t v + Δ v + |v|^2 v = 0,    v: ℝ_t × ℝ^d → ℂ,
where d = 2 or d = 3, ε > 0 is a fixed parameter, and P(ε∇) is a positive self-adjoint Fourier multiplier with symbol P(εξ) (ξ ∈ ℝ^d) satisfying the partial off-axis coercivity estimate
   (P(ε∇) v, v)_{L^2} ≳ ‖v‖_{L^2}^2 + ε^2 Σ_{k=1}^{j} ‖ v_k · ∇ v ‖_{L^2}^2,
for fixed unit vectors v_1, …, v_j ∈ ℝ^d, with j = 1 when d = 2, and j ∈ {1, 2} when d = 3, so that the right-hand side does not control the full H^1 norm of v (i.e. derivatives are controlled only along a proper subset of directions). The equation possesses formally conserved mass and a modified energy
   E(v) = ½ ‖∇ v‖_{L^2}^2 − ¼ ‖v‖_{L^4}^4.

(a) Develop a local well-posedness theory for the Cauchy problem associated with this equation in a natural function space adapted to the partial off-axis regularization provided by P(ε∇).

(b) Develop a global well-posedness theory using the available conserved quantities.

(c) Decide whether the partial off-axis dependence is sufficient to prevent finite-time blow-up of solutions; that is, determine whether all (or a large class of) sufficiently regular solutions extend globally in time, in contrast to the standard focusing cubic NLS (P ≡ 1), for which finite-time blow-up occurs for a large class of initial data in dimensions d = 2, 3.
status_search_result: Subsequent work has addressed the partial off-axis case: a SIAM J. Math. Anal. paper "Regularizing Nonlinear Schrödinger Equations Through Partial Off-axis Variations" establishes local and global well-posedness for cubic-type focusing NLS with only partial off-axis regularization, showing that the partial off-axis dependence yields a regularizing mechanism preventing the standard focusing-NLS finite-time blow-up in supercritical regimes. This indicates the open problem has been resolved affirmatively.

original_question:
For the self-steepening model

 i partial_t v + Delta v + (1 + i epsilon alpha_3 . nabla)(|v|^2 v) = 0

in dimension 2 for no group velocity dispersion or dimension 3 for anomalous group velocity dispersion, how can the finite-time blow-up solutions behave? In particular, can one rigorously describe the blow-up scenarios, including whether solutions can develop the shock-like profiles that the paper associates with optical self-steepening?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the self-steepening modification of the cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation
$$i\,\partial_t v + \Delta v + (1 + i\varepsilon\, \alpha_3 \cdot \nabla)\bigl(|v|^2 v\bigr) = 0,$$
where $v : [0,T) \times \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{C}$, $\varepsilon > 0$ is a small parameter, $\alpha_3 \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is a fixed nonzero vector (a distinguished "propagation" direction), and the spatial dimension is either $d = 2$ (the case modeling absence of group velocity dispersion) or $d = 3$ (the case of anomalous group velocity dispersion). The Laplacian and gradient act on the spatial variables $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$.

Provide a rigorous description of the possible finite-time blow-up scenarios for solutions of this equation. In particular:

1. Classify the dynamical behaviors (e.g.\ blow-up rates, concentration profiles, stability, universality classes) of solutions $v(t,x)$ that develop a singularity at some finite time $T^* < \infty$, in the sense that $\limsup_{t \to T^*} \|v(t,\cdot)\|_{H^1(\mathbb{R}^d)} = \infty$.

2. Determine whether there exist initial data leading to solutions whose corresponding profile develops a shock-like singularity (i.e.\ the gradient of an appropriately rescaled amplitude/phase profile blows up while the amplitude remains bounded, mimicking optical self-steepening shock formation), and if so, construct such solutions and describe the associated shock formation mechanism.
status_search_result: A web search did not return any rigorous results describing blow-up scenarios or shock formation for this self-steepening NLS model. Available literature on self-steepening solitons and supercritical NLS blow-up (Merle–Raphaël–Rodnianski–Szeftel and related works) addresses different equations, and no construction of shock-developing blow-up solutions for this specific equation was located. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question:
For the hyperbolic or non-elliptic cubic NLS

 i partial_t v + (Delta_perp - partial_z^2)v + |v|^2 v = 0

in dimensions 2 and 3, can one prove that every H^1 solution is global, despite the lack of the standard elliptic structure of the usual focusing cubic NLS?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the hyperbolic (non-elliptic) cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation
  i ∂_t v + (Δ_⊥ − ∂_z^2) v + |v|^2 v = 0,
where v = v(t, x_⊥, z) is a complex-valued function with (x_⊥, z) ∈ R^{d−1} × R and d ∈ {2, 3}. Here Δ_⊥ denotes the Laplacian in the transverse variables x_⊥ (in dimension d = 2, x_⊥ ∈ R and Δ_⊥ = ∂_{x}^2; in dimension d = 3, x_⊥ ∈ R^2 and Δ_⊥ = ∂_{x_1}^2 + ∂_{x_2}^2), so that the spatial operator Δ_⊥ − ∂_z^2 is of mixed (indefinite, hyperbolic) signature rather than elliptic. The equation is locally well-posed in H^1(R^d) and conserves the mass ∫|v|^2 dx and the (indefinite) energy
  E(v) = (1/2) ∫(|∇_⊥ v|^2 − |∂_z v|^2) dx − (1/4) ∫|v|^4 dx.
Because of the indefinite sign of the quadratic part of the energy, the standard variational/coercivity argument that yields global existence for the elliptic defocusing cubic NLS, and the Glassey-type virial obstruction for the elliptic focusing cubic NLS, do not apply directly.

Problem: Prove that for every initial datum v(0, ·) ∈ H^1(R^d) (with d = 2 or d = 3), the corresponding solution v of the above hyperbolic cubic NLS exists globally in time in H^1, i.e. no finite-time blow-up (whether by pulse splitting or any other mechanism) occurs.
status_search_result: A web search reveals active research on the hyperbolic (non-elliptic) cubic NLS in two and three dimensions, including recent well-posedness results on T^2 and analyses of radial standing/self-similar waves, but no source establishes global existence in H^1 on R^2 or R^3 for the hyperbolic cubic NLS. The problem of ruling out finite-time blow-up in this setting appears to remain open.

original_question:
For the hyperbolic cubic NLS

 i partial_t v + (Delta_perp - partial_z^2)v + |v|^2 v = 0,

can one rigorously prove and describe the pulse-splitting phenomenon seen in simulations, where a concentrating pulse reaches a threshold and then separates into lower-amplitude pulses moving apart instead of forming a singularity?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the hyperbolic cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation in dimension d = d_⊥ + 1, for a complex-valued function v(t, x_⊥, z) with t ∈ ℝ, x_⊥ ∈ ℝ^{d_⊥}, z ∈ ℝ:

   i ∂_t v + (Δ_⊥ − ∂_z^2) v + |v|^2 v = 0,

where Δ_⊥ = Σ_{j=1}^{d_⊥} ∂_{x_j}^2 denotes the Laplacian in the transverse variables x_⊥, and the dispersive operator Δ_⊥ − ∂_z^2 has indefinite (hyperbolic) signature.

Numerical simulations of this equation reveal a "pulse-splitting" phenomenon: starting from suitable focusing initial data, the solution concentrates and its amplitude grows until it reaches a certain threshold, after which, instead of forming a finite-time singularity, the pulse splits into two pulses of smaller amplitude that move away from each other.

Provide a rigorous mathematical description and proof of this pulse-splitting phenomenon. Specifically:
(a) Identify a class of initial data v(0, ·) for which the solution exhibits pulse splitting.
(b) Define rigorously what is meant by pulse splitting (e.g., describe the asymptotic profile, the threshold amplitude, the locations and velocities of the emerging pulses, and the regime of validity).
(c) Prove that for such initial data the solution is global in time and decomposes asymptotically (in a suitable norm) into at least two separating localized pulses, ruling out finite-time blow-up in this regime.

original_question:
When partial off-axis variation of the group velocity and longitudinal self-steepening are both present in the same direction, namely for

 i(1 - epsilon^2 partial_z^2) partial_t v + Delta v + (1 + i epsilon partial_z)(|v|^2 v) = 0,

do solutions still exhibit self-steepening, or does the off-axis regularization suppress or qualitatively change that shock-like steepening effect?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\varepsilon>0$ be a small parameter, and consider a complex-valued function $v=v(t,z,x_\perp)$ with $t\in\mathbb{R}$, $z\in\mathbb{R}$, and $x_\perp\in\mathbb{R}^{d-1}$ (with $d\in\{2,3\}$ the physically relevant cases). Let $\Delta=\partial_z^2+\Delta_{x_\perp}$ denote the full spatial Laplacian (or, in the partial off-axis context, write $\Delta v$ for the standard Laplacian acting on $v$). Consider the modified focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation combining a partial off-axis regularization of the group velocity with a longitudinal self-steepening term, both acting along the propagation direction $z$:
$$ i\bigl(1-\varepsilon^2\partial_z^2\bigr)\partial_t v \;+\; \Delta v \;+\; \bigl(1+i\varepsilon\partial_z\bigr)\bigl(|v|^2 v\bigr) \;=\; 0. $$
The classical NLS with self-steepening term $i\varepsilon\partial_z(|v|^2 v)$ is known to produce a shock-like steepening of the pulse profile in $z$ (formation of large gradients in finite time). The off-axis operator $1-\varepsilon^2\partial_z^2$ on the left-hand side acts as a regularization of the time derivative.

Question: Do solutions of the above equation still exhibit self-steepening (the formation of shock-like longitudinal gradients), or does the partial off-axis regularization of the group velocity suppress or qualitatively alter this steepening phenomenon? Specifically, determine whether there exist smooth, suitably localized initial data $v(0,\cdot)$ for which $\|\partial_z v(t,\cdot)\|_{L^\infty}$ becomes arbitrarily large in finite time, or prove that the off-axis term enforces a uniform bound preventing such steepening.
status_search_result: The equation appears as an open problem in a survey on variants of the focusing NLS equation related to laser filamentation. No subsequent work directly resolving whether solutions to this combined off-axis/self-steepening NLS variant exhibit self-steepening was located; related works treat self-steepening or off-axis regularization separately rather than the combined equation.

original_question: The paper rigorously derives several NLS-type asymptotic models from Maxwell's equations and justifies them on times of order T/epsilon only while the approximating NLS-type solution stays bounded, which in the standard focusing case means times strictly before the focusing time T_foc. Can one rigorously justify at least one of these derived NLS-type models on a time interval [0, T/epsilon] with T greater than or equal to the focusing time T_foc, so that the approximation remains valid in the regime where the different models begin to differ in a physically meaningful way?
self_contained_problem:
Consider Maxwell's equations in a nonlinear isotropic dielectric medium in $\mathbb{R}^3$,
$$\partial_t D = \nabla \times H, \qquad \partial_t B = -\nabla \times E, \qquad \nabla\cdot B = 0,\ \nabla\cdot D = 0,$$
with constitutive laws $B = \mu_0 H$ and $D = \varepsilon_0 E + P(E)$, where the polarization $P(E)$ has a linear part with susceptibility kernel giving rise to a smooth dispersion relation $\omega = \omega(k)$ and a cubic instantaneous nonlinear part of Kerr type. Let $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$ be a small parameter measuring the ratio of the wavelength to the typical longitudinal scale of the envelope, and let
$$E_{\mathrm{NLS}}^\varepsilon(t,x) = \varepsilon\, A(\varepsilon t,\varepsilon(x_\parallel - v_g t),\varepsilon^{1/2} x_\perp)\, e^{i(k\cdot x-\omega(k)t)/\varepsilon} + \mathrm{c.c.}$$
denote a quasi-monochromatic wave packet ansatz, where the slowly varying complex envelope $A(\tau,X)$ satisfies a focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation (or one of its standard variants: full-dispersion NLS, NLS with self-steepening, NLS with mean-field coupling, off-axis NLS, etc.) of the form
$$i\partial_\tau A + \alpha\, \partial_{X_\parallel}^2 A + \beta\, \Delta_{X_\perp} A + \gamma\, |A|^2 A + (\text{lower-order corrections}) = 0,$$
with coefficients computed from $\omega$ and the cubic susceptibility, and prescribed initial data $A|_{\tau=0}=A_0\in H^s(\mathbb{R}^3)$ for $s$ sufficiently large.

In the focusing regime, the envelope solution $A$ blows up at a finite focusing time $T_{\mathrm{foc}}\in(0,\infty)$, in the sense that $\|A(\tau)\|_{H^s}\to\infty$ as $\tau\to T_{\mathrm{foc}}^-$. Standard rigorous justification yields, for any $T<T_{\mathrm{foc}}$, an exact Maxwell solution $E^\varepsilon$ with the same initial data such that
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T/\varepsilon} \|E^\varepsilon(t,\cdot) - E_{\mathrm{NLS}}^\varepsilon(t,\cdot)\|_{L^\infty} \le C(T)\, \varepsilon^\theta$$
for some $\theta>0$.

Problem. For at least one such NLS-type envelope model (chosen among the variants derivable from the above Maxwell system at the relevant order), prove a rigorous justification estimate of the above type on a time interval $[0,T/\varepsilon]$ with $T\ge T_{\mathrm{foc}}$; equivalently, establish that the Maxwell solution $E^\varepsilon$ remains $o(1)$-close in a suitable norm to the chosen NLS-type envelope solution on a time scale reaching or surpassing the envelope focusing time, where the various derived variants begin to differ in a physically meaningful way.
status_search_result: A subsequent 2018 exposition by the same line of work restates the question as an open problem related to filamentation, and no later paper appears to give a rigorous justification of any NLS-type model derived from Maxwell's equations on a time interval reaching or exceeding the focusing time. Standard justification results in the literature remain confined to times strictly before envelope blow-up.

original_question: In bootstrap algebraic multigrid, how should one define a form of compatible relaxation together with a convergence-rate estimate derived from the compatible-relaxation factor rho_cr so that, for a chosen interpolation strategy, the estimate accurately predicts the performance of the resulting two-grid method?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be a symmetric positive definite matrix and consider the linear system $A\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{f}$. A two-grid algebraic multigrid method is defined by:
(i) a splitting of the index set $\{1,\dots,n\} = C \cup F$ (with $|C| = n_c$);
(ii) a smoother $M$ (with error-propagation $E_s = I - M^{-1}A$);
(iii) an interpolation operator $P \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n_c}$ with $P|_C = I$, giving the coarse-grid correction $E_c = I - P(P^T A P)^{-1} P^T A$. The two-grid error-propagation operator is $E_{TG} = E_s\, E_c\, E_s$, and its convergence rate is $\rho_{TG} := \|E_{TG}\|_A$.

Compatible relaxation (CR), as introduced by Brandt, is a relaxation scheme on the $F$-variables only, with error-propagation $E_F = I_F - M_{FF}^{-1} A_{FF}$ (or a more general $F$-restricted iteration). Its asymptotic convergence factor is
$$\rho_{cr} := \lim_{k\to\infty} \|E_F^k\|^{1/k}_{A_{FF}}.$$
It is known that a small $\rho_{cr}$ is necessary for the existence of a sparse interpolation $P$ yielding a uniformly convergent two-grid method.

Problem. Construct a definition of compatible relaxation and an associated convergence-rate estimate $\Phi(\rho_{cr})$ (possibly involving auxiliary quantities determined by the smoother and the $C/F$ splitting) such that, for a prescribed interpolation strategy $\mathcal{I}$ that produces $P$ from $(A,C,F)$, the estimate sharply predicts the actual two-grid convergence rate; that is, exhibit functions $\Phi$ and a CR formulation for which
$$\rho_{TG}(A,C,F,\mathcal{I}) \approx \Phi(\rho_{cr})$$
holds with provable two-sided bounds, uniformly over a specified class of SPD matrices $A$ and admissible splittings.
status_search_result: Compatible relaxation provides necessary conditions and lower bounds for two-grid convergence, and recent work (e.g., Brannick–Cao–Kahl–Falgout–Zikatanov, 2017–2025) has produced sharper CR-type estimates and optimal-interpolation frameworks. However, deriving a CR-based estimate that sharply predicts (with matching upper and lower bounds) the two-grid convergence rate for a given practical interpolation strategy across general SPD problems remains an active research question without a definitive resolution.

original_question: How can least-squares interpolation and the bootstrap setup used to compute test vectors be combined in a way that is simultaneously optimal and robust for defining algebraic multigrid interpolation?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an algebraic multigrid (AMG) framework for solving linear systems $A x = b$ with $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ a large sparse matrix (e.g., arising from a discretized PDE). In AMG one selects a set of coarse-grid degrees of freedom $\mathcal{C} \subset \{1,\dots,n\}$ together with a prolongation (interpolation) operator $P \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times |\mathcal{C}|}$ that maps coarse-grid vectors to fine-grid vectors and is used recursively to define a multilevel solver.

In the bootstrap algebraic multigrid (BAMG) approach, the rows of $P$ are determined by a weighted least-squares fit. Concretely, given a set of test vectors $\{v^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K} \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ together with positive weights $\{\omega_k\}_{k=1}^K$, the interpolation weights $(p_{ij})_{j \in \mathcal{C}_i}$ for each fine-grid point $i \notin \mathcal{C}$ (with neighboring coarse set $\mathcal{C}_i$) are defined by
$$
\min_{(p_{ij})_{j \in \mathcal{C}_i}} \sum_{k=1}^{K} \omega_k \Big( v^{(k)}_i - \sum_{j \in \mathcal{C}_i} p_{ij}\, v^{(k)}_j \Big)^2 .
$$
The test vectors $\{v^{(k)}\}$ are themselves computed by a "bootstrap" setup procedure: starting from random initial vectors, one applies relaxation to the homogeneous equation $A x = 0$, then iteratively improves the test vectors via a multilevel eigensolver applied to the current multigrid hierarchy, possibly combined with adaptive residual-based relaxation.

Problem. Devise and analyze a procedure that combines the least-squares definition of the prolongation $P$ with the bootstrap setup for generating test vectors so that the resulting interpolation operator is simultaneously:

(i) Optimal, in the sense that for an appropriate quantitative measure of two-grid (or multigrid) convergence — for example, the asymptotic convergence factor of the resulting V-cycle, or the constant in the weak approximation property
$$
\inf_{x_c} \| x - P x_c \|_{D}^2 \le C\, \langle A x, x \rangle \qquad \forall x \in \mathbb{R}^n,
$$
where $D$ is a suitable diagonal scaling — the constructed $P$ achieves (or provably approaches) the best possible value of that measure over the class of interpolation operators with the given sparsity pattern.

(ii) Robust, in the sense that the construction yields uniformly bounded multigrid convergence factors across a broad class of problems (including, e.g., scalar elliptic problems with strongly varying or anisotropic coefficients, indefinite systems, and systems of PDEs) without requiring problem-specific parameter tuning, and is stable with respect to the number, accuracy, and choice of test vectors produced by the bootstrap cycle (avoiding overfitting and degenerate least-squares systems).

Specify (a) how the test-vector set, weights, and least-squares regularization should be chosen as functions of the bootstrap iterates, (b) the precise sense in which the resulting $P$ is optimal, and (c) prove a robustness theorem giving an a priori bound on the multigrid convergence factor that depends only on natural properties of $A$ and not on problem-specific parameters.
status_search_result: The combination of least-squares interpolation with bootstrap test-vector setup remains an active area of research in algebraic multigrid. Status reports and recent works (e.g., on bootstrap AMG with operator-based interpolation, least-angle-regression coarsening, and learning-based weighted least-squares variants) continue to propose and refine such combinations, indicating the question of a simultaneously optimal and robust integration is still open and being explored, rather than definitively resolved.

original_question: For Hermitian positive definite problems, how should the compatible relaxation, algebraic distance, least-squares interpolation, test-vector generation, and related bootstrap algebraic multigrid components be integrated into a practical overall algorithm, validated on a carefully chosen and diverse collection of test problems including systems of partial differential equations, so that the method becomes a fast solver usable in practice?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the class of Hermitian positive definite (HPD) linear systems $A x = b$, where $A \in \mathbb{C}^{n	imes n}$ satisfies $A = A^*$ and $x^* A x > 0$ for all nonzero $x \in \mathbb{C}^n$. A bootstrap algebraic multigrid (BAMG) solver for such systems is built from the following components:

1. Compatible relaxation: an iterative relaxation scheme restricted to a candidate set of fine-grid variables, used to assess the quality of a coarse-variable set $C \subset \{1,\dots,n\}$ via its convergence rate.
2. Algebraic distance: a notion of strength of connection between variables derived from the smoothed behavior of test vectors, used to guide coarsening and sparsity patterns of interpolation.
3. Least-squares interpolation: for each fine variable $i 
otin C$, an interpolation operator row obtained by solving a weighted least-squares problem that fits a collection of test vectors $\{v^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K}$ on a chosen neighborhood in $C$.
4. Test-vector generation: a bootstrap process in which test vectors are produced and iteratively improved by applying the current multigrid hierarchy (e.g. via multigrid eigensolver / setup cycles) to expose algebraically smooth error.
5. Auxiliary BAMG ingredients: coarse-grid construction, choice of smoother, cycling strategy, and adaptive updating of the hierarchy.

Problem. Design a complete, practical BAMG algorithm for general HPD problems that specifies precisely how components (1)–(5) are combined, including all algorithmic parameters and stopping criteria, and prove or empirically demonstrate, on a carefully chosen and diverse collection of HPD test problems (including discretizations of scalar PDEs, anisotropic and jump-coefficient diffusion, and systems of PDEs such as elasticity and Stokes-type saddle-free reductions), that the resulting solver achieves grid-independent or nearly grid-independent convergence with optimal or near-optimal computational complexity, qualifying it as a fast solver usable in practice.
status_search_result: This is a broad research program rather than a single sharply-posed conjecture. While many BAMG components and integrated algorithms have been proposed and tested for various HPD problems, no universally validated, practical BAMG fast solver covering the full range of HPD systems (including general systems of PDEs) has been established. The problem is best classified as open / ongoing research.

original_question: For non-Hermitian problems treated with Galerkin-based algebraic multigrid, how can one correctly characterize the algebraically smooth error, or near-kernel components, that restriction and interpolation must approximate on coarse levels when small-singular-vector information can fail to describe that near kernel unless the matrix is normal?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A \in \mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$ be a (possibly non-normal, non-Hermitian) invertible matrix arising from the discretization of a linear problem $Ax = b$, and consider a two-level Galerkin algebraic multigrid scheme: choose a relaxation (smoothing) iteration with error-propagation matrix $S$, and choose interpolation $P \in \mathbb{C}^{n\times m}$ and restriction $R \in \mathbb{C}^{m\times n}$ with coarse operator $A_c = R A P$, so that the coarse-grid correction operator is $T = I - P A_c^{-1} R A$ and the two-level error propagation is $E = S^{\nu_2} T S^{\nu_1}$.

Call an error vector $e$ "algebraically smooth" if relaxation reduces it slowly, i.e., $\|S e\| \approx \|e\|$. For Hermitian positive-definite $A$, algebraically smooth errors coincide with the near-kernel of $A$, namely vectors $v$ with $\|Av\|/\|v\|$ small, equivalently right singular vectors associated with small singular values; this is also equivalent for normal $A$. For general non-normal $A$, however, vectors $v$ with $\|Av\|$ small need not be slow to be reduced by typical relaxation schemes, so the small-singular-vector subspace need not describe the components that $P$ and $R$ must capture.

Problem. Provide a precise, computable characterization of the subspaces of slow-to-reduce errors of $A$ and $A^*$ under a given relaxation $S$ when $A$ is non-Hermitian and non-normal, such that:

(i) the characterization reduces to the near-kernel / small-singular-vector description in the normal case;

(ii) it identifies the right and left subspaces that the columns of $P$ and the rows of $R$ must respectively approximate in order to guarantee uniform two-level convergence, i.e., a bound $\|E\| \le \rho < 1$ independent of $n$;

(iii) it can be used as the target subspace in an adaptive/bootstrap AMG setup procedure.

Equivalently: identify the correct analogue of the "algebraically smooth error" / near-kernel for non-normal $A$ that restriction and interpolation must approximate on coarse levels in Galerkin-based AMG.
status_search_result: Several lines of work address this question. Energy-minimization interpolation strategies and generalized smoothed-aggregation setups have been extended to non-Hermitian/indefinite problems by targeting the right and left near-null-spaces of $A$ separately (so $P$ approximates right near-kernel, $R$ approximates left near-kernel). Adaptive/bootstrap AMG and reduction-based multigrid for nearly singular non-symmetric operators address the characterization in practice, and recent (2025) work explicitly studies "characterization of the near-null error components utilized in composite adaptive AMG solvers." A fully general, theoretically tight characterization that guarantees uniform convergence for arbitrary non-normal $A$ remains incomplete, so the problem is best described as partially solved.

original_question: For indefinite, non-elliptic problems such as Helmholtz and Schroedinger operators in higher dimensions, how can bootstrap algebraic multigrid be developed so that several locally orthogonal prolongation operators and the resulting multiple Galerkin coarse-grid operators are constructed efficiently, and to what extent can those techniques be extended into fast solvers for general sparse matrix equations?
self_contained_problem:
Consider linear systems Au = f arising from discretizations of indefinite, non-elliptic operators in dimension d ≥ 2, in particular the Helmholtz operator -Δ - k^2 with wavenumber k > 0 and the (real or complex) Schrödinger operator -Δ + V(x) with sign-changing or oscillatory potentials. The bootstrap algebraic multigrid (BAMG) framework constructs a hierarchy of coarse spaces by:
  (i) generating a set of test vectors that approximate the algebraically smooth (near-null-space) components of A,
  (ii) defining one or more prolongation operators P_1, …, P_m: ℝ^{n_c} → ℝ^{n_f} of small caliber (each fine point interpolated from a uniformly bounded number of coarse points),
  (iii) forming Galerkin coarse-grid operators A_c^{(j)} = P_j^T A P_j (or their complex/non-symmetric analogues), and
  (iv) recursively repeating the construction on each coarse level.

For indefinite non-elliptic problems, the algebraically smooth (near-kernel) modes are highly oscillatory plane-wave-like functions whose direction depends on local geometry, and they cannot be accurately captured by a single small-caliber prolongation on sufficiently fine scales; multiple prolongations are therefore required. To preserve optimal O(n) complexity per V-cycle, the multiple prolongations P_1, …, P_m must be locally orthogonal in the sense that, for each fine degree of freedom, the rows of the P_j associated with that point are mutually orthogonal (so that the resulting hierarchy of coarse operators stays sparse and the work per level decays geometrically).

Problem. 
(a) Devise a constructive BAMG algorithm for indefinite, non-elliptic problems (Helmholtz and Schrödinger in d ≥ 2) that produces several locally orthogonal small-caliber prolongation operators P_1, …, P_m together with their Galerkin coarse-grid operators A_c^{(j)}, with total setup and per-cycle cost that is provably linear (or quasi-linear) in the number of unknowns, and prove that the resulting multilevel iteration converges with a contraction factor bounded independently of the mesh size h and (ideally) the wavenumber k or potential V.
(b) Determine to what extent such a multiple-prolongation, locally orthogonal BAMG construction can be developed into a fast (linear or quasi-linear complexity) solver for general sparse matrix equations Au = f, identifying structural conditions on A under which uniform convergence and optimal complexity hold.
status_search_result: Recent work (e.g., a 2024–2025 SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing paper "Toward an Algebraic Multigrid Method for the Indefinite Helmholtz Equation" and the 2023 preprint "Stand-alone multigrid for Helmholtz revisited") explicitly states that designing a robust, optimal-complexity AMG (including bootstrap-style approaches with multiple coarse spaces) for indefinite Helmholtz/Schrödinger problems remains an open challenge, and that extending such ideas to general sparse systems is not yet achieved. The problem is therefore still open, with active partial progress.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in particle physics
original_question: Do short-baseline and other neutrino anomalies—LSND and MiniBooNE antimuon-to-antielectron appearance, reactor antineutrino disappearance, gallium calibration deficits, possible differences between neutrino and antineutrino oscillations, low-energy MiniBooNE excesses, possible seasonal variations, and OPERA's reported superluminal muon-neutrino velocity—represent real physics beyond standard three-flavour neutrino oscillations, and if so can a single theory explain them quantitatively, for example by sterile neutrinos, CPT violation, or nonstandard matter interactions, while satisfying the existing oscillation and Lorentz-invariance constraints?
status_search_result: The OPERA superluminal-neutrino result was retracted in 2012 after a faulty fibre-optic timing connection was identified, removing item (g). original_question: Determine the exact asymptotic growth of D(n), where D(n) is the minimum number of distinct Euclidean distances determined by an n-point set in the plane.
self_contained_problem:
For a finite set $P\subset\mathbb{R}^2$, let $D(P)$ denote the number of distinct Euclidean distances determined by pairs of points of $P$, i.e.,
$$D(P) = \bigl|\{\,\|p-q\| : p,q\in P,\ p\neq q\,\}\bigr|.$$
Define
$$D(n) = \min_{\substack{P\subset\mathbb{R}^2\\ |P|=n}} D(P),$$
the minimum number of distinct distances determined by an $n$-point planar set. Determine the exact asymptotic growth rate of $D(n)$ as $n\to\infty$. In particular, close the gap between the known lower bound $D(n)=\Omega(n/\log n)$ and the known upper bound $D(n)=O(n/\sqrt{\log n})$ achieved by a $\sqrt{n}\times\sqrt{n}$ section of the integer lattice.
status_search_result: The Erdős distinct distances problem in the plane remains open. Guth and Katz (2015) established the lower bound $D(n)=\Omega(n/\log n)$, while Erdős's $\sqrt{n}\times\sqrt{n}$ lattice gives $D(n)=O(n/\sqrt{\log n})$. The exact asymptotic (in particular, whether the upper bound is tight) is still unresolved.
