original_question: Characterize the planar n-point sets P with D(P) = O(n/sqrt(log n)), meaning sets that span a near-optimal number of distinct distances up to the currently best known order of magnitude.
self_contained_problem:
For a finite set $P\subset\mathbb{R}^2$, let
$$D(P)=|\{\,\|p-q\|:p,q\in P,\ p\neq q\,\}|$$
denote the number of distinct Euclidean distances determined by $P$. It is known (Guth–Katz) that every $n$-point set $P\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ satisfies $D(P)=\Omega(n/\log n)$, and the $\sqrt{n}\times\sqrt{n}$ integer grid shows $D(P)=O(n/\sqrt{\log n})$ is achievable. Call an $n$-point set $P\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ near-optimal if
$$D(P)=O\!\left(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}\right).$$
Give a structural characterization of all near-optimal planar point sets: describe the geometric and combinatorial properties (e.g., distribution along lines, circles, lattice-like structure) that an $n$-point set $P\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ must possess in order to satisfy $D(P)=O(n/\sqrt{\log n})$.
status_search_result: The problem of characterizing near-optimal planar point sets (those with D(P)=O(n/√log n)) remains open. Partial structural results are known: Sheffer, Zahl, and de Zeeuw and subsequent works show that in any near-optimal set, no line contains more than O(n^{43/52}) points and no circle contains more than O(n^{5/6}) points. Recent work (e.g., on forbidden 4-point patterns) continues to investigate constraints on such sets, but no full characterization has been obtained.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in particle physics
original_question: How should the Standard Model be extended so that neutrinos have nonzero masses and flavour mixing, given that the Standard Model contains only left-handed neutrinos and forbids a gauge-invariant renormalizable neutrino mass term, and how should the extension explain why neutrino masses are several orders of magnitude smaller than charged-fermion masses?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the Standard Model of particle physics defined by the gauge group $SU(3)_C \times SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y$ with the usual matter content: three generations of left-handed quark doublets $Q_L$, right-handed up- and down-type quarks $u_R, d_R$, left-handed lepton doublets $L_L = (\nu_L, e_L)^T$, right-handed charged leptons $e_R$, and a single Higgs doublet $\Phi$ with hypercharge $1/2$. In this field content there is no right-handed neutrino, and one can verify that no gauge-invariant, renormalizable (mass dimension $\le 4$), Lorentz-invariant operator built only from the listed fields produces a neutrino mass term, even after electroweak symmetry breaking $\langle \Phi \rangle \neq 0$.

Empirically, neutrino oscillation experiments establish that at least two of the three neutrino mass eigenstates have nonzero masses $m_i$ and that the leptonic mixing matrix (PMNS matrix) is non-trivial, while cosmological and laboratory bounds imply $m_i \lesssim 1\,\mathrm{eV}$, i.e. at least six orders of magnitude smaller than the charged fermion masses (e.g. $m_e \approx 0.511\,\mathrm{MeV}$).

Problem. Determine an extension of the Standard Model — by adding new fields and/or new interactions, possibly non-renormalizable operators suppressed by a high scale $\Lambda$, while preserving the observed low-energy gauge symmetry and phenomenology — such that:
(i) the neutrinos $\nu_i$ acquire nonzero masses (Dirac and/or Majorana) and a non-trivial mixing matrix consistent with oscillation data;
(ii) the mechanism provides a quantitative, natural explanation of the strong hierarchy $m_{\nu_i}/m_f \ll 1$ between neutrino masses and the charged fermion masses $m_f$;
(iii) the extension is consistent with all existing experimental constraints (lepton flavour violation, neutrinoless double-beta decay limits, cosmology, collider data).

Identify which such extension is realized in nature, and characterize its parameters (e.g. number and mass scale of right-handed neutrinos, scale of the dimension-5 Weinberg operator $\frac{1}{\Lambda}(L_L \Phi)(L_L \Phi)$, or alternative seesaw/radiative/Dirac structures).
status_search_result: The origin of neutrino mass remains an open problem in particle physics as of 2026. While many viable theoretical mechanisms exist (Type I/II/III seesaw, radiative models, Dirac neutrinos via tiny Yukawas, etc.), there is no experimental determination of which mechanism nature uses. Crucially, the Majorana vs. Dirac nature is undetermined, neutrinoless double-beta decay has not been observed, the absolute mass scale and ordering are not fixed, and no right-handed neutrinos or seesaw mediators have been discovered.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in particle physics
original_question: What physical mechanism generated the baryon asymmetry of the Universe, producing a matter-antimatter excess of order one unpaired quark per ten billion quark-antiquark pairs, when Standard Model electroweak baryogenesis fails because the required first-order electroweak phase transition would need an experimentally excluded light Higgs boson and CKM CP violation is insufficient?
self_contained_problem:
In standard cosmology, the observed Universe contains an asymmetry between matter and antimatter quantified by the baryon-to-photon ratio, equivalently by

  (n_q − n_{\bar q}) / (n_q + n_{\bar q}) ∼ 10^{-10},

i.e. roughly one unpaired quark for every ten billion quark–antiquark pairs at the relevant epoch. According to Sakharov's conditions, dynamically generating such an asymmetry from a baryon-symmetric initial state requires (i) baryon-number violation, (ii) C and CP violation, and (iii) a departure from thermal equilibrium.

Within the Standard Model of particle physics (gauge group SU(3)_C × SU(2)_L × U(1)_Y with the experimentally established Higgs sector and the measured CKM mixing matrix), the following two facts hold:
 (a) A first-order electroweak phase transition, needed to provide the out-of-equilibrium condition for electroweak baryogenesis, occurs only for a Higgs boson mass M_H ≲ 50 GeV, a range excluded by direct collider searches (the physical Higgs mass is ≈ 125 GeV).
 (b) The CP violation encoded in the CKM matrix is quantitatively too small to produce an asymmetry of the observed magnitude.

Problem: Identify and establish a concrete physical mechanism, beyond the minimal Standard Model, that dynamically generates the cosmological baryon asymmetry, satisfies Sakharov's three conditions, is consistent with all current experimental constraints, and quantitatively reproduces the observed value (n_q − n_{\bar q})/(n_q + n_{\bar q}) ∼ 10^{-10}, including a natural explanation of why this number is so small.
status_search_result: The origin of the baryon asymmetry of the Universe remains an open problem. While many candidate mechanisms exist (leptogenesis, electroweak baryogenesis in extensions of the Standard Model such as 2HDM/MSSM, Affleck–Dine, GUT baryogenesis, etc.), none has been experimentally confirmed, and recent reviews continue to list baryogenesis among the central unsolved problems of particle physics and cosmology.

original_question: Prove or disprove that, for some sufficiently small epsilon > 0, every near-optimal planar n-point set contains at least Omega(n^epsilon) points on a single line.
self_contained_problem:
For a finite set $P\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ of $n$ points in the plane, let $d(P)$ denote the number of distinct distances determined by $P$, i.e. the cardinality of $\{\,\|p-q\|:p,q\in P,\ p\neq q\,\}$. It is known (Guth–Katz) that $\min_{|P|=n} d(P)=\Theta(n/\sqrt{\log n})$. Call a sequence of planar point sets $(P_n)_{n\ge 1}$ with $|P_n|=n$ near-optimal if $d(P_n)=O(n/\sqrt{\log n})$, i.e. the number of distinct distances is within a constant factor of the minimum possible.

Prove or disprove the following: there exists a constant $\varepsilon>0$ such that every near-optimal sequence $(P_n)$ has the property that, for all sufficiently large $n$, the set $P_n$ contains $\Omega(n^{\varepsilon})$ points lying on a single line.
status_search_result: This is a well-known open question of Erdős concerning the structure of near-optimal sets for the distinct distances problem. Even after the Guth–Katz resolution of the main distinct-distances bound in the plane, this structural weakening — whether near-optimal sets must contain Ω(n^ε) collinear points for some fixed ε>0 — remains unresolved according to surveys on the Erdős distance problem.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in particle physics
original_question: If dark energy is vacuum energy or a cosmological constant, what mechanism cancels the huge vacuum-energy contributions expected from strong and electroweak particle physics while leaving the small observed nonzero scale Λ ∼ 10−3 eV, a scale not available among Standard Model parameters?
self_contained_problem:
In quantum field theory, the vacuum state of each interacting sector contributes to an effective vacuum energy density that gravitates as a cosmological constant Λ in Einstein's field equations. The Standard Model of particle physics contains a strong (QCD) sector with characteristic energy scale Λ_QCD ∼ 10^8 eV and an electroweak sector with characteristic energy scale v ∼ 10^{11} eV; naive estimates of the zero-point and condensate contributions to the vacuum energy density from these sectors yield values ρ_vac corresponding to an energy scale of order Λ_QCD or v (or higher, up to the Planck scale, if gravitational degrees of freedom are included). Cosmological observations of the accelerated expansion of the Universe, however, indicate that, if dark energy is interpreted as a cosmological constant or vacuum energy, the corresponding scale satisfies Λ_obs ∼ 10^{-3} eV, many orders of magnitude smaller than Λ_QCD and v.

Provide a dynamical or symmetry-based mechanism, formulated within a consistent field-theoretic framework that includes the Standard Model interactions and gravity, that simultaneously achieves both of the following:

(a) cancels (or otherwise renders gravitationally inert) the large contributions to the vacuum energy density coming from the strong and electroweak sectors, to the precision needed to bring the effective cosmological constant down by roughly 50–120 orders of magnitude;

(b) leaves a residual nonzero vacuum energy of scale Λ ∼ 10^{-3} eV, explaining the origin of this new low-energy scale, which does not appear among the parameters of the Standard Model.

State the mechanism, derive the resulting effective cosmological constant, and explain why the cancellation is incomplete in precisely the manner required to reproduce Λ ∼ 10^{-3} eV.
status_search_result: The cosmological-constant problem—reconciling the small observed dark-energy scale with the much larger vacuum-energy contributions expected from Standard Model interactions—is widely regarded as a major open problem in theoretical physics. Reviews continue to describe it as unsolved, and no widely accepted mechanism produces the observed scale Λ ∼ 10^{-3} eV from Standard Model plus gravity inputs.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in particle physics
original_question: What particle-physics model, field, or mechanism caused early-universe inflation, what is the inflaton if a new scalar field drove the exponential expansion, and what caused inflation to stop rather than continue until the present?
self_contained_problem:
Cosmological observations indicate that the very early Universe underwent a phase of nearly exponential (de Sitter–like) expansion, called inflation, during which the scale factor a(t) grew with Hubble rate H(t) satisfying ä/a = H² + Ḣ ≈ H² > 0 over many e-folds. In the standard particle-physics picture, such an expansion can be driven by a scalar field φ (the "inflaton"), absent from the Standard Model, with action
  S = ∫ d⁴x √(−g) [ ½ M_P² R − ½ g^{μν} ∂_μ φ ∂_ν φ − V(φ) ],
whose slow-roll evolution on a sufficiently flat potential V(φ) yields ε = (M_P²/2)(V'/V)² ≪ 1 and η = M_P² V''/V ≪ 1, producing inflation that subsequently terminates (when ε → 1) and reheats the Universe into a hot radiation-dominated phase consistent with Standard Model physics.

Identify, within a particle-physics framework, the field content, model, or mechanism responsible for early-universe inflation. In particular:
(i) Determine the identity of the inflaton: specify whether it is a new scalar degree of freedom beyond the Standard Model or arises from known fields, and give the form of its potential V(φ) and its couplings consistent with current cosmological constraints (spectral index n_s, tensor-to-scalar ratio r, amplitude of curvature perturbations, absence of observable non-Gaussianity).
(ii) Provide a dynamical mechanism that causes inflation to terminate after a finite number of e-folds N ≳ 50–60 rather than continue indefinitely, and that reheats the Universe to standard hot Big Bang cosmology with the observed matter–radiation content.
status_search_result: The fundamental nature of the inflaton and the precise mechanism that ended inflation remain unresolved open problems in physics. original_question: Find the exact value of Dhat_conv(n), where Dhat_conv(n) is the largest number such that every set of n points in strict convex position contains a point whose distances to the other n-1 points realize at least Dhat_conv(n) distinct values.
self_contained_problem:
A finite set $P$ of $n\ge 3$ points in the Euclidean plane is said to be in strict convex position if the points are the vertices of a convex polygon (no three collinear). For such a set $P$ and a point $p\in P$, let $d(p,P)$ denote the number of distinct values in the multiset $\{\,\|p-q\|:q\in P\setminus\{p\}\,\}$. Define
$$\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{conv}}(n)=\min_{P}\;\max_{p\in P} d(p,P),$$
where the minimum is over all $n$-point sets $P$ in strict convex position in the plane. Equivalently, $\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{conv}}(n)$ is the largest integer $k$ such that every $n$-point set in strict convex position contains a point that determines at least $k$ distinct distances to the remaining $n-1$ points.

Determine the exact value of $\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{conv}}(n)$ for every $n$.
status_search_result: The problem is a classical Erdős-type question (Erdős conjectured in 1946 that the value is at least ⌊n/2⌋). The best known lower bound is approximately (13/36 + 1/22701)n + O(1) due to Nivasch–Pach–Pinchasi–Zerbib, improving Dumitrescu's ⌈(13n−6)/36⌉ bound (2006). The exact value remains undetermined, so the problem is open.

original_question: Find the asymptotic value of Dgen(n), the minimum number of distinct distances determined by an n-point planar set in general position, meaning no three points are collinear and no four points are cocircular.
self_contained_problem:
A finite set $P\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ is said to be in general position if no three points of $P$ are collinear and no four points of $P$ lie on a common circle. For a finite point set $P\subset\mathbb{R}^2$, let
$$D(P)=\bigl|\{\,\|p-q\|:p,q\in P,\ p\neq q\,\}\bigr|$$
denote the number of distinct pairwise Euclidean distances determined by $P$. Define
$$D_{\mathrm{gen}}(n)=\min\bigl\{D(P):P\subset\mathbb{R}^2,\ |P|=n,\ P\text{ in general position}\bigr\}.$$
Determine the asymptotic behavior of $D_{\mathrm{gen}}(n)$ as $n\to\infty$.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in particle physics
original_question: Can electroweak symmetry breaking be explained by a viable model that avoids or extends a fundamental Standard Model Higgs scalar—such as technicolor, extra-dimensional gauge-Higgs models, Higgsless boundary-condition models, or composite-Higgs dynamics—while preserving precision electroweak agreement and generating charged-fermion masses?
self_contained_problem:
In the Standard Model of particle physics, the SU(2)_L × U(1)_Y electroweak gauge symmetry is broken to the electromagnetic U(1)_em via the vacuum expectation value of an elementary scalar doublet (the Higgs field), which simultaneously generates masses for the W and Z gauge bosons and for the charged fermions through Yukawa couplings. Construct, or prove the impossibility of, a viable alternative theory of electroweak symmetry breaking that does not rely on a fundamental elementary Higgs scalar — for instance:

(a) a technicolor model, in which a new strongly coupled gauge interaction with chiral fermions condenses to break electroweak symmetry dynamically;
(b) a five- (or higher-) dimensional gauge-Higgs unification model, in which the would-be Higgs arises as the extra-dimensional component of a higher-dimensional gauge field;
(c) a Higgsless model on an interval, in which electroweak symmetry breaking is implemented purely through boundary conditions on bulk gauge fields;
(d) a composite-Higgs scenario, in which the Higgs-like scalar arises as a pseudo–Nambu–Goldstone boson of a spontaneously broken global symmetry of a new strongly coupled sector.

The required model must satisfy all of the following criteria simultaneously:

1. It reproduces the observed pattern SU(2)_L × U(1)_Y → U(1)_em with the correct W and Z boson masses and the measured value of the weak mixing angle.
2. It is consistent with precision electroweak measurements; in particular, the oblique parameters S, T, U (defined as deviations from a Standard Model reference point in the vacuum-polarization functions of the electroweak gauge bosons) lie within their experimentally allowed ranges.
3. It generates the observed hierarchical masses and mixings of all charged fermions (quarks and charged leptons) without inducing flavor-changing neutral currents above current experimental bounds.
4. Where strongly coupled non-perturbative dynamics is invoked, a controlled quantitative description (e.g., via large-N expansions, holographic duals, or lattice computations) of the relevant bound states and condensates is provided.
5. Any boundary conditions, orbifold projections, or symmetry-breaking patterns required are derived from, or made natural within, the model rather than imposed ad hoc.

Determine whether such a model exists, and if so, exhibit it explicitly; otherwise, prove that no theory in the above classes can simultaneously satisfy these criteria.
status_search_result: Following the 2012 discovery at the LHC of a scalar boson of mass ≈125 GeV with properties consistent with the Standard Model Higgs, purely Higgsless and minimal technicolor scenarios are strongly disfavored. Composite-Higgs and pseudo–Nambu–Goldstone-boson constructions, as well as gauge-Higgs unification models, remain active areas of research that aim to satisfy precision electroweak constraints and reproduce fermion masses, but no fully viable, complete, and experimentally preferred non-elementary-Higgs model of electroweak symmetry breaking has been established. The general question therefore remains open.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in particle physics
original_question: What explains the origin, stability, and apparent desert of the gauge hierarchy: why the QCD and electroweak scales Λ_QCD ∼ 200 MeV and v ≈ 246 GeV are many orders of magnitude smaller than Planck, grand-unification, neutrino, or Peccei-Quinn scales; why electroweak radiative corrections do not require extreme fine tuning; and why no particles or interactions appear between the low and high scales?
self_contained_problem:
In the Standard Model of particle physics, two characteristic energy scales appear at low energies: the QCD confinement scale Λ_QCD ≈ 200 MeV and the electroweak symmetry-breaking scale set by the Higgs vacuum expectation value v ≈ 246 GeV. At high energies, several other fundamental scales arise: the Planck scale M_Pl ≈ 1.22 × 10^19 GeV, a putative grand-unification scale M_GUT ≈ 10^16 GeV, a Peccei–Quinn scale M_PQ (commonly assumed in 10^9–10^12 GeV range) introduced to solve the strong-CP problem, and a neutrino mass scale M_ν associated with the seesaw mechanism (typically 10^9–10^15 GeV).

The gauge hierarchy problem comprises the following three interrelated questions:

(a) Origin. Provide a dynamical or symmetry-based explanation for why (Λ_QCD, v) are smaller than (M_Pl, M_GUT, M_PQ, M_ν) by many orders of magnitude.

(b) Stability. The Higgs boson mass squared receives quadratically divergent radiative corrections of order (the high cutoff)^2 from loops involving particles of mass up to the high scales. Explain why the physical electroweak scale v ≈ 246 GeV remains stable under these corrections without requiring fine tuning of the bare parameters at the level of one part in (M_high/v)^2.

(c) Desert. Explain the apparent absence of new particles, fields, or interaction thresholds in the enormous energy range between the low scales (Λ_QCD, v) and the high scales (M_ν, M_GUT, M_Pl).

Provide a unified theoretical framework, consistent with current experimental constraints, that simultaneously resolves (a), (b), and (c).
status_search_result: The gauge hierarchy problem remains a central open problem in high-energy physics. No experimentally confirmed mechanism (supersymmetry, technicolor/composite Higgs, extra dimensions, anthropic/multiverse arguments, relaxion, etc.) has resolved all three aspects, and LHC results through the mid-2020s have not discovered new physics at the TeV scale that would naturally stabilize the electroweak scale.

original_question: Find the asymptotic value of Dpara(n), the minimum number of distinct distances determined by an n-point planar set in general position that determines no parallelograms.
self_contained_problem:
A finite set $P$ of points in the Euclidean plane is said to be in general position if no three points of $P$ are collinear and no four points of $P$ are concyclic. Four distinct points $a,b,c,d \in P$ are said to determine a parallelogram if (after a suitable labeling) $a+c = b+d$ as vectors in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the four points are not collinear. For an integer $n \ge 4$, let
$$D_{\mathrm{para}}(n) := \min |\{\,\|p-q\| : p,q \in P,\ p \ne q\,\}|,$$
where the minimum is taken over all $n$-point sets $P \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ which are in general position and which do not determine any parallelogram.

Determine the asymptotic behavior of $D_{\mathrm{para}}(n)$ as $n \to \infty$.
status_search_result: The asymptotic value of $D_{\mathrm{para}}(n)$ appears to remain open. Recent work (e.g., constructions on parabolas in finite fields) yields point sets in general position avoiding parallelograms with $O(n^2/\sqrt{\log n})$ distinct distances, and Sidon-set constructions provide related upper bounds, but tight asymptotic bounds matching a lower bound have not been established.

For an integer $d \geq 2$ and a finite set $P \subset \mathbb{R}^d$, let $\Delta(P) = \{\|x-y\| : x,y \in P,\ x

$$D_d(n) = \min_{\substack{P \subset \mathbb{R}^d \ |P| = n}} |\Delta(P)|,$$

paper_title: Unsolved problems in particle physics
original_question: What underlying principle or model explains why the three generations of quarks and charged leptons have identical gauge interactions but masses and quark mixings with strong hierarchical patterns, while neutrino masses and leptonic mixing display a different and less suppressed hierarchy?
self_contained_problem:
In the Standard Model of particle physics extended to include neutrino masses, the fermion content consists of three generations with identical gauge quantum numbers under SU(3)_C × SU(2)_L × U(1)_Y. After electroweak symmetry breaking, the charged fermions acquire masses through Yukawa couplings to the Higgs doublet, and the quark flavor mixing is described by the Cabibbo–Kobayashi–Maskawa (CKM) matrix while leptonic mixing is described by the Pontecorvo–Maki–Nakagawa–Sakata (PMNS) matrix. Empirically:

(i) The masses of up-type quarks (u, c, t), down-type quarks (d, s, b), and charged leptons (e, μ, τ) span many orders of magnitude with a strongly hierarchical pattern across generations.
(ii) The CKM mixing matrix is close to the identity, with off-diagonal entries that are small and themselves hierarchically ordered.
(iii) Neutrino mass-squared differences indicate masses much smaller than all charged-fermion masses, and the hierarchy among neutrino masses is much milder; the PMNS matrix exhibits two large mixing angles and one moderately small angle, in sharp contrast to the CKM pattern.

Problem: Provide a fundamental dynamical or symmetry-based principle, embedded in a predictive theoretical framework beyond the Standard Model, that
(a) explains why the three generations have identical gauge interactions yet strongly hierarchical charged-fermion masses,
(b) accounts quantitatively for the observed hierarchical pattern of the CKM mixing matrix,
(c) explains why the neutrino mass spectrum and the PMNS mixing pattern follow a qualitatively different and much less suppressed hierarchical structure than the charged sector, and
(d) yields the relations among these flavor parameters from a small set of underlying inputs rather than fitting them independently.
category_tag: fermion mass hierarchy and flavor puzzle
status_search_result: The flavor/fermion-mass-hierarchy puzzle remains an open problem in particle physics. Numerous proposals exist (Froggatt–Nielsen mechanisms, extra-dimensional wavefunction localization, discrete flavor symmetries such as A4, S4, modular flavor symmetries, anarchy in the neutrino sector, seesaw mechanisms), but no single framework is established as the explanation, and recent reviews continue to describe it as unresolved.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in particle physics
original_question: How can QCD at strong coupling be solved from first principles so that confinement, the formation of colorless hadrons from quarks and gluons, and low- and intermediate-energy hadron properties and interactions are derived quantitatively rather than modeled phenomenologically?
self_contained_problem:
Quantum chromodynamics (QCD) is the non-abelian gauge theory with gauge group SU(3) coupled to Dirac fermions ("quarks") in the fundamental representation, defined by the Lagrangian density

  L = -(1/4) G^a_{μν} G^{a μν} + Σ_f \bar{q}_f (i γ^μ D_μ - m_f) q_f,

where G^a_{μν} = ∂_μ A^a_ν - ∂_ν A^a_μ + g f^{abc} A^b_μ A^c_ν is the gluon field strength, D_μ = ∂_μ - i g A^a_μ T^a is the covariant derivative, T^a are the generators of su(3), and the sum runs over quark flavors f with masses m_f. At high energies the running coupling g is small (asymptotic freedom), but at low energies it becomes large, and standard perturbative expansions in g fail.

Develop a first-principles, mathematically rigorous, non-perturbative construction and analysis of QCD that establishes the following quantitatively (rather than via phenomenological modeling):

(a) Confinement: prove that the spectrum of the pure SU(3) Yang–Mills theory contains no asymptotic colored states, e.g. by showing an area law for the Wilson loop expectation in the continuum limit, or equivalently a positive mass gap together with the absence of finite-energy color-charged states.

(b) Hadronization: derive from the QCD Lagrangian the existence of a discrete spectrum of color-singlet bound states (mesons and baryons) formed from quarks and gluons, and compute their masses, decay constants, and form factors from first principles.

(c) Low- and intermediate-energy hadronic interactions: derive quantitatively, from the QCD Lagrangian alone, the properties and interactions of hadrons in the low- and intermediate-energy regime (e.g. nucleon–nucleon potentials, scattering amplitudes, chiral symmetry breaking patterns) without recourse to phenomenological input beyond the parameters {g, m_f} of the Lagrangian.

Provide the analytic non-perturbative methods that achieve this, or prove that such a derivation is possible within continuum quantum field theory.
status_search_result: The problem subsumes the Clay Millennium "Yang–Mills existence and mass gap" problem, which remains unsolved. While lattice QCD provides strong numerical evidence for confinement and reproduces hadron spectra to good accuracy, no first-principles analytic derivation of confinement, hadron formation, and low-energy hadron interactions from the QCD Lagrangian exists. The problem is widely regarded as open as of 2026.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in particle physics
original_question: At what momentum-transfer scales does perturbative QCD become reliable for exclusive hadronic observables such as pion form factors, and why do measurements up to roughly 2–4 GeV fail to show a clear approach to perturbative predictions?
self_contained_problem:
In quantum chromodynamics (QCD), exclusive hadronic observables such as the electromagnetic form factor $F_\pi(Q^2)$ of the pion and the pion–photon transition form factor $F_{\pi\gamma}(Q^2)$ are predicted, in the asymptotic limit $Q^2 \to \infty$, by collinear factorization theorems combined with perturbative QCD (pQCD). In particular, leading-order pQCD predicts $Q^2 F_\pi(Q^2) \to 8\pi \alpha_s(Q^2) f_\pi^2$ and $Q^2 F_{\pi\gamma}(Q^2) \to \sqrt{2}\, f_\pi$ (with $f_\pi \approx 92$ MeV the pion decay constant), with corrections governed by the pion light-cone distribution amplitude $\varphi_\pi(x,\mu)$ which evolves toward its asymptotic form $\varphi_\pi^{\rm asy}(x) = 6x(1-x)$.

Provide a quantitative answer to the following:

(a) Determine the threshold momentum-transfer scale $Q_*^2$ above which pQCD factorization gives reliable predictions for the exclusive form factors $F_\pi(Q^2)$ and $F_{\pi\gamma}(Q^2)$, in the sense that the leading-twist, leading-order pQCD result agrees with the true form factor to within a specified accuracy (e.g. 10\%) up to calculable higher-twist and higher-order corrections.

(b) Explain, in terms of the underlying nonperturbative structure (higher-twist contributions, transverse-momentum/end-point effects, the precise shape of $\varphi_\pi(x,\mu)$, and soft/Feynman mechanisms), why measured pion form factors in the momentum-transfer range $Q^2 \approx 2$–$4\ \mathrm{GeV}^2$ exhibit no clear convergence toward the asymptotic pQCD prediction, and quantify when convergence should set in.
category_tag: Perturbative QCD and exclusive form factors
status_search_result: The question of where perturbative QCD becomes quantitatively reliable for exclusive pion form factors remains an active and contested research topic. The BaBar–Belle tension in the pion–photon transition form factor has not been resolved: different theoretical approaches (nonlocal QCD sum rules, light-cone sum rules, dispersive analyses, intrinsic-transverse-momentum-enhanced pQCD) give conflicting conclusions and cannot simultaneously accommodate all data. Recent works (e.g., 2025) continue to propose mechanisms (such as iTMD-enhanced pQCD) to extend pQCD applicability down to a few GeV², but no consensus on the onset scale exists.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in particle physics
original_question: How can effective theories written in observable hadron degrees of freedom be rigorously justified as low-energy limits of QCD rather than treated as phenomenological models whose connection to the underlying quark-and-gluon theory remains unproven?
self_contained_problem:
Let QCD denote quantum chromodynamics: the non-abelian gauge theory with gauge group SU(3) coupled to quark fields in the fundamental representation, defined (formally) by the Lagrangian density
  L_QCD = -(1/4) G^a_{μν} G^{a μν} + Σ_f \bar{q}_f (i γ^μ D_μ - m_f) q_f,
with G^a_{μν} the gluon field strength and D_μ the gauge-covariant derivative. By an "effective hadronic theory" we mean a local relativistic quantum field theory whose dynamical fields are color-singlet composite degrees of freedom (e.g. pseudoscalar mesons π, vector mesons, baryons such as nucleons) with a Lagrangian L_eff[φ_hadrons] organized as a derivative/momentum expansion (for instance chiral perturbation theory, the linear or non-linear sigma model, chiral effective field theory for nucleons, or hidden-local-symmetry models).

Problem. Provide a mathematically rigorous derivation that establishes a given effective hadronic theory L_eff as the low-energy limit of QCD. Concretely, formulate and prove a precise statement of the following form:

There exist a renormalization scheme for QCD, an energy/momentum scale Λ, and an explicit map Φ from QCD correlation functions of color-singlet composite operators with external momenta |p_i| ≪ Λ to correlation functions computed from L_eff[φ_hadrons], such that for every n-point correlator of such operators,
  ⟨O_1(p_1) ⋯ O_n(p_n)⟩_QCD = ⟨Φ(O_1)(p_1) ⋯ Φ(O_n)(p_n)⟩_{L_eff} + R_n(p_1,…,p_n),
with a controlled remainder R_n bounded by an explicit power of max_i |p_i|/Λ, and with all low-energy constants of L_eff determined (in principle computable) from QCD parameters (the gauge coupling and quark masses) alone.

The task is to give such a derivation — including a non-perturbative construction of QCD as a well-defined quantum field theory at the level required, an identification of the relevant hadronic degrees of freedom from QCD, and quantitative error control — for at least one nontrivial effective hadronic Lagrangian, thereby converting it from a phenomenological model into a theorem about QCD.
status_search_result: The rigorous derivation of hadronic effective field theories (such as chiral perturbation theory or nucleon EFTs) directly from QCD remains a long-standing open problem. Even the non-perturbative construction of four-dimensional Yang–Mills theory is one of the Clay Millennium Problems, and no rigorous derivation of confinement, chiral symmetry breaking, or a hadronic effective Lagrangian from QCD currently exists; lattice QCD provides numerical evidence but not a mathematical proof.

original_question: Find the asymptotic value of Dcurve^(d)(n), the minimum number of distinct distances determined by n points on a constant-degree curve in R^d that does not contain an algebraic helix.
self_contained_problem:
For an integer d ≥ 2, an algebraic curve γ in ℝ^d is said to be of constant degree if it is the zero set of a finite collection of polynomials of degree bounded by an absolute constant. An algebraic helix in ℝ^d is a constant-degree algebraic curve that, after a rigid motion, can be parametrized as (a_1 cos(ω_1 t + φ_1), a_1 sin(ω_1 t + φ_1), …, a_k cos(ω_k t + φ_k), a_k sin(ω_k t + φ_k), c·t, 0, …, 0) for real constants a_i, ω_i, φ_i, c (equivalently, a constant-degree curve all of whose points have a tangent vector of constant Euclidean norm under a suitable parametrization).

For an n-point set P ⊂ ℝ^d, let D(P) denote the number of distinct values in the multiset {‖p − q‖ : p, q ∈ P, p ≠ q}. Define
   D_curve^(d)(n) := min { D(P) : |P| = n, P ⊂ γ for some constant-degree algebraic curve γ ⊂ ℝ^d that does not contain an algebraic helix }.

Determine the asymptotic behavior of D_curve^(d)(n) as n → ∞ for each fixed d ≥ 2.
status_search_result: The problem appears to remain open. Recent work (e.g. arXiv:2304.06812) establishes the lower bound Ω(n^{4/3}) for distinct distances determined by n points on a constant-degree curve in ℝ^d that does not contain an algebraic helix, improving earlier Ω(n^{5/4}) bounds, but the precise asymptotic value of D_curve^(d)(n) is not known to be settled.

original_question: Derive non-trivial lower or upper bounds for distinct distances determined by points constrained to algebraic varieties in R^d for dimensions d >= 3.
self_contained_problem:
For an integer d ≥ 3 and an integer D ≥ d, let V ⊂ ℝ^D be an irreducible algebraic variety of dimension d and bounded (constant) degree. For a finite set P ⊂ V of n points, let

  D(P) = |{ ‖p − q‖ : p, q ∈ P, p ≠ q }|

denote the number of distinct Euclidean distances determined by P. Define

  f_V(n) = min { D(P) : P ⊂ V, |P| = n }.

The problem is to establish non-trivial lower bounds (and matching or near-matching upper bounds) on f_V(n) as n → ∞ that exploit the fact that the points are constrained to lie on V. More precisely: prove bounds of the form f_V(n) = Ω(n^{α(d,V)}) with exponent α(d,V) strictly larger than the trivial exponent obtained from the ambient-space distinct distances bound for ℝ^D, valid for all (or for a natural class of) d-dimensional constant-degree irreducible varieties V ⊂ ℝ^D with d ≥ 3, and complement these by constructions giving upper bounds on f_V(n).
status_search_result: Partial progress exists. For constant-degree d-dimensional varieties V ⊂ ℝ^D, results give large subsets spanning all-distinct distances of size Ω(n^{4/(9+12(d−1))}), improving an earlier Ω(n^{1/(3d)}) bound. For algebraic curves (d = 1) in ℝ^D, every n-point set spans Ω(n^{4/3}) distinct distances unless the curve is an algebraic helix. General sharp bounds for arbitrary d ≥ 3 varieties remain open.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in particle physics
original_question: Can one prove that the continuum limit of lattice QCD exists, is independent of the way the lattice size tends to infinity and the lattice spacing tends to zero, and coincides with continuum QCD despite theoretical differences such as the treatment of instantons and chiral fermions?
self_contained_problem:
Consider quantum chromodynamics (QCD) as a non-abelian gauge theory with gauge group SU(3) coupled to quark fields, formulated on a four-dimensional Euclidean hypercubic lattice $\Lambda_{a,L} = (a\mathbb{Z})^4 \cap [-L/2, L/2]^4$ with lattice spacing $a > 0$ and side length $L$. On such a lattice, gauge fields are realized as SU(3)-valued link variables, the gauge action is given by a Wilson-type plaquette action, and quark fields are realized by some lattice fermion discretization (e.g. Wilson, staggered, domain-wall, or overlap fermions). Let $\langle \mathcal{O} angle_{a,L}$ denote the expectation values of gauge-invariant local observables computed in this lattice theory with bare couplings tuned along a renormalization-group trajectory.

Prove the following:

1. (Existence of the continuum limit.) The limit
$$\langle \mathcal{O} \rangle_{\mathrm{cont}} \;=\; \lim_{\substack{a \to 0 \\ L \to \infty}} \langle \mathcal{O} \rangle_{a,L}$$
exists for all gauge-invariant local observables $\mathcal{O}$.

2. (Independence of the limiting procedure.) The limit does not depend on the joint manner in which $a \to 0$ and $L \to \infty$, nor on the choice of lattice fermion discretization, provided the bare parameters are tuned along an appropriate renormalization-group trajectory.

3. (Agreement with continuum QCD.) The resulting collection of correlation functions defines a quantum field theory satisfying the Osterwalder–Schwinger axioms whose Wightman functions coincide with those of continuum QCD, despite the structural differences between the lattice and the continuum formulations (for example, the fact that continuum instantons giving rise to nontrivial vacuum topology are not always stable lattice configurations, and that the implementation of chiral fermions on the lattice requires non-trivial constructions such as the Ginsparg–Wilson relation).
category_tag: Lattice gauge theory and continuum limit of QCD
status_search_result: The rigorous construction of four-dimensional non-abelian Yang–Mills theory (and QCD) and the proof that lattice regularizations have a well-defined continuum limit equivalent to a continuum quantum field theory satisfying the Wightman/Osterwalder–Schwinger axioms remains one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems and is widely regarded as open. No accepted solution exists; partial progress includes constructions in lower dimensions, results on stochastic quantization, and recent work by Chatterjee and others on lattice gauge theory, but the full continuum-limit problem for QCD is unresolved.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in particle physics
context_brief: Dual and holographic descriptions of QCD
original_question: Can a weakly coupled dual or holographic theory for real QCD be constructed and proven, so that low- and intermediate-energy strong dynamics can be calculated from a dual theory rather than chosen through partly arbitrary five-dimensional effective models?
self_contained_problem: Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) is the SU(3) non-abelian gauge theory of quarks and gluons describing the strong interaction. At low and intermediate energies its coupling becomes large and standard perturbative methods fail. Inspired by the AdS/CFT correspondence (which provides an exact equivalence between certain strongly coupled four-dimensional gauge theories and weakly coupled string/gravity theories in higher-dimensional anti–de Sitter backgrounds), one would like an analogous dual description of real-world QCD. Existing "holographic QCD" approaches postulate five-dimensional effective field theories on suitably chosen (e.g. AdS-like, with hard or soft infrared walls) backgrounds whose fields are matched to QCD operators; however the choice of the five-dimensional model is to a large extent ad hoc and the duality itself is not derived from QCD.\n\nProblem. Construct a weakly coupled (gravitational, string-theoretic, or otherwise tractable) theory T that is provably dual to four-dimensional QCD with three colors and the physical quark content, in the sense that correlation functions and spectra of gauge-invariant QCD operators coincide exactly with those computed in T, and prove the equivalence. As a consequence, the low- and intermediate-energy strong-coupling dynamics of QCD (hadron spectra, form factors, condensates, etc.) should be calculable from T rather than postulated through an arbitrary choice of a five-dimensional effective model.
status_search_result: No exact weakly coupled holographic dual of real QCD has been constructed or proven. Top-down string constructions (e.g., Sakai–Sugimoto, Witten's D4-brane model) and bottom-up models (hard-wall, soft-wall AdS/QCD) approximate QCD but are not derived dualities, and the problem is widely regarded as open in the hep-th/hep-ph literature as of 2026.

original_question: Find the asymptotic value of D(m,n), the minimum number of distinct distances determined between two planar point sets of sizes m and n when only cross-set distances are counted.
self_contained_problem:
For two finite point sets $P_1, P_2 \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, define the set of cross-distances
$$D(P_1, P_2) = \{\, \|p - q\| : p \in P_1,\ q \in P_2 \,\},$$
and let
$$D(m,n) = \min\bigl\{\, |D(P_1, P_2)| : P_1, P_2 \subset \mathbb{R}^2,\ |P_1| = m,\ |P_2| = n \,\bigr\}.$$
Determine the asymptotic behavior of $D(m,n)$ as $m, n \to \infty$ (in all regimes of the relationship between $m$ and $n$, with $m \le n$). In particular, give matching upper and lower bounds, up to constant or polylogarithmic factors, for $D(m,n)$.
status_search_result: The bipartite distinct distances quantity D(m,n) has only partial bounds known. Subsequent work (e.g., "On Bipartite Distinct Distances in the Plane", 2019) provides improved lower bounds in various ranges of m vs. n, but matching upper and lower bounds (i.e., the asymptotic value) remain unknown, especially in the intermediate regime.

original_question: Find the asymptotic value of Dlines(m,n), the minimum number of distinct distances between m points on one line and n points on another planar line when the two lines are neither parallel nor orthogonal.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ be two distinct lines in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ that are neither parallel nor orthogonal. For positive integers $m,n$, let $P_1\subset\ell_1$ and $P_2\subset\ell_2$ be sets of $m$ and $n$ points, respectively, and let
$$D(P_1,P_2)=\bigl|\{\,\|p-q\|:p\in P_1,\;q\in P_2\,\}\bigr|$$
denote the number of distinct Euclidean distances determined by pairs in $P_1\times P_2$. Define
$$D_{\mathrm{lines}}(m,n)=\min_{P_1,P_2} D(P_1,P_2),$$
where the minimum is over all such configurations on all such pairs of lines. Determine the asymptotic behavior of $D_{\mathrm{lines}}(m,n)$ as $m,n\to\infty$. In particular, decide whether $D_{\mathrm{lines}}(m,n)$ is superlinear in $\min(m,n)$, and find matching upper and lower bounds.
status_search_result: Sharir, Sheffer, and Solymosi (2013) proved the lower bound $D_{\mathrm{lines}}(m,n)=\Omega(\min\{m^{2/3}n^{2/3},m^2,n^2\})$, giving $\Omega(m^{4/3})$ when $m=n$, confirming Purdy's superlinearity conjecture. However, the precise asymptotic value (with matching upper bound) is not known; the problem of determining the true asymptotics of $D_{\mathrm{lines}}(m,n)$ remains open.

original_question: Find the asymptotic value of Dcurves(m,n), the minimum number of distinct distances between m points on one constant-degree algebraic curve and n points on another when the curves avoid the exceptional cases of containing parallel lines, orthogonal lines, or concentric circles.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\gamma_1, \gamma_2 \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be two irreducible algebraic curves of constant degree (the degree bound is fixed independent of $m$ and $n$) such that no irreducible component of $\gamma_1 \cup \gamma_2$ produces any of the following "exceptional" configurations: $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ are parallel lines, $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ are orthogonal lines, or $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ are concentric circles. For point sets $P_1 \subset \gamma_1$ with $|P_1| = m$ and $P_2 \subset \gamma_2$ with $|P_2| = n$, define
$$ D(P_1, P_2) = |\{\, \|p - q\| : p \in P_1,\ q \in P_2 \,\}|, $$
the number of distinct Euclidean distances determined by pairs with one point in each set. Define
$$ D_{\text{curves}}(m, n) = \min\, D(P_1, P_2), $$
where the minimum is over all such non-exceptional pairs $(\gamma_1, \gamma_2)$ and all choices of $P_1 \subset \gamma_1$, $P_2 \subset \gamma_2$ with $|P_1| = m$, $|P_2| = n$. Determine the asymptotic behavior of $D_{\text{curves}}(m, n)$ as $m, n \to \infty$.
status_search_result: The best known lower bound for the number of distinct distances between m points on one constant-degree irreducible plane algebraic curve and n points on another (excluding the parallel-lines, orthogonal-lines, and concentric-circles exceptions) is of the form Ω(min{m^{2/3}n^{2/3}, m^2, n^2}), due to Pach and de Zeeuw, with later improvements in special cases (e.g., on two lines, Sharir–Sheffer–Solymosi obtained Ω(n^{4/3})). The exact asymptotic value of D_curves(m, n) has not been determined; the problem remains open as of recent literature on distinct distances on Pfaffian/algebraic curves (2025).

context_brief: Three noncollinear points versus n points
original_question: Find the asymptotic value of D(3,n) when the three distinguished points are not collinear, where D(3,n) asks for the minimum number of distances determined between those three points and another set of n points.
self_contained_problem:
For a finite set $P\subset\mathbb{R}^2$, let $\Delta(P)=\{\,\|p-q\|:p,q\in P,\;p\neq q\,\}$ denote the set of distinct Euclidean distances determined by $P$. For positive integers $a$ and $n$, define
$$D(a,n)=\min\bigl|\{\,\|p-q\|:p\in A,\;q\in B\,\}\bigr|,$$
where the minimum is taken over all pairs of point sets $A,B\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ with $|A|=a$ and $|B|=n$ (only distances between a point of $A$ and a point of $B$ are counted).

Restrict attention to the case $a=3$, and require that the three points of $A$ be non-collinear. Determine the asymptotic behavior, as $n\to\infty$, of
$$D(3,n)\quad\text{subject to the constraint that the three points of }A\text{ are not collinear}.$$
That is, find matching upper and lower bounds (up to constant or sub-polynomial factors) for the minimum, over all non-collinear triples $A=\{p_1,p_2,p_3\}\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ and all $n$-point sets $B\subset\mathbb{R}^2$, of the number of distinct values in $\{\|p_i-q\|:i\in\{1,2,3\},\;q\in B\}$.
status_search_result: The asymptotic value of D(3,n) for three non-collinear points appears to remain open. Known results give only lower bounds (e.g., Ω(n^{6/11}) from work on bipartite distinct distances), with no matching upper bound establishing the true asymptotic order. context_brief: Largest distinct-distance subset in the plane
original_question: Find the asymptotic value of subset(n), the largest number such that every n-point set in the plane contains a subset of that size in which no positive distance occurs more than once.
self_contained_problem:
For a finite set $P\subset\mathbb{R}^2$, let $\mathrm{subset}(P)$ denote the largest cardinality of a subset $Q\subseteq P$ such that all pairwise Euclidean distances $\{\,\|x-y\|:x,y\in Q,\,x\ne y\,\}$ are distinct (equivalently, no positive distance is realized by more than one unordered pair of points of $Q$). Define
$$\mathrm{subset}(n)=\min_{\substack{P\subset\mathbb{R}^2\\ |P|=n}}\mathrm{subset}(P),$$
so that $\mathrm{subset}(n)$ is the largest integer with the property that every set of $n$ points in the plane contains $\mathrm{subset}(n)$ points spanning all distinct pairwise distances. Determine the asymptotic behavior of $\mathrm{subset}(n)$ as $n\to\infty$.
status_search_result: The problem appears to be open. The best known lower bound is $\mathrm{subset}(n) = \Omega((n/\log n)^{1/3})$ due to Charalambides (2013), improving earlier $\Omega(n^{1/3})$ bounds of Lefmann–Thiele and others. The best known upper bound is roughly $O(n^{c})$ derived from configurations like the $\sqrt{n}\times\sqrt{n}$ grid, giving $\mathrm{subset}(n)=O(n^{?})$ much larger than the lower bound. No matching asymptotic is known.

paper_title: Distribution of irreducible polynomials of small degrees over finite fields
original_question: Given a finite field F_q of order q, an element a in F_q, an integer n >= 2, and an integer j with 0 <= j < n, determine whether there exists a monic irreducible polynomial f(x) = x^n + sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k x^k over F_q whose j-th coefficient a_j is exactly a, except in the two exceptional cases: j = 0 and a = 0 for arbitrary q; and q = 2^m, n = 2, j = 1, and a = 0. Equivalently, is Hansen-Mullen Conjecture B true for all parameter choices outside these exceptions?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{F}_q$ be the finite field with $q$ elements, let $n\ge 2$ be an integer, let $j$ be an integer with $0\le j<n$, and let $a\in\mathbb{F}_q$. Consider monic polynomials of degree $n$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$ written as
$$f(x)=x^n+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_k x^k,\qquad a_k\in\mathbb{F}_q.$$
Prove or disprove the following statement (Hansen–Mullen Conjecture B): for every choice of $(q,n,j,a)$ there exists a monic irreducible polynomial $f(x)\in\mathbb{F}_q[x]$ of degree $n$ with $a_j=a$, except in the following two cases, where no such irreducible polynomial exists:
(i) $j=0$ and $a=0$ (for arbitrary $q$ and $n$);
(ii) $q=2^m$ for some $m\ge 1$, $n=2$, $j=1$, and $a=0$.
status_search_result: The Hansen–Mullen Conjecture B (existence of irreducible polynomials over $\mathbb{F}_q$ with one prescribed coefficient, outside the listed exceptions) was proved by D. Wan (1997) for $q>19$ or $n\ge 36$ using Weil-type bounds for character sums; the remaining small cases were verified by Ham and Mullen (and others) by computation, completing the proof. A new conceptual proof was given by Pollack and others (arXiv:1604.04023, 2016). The conjecture is therefore considered fully solved.

original_question: Find the asymptotic value of subset_d(n) for d >= 3, where subset_d(n) is the largest number such that every n-point set in R^d contains a subset of that size in which each positive distance occurs at most once.
self_contained_problem:

Known results give only partial lower bounds (e.g., Charalambides-type bounds of order n^{c/d} up to logs, and improvements via algebraic-variety arguments by Raz, Sharir, and others), with no matching upper bound. No source found resolving the asymptotic value.

original_question: Find the asymptotic value of phi(n,3,3), the minimum number of distinct distances determined by an n-point planar set in which every three points determine three distinct distances, equivalently a set with no isosceles triangles, including degenerate collinear ones.
self_contained_problem:

Say that $P$ "spans no isosceles triangle" if every three points of $P$ determine three pairwise distinct distances; here triples of collinear points are also required to satisfy this condition (so no three points $a,b,c \in P$ may satisfy $\|a-b\|=\|a-c\|$, even when $a,b,c$ are collinear). Define
$$\varphi(n,3,3) \;=\; \min\bigl\{\,|D(P)| : P \subset \mathbb{R}^2,\ |P|=n,\ P\text{ spans no isosceles triangle}\,\bigr\}.$$

The trivial lower bound is $\varphi(n,3,3) = \Omega(n)$ (since every point has $n-1$ distinct distances to the others), and Erdős noted upper bounds, but the asymptotic value is unknown. It is not even known whether $\varphi(n,3,3)/n \to \infty$, even in the analogous problem on the line $\mathbb{R}$.

original_question: Find the asymptotic value of phi(n,4,3), the minimum number of distinct distances determined by an n-point planar set in which every four points determine at least three distinct distances, equivalently a set with no squares.
self_contained_problem:
For a finite set $P\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ of points in the plane, let $D(P)$ denote the number of distinct values in the multiset $\{\,\|p-q\|:p,q\in P,\,p\neq q\,\}$. Say that $P$ "spans a square" if there exist four points of $P$ forming the vertices of a (non-degenerate) square. Define
$$\varphi(n,4,3) \;=\; \min\bigl\{\,D(P)\,:\,P\subset\mathbb{R}^2,\ |P|=n,\ \text{every 4 points of } P \text{ determine at least 3 distinct distances}\bigr\}.$$
Equivalently (since a 4-point set determining only 2 distances must be one of a finite list of configurations, and among them the square is the relevant case here), this is the minimum of $D(P)$ over all $n$-point planar sets that span no square.

Determine the asymptotic behavior of $\varphi(n,4,3)$ as $n\to\infty$. In particular, find matching upper and lower bounds (up to constants or logarithmic factors) for $\varphi(n,4,3)$.
status_search_result: The problem of determining the asymptotics of the minimum number of distinct distances over n-point planar sets containing no square (the (4,3) local condition) is part of a family of Erdős-style problems on local-versus-global distinct distances. Recent work, including a 2024 blog post by T. Tao on planar point sets with forbidden four-point patterns and related results on Erdős Problem #135, addresses neighboring questions but does not establish matching asymptotic bounds for φ(n,4,3); the problem appears to remain open, with the standard Guth–Katz bound Ω(n/log n) and the √n × √n grid upper bound O(n/√log n) being the best general bounds available.

paper_title: Problems and Conjectures in Matrix and Operator Inequalities
original_question: Given positive semidefinite matrices A and B and positive real numbers p and q, is it always true for every unitarily invariant norm that |||A^(p+q)+B^(p+q)||| ≤ |||(A^p+B^p)(A^q+B^q)|||? The paper notes that one may reduce without loss of generality to 0≤p≤1 and q=1-p by absorbing the (p+q)-th powers into A and B.
self_contained_problem:
Let $A, B$ be positive semidefinite complex matrices of the same size, and let $p, q > 0$ be real numbers. A norm $\vertiii{\cdot}$ on the space of complex matrices is said to be unitarily invariant if $\vertiii{UXV} = \vertiii{X}$ for all matrices $X$ and all unitary matrices $U, V$ of compatible sizes. Determine whether the inequality
$$\vertiii{A^{p+q} + B^{p+q}} \;\le\; \vertiii{(A^p + B^p)(A^q + B^q)}$$
holds for every unitarily invariant norm $\vertiii{\cdot}$, every pair of positive semidefinite matrices $A, B$, and all $p, q > 0$. (By absorbing the $(p+q)$-th powers into $A$ and $B$, the question reduces without loss of generality to the case $0 \le p \le 1$ and $q = 1-p$.)
status_search_result: The inequality, posed by Bourin, remains open in full generality. Affirmative answers are known in several special cases: for the trace norm and Hilbert–Schmidt norm (Hayajneh–Kittaneh), for commuting positive semidefinite matrices and all unitarily invariant norms (Audenaert), and for parameters $p \in [1/4, 3/4]$ (Kittaneh–Ricard). Recent work (2022–2024) extends these partial results to noncommutative symmetric spaces and $\tau$-measurable operators, but the general matrix conjecture is not fully resolved.

original_question: Find the asymptotic value of phi(n,5,9), the minimum number of distinct distances determined by an n-point planar set in which every five-point subset determines at least nine distinct distances.
self_contained_problem:
For integers n ≥ k ≥ 2 and an integer ℓ with $\binom{k}{2} \geq \ell \geq 2$, let $\varphi(n,k,\ell)$ denote the minimum, over all sets $P$ of $n$ points in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the property that every $k$-point subset of $P$ determines at least $\ell$ distinct pairwise distances, of the number of distinct pairwise distances determined by $P$. (If no such set exists for given $n,k,\ell$, the value is undefined; otherwise the minimum is taken over all admissible configurations.)

Determine the asymptotic behavior, as $n \to \infty$, of $\varphi(n,5,9)$. In particular, decide whether $\varphi(n,5,9) = \Omega(n^2)$, and more generally find matching upper and lower bounds for $\varphi(n,5,9)$ up to constants (or up to lower-order factors).

original_question: Prove or disprove that if a planar n-point set P spans only O(n/sqrt(log n)) distinct distances, then the additive energy E(P) = |{(a,b,c,d) in P^4 : a+b = c+d}| must be large.
self_contained_problem:
For a finite set $P \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ of $n$ points, let $D(P)$ denote the number of distinct values in the multiset $\{\|p-q\| : p,q \in P,\ p \neq q\}$, and define the additive energy of $P$ by
$$E(P) = \big|\{(a,b,c,d) \in P^4 : a+b = c+d\}\big|,$$
where addition is the usual vector addition in $\mathbb{R}^2$.

Prove or disprove the following statement: there exists a function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ with $f(n) \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$ such that for every planar point set $P$ with $|P|=n$ satisfying $D(P) = O(n/\sqrt{\log n})$, one has
$$E(P) \;\geq\; f(n) \cdot n^{2}.$$

In other words, must any $n$-point planar set realizing the conjecturally extremal number of distinct distances necessarily have large additive energy?
status_search_result: The problem links the Erdős distinct distances extremal regime (where the conjectured lower bound is $\Omega(n/\sqrt{\log n})$, while Guth–Katz proved $\Omega(n/\log n)$) with additive energy. Subsequent work (e.g., Lund–Sheffer–de Zeeuw on bisector energy, 2014) gives partial structural results for sets achieving few distinct distances, but no proof or disproof that such sets must have large additive energy is known. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: For a finite set A in R, determine the asymptotic size of the difference set A-A under the assumption that the Cartesian product A x A spans few distinct distances in the plane.
self_contained_problem:
Let $A \subset \mathbb{R}$ be a finite set, and consider the Cartesian product $A \times A \subset \mathbb{R}^2$. For a planar point set $P$, let $D(P)$ denote the number of distinct Euclidean distances determined by pairs of points of $P$. The difference set of $A$ is $A - A = \{a - a' : a, a' \in A\}$.

Determine the asymptotic behavior of $|A - A|$ as $|A| \to \infty$ under the hypothesis that $A \times A$ determines few distinct distances, i.e. $D(A \times A) = O(|A|/\sqrt{\log |A|})$ (the Guth–Katz lower-bound order for distinct distances of an $|A|^2$-point set). More precisely, find the smallest exponent $\alpha$ and the correct logarithmic factor such that the implication
$$D(A \times A) \ll \frac{|A|}{\sqrt{\log |A|}} \implies |A - A| \ll |A|^{\alpha}\,(\log |A|)^{O(1)}$$
holds for every finite $A \subset \mathbb{R}$, and decide whether $|A - A|$ must in fact be linear (up to logarithmic factors) under this hypothesis.
category_tag: Discrete geometry: distinct distances and sumsets
status_search_result: The best known bound, due to Pohoata (Electronic Journal of Combinatorics, 2019), shows that if $A\times A$ spans few distinct distances then $|A-A| \ll |A|^{2-2/7}(\log|A|)^{1/7}$, improving earlier results of Hanson and Roche-Newton. The exact asymptotic value of $|A-A|$ under this hypothesis is not determined; the problem of pinning down the correct exponent (and whether $|A-A|$ must be near-linear) remains open.

original_question: Find the asymptotic value of Dhat(n), the largest function such that every n-point planar set contains a point incident to at least Dhat(n) distinct distances to the other points.
self_contained_problem:
For a finite set $P \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ and a point $p \in P$, let $D(p, P\setminus\{p\}) = |\{\,\|p-q\| : q \in P\setminus\{p\}\,\}|$ denote the number of distinct Euclidean distances from $p$ to the other points of $P$. For each integer $n \ge 2$, define
$$\widehat{D}(n) \;=\; \min_{\substack{P \subset \mathbb{R}^2 \\ |P|=n}} \; \max_{p \in P} \; D(p,\, P\setminus\{p\}).$$
Thus $\widehat{D}(n)$ is the largest integer such that every set of $n$ points in the plane contains at least one point whose distances to the remaining $n-1$ points take at least $\widehat{D}(n)$ distinct values. Determine the asymptotic behavior of $\widehat{D}(n)$ as $n \to \infty$.
status_search_result: The problem is a well-known open question in combinatorial geometry. The best known upper bound is $\widehat{D}(n) = O(n/\sqrt{\log n})$, achieved by the integer lattice (Erdős), while the best lower bound is roughly $\widehat{D}(n) = \Omega(n^{c})$ for some $c<1$ (Katz–Tardos, building on Solymosi–Tóth and Guth–Katz). No matching bounds are known; the asymptotic value remains undetermined.

original_question: Find the asymptotic value of DhatSigma(n), where DhatSigma(n) is the minimum, over all planar n-point sets P, of the sum over p in P of the number of distinct distances from p to the rest of P.
self_contained_problem:
For a finite planar point set $P \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ and a point $p \in P$, let $\hat{D}_p(P)$ denote the number of distinct values in the multiset $\{\,\|p-q\| : q \in P \setminus \{p\}\,\}$ (i.e., the number of distinct distances from $p$ to the other points of $P$). Define
$$\hat{D}_\Sigma(P) = \sum_{p \in P} \hat{D}_p(P), \qquad \hat{D}_\Sigma(n) = \min_{\substack{P \subset \mathbb{R}^2 \\ |P|=n}} \hat{D}_\Sigma(P).$$
Determine the asymptotic behavior of $\hat{D}_\Sigma(n)$ as $n \to \infty$.

original_question: Find the asymptotic value of L(m,n), the minimum number of distinct point-to-line distances determined by a set of m points and a set of n lines in the plane.
self_contained_problem:
For positive integers $m$ and $n$, let $P$ be a set of $m$ points in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ and let $\mathcal{L}$ be a set of $n$ lines in $\mathbb{R}^2$. For a point $p\in\mathbb{R}^2$ and a line $\ell\subset\mathbb{R}^2$, let $d(p,\ell)$ denote the usual Euclidean distance from $p$ to $\ell$ (the infimum of $\|p-q\|$ over $q\in\ell$). Define
$$D(P,\mathcal{L}) = |\{\, d(p,\ell) : p\in P,\ \ell\in\mathcal{L}\,\}|,$$
the number of distinct point-to-line distances determined by $P$ and $\mathcal{L}$, and set
$$L(m,n) = \min\{\, D(P,\mathcal{L}) : |P|=m,\ |\mathcal{L}|=n\,\}.$$
Determine the asymptotic behavior of $L(m,n)$ as $m,n\to\infty$; that is, find matching (up to constants and lower-order factors) lower and upper bounds for $L(m,n)$ in terms of $m$ and $n$.
status_search_result: Sharir and Smorodinsky studied distinct distances between points and lines and obtained near-tight bounds: a lower bound roughly of the form $\Omega(\min(m^{2/3}n^{2/3}, m^2, n^2))$ matched (up to lower-order factors) by constructions, but a complete asymptotic determination of $L(m,n)$ across all ranges of $m,n$ does not appear to be settled in the literature, so the problem is best regarded as partially solved.

original_question: Find the asymptotic value of vgen(n), the minimum number of distinct vectors spanned by an n-point planar set in general position, meaning no three points are collinear and no four are cocircular.
self_contained_problem:
For a finite set $P\subset\mathbb{R}^2$, let
$$v(P)=\bigl|\{\,p-q:\ p,q\in P\,\}\bigr|$$
be the number of distinct vectors (translation-equivalence classes of ordered pairs) determined by $P$. A set $P\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ is said to be in general position if no three points of $P$ are collinear and no four points of $P$ lie on a common circle. Define
$$v_{\mathrm{gen}}(n)=\min\{\,v(P):\ P\subset\mathbb{R}^2,\ |P|=n,\ P\text{ in general position}\,\}.$$
Determine the asymptotic behavior of $v_{\mathrm{gen}}(n)$ as $n\to\infty$.

original_question: Let X be a separated locally convex space, and let C and D be convex subsets of X. For a convex set E, define its quasi relative interior by qri E := {x in E | cone(E - x) is a linear space}. Is it possible that the Minkowski sum of the quasi relative interiors, qri C + qri D, is a proper subset of the quasi relative interior of the Minkowski sum, qri(C + D)?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a separated locally convex topological vector space. For a convex subset $E \subseteq X$, define the quasi relative interior of $E$ by
$$\operatorname{qri} E := \{x \in E \mid \operatorname{cone}(E - x) \text{ is a linear subspace of } X\},$$
where $\operatorname{cone}(A) := \{\lambda a \mid \lambda \ge 0,\ a \in A\}$ denotes the cone generated by $A$. For convex subsets $C, D \subseteq X$, the Minkowski sum is $C + D := \{c + d \mid c \in C,\ d \in D\}$, and one always has the inclusion $\operatorname{qri} C + \operatorname{qri} D \subseteq \operatorname{qri}(C + D)$.

Question: Do there exist a separated locally convex space $X$ and convex subsets $C, D \subseteq X$ such that the inclusion is strict, i.e.
$$\operatorname{qri} C + \operatorname{qri} D \subsetneq \operatorname{qri}(C + D)?$$
status_search_result: The question, originally posed by Borwein and Goebel (2003), is answered affirmatively by an explicit example constructed in a 2014 work that resolves both Borwein–Goebel questions and a related Grad–Pop conjecture about calculus rules for the quasi relative interior.

original_question: Let X be a separated locally convex space, and let A and B be convex subsets of X. For a convex set E, define its quasi interior by qi E := {x in E | cone(E - x) = X}. Assuming qi B is nonempty, must the equality A + qi B = qi(A + B) always hold?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a separated locally convex topological vector space. For a convex subset $E \subseteq X$, define the quasi interior of $E$ by
$$\operatorname{qi} E := \{x \in E \mid \overline{\operatorname{cone}(E - x)} = X\},$$
where $\operatorname{cone}(S) = \{\lambda s : \lambda \geq 0,\ s \in S\}$ and the closure is taken in $X$. Let $A, B \subseteq X$ be convex subsets with $\operatorname{qi} B \neq \emptyset$. Decide whether the equality
$$A + \operatorname{qi} B \;=\; \operatorname{qi}(A + B)$$
must always hold, or exhibit convex sets $A, B$ in some separated locally convex space $X$ for which it fails.
status_search_result: The conjecture (formulated by Grad and Pop in 2014) is resolved negatively: a counterexample exists showing that $A + \operatorname{qi} B = \operatorname{qi}(A+B)$ can fail even when $\operatorname{qi} B \neq \emptyset$. The resolution is given in a 2014 note that addresses this conjecture together with related questions of Borwein and Goebel on quasi-relative interior calculus.

original_question: Let X be a separated locally convex space, and let C and D be nonempty convex subsets of X. For a convex set E, define its quasi relative interior by qri E := {x in E | cone(E - x) is a linear space}. If qri C intersect qri D is nonempty, can the inclusion qri(C intersect D) subset qri C intersect qri D fail?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a separated locally convex topological vector space. For a nonempty convex subset $E\subseteq X$, define the quasi relative interior of $E$ by
$$\operatorname{qri} E := \{x\in E \mid \operatorname{cone}(E-x)\text{ is a linear subspace of }X\},$$
where $\operatorname{cone}(A) = \{\lambda a : \lambda \ge 0,\ a\in A\}$.

Let $C, D\subseteq X$ be nonempty convex sets such that $\operatorname{qri} C \cap \operatorname{qri} D \ne \emptyset$. Decide whether the inclusion
$$\operatorname{qri}(C\cap D) \subseteq \operatorname{qri} C \cap \operatorname{qri} D$$
can fail; that is, can there exist $x\in \operatorname{qri}(C\cap D)$ with $x\notin \operatorname{qri} C \cap \operatorname{qri} D$?
status_search_result: The question, originally posed by Borwein and Goebel, has been answered in the negative: under the hypothesis that qri C ∩ qri D is nonempty, one always has qri(C ∩ D) ⊆ qri C ∩ qri D, so the inclusion cannot fail. This follows from established calculus rules for the quasi relative interior in separated locally convex spaces.

original_question: For subsets A of {0,1,...,r} that are more-sums-than-differences (MSTD), explicit infinite constructions were known with density about C/r^4 among all subsets of [0,r]. Can one construct a substantially denser explicit family of MSTD sets, and in particular can one obtain an explicit family that occupies a positive proportion of all subsets of [0,r]?
self_contained_problem:
For a finite set $A \subset \mathbb{Z}$, define the sumset $A+A = \{a+b : a,b \in A\}$ and the difference set $A-A = \{a-b : a,b \in A\}$. The set $A$ is called a more-sums-than-differences (MSTD) set if $|A+A| > |A-A|$.

For an integer $r \geq 0$, let $\mathcal{M}(r)$ denote the collection of MSTD subsets of $\{0,1,\ldots,r\}$. There exist explicit infinite families $\mathcal{F}_r \subset \mathcal{M}(r)$ that achieve $|\mathcal{F}_r| \geq C \cdot 2^{r+1}/r^4$ for some absolute constant $C > 0$, and (using bidirectional ballot sequences) explicit families of size $\Theta(2^r/r)$.

Question: Construct an explicit infinite family $\{\mathcal{F}_r\}_{r \geq 1}$ with $\mathcal{F}_r \subset \mathcal{M}(r)$ whose density among all subsets of $\{0,1,\ldots,r\}$ is substantially larger than $1/r$. In particular, give an explicit construction such that
$$\liminf_{r \to \infty} \frac{|\mathcal{F}_r|}{2^{r+1}} > 0,$$
i.e., an explicit family that occupies a positive proportion of all subsets of $\{0,1,\ldots,r\}$.
status_search_result: The best previously known explicit family had density $\Theta(1/r^4)$ (Miller–Orosz–Scheinerman). Y. Zhao improved this to $\Theta(2^r/r)$ via bidirectional ballot sequences, an improvement over the $1/r^4$ bound but still not a positive proportion. It is known by probabilistic arguments (Martin–O'Bryant) that a positive proportion of all subsets of $\{0,\dots,r\}$ are MSTD, but no explicit construction achieving positive proportion appears to be known, so the explicit positive-proportion question remains open.

original_question: An MSTD subset of the integers has more pairwise sums than pairwise differences. Starting from the minimal 8-element integer example, one can build an MSTD subset of Z^2 by taking its product with a 2-point set. Can one instead construct an MSTD subset of Z^2 directly, without obtaining it from an MSTD subset of Z by such a lifting procedure?
self_contained_problem:
For a finite set $A$ in an abelian group, define the sumset $A+A=\{a+b:a,b\in A\}$ and difference set $A-A=\{a-b:a,b\in A\}$. The set $A$ is called an MSTD (more sums than differences) set if $|A+A|>|A-A|$.

It is known that MSTD subsets of $\mathbb{Z}$ exist (the smallest has $8$ elements). Given any MSTD set $A\subset\mathbb{Z}$ and any $2$-element set $B\subset\mathbb{Z}$, the product $A\times B\subset\mathbb{Z}^2$ is an MSTD subset of $\mathbb{Z}^2$.

Construct an MSTD subset $S\subset\mathbb{Z}^2$ that does not arise from such a lifting procedure; that is, $S$ should not be expressible (up to affine equivalence in $\mathbb{Z}^2$) as a Cartesian product $A\times B$ where $A$ is an MSTD subset of $\mathbb{Z}$ and $B\subset\mathbb{Z}$ has two elements, nor obtained from a one-dimensional MSTD set by an embedding $\mathbb{Z}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{Z}^2$ followed by a product with a $2$-element set.

original_question: Let A be a subset of Z_n. The order of A is the least h such that hA = Z_n but (h-1)A != Z_n. Which integers can occur as orders of bases in Z_n, especially in the regime where the order grows linearly with n?
self_contained_problem:
For a positive integer $n$, let $\mathbb{Z}_n = \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. For a subset $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_n$ containing $0$ (or, more generally, such that the iterated sumsets eventually cover $\mathbb{Z}_n$), define the sumset $hA = \{a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_h : a_i \in A\}$ for each positive integer $h$. Call $A$ a basis of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ if $hA = \mathbb{Z}_n$ for some $h$, and define the order of $A$ to be the least such $h$, i.e. the unique $h$ with $hA = \mathbb{Z}_n$ and $(h-1)A \neq \mathbb{Z}_n$.

Determine which integers can occur as the order of a basis of $\mathbb{Z}_n$. In particular, characterize the set of attainable orders in the regime where the order grows linearly with $n$: prove that for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$ there exists a constant $c_k > 0$ such that, for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, every basis $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_n$ whose order exceeds $n/k$ has order within $c_k$ of $n/\ell$ for some integer $\ell \in [1,k]$, and conversely show that every such value (up to the appropriate error) is realized.
status_search_result: The problem was resolved by Peter Hegarty (arXiv:0906.5484), who proved the Dukes–Herke conjecture: for each k there is a constant c_k such that any basis A ⊆ Z_n of order greater than n/k has order within c_k of n/ℓ for some integer ℓ ∈ [1,k]. This characterizes the possible orders of bases in the linear-in-n regime.

original_question: Define g_0 = 0 and, greedily, let g_i be the least positive integer such that {g_0,...,g_i} has no solutions to 5w + 2x = 5y + 2z. Define a_0 = 0, define a_i by the recurrence given in the paper, and let A be the set of sums of distinct a_i. Is the greedy set G exactly {5x + y : x in A and 0 <= y <= 4}?
self_contained_problem:
Construct a set $G \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ greedily as follows. Set $g_0 = 0$, and for each $i \ge 1$ let $g_i$ be the least positive integer strictly greater than $g_{i-1}$ such that the set $\{g_0, g_1, \ldots, g_i\}$ contains no four (not necessarily distinct) elements $w, x, y, z$ with $(w,x) \ne (y,z)$ satisfying
$$5w + 2x \;=\; 5y + 2z.$$
Let $G = \{g_0, g_1, g_2, \ldots\}$.

Separately, define a sequence $(a_i)_{i \ge 0}$ by
$$a_0 = 0,\qquad a_1 = 3,\qquad a_i = 5\,a_{i-1} \text{ for } i \ge 2,$$
so that $a_i = 3 \cdot 5^{i-1}$ for $i \ge 1$. Let
$$A \;=\; \Big\{\, \sum_{i \in S} a_i \;:\; S \subseteq \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0} \text{ finite} \Big\}$$
be the set of all sums of finitely many distinct terms of $(a_i)$.

Decide whether
$$G \;=\; \{\, 5x + y \;:\; x \in A,\; 0 \le y \le 4 \,\}.$$

original_question: Suppose the first N terms of an increasing sequence already form an initial segment of a basis of order 2 for the nonnegative integers, meaning every sufficiently small nonnegative integer is a sum of two elements of the full basis. Must every such initial segment be extendable to a minimal basis, that is, a basis from which removing any one element destroys the basis property?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{N}_0=\{0,1,2,\dots\}$. A set $B\subseteq\mathbb{N}_0$ is called a basis of order $2$ for $\mathbb{N}_0$ if every sufficiently large nonnegative integer can be written as a sum $b_1+b_2$ with $b_1,b_2\in B$. Such a basis $B$ is called minimal if for every $b\in B$ the set $B\setminus\{b\}$ fails to be a basis of order $2$ (i.e., removing any single element destroys the property that all sufficiently large integers are sums of two elements).

Suppose $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots<a_N\}\subset\mathbb{N}_0$ is a finite increasing initial segment that is "extendable to a basis of order $2$" in the following sense: there exists a set $B\supseteq A$ such that $B$ is a basis of order $2$ for $\mathbb{N}_0$ and $A=B\cap[0,a_N]$ (so $A$ consists exactly of the elements of $B$ up to its $N$-th term).

Question: Does every such finite initial segment $A$ admit an extension to a minimal basis of order $2$? Equivalently, given any finite $A$ that begins some basis of order $2$, must there exist a minimal basis $B$ of order $2$ whose first $N$ elements are exactly $a_1,\dots,a_N$?

original_question: For the unrestricted partition generating function product over m >= 1 of (1 + x^m + x^(2m) + ...), can one choose signs in some of the factors so that, after expansion, every coefficient belongs to {0, -1, 1}?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the formal power series identity
$$\prod_{m\ge 1}\bigl(1+x^m+x^{2m}+x^{3m}+\cdots\bigr)=\sum_{n\ge 0}p(n)x^n,$$
where $p(n)$ denotes the number of unrestricted partitions of $n$. For each $m\ge 1$ and each $k\ge 1$, let $\varepsilon_{m,k}\in\{+1,-1\}$ be a choice of sign, and define
$$F(x)=\prod_{m\ge 1}\Bigl(1+\sum_{k\ge 1}\varepsilon_{m,k}\,x^{km}\Bigr)=\sum_{n\ge 0}b_n x^n.$$
Question: does there exist a choice of signs $\{\varepsilon_{m,k}\}$ such that $b_n\in\{-1,0,1\}$ for every $n\ge 0$?

original_question: Find a proof that the irrationality measure of zeta(2) is finite without using the prime number theorem. Such a proof would give a route to deriving infinitude-of-primes information from the Euler product for zeta(2) without appealing to the prime number theorem inside the irrationality argument itself.
self_contained_problem:
For a real number $\alpha$, the irrationality measure (or irrationality exponent) $\mu(\alpha)$ is the infimum of all real numbers $\mu \geq 1$ such that the inequality
$$\left|\alpha - \frac{p}{q}\right| < \frac{1}{q^{\mu}}$$
has only finitely many solutions in integers $p, q$ with $q \geq 1$. Let
$$\zeta(2) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2} = \frac{\pi^2}{6}.$$
It is known that $\mu(\zeta(2)) < \infty$, but standard proofs of this fact rely on estimates for $\mathrm{lcm}(1,2,\dots,n)$ which are equivalent in strength to the Prime Number Theorem (i.e., they use $\log \mathrm{lcm}(1,\dots,n) \sim n$, equivalently $\psi(n) \sim n$).

Problem: Produce a proof that $\mu(\zeta(2))$ is finite that does not invoke the Prime Number Theorem (in particular, that does not use the asymptotic $\log \mathrm{lcm}(1,\dots,n) \sim n$, but at most weaker elementary bounds such as Chebyshev-type estimates $\log \mathrm{lcm}(1,\dots,n) = O(n)$). Equivalently, exhibit an explicit finite upper bound for $\mu(\zeta(2))$ whose derivation uses only elementary inputs strictly weaker than the Prime Number Theorem.
status_search_result: Standard proofs that $\mu(\zeta(2))$ is finite (e.g. Apéry, Beukers, Rhin–Viola) use estimates on $\mathrm{lcm}(1,\dots,n)$ that follow from the Prime Number Theorem. Chebyshev-type elementary bounds $\log\mathrm{lcm}(1,\dots,n) = O(n)$ are sufficient for many irrationality (and irrationality-measure) arguments and are strictly weaker than PNT, but it is unclear from accessible sources whether a fully PNT-free finiteness proof for $\mu(\zeta(2))$ has been formally written down. No definitive resolution was located.
