original_question: Which pairs of rooted polytopes have the property that their mix is itself a polytope?
self_contained_problem:
An abstract polytope of rank $n$ is a partially ordered set $P$ (with a minimum element $F_{-1}$ and a maximum element $F_n$) whose elements (called faces) are graded by a rank function with values in $\{-1,0,\dots,n\}$, in which every maximal chain (flag) contains exactly one face of each rank, which satisfies the diamond condition (for any face $F$ of rank $i-1$ and any face $H$ of rank $i+1$ with $F<H$, there are exactly two faces of rank $i$ strictly between $F$ and $H$), and which is strongly flag-connected. The automorphism group of $P$ acts on the set of flags; $P$ is called regular if this action is transitive. A regular polytope is generated, as a poset with distinguished base flag, by the involutions $\rho_0,\rho_1,\dots,\rho_{n-1}$ that send the base flag to its $i$-adjacent flags, and these generators satisfy a string Coxeter-type presentation.

A rooted polytope is a regular abstract polytope $P$ together with a choice of base flag, equivalently a choice of distinguished generators $(\rho_0,\dots,\rho_{n-1})$ of its automorphism group. Given two rooted regular polytopes $P$ and $Q$ of the same rank $n$, with distinguished generators $(\rho_0,\dots,\rho_{n-1})$ and $(\rho'_0,\dots,\rho'_{n-1})$ respectively, their mix $P\diamond Q$ is the poset associated with the group generated by the diagonal involutions $(\rho_i,\rho'_i)$, $i=0,\dots,n-1$, inside the direct product $\mathrm{Aut}(P)\times \mathrm{Aut}(Q)$, viewed as a string C-group construction. The resulting structure $P\diamond Q$ is always a pre-polytope, but it need not satisfy the intersection property required for it to be an abstract polytope.

Problem: Give a characterization of all pairs $(P,Q)$ of rooted regular abstract polytopes (of the same rank) such that the mix $P\diamond Q$ is itself an abstract polytope.
status_search_result: The general characterization problem for when the mix of two rooted (regular) abstract polytopes is itself a polytope appears to remain open. While partial results are known (e.g., for specific families of regular convex polytopes and for mixes with small polytopes), no general criterion has been published. Searches turn up the operation in works on mixing regular convex polytopes and in Abstract Regular Polytopes (McMullen–Schulte), but no complete characterization is reported.

original_question: For every k >= 1 and every n >= 3, does there exist a k-orbit n-polytope with no rank-2 section that is a digon?
self_contained_problem:
An abstract n-polytope is a partially ordered set P (with elements called faces) satisfying the standard axioms: P has a unique minimum face F_{-1} and a unique maximum face F_n; every maximal chain (flag) has exactly n+2 elements, giving each face a well-defined rank in {-1,0,1,...,n}; P is strongly flag-connected; and P satisfies the diamond condition (for any faces F < G with rank(G) - rank(F) = 2, there are exactly two faces H with F < H < G). For faces F ≤ G, the section G/F is the subposet { H : F ≤ H ≤ G }; a section of rank 2 is a section G/F with rank(G) - rank(F) = 2, and such a section is a digon if it consists of exactly two faces strictly between F and G (so the rank-1 section G/F is combinatorially a 2-gon with two vertices and two edges).

The automorphism group Aut(P) acts on the set of flags of P; the polytope P is called a k-orbit polytope if Aut(P) has exactly k orbits on the flags of P. (1-orbit polytopes are the regular abstract polytopes.)

Question: For every integer k ≥ 1 and every integer n ≥ 3, does there exist a k-orbit abstract n-polytope P such that no rank-2 section of P is a digon?

original_question: Given a group Gamma, for which integers k >= 1 and n >= 3 is Gamma the automorphism group of a k-orbit polytope or maniplex of rank n?
self_contained_problem:
A maniplex of rank n (with n ≥ 3) is a connected n-valent properly edge-colored graph with colors {0, 1, …, n−1} such that, for any two colors i, j with |i − j| ≥ 2, every connected component of the subgraph induced by edges of colors i and j is a 4-cycle. The vertices of a maniplex are called flags. An automorphism of a maniplex is a color-preserving graph automorphism, and the automorphism group acts freely on flags. Abstract polytopes of rank n correspond to a special class of rank-n maniplexes (those satisfying the diamond and strong flag-connectedness conditions and giving rise to a partial order on faces). A maniplex (or polytope) is called k-orbit if its automorphism group has exactly k orbits on the set of flags.

Problem: Given an abstract group Γ, determine all pairs of integers (k, n) with k ≥ 1 and n ≥ 3 for which there exists a k-orbit maniplex of rank n whose automorphism group is isomorphic to Γ, and, separately, all such pairs for which there exists a k-orbit abstract polytope of rank n with automorphism group isomorphic to Γ.
status_search_result: The general question remains open. Complete characterizations of automorphism groups of k-orbit polytopes/maniplexes are known only for small k (e.g., k = 1, 2 and partial results for k = 3) and for specific group families (such as PSL_2(q)). Recent work (2022–2024) on 3-orbit polyhedra, coset-geometry characterizations, and prescribing automorphism groups for polytopes provides only partial progress toward the general problem.

original_question: If a connected properly edge-colored n-regular graph satisfies the usual allowable-graph condition that every alternating i,j,i,j walk with |i-j| > 1 returns to its starting point, must it be the symmetry type graph of some maniplex?
self_contained_problem:
Let n be a positive integer. Consider connected graphs G (allowing multiple edges and loops) whose edges are properly colored with the colors {0, 1, ..., n-1} so that at every vertex v and every color i ∈ {0, ..., n-1} there is exactly one edge of color i incident to v (a loop counts as the unique edge of its color at that vertex); such a G is called a properly edge-colored n-regular graph. For colors i, j with |i - j| > 1, an alternating (i,j)-walk of length 4 starting at a vertex v is the walk obtained by traversing, in order, the unique edges of colors i, j, i, j incident to the successive vertices. Call G allowable if it is connected, properly n-edge-colored as above, and every alternating (i,j,i,j)-walk with |i - j| > 1 closes up (i.e., returns to its starting vertex after these four steps), for all such pairs i, j.

A maniplex of rank n is a connected properly n-edge-colored graph (with the same regularity convention) in which every alternating (i,j,i,j)-walk closes up whenever |i - j| > 1. Given a maniplex M with automorphism group Γ = Aut(M), the symmetry type graph T(M) of M is the quotient multigraph G/Γ: its vertices are the Γ-orbits of vertices of M, and for each color i, an edge of color i joins the orbit of v to the orbit of its i-neighbor (with appropriate loops/multiple edges).

Question: Is it true that for every n ≥ 1, every allowable graph (in the sense above) arises as the symmetry type graph T(M) of some maniplex M of rank n?
status_search_result: The question (often phrased in terms of premaniplexes/admissible graphs) is generally regarded as a difficult open problem. Partial results are known: every premaniplex with 2 vertices of rank ≥ 3 is the symmetry type graph of some maniplex, and every premaniplex with 3 vertices of rank ≥ 3 is the symmetry type graph of some polytope. Voltage-operation constructions (Hubard et al.) realize many further premaniplexes as symmetry type graphs of maniplexes, but the full question for arbitrary allowable graphs remains unresolved.

original_question: Are there constructions of (n + 1)-polytopes from n-polytopes whose resulting symmetry type graphs differ from the families produced in Theorem 4.2 and from their duals?
self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. Let P be an abstract n-polytope with flag set F(P) and automorphism group Γ(P). The flag graph G(P) is the edge-colored graph with vertex set F(P), where two flags are joined by an edge of color i (for i ∈ {0,1,...,n−1}) whenever they are i-adjacent (i.e., differ exactly in their i-face). The symmetry type graph T(P) of P is the quotient multigraph G(P)/Γ(P), whose vertices are the Γ(P)-orbits on flags and which has, for each i, an i-colored edge between orbits O and O' whenever some flag in O is i-adjacent to some flag in O'. Thus T(P) is an n-edge-colored (multi)graph in which every vertex is incident with exactly one edge of each color (counting loops appropriately), and it captures the combinatorial type of the action of Γ(P) on flags.

A construction is a procedure that, given an n-polytope P, produces an (n+1)-polytope Q = C(P) (such as the pyramid, prism, antiprism, dual, medial, truncation, or other functorial constructions). Suppose one is given a finite list of families F_1, F_2, ..., F_k of admissible symmetry type graphs of (n+1)-polytopes, together with the family of duals of those (where the dual operation reverses the color ordering 0 ↔ n, 1 ↔ n−1, ...).

Question. Does there exist a construction C taking an n-polytope P to an (n+1)-polytope C(P) such that the symmetry type graph T(C(P)) does not belong to any of the families F_1, ..., F_k nor to the family of their duals? Equivalently, can one construct (n+1)-polytopes from n-polytopes whose resulting symmetry type graphs realize patterns outside the prescribed list and its duals?

original_question: Which combinatorial symmetry type graphs occur among convex polytopes, and which geometric symmetry type graphs occur among convex polytopes?
self_contained_problem:
Let P be a convex polytope in Euclidean space (of arbitrary finite dimension), and let F(P) denote the set of flags of P (a flag being a maximal chain of faces ordered by inclusion). For each i in {0,1,...,dim(P)-1}, two flags are i-adjacent if they differ exactly in their i-dimensional face. 

The combinatorial symmetry type graph T_c(P) is defined as the quotient multigraph F(P)/Γ(P), where Γ(P) is the combinatorial automorphism group of the face lattice of P; the vertices of T_c(P) are the orbits of flags under Γ(P), and for each i there is an edge labeled i between (possibly equal) orbits whenever a flag in one orbit is i-adjacent to a flag in the other.

The geometric symmetry type graph T_g(P) is defined analogously as F(P)/G(P), where G(P) is the group of Euclidean isometries of the ambient space that map P to itself.

original_question: Do there exist polytopes P and Q such that the amalgamation class hP, Qi is nonempty and P has at least two non-isomorphic vertex-figures?
self_contained_problem:
Work in the category of abstract polytopes. Recall that an abstract polytope of rank n is a partially ordered set with a strictly monotone rank function onto {-1, 0, …, n}, having a unique minimum element (of rank -1) and a unique maximum element (of rank n), in which every maximal chain (flag) has the same length, which satisfies the diamond condition (any element of rank i with 0 ≤ i ≤ n−1 covered by an element two ranks above is succeeded by exactly two elements at the intermediate rank), and which is strongly flag-connected. The faces of rank 0 are vertices and the faces of rank n−1 are facets. For a face F of rank i, the vertex-figure of an abstract polytope at a vertex v is the section v/⊥ = {G : v ≤ G}, where ⊥ is the unique minimum element; equivalently the vertex-figure at v is the polytope of rank n−1 whose elements are those faces of the polytope incident to v.

Given two abstract polytopes P (of rank n) and Q (of rank n), the amalgamation class ⟨P, Q⟩ is the class of all abstract polytopes R of rank n+1 such that every facet of R is isomorphic to P and every vertex-figure of R is isomorphic to Q.

Question: Do there exist abstract polytopes P and Q such that the amalgamation class ⟨P, Q⟩ is nonempty and the polytope P has at least two non-isomorphic vertex-figures?

original_question: Whenever there is a rooted amalgamation of polytopes P and Q, is there always a universal rooted amalgamation of P and Q?
self_contained_problem:
Let P and Q be abstract polytopes equipped with distinguished base flags (i.e., rooted polytopes). A rooted amalgamation of P and Q is a rooted polytope R together with structure-preserving (rooted) coverings exhibiting P as the facet type and Q as the vertex-figure type at the root, in the sense appropriate to the rooted setting (so that every facet of R containing the root is isomorphic to P as a rooted polytope, and the vertex figure of R at the root is isomorphic to Q as a rooted polytope). A universal rooted amalgamation of P and Q is a rooted amalgamation U of P and Q such that, for every rooted amalgamation R of P and Q, there exists a rooted covering U → R that maps the base flag of U to the base flag of R.

original_question: Which pairs of polytopes P and Q have a nonempty amalgamation class hP, Qi for which the number of flag orbits among polytopes in hP, Qi is bounded?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. An abstract polytope of rank n is a partially ordered set P (whose elements are called faces) satisfying the standard axioms: P has a unique least face F_{-1} and a unique greatest face F_n; every maximal chain (called a flag) of P contains exactly n+2 faces, one of each rank in {-1,0,1,...,n}; P is strongly flag-connected; and P satisfies the diamond condition (whenever F < G with rank(G) - rank(F) = 2, there are exactly two faces H with F < H < G). The automorphism group Γ(P) of P acts on the set F(P) of flags of P; the orbits of this action are called the flag orbits of P, and their number is denoted by |F(P)/Γ(P)|.

For a face F of P with rank(F) = -1,...,n, the section F_n/F is the subposet of faces G with F ≤ G ≤ F_n, and similarly F/F_{-1} for sections from below. The facets of P are the sections F_n/F with rank(F) = n-1 (these are themselves abstract polytopes of rank n-1), and the vertex figures are the sections F_n/v for vertices v (also abstract polytopes of rank n-1).

Given two abstract polytopes K and L of rank n-1, the amalgamation class ⟨K, L⟩ is defined as the class of all abstract polytopes P of rank n such that every facet of P is isomorphic to K and every vertex figure of P is isomorphic to L.

original_question: Which k-orbit polytopes P admit a universal k-orbit extension that covers every other k-orbit extension of P?
self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. An abstract polytope of rank $n$ is a partially ordered set $P$ whose elements are called faces, equipped with a strictly monotone rank function with values in $\{-1,0,1,\dots,n\}$, satisfying: (i) $P$ has a unique minimum face (of rank $-1$) and a unique maximum face (of rank $n$); (ii) every maximal chain (flag) of $P$ contains exactly $n+2$ faces, one of each rank; (iii) $P$ is strongly flag-connected; and (iv) the diamond condition holds: whenever $F<G$ with $\operatorname{rank}(G)-\operatorname{rank}(F)=2$, there are exactly two faces $H$ with $F<H<G$. The automorphism group $\Gamma(P)$ acts on the set of flags of $P$, and $P$ is called a $k$-orbit polytope if this action has exactly $k$ orbits.

A polytope $Q$ of rank $n+1$ is called an extension of a polytope $P$ of rank $n$ if all of the rank-$n$ faces (facets) of $Q$ are isomorphic to $P$. An extension $Q$ of $P$ is called a $k$-orbit extension if $Q$ itself is a $k$-orbit polytope. Given two extensions $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ of $P$, we say that $Q_1$ covers $Q_2$ if there exists a rank- and incidence-preserving surjection $Q_1\to Q_2$ that restricts to an isomorphism on each facet.

A $k$-orbit extension $U$ of $P$ is called a universal $k$-orbit extension of $P$ if $U$ is a $k$-orbit extension of $P$ and, for every $k$-orbit extension $Q$ of $P$, the polytope $U$ covers $Q$.

Problem. Characterize the $k$-orbit polytopes $P$ that admit a universal $k$-orbit extension.

A subsequent work characterizes automorphism groups of k-orbit polytopes via coset geometries, but no source found resolves the existence question of universal k-orbit extensions in general. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Describe all chiral polytopes of full rank.
self_contained_problem:
An abstract polytope of rank n is a partially ordered set whose elements (called faces) are stratified into ranks -1, 0, 1, …, n, satisfying the standard diamond condition and strong flag-connectedness conditions. Such a polytope is called chiral if its automorphism group has exactly two orbits on the set of flags (maximal chains), with adjacent flags lying in different orbits. A geometric (skeletal) realization of an abstract n-polytope in Euclidean space E^d assigns to each face a corresponding affine subspace in a way that respects incidence and the symmetry of the polytope. A finite skeletal polytope of rank n in E^d necessarily satisfies d ≥ n, and an infinite (apeirotopic) one satisfies d ≥ n-1; when equality holds, the polytope is said to be of full rank.

Problem: Determine, up to similarity, all chiral polytopes of full rank. That is, classify all chiral abstract n-polytopes admitting a faithful skeletal realization in Euclidean space of dimension n (finite case) or n-1 (infinite case).
status_search_result: The classification has been completed. It is established that chiral polytopes of full rank exist only in ranks 4 and 5. In rank 4, three chiral polytopes in Euclidean 3-space (including Roli's cube) were enumerated and shown to be complete; in rank 5, a chiral 5-polytope of full rank was constructed and the enumeration finalized, concluding the classification.

original_question: Describe all chiral polytopes of nearly full rank.
self_contained_problem:
An abstract n-polytope is a partially ordered set with a strict rank function taking values in {-1, 0, ..., n}, with a unique least face F_{-1} and unique greatest face F_n, in which every maximal chain (flag) contains exactly n+2 faces, that satisfies the diamond condition (for any two faces F < G with rank(G) - rank(F) = 2, there are exactly two faces strictly between F and G), and that is strongly flag-connected. Its automorphism group acts on the set of flags. The polytope is called regular if this action is transitive, and chiral if it has exactly two flag orbits such that adjacent flags lie in different orbits.

A faithful (geometric) realization of an abstract n-polytope P in Euclidean space E^d is an injective map from the vertex set of P into E^d that extends to higher-rank faces (sending each face to the convex hull, affine hull, or appropriate geometric object spanned by its vertices) in such a way that every automorphism of P is induced by an isometry of E^d. The (geometric) dimension of P is the smallest d for which such a faithful realization exists. The polytope P (or its faithful realization in E^d) is said to be of nearly full rank if d = n - 1 in the finite case or d = n in the infinite (apeirotope) case; equivalently, the realization dimension is one less than the maximum possible "full rank" value.

Problem. Describe (classify up to similarity) all chiral abstract polytopes of nearly full rank: that is, determine, for every rank n ≥ 3, all chiral n-polytopes that admit a faithful realization in Euclidean space of dimension n-1 (when finite) or n (when infinite, i.e. as an apeirotope), and exhibit the complete list together with their automorphism groups and combinatorial Schläfli-type data.
status_search_result: The classification of chiral polytopes of nearly full rank appears to be open. The analogous classification for regular polytopes/apeirotopes of nearly full rank has been completed (McMullen and subsequent work), and the full-rank chiral case has been resolved (chiral polytopes of full rank exist only in ranks 4 and 5, with concrete examples including Roli's cube and a chiral 5-polytope of full rank). However, no source found provides a complete description of the chiral nearly-full-rank case; recent literature (including a 2025 monograph on abstract chiral polytopes) still lists related questions among open problems.

original_question: Describe all two-orbit polytopes of full rank.
self_contained_problem:
An abstract polytope of rank $n$ is a partially ordered set $\mathcal{P}$ whose elements (called faces) have ranks in $\{-1, 0, 1, \dots, n\}$, that contains a unique minimum face of rank $-1$ and a unique maximum face of rank $n$, in which every maximal chain (called a flag) contains exactly $n+2$ faces, that is strongly flag-connected, and that satisfies the diamond condition: whenever $F < G$ with $\mathrm{rank}(G)-\mathrm{rank}(F)=2$, there are exactly two faces $H$ with $F<H<G$. The automorphism group $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ acts freely on the set of flags. The polytope $\mathcal{P}$ is called a two-orbit polytope if $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ has exactly two orbits on flags.

A faithful realization of an abstract polytope $\mathcal{P}$ of rank $n$ in Euclidean space $\mathbb{E}^d$ is a map sending each face to an affine subspace of $\mathbb{E}^d$ in a way compatible with the partial order, such that the symmetry group of the realized polytope induces $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$. The dimension of a realization is the dimension of the affine hull of its vertices. A realization is said to be of full rank if its dimension equals the rank $n$ of $\mathcal{P}$.

Problem: Describe (classify up to similarity) all two-orbit polytopes of full rank, i.e., all pairs $(\mathcal{P}, \rho)$ where $\mathcal{P}$ is an abstract polytope of rank $n$ with two flag orbits under its automorphism group and $\rho$ is a faithful realization of $\mathcal{P}$ in $\mathbb{E}^n$.

The status of the problem could not be definitively verified.

original_question: For k <= d, find all k-orbit realizations in Euclidean space E^d of regular d-polytopes.
self_contained_problem:
Background. A regular d-polytope is a convex polytope P in some Euclidean space whose symmetry group acts transitively on its set of complete flags (chains consisting of one face of each dimension 0,1,…,d−1). More generally, given an abstract regular d-polytope 𝒫 with automorphism group Γ(𝒫), a realization of 𝒫 in Euclidean space E^d is a homomorphism that assigns to each vertex of 𝒫 a point of E^d, extended to faces as the convex hulls (or appropriate geometric span) of their vertex sets, in such a way that every automorphism of 𝒫 is induced by an isometry of E^d. A realization is called a k-orbit realization if the induced isometry group of the realized polytope partitions its set of flags into exactly k orbits. (In particular, 1-orbit realizations are the geometrically regular ones.)

Problem. For each integer k with 1 ≤ k ≤ d, classify all k-orbit realizations in Euclidean space E^d of regular d-polytopes. That is, determine, up to similarity, every pair (𝒫, f), where 𝒫 is an abstract regular d-polytope and f : 𝒫 → E^d is a realization, such that the resulting geometric polytope has exactly k flag orbits under its full Euclidean symmetry group.
status_search_result: The general classification of k-orbit realizations of regular d-polytopes in E^d for all k ≤ d does not appear to have been completed. McMullen and Schulte's realization theory, and follow-up work (e.g., on regular polytopes of full and nearly full rank), addresses important special cases (notably k = 1, regular realizations), but a comprehensive classification for arbitrary k ≤ d has not been reported in the literature found, and the problem appears to remain open.

context_brief: Dimension bounds for convex k-orbit polytopes
original_question: Determine the number N_k for each k, or improve the known bounds on N_k, where N_k bounds the dimensions in which geometrically k-orbit convex polytopes can exist.
self_contained_problem:
A convex polytope $P\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ is a bounded intersection of finitely many closed half-spaces. Its face lattice, ordered by inclusion (including the empty face and $P$ itself), gives rise to flags: maximal chains $\Phi=(F_{-1}\subset F_0\subset F_1\subset\cdots\subset F_{n-1}\subset F_n)$ in which $\dim F_i=i$. The (geometric) symmetry group $G(P)$ consists of all isometries of $\mathbb{R}^n$ that map $P$ onto itself; it acts naturally on the set of flags of $P$. The polytope $P$ is called geometrically $k$-orbit if $G(P)$ partitions the flags of $P$ into exactly $k$ orbits.

For each positive integer $k$, define
\[ N_k = \sup\{\,n\in\mathbb{N} : \text{there exists a geometrically $k$-orbit convex polytope } P\subset\mathbb{R}^n\,\}, \]
where $N_k=\infty$ if such polytopes exist in arbitrarily high dimensions, and $N_k$ is otherwise the largest dimension in which such a polytope exists.

Problem: Determine the value of $N_k$ for every $k\ge 1$, or improve the currently known upper and lower bounds on $N_k$.
status_search_result: The problem of determining $N_k$ for geometrically $k$-orbit convex polytopes appears as a well-known open problem in the theory of $k$-orbit polytopes. Web search returned no publication establishing the exact values of $N_k$ in general, and recent work on $k$-orbit polytopes (e.g., on automorphism groups of abstract $k$-orbit polytopes) does not resolve the geometric dimension bounds. The problem is therefore considered open.

paper_title: On some open questions in bilinear quantum control
context_brief: Positive minimal time in infinite-dimensional approximate control
original_question: Let (A,B) satisfy Assumption 1 for the bilinear quantum system dψ/dt = (A + u(t)B)ψ, and suppose (A,B) admits a non-degenerate chain of connectedness, so the reachable set from φ_1 is dense in H. Define ρ to be the infimum of all T ≥ 0 such that the union of states reachable from φ_1 by piecewise-constant controls over times 0 ≤ t ≤ T is dense in H. Does there exist a system (A,B) that is k-weakly-coupled for every k > 0, whose drift operator A is unbounded, whose control operator B has no eigenvector, and for which the minimal approximate-controllability time satisfies ρ > 0?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a separable complex Hilbert space H with Hermitian inner product, and a bilinear control system of the form

  dψ/dt = (A + u(t) B) ψ,   ψ(0) = φ_1,

where:

• A is a (possibly unbounded) skew-adjoint operator on H with purely discrete spectrum, having an orthonormal basis (φ_k)_{k≥1} of eigenvectors with A φ_k = i λ_k φ_k, λ_k ∈ ℝ;
• B is a skew-symmetric operator on H such that A + uB generates a unitary propagator Υ^u_{t,0} on H for every piecewise-constant control u : [0,∞) → ℝ (denote by PC the set of such controls);
• (A,B) is assumed to admit a non-degenerate chain of connectedness, i.e. there is a graph on the indices {1,2,…} whose edges are the pairs (j,k) with ⟨φ_j, B φ_k⟩ ≠ 0 such that the graph is connected, and along every cycle of edges the spectral gaps |λ_j − λ_k| are non-resonant in the standard sense used to guarantee approximate controllability.

For a real number k > 0, the system (A,B) is called k-weakly-coupled if |A|^{k/2} is well-defined via functional calculus, B maps the domain D(|A|^{k/2}) into itself, and there exists a constant C_k such that

  |Re ⟨ |A|^k ψ , B ψ ⟩ | ≤ C_k ⟨ |A|^k ψ , ψ ⟩   for all ψ ∈ D(|A|^k).

Under these assumptions, the reachable set ⋃_{t ≥ 0} { Υ^u_{t,0} φ_1 : u ∈ PC } is dense in the unit sphere of H. Define

  ρ(A,B) = inf { T ≥ 0 : ⋃_{0 ≤ t ≤ T} { Υ^u_{t,0} φ_1 : u ∈ PC } is dense in the unit sphere of H }.

Question: Does there exist a pair (A,B) satisfying all the hypotheses above such that

  (i) (A,B) is k-weakly-coupled for every k > 0,
  (ii) A is unbounded,
  (iii) B has no eigenvector in H, and
  (iv) ρ(A,B) > 0 ?

Subsequent works (e.g., Beauchard–Coron–Marbach on minimal time for approximate bilinear control, and Boscain–Caponigro–Chambrion–Sigalotti and Duca–Nersesyan on small-time controllability examples) have produced both examples of positive minimal time and examples of small-time approximate controllability, but no source found explicitly resolves the specific question of producing such an example simultaneously k-weakly-coupled for all k>0, with A unbounded and B having no eigenvector. context_brief: Combinatorial flag orbits in convex polytopes
original_question: For which values of k and d does there exist a convex d-polytope with exactly k combinatorial flag orbits?
self_contained_problem:
Let $P$ be a convex $d$-dimensional polytope, with face lattice ordered by inclusion (including the empty face $\hat{0}$ and $P$ itself as $\hat{1}$). A flag of $P$ is a maximal chain in this face lattice; equivalently, a sequence $(F_{-1}, F_0, F_1, \ldots, F_{d-1}, F_d)$ with $F_{-1} = \emptyset$, $F_d = P$, and $F_i$ a proper $i$-face of $P$ with $F_i \subset F_{i+1}$ for all $i$. The combinatorial automorphism group $\Gamma(P)$ consists of all order-preserving bijections of the face lattice of $P$ to itself, and acts on the set of flags. The combinatorial flag orbits of $P$ are the orbits of this action; $P$ is called combinatorially $k$-orbit if it has exactly $k$ combinatorial flag orbits.

Determine, for every pair of positive integers $(k, d)$ with $d \geq 2$, whether there exists a convex $d$-polytope that is combinatorially $k$-orbit. In particular, characterize the set $\{(k,d) : \text{such a polytope exists}\}$.
status_search_result: The problem appears to be open in general. The case $k=1$ (regular convex polytopes) is classical. For $k=2$, it has been shown that combinatorially two-orbit convex polytopes exist only in dimension 3 and form a finite known list (cuboctahedron, icosidodecahedron, rhombic dodecahedron, rhombic triacontahedron). For general $k \geq 3$ and arbitrary $d$, no full classification of admissible pairs $(k,d)$ is known; surveys of open problems on k-orbit polytopes list this as an open question, and recent work on k-orbit and few-flag-orbit polytopes (e.g., Matteo's thesis and work on 3-orbit polyhedra) addresses partial cases without resolving it.

context_brief: Geometric flag orbits in convex polytopes
original_question: For which values of k and d does there exist a convex d-polytope with exactly k geometric flag orbits?
self_contained_problem:
Let P be a convex d-polytope in Euclidean space, i.e., the convex hull of finitely many points in R^d with affine dimension d. A flag of P is a maximal chain (F_{-1}, F_0, F_1, ..., F_{d-1}, F_d) of faces of P, where F_{-1} = ∅, F_d = P, dim F_i = i, and F_i ⊂ F_{i+1} for each i. The geometric symmetry group G(P) of P is the group of Euclidean isometries of R^d that map P onto itself; G(P) acts naturally on the set of flags of P. The orbits of this action are called the geometric flag orbits of P, and P is said to be geometrically k-orbit if G(P) has exactly k orbits on the flags of P.

Determine all pairs (k, d) of positive integers (with d ≥ 1) for which there exists a convex d-polytope that is geometrically k-orbit.
status_search_result: The classifications for k=1 (regular convex polytopes, classical, due to Schläfli), k=2 (only in dimensions 2 and 3, classified), and k=3 (classified, existing in dimensions 2 through 8) are known. The general problem of determining all pairs (k,d) for which a geometrically k-orbit convex d-polytope exists appears to remain open in full generality.

paper_title: On some open questions in bilinear quantum control
context_brief: Time-optimal transfer under an L1 control budget
original_question: Fix a bilinear quantum system dψ/dt = (A + u(t)B)ψ with first and second eigenstates φ_1 and φ_2 of the drift operator A. Suppose one imposes an a priori upper bound on the L^1 norm of the control u. Under that control-budget constraint, what is the smallest possible transfer time needed to steer the system from the first eigenstate φ_1 to the second eigenstate φ_2?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a bilinear quantum control system on a complex Hilbert space H of the form
    i dψ/dt = (A + u(t) B) ψ,
where A is a (possibly unbounded) self-adjoint operator on H with pure point spectrum and a complete orthonormal basis of eigenstates (φ_k)_{k≥1} corresponding to eigenvalues (λ_k)_{k≥1}, B is a self-adjoint operator on H coupling the eigenstates of A, and u : [0,T] → R is a real-valued measurable control function. Assume the pair (A,B) is such that the system is approximately controllable in the unit sphere of H.

Fix a constant K > 0 and consider only controls u satisfying the L^1 budget constraint
    ‖u‖_{L^1([0,T])} = ∫_0^T |u(t)| dt ≤ K.

Define
    T*(K) = inf { T > 0 : there exists u ∈ L^1([0,T]) with ‖u‖_{L^1} ≤ K such that the solution ψ of the system with ψ(0) = φ_1 satisfies ψ(T) = φ_2 (or, in the approximate sense, ‖ψ(T) − φ_2‖ is arbitrarily small) }.

Determine T*(K) — that is, given the L^1 bound K on the control, find the smallest possible time needed to transfer the system from the first eigenstate φ_1 of A to the second eigenstate φ_2.
status_search_result: Related work establishes that for weakly-coupled systems an L^1 bound on the control prevents approximate controllability in arbitrarily small time, and explicit minimal L^1 costs have been computed for some examples; however, no general formula for the minimum transfer time T*(K) between the first two eigenstates under an a priori L^1 bound appears in the literature, so the problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: On some open questions in bilinear quantum control
context_brief: Reducing the switch complexity of approximate steering controls
original_question: Let (A,B) satisfy Assumption 1 and admit a non-degenerate chain of connectedness. Then for every target state ψ_b on the unit sphere of H and every ε > 0, one can find a piecewise-constant control u_ε : [0,T_ε] → {0,1} such that the propagated first eigenstate Υ^{u_ε}_{T_ε,0} φ_1 is within ε of ψ_b. Existing constructions can produce such controls with a number of discontinuities of order 1/ε. Is it possible instead to construct controls u_ε whose number of discontinuities is little-o of 1/ε as ε → 0?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let H be a separable complex Hilbert space with inner product ⟨·,·⟩ and norm ∥·∥. Consider a bilinear control system on H of the form

  i d/dt ψ(t) = (A + u(t) B) ψ(t),

where:
- A is a (possibly unbounded) self-adjoint operator on H with domain D(A), having purely discrete spectrum and a complete orthonormal basis (φ_k)_{k≥1} of eigenvectors, with A φ_k = λ_k φ_k and simple eigenvalues λ_1 < λ_2 < ….
- B is a symmetric operator on H such that A + uB is essentially self-adjoint on D(A) for every u in some interval containing {0,1}, and such that the well-posedness assumption (henceforth "Assumption 1") holds: for every piecewise-constant u : [0,T] → {0,1} the Schrödinger equation above generates a unitary propagator Υ^u_{t,s} on H with Υ^u_{T,0} φ_1 ∈ H of unit norm.
- (A,B) admits a non-degenerate chain of connectedness, meaning there exists a permutation σ of ℕ* such that for every k ≥ 1 one has ⟨B φ_{σ(k)}, φ_{σ(k+1)}⟩ ≠ 0, the differences λ_{σ(k+1)} − λ_{σ(k)} are all distinct, and these gaps are non-resonant in the standard sense used for approximate controllability via adiabatic/Lie–Galerkin techniques.

Known fact. Under these hypotheses, for every target state ψ_b on the unit sphere of H and every ε > 0 there exist T_ε > 0 and a piecewise-constant control u_ε : [0,T_ε] → {0,1} such that

  ∥ Υ^{u_ε}_{T_ε,0} φ_1 − ψ_b ∥ < ε.

Moreover, classical constructions yield such u_ε with N(ε) discontinuities, where N(ε) = O(1/ε) as ε → 0+.

Question. Does there exist, under the same hypotheses, a family of piecewise-constant controls (u_ε)_{ε>0} : [0,T_ε] → {0,1} satisfying the approximate steering bound ∥Υ^{u_ε}_{T_ε,0} φ_1 − ψ_b∥ < ε whose number of discontinuities N(ε) satisfies

  N(ε) = o(1/ε)  as  ε → 0+ ?

That is, can the switch-complexity of approximate steering from the ground state φ_1 to an arbitrary unit target be made asymptotically smaller than 1/ε?

The status of this specific switch-complexity improvement could not be verified from available search results.

context_brief: When convex realization preserves k-orbit geometry
original_question: For which values of k and d is the following true: if a k-orbit d-polytope P is realized as a convex d-polytope, then P must be isomorphic to a geometrically k-orbit convex polytope?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. An abstract polytope of rank d (an abstract d-polytope) is a partially ordered set P, with a unique minimum and maximum element, whose elements (called faces) are graded by a rank function taking values in {-1, 0, 1, …, d}, satisfying the usual diamond condition and strong flag-connectivity. A flag of P is a maximal chain. The automorphism group Γ(P) acts on the set of flags of P; the number of orbits of this action is called the number of flag orbits. P is said to be a k-orbit polytope if Γ(P) has exactly k orbits on flags.

A convex d-polytope Q ⊂ ℝ^d is the convex hull of finitely many points with full-dimensional interior; its face lattice is naturally an abstract d-polytope. We say that an abstract d-polytope P is realized as a convex d-polytope if P is isomorphic, as a poset, to the face lattice of some convex d-polytope Q. The Euclidean symmetry group G(Q) of Q ⊂ ℝ^d is the group of isometries of ℝ^d that map Q to itself; G(Q) acts on the flags of Q. A convex d-polytope Q is called geometrically k-orbit if its Euclidean symmetry group G(Q) has exactly k orbits on the flags of Q.

Problem. Determine all pairs of positive integers (k, d) with d ≥ 2 for which the following implication holds: whenever a k-orbit abstract d-polytope P admits a realization as a convex d-polytope, there exists a convex d-polytope Q, isomorphic to P as an abstract polytope, that is geometrically k-orbit (i.e., its Euclidean symmetry group has exactly k flag orbits).
status_search_result: The problem appears in a list of open problems on k-orbit polytopes published in Discrete Mathematics. Subsequent literature on k-orbit polytopes (e.g., work characterizing automorphism groups via coset geometries) treats the geometric vs. combinatorial symmetry question as ongoing, with no general resolution found for arbitrary (k, d). Partial answers exist for small k and low d (e.g., regular k=1 case), but no comprehensive solution was located.

original_question: Classify all two-orbit polyhedra in hyperbolic 3-space H^3.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{H}^3$ denote hyperbolic 3-space, and let $\mathrm{Isom}(\mathbb{H}^3)$ denote its isometry group. A polyhedron $P \subset \mathbb{H}^3$ is a 3-dimensional convex body bounded by finitely many geodesic faces (allowing finite, ideal, or hyperideal vertices as appropriate). The symmetry group of $P$ is $G(P) = \{g \in \mathrm{Isom}(\mathbb{H}^3) : g(P) = P\}$. The group $G(P)$ acts on the set of flags of $P$, where a flag is an incident triple (vertex, edge, face). The polyhedron $P$ is said to be a two-orbit polyhedron if $G(P)$ partitions the set of flags of $P$ into exactly two orbits.

Problem: Classify, up to isometry of $\mathbb{H}^3$, all two-orbit polyhedra in $\mathbb{H}^3$.

paper_title: On some open questions in bilinear quantum control
context_brief: Good Galerkin approximations beyond weak coupling
original_question: Does there exist a bilinear quantum system dψ/dt = (A + u(t)B)ψ in which the control operator B is unbounded, the pair (A,B) satisfies Assumption 1, the system is not k-weakly-coupled for any k > 0, and nevertheless the infinite-dimensional dynamics can still be approximated uniformly by its Galerkin truncations with respect to the L^1 norm of the control? Here the intended uniform approximation is the same type discussed earlier in the paper for weakly-coupled systems, where for every control with bounded L^1 norm the Galerkin evolution stays uniformly close to the full evolution.
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Consider a separable complex Hilbert space $H$ with inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $A: D(A)\subset H\to H$ be a (densely defined) skew-adjoint operator such that $iA$ has purely discrete spectrum, with eigenvalues $(\lambda_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ and an associated Hilbert basis $(\phi_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ of eigenvectors. Let $B:D(B)\subset H\to H$ be a (possibly unbounded) skew-symmetric operator. For $s\geq 0$, let $|A|^{s/2}$ denote the absolute value of $A$ to the power $s/2$ defined by functional calculus, with domain $D(|A|^{s/2})$ and graph norm $\|\psi\|_{s/2}=\big\|(I+|A|^{s/2})\psi\big\|$.

Consider the bilinear control system
$$\frac{d\psi}{dt}(t) = \big(A + u(t)\,B\big)\psi(t), \qquad \psi(t)\in H,$$
where the control $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R};\mathbb{R})$.

Assumption 1. The pair $(A,B)$ is admissible: $A$ is skew-adjoint with discrete spectrum and a Hilbert basis of eigenvectors $(\phi_n)$, $B$ is skew-symmetric, and the products of operators are well defined on suitable common cores so that for every $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ the system admits a unique unitary propagator $\Upsilon^u_t$ on $H$.

For $N\in\mathbb{N}$ let $\pi_N$ denote the orthogonal projection of $H$ onto $\mathrm{span}(\phi_1,\dots,\phi_N)$, and let $\Upsilon^{u,N}_t$ be the propagator of the Galerkin truncation
$$\frac{d\psi_N}{dt} = \pi_N(A+u(t)B)\pi_N\psi_N$$
on the finite-dimensional subspace $\pi_N H$.

$k$-Weak coupling. For $k>0$, the pair $(A,B)$ is called $k$-weakly-coupled if $D(|A|^{k/2})$ is invariant under the propagator $\Upsilon^u_t$ for every $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$, and there exist $d>0$ and $0\le r<k$ such that $\|B\psi\|\le d\,\|\psi\|_{r/2}$ for every $\psi\in D(|A|^{r/2})$.

Uniform Galerkin approximation in $L^1$. The system $(A,B)$ is said to admit Galerkin approximations uniform with respect to the $L^1$ norm of the control if, for every $\varepsilon>0$ and every $K>0$, there exists $N_0\in\mathbb{N}$ such that for all $N\ge N_0$, all $\psi_0\in H$ with $\|\psi_0\|=1$ and $\psi_0\in\pi_N H$, all controls $u\in L^1(\mathbb{R};\mathbb{R})$ with $\|u\|_{L^1}\le K$, and all $t\in\mathbb{R}$,
$$\big\|\Upsilon^u_t\psi_0 - \Upsilon^{u,N}_t\psi_0\big\| \le \varepsilon.$$

Question. Does there exist a pair $(A,B)$ with $B$ unbounded, satisfying Assumption 1, which is not $k$-weakly-coupled for any $k>0$, yet which nonetheless admits Galerkin approximations uniform with respect to the $L^1$ norm of the control in the sense above?
status_search_result: Searches around Boussaid–Caponigro–Chambrion's framework on weakly-coupled bilinear quantum systems and good Galerkin approximations did not surface a published resolution of this specific question (existence of an admissible non-k-weakly-coupled system with unbounded B that still admits uniform-in-L^1 Galerkin approximation). Subsequent works on energy estimates for low-regularity bilinear Schrödinger equations and obstructions for unbounded potentials are related but do not appear to settle it. Status seems unresolved in the literature available.

original_question: Classify all two-orbit 4-polytopes in hyperbolic 3-space H^3.
self_contained_problem:
An abstract polytope of rank n is a partially ordered set $\mathcal{P}$ (with a least and greatest face) whose maximal chains, called flags, all have length n+1, that is strongly flag-connected, and that satisfies the diamond condition: whenever $F<G$ with $\mathrm{rank}(G)-\mathrm{rank}(F)=2$, there are exactly two faces $H$ with $F<H<G$. Two flags are called adjacent if they differ in exactly one face. The automorphism group $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ acts freely on flags; $\mathcal{P}$ is called regular if this action is transitive, and two-orbit if there are exactly two orbits of flags under $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$.

A rank-4 polytope (a "4-polytope") in hyperbolic 3-space $\mathbb{H}^3$ is a faithful realization of an abstract rank-4 polytope as a locally finite, face-to-face tessellation of $\mathbb{H}^3$ by hyperbolic polyhedra (the 3-faces), in which every symmetry of the realization is induced by an isometry of $\mathbb{H}^3$. Such a polytope is called two-orbit in $\mathbb{H}^3$ if its isometry group has exactly two orbits on the flags of the underlying abstract polytope.

Problem. Classify, up to isometry of $\mathbb{H}^3$, all two-orbit rank-4 polytopes (tessellations) realized in hyperbolic 3-space $\mathbb{H}^3$. For each two-orbit symmetry class (i.e., each proper nonempty subset $I\subsetneq\{0,1,2,3\}$ describing which $i$-adjacencies preserve the flag-orbit), determine whether a realization in $\mathbb{H}^3$ exists, and enumerate all such realizations.

The status appears to remain open or only partially addressed.

original_question: Develop a theory of k-orbit realizations of k-orbit polytopes.
self_contained_problem:
An abstract polytope is a ranked partially ordered set whose maximal chains are called flags, satisfying the standard diamond and connectedness conditions of the theory of abstract polytopes. The automorphism group of an abstract polytope acts on the set of its flags, and the polytope is called a k-orbit polytope when this action has exactly k orbits. A (geometric) realization of an abstract polytope P is a mapping of its vertex set into a Euclidean space such that every automorphism of P extends to an isometry of the ambient space permuting the images of the faces consistently with P's structure. A realization of a k-orbit polytope is called matched (or k-orbit) if the symmetry group of the realization also acts on the flags of P with exactly k orbits, matching the combinatorial flag-orbit structure of P.

Develop a general theory of k-orbit realizations of k-orbit abstract polytopes. In particular, for each k ≥ 1 and each combinatorial type of k-orbit abstract polytope P, characterize the set of Euclidean realizations of P whose geometric symmetry group induces exactly k orbits on the flags of P; describe the structure of the space of such realizations (including its dimension, faithfulness, and decomposition into irreducible/pure realizations), establish operations such as blending and direct sums within this class, and determine necessary and sufficient combinatorial conditions on P for the existence of a faithful k-orbit realization.
status_search_result: The problem appears in a list of open problems on k-orbit polytopes. While realization theory for regular (1-orbit) polytopes is well developed and partial results exist for 2-orbit polytopes, no general theory of k-orbit realizations of k-orbit polytopes has been established. Recent works on k-orbit polytopes (e.g., on automorphism groups, orbit graphs, and 3-orbit polyhedra) address related structural questions but do not provide such a general realization theory.

original_question: Which k-orbit d-polytopes admit a faithful realization in Euclidean space E^d as geometrically k-orbit polytopes?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. An abstract d-polytope is a partially ordered set $\mathcal{P}$ whose elements (called faces) have ranks in $\{-1,0,1,\dots,d\}$, with a unique least face (rank $-1$) and unique greatest face (rank $d$), in which every maximal chain (flag) contains exactly $d+2$ faces, which is strongly flag-connected, and which satisfies the diamond condition: whenever $F<G$ with $\mathrm{rank}(G)=\mathrm{rank}(F)+2$, there are exactly two faces strictly between $F$ and $G$. The automorphism group $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ acts on the set of flags of $\mathcal{P}$. The polytope $\mathcal{P}$ is called a k-orbit polytope if $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ has exactly $k$ orbits on the flags of $\mathcal{P}$.

A (faithful) realization of $\mathcal{P}$ in Euclidean space $\mathbb{E}^d$ is an injective map $\beta$ from the vertex set (rank-$0$ faces) of $\mathcal{P}$ to $\mathbb{E}^d$ such that the induced assignment of every face to the convex hull (or appropriate geometric figure) of the images of its vertices is also injective on faces and respects the incidence structure. Given such a realization, let $G(\beta)\le \mathrm{Iso}(\mathbb{E}^d)$ be the group of Euclidean isometries that permute the realized faces compatibly with the abstract structure. The realization is said to be geometrically k-orbit if $G(\beta)$ has exactly $k$ orbits on the flags of $\mathcal{P}$ — equivalently, every combinatorial automorphism of $\mathcal{P}$ is induced by some Euclidean isometry of the realization.

Problem. Characterize precisely which k-orbit abstract d-polytopes $\mathcal{P}$ admit a faithful realization in $\mathbb{E}^d$ that is geometrically k-orbit (i.e., for which the full combinatorial symmetry of $\mathcal{P}$ is realized by Euclidean isometries of the realization).

original_question: Develop a theory of k-orbit realizations of m-orbit polytopes.
self_contained_problem:
An abstract polytope $\mathcal{P}$ is a ranked partially ordered set generalizing the face lattice of a convex polytope. A flag of $\mathcal{P}$ is a maximal chain. original_question: Develop a theory of k-orbit realizations of regular polytopes.
self_contained_problem:
An abstract polytope P of rank n is a partially ordered set of "faces" (with a least and greatest element) satisfying the standard diamond and connectedness conditions of abstract polytope theory; a flag of P is a maximal chain. The automorphism group Γ(P) acts on the set of flags, and P is called regular if this action is transitive. More generally, P is a k-orbit polytope if Γ(P) has exactly k orbits on flags.

A realization of an abstract polytope P is a mapping β from the vertex set of P into a Euclidean space E (extended recursively to higher faces by taking β(F) to be the family of images of the vertices contained in F) such that every automorphism g ∈ Γ(P) is induced by an isometry of E permuting the realized faces accordingly. For regular polytopes (k = 1), there is a well-developed theory of the realization cone: the set of (congruence classes of) realizations forms a closed convex cone whose fine structure is governed by the irreducible orthogonal representations of Γ(P), with extreme rays corresponding to "pure" realizations.

Problem. Develop an analogous theory of realizations for k-orbit regular polytopes — that is, for abstract polytopes whose automorphism group has exactly k orbits on flags (with k ≥ 2). Specifically, define an appropriate notion of realization compatible with the partial symmetry, describe the structure of the resulting space (or cone) of realizations up to congruence, identify its extreme/pure elements, and relate this structure to the representation theory of Γ(P) and to the symmetry type graph encoding the flag-orbit structure of P.
status_search_result: The problem of developing a theory of realizations for k-orbit (in particular non-regular but symmetric) abstract polytopes is listed among open problems on k-orbit polytopes, and recent work has explored related structural questions (e.g., automorphism groups of k-orbit polytopes, finite 3-orbit polyhedra), but no comprehensive realization theory analogous to McMullen–Schulte's regular case appears to have been established. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Develop a theory of realizations of regular polytopes in hyperbolic spaces.
self_contained_problem:
An abstract regular polytope is a partially ordered set $\mathcal{P}$ (with elements called faces, ranked by dimension) satisfying the standard axioms of an abstract polytope, whose automorphism group $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ acts transitively on the set of flags (maximal chains). For abstract regular polytopes, a well-developed theory of realizations in Euclidean spaces exists: a Euclidean realization is a map $\beta$ from the vertex set $\mathcal{P}_0$ of $\mathcal{P}$ into a Euclidean space $\mathbb{E}$ such that every automorphism of $\mathcal{P}$ extends to an isometry of $\mathbb{E}$ permuting $\beta(\mathcal{P}_0)$; the set of realizations (modulo congruence) forms a convex cone admitting a decomposition into irreducible subcones, related to the orthogonal/unitary representations of $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$.

Develop an analogous theory of realizations of abstract regular polytopes in hyperbolic spaces $\mathbb{H}^n$. Specifically, define an appropriate notion of a hyperbolic realization $\beta:\mathcal{P}_0\to\mathbb{H}^n$ such that every automorphism of $\mathcal{P}$ extends to an isometry of $\mathbb{H}^n$ permuting the image; classify and parametrize such realizations up to congruence; identify a structure on the space of realizations analogous to the Euclidean realization cone and its irreducible decomposition; and relate the theory to the representation theory of $\Gamma(\mathcal{P})$ in the isometry groups $O(n,1)$ of hyperbolic spaces.
status_search_result: McMullen's theory of realizations of abstract regular polytopes is well developed in the Euclidean setting (with extensions involving representation-theoretic decompositions of the realization cone). Search results indicate work on regular honeycombs and compounds in hyperbolic spaces, but no comprehensive analogue of the Euclidean realization theory in hyperbolic spaces appears to have been established. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Let (X, d) be a metric space, let 2^X denote the family of all non-empty closed subsets of X, and let T_W(d) be the Wijsman topology on 2^X, meaning the weakest topology that makes each distance functional A -> d(x, A) continuous for every x in X. self_contained_problem: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and let $2^X$ denote the collection of all non-empty closed subsets of $X$. For each $x \in X$, define the distance functional $\mathrm{dist}(x,\cdot): 2^X \to \mathbb{R}$ by $\mathrm{dist}(x,A) = \inf\{d(x,a) : a \in A\}$. The Wijsman topology $\tau_W(d)$ on $2^X$ is the weakest topology on $2^X$ such that for every $x \in X$ the map $A \mapsto \mathrm{dist}(x,A)$ is continuous from $(2^X,\tau_W(d))$ to $\mathbb{R}$. Provide a characterization, in terms of intrinsic properties of $(X,d)$, of exactly those metric spaces $(X,d)$ for which the Wijsman hyperspace $(2^X,\tau_W(d))$ is a normal topological space (i.e.\ Hausdorff and any two disjoint closed sets can be separated by disjoint open sets).

A full intrinsic characterization is not available.

original_question: For a metric space (X, d), it is known that if (X, d) is separable then the Wijsman hyperspace (2^X, T_W(d)) is metrizable and therefore paracompact and normal. Is the converse true? Equivalently, is (2^X, T_W(d)) normal if and only if it is metrizable?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and let $2^X$ denote the collection of all nonempty closed subsets of $X$. The Wijsman topology $\tau_W(d)$ on $2^X$ is the weakest topology such that for every $x\in X$ the distance functional 
$$d_x:2^X\to\mathbb{R},\qquad d_x(A)=d(x,A)=\inf\{d(x,a):a\in A\},$$ 
is continuous. It is known that if $(X,d)$ is separable, then $(2^X,\tau_W(d))$ is metrizable, hence paracompact and normal.

Determine whether the converse holds. Specifically: is it true that for every metric space $(X,d)$, the Wijsman hyperspace $(2^X,\tau_W(d))$ is normal if and only if it is metrizable?
status_search_result: The problem (originally posed by Di Maio and Meccariello) has significant partial progress but does not appear to be fully resolved. Cao and Junnila (2012, "Hereditarily Normal Wijsman Hyperspaces Are Metrizable") proved that hereditary normality of the Wijsman hyperspace implies metrizability. Further partial results show that for linear metric spaces, normality of the Wijsman hyperspace is equivalent to metrizability, and that locally separable spaces of regular uncountable weight have non-normal Wijsman hyperspaces. The full equivalence between normality and metrizability of the Wijsman hyperspace for arbitrary metric spaces appears to remain open.

original_question: If (X, d) is completely metrizable, with no separability assumption, is that equivalent to some completeness-type topological property of the Wijsman hyperspace (2^X, T_W(d))?
self_contained_problem:
Let (X, d) be a metric space (no separability assumed). The Wijsman topology T_W(d) on the hyperspace 2^X (the family of nonempty closed subsets of X) is the weakest topology on 2^X such that for every x ∈ X the distance functional A ↦ d(x, A) := inf{d(x, a) : a ∈ A} is continuous from (2^X, T_W(d)) to ℝ.

Recall that a topological space is completely metrizable if it admits a compatible complete metric, and various weaker "completeness-type" topological properties exist (for example: Čech-completeness, sieve-completeness, hereditary Baireness, the Amsterdam properties such as α-favorability in the strong Choquet game, domain-representability, etc.).

Equivalently, characterize complete metrizability of (X, d), without any separability hypothesis on X, by means of an intrinsic completeness-type topological property of the Wijsman hyperspace (2^X, T_W(d)).

No characterization of non-separable complete metrizability via a completeness-type property of the Wijsman hyperspace appears to have been established in subsequent literature, so the problem appears to remain open.

The space $Y$ is called strongly Choquet if $\alpha$ has a winning strategy, and strongly $\alpha$-favorable if $\alpha$ has a stationary (tactical) winning strategy depending only on $\beta$'s last move.

original_question: Let X be a metrizable space. If, for every metric d compatible with the topology of X, the Wijsman hyperspace (2^X, T_W(d)) is strongly Choquet or strongly alpha-favorable, must X itself be completely metrizable?
self_contained_problem:
Let X be a metrizable topological space. For a metric d compatible with the topology of X, let 2^X denote the collection of all nonempty closed subsets of X, and let T_W(d) denote the Wijsman topology on 2^X, namely the weakest topology on 2^X for which, for every x in X, the distance functional A ↦ d(x, A) := inf{d(x, a) : a ∈ A} (from 2^X to the real line) is continuous.

Recall the strong Choquet game on a topological space Y: players α and β alternate moves, β first. At round n, β picks a pair (y_n, V_n) where V_n is a nonempty open set of Y and y_n ∈ V_n; α responds with an open set U_n with y_n ∈ U_n ⊆ V_n; then β must choose (y_{n+1}, V_{n+1}) with V_{n+1} ⊆ U_n and y_{n+1} ∈ V_{n+1}. Player α wins the play if the intersection of the U_n is nonempty. The space Y is strongly Choquet if α has a winning strategy, and strongly α-favorable if α has a stationary winning strategy (one that depends only on β's last move).

Question: Suppose that, for every metric d compatible with the topology of X, the Wijsman hyperspace (2^X, T_W(d)) is strongly Choquet (respectively, strongly α-favorable). Must X then be completely metrizable?
status_search_result: Searches reveal results in the forward direction (if X is completely metrizable, the Wijsman hyperspace is strongly α-favorable for every compatible metric) and a partial converse for locally separable metrizable X (where α having a winning strategy on the Wijsman hyperspace for each compatible metric is equivalent to α having one on X, hence to complete metrizability). No source verifying the full converse for arbitrary metrizable X was located, so the general question appears to remain open.

original_question: If a metric space (X, d) is pseudocomplete, must its Wijsman hyperspace (2^X, T_W(d)) also be pseudocomplete? Likewise, if (X, d) is subcompact or base-compact, must (2^X, T_W(d)) inherit the corresponding property?
self_contained_problem:
Let (X, d) be a metric space, and let 2^X denote the family of all nonempty closed subsets of X. The Wijsman topology T_W(d) on 2^X is the weakest topology making, for every x ∈ X, the distance functional d_x : 2^X → ℝ defined by d_x(A) = inf{d(x, a) : a ∈ A} continuous.

Recall the following "Amsterdam-style" completeness properties of a topological space Y:
• Y is pseudocomplete if it has a sequence (B_n) of π-bases such that for every choice of sets U_n ∈ B_n with cl(U_{n+1}) ⊆ U_n, the intersection ∩_n U_n is nonempty.
• Y is subcompact if it has a base B such that every regular filter base in B (every subfamily F ⊆ B with the property that for any F_1, F_2 ∈ F there exists F_3 ∈ F with cl(F_3) ⊆ F_1 ∩ F_2) has nonempty intersection.
• Y is base-compact if it has a base B such that every centered subfamily of {cl(B) : B ∈ B} has nonempty intersection.

Question: If (X, d) is pseudocomplete, must (2^X, T_W(d)) be pseudocomplete? If (X, d) is subcompact, must (2^X, T_W(d)) be subcompact? If (X, d) is base-compact, must (2^X, T_W(d)) be base-compact?
status_search_result: The question of whether the Amsterdam-style completeness properties (pseudocompleteness, subcompactness, base-compactness) transfer from a metric space (X, d) to its Wijsman hyperspace (2^X, T_W(d)) appears to remain open. It is listed as an open problem in the literature on Amsterdam properties of Wijsman hyperspaces, and partial results are known only for weakened variants such as countable subcompactness and countable base-compactness in special examples.

original_question: Given a metric space (X, d), characterize when the Wijsman hyperspace (2^X, T_W(d)) is a Baire space, using properties of the underlying metric space (X, d).
self_contained_problem:
Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space, and let $2^X$ denote the collection of all nonempty closed subsets of $X$. The Wijsman topology $\tau_W(d)$ on $2^X$ is the weakest topology making, for each fixed $x\in X$, the distance functional
$$d_x : 2^X \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad d_x(A) = d(x,A) := \inf_{a\in A} d(x,a)$$
continuous. A topological space is called a Baire space if the intersection of every countable family of dense open sets is dense (equivalently, no nonempty open set is of first category).

Find a characterization, expressed purely in terms of properties of the metric space $(X,d)$, of when the Wijsman hyperspace $(2^X,\tau_W(d))$ is a Baire space.

Pol and Zsilinszky showed completeness is not necessary. A full characterization in terms of (X,d) alone has not been established.

paper_title: Some remarks concerning the Grothendieck Period Conjecture
original_question: Let Qbar be the algebraic closure of Q in C. Let X be a smooth projective variety over Qbar, and let X_C^an be the compact complex analytic manifold associated to X after base change to C. For an integer k, set H_Gr^{2k}(X,Q(k)) = H_dR^{2k}(X/Qbar) intersect H^{2k}(X_C^an,Q(k)) inside H^{2k}(X_C^an,C), where Q(k) = (2*pi*i)^k Q. Let cl_Gr^X: Z^k(X)_Q -> H_Gr^{2k}(X,Q(k)) be the Q-linear cycle-class map from codimension-k algebraic cycles with rational coefficients. Is cl_Gr^X surjective; equivalently, is every cohomology class that is both algebraic-de-Rham rational and Betti-rational with Tate twist Q(k) the class of a codimension-k algebraic cycle with rational coefficients?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ denote the algebraic closure of $\mathbb{Q}$ inside $\mathbb{C}$. Let $X$ be a smooth projective variety over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, and let $X_{\mathbb{C}}^{\mathrm{an}}$ denote the compact complex analytic manifold associated to the base change $X \times_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}} \mathbb{C}$. For an integer $k \ge 0$, the algebraic de Rham cohomology $H^{2k}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X/\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ embeds (after extending scalars to $\mathbb{C}$ and using the period comparison isomorphism) into the Betti cohomology $H^{2k}(X_{\mathbb{C}}^{\mathrm{an}}, \mathbb{C})$. Define the Grothendieck (de Rham–Betti) cohomology with Tate twist by
$$H^{2k}_{\mathrm{Gr}}(X, \mathbb{Q}(k)) \;:=\; H^{2k}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}) \;\cap\; H^{2k}(X_{\mathbb{C}}^{\mathrm{an}}, \mathbb{Q}(k)) \;\subset\; H^{2k}(X_{\mathbb{C}}^{\mathrm{an}}, \mathbb{C}),$$
where $\mathbb{Q}(k) = (2\pi i)^k \mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbb{C}$. Let
$$\mathrm{cl}^X_{\mathrm{Gr}} : Z^k(X)_{\mathbb{Q}} \longrightarrow H^{2k}_{\mathrm{Gr}}(X, \mathbb{Q}(k))$$
be the $\mathbb{Q}$-linear cycle class map sending a codimension-$k$ algebraic cycle on $X$ (with rational coefficients) to its de Rham–Betti class. Is $\mathrm{cl}^X_{\mathrm{Gr}}$ surjective? Equivalently: must every cohomology class on $X_{\mathbb{C}}^{\mathrm{an}}$ that is simultaneously rational over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ in algebraic de Rham cohomology and rational (with twist $\mathbb{Q}(k)$) in Betti cohomology be the class of a codimension-$k$ algebraic cycle with rational coefficients?
category_tag: Grothendieck period conjecture / de Rham–Betti cycle classes
status_search_result: The surjectivity of the de Rham–Betti cycle class map (the strong form of the Grothendieck Period Conjecture for smooth projective varieties over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$) is widely regarded as open. Only partial results are known, e.g. de Rham–Betti classes on products/powers of elliptic curves (with CM cases going back to Chudnovsky) are known to be algebraic. The general conjecture remains unresolved.

paper_title: Some remarks concerning the Grothendieck Period Conjecture
original_question: Let X be a smooth projective variety over Qbar. Let Z_X be the Zariski closure of the comparison isomorphism between total algebraic de Rham cohomology H_dR^*(X/Qbar) and total Betti cohomology H_B^*(X,Q) after extension to C, and let Omega_mot_X be the motivic torsor of periods of X. Is Z_X equal to Omega_mot_X, so that the comparison isomorphism is dense in the motivic torsor of periods and all polynomial relations between periods of cohomology classes on self-products of X are induced by algebraic cycles on those self-products?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a smooth projective variety over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$. Consider its algebraic de Rham cohomology $H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}) = \bigoplus_i H^i_{\mathrm{dR}}(X/\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ and its Betti cohomology $H^*_B(X,\mathbb{Q}) = \bigoplus_i H^i(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Q})$. The classical comparison theorem gives, after extending scalars to $\mathbb{C}$, an isomorphism
\[ \mathrm{comp}_X\colon H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X/\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\otimes_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}\mathbb{C} \;\xrightarrow{\sim}\; H^*_B(X,\mathbb{Q})\otimes_{\mathbb{Q}}\mathbb{C}. \]
Regard $\mathrm{comp}_X$ as a $\mathbb{C}$-point of the affine $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$-scheme of graded vector space isomorphisms $\mathrm{Isom}^*\bigl(H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X/\overline{\mathbb{Q}}),\,H^*_B(X,\mathbb{Q})\otimes_{\mathbb{Q}}\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\bigr)$, and let $Z_X$ denote the Zariski closure of $\mathrm{comp}_X$ in this scheme.

Working in a Tannakian category of motives over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ generated by $X$ (e.g.\ André's category of motives), let $G_{\mathrm{mot}}(X)$ be the motivic Galois group of $X$ — the Tannaka group of the de Rham fibre functor on the Tannakian subcategory generated by the motive of $X$. Let $\Omega^{\mathrm{mot}}_X$ be the motivic torsor of periods of $X$, namely the affine $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$-scheme of tensor isomorphisms from the Betti to the de Rham fibre functor on this subcategory. Then $\Omega^{\mathrm{mot}}_X$ is a torsor under $G_{\mathrm{mot}}(X)$ and contains $\mathrm{comp}_X$ as a $\mathbb{C}$-point, so $Z_X \subseteq \Omega^{\mathrm{mot}}_X$.

Question: Is the equality $Z_X = \Omega^{\mathrm{mot}}_X$ valid for every smooth projective variety $X$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$? Equivalently, is $\mathrm{comp}_X$ Zariski-dense in the motivic torsor of periods, so that every polynomial relation with $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$-coefficients among the periods of cohomology classes on the self-products $X^n$ ($n\geq 1$) is induced by algebraic cycles on those self-products?
status_search_result: The Grothendieck period conjecture, in the form asserting that the comparison isomorphism is a Zariski-dense (generic) point of the motivic torsor of periods — equivalently, that all polynomial relations among periods are induced by algebraic cycles — is widely regarded as open in general. Only special cases are known (e.g. certain CM abelian varieties, certain Kummer surfaces of self-product CM type), and the geometric/functional analogue has been established by Ayoub and by Nori, but the arithmetic conjecture for arbitrary smooth projective varieties over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ remains unresolved.

paper_title: Some remarks concerning the Grothendieck Period Conjecture
original_question: Let X be a smooth projective variety over Qbar. For all nonnegative self-products X^n and all integers j and k, must the Grothendieck cohomology group H_Gr^j(X^n,Q(k)) vanish unless j = 2k? Equivalently, outside the degree equal to twice the Tate twist, are there no de Rham-Betti classes on self-products that are simultaneously rational in the algebraic de Rham and Betti realizations?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a smooth projective variety over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$. For each integer $n\geq 0$, equip the self-product $X^n$ with its algebraic de Rham cohomology $H^j_{\mathrm{dR}}(X^n/\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ and its Betti cohomology $H^j_B(X^n(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Q})$, related by the period comparison isomorphism
$$\alpha:H^j_{\mathrm{dR}}(X^n/\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\otimes_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}\mathbb{C}\xrightarrow{\sim}H^j_B(X^n(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Q})\otimes_{\mathbb{Q}}\mathbb{C}.$$
For an integer $k$, define the de Rham–Betti cohomology group with Tate twist $k$ by
$$H^j_{\mathrm{Gr}}(X^n,\mathbb{Q}(k))=\{c\in (2\pi i)^k\,H^j_B(X^n(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Q})\;\mid\;\alpha^{-1}(c\otimes 1)\in H^j_{\mathrm{dR}}(X^n/\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\}.$$
Question: Is it true that for every smooth projective variety $X$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, every integer $n\geq 0$, and all integers $j,k$, one has $H^j_{\mathrm{Gr}}(X^n,\mathbb{Q}(k))=0$ whenever $j\neq 2k$? Equivalently, do nonzero de Rham–Betti classes on self-products $X^n$ exist only in degree $j=2k$?
category_tag: Grothendieck period conjecture / de Rham-Betti classes
status_search_result: The conjectural vanishing of $H^j_{\mathrm{Gr}}(X^n,\mathbb{Q}(k))$ for $j\neq 2k$ is a form of the Grothendieck period conjecture reflecting absence of weights for the de Rham–Betti realization. It remains open in general, but has been verified in special cases: degree 1 for products of curves, abelian varieties, and K3 surfaces, and degree 2 for smooth cubic fourfolds. Subsequent work (e.g. on de Rham–Betti classes with coefficients) extends but does not resolve the general statement.

paper_title: Some remarks concerning the Grothendieck Period Conjecture
original_question: Let X be a smooth quasi-projective variety over Qbar. Its de Rham-Betti cohomology groups H_dRB^k(X,Q(j)) have a canonical increasing weight filtration W_*. For any integers j and k, must all Grothendieck classes in H_dRB^k(X,Q(j)) lie in weight zero, in the precise sense that W_{-1} H_dRB^k(X,Q(j))_Gr = 0 and the natural injection W_0 H_dRB^k(X,Q(j))_Gr -> H_dRB^k(X,Q(j))_Gr is an isomorphism?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a smooth quasi-projective variety over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$. For integers $k\ge 0$ and $j\in\mathbb{Z}$, consider the de Rham–Betti cohomology group
$$H_{\mathrm{dRB}}^{k}(X,\mathbb{Q}(j)),$$
which by definition consists of triples $(\alpha_{B},\alpha_{\mathrm{dR}},c)$ where $\alpha_{B}\in H_{B}^{k}(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Q}(j))$, $\alpha_{\mathrm{dR}}\in F^{0}H_{\mathrm{dR}}^{k}(X/\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ (with the Tate twist normalization), and $c$ is the identification of their complexifications via the period comparison isomorphism. A class in $H_{\mathrm{dRB}}^{k}(X,\mathbb{Q}(j))$ is called a Grothendieck class (the subgroup of such classes is denoted $H_{\mathrm{dRB}}^{k}(X,\mathbb{Q}(j))_{\mathrm{Gr}}$). 

The Betti cohomology $H_{B}^{k}(X(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Q}(j))$ carries Deligne's canonical increasing weight filtration $W_{\bullet}$, which by transport induces a weight filtration $W_{\bullet}H_{\mathrm{dRB}}^{k}(X,\mathbb{Q}(j))$ on the de Rham–Betti cohomology, and hence on its subgroup $H_{\mathrm{dRB}}^{k}(X,\mathbb{Q}(j))_{\mathrm{Gr}}$.

Prove or disprove: for every smooth quasi-projective variety $X$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ and all integers $j,k$, every Grothendieck class lies in weight zero, in the sense that
$$W_{-1}H_{\mathrm{dRB}}^{k}(X,\mathbb{Q}(j))_{\mathrm{Gr}}=0\quad\text{and}\quad W_{0}H_{\mathrm{dRB}}^{k}(X,\mathbb{Q}(j))_{\mathrm{Gr}}\;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\;H_{\mathrm{dRB}}^{k}(X,\mathbb{Q}(j))_{\mathrm{Gr}}.$$
status_search_result: The conjecture that Grothendieck cohomology classes on smooth quasi-projective varieties over number fields lie in weight zero remains open in general. Partial results are known: for example, the Grothendieck period conjecture in degree 1 has been established for products of curves, abelian varieties and K3 surfaces, and in degree 2 for smooth cubic fourfolds, but no general proof of the weight-zero statement has appeared.

original_question: Let X be a smooth projective variety over Qbar, let k be a nonnegative integer, and let K be an algebraically closed field of finite transcendence degree over Q containing Qbar. For a class alpha in H_dR^{2k}(X_K/K), say alpha is absolute rational if it is rational relative to every embedding K -> C, and say alpha is absolute Hodge if it is absolute rational and belongs to the k-th Hodge filtration piece F^k H_dR^{2k}(X_K/K). Does every absolute rational class alpha necessarily have to be an absolute Hodge class?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a smooth projective variety over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, and let $k$ be a nonnegative integer. Let $K$ be an algebraically closed field of finite transcendence degree over $\mathbb{Q}$ containing $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, and write $X_K = X \times_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}} K$. Consider the algebraic de Rham cohomology $H^{2k}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X_K/K)$, equipped with its Hodge filtration $F^\bullet$.

For each embedding $\sigma\colon K \hookrightarrow \mathbb{C}$, base change yields a comparison isomorphism
$$H^{2k}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X_K/K) \otimes_{K,\sigma} \mathbb{C} \;\cong\; H^{2k}_{\mathrm{B}}(X_\sigma(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Q}) \otimes_{\mathbb{Q}} \mathbb{C}.$$

A class $\alpha \in H^{2k}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X_K/K)$ is called:
- *absolute rational* if, for every embedding $\sigma\colon K \hookrightarrow \mathbb{C}$, the image of $\alpha$ under the above comparison lies in $(2\pi i)^k \cdot H^{2k}_{\mathrm{B}}(X_\sigma(\mathbb{C}),\mathbb{Q})$;
- *absolute Hodge* if it is absolute rational and additionally satisfies $\alpha \in F^k H^{2k}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X_K/K)$.

Question: Must every absolute rational class $\alpha \in H^{2k}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X_K/K)$ automatically be absolute Hodge? Equivalently, does absolute rationality force $\alpha$ to lie in the $k$-th piece $F^k$ of the Hodge filtration?

status_search_result: The implication "absolute rational ⇒ absolute Hodge" is a refinement related to the Grothendieck period conjecture and the theory of absolute Hodge classes. Web search did not surface any published proof or disproof of this specific implication; partial results on the Grothendieck period conjecture exist (e.g., in degree 1 for products of curves, abelian varieties, K3 surfaces, and in degree 2 for cubic fourfolds), but the general question of whether absolute rationality forces a class to lie in $F^k$ appears not to have a known resolution.

original_question: For a smooth projective holomorphic symplectic variety over Qbar with second Betti number at least 4, the Kuga-Satake correspondence gives an absolute Hodge injective morphism from H^2(X_C^an,Q(1)) to H^2(A_C^an,Q(1)) for some abelian variety A over Qbar, and the source describes this correspondence as analytically defined through algebraic-group arguments on moduli spaces of holomorphic symplectic varieties and abelian varieties. Is this Kuga-Satake correspondence induced by an algebraic cycle?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a smooth projective holomorphic symplectic variety defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ with second Betti number $b_2(X) \geq 4$. The Kuga–Satake construction, applied to the polarized weight-two Hodge structure on $H^2(X_{\mathbb{C}}^{\mathrm{an}}, \mathbb{Q}(1))$, produces an abelian variety $A$ defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ together with an injective morphism of rational Hodge structures
$$\kappa : H^2(X_{\mathbb{C}}^{\mathrm{an}}, \mathbb{Q}(1)) \hookrightarrow H^2(A_{\mathbb{C}}^{\mathrm{an}}, \mathbb{Q}(1)),$$
which is known to be absolute Hodge and is naturally defined analytically via algebraic-group constructions on the moduli spaces of polarized holomorphic symplectic varieties and of polarized abelian varieties. By the Künneth formula, $\kappa$ may be viewed as a Hodge class in $H^4(X \times A, \mathbb{Q}(2))$.

Question: Is the class $\kappa$ the cohomology class of an algebraic cycle on $X \times A$? Equivalently, is the Kuga–Satake correspondence between $X$ and $A$ induced by an algebraic cycle?
status_search_result: The algebraicity of the Kuga–Satake correspondence is open in general. It is known in classical low-dimensional cases (e.g., for many K3 surfaces, via work of Morrison, Paranjape, van Geemen–Voisin, and others), and recent work of O'Grady and Markman (around 2022–2023) established it for projective hyper-Kähler manifolds of generalized Kummer deformation type. However, for arbitrary projective holomorphic symplectic varieties with $b_2 \geq 4$, the question remains open.

original_question: Let F be the abelian group of algebraic functions with the Fermat property. Let D be the subgroup generated by logarithmic derivatives U^(partial)(x) = xU'(x) of algebraic functions U(x), let Z[x] be the polynomial subgroup, and let P be the subgroup generated by finite sums of power-substituted algebraic functions U_j(x^{M_j}) with M_j >= 2. For an algebraic function U over Q(x) that is unramified at x = 0, let F_U = F intersect Q(x, U), D_U = D intersect Q(x, U), and P_U = P intersect Q(x, U). Determine the structure of the quotient groups F/(D + Z[x] + P), A_U = F_U/(D_U + Z[x]), and P_U = F_U/(D_U + Z[x] + P_U). In particular, determine the corresponding quotient in the purely rational case Q(x).
self_contained_problem:
Consider algebraic functions $U(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a(n) x^n \in \mathbb{Z}[[x]]$ over $\mathbb{Q}(x)$ that are unramified at $x=0$ and have no pole at $x=0$. Say that such $U$ has the Fermat property if for every prime $p$ and every $n \geq 1$, $a(pn) \equiv a(n) \pmod{p}$ (equivalently, $U(x^p) \equiv U(x)^p$ in a suitable sense modulo $p$). Let $F$ denote the abelian group (under addition) of all algebraic functions with the Fermat property.

Define the following subgroups of $F$:
\begin{itemize}
\item $D$ ("differential"): the subgroup generated by all logarithmic-type derivatives $U^{\partial}(x) := x\, U'(x)$, where $U$ ranges over algebraic functions for which $U^{\partial} \in F$.
\item $\mathbb{Z}[x]$: the subgroup of polynomials with integer coefficients.
\item $P$ ("power"): the subgroup generated by all finite sums $\sum_{j=1}^s U_j(x^{M_j})$ with $M_j \geq 2$ and each $U_j$ an algebraic function unramified and regular at $0$ such that the sum lies in $F$.
\end{itemize}

For an algebraic function $U$ over $\mathbb{Q}(x)$, unramified at $x=0$, set
$$F_U = F \cap \mathbb{Q}(x,U), \qquad D_U = D \cap \mathbb{Q}(x,U), \qquad P_U = P \cap \mathbb{Q}(x,U).$$

Determine the structure of the abelian groups
$$F/(D + \mathbb{Z}[x] + P), \qquad A_U = F_U/(D_U + \mathbb{Z}[x]), \qquad \mathcal{P}_U = F_U/(D_U + \mathbb{Z}[x] + P_U).$$
In particular, determine $\mathcal{P}_\emptyset$, i.e., the corresponding quotient in the purely rational case where one restricts to $\mathbb{Q}(x)$.
