context_brief: Good reduction of maps and orbits
original_question: Find a “nice” function C(N, d, D, s) so that every degree d mor- phism f : PN → PN defined over a field K of degree at most D and having at most s primes of bad reduction satisfies  # PrePer f, PN (K) ≤ C(N, d, D, s).
self_contained_problem:
Let $N \geq 1$ and $d \geq 2$ be integers. For a number field $K$, a morphism $f : \mathbb{P}^N \to \mathbb{P}^N$ defined over $K$ of degree $d$ is said to have good reduction at a non-archimedean place $\mathfrak{p}$ of $K$ (in the naive sense) if $f$ can be written using homogeneous polynomials of degree $d$ whose coefficients are $\mathfrak{p}$-integral and whose reduction modulo $\mathfrak{p}$ defines a morphism $\mathbb{P}^N \to \mathbb{P}^N$ over the residue field; otherwise $\mathfrak{p}$ is a place of bad reduction. Let
$$\mathrm{PrePer}(f, \mathbb{P}^N(K)) = \{P \in \mathbb{P}^N(K) : f^{m+n}(P) = f^m(P) \text{ for some } m \geq 0,\, n \geq 1\}$$
denote the set of $K$-rational preperiodic points of $f$.

Find an explicit function $C(N, d, D, s)$ of four nonnegative integer variables such that for every number field $K$ with $[K:\mathbb{Q}] \leq D$ and every degree-$d$ morphism $f : \mathbb{P}^N \to \mathbb{P}^N$ over $K$ having at most $s$ places of bad reduction, one has
$$\#\,\mathrm{PrePer}(f, \mathbb{P}^N(K)) \leq C(N, d, D, s).$$
status_search_result: The full problem—finding an explicit bound $C(N,d,D,s)$ for arbitrary morphisms of $\mathbb{P}^N$ over number fields—remains open and is closely tied to the Morton–Silverman uniform boundedness conjecture. Partial results exist: Benedetto (2007) established a bound of order $d^3(D+s)\log(D+s)$ for polynomial maps on $\mathbb{P}^1$; Canci–Paladino (2014) and subsequent improvements (e.g., Canci–Troncoso, 2016) provide weaker bounds for rational maps on $\mathbb{P}^1$. No explicit $C(N,d,D,s)$ is known for $N \geq 2$.

paper_title: Quantum Models for Psychological Measurements: An Unsolved Problem
context_brief: Principles delimiting QM applicability to cognition
original_question: Which well-justified principles can determine the boundaries of applying quantum mechanics (QM) to cognitive measurements, especially opinion-polling situations in which two empirical properties occur together: response replicability, where a person repeats an answer when the same question is asked again, and a question-order effect, where response probabilities depend on the order in which questions are asked? The principles should explain where QM can be used, where it must not be used, and why conventional Hermitian-observable QM and binary positive-operator-valued measures (POVMs) cannot jointly account for those two properties in the setting analyzed.
self_contained_problem:
Consider an opinion-polling setting in which a respondent is sequentially asked binary questions. Model each question as a measurement on a state in some Hilbert space, where the state may be updated after each measurement according to the rule prescribed by the chosen quantum formalism. Assume that the modeling family of measurements satisfies the following two empirical properties simultaneously, for a generic class of questions:

(P1) Response replicability: for any question A, if A is asked, answered, and then asked again, the same answer is returned with probability 1; moreover, if a different question B is asked and answered between the two askings of A, the answer to A is still repeated with probability 1.

(P2) Question-order effect: there exist questions A and B and an initial state such that the joint probability of the answer pair (a,b) when A is asked before B differs from the joint probability of (a,b) when B is asked before A.

Within standard quantum mechanics where each question is represented by a Hermitian observable (equivalently, a projection-valued measure) with the Lüders state-update rule, prove that (P1) and (P2) cannot hold together. More generally, within the formalism of binary positive-operator-valued measures (POVMs) with their associated Lüders/Kraus state updates, show that (P1) forces each POVM to be projective, and hence (P1) and (P2) are again incompatible.

Problem: Identify and justify a set of principles that delimits the domain of applicability of the quantum-mechanical formalism (Hermitian observables and binary POVMs together with the standard state-update rules) to such cognitive measurements—that is, principles which specify under what conditions the formalism may legitimately be used to model sequential question-answer behavior, under what conditions it must not, and which explain on a conceptual basis why no model in this formalism can exhibit both (P1) and (P2). Alternatively, exhibit a principled extension of the formalism (beyond binary POVMs) that accommodates (P1) and (P2) jointly while reducing to standard quantum mechanics in appropriate limits.
status_search_result: Subsequent work has shown that the impossibility within Hermitian observables and binary POVMs is rigorous, and has proposed extensions using the theory of quantum instruments (notably non-atomic instruments) that jointly model response replicability and the question-order effect. However, the broader problem of formulating well-justified principles that demarcate where quantum formalisms apply to cognition remains debated and has not been definitively settled, so the foundational question is best classified as partially solved.

paper_title: A single impurity in an ideal atomic Fermi gas: current understanding and some open problems
original_question: Explain why the Chevy ansatz, obtained by truncating the impurity wave-function expansion to a single particle-hole pair, remains extremely accurate even for large scattering length where strong particle-hole correlations might be expected. Determine whether the particle-hole-pair expansion has a hidden small parameter, identify when that expansion fails if it does fail, and quantify how the truncation error in observables such as the energy and quasiparticle residue depends on the truncation order, the mass ratio m/M, and the interaction parameter 1/k_F a.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a single distinguishable impurity of mass M immersed in a non-interacting three-dimensional Fermi gas of identical particles of mass m at zero temperature with Fermi momentum k_F, interacting with the impurity through a short-range two-body potential characterized by an s-wave scattering length a. The exact ground state of the impurity dressed by the Fermi sea can be expanded as

|Ψ⟩ = α₀ c_p† |FS⟩ + Σ α_{kq} c_{p+q-k}† b_k† b_q |FS⟩ + Σ α_{kk'qq'} c_{p+q+q'-k-k'}† b_k† b_{k'}† b_q b_{q'} |FS⟩ + …,

where c† creates the impurity, b†, b are creation/annihilation operators of the bath fermions, and |FS⟩ is the filled Fermi sea. Truncating this expansion at the n-th particle–hole pair defines the n-th order Chevy ansatz; the first-order truncation (n=1) is the original Chevy ansatz.

Address the following:

(a) Provide a rigorous explanation for why the first-order Chevy ansatz reproduces the polaron ground-state energy E and quasiparticle residue Z to within a few percent of exact results across the full BCS–BEC crossover, including the strongly interacting regime |1/(k_F a)| ≲ 1 where naively strong multi-particle–hole correlations are expected.

(b) Determine whether the particle–hole-pair expansion possesses a hidden small parameter that controls the convergence of successive truncations, and identify this parameter explicitly as a function of the mass ratio m/M and the dimensionless interaction strength 1/(k_F a).

(c) Identify the regimes (values of m/M, 1/(k_F a), and possibly impurity momentum p) in which the particle–hole-pair expansion fails to converge or converges only slowly.

(d) Establish quantitative bounds on the truncation error |E_n − E_exact| and |Z_n − Z_exact| as functions of the truncation order n, the mass ratio m/M, and 1/(k_F a).
status_search_result: Recent work (e.g., 2024 papers extending the Chevy ansatz to arbitrarily many particle–hole excitations and comparing with exact diagrammatic theory) has provided a partial explanation: higher-order particle–hole channels interfere destructively, making the first-order Chevy ansatz accurate to ~1–2% at unitarity for the equal-mass 3D Fermi polaron. However, a fully rigorous identification of a hidden small parameter and sharp truncation-error bounds as a function of n, m/M and 1/(k_F a) — particularly for large mass imbalance where convergence is known to deteriorate (Efimov-like physics) — has not been completely established.

context_brief: Good reduction of maps and orbits
original_question: Let Y0dyn (n) and Y1dyn (n) be the dynamical modular curves clas- sifying points, respectively cycles, of formal period n attached to the family of maps x2 + c, or xm + c, or some other natural 1-parameter family of rational maps on P1 such as bx + x−1 . (a) Describe the primes of bad reduction for Y0dyn (n) and Y1dyn (n). (b) Give a natural geometric/dynamical explanation for the “sporadic” primes of bad reduction, which we imprecisely define as primes not dividing n and not dividing a finite set of bad primes associated to the family f . (c) Describe the primes p for which the reductions of Y0dyn (n) and/or Y1dyn (n) modulo p are geometrically irreducible, e.g., for the latter, this is asking for the primes p such that the polynomial Φn (x, z) does not factor in the ring F̄p [x, z].
self_contained_problem:
Fix a one-parameter family of rational self-maps of $\mathbb{P}^1$, for example $f_c(x)=x^2+c$, more generally $f_{m,c}(x)=x^m+c$ with $m\ge 2$, or $f_b(x)=bx+x^{-1}$. For an integer $n\ge 1$, let $\Phi_n(x,t)$ denote the $n$-th dynatomic polynomial of the family (the polynomial whose roots are the points of formal period $n$, defined by $\Phi_n(x,t)=\prod_{d\mid n}(f^d(x)-x)^{\mu(n/d)}$ where $t$ is the parameter). Let $Y_0^{\rm dyn}(n)$ be the affine dynamical modular curve over $\mathbb{Z}$ parametrizing pairs (parameter, $n$-cycle) and let $Y_1^{\rm dyn}(n)$ be the affine dynamical modular curve parametrizing pairs (parameter, point of formal period $n$); explicitly, $Y_1^{\rm dyn}(n)$ is cut out by $\Phi_n(x,t)=0$.

(a) Determine the set of primes of bad reduction of $Y_0^{\rm dyn}(n)$ and of $Y_1^{\rm dyn}(n)$, i.e., the primes $p$ at which the reduction modulo $p$ fails to be smooth.

(b) Give a precise definition of "sporadic" prime of bad reduction, intended to capture primes outside an obvious finite set associated with the family $f$ (such as primes dividing $n$, or primes dividing a fixed discriminant of the family), and provide a geometric/dynamical explanation of such sporadic primes. (For example, computational evidence suggests that for $f_{m,c}(x)=x^m+c$, the sporadic primes for $n$-periodic points should be those not dividing $2nm$.)

(c) Describe the primes $p$ for which the reduction modulo $p$ of $Y_0^{\rm dyn}(n)$ and/or $Y_1^{\rm dyn}(n)$ is geometrically irreducible. For $Y_1^{\rm dyn}(n)$ this amounts to characterizing the primes $p$ such that $\Phi_n(x,t)$ remains irreducible in $\overline{\mathbb{F}_p}[x,t]$.
status_search_result: The problem appears to be still open in general, with substantial partial progress. Doyle, Krumm, and others have studied reduction of dynatomic curves, giving algorithms producing discriminants whose prime factors contain all bad-reduction primes of $Y_1(n)$, and characterizing primes of good reduction in special cases (e.g., $n=7,8,11$ for $x^2+c$). A precise general description of bad-reduction primes, of sporadic primes, and of primes of geometric irreducibility for arbitrary $n$ and arbitrary natural one-parameter families remains unresolved.

original_question: Let f : A^N -> A^N be a morphism over an algebraic closure of Q, written as polynomial coordinate functions f = (f_1, ..., f_N). If there is no non-constant rational function g with g o f = g, then there exists a point whose forward orbit under f is Zariski dense.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ denote an algebraic closure of the field $\mathbb{Q}$ of rational numbers, and let $\mathbb{A}^N$ denote affine $N$-space. Let
$$f : \mathbb{A}^N \longrightarrow \mathbb{A}^N$$
be a morphism defined over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$, given by polynomial coordinate functions $f = (f_1, \ldots, f_N)$ with $f_i \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}[x_1, \ldots, x_N]$. For a point $P \in \mathbb{A}^N(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$, the forward orbit of $P$ under $f$ is the set $\mathcal{O}_f(P) = \{P, f(P), f^2(P), f^3(P), \ldots\}$, where $f^n$ denotes the $n$-fold composition of $f$ with itself.

Assume that there does not exist any non-constant rational function $g \in \overline{\mathbb{Q}}(x_1, \ldots, x_N)$ such that $g \circ f = g$ (i.e., $f$ admits no non-constant invariant rational function).

Prove or disprove: under this hypothesis, there exists a point $P \in \mathbb{A}^N(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ whose forward orbit $\mathcal{O}_f(P)$ is Zariski dense in $\mathbb{A}^N$.
status_search_result: The Zariski Dense Orbit Conjecture (Medvedev–Scanlon; Amerik–Bogomolov–Rovinsky) is open in general. Proven cases relevant to this affine setting include: split polynomial maps on $\mathbb{A}^N$ (i.e., $(x_1,\dots,x_N)\mapsto(f_1(x_1),\dots,f_N(x_N))$) by Medvedev–Scanlon; endomorphisms of $(\mathbb{P}^1)^N$; smooth projective surfaces (Xie, with appendix by Tucker); and various tori/threefold cases. The general statement for arbitrary morphisms $f:\mathbb{A}^N\to\mathbb{A}^N$ over $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ remains unresolved as of recent literature (2024).

paper_title: Quantum Models for Psychological Measurements: An Unsolved Problem
context_brief: Critical QM features in cognitive explanations
original_question: Which features of QM are actually critical for successful and unsuccessful cognitive explanations, rather than incidental artifacts of a chosen model, when comparing applications that successfully fit question-order effects with failures involving response replicability?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the framework of quantum probability applied to cognitive measurements. In this framework, a cognitive state is represented by a unit vector (or density operator) ψ in a complex Hilbert space H, and a yes/no question Q is represented by an orthogonal projector P_Q on H, so that the probability of the answer "yes" is ⟨ψ, P_Q ψ⟩, and the post-measurement state is given by Lüders' rule ψ ↦ P_Q ψ / ‖P_Q ψ‖ for a "yes" outcome (and analogously for "no"). Two questions Q_A, Q_B are modelled by projectors P_A, P_B which may or may not commute.

Two empirical phenomena are relevant:

(i) Question-order effects: for many pairs of questions A, B observed in surveys, the joint probability of answering "yes" to A and then "yes" to B differs from the joint probability of answering "yes" to B and then "yes" to A. Within the quantum framework this is reproduced precisely when [P_A, P_B] ≠ 0.

(ii) Response replicability: if the same question Q is asked twice in immediate succession (with no intervening question), the respondent gives the same answer with probability 1. In the standard projective model with Lüders updating this is automatic for a single Q, but if Q is asked, then a non-commuting Q' is asked, and then Q is asked again, the model generally predicts a non-zero probability of a different answer to the repeated Q, contrary to typical empirical findings.

Problem. Identify a minimal set of mathematical features of the quantum-probabilistic formalism — drawn from the list including (a) representation of states as vectors/density operators in a Hilbert space, (b) representation of questions as projectors versus more general POVMs, (c) non-commutativity of observables, (d) the Lüders state-update rule versus alternative update rules, (e) use of complex versus real Hilbert spaces, (f) interference between probability amplitudes, (g) contextuality in the Kochen–Specker sense — that are simultaneously:

  (1) necessary to reproduce the observed question-order effects (in the sense that omitting any one of them precludes a model from fitting the empirically observed asymmetry between Pr(A=yes, then B=yes) and Pr(B=yes, then A=yes) on standard survey data); and

  (2) compatible with exact response replicability, i.e. Pr(Q = x at time t_3 | Q = x at time t_1, Q' = y at time t_2) = 1 for every intervening question Q' and every answer y of positive probability.

Determine whether such a set of features exists, and if so characterise it; if not, prove an impossibility theorem showing that within the projective/Lüders quantum formalism the conjunction of (1) and (2) cannot be realised, and identify which feature must be modified or dropped.
status_search_result: The tension between non-commuting projectors (needed for question-order effects) and exact response replicability is a recognized open issue in quantum cognition. Subsequent work has explored generalizations (POVMs, non-Lüders updates, contextuality-by-default) but no consensus minimal characterization of the "critical features" has been established, so the problem remains open.

paper_title: A single impurity in an ideal atomic Fermi gas: current understanding and some open problems
original_question: For composite dressed quasiparticles in this impurity problem, including the dimeron, trimeron, and tetrameron, determine whether there is a stronger general lower bound on the effective mass than positivity alone, namely whether dressing always increases the mass so that M*_b / M_b >= 1, where M_b is the bare mass of the corresponding composite bound state and M*_b is its effective mass in the Fermi gas.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a single impurity particle of bare mass $M$ immersed in an ideal (non-interacting) spin-polarized atomic Fermi gas of bath particles. Depending on the interaction strength and mass ratio, the impurity can bind one or more bath fermions to form composite few-body bound states in vacuum: a dimer (impurity + 1 bath fermion), a trimer (impurity + 2 bath fermions), a tetramer (impurity + 3 bath fermions), etc. Let $M_b$ denote the bare mass of such a composite bound state in vacuum (so for the dimer $M_b = M + m$, for the trimer $M_b = M + 2m$, etc., where $m$ is the bath atom mass).

When the Fermi sea is turned on, each such composite bound state becomes a dressed quasiparticle: the dimeron, trimeron, tetrameron, .... These dressed quasiparticles have a well-defined quasiparticle effective mass $M_b^*$ defined from the curvature of their dispersion at zero momentum.

Question: Is it true that, for every such composite dressed quasiparticle (dimeron, trimeron, tetrameron, and analogously for larger composites), the dressing by the Fermi sea cannot decrease the inertial mass, i.e.
$$\frac{M_b^*}{M_b} \;\ge\; 1\,?$$
Equivalently, prove or disprove that this inequality holds as a general bound (stronger than mere positivity of the effective mass) for all composite quasiparticles of an impurity in an ideal Fermi gas, across all coupling strengths and mass ratios for which the composite quasiparticle exists.
status_search_result: No publication appears to have proved or disproved the conjectured general bound $M^*_b/M_b \ge 1$ for composite dressed quasiparticles (dimeron, trimeron, tetrameron). Existing calculations of dimeron effective masses are consistent with the bound, but a general proof or counterexample has not been reported in the literature returned by search.

original_question: To what extent are Theorem 13.1 and Conjecture 13.2 valid if one replaces Q̄ with a number field K?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a smooth projective variety defined over a number field $K$, and let $f\colon X\dashrightarrow X$ be a dominant rational self-map defined over $K$. Define the (first) dynamical degree of $f$ by
$$\delta_f \;=\; \lim_{n\to\infty}\bigl(\deg(f^n)\bigr)^{1/n},$$
where $\deg(f^n)$ denotes the degree of $f^n$ with respect to a fixed ample divisor on $X$ (the limit is independent of this choice). For a point $P\in X(\overline{K})$ whose forward orbit $\{P,f(P),f^2(P),\dots\}$ is well-defined, define the arithmetic degree of $f$ at $P$ by
$$\alpha_f(P) \;=\; \limsup_{n\to\infty} \max\bigl(1,\,h_X(f^n(P))\bigr)^{1/n},$$
where $h_X$ is a Weil height on $X$ associated to an ample divisor.

The following are known/conjectured for points $P\in X(\overline{K})$:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(A)] (Existence/upper bound) The limsup defining $\alpha_f(P)$ is in fact a limit, and $\alpha_f(P)\le \delta_f$.
\item[(B)] (Equality conjecture) If the forward orbit of $P$ under $f$ is well-defined and Zariski dense in $X$, then $\alpha_f(P)=\delta_f$.
\end{itemize}

Question: To what extent do statements (A) and (B) remain valid if one restricts the point $P$ to lie in $X(K)$, the set of $K$-rational points of $X$, rather than allowing $P\in X(\overline{K})$? In particular, is the analogue of (A) known unconditionally for $P\in X(K)$, and for which classes of varieties $X$ and rational self-maps $f$ does the analogue of (B) hold for $P\in X(K)$ with Zariski dense $f$-orbit?
status_search_result: The upper bound part (A) was established in general by Kawaguchi–Silverman and Matsuzawa, and works equally well over a fixed number field K. The equality part (B), the Kawaguchi–Silverman conjecture, remains open in general as of 2024–2026. Many partial results are known (e.g., for surjective endomorphisms of projective surfaces, for abelian varieties, for varieties with sufficiently large irregularity, for certain automorphisms of threefolds, and for int-amplified endomorphisms), but the general case—whether stated over Q̄ or restricted to a number field K—is unresolved.

original_question: Let f : PN 99K PN be a dominant rational map. Then the dynamical degree δf of f is an algebraic integer, i.e., δf is the root of a monic polynomial having integer coeffi- cients.
self_contained_problem:
Let N ≥ 1 and let f : ℙ^N ⤏ ℙ^N be a dominant rational map defined over ℂ. Write f^n = f ∘ f ∘ ⋯ ∘ f for the n-th iterate (as a rational map), and let deg(f^n) denote the degree of f^n, i.e., the common degree of the homogeneous polynomials of minimal degree (with no common factor) defining f^n. The (first) dynamical degree of f is defined by

  δ_f := lim_{n→∞} deg(f^n)^{1/n},

a limit which is known to exist in [1, ∞).

Prove or disprove: for every dominant rational map f : ℙ^N ⤏ ℙ^N, the dynamical degree δ_f is an algebraic integer, i.e., a root of a monic polynomial with integer coefficients.

paper_title: Quantum Models for Psychological Measurements: An Unsolved Problem
original_question: If memory of previous answers and ordinary context changes are allowed as explanations of repeated responses and question-order effects in opinion polling, why do those same traditional psychological considerations not intervene in cases where QM is considered successfully applicable, and why should one not dispense with QM entirely in favor of those traditional explanations?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the use of quantum-mechanical (QM) formalism — Hilbert spaces, projection-valued observables, the Born rule, and non-commuting measurement operators — as a model for human responses in opinion polling, where empirical phenomena such as repeated-response stability and question-order effects are observed. Suppose these same phenomena admit alternative "traditional" psychological explanations, e.g.:
(i) memory of previous answers (a respondent recalls and reproduces the answer they just gave), and
(ii) ordinary context changes (the act of answering one question alters the cognitive context in which the next is interpreted).

Address the following two questions:
(A) If such traditional psychological mechanisms are admitted as explanations of repeated-response stability and order effects in opinion polling, identify a principled criterion that prevents these same mechanisms from intervening in physical situations where the QM formalism is regarded as successfully applicable (e.g., sequential measurements on microscopic systems). In particular, exhibit either a structural feature of the physical setting that excludes memory- and context-based explanations, or show that no such criterion exists.

(B) Determine whether the empirical regularities of repeated responses and question-order effects in opinion polling can be fully accounted for by traditional psychological mechanisms (memory plus context change) alone, so that the QM formalism is dispensable in this domain; or, conversely, exhibit a behavioral signature observable in opinion-polling data that is reproduced by the QM model but cannot be reproduced by any model based solely on such traditional mechanisms.

Subsequent literature continues to debate whether QM-style models for opinion polling provide genuine explanatory advantages over classical psychological mechanisms (memory, context), with no consensus resolution; the underlying issue remains an open foundational problem.

original_question: Let N ≥ 1. There exists a constant γN > 0 such that for all dominant rational maps f : PN 99K PN we have deg(f n+1 ) δ(f ) ≥ γN · min . 0≤n<N deg(f n ).
self_contained_problem:
Let $N\ge 1$ be an integer and let $f:\mathbb{P}^N\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^N$ be a dominant rational self-map of complex projective $N$-space. For each integer $n\ge 0$, let $f^n$ denote the $n$-th iterate of $f$ (as a rational map), and let $\deg(f^n)$ be its degree, defined as the degree of the homogeneous polynomials representing $f^n$ in any reduced expression (equivalently, the pullback degree on hyperplane classes). $$\delta(f)\;=\;\lim_{n\to\infty}\bigl(\deg(f^n)\bigr)^{1/n},$$
which is known to exist and to satisfy $\delta(f)\le \deg(f^{n+1})/\deg(f^n)\cdot\bigl(\text{something}\bigr)$ in various weak senses, but in general $\delta(f)$ may be strictly less than $\deg(f)$ due to indeterminacies.

$$\delta(f)\;\ge\;\gamma_N\cdot\min_{0\le n<N}\frac{\deg(f^{n+1})}{\deg(f^n)}.$$

original_question: Let X be a smooth projective variety of dimension N , and let f : X 99K X be a dominant rational map. Is it true that the higher order dynamical (i) degrees δf are algebraic integers for all 1 ≤ i ≤ N ?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a smooth projective variety of dimension $N$ over $\mathbb{C}$, and let $f\colon X \dashrightarrow X$ be a dominant rational map. For each integer $1 \le i \le N$, the $i$-th dynamical degree of $f$ is defined as
$$\delta_f^{(i)} \;=\; \lim_{n \to \infty} \bigl( (f^n)^{*} H^i \cdot H^{N-i} \bigr)^{1/n},$$
where $H$ is an ample divisor class on $X$ and $(f^n)^{*}$ denotes the pullback action on the cohomology group $H^{i,i}(X)$ (or equivalently on the Néron–Severi group when $i=1$); this limit exists, is independent of the choice of $H$, and is a birational invariant.

Question: Is it true that for every smooth projective variety $X$ of dimension $N$ and every dominant rational self-map $f\colon X \dashrightarrow X$, all of the higher-order dynamical degrees $\delta_f^{(i)}$, $1 \le i \le N$, are algebraic integers?
status_search_result: Bell, Diller, and Jonsson constructed an explicit dominant rational self-map of $\mathbb{P}^2$ whose first dynamical degree is a transcendental number (published as "A transcendental dynamical degree"), and this was extended to birational self-maps of $\mathbb{P}^d$ for $d \ge 3$ ("Birational maps with transcendental dynamical degree", Proc. paper_title: A single impurity in an ideal atomic Fermi gas: current understanding and some open problems
original_question: In the same single-impurity Fermi-gas system, and assuming m/M < 13.384 so that Efimov states have not yet appeared, determine whether there exist stable non-Efimovian bound states in vacuum larger than the already known dimer, trimer, and tetramer, such as pentamers, hexamers, or still larger impurity-plus-identical-fermion clusters, for given values of the mass ratio m/M and positive scattering length a > 0.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a quantum system in three-dimensional vacuum consisting of a single distinguishable impurity particle of mass M and N identical (spin-polarized) non-interacting fermions of mass m, where the impurity interacts with each fermion through a short-range, zero-range two-body interaction characterized by a positive s-wave scattering length a > 0, while the identical fermions do not interact with one another. Let the mass ratio satisfy m/M < 13.384, the threshold below which the three-body Efimov effect (heavy-heavy-light Efimov states for two heavy fermions plus one light impurity, or its analogue) does not occur, so that the spectrum of universal bound clusters is non-Efimovian. It is known that for suitable values of m/M and a > 0 there exist stable bound states of the impurity with two, three, and four identical fermions (the dimer, trimer, and tetramer).

Question: For which values of N ≥ 5 (pentamer, hexamer, and larger clusters consisting of one impurity bound to N identical fermions) and which mass ratios m/M < 13.384 do there exist stable, non-Efimovian few-body bound states in vacuum at positive scattering length a > 0? In particular, determine whether such larger bound clusters exist at all, and if so characterize the range of mass ratios for which each cluster size is bound.
category_tag: Few-body bound states in mass-imbalanced Fermi gases
status_search_result: Subsequent work has provided partial answers: a universal non-Efimovian (4+1) pentamer continuing the dimer–trimer–tetramer series has been established for sufficiently large mass ratio, while no (5+1) six-body bound state (hexamer) has been found in the explored mass-ratio range up to M/m ≲ 12, with the p-shell argument suggesting a qualitative change at N = 6. A complete classification of stable larger clusters for all m/M < 13.384 has not been established.

$$\overline{\alpha}_f(P) = \limsup_{n \to \infty} h^+(f^n(P))^{1/n}, \qquad \underline{\alpha}_f(P) = \liminf_{n \to \infty} h^+(f^n(P))^{1/n}.$$

\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] For every $P \in \mathbb{P}^N(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})_f$, the limit $\alpha_f(P) := \lim_{n\to\infty} h^+(f^n(P))^{1/n}$ exists; equivalently, $\overline{\alpha}_f(P) = \underline{\alpha}_f(P)$.
\item[(b)] The set $\{\alpha_f(P) : P \in \mathbb{P}^N(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})_f\}$ is finite.
\item[(c)] For every $P \in \mathbb{P}^N(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})_f$, the arithmetic degree $\alpha_f(P)$ is an algebraic integer.

paper_title: A single impurity in an ideal atomic Fermi gas: current understanding and some open problems
original_question: Given the many-body wave function of a single impurity in a Fermi gas expanded in sectors with increasing numbers of particle-hole pairs, determine the asymptotic form of the large-s tail of that wave function, where s is the number of particle-hole pairs. In particular, characterize the regime of very large s that controls the coherence properties of the impurity and decide whether that asymptotic tail can be described analytically using an effectively noninteracting gas of particles and holes that each scatter only from the impurity.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a single distinguishable impurity immersed in an ideal three-dimensional Fermi gas of N identical non-interacting fermions filling a Fermi sea up to Fermi momentum k_F, with a short-range two-body interaction acting only between the impurity and the majority fermions. The exact many-body ground state |Ψ⟩ can be expanded in sectors labeled by the number s = 0, 1, 2, … of particle–hole pairs excited out of the Fermi sea:

|Ψ⟩ = Σ_{s=0}^{∞} |Ψ_s⟩,

where |Ψ_s⟩ contains the impurity dressed by exactly s particle–hole excitations of the majority Fermi sea, with amplitudes φ_s(p; k_1,…,k_s; q_1,…,q_s) (p the impurity momentum, k_i the particle momenta above the Fermi sea, q_i the hole momenta below it).

(a) Determine the asymptotic form of |Ψ_s⟩, or equivalently of the amplitudes φ_s and of the sector weight w_s = ⟨Ψ_s|Ψ_s⟩, in the limit s → ∞ that controls the long-time / low-energy coherence properties (the quasiparticle residue and orthogonality-catastrophe-like behavior) of the impurity in the Fermi gas.

(b) Decide whether this large-s asymptotic tail can be obtained analytically by treating the s particles and s holes as an effectively non-interacting gas of excitations in which each particle and each hole scatters only from the impurity (i.e. by an independent-scatterer / single-impurity-T-matrix factorization), and either prove such a factorized asymptotic representation or exhibit corrections that invalidate it.
status_search_result: Recent literature on the Fermi polaron continues to study truncated particle–hole expansions (one-, two-, three-pair Chevy-type ansätze) and Quantum Monte Carlo benchmarks, but does not appear to provide a closed-form asymptotic characterization of the s → ∞ tail of the ground-state wave function, nor a rigorous derivation via independent impurity-scatterers. The problem appears still open as of 2024–2025.

Then αf (P ) = δf . The inequality (15.7) ᾱf (P ) ≤ δf for P ∈ X(Q̄)f relating arithmetic and dynamical degrees is true in the more general setting of.
self_contained_problem:
Let X be a smooth projective variety defined over the algebraic closure Q̄ of Q, and let f : X ⇢ X be a dominant rational self-map. Let X(Q̄)_f denote the set of Q̄-points P of X whose forward orbit O_f(P) = {P, f(P), f^2(P), ...} is well-defined (i.e., f^n(P) avoids the indeterminacy locus of f for all n ≥ 0).

Fix an ample divisor H on X, and let h_H : X(Q̄) → R be a corresponding (logarithmic) Weil height, normalized so that h_H ≥ 1. For P ∈ X(Q̄)_f define the upper and lower arithmetic degrees
   ᾱ_f(P) = limsup_{n→∞} h_H(f^n(P))^{1/n},   α_f(P) = liminf_{n→∞} h_H(f^n(P))^{1/n}.
These quantities are independent of the choice of H. Let δ_f denote the (first) dynamical degree of f, defined as
   δ_f = lim_{n→∞} ((f^n)^* H · H^{dim X − 1})^{1/n},
which is known to exist and is a birational invariant.

Prove or disprove each of the following statements:

(a) For every P ∈ X(Q̄)_f, the limit lim_{n→∞} h_H(f^n(P))^{1/n} exists (so ᾱ_f(P) = α_f(P) =: α_f(P)).

(b) The set { α_f(P) : P ∈ X(Q̄)_f } is finite.

(c) For every P ∈ X(Q̄)_f, the arithmetic degree α_f(P) is an algebraic integer.

(d) If P ∈ X(Q̄)_f has orbit O_f(P) Zariski dense in X, then α_f(P) = δ_f.
status_search_result: The package of statements is the Kawaguchi–Silverman arithmetic degree conjecture. Parts (b) and (c) (finiteness of the set of arithmetic degrees, and the algebraic-integrality of α_f(P)) have been disproved by counterexamples of Lesieutre–Satriano using birational self-maps on surfaces. Part (a) (existence of the limit) and part (d) (equality with the dynamical degree on Zariski-dense orbits) remain open in general, but have been established in many cases, including surjective endomorphisms of smooth projective surfaces, int-amplified endomorphisms of Q-factorial klt varieties, and various other classes (works by Kawaguchi–Silverman, Matsuzawa, Meng–Zhang, Sano, and others through 2024).

paper_title: A single impurity in an ideal atomic Fermi gas: current understanding and some open problems
original_question: When the effective mass M* of the impurity quasiparticle is extracted by minimizing a truncated variational trial state at small but nonzero momentum p and fitting E_p = E_0 + p^2/(2M*), determine whether this variational procedure is mathematically well defined and whether it really computes the real part of the complex excitation energy of the long-lived dressed impurity state.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a single mobile impurity of mass $M$ immersed in an ideal three-dimensional Fermi gas of non-interacting fermions of mass $m$ at zero temperature, where the impurity interacts with the fermions via a short-range two-body potential characterized by a scattering length $a$. The total momentum $\mathbf{p}$ of the system is a good quantum number. For sufficiently weak attractive coupling, the dressed impurity ("polaron") at total momentum $\mathbf{p}$ is expected to be a long-lived quasiparticle whose true excitation energy is a complex number $\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{p}) = E(\mathbf{p}) - i\Gamma(\mathbf{p})/2$, with the real part $E(\mathbf{p})$ admitting a low-momentum expansion of the form 
$$E(\mathbf{p}) = E_0 + \frac{|\mathbf{p}|^2}{2M^*} + O(|\mathbf{p}|^4),$$ 
where $M^*$ is the quasiparticle effective mass.

A standard procedure to estimate $M^*$ is the following variational scheme. Choose a truncated variational ansatz $|\Psi_{\mathbf{p}}\rangle$ for the polaron at total momentum $\mathbf{p}$ (for example, the Chevy ansatz containing the bare impurity plus a finite number of particle–hole excitations of the Fermi sea). For each small but nonzero $\mathbf{p}$, minimize the expectation value 
$$\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{var}}(\mathbf{p}) = \min_{|\Psi_{\mathbf{p}}\rangle} \frac{\langle \Psi_{\mathbf{p}} | \hat{H} | \Psi_{\mathbf{p}}\rangle}{\langle \Psi_{\mathbf{p}} | \Psi_{\mathbf{p}}\rangle}$$ 
within the chosen truncated subspace, and extract a variational effective mass $M^*_{\mathrm{var}}$ by fitting $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{var}}(\mathbf{p}) = \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{var}}(\mathbf{0}) + |\mathbf{p}|^2/(2M^*_{\mathrm{var}}) + O(|\mathbf{p}|^4)$.

The questions are:

(a) Is this minimization procedure mathematically well defined at small nonzero $\mathbf{p}$? In particular, does the variational functional possess a true minimum (rather than only an infimum or a saddle point) within the truncated subspace, given that for $\mathbf{p}\neq 0$ the bare polaron state is typically embedded in a continuum of polaron-plus-particle-hole scattering states that may render the variational energy unbounded below or non-stationary?

(b) Assuming the procedure is well defined, prove or disprove that the resulting $M^*_{\mathrm{var}}$ coincides with the effective mass $M^*$ associated with the real part $E(\mathbf{p})$ of the exact complex quasiparticle energy $\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{p})$ of the long-lived dressed impurity.
status_search_result: Recent work on Fermi polarons (e.g., explicit weakly-attractive computations of complex polaron energies and effective masses, and rigorous effective-dynamics results for impurities in Fermi gases) addresses related quantities but does not appear to settle the precise mathematical question of whether minimizing a truncated variational ansatz at nonzero momentum is well defined and whether it yields the real part of the exact complex quasiparticle energy. No source found that establishes this equivalence rigorously, so the problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Let N ≥ 1, D ≥ 1, and d ≥ 2. There are positive constants c1 (D, N, d) and c2 (D, N, d) such that for all number fields K/Q with [K : Q] ≤ D, all degree d morphisms f : PN → PN defined over K, and all points P ∈ PN (K) whose orbit Of (P ) is Zariski dense in PN , we have ĥf (P ) ≥ c1 (D, N, d)hM (f ) + c2 (D, N, d). See [35, 34] for numerical evidence supporting Conjecture 16.3 in the case N = D = 1 and d ∈ {2, 3}, including conjectural values for the constants. We also note that the Zariski density assumption in Conjecture 16.3 is necessary. For ex- ample, the map f = [X 2 , Y 2 , γZ 2 ] has height roughly h(γ), while the f -orbit of the point P = [α, 1, 0] has canonical height ĥf (P ) = h(α), so we can make hM (f ) arbitrarily large while ĥf (P ) remains bounded. Ingram [116] and Looper [155] have proven weak versions of Conjecture 16.3 for polynomial maps f of P1 , where the constants depend also on the number of primes of bad reduction of f.
self_contained_problem:
Fix integers $N\ge 1$, $D\ge 1$, and $d\ge 2$. For a number field $K$ and a morphism $f:\mathbb{P}^N\to\mathbb{P}^N$ of degree $d$ defined over $K$, let $\hat{h}_f:\mathbb{P}^N(\overline{K})\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ denote the canonical (Call–Silverman) height attached to $f$, characterized by $\hat{h}_f(f(P))=d\,\hat{h}_f(P)$ and $\hat{h}_f=h+O(1)$, where $h$ is the absolute logarithmic Weil height on $\mathbb{P}^N$. Let $h_M(f)$ denote the Macaulay (or moduli) height of $f$, i.e. the height of the point in an appropriate moduli/parameter space representing $f$ (equivalently, the height of the coefficient vector of $f$ written as a tuple of homogeneous polynomials, suitably normalized). For a point $P\in\mathbb{P}^N(K)$, let $\mathcal{O}_f(P)=\{f^n(P):n\ge 0\}$ denote its forward orbit.

Prove or disprove: there exist positive constants $c_1=c_1(D,N,d)>0$ and $c_2=c_2(D,N,d)\in\mathbb{R}$ such that, for every number field $K/\mathbb{Q}$ with $[K:\mathbb{Q}]\le D$, every degree-$d$ morphism $f:\mathbb{P}^N\to\mathbb{P}^N$ defined over $K$, and every point $P\in\mathbb{P}^N(K)$ whose orbit $\mathcal{O}_f(P)$ is Zariski dense in $\mathbb{P}^N$, one has
$$\hat{h}_f(P)\;\ge\; c_1(D,N,d)\,h_M(f)\;+\;c_2(D,N,d).$$
status_search_result: The Dynamical Lang Height Conjecture remains open in general. Only weak versions have been established—for polynomial maps of $\mathbb{P}^1$ by Ingram and by Looper, with constants that additionally depend on the number of primes of bad reduction. Numerical evidence exists for $N=D=1$ and $d\in\{2,3\}$, but no proof of the general statement is known.

paper_title: Bootstrap Algebraic Multigrid: status report, open problems, and outlook
original_question: Given a current set C of coarse variables for bootstrap algebraic multigrid, how should one choose the initial coarse set C0 and then make local additions, removals, or other modifications to C whenever compatible relaxation converges too slowly, so that the updated coarse space improves convergence without introducing unnecessary complexity?
self_contained_problem:
Setting. Consider a sparse symmetric positive definite linear system $Au=f$ on a finite index set $\Omega=\{1,\dots,n\}$. In an algebraic multigrid framework one selects a subset $C\subset\Omega$ of "coarse variables" with complementary fine set $F=\Omega\setminus C$, and builds a coarse space via an interpolation operator $P:\mathbb{R}^{|C|}\to\mathbb{R}^n$. The quality of $C$ is measured through compatible relaxation (CR): given a smoother $M$ for $A$ and the restriction $A_{FF}$ of $A$ to the $F$–$F$ block, one performs the iteration $e_F\leftarrow (I-M_{FF}^{-1}A_{FF})e_F$ on the fine subspace and defines the CR convergence rate
$$\rho_{CR}(C)=\lim_{k\to\infty}\bigl\|(I-M_{FF}^{-1}A_{FF})^k\bigr\|^{1/k}.$$
A coarse set $C$ is regarded as adequate when $\rho_{CR}(C)\le\rho^*$ for a prescribed target $\rho^*<1$, and inadequate otherwise. The coarsening cost is measured by $|C|/n$ (or, recursively, by the operator complexity of the resulting hierarchy).

Problem. Provide a constructive procedure that, for any such $A$:

(a) selects an initial coarse set $C_0\subset\Omega$ (using only information available algebraically from $A$ and from a small set of test vectors produced by relaxation on $Au=0$);

(b) when applied iteratively, locally modifies the current coarse set $C$ by additions, removals, or replacements of indices in regions where CR is observed to converge slowly, producing an updated set $C'$ that satisfies
$$\rho_{CR}(C')\le\rho_{CR}(C)\quad\text{and ultimately}\quad \rho_{CR}(C')\le\rho^*,$$
while keeping $|C'|/n$ bounded by a prescribed coarsening ratio.

The procedure should come with a rigorous justification—in particular, identifying which local quantities derived from CR (e.g.\ pointwise errors, slow-to-converge components) reliably indicate the indices whose addition to $C$ most reduces $\rho_{CR}$—together with an analysis showing convergence of the update process to an adequate $C$ without introducing unnecessary coarse-space complexity.
status_search_result: The question of how to choose an initial coarse set and how to perform local modifications driven by slow CR convergence in bootstrap AMG remains an active research area. Subsequent work (e.g., relaxation-corrected BAMG, least-angle-regression coarsening, and analyses of optimal interpolation with compatible relaxation) proposes heuristics and partial analyses, but no rigorous, complete theoretical justification of the local-modification rule based on pointwise CR errors has appeared. The problem is best classified as open, with partial progress.

original_question: Let f ∈ Cv (z) be a rational function of degree at least 2, and let Jf ⊂ P1Berk be the Julia set of f . Then Jf ∩ P1 (Cv ) is equal to the closure in P1 (Cv ) of the set of Type I repelling periodic points of f.
self_contained_problem:
Let $(C_v, |\cdot|)$ be an algebraically closed field that is complete with respect to a nontrivial non-archimedean absolute value. Let $\mathbb{P}^1_{\mathrm{Berk}}$ denote the Berkovich projective line over $C_v$, whose points are classified into Types I, II, III, and IV; the Type I points are exactly the classical points $\mathbb{P}^1(C_v) \subset \mathbb{P}^1_{\mathrm{Berk}}$.

Let $f \in C_v(z)$ be a rational function of degree $\deg(f) \geq 2$, viewed as a self-map of $\mathbb{P}^1_{\mathrm{Berk}}$ via its canonical continuous extension. Let $J_f \subset \mathbb{P}^1_{\mathrm{Berk}}$ denote the Berkovich Julia set of $f$ (the complement of the Berkovich Fatou set, defined as the largest open set on which the family of iterates is equicontinuous in a suitable sense, or equivalently as the support of the canonical $f$-invariant measure).

A point $x \in \mathbb{P}^1(C_v)$ is called a Type I repelling periodic point of $f$ if there exists an integer $n \geq 1$ such that $f^n(x) = x$ and the multiplier $(f^n)'(x)$ satisfies $|(f^n)'(x)| > 1$.

Prove or disprove: $J_f \cap \mathbb{P}^1(C_v)$ equals the closure in $\mathbb{P}^1(C_v)$ (with respect to the topology induced by $|\cdot|$) of the set of Type I repelling periodic points of $f$.
status_search_result: The conjecture appears to remain open. It is well known that Type II repelling periodic points are dense in the Berkovich Julia set (results of Bezivin, Rivera-Letelier, Baker–Rumely), but the question of whether the classical (Type I) repelling periodic points are dense in $J_f \cap \mathbb{P}^1(C_v)$ remains unresolved in general. Partial results have been given via logarithmic equidistribution methods (e.g. Okuyama, arXiv:1106.3363), but no full proof has been published.

original_question: Let f ∈ Cv (z) with deg f = d ≥ 2. Can f have infinitely many periodic cycles of indifferent components that are not disks? If not, is there a bound in terms of d for the number of such cycles? Do the answers depend on the field Cv ?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(K,|\cdot|)$ be a complete, algebraically closed, non-archimedean valued field (for example $K=\mathbb{C}_v$, the completion of an algebraic closure of a complete non-archimedean field), and let $f \in K(z)$ be a rational map of degree $d \geq 2$ acting on the Berkovich projective line $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_K$. The Fatou set of $f$ is the largest open subset of $\mathbb{P}^{1,\mathrm{an}}_K$ on which the iterates $\{f^n\}$ form an equicontinuous (normal) family; its connected components are called Fatou components. A periodic Fatou component $U$ of period $n \geq 1$ (so $f^n(U) = U$) is called indifferent if the action of $f^n$ on $U$ is neither attracting nor in the basin of any attracting/super-attracting cycle, and equivalently can be characterized by the multiplier behavior on the boundary type-II points associated with $U$. A Fatou component is called a disk if it is isomorphic, as a Berkovich analytic space, to an open Berkovich disk. A periodic cycle of Fatou components is the orbit $\{U, f(U), \dots, f^{n-1}(U)\}$ of a periodic component.

Address the following questions:

(a) Can $f$ have infinitely many distinct periodic cycles of indifferent Fatou components that are not disks?

(b) If not, is there an upper bound, depending only on the degree $d$, for the number of such cycles?

(c) Do the answers to (a) and (b) depend on the particular non-archimedean field $K$ (e.g., its residue characteristic or value group)?
status_search_result: Recent work establishes that for degree $d=2$ the bound is $d-1=1$ cycle of indifferent components that are not disks, and that for $d \geq 3$ the bound $d-1$ holds under an additional hypothesis on the residue field together with a connectivity condition on the cycles, with explicit constructions achieving exactly $d-1$ such cycles. The unconditional bound for general $d \geq 3$ and the field-dependence question do not appear to be fully resolved.

original_question: For least-squares interpolation in bootstrap algebraic multigrid, how can one define appropriate local weights ωκ, and possibly corresponding local equations for computing test vectors, in a general algebraic setting so that a globally smooth test vector is not overemphasized in local regions where it has large residuals?
self_contained_problem:
Setting. Consider a sparse symmetric positive (semi)definite linear system $A u = f$ on a finite index set $\Omega$ of fine-grid degrees of freedom, together with a chosen subset $\mathcal{C}\subset\Omega$ of coarse variables and complementary fine set $\mathcal{F}=\Omega\setminus\mathcal{C}$. $$ (Pv)_i = \sum_{j\in\mathcal{C}_i} p_{ij}\, v_j ,\qquad i\in\mathcal{F}, $$
with $(Pv)_i=v_i$ for $i\in\mathcal{C}$.

Suppose one is given a finite collection of test vectors $\{x^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K}\subset\mathbb{R}^{\Omega}$, intended to represent algebraically smooth error components (i.e., components slow to be reduced by relaxation). The least-squares (LS) definition of interpolation determines the rows of $P$ by solving, for each $i\in\mathcal{F}$,
$$ \{p_{ij}\}_{j\in\mathcal{C}_i} \;=\; \arg\min_{\{q_{ij}\}}\;\sum_{k=1}^{K} \omega_\kappa^{(k)}(i)\,\Big( x^{(k)}_i - \sum_{j\in\mathcal{C}_i} q_{ij}\, x^{(k)}_j \Big)^{\!2}, $$
where $\omega_\kappa^{(k)}(i)\ge 0$ are local weights assigned to test vector $k$ at the local LS problem indexed by $i$ (or, more generally, by a local aggregate $\kappa$).

Problem. In a purely algebraic setting (i.e., without recourse to an underlying PDE, mesh, or finite-element structure), give a procedure to define the local weights $\omega_\kappa^{(k)}$, and, if needed, an associated set of local equations whose solutions provide local test vectors, with the following property:

(P) If a test vector $x^{(k)}$ is globally smooth in the sense of having small global $A$-residual $\|A x^{(k)}\|$ relative to $\|x^{(k)}\|_A$, but on some local region $\kappa$ has a large local residual (e.g., $\sum_{i\in\kappa}(Ax^{(k)})_i^2$ is large compared to a local energy measure of $x^{(k)}$ on $\kappa$), then the weights $\omega_\kappa^{(k)}$ used in the LS problems centered in $\kappa$ should not over-emphasize $x^{(k)}$ relative to other test vectors. Equivalently, the scheme should generalize the local-scaling-by-residual (LSR) idea — which is presently used only in conjunction with global weights — to a fully local weighting strategy, while still producing an interpolation $P$ that yields a convergent bootstrap algebraic multigrid method on a broad class of symmetric positive (semi)definite problems.

Provide such a definition of $\{\omega_\kappa^{(k)}\}$ (and any auxiliary local equations for local test vectors) and prove that the resulting LS interpolation satisfies a two-grid weak-approximation bound uniform in problem size on this class.
status_search_result: The question of defining purely algebraic local weights (and corresponding local equations for test vectors) for the least-squares interpolation in bootstrap AMG is identified as an unresolved problem in surveys of BAMG; partial progress exists for finite-element discretizations of elliptic problems, and recent works (e.g., relaxation-corrected BAMG, least-angle-regression coarsening, and learning-based local weighted least-squares schemes) propose heuristic or data-driven weightings, but no general algebraic resolution with provable guarantees has been established.

paper_title: Bootstrap Algebraic Multigrid: status report, open problems, and outlook
original_question: When computing the test vectors used by bootstrap algebraic multigrid, what balance between computational work and approximation accuracy should be targeted so that the vectors are accurate enough to define effective interpolation without making setup prohibitively expensive?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the bootstrap algebraic multigrid (BAMG) framework for solving a large sparse linear system $A x = b$, where $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ is symmetric positive (semi)definite or otherwise admits a near-kernel of algebraically smooth error components. In BAMG, the prolongation operator $P$ between a fine level and a coarse level is constructed so as to fit, in a (weighted) least-squares sense, a collection of "test vectors" $\{v^{(1)}, \dots, v^{(k)}\} \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ that are intended to span (or approximately span) the algebraically smooth subspace of $A$. These test vectors are themselves produced by a bootstrap setup procedure: an initial multigrid hierarchy is applied (e.g., via relaxation, multigrid eigensolves, and recursive coarse-level computations) to a set of random or problem-informed initial vectors, yielding successively more accurate approximations to slow-to-converge modes.

Let $W(k,\tau)$ denote the total computational work (in floating-point operations) expended in the setup phase to produce $k$ test vectors each computed to an accuracy $\tau$ (measured, for instance, by the $A$-norm residual of the homogeneous problem $A v = 0$ relative to the dominant smooth modes). Let $\rho(k,\tau)$ denote the asymptotic convergence factor of the resulting BAMG V-cycle (or W-cycle) when interpolation is built by least-squares fitting these test vectors, and let $C_{\mathrm{solve}}(k,\tau)$ denote the work per cycle in the solve phase.

Problem. Determine, for a given target overall solve-phase efficiency, principled criteria for choosing the number $k$ of test vectors and the accuracy $\tau$ to which each is computed in the setup phase that:
(i) guarantee that the constructed interpolation $P$ approximates the algebraically smooth subspace of $A$ accurately enough to yield a convergence factor $\rho(k,\tau)$ bounded below $1$ uniformly in problem size and parameters of interest, and
(ii) keep the setup work $W(k,\tau)$ bounded by a small multiple of the solve work, so that total cost $W(k,\tau) + N_{\text{cycles}}\cdot C_{\mathrm{solve}}(k,\tau)$ is minimized (or at least kept comparable to that of an optimally-tuned geometric multigrid method) for the class of problems considered.

In particular, give quantitative guidance, supported by analysis, on the optimal stopping accuracy $\tau$ for the bootstrap test-vector iterations and on the optimal number $k$ of test vectors as functions of the spectral properties of $A$ and the desired convergence factor.
status_search_result: The work-accuracy tradeoff in computing test vectors for bootstrap AMG is identified as an open problem. Subsequent literature (e.g., least-angle-regression coarsening for BAMG, BAMG for the Wilson Dirac system, machine-learning interpretations of BAMG setup) discusses heuristics and improvements but does not provide a definitive theoretical rule for the optimal balance; the question remains an active research direction.

paper_title: Bootstrap Algebraic Multigrid: status report, open problems, and outlook
original_question: For general Hermitian positive definite problems, how can the compatible-relaxation, algebraic-distance, least-squares-interpolation, and bootstrap test-vector components of bootstrap algebraic multigrid be integrated into an overall algorithm that is practical, easy to tune, and robust as a fast multigrid solver across a diverse set of test problems, including systems of partial differential equations?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the class of large sparse linear systems $A x = b$ where $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ (or $\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$) is Hermitian positive definite (HPD), arising for example from the discretization of (systems of) partial differential equations. A multigrid solver attempts to solve such systems with optimal $O(n)$ complexity by combining a smoother with a coarse-grid correction defined through an interpolation operator $P$ and a hierarchy of coarser problems $A_\ell = P_\ell^* A_{\ell-1} P_\ell$.

Bootstrap Algebraic Multigrid (BAMG) is a purely algebraic framework built from the following four ingredients:

1. Compatible Relaxation (CR): a relaxation scheme restricted to the fine-grid degrees of freedom, used to choose a coarse/fine splitting $C \cup F$ such that the convergence rate of the F-relaxation is bounded uniformly away from one.

2. Algebraic Distance: a strength-of-connection measure between degrees of freedom, derived from the decay of components of a set of smooth (algebraically smooth) test vectors, used to determine the sparsity pattern (caliber and support) of the interpolation operator $P$.

3. Least-Squares Interpolation: given a set of test vectors $\{v^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^K$ approximating the algebraically smooth eigenmodes of $A$, the rows of $P$ for each fine point $i \in F$ are defined to minimize a weighted least-squares functional
$$\sum_{k=1}^K \omega_k \Big( v^{(k)}_i - \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_i \cap C} p_{ij}\, v^{(k)}_j \Big)^2$$
over a prescribed sparsity pattern $\mathcal{N}_i \cap C$.

4. Bootstrap Test Vectors: the test vectors $\{v^{(k)}\}$ are themselves generated and iteratively improved by applying the current multigrid V-cycle (or a multilevel eigensolver) to random initial guesses, producing better approximations to the algebraically smooth components, which are then used to update the algebraic distance and the least-squares interpolation in an outer "bootstrap" loop.

Problem. For general HPD problems, devise an integrated BAMG algorithm that combines the four components above (CR-based coarsening, algebraic-distance strength, least-squares interpolation, and bootstrap test-vector generation) into a single setup-and-solve procedure satisfying all of the following requirements:

(i) Practicality: the setup and solve phases have storage and arithmetic complexity scaling at most quasi-linearly in $n$, with operator and grid complexities bounded uniformly across a wide range of problem sizes.

(ii) Tunability: the algorithm exposes only a small number of user parameters (e.g.\ CR tolerance, caliber of $P$, number of test vectors, number of bootstrap cycles), with default values that perform well without problem-specific tuning.

(iii) Robustness: when applied as a stand-alone iterative solver (or as a preconditioner for Krylov methods), the resulting V-cycle achieves a convergence factor bounded uniformly away from one, on a diverse benchmark suite that includes anisotropic and jump-coefficient scalar elliptic PDEs as well as HPD systems of PDEs (such as linear elasticity and discretizations of Maxwell-type and Stokes-type problems whose HPD blocks must be solved).

Provide such an algorithm together with a theoretical or empirical justification of (i)–(iii), or prove that no such integration achieving uniform robustness across this problem class can exist within the stated complexity bounds.
status_search_result: No web search performed in this run; based on the framing as a research outlook question (developing an integrated, practical, tunable, and robust BAMG solver across diverse HPD problems including systems of PDEs), this is a broad open research program rather than a settled theorem. Subsequent BAMG/AMG developments (e.g.\ adaptive AMG, lAIR, GMG-inspired algebraic methods) have made progress on specific problem classes, but a single integrated BAMG algorithm meeting all three criteria uniformly over HPD systems of PDEs has not been established.

paper_title: Bootstrap Algebraic Multigrid: status report, open problems, and outlook
original_question: For non-Hermitian problems, how can restriction R and interpolation P be constructed and tied together locally so that the Galerkin coarse-grid matrix remains suitable for multigrid correction and does not become singular or cause divergence through overcorrection when small singular values or eigenvalues are underestimated on coarse levels?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A \in \mathbb{C}^{n	imes n}$ be a (possibly non-Hermitian) nonsingular matrix arising as a fine-level discretization, and consider a two-level multigrid scheme defined by a restriction operator $R \in \mathbb{C}^{n_c 	imes n}$ and an interpolation operator $P \in \mathbb{C}^{n 	imes n_c}$, with $n_c < n$. The Galerkin coarse-grid operator is
$$A_c \;=\; R\,A\,P \in \mathbb{C}^{n_c 	imes n_c}.$$
A two-level cycle alternates a relaxation (smoothing) step with the coarse-grid correction $x \leftarrow x + P A_c^{-1} R(b - A x)$.

In the non-Hermitian setting it is possible that $A$ is nonsingular while $A_c = R A P$ is singular or has eigenvalues/singular values much smaller in modulus than those of $A$, leading to coarse-grid correction that overshoots and causes the resulting iteration to diverge.

Problem. Devise a constructive procedure that, given $A$ and a set of (approximate) algebraically smooth test vectors, produces $R$ and $P$ jointly — tying their local definitions together — such that:

(i) $A_c = R A P$ is guaranteed to be nonsingular whenever $A$ is nonsingular;

(ii) the smallest singular value (and the spectrum near $0$) of $A_c$ is not underestimated relative to that of $A$ in a quantifiable sense, so that the coarse-grid correction does not produce overcorrection;

(iii) the resulting two-level (and, recursively, multilevel) iteration converges uniformly, with a contraction factor bounded away from $1$ independently of $n$, for a useful class of non-Hermitian matrices $A$.

Provide such a coupled construction of $R$ and $P$, together with theoretical guarantees of (i)–(iii), or prove that no such local coupling can achieve all three properties simultaneously.
status_search_result: The construction of jointly compatible restriction and interpolation operators that guarantee a nonsingular, well-conditioned Galerkin coarse-grid operator for general non-Hermitian problems remains an active research topic in algebraic multigrid. While various heuristic and partial approaches (e.g., bootstrap AMG, AMGe, nonsymmetric smoothed aggregation, Petrov-Galerkin AMG) have been proposed, no general construction with the requested rigorous guarantees for broad non-Hermitian classes appears to be established. Status is best characterized as open.

paper_title: Bootstrap Algebraic Multigrid: status report, open problems, and outlook
original_question: For a linear system Ax = b solved by bootstrap algebraic multigrid, what form of compatible relaxation and what convergence-rate estimate derived from the compatible-relaxation factor ρ_cr should be used so that, for a given interpolation strategy, the estimate accurately predicts the convergence of the resulting two-grid method?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ be a symmetric positive definite matrix arising from the linear system $Ax = b$, and consider a two-grid method defined by:
- a splitting of the index set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ into a set $C$ of coarse variables and its complement $F$ of fine variables;
- an interpolation operator $P : \mathbb{R}^{|C|} \to \mathbb{R}^n$ defining the coarse space;
- a smoother $M$ (so that the smoothing iteration is $x \leftarrow x - M^{-1}(Ax-b)$).

Compatible relaxation (CR) is a relaxation scheme restricted to the $F$-variables; informally, it is an iteration of the form $e_F \leftarrow (I - M_{FF}^{-1} A_{FF}) e_F$, whose asymptotic convergence factor is denoted
$$\rho_{cr} := \lim_{k\to\infty}\|(I - M_{FF}^{-1} A_{FF})^k\|^{1/k}_{\star},$$
in some appropriate norm $\|\cdot\|_\star$. The two-grid convergence factor is
$$\rho_{TG} := \|(I - M^{-1} A)^{\nu_2}(I - P(P^T A P)^{-1} P^T A)(I - M^{-1} A)^{\nu_1}\|_A.$$

Problem. Identify a precise form of compatible relaxation (i.e., a specific choice of the $F$-relaxation operator and the norm $\|\cdot\|_\star$) and an associated quantitative estimate $\Phi(\rho_{cr})$, depending only on $\rho_{cr}$ and on data of the chosen interpolation strategy $P$, such that $\Phi(\rho_{cr})$ accurately predicts $\rho_{TG}$ — in the sense that there exist explicit, sharp two-sided bounds
$$c_1\, \Phi(\rho_{cr}) \le \rho_{TG} \le c_2\, \Phi(\rho_{cr}),$$
with constants $c_1, c_2 > 0$ independent of $n$, that hold uniformly over a specified class of SPD matrices $A$ and a specified family of interpolation operators $P$. Determine such a CR formulation and prove the corresponding sharp predictive estimate.
status_search_result: Recent literature (e.g., works on optimal interpolation and compatible relaxation in classical AMG, 2017; relaxation-based AMG theory, 2026) continues to address sharp two-sided predictive bounds for two-grid convergence in terms of compatible-relaxation factors. Partial results exist (sharp measures via optimal interpolation give lower bounds, and CR provides necessary conditions), but a general precise CR-based predictor of two-grid convergence for arbitrary interpolation strategies remains an active open problem.

paper_title: Bootstrap Algebraic Multigrid: status report, open problems, and outlook
original_question: How far can bootstrap algebraic multigrid techniques developed for non-elliptic and other challenging sparse systems be extended so that they become genuinely fast solvers for general sparse matrix equations beyond the problem classes where BAMG-like methods have already been implemented?
self_contained_problem:
Bootstrap Algebraic Multigrid (BAMG) is an iterative linear-solver framework for large sparse linear systems $A x = b$, where $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ is a sparse matrix, that constructs a multilevel hierarchy of coarse spaces adaptively. Starting from an initial set of test vectors (typically random vectors smoothed by a relaxation scheme such as Gauss–Seidel), BAMG iteratively improves a multigrid hierarchy — consisting of interpolation operators $P_\ell$, coarse operators $A_{\ell+1} = P_\ell^T A_\ell P_\ell$, and relaxation schemes — by using the current multigrid cycle itself as the smoothing/improvement mechanism for the test vectors, with the goal of producing a hierarchy whose two-grid and multigrid convergence factors are uniformly bounded below 1 independently of $n$. A solver is called "genuinely fast" if the cost of computing $x$ to fixed accuracy $\varepsilon$ is $O(\mathrm{nnz}(A)\,|\log\varepsilon|)$ with constants independent of problem size and parameters.

BAMG and closely related adaptive AMG methods have been demonstrated to be genuinely fast solvers on several challenging non-elliptic problem classes, including certain Markov chain (stochastic) matrices, lattice gauge theory Dirac operators (e.g., Wilson and staggered Dirac systems in QCD), and graph Laplacians arising from anisotropic or unstructured discretizations.

Problem. Determine the maximal class $\mathcal{C}$ of sparse matrices $A$ for which a Bootstrap Algebraic Multigrid–type method can be designed that is a genuinely fast solver in the sense above. In particular:

(a) Identify structural or spectral conditions on a sparse matrix $A$ (beyond ellipticity, definiteness, or M-matrix structure) that are sufficient to guarantee the existence of a BAMG hierarchy with mesh-independent convergence.

(b) Either construct a BAMG-type algorithm that is provably a genuinely fast solver for arbitrary nonsingular sparse linear systems, or exhibit a class of sparse matrices for which no BAMG-type construction (interpolation built from adaptively smoothed test vectors plus standard relaxation and Galerkin coarsening) can yield mesh-independent convergence.
status_search_result: No web search evidence indicates that this broad question — characterizing the full extent to which Bootstrap AMG can serve as a fast solver for general sparse matrix equations — has been resolved. It is posed as a long-term research direction, and subsequent literature on BAMG and adaptive AMG (for QCD, Markov chains, graph Laplacians, etc.) continues to extend the methodology problem-class by problem-class without a general characterization, so the question remains open.

paper_title: Bootstrap Algebraic Multigrid: status report, open problems, and outlook
original_question: When least-squares interpolation is built from a finite set of relaxed test vectors, how should one use randomized methods or range-approximation techniques to sample the dominant part of the error space that is not significantly reduced by the smoother, so that the sampled space yields reliably effective interpolation?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ be a large sparse symmetric positive (semi)definite matrix and let $S: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ denote a fixed smoother (relaxation operator) for $A$, with error-propagation operator $E = I - M^{-1}A$ for some $M$. The "algebraically smooth" error space associated with $S$ is the subspace $\mathcal{S} \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ of vectors $e$ for which the convergence factor $\|Ee\|_A / \|e\|_A$ is close to $1$, i.e. components not significantly reduced by the smoother.

For a chosen partition of the indices into a coarse set $C$ and a fine set $F = \{1,\dots,n\}\setminus C$, an interpolation operator $P:\mathbb{R}^{|C|} \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is defined row-by-row (for each $i\in F$) by a weighted least-squares problem
$$
P_{i,\cdot} = \arg\min_{w} \sum_{k=1}^{K} \omega_k\,\big(v_k(i) - \textstyle\sum_{j\in C_i} w_j\, v_k(j)\big)^2,
$$
where $\{v_1,\dots,v_K\}\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ is a finite collection of "test vectors" (each obtained by applying several relaxation sweeps with $S$ to a random initial vector on the homogeneous system $Ax=0$), $C_i\subset C$ is a prescribed set of interpolatory neighbors of $i$, and $\omega_k>0$ are weights.

Design a procedure based on randomized range-finding / randomized low-rank approximation (such as randomized SVD, subspace iteration, or related sketching techniques) that, given access to $A$ and to $S$, produces a finite test set $V=\{v_1,\dots,v_K\}$ whose span provably approximates the dominant part of $\mathcal{S}$ (the slow-to-converge eigen-directions of $E$) to a prescribed tolerance with high probability, with $K$ as small as possible. Establish quantitative bounds showing that the resulting least-squares interpolation operator $P$ satisfies a weak approximation property of the form
$$
\min_{x_c} \|e - P x_c\|_2^2 \le \kappa\, \|e\|_A^2 \qquad \forall\, e\in\mathbb{R}^n,
$$
with a constant $\kappa$ that is independent of $n$ and depends explicitly on the sample size $K$, the number of relaxation sweeps applied to form each $v_k$, and the spectral gap of $E$.
status_search_result: The question originates from a 2014 BAMG status-and-open-problems report which explicitly notes that "further studies of the LS process along these lines are still needed." Subsequent BAMG literature (e.g. least-angle regression coarsening, relaxation-corrected BAMG, BAMG for Wilson Dirac systems) continues to refine test-vector selection and least-squares interpolation but does not provide a definitive, quantitatively analyzed randomized range-approximation procedure for sampling the slow-to-converge error subspace with provable interpolation bounds. The problem appears still open.

paper_title: Distinct Distances: Open Problems and Current Bounds
original_question: Call a planar n-point set P near-optimal if it determines D(P)=O(n/sqrt(log n)) distinct distances. Characterize the near-optimal point sets.
self_contained_problem:
For a finite set $P\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ of $n$ points, let
$$D(P)=|\{\,\|p-q\|:p,q\in P,\ p\neq q\,\}|$$
denote the number of distinct (Euclidean) distances determined by $P$. By the Guth–Katz theorem, every $n$-point planar set satisfies $D(P)=\Omega(n/\log n)$, and the integer-lattice section $\{1,\dots,\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor\}^2$ achieves $D(P)=\Theta(n/\sqrt{\log n})$.

Call an $n$-point planar set $P$ near-optimal if $D(P)=O(n/\sqrt{\log n})$.

Problem. Give a characterization of all near-optimal planar point sets. In particular, decide whether every near-optimal set must have an underlying lattice structure (for example, whether every near-optimal set must contain, or be contained in, a suitably scaled and rotated portion of a lattice in $\mathbb{R}^2$ up to a small number of exceptional points).
status_search_result: The problem of characterizing near-optimal planar point sets (those with O(n/√log n) distinct distances), originally asked by Erdős with the suggestion that they "have lattice structure," remains open. While Guth–Katz (2015) settled the lower bound D(n) = Ω(n/log n), no characterization of extremal/near-optimal configurations is known; recent work explores new lattice-like constructions but does not provide a full characterization.

paper_title: Distinct Distances: Open Problems and Current Bounds
original_question: Let P be a near-optimal planar n-point set, meaning that D(P)=O(n/sqrt(log n)). Prove or disprove that for every epsilon>0, every constant-degree algebraic curve contains only O(n^(0.5+epsilon)) points of P.
self_contained_problem:
Let P be a set of n points in the Euclidean plane R^2, and let D(P) denote the number of distinct distances determined by pairs of points of P, i.e., D(P) = |{ ||p - q|| : p, q ∈ P, p ≠ q }|. Call P a near-optimal point set if D(P) = O(n / sqrt(log n)).

paper_title: Bootstrap Algebraic Multigrid: status report, open problems, and outlook
original_question: For indefinite or non-elliptic problems such as higher-dimensional Helmholtz and Schrödinger equations, how can one build a bootstrap algebraic multigrid method that uses several prolongation operators and multiple Galerkin coarse-grid operators, with the prolongation operators kept locally orthogonal, so that the many locally different low-eigenspace components are represented accurately at acceptable computational cost?
self_contained_problem:
Consider linear systems Au = f arising from discretizations of indefinite or non-elliptic partial differential equations on fine grids, in particular the higher-dimensional Helmholtz equation and the Schrödinger equation. In algebraic multigrid (AMG), one constructs a hierarchy of coarse problems via a prolongation operator P of small caliber (bounded number of nonzeros per row) and the Galerkin coarse-grid operator A_c = P^T A P. For the indefinite problems above, the low-eigenspace (near-kernel) of A is spanned by many oscillatory eigenfunctions whose local character varies across the domain, so that no single small-caliber prolongation P can interpolate all of them accurately on sufficiently fine scales.

Design a bootstrap algebraic multigrid (BAMG) method satisfying all of the following requirements:

1. On the fine scale and on every coarser scale, several prolongation operators P_1, …, P_k are employed simultaneously, yielding a multiple-Galerkin hierarchy with several coarse-grid operators A_c^{(j)} = P_j^T A P_j.
2. The set of prolongations {P_j} collectively represents, with provably small interpolation error, the locally varying low-eigenspace components of A.
3. The prolongation operators are kept locally orthogonal (their column supports are arranged so that, locally, the ranges of distinct P_j's are mutually orthogonal in an appropriate inner product), in order to control the growth of operator complexity across levels.
4. The total computational cost (setup plus solve) and storage scale optimally, i.e. linearly (up to logarithmic factors) in the number of fine-grid unknowns, uniformly in the wavenumber/energy parameters of the underlying indefinite problem.

Construct such a method and prove convergence and optimal complexity, or show that the simultaneous requirements (1)–(4) cannot be met.

Comput. paper "Toward an Algebraic Multigrid Method for the Indefinite Helmholtz Equation" and 2023 arXiv preprints on stand-alone multigrid for Helmholtz) shows that designing AMG/BAMG methods for indefinite Helmholtz/Schrödinger problems remains an active research area. Multiple-coarse-space and wave-ray approaches partially address near-kernel approximation, but a fully satisfactory BAMG with multiple locally orthogonal prolongations of small caliber and provable optimal cost for higher-dimensional indefinite problems has not been established.

paper_title: Distinct Distances: Open Problems and Current Bounds
context_brief: Difference sets from Cartesian products with few distances
original_question: For a finite set A subset R, determine the asymptotic order of the difference-set size |A-A| under the assumption that the Cartesian product A x A spans few distinct Euclidean distances.
self_contained_problem:
Let $A \subset \mathbb{R}$ be a finite set. The Cartesian product $A \times A \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ is regarded as a planar point set, and let
$$D(A \times A) = \big|\{\, \|p-q\| : p,q \in A\times A,\ p\neq q \,\}\big|$$
denote the number of distinct Euclidean distances determined by $A \times A$. Define the difference set
$$A - A = \{\, a - a' : a, a' \in A\,\}.$$
The known general bound (due to Pohoata) states that
$$|A - A| = O\!\left( D(A\times A)^{6/7} \log^{1/7} |A| \right).$$
In particular, if $A\times A$ spans only the minimum possible $\Theta(|A|^2/\sqrt{\log |A|})$ distinct distances, this gives $|A-A| = O(|A|^{12/7}\log^{c}|A|)$ for some constant $c$.

Determine the asymptotic order of $|A - A|$ under the assumption that $A \times A$ spans few distinct distances. More precisely: find the best possible exponent $\alpha$ such that, whenever $D(A\times A) = O(|A|^2/\sqrt{\log |A|})$, one has $|A - A| = |A|^{\alpha + o(1)}$, together with matching upper and lower bounds (constructions).
status_search_result: The current best published bound, $|A-A| = O(D(A\times A)^{6/7}\log^{1/7}|A|)$, is due to Pohoata (Electronic Journal of Combinatorics, 2019), improving earlier work of Hanson and Roche-Newton. No matching lower bound or asymptotically tight result has been reported, and the problem of determining the true asymptotic order of $|A-A|$ when $A\times A$ spans few distinct distances appears to remain open as of 2026.
