paper_title: What Regulates Galaxy Evolution? Open Questions in our Understanding of Galaxy Formation and Evolution.
context_brief: Model extensions for upcoming galaxy-evolution data
original_question: How should next-generation galaxy-formation models be extended to exploit upcoming resolved spectroscopy, atomic hydrogen, and molecular-gas observations, including explicit treatment of the transition from atomic to molecular gas, possible modeling of spatially resolved physical properties, and detailed chemical evolution with abundance ratios as constraints?
self_contained_problem:
Consider theoretical models of galaxy formation and evolution (e.g., semi-analytic models and hydrodynamical simulations) that track the assembly history of galaxies inside dark-matter halos, the cooling of gas, star formation, stellar feedback, and the production and recycling of metals. Existing implementations typically parametrize star formation in terms of total cold gas, treat galaxies as one-zone systems, and follow only bulk metallicity.

Develop a framework that extends such models so that they can be quantitatively confronted with upcoming observational datasets that provide (i) spatially resolved optical/IR spectroscopy of galaxies (resolved kinematics, ages, and metallicities on sub-galactic scales), (ii) resolved measurements of atomic hydrogen (HI) and molecular gas (H2/CO) content. Specifically, address the following:

1. Atomic-to-molecular transition. Formulate an explicit prescription, derivable from the local interstellar medium properties (gas surface density, metallicity, radiation field, dust shielding), that partitions cold gas into atomic and molecular components in each modeled resolution element, and tie the star-formation rate to the molecular component. Demonstrate that the prescription reproduces simultaneously the observed HI and H2 mass functions, the H2/HI ratio as a function of stellar mass, and the Kennicutt–Schmidt relation across redshift.

2. Spatially resolved galaxy properties. Extend galaxy models from one-zone descriptions to spatially resolved (e.g., axisymmetric multi-ring or full 3D) descriptions, evolving radial profiles of gas surface density, stellar mass, star-formation rate, and metallicity. Identify the minimal set of physical ingredients (gas inflow with prescribed angular momentum, radial transport, feedback-driven outflows, satellite accretion) needed to reproduce, jointly, observed radial profiles of stellar age, metallicity, and star-formation rate in galaxies of different masses and morphologies.

3. Detailed chemical evolution. Replace single-metallicity tracking with explicit, time-resolved nucleosynthetic yields for individual elements (at minimum H, He, C, N, O, Mg, Si, Fe), incorporating delay-time distributions for Type Ia supernovae, mass- and metallicity-dependent yields from core-collapse supernovae and AGB stars, and the impact of finite stellar lifetimes (no instantaneous-recycling approximation). Use abundance-ratio diagnostics (e.g., [α/Fe] vs. [Fe/H], [N/O] vs. [O/H]) of stars and gas as primary constraints, and quantify the resulting constraints on star-formation timescales, IMF, and feedback efficiencies.

Provide such an integrated extension and demonstrate, through comparison with current and forthcoming resolved spectroscopic surveys and HI/H2 surveys, that it yields a self-consistent description of galaxy evolution under these combined constraints.
status_search_result: This is a broad research-program question about extending galaxy-evolution models with explicit H I↔H2 chemistry, spatially resolved descriptions, and detailed chemical evolution. While substantial progress has been made on each individual ingredient (H2-based star-formation laws in semi-analytic and hydrodynamic models, resolved SAMs, and chemical-evolution post-processing), no single framework simultaneously and fully satisfies all three desiderata as primary constraints. The overall program remains an active, open research direction.

paper_title: On open problems in polling systems
context_brief: Renewal-arrival polling systems with large deterministic switch-over times
original_question: Consider a cyclic polling system with finitely many queues, deterministic switch-over times between successive queues, and general renewal arrival processes at the queues. The source conjectures that, when the deterministic switch-over times tend to infinity, the polling system converges to a deterministic cyclic system. Provide a rigorous proof of that conjecture.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a cyclic polling system defined as follows. There are $N\ge 2$ queues $Q_1,\dots,Q_N$ served by a single server that visits them in the fixed cyclic order $Q_1\to Q_2\to\cdots\to Q_N\to Q_1$. Customers arrive at queue $Q_i$ according to an independent renewal process with i.i.d. interarrival times of finite mean $1/\lambda_i$, and require i.i.d. service times with finite mean $1/\mu_i$; assume the system is stable, i.e. $\rho:=\sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i/\mu_i<1$. Between leaving $Q_i$ and starting service at $Q_{i+1}$ the server incurs a deterministic switch-over time $s_i\ge 0$. Fix a service discipline at each queue (for instance exhaustive or gated). Let $S=\sum_{i=1}^N s_i$ denote the total switch-over time per cycle, and consider scaling all $s_i$ proportionally so that $S\to\infty$.

Prove rigorously that, in this large-switch-over limit, the polling system converges (in an appropriate distributional/sample-path sense to be specified) to a deterministic cyclic system: that is, the cycle times, the visit instants, and the queue-length and workload processes (suitably normalized) converge to those of a deterministic periodic system in which each queue is served for a deterministic amount of time per cycle determined by $\lambda_i$, $\mu_i$, and $s_i$.
status_search_result: Web search did not surface a published rigorous proof of the conjectured convergence of a cyclic polling system with general renewal arrivals to a deterministic cyclic system as the deterministic switch-over times tend to infinity. Related work establishes heavy-traffic results and periodicity in transient regimes, and proofs exist for special cases (e.g. N=2), but the general renewal-arrival statement appears to remain a conjecture.

paper_title: What Regulates Galaxy Evolution? Open Questions in our Understanding of Galaxy Formation and Evolution.
context_brief: Age uncertainties in low-mass star formation histories
original_question: How should age uncertainties in low-mass galaxies be understood and reduced so that star formation histories inferred from spectral energy distribution fitting, main sequence integration, and color-magnitude diagrams can be reconciled, especially when color-magnitude-diagram estimates suggest dwarf galaxies formed large fractions of their stars at redshifts greater than one?
self_contained_problem:
Consider three independent methods used to infer the star formation history (SFH) of a low-mass galaxy (stellar mass roughly $10^7$–$10^9 \, M_\odot$):

1. Spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting, in which a galaxy's broadband photometry is fit by stellar population synthesis models that yield a parametric or non-parametric SFH and a mean stellar age.
2. Main-sequence integration, in which the observed star-formation-rate vs. stellar-mass relation at successive redshifts is integrated backward in time to reconstruct the cumulative stellar mass growth of a galaxy of given present-day mass.
3. Color–magnitude diagram (CMD) analysis of resolved stellar populations, in which the distribution of stars in the CMD is decomposed into coeval stellar populations to recover the cumulative fraction of stellar mass formed as a function of lookback time.

Empirically, for dwarf galaxies the CMD method indicates that a large fraction of the stellar mass was formed at redshifts $z > 1$, while extrapolations of SED-fitting and main-sequence-integration methods yield substantially younger mean ages and later assembly times.

Quantify and reconcile this discrepancy. Specifically:
(a) Identify the dominant sources of systematic age uncertainty in each of the three methods (e.g., age–metallicity–dust degeneracies in SED fitting, scatter and selection effects in the main sequence, isochrone and IMF assumptions in CMD fitting).
(b) Determine how these uncertainties propagate to the inferred cumulative SFH at lookback times corresponding to $z>1$.
(c) Propose a methodological framework (data, priors, modeling choices) under which the three SFH estimators become statistically consistent for galaxies in this mass range.
status_search_result: This is a domain-level open question in extragalactic astrophysics about reconciling SFH estimators for low-mass galaxies. Subsequent literature (e.g., works on non-parametric SED fitting such as Prospector by Leja et al., and CMD-based SFH studies by Weisz et al.) has narrowed but not eliminated the discrepancy: non-parametric SED priors yield older ages closer to CMD results, but full reconciliation across mass and redshift remains unresolved. The problem therefore appears still open / partially addressed.

paper_title: What Regulates Galaxy Evolution? Open Questions in our Understanding of Galaxy Formation and Evolution.
context_brief: Information loss in Local-Group-like central-satellite assignments
original_question: For galaxy systems like the Local Group, where the Milky Way and M31 each have their own satellite populations but may be assigned to a single halo by group-finding algorithms, what physical information is lost by forcing the system into a single central-satellite hierarchy, how can that lost information be measured, and which lost information matters most for understanding galaxy evolution?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a galaxy system analogous to the Local Group, in which two comparably massive galaxies (call them G1 and G2, playing the roles of the Milky Way and M31) each host their own bound population of smaller satellite galaxies, while G1 and G2 are themselves gravitationally interacting and will eventually merge. Suppose a group-finding algorithm enforces a strict single central / satellite hierarchy on this system, designating exactly one of {G1, G2} as the unique central halo and reclassifying the other together with all its satellites as satellites of that central.

(a) Provide a quantitative characterization of the physical and statistical information about the system that is destroyed by such a forced single-central assignment, relative to the true two-center hierarchy. Examples of information potentially lost include: the multiplicity and mass function of distinct host halos, the kinematic association of each satellite with its true host, the merger history and future dynamical evolution of the subsystems, the radial profiles and quenching environments experienced by satellites, and the conditional luminosity / stellar mass functions of secondary hosts.

(b) Define one or more measurable indicators (e.g. information-theoretic divergences between the true and assigned satellite-host probability distributions, or differences in summary statistics such as satellite kinematics, quenched fractions, and host stellar-mass functions) by which this lost information can be quantified for an ensemble of Local-Group-like systems drawn from a cosmological simulation or mock catalog.

(c) Determine which components of the lost information are the most consequential for inferring the physics of galaxy evolution (star formation histories, quenching, environmental processing, satellite accretion histories) in Local-Group-like systems, and quantify their impact.

The problem is best classified as open.

paper_title: What Regulates Galaxy Evolution? Open Questions in our Understanding of Galaxy Formation and Evolution.
original_question: What causes galaxy conformity, the observation that satellites appear to correlate with the star formation properties of their central galaxy, such that star-forming central galaxies have a higher fraction of late-type satellites than halos with early-type central galaxies?
self_contained_problem:
In the standard cosmological framework, dark matter halos host a single "central" galaxy at their center together with a population of "satellite" galaxies. Galaxies are commonly classified by their star formation properties (e.g., star-forming vs. quiescent, or late-type vs. early-type morphology). Empirically, one observes the phenomenon known as galaxy conformity: at fixed halo mass, halos whose central galaxy is star-forming (late-type) host a significantly higher fraction of late-type, star-forming satellites than halos whose central galaxy is quiescent (early-type). This correlation has been reported both within single halos (one-halo conformity, on scales comparable to the virial radius) and between neighboring halos (two-halo conformity, extending well beyond the virial radius, in some cases out to several Mpc).

Identify and characterize the physical mechanism (or combination of mechanisms) responsible for galaxy conformity. Specifically, determine why the star-formation state of a central galaxy correlates with the star-formation states of its satellite galaxies and of galaxies in neighboring halos, including the dependence of this effect on halo mass, central stellar mass, environment, and spatial scale, and decide to what extent conformity reflects (i) correlated assembly histories of dark matter halos ("assembly bias"), (ii) large-scale environmental pre-heating or other intergalactic-medium effects, (iii) baryonic feedback processes coupling centrals to their surroundings, or (iv) systematic effects in the identification of central galaxies.
status_search_result: The origin of galaxy conformity remains an active area of research without a definitive consensus. Proposed explanations include halo assembly bias, large-scale pre-heating of intergalactic gas (especially for low-mass, gas-poor centrals), and feedback processes operating near the virial scale, while some studies have argued that two-halo conformity signals are partly contaminated by central/satellite misclassification. No single mechanism has been broadly accepted as fully explaining the observed effect across all mass and scale regimes.

paper_title: What Regulates Galaxy Evolution? Open Questions in our Understanding of Galaxy Formation and Evolution.
original_question: For galaxy groups, which are likely the most common environments experienced by galaxies, how important are different environmental processes such as ram-pressure stripping, tidal effects, and evolution of gaseous components at typical group velocity dispersions, and to what degree do shortcomings in modeling these processes explain problems with satellite galaxy evolution?
self_contained_problem:
Galaxy groups are gravitationally bound associations of galaxies whose typical one-dimensional velocity dispersions lie roughly in the range 100–500 km/s, intermediate between isolated field galaxies and massive clusters; they are believed to be the most common environment in which galaxies reside. Several physical processes are thought to transform satellite galaxies inside such groups, including: (i) ram-pressure stripping, the removal of a galaxy's interstellar gas by the hydrodynamic pressure of the surrounding hot intragroup medium as the galaxy moves through it; (ii) tidal effects, the gravitational stripping and heating of a satellite's stars, gas, and dark matter by the host group potential and by encounters with other group members; and (iii) the dynamical evolution of the gaseous components of satellites, including starvation/strangulation through removal of an extended hot gas reservoir, turbulent viscous stripping, and thermal evaporation. paper_title: Some open questions in hydrodynamics
original_question: How can one define the most plausible initial conditions at the beginning of the hydrodynamic stage in a relativistic heavy-ion collision? The issue is to specify the initial relativistic-fluid state at the start of stage (ii), even though the experimentally observed hadrons are produced only much later and the earlier state cannot be measured directly.
self_contained_problem:
In the standard multi-stage description of an ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collision, the evolution of the produced matter is decomposed into successive stages: (i) a pre-equilibrium stage immediately following the collision of the two highly Lorentz-contracted nuclei, in which the produced partonic system is far from local thermal equilibrium; (ii) a relativistic hydrodynamic stage, during which the matter is modeled as a relativistic fluid governed by the conservation laws ∂_μ T^{μν} = 0 (and conserved-charge currents ∂_μ J^μ = 0) supplemented by an equation of state and, in viscous hydrodynamics, by constitutive/relaxation equations for dissipative currents; (iii) a hadronic freeze-out stage, in which the fluid converts to free-streaming hadrons that are eventually detected.

To run the hydrodynamic stage (ii) one must prescribe, on some initial Cauchy hypersurface Σ_0 (typically a constant proper-time surface τ = τ_0), the full set of fluid fields: the energy density ε(x), the flow four-velocity u^μ(x) (with u^μ u_μ = 1), any conserved-charge densities, and—if dissipative hydrodynamics is used—the initial values of the shear-stress tensor π^{μν}(x), bulk viscous pressure Π(x), and any diffusion currents. Direct experimental access to these fields is impossible: only the asymptotic hadrons produced after stage (iii) are measured.

Problem. Provide a principled, predictive prescription that determines, from the properties of the two incoming nuclei and the collision kinematics alone, the most plausible initial data {ε(x), u^μ(x), π^{μν}(x), Π(x), …} on the hypersurface Σ_0 at which relativistic hydrodynamics begins. The prescription should specify the initialization time τ_0, the spatial profiles of all required fluid fields, and their dissipative components, in a way that is consistent with the underlying microscopic (quantum chromodynamic) dynamics of the pre-equilibrium stage and that yields, after hydrodynamic evolution and freeze-out, agreement with the measured hadronic observables.
status_search_result: Recent reviews of relativistic hydrodynamics in heavy-ion collisions (e.g., Jaiswal–Roy 2016 and subsequent literature) explicitly identify the specification of initial conditions for the hydrodynamic stage as a major source of uncertainty, with several competing models (Glauber, KLN, IP-Glasma, EKRT, dynamical initialization schemes) but no first-principles consensus. The pre-equilibrium dynamics linking the collision to a thermalized fluid state is still not fully understood, so the problem remains open.

original_question: In relativistic heavy-ion collisions, can the pre-hydrodynamic stage create the condition needed for relativistic hydrodynamics to apply at the later hydrodynamic stage, namely local thermodynamic equilibrium in which the mean free path λmfp of the elementary constituents is much smaller than a characteristic system size L? Consider a relativistic heavy-ion collision modeled as a multi-stage process: (i) a pre-hydrodynamic stage immediately after the collision, during which the produced matter is generally far from equilibrium, followed by (ii) a hydrodynamic stage in which the evolution of the medium is described by relativistic fluid dynamics. The applicability of relativistic hydrodynamics requires the existence of local thermodynamic equilibrium, which in kinetic terms demands that the mean free path λ_mfp of the elementary constituents (quarks and gluons, or hadrons) be much smaller than a characteristic spatial scale L of the system, i.e. λ_mfp ≪ L (the Knudsen number Kn = λ_mfp/L is small).

paper_title: Some open questions in hydrodynamics
context_brief: Recovering collision geometry from final observables
original_question: To what extent do the experimental observables measured after hadron formation in relativistic heavy-ion collisions mainly reflect the geometry of the collision, and how can that collision geometry be inferred from those final-state hadronic observables? Consider a relativistic heavy-ion collision modeled as a relativistic fluid. Assume that at an initial proper time $t_0$ the system is specified by initial conditions consisting of: (a) the three spatial components of a fluid velocity field $u^i(\mathbf{x}, t_0)$, (b) an energy density $\varepsilon(\mathbf{x}, t_0)$, and (c) an entropy density $s(\mathbf{x}, t_0)$, all defined on a spatial slice. The subsequent dynamics is governed by the relativistic hydrodynamic equations $\partial_\mu T^{\mu\nu} = 0$ together with a prescribed equation of state $p = p(\varepsilon, s)$, evolved until a freeze-out hypersurface on which the fluid is converted into hadrons whose momenta and yields constitute the final-state observables (e.g. single-particle spectra and azimuthal Fourier coefficients $v_n$).

1. To what extent are the final-state hadronic observables determined predominantly by the geometric component of the initial conditions, as opposed to the non-geometric components, after the full hydrodynamic evolution and freeze-out?

2. Provide an explicit reconstruction map (or prove an inversion theorem) that, given the final-state hadronic observables on the freeze-out hypersurface, recovers the geometric component of the initial conditions at time $t_0$, and characterize its stability and uniqueness.

Consider a spacetime modeled by a 4-dimensional smooth manifold M endowed with a Lorentzian metric g of signature (-,+,+,+) and an affine connection Γ on the tangent bundle TM. Two formulations of a gravitational theory on (M, g, Γ) are distinguished:

(i) Purely metric formulation: Γ is identified a priori with the Levi-Civita connection of g, i.e. the unique torsion-free connection satisfying ∇g = 0. The dynamical variable is g alone.

(ii) Palatini (metric-affine) formulation: g and Γ are treated as independent dynamical variables, with Γ a general (possibly non-metric, possibly with torsion) affine connection that need not coincide with the Levi-Civita connection of g. The relation between Γ and g is then a consequence of the field equations rather than an a priori identification.

The Einstein Equivalence Principle (EEP) asserts that (a) the trajectory of a freely falling structureless test body is independent of its internal composition (Weak Equivalence Principle / Universality of Free Fall), (b) the outcome of any local non-gravitational experiment is independent of the velocity of the freely falling reference frame in which it is performed (Local Lorentz Invariance), and (c) the outcome of any local non-gravitational experiment is independent of where and when in the universe it is performed (Local Position Invariance).

Question: Determine whether arbitrarily precise experimental tests of the Einstein Equivalence Principle can, in principle, discriminate between formulations (i) and (ii). Concretely, identify observable signatures (in the dynamics of test particles, in atomic-clock comparisons, or in other local non-gravitational experiments) by which a non-Levi-Civita independent connection Γ in formulation (ii) would produce deviations from the EEP that are absent in formulation (i), and quantify the precision required to detect or rule out such deviations; or, alternatively, prove that no EEP-based experiment can distinguish the two formulations.
status_search_result: The question of whether Equivalence Principle tests can distinguish purely metric gravity from Palatini/metric-affine formulations remains an open conceptual and experimental problem. Ongoing and proposed EP tests (e.g., MICROSCOPE, STEP, atom-interferometry experiments) continue to push precision, and theoretical work on metric-affine and Palatini f(R) gravity continues without a definitive verdict; no proof of equivalence or experimental discrimination has been established.

paper_title: OPEN PROBLEMS IN GRAVITATIONAL PHYSICS
context_brief: Physical meaning of Jordan and Einstein frames
original_question: When modified gravitational dynamics are written in the Jordan frame, where Einstein field equations are modified and matter fields are minimally coupled to gravity, or in the Einstein frame, where Einstein field equations are preserved and matter fields are non-minimally coupled, does passing from one conformal frame to the other have genuine physical significance?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a modified theory of gravity formulated on a four-dimensional spacetime (M, g) with a scalar degree of freedom φ that couples to gravity. Two equivalent mathematical formulations of such a theory can be obtained by a conformal rescaling of the metric, g̃_{μν} = Ω²(φ) g_{μν}:

(a) The Jordan frame, in which the Einstein field equations are modified (the gravitational Lagrangian contains a non-trivial coupling, e.g. f(φ) R, or a function f(R) of the Ricci scalar) and matter fields are minimally coupled to the metric g_{μν}.

(b) The Einstein frame, obtained by the conformal transformation above (with a suitable redefinition of φ), in which the gravitational sector takes the standard Einstein–Hilbert form R̃ and matter fields acquire a non-minimal coupling to the rescaled metric g̃_{μν} through φ-dependent factors.

The two frames are related by a field redefinition (a conformal transformation of the metric together with a rescaling of the scalar) and are therefore mathematically equivalent at the level of the action.

Question: Determine whether the choice of conformal frame (Jordan vs. Einstein) carries genuine physical significance. Specifically, is there an observable or operationally well-defined physical quantity — at the classical level, at the semiclassical level, or at the quantum level — that distinguishes predictions made in the Jordan frame from those made in the Einstein frame, or are the two frames physically equivalent in every operational sense (so that the passage between them is merely a change of variables)?
status_search_result: The physical equivalence (or non-equivalence) of the Jordan and Einstein conformal frames remains an actively debated open problem. Recent works argue for classical/canonical equivalence on a reduced phase space, while others present arguments for non-equivalence at the quantum level (e.g., differences detectable via entanglement, or via differential matter couplings). No consensus has been reached.

paper_title: Recent results and open questions on collective type phenomena from A-A to pp collisions
context_brief: laboratory access to QCD matter states
original_question: To what extent can strongly interacting QCD matter states resembling (i) high-temperature matter with negligible baryon chemical potential, as in the early universe, or (ii) low-temperature QCD matter, as may exist in neutron-star cores, be produced and studied in terrestrial laboratories through relativistic or ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions?
self_contained_problem:
Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) predicts that strongly interacting matter, composed of quarks and gluons, can exist in distinct thermodynamic phases parameterized by temperature T and baryon chemical potential μ_B. Two physically motivated regions of the (T, μ_B) phase diagram are: (i) the high-temperature, near-zero baryon chemical potential regime (T large, μ_B ≈ 0), believed to describe the matter present a few microseconds after the Big Bang; and (ii) the low-temperature, high baryon chemical potential regime (T small, μ_B large), believed to describe the matter in the cores of neutron stars.

Relativistic and ultra-relativistic collisions of heavy nuclei produce transient regions of strongly interacting matter at high energy densities and temperatures. Determine to what extent QCD matter states corresponding to regimes (i) and (ii) above can actually be created, controlled, and quantitatively characterized in terrestrial heavy-ion collision experiments. In particular, identify what observable signatures (collective flow, thermal radiation, particle yields, fluctuations, jet modification, etc.) and what range of collision energies and system sizes give experimental access to these regimes, and clarify which thermodynamic and transport properties of QCD matter near regime (i) and regime (ii) can be inferred from such measurements.
status_search_result: This is a broad foundational question of relativistic heavy-ion physics rather than a specific theorem to be solved. While substantial progress has been made on regime (i) (high-T, μ_B≈0) at RHIC and LHC, including measurements of the quark-gluon plasma's transport properties, the high-μ_B/low-T regime relevant to neutron star cores remains a major open frontier targeted by ongoing and planned programs (RHIC Beam Energy Scan II, NICA, FAIR/CBM, J-PARC-HI). The question is therefore best characterized as still open / partially explored.

paper_title: Recent results and open questions on collective type phenomena from A-A to pp collisions
context_brief: deconfinement and hydrodynamic expansion in high-multiplicity pp
original_question: In very high-energy proton-proton collisions with low impact parameter and high charged-particle multiplicity, do multiparton interactions and rescatterings transfer enough energy into a proton-sized volume to create a close-to-equilibrium deconfined initial state, allow thermalization despite the small system size, and produce a proton-sized fireball that expands hydrodynamically or collectively?
self_contained_problem:
Consider proton–proton collisions at very high center-of-mass energies (LHC-scale and beyond) restricted to events with low impact parameter and high charged-particle multiplicity. Model the partonic activity in such events as a superposition of multiparton interactions accompanied by subsequent rescatterings of the produced partons. Assume that the resulting deconfined-phase constituents have a mean free path of order λ ≈ 0.2–0.3 fm, and that the transverse extent of the interaction region is of order the proton radius R ≈ 0.8 fm, so that R/λ is only a few.

Determine whether the following three propositions hold simultaneously in this regime:

(a) The cumulative energy transferred by the multiparton interactions and rescatterings into a volume of proton size is sufficient to reach (or exceed) the QCD deconfinement energy density, producing a close-to-equilibrium deconfined initial state.

(b) Despite the smallness of the system (only a few mean free paths across), the constituents of this initial state thermalize on a timescale shorter than the system's lifetime.

(c) The thermalized, proton-sized fireball thereafter undergoes a hydrodynamic / collective expansion describable by relativistic fluid dynamics, with collective observables (radial flow, anisotropic flow harmonics, strangeness enhancement, etc.) analogous to those seen in heavy-ion collisions.

Provide a rigorous theoretical or phenomenological resolution of (a)–(c): either establish all three within a controlled framework, or identify which fail and characterize the regime of validity.
status_search_result: Recent reviews (2024–2025) report mounting experimental signatures of collective, QGP-like behavior in high-multiplicity pp collisions—long-range ridge correlations, strangeness enhancement, mass-ordered radial flow—and successful descriptions by hydrodynamic and hybrid models. However, a first-principles demonstration that thermalization is achieved in such a small system, and that a genuine deconfined fireball is formed rather than alternative non-thermal mechanisms (e.g., color reconnection, initial-state CGC correlations, string interactions), remains unsettled. The questions of whether MPI/rescatterings drive the system to local equilibrium and whether the expansion is truly hydrodynamic in pp are still actively debated.

original_question: What experimental and theoretical mechanism explains the multiplicity-dependent collective-type trends observed in proton-proton collisions at √s = 7 TeV, including the decrease of kinetic freeze-out temperature, the increase of average transverse expansion velocity, and identified-hadron transverse-momentum spectral changes that resemble trends seen in heavy-ion collisions?
self_contained_problem:
In inelastic proton–proton collisions at center-of-mass energy √s = 7 TeV, identify and justify the experimental and theoretical mechanism(s) responsible for the following multiplicity-dependent "collective-type" trends observed for identified charged hadrons (π, K, p, etc.):

1. The kinetic freeze-out temperature T_kin extracted from a simultaneous blast-wave fit to the transverse-momentum spectra of identified hadrons decreases as a function of charged-particle multiplicity.
2. The mean transverse radial-flow velocity ⟨β_T⟩ obtained from the same fit increases as a function of charged-particle multiplicity.
3. The transverse-momentum spectra of identified hadrons exhibit a mass-dependent hardening with increasing multiplicity, qualitatively reproducing the patterns observed in nucleus–nucleus collisions when plotted against centrality.

Specifically: provide a quantitative dynamical description (e.g., hydrodynamic evolution, multi-parton interactions with color reconnection, string percolation, or an alternative microscopic framework) that simultaneously accounts for the (T_kin, ⟨β_T⟩) anti-correlation and the identified-hadron spectral shape evolution observed in high-multiplicity pp events, and determine whether such a description requires the formation of a thermalized partonic medium analogous to that produced in heavy-ion collisions.
status_search_result: The origin of collective-like behavior in high-multiplicity pp collisions remains an active and unresolved research topic. paper_title: OPEN PROBLEMS IN GRAVITATIONAL PHYSICS
context_brief: Metric versus independent connection in gravitational theory
original_question: In a relativistic theory of gravitation on a four-dimensional spacetime manifold, where a Lorentzian metric g fixes the causal structure of spacetime and a linear connection Γ fixes free fall, must Γ necessarily be the Levi-Civita connection determined by g, or can Γ instead be an independent, more general connection constrained only a posteriori by physical restrictions such as compatibility with photon trajectories? Equivalently, can the geodesic structure and the causal structure of spacetime be genuinely disentangled rather than both being fixed by the same metric object?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a four-dimensional smooth spacetime manifold $M$ equipped with two a priori independent geometric structures:

(i) a Lorentzian metric $g$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, which determines the causal structure of $M$ (in particular, the null cones along which photons propagate); and

(ii) a torsion-free linear connection $\Gamma$ on $TM$, whose autoparallel curves are postulated to describe the worldlines of freely falling test particles (free fall).

Impose only the following physical compatibility requirement: photon worldlines, which are null geodesics of $g$, must also be (unparametrized) autoparallels of $\Gamma$, i.e. the null geodesics of $g$ coincide as point sets with null autoparallels of $\Gamma$.

Question: Does this compatibility requirement, together with the standard principles of a relativistic theory of gravitation, force $\Gamma$ to be the Levi-Civita connection of $g$? Equivalently, can one consistently formulate a relativistic theory of gravitation on $(M,g,\Gamma)$ in which $\Gamma$ is a genuinely independent connection (not equal to the Levi-Civita connection of $g$), so that the geodesic structure (free fall) and the causal structure (light propagation) of spacetime are physically disentangled?
status_search_result: Metric-affine and Palatini-type formulations of gravity, in which the connection is taken to be independent of the metric, remain an active area of theoretical research with ongoing observational and theoretical investigations. There is no consensus result forcing the connection to be Levi-Civita under only the photon-null-geodesic compatibility constraint, and the disentanglement of causal and geodesic structure continues to be explored in current literature.

original_question: Can a two-dimensional event-selection condition that combines charged-particle multiplicity with global event-shape observables such as Directivity, Sphericity, Thrust, or Fox-Wolfram moments reliably isolate soft, nearly azimuthally isotropic proton-proton events with specific azimuthal distributions at a given multiplicity?
self_contained_problem:
In high-energy proton-proton collisions, each event produces a set of charged particles whose transverse momenta $\vec{p}_{T,i}$ in the plane transverse to the beam axis can be measured. For an event with $N$ charged particles, define the following global event-shape observables:

(i) The transverse sphericity tensor $S^{xy}_{\alpha\beta} = \frac{\sum_i p_{T,i,\alpha}\,p_{T,i,\beta}}{\sum_i |\vec{p}_{T,i}|^2}$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq 0$, and the transverse sphericity $S_T = 2\lambda_2/(\lambda_1+\lambda_2) \in [0,1]$, where $S_T \to 1$ corresponds to azimuthal isotropy and $S_T \to 0$ corresponds to a pencil-like event.

(ii) The transverse thrust $T_\perp = \max_{\hat{n}_T} \frac{\sum_i |\vec{p}_{T,i}\cdot\hat{n}_T|}{\sum_i |\vec{p}_{T,i}|}$, maximized over unit vectors $\hat{n}_T$ in the transverse plane.

(iii) The Fox–Wolfram moments $H_\ell = \sum_{i,j} \frac{|\vec p_i||\vec p_j|}{E_{vis}^2}\, P_\ell(\cos\theta_{ij})$ for $\ell=0,1,2,\dots$, where $P_\ell$ are Legendre polynomials and $\theta_{ij}$ is the angle between particle momenta.

(iv) The directivity $D = \frac{|\sum_i \vec{p}_{T,i}|}{\sum_i |\vec{p}_{T,i}|} \in [0,1]$.

Let $N_{ch}$ denote the charged-particle multiplicity of an event. Consider applying a two-dimensional event-selection cut of the form $\{N_{ch}\geq N_{\min}\}\cap\{X \in I\}$, where $X$ is one of the above event-shape variables and $I$ is an interval chosen to enforce near azimuthal isotropy.

Question: Does there exist such a two-dimensional selection $(N_{ch},X)$ that, at any fixed value of $N_{ch}$, reliably isolates a sub-ensemble of events whose single-particle azimuthal distribution $dN/d\varphi$ is nearly uniform (soft, isotropic), as opposed to events dominated by hard back-to-back jet structures, given that the marginal distributions of $X$ remain broad even at the largest accessible multiplicities?
status_search_result: Subsequent experimental and phenomenological studies (e.g. ALICE measurements of transverse sphericity and the "spherocity" variable, and CMS/ATLAS event-shape analyses) have demonstrated that combining multiplicity with event-shape observables such as transverse sphericity or spherocity does separate jetty from isotropic pp events and reveals different particle-production properties. The procedure is feasible and is used in practice, though no single optimal observable has been identified as definitive; the broader question of fully isolating "soft isotropic" events at fixed multiplicity remains an active area of investigation.

paper_title: OPEN PROBLEMS IN GRAVITATIONAL PHYSICS
context_brief: Quantum-level status of the Equivalence Principle
original_question: Is the Equivalence Principle universally valid, or can it fail once gravity is considered together with quantum theory? In particular, if the Equivalence Principle holds at the classical level, can it nevertheless be violated at the quantum level, and is the principle consistent with Quantum Mechanics when one tries to connect gravitation with the other interactions?
self_contained_problem:
The Equivalence Principle (EP) asserts the local indistinguishability between the effects of a uniform gravitational field and those of a uniformly accelerated reference frame; equivalently, in its weak form, it states that the inertial mass and the gravitational (passive and active) mass of any test body coincide, so that the trajectories of freely falling bodies in a given gravitational field are independent of their internal composition and mass.

Address the following questions concerning the status of this principle when gravity is combined with quantum theory:

(a) Is the Equivalence Principle universally valid in nature, or can it fail in regimes where gravitational and quantum effects are simultaneously relevant?

(b) Suppose that the Equivalence Principle holds exactly at the classical level (i.e., for classical point particles and classical fields on a classical spacetime). Can it nevertheless be violated at the quantum level, for example through the dynamics of quantum test particles, quantum fields, or quantum superpositions of mass/energy states propagating in a gravitational background?

(c) Is the Equivalence Principle, formulated in a precise operational way, logically consistent with the principles of Quantum Mechanics (linearity, superposition, the standard formalism of observables and states) when one attempts to incorporate gravitation alongside the other fundamental interactions in a unified quantum framework?

Provide a definitive resolution of (a)–(c), either by exhibiting a consistent formulation of the Equivalence Principle compatible with Quantum Mechanics in a unified theory, or by identifying an unavoidable mechanism by which the principle must be violated at the quantum level.
status_search_result: The compatibility of the Equivalence Principle with Quantum Mechanics, and whether it is violated at the quantum level, remains an active and unresolved research topic. Recent works (2018–2023) propose general formalisms for a "quantum equivalence principle," argue for explicit mass-dependent quantum corrections incompatible with the weak EP, and note that candidate quantum-gravity theories (string theory, loop quantum gravity) generically predict EP violations at the 10^-13–10^-18 level. No consensus or definitive answer has been reached, and high-precision experimental tests are ongoing.

paper_title: Current Open Questions in Complete Mixability
original_question: Let n be a positive integer and let M_n(μ) denote the set of distributions on ℝ that are n-completely mixable with center μ. If a distribution F on ℝ or on ℝ^d is n-completely mixable, must its center be unique? Equivalently, for distinct μ, ν ∈ ℝ, is M_n(μ) ∩ M_n(ν) empty?
self_contained_problem:
Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. A probability distribution $F$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ is called $n$-completely mixable with center $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^d$ if there exist random vectors $X_1, \dots, X_n$, each with distribution $F$, such that
$$X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_n = n\mu \quad \text{almost surely}.$$
Let $\mathcal{M}_n(\mu)$ denote the set of all distributions on $\mathbb{R}^d$ that are $n$-completely mixable with center $\mu$.

Question: Is the center of complete mixability always unique? Equivalently, is it true that for every pair of distinct points $\mu, \nu \in \mathbb{R}^d$ with $\mu \ne \nu$, one has
$$\mathcal{M}_n(\mu) \cap \mathcal{M}_n(\nu) = \emptyset\,?$$
status_search_result: The question was resolved in the negative by Puccetti, Rigo, Wang and Wang ("Centers of probability measures without the mean", J. Theoret. Probab., 2019). They show that if a distribution has finite mean, its mixability center must equal that mean (so it is unique), but for heavy-tailed distributions without a finite mean (e.g., Cauchy) a whole interval of centers can be achieved. Explicitly, for $n \ge 2$ standard Cauchy random variables, the achievable constants $C$ form the interval $|C| \le n\log(n-1)/\pi$, so the center is not unique in general.

original_question: In the QCD phase diagram for strongly interacting matter, statistical-model fits to yield ratios identify a transitional point (T_H, μ_H) where the thermodynamic role of baryons surpasses that of mesons, located around μ_H = 350–400 MeV and T_H = 150–160 MeV. To what extent does this point correspond to a finite-number-of-colors (finite-N_c) triple point separating hadronic, deconfined, and quarkyonic regimes?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the phase diagram of strongly interacting matter parameterized by temperature $T$ and baryon chemical potential $\mu_B$. Statistical-thermal model fits to hadron yield ratios measured in heavy-ion collisions at various energies populate a chemical-freeze-out curve in the $(T,\mu_B)$ plane. Along this curve, for $\mu_B \ll M_N$ (the nucleon mass) the thermodynamic degrees of freedom are dominated by mesons, while for larger $\mu_B$ baryonic degrees of freedom dominate. Define $(T_H,\mu_H)$ as the transitional point on this freeze-out curve where the baryonic contribution to the thermodynamics surpasses the mesonic contribution; statistical-model fits place it in the region $\mu_H \in [350,400]$ MeV, $T_H \in [150,160]$ MeV.

Independently, large-$N_c$ analyses of QCD predict a phase structure with three distinct regions — a confined hadronic phase, a deconfined quark–gluon plasma phase, and a quarkyonic phase (in which the pressure scales as $p\sim N_c$, intermediate between $p\sim N_c^0$ for a hadron gas and $p\sim N_c^2$ for the QGP) — that meet at a triple point in the $(T,\mu_B)$ plane. Extending this picture to the physical case $N_c=3$ yields a conjectured finite-$N_c$ triple point.

Problem: Determine to what extent the statistically determined transitional point $(T_H,\mu_H)$ coincides with, or can be identified as, the finite-$N_c$ triple point separating the hadronic, deconfined, and quarkyonic regimes of QCD matter.
status_search_result: The identification of the meson/baryon transitional point on the chemical freeze-out curve with a finite-$N_c$ hadronic–deconfined–quarkyonic triple point remains a topic of active discussion. No definitive resolution is established.

paper_title: Current Open Questions in Complete Mixability
original_question: Theorem 3 states that a ℤ_+-valued random vector X is a joint mix with joint center N if and only if it can be written as X = ∑_{k=1}^N X_k, where each X_k is a binary multinomial random vector. Can this decomposition be used in a nontrivial way to characterize additional classes of completely mixable or jointly mixable distributions, and if so how?
self_contained_problem:
A random vector $X = (X^{(1)}, \dots, X^{(d)})$ taking values in $\mathbb{Z}_+^d$ is called a joint mix with joint center $N \in \mathbb{Z}_+$ if $X^{(1)} + X^{(2)} + \cdots + X^{(d)} = N$ almost surely. A binary multinomial random vector is a $\{0,1\}^d$-valued random vector whose components sum to $1$ almost surely (equivalently, exactly one coordinate equals $1$ with some probability distribution over the $d$ coordinates).

It is known that a $\mathbb{Z}_+^d$-valued random vector $X$ is a joint mix with joint center $N \in \mathbb{Z}_+$ if and only if it admits a representation
$$X = \sum_{k=1}^{N} X_k,$$
where $X_1, \dots, X_N$ are (not necessarily independent) binary multinomial random vectors.

A tuple of univariate marginal distributions $(F_1, \dots, F_d)$ is called jointly mixable (JM) if there exist random variables $Y_1 \sim F_1, \dots, Y_d \sim F_d$ on a common probability space such that $Y_1 + \cdots + Y_d$ is almost surely a constant; in the case $F_1 = \cdots = F_d = F$, $F$ is called completely mixable (CM).

Question: Can the binary-multinomial decomposition above be used in a nontrivial way to characterize new classes of completely mixable or jointly mixable distributions? More precisely, identify a class $\mathcal{C}$ of univariate distributions (or tuples thereof), not previously known to be CM (resp. JM), and use the decomposition $X = \sum_{k=1}^N X_k$ into binary multinomial random vectors to give necessary and/or sufficient conditions for membership of $\mathcal{C}$ in the CM (resp. JM) class.
status_search_result: A full characterization of completely mixable and jointly mixable distributions for $d \geq 3$ remains open in the probability literature. Necessary and sufficient conditions are known for restricted families (uniform, monotone-density, unimodal-symmetric, and elliptical distributions with common characteristic generator), but no general characterization leveraging the binary-multinomial decomposition for $\mathbb{Z}_+$-valued joint mixes has been published, and the question of whether this decomposition yields new CM/JM classes appears unresolved.

context_brief: reconstructing collision evolution from final observables
original_question: How can detailed information about the dynamics and properties of each stage after the initial phase of a relativistic heavy-ion collision be reconstructed from the final particles and electromagnetic radiation that reach detectors, given that even the heaviest colliding nuclei create a small, highly non-homogeneous system with violent dynamical evolution?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a relativistic heavy-ion collision in which two nuclei (possibly the heaviest available, e.g. Pb or Au) collide at ultra-relativistic energies, producing a small, spatially highly non-homogeneous, rapidly evolving strongly interacting system. After the initial impact the system passes through several stages (e.g. pre-equilibrium dynamics, a possibly thermalized quark–gluon plasma phase, hadronization, and a hadronic rescattering/freeze-out phase). The only experimentally accessible information consists of the momenta, identities, and correlations of the hadrons, leptons, and photons that reach detectors in the final state, together with electromagnetic radiation emitted during the evolution.

Develop a quantitative framework — including a set of final-state observables and an inversion procedure — that allows one to reconstruct, from these final-state particles and electromagnetic radiation alone, detailed information about the dynamics (equation of state, transport coefficients such as shear and bulk viscosity, thermalization time, expansion profile) and properties (temperature, energy density, chemical composition) of each successive stage of the post-initial evolution of the collision, while consistently accounting for the small system size, large initial-state spatial inhomogeneities and event-by-event fluctuations, and the strongly non-equilibrium dynamical character of the evolution.
status_search_result: The reconstruction of the full space-time evolution of heavy-ion collisions from final-state observables remains an active and open research program. Modern Bayesian analyses combining hydrodynamic + transport models with LHC and RHIC data (e.g., JETSCAPE, Trajectum) have produced posterior estimates of QGP transport coefficients but no closed-form inversion exists, and significant uncertainties remain about the pre-equilibrium stage, initial conditions, and small-system applicability.

original_question: If C is a convex subset of ℝ^d, is the uniform distribution on C necessarily n-completely mixable for every n ≥ d + 1?

paper_title: Recent results and open questions on collective type phenomena from A-A to pp collisions
context_brief: multiplicity and geometry across A-A, p-A, and pp
original_question: How should charged-particle multiplicity, impact parameter, and centrality be related and compared across nucleus-nucleus, proton-nucleus, and proton-proton collisions, given that A-A collisions allow relatively good impact-parameter selection, p-A collisions have a broad wounded-nucleon versus impact-parameter correlation, and direct multiplicity-based comparisons among pp, p-Pb, and Pb-Pb can be misleading?
self_contained_problem:
Consider high-energy hadronic collisions of three types: nucleus-nucleus (A-A), proton-nucleus (p-A), and proton-proton (pp). For each collision event, define the impact parameter b as the transverse distance between the centers of the incoming objects, the number of wounded nucleons N_part as the number of nucleons that undergo at least one inelastic interaction (computed in a Glauber Monte Carlo model), and the charged-particle multiplicity N_ch as the number of produced charged hadrons in a fixed pseudorapidity window. Centrality classes are defined as percentiles of the N_ch distribution. Assume that nucleon-nucleon charged-particle multiplicities follow a negative binomial distribution, and that A-A multiplicity distributions can be fitted by a Glauber-based ancestor model from which a relatively narrow correlation between b and N_ch is obtained.

(a) Provide a quantitative framework that relates b, N_part, and N_ch consistently across A-A, p-A, and pp collisions, characterizing the conditional distributions P(b | N_ch), P(N_part | b), and P(N_ch | N_part, b) for each system.

(b) In p-A collisions, quantify how broad the correlation between N_part and b is compared to A-A, and determine to what extent (and under which selection observables) a meaningful centrality / impact-parameter selection is possible.

(c) For pp collisions, where there is no direct experimental access to b, determine whether (and how) the dependence of observables on the nucleon-level impact parameter can be inferred from the dependence on N_ch, given that the geometry-multiplicity interplay is complex.

(d) Establish under what conditions a direct comparison of pp, p-Pb, and Pb-Pb observables at fixed N_ch (or fixed centrality percentile) is physically meaningful, and provide the appropriate rescaling or matching prescription that should replace naive multiplicity-based comparisons.
status_search_result: The question concerns an ongoing program in high-energy nuclear physics. Centrality determination in p-Pb is known to be ambiguous (ALICE has published methods using ZNA, V0A, and hybrid estimators), but a unified, model-independent framework relating b, N_part, and N_ch consistently across pp, p-Pb, and Pb-Pb remains an active research topic without a definitive resolution.

original_question: Is every absolutely continuous distribution supported on a bounded interval n-completely mixable once n is large enough?
self_contained_problem:
A random vector $(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ has marginal distributions all equal to a probability distribution $F$ on $\mathbb{R}$. The distribution $F$ is called $n$-completely mixable ($n$-CM) if there exists a random vector $(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ with each $X_i \sim F$ such that
$$P(X_1+X_2+\cdots+X_n = n\mu) = 1$$
for some constant $\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ (necessarily equal to the mean of $F$ when $F$ has finite mean). A distribution $F$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is absolutely continuous if it admits a density with respect to Lebesgue measure.

paper_title: Current Open Questions in Complete Mixability
original_question: What happens if the definition of mixability uses a multivariate function other than the sum x_1 + ⋯ + x_n? Which alternative multivariate functions lead to useful notions of mixability, and how should those notions be characterized?
self_contained_problem:
Background. A tuple of univariate distributions $F_1,\dots,F_n$ is called jointly mixable if there exist random variables $X_1,\dots,X_n$ defined on a common probability space such that $X_i\sim F_i$ for each $i$ and the sum $X_1+\cdots+X_n$ is almost surely equal to a constant. When $F_1=\cdots=F_n=F$, the distribution $F$ is called $n$-completely mixable.

Problem. Replace the additive aggregation function $S(x_1,\dots,x_n)=x_1+\cdots+x_n$ by a general measurable function $\Phi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ (or more generally $\Phi:\mathcal{X}^n\to\mathcal{Y}$ for a suitable measurable space). Say that distributions $F_1,\dots,F_n$ are $\Phi$-mixable if there exist random variables $X_i\sim F_i$ on a common probability space with $\Phi(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ almost surely constant.

(a) Identify the classes of functions $\Phi$ for which $\Phi$-mixability yields a non-trivial and useful theory (e.g., functions invariant under permutations of coordinates, continuous, monotone in each argument, or Schur-concave/convex aggregations such as $\max$, $\min$, products, $L^p$-norms, or quasi-arithmetic means $\phi^{-1}\!\big(\tfrac{1}{n}\sum\phi(x_i)\big)$).

(b) For such classes, give a characterization (necessary and sufficient conditions on $F_1,\dots,F_n$) for $\Phi$-mixability, generalizing known characterizations available for $\Phi=S$ (e.g., the mean condition and the variance/length conditions for monotone marginal densities).

(c) Determine the analogue of the "center" (the almost-sure constant value of $\Phi(X_1,\dots,X_n)$) and the set of admissible centers.
status_search_result: No general theory characterizing $\Phi$-mixability for arbitrary aggregation functions $\Phi$ replacing the sum appears in the literature. Some related generalizations exist (e.g., joint mixability with center, and unrelated "Φ-mixability" in online learning by Reid et al., 2015), but a systematic answer to which alternative multivariate aggregation functions yield a useful mixability theory and how to characterize them remains, to current knowledge, open.

paper_title: Current Open Questions in Complete Mixability
original_question: Suppose a distribution F satisfies a known sufficient condition for n-complete mixability, such as one of the conditions listed earlier in Section 2.2. Is there a way to simulate samples from an n-complete mix with margins F?
self_contained_problem:
Let $n \geq 2$ be an integer and let $F$ be a univariate cumulative distribution function on $\mathbb{R}$. Call $F$ $n$-completely mixable ($n$-CM) if there exist random variables $X_1, \dots, X_n$, each with marginal distribution $F$, such that
$$X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_n = c \quad \text{almost surely}$$
for some constant $c \in \mathbb{R}$. Any random vector $(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ with these properties is called an $n$-complete mix with margins $F$.

Several sufficient conditions for $n$-complete mixability are known; for example, any continuous distribution $F$ on a bounded interval whose density is symmetric and unimodal is $n$-CM for every $n \geq 2$, and any continuous distribution with a concave density on its support is $n$-CM for every $n \geq 3$.

Problem. Assume $F$ satisfies such a sufficient condition for $n$-complete mixability. Provide an explicit and implementable algorithm that, given $F$ and $n$ as input, generates exact samples from the joint distribution of an $n$-complete mix $(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ whose marginals are all equal to $F$ and whose components sum to a constant almost surely.
status_search_result: The problem of simulating samples from an n-complete mix with given margins F (under the standard sufficient conditions for n-complete mixability) appears in the open-problem list on complete mixability and no general-purpose simulation algorithm appears to have been published. Recent literature on complete mixability (e.g., detecting complete and joint mixability, advances in complete mixability) treats existence and characterization rather than exact simulation, suggesting the problem remains open.

paper_title: Recent results and open questions on collective type phenomena from A-A to pp collisions
original_question: At higher LHC proton-proton collision energy and with higher statistics, how can collective-type studies be extended to heavy-flavor hadrons and used for detailed comparisons with corresponding results from nucleus-nucleus collisions?
self_contained_problem:
In high-energy proton-proton (pp) collisions at the LHC, transverse momentum (p_T) distributions of identified light hadrons (π±, K±, p, p̄) at mid-rapidity (|y| < 0.5), measured in bins of charged-particle multiplicity, exhibit a progressive depletion of heavier species relative to lighter ones at low p_T as multiplicity increases. Simultaneous fits of these spectra with the Boltzmann–Gibbs Blast-Wave model — characterized by a kinetic freeze-out temperature T_kin, an average transverse expansion (radial flow) velocity ⟨β_T⟩, and a transverse-velocity profile exponent n — yield multiplicity-dependent parameters whose trends mimic those extracted in nucleus–nucleus (A–A) collisions, suggesting collective-type behavior in high-multiplicity pp events.

Formulate and carry out a quantitative program that extends such collective-type analyses to heavy-flavor hadrons (open-charm hadrons such as D⁰, D±, D_s, Λ_c and charmonia such as J/ψ, ψ(2S), as well as open-beauty states) in pp collisions at center-of-mass energies a factor of two beyond 7 TeV (i.e. around 13–14 TeV) with substantially higher integrated luminosity. Specifically:

(i) Measure the multiplicity-differential p_T spectra and yields of the above heavy-flavor hadrons at mid-rapidity in pp collisions, and fit them simultaneously (together with light-flavor spectra) with a Blast-Wave-type parameterization
   dN/(p_T dp_T) ∝ ∫₀^R r dr · m_T I₀(p_T sinh ρ / T_kin) K₁(m_T cosh ρ / T_kin),
   with ρ(r) = tanh⁻¹(β_T(r)) and β_T(r) = β_s (r/R)^n, extracting (T_kin, ⟨β_T⟩, n) and their evolution with charged-particle multiplicity.

(ii) Quantify whether heavy-flavor hadrons participate in the same collective transverse expansion as light hadrons in pp collisions, by comparing the heavy-flavor-inferred (T_kin, ⟨β_T⟩) with those obtained from light hadrons at matched multiplicities.

(iii) Perform a systematic comparison of the multiplicity-dependent heavy-flavor blast-wave parameters, nuclear-modification-type ratios, and azimuthal anisotropy coefficients (v_2, v_3) in pp collisions with the corresponding observables in A–A collisions at similar charged-particle multiplicities, and assess to what extent the apparent collectivity in small systems extends to the heavy-flavor sector.

The problem is to determine whether and how heavy-flavor production in high-multiplicity pp collisions exhibits collective behavior consistent with that observed in A–A collisions, within a unified Blast-Wave / hydrodynamic framework.
category_tag: heavy-flavor collective flow in pp collisions
status_search_result: Subsequent LHC measurements (ALICE, CMS, LHCb at 13 TeV) have reported multiplicity-dependent enhancement of D-meson and J/ψ production in pp collisions, and non-zero v_2 for D mesons in high-multiplicity pp/p–Pb events, indicating partial progress. However, a comprehensive Blast-Wave characterization of heavy-flavor collectivity in pp matched to A–A remains incomplete, and the microscopic origin (hydrodynamics vs. initial-state/MPI effects) is still debated. The broader question is therefore considered open with partial experimental progress.

original_question: Let D_n be the aggregation set of sums X_1 + ⋯ + X_n formed from random variables with prescribed marginal distributions F_1, …, F_n. What are necessary and sufficient conditions for D_n to contain a smallest element with respect to convex order?
self_contained_problem:
Let $F_1, \dots, F_n$ be probability distributions on $\mathbb{R}$ with finite means. Define the aggregation set
$$\mathcal{D}_n(F_1,\dots,F_n) = \{X_1 + \cdots + X_n : X_i \sim F_i \text{ for } i=1,\dots,n\},$$
where the $X_i$ are defined on a common (atomless) probability space and may have arbitrary joint distribution. For random variables $Y, Z$ with finite means, recall the convex order: $Y \leq_{cx} Z$ iff $\mathbb{E}[\varphi(Y)] \leq \mathbb{E}[\varphi(Z)]$ for every convex function $\varphi: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that the expectations exist. An element $S^* \in \mathcal{D}_n$ is called a smallest element with respect to convex order if $S^* \leq_{cx} S$ for every $S \in \mathcal{D}_n$.

Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the marginal distributions $F_1, \dots, F_n$ under which $\mathcal{D}_n(F_1, \dots, F_n)$ contains such a smallest element with respect to convex order.

Subsequent work (e.g., Jakobsons–Han–Wang on general convex order in risk aggregation) provides counterexamples showing such a smallest element need not exist and gives sufficient conditions (notably involving complete mixability), but a full necessary-and-sufficient characterization does not appear to have been established.

A univariate distribution function $F$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is said to be $n$-completely mixable ($n$-CM) if there exist random variables $X_1, \dots, X_n$, each with distribution $F$, such that
$$P\!\left(X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_n = n\mu\right) = 1$$
for some constant $\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ (called a center of $F$). More generally, an $n$-tuple of univariate distributions $(F_1, \dots, F_n)$ is said to be jointly mixable (JM) if there exist random variables $X_i \sim F_i$, $i = 1,\dots,n$, such that $X_1 + \cdots + X_n$ is almost surely constant.

The main known results characterizing complete and joint mixability — for example, that any distribution with a monotone density on a bounded interval and mean satisfying the obvious necessary condition is completely mixable, and the corresponding results for distributions with concave or unimodal-symmetric densities, and the analogous joint mixability theorems — have so far been established by arguments relying on combinatorial constructions, discretization of distributions into atomic distributions, and mathematical induction on the number of atoms.

Problem. Develop a generic probabilistic or analytic proof of the main complete-mixability and joint-mixability theorems that does not rely on combinatorics, discretization, or induction over discrete approximations. Equivalently, find a unified continuous (e.g., coupling-based, measure-theoretic, or functional-analytic) framework that yields these characterizations directly.
status_search_result: Subsequent literature on complete and joint mixability (e.g., works by Puccetti–Wang, Wang–Wang on joint mixability, and the 2017 paper on joint mixability of elliptical distributions) continues to rely on combinatorial/discretization/induction techniques or on specific structural properties (e.g., elliptical families). No source located provides a generic probabilistic or analytic proof of the main CM/JM theorems, so the problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Given positive numbers a_{i,j} representing the time taken by worker (i, j) to complete production step j, and using permutations σ_1, …, σ_n ∈ S_m to assign one worker from each step to each of m equipments, minimize max_{i=1,…,m} ∑_{j=1}^n a_{σ_j(i),j}. What assignment of workers is optimal, and how can an optimal assignment be computed?
self_contained_problem:
Let m, n be positive integers and let (a_{i,j})_{1 ≤ i ≤ m, 1 ≤ j ≤ n} be a given matrix of positive real numbers. Interpret a_{i,j} as the time taken by worker i to perform production step j; there are m workers available for each of the n steps. An assignment is a tuple (σ_1, …, σ_n) of permutations σ_j ∈ S_m, where σ_j(i) denotes which worker is assigned to step j on equipment i. The total time spent on equipment i is

  T_i(σ_1, …, σ_n) = ∑_{j=1}^n a_{σ_j(i), j},

and the makespan of the assignment is

  M(σ_1, …, σ_n) = max_{1 ≤ i ≤ m} T_i(σ_1, …, σ_n).

Problems:
(a) Characterize the assignments (σ_1*, …, σ_n*) ∈ (S_m)^n that minimize M(σ_1, …, σ_n).
(b) Provide an algorithm that computes such an optimal arrangement (σ_1*, …, σ_n*) for given input (a_{i,j}).

In particular, identify structural properties of optimal arrangements (e.g., relation to "completely mixable" or "jointly mixable" rearrangements of the columns of (a_{i,j})) and determine the computational complexity of finding one.
status_search_result: No source was found that resolves the characterization or efficient computation of optimal arrangements for this minimax row-sum permutation problem in its general form. The problem is closely linked to the theory of complete/joint mixability of distributions, where exact optima are known only in special cases (e.g., monotone or identically distributed marginals). General characterizations and algorithms appear to remain open.

paper_title: Current Open Questions in Complete Mixability
original_question: For given distributions, can one design effective algorithms to decide whether they are jointly mixable or to solve the minimax assignment problem from Section 1? In particular, under what conditions do the swapping algorithms discussed in the paper converge?
self_contained_problem:
Let $F_1, \ldots, F_d$ be one-dimensional probability distributions on $\mathbb{R}$ with finite mean. The tuple $(F_1, \ldots, F_d)$ is called jointly mixable if there exist random variables $X_1, \ldots, X_d$ defined on a common probability space, with $X_i \sim F_i$ for each $i$, such that the sum $X_1 + \cdots + X_d$ is almost surely constant. The associated minimax assignment problem asks, given samples (or discretizations) $x_{i,1}, \ldots, x_{i,n}$ from each $F_i$ arranged as the rows of a $d \times n$ matrix $A$, for permutations $\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_d$ of $\{1, \ldots, n\}$ minimizing
$$\max_{1 \le j \le n} \sum_{i=1}^{d} x_{i,\sigma_i(j)} \;-\; \min_{1 \le j \le n} \sum_{i=1}^{d} x_{i,\sigma_i(j)}.$$
A swapping (rearrangement) algorithm iteratively replaces each row of $A$ by a permutation of its entries so that this row becomes oppositely ordered (countermonotonic) with respect to the sum of the remaining rows, repeating until no further reduction is achieved.

Address the following:

(a) Design an effective algorithm that decides, for given distributions $F_1, \ldots, F_d$, whether $(F_1, \ldots, F_d)$ is jointly mixable, and an effective algorithm to (approximately) solve the minimax assignment problem above.

(b) Determine necessary and sufficient (or otherwise sharp) conditions on the input matrix $A$ — or on the underlying distributions $F_1, \ldots, F_d$ — under which the swapping algorithm described above converges to an optimal solution of the minimax assignment problem.
status_search_result: Subsequent work (Puccetti–Wang on detecting complete and joint mixability; the Block Rearrangement Algorithm of Bernard–McLeish and follow-ups; Haus 2015 on hardness of the assignment problem) has produced improved heuristics, partial complexity results, and convergence-rate estimates in special cases (e.g., Gaussian marginals). However, a complete characterization of when the swapping/rearrangement algorithm provably converges to the optimum, and a fully effective algorithm to decide joint mixability for arbitrary distributions, are not established in the literature located. The problem appears to remain open in general.

paper_title: Current Open Questions in Complete Mixability
original_question: Let F be a distribution on ℝ^d with d > 1. If the projection of F onto every essential subspace of ℝ^d is n-completely mixable, under what additional conditions does it follow that F itself is n-completely mixable on ℝ^d?
self_contained_problem:
A probability distribution F on ℝ^d (with d ≥ 1) is called n-completely mixable (n-CM) if there exist d-dimensional random vectors X_1, …, X_n, each with distribution F, such that
    X_1 + X_2 + ⋯ + X_n = c   almost surely,
for some constant vector c ∈ ℝ^d. For a linear subspace V ⊆ ℝ^d, the projection of F onto V is the law of π_V(X), where X ~ F and π_V denotes orthogonal projection onto V. A subspace V ⊆ ℝ^d is called essential for F if the projection π_V(X) is non-degenerate (i.e., its support is not concentrated at a single point).

Now suppose d > 1 and F is a distribution on ℝ^d such that, for every essential subspace V of ℝ^d, the projection of F onto V is n-completely mixable. Determine additional conditions on F under which it follows that F itself is n-completely mixable on ℝ^d. In particular, find a (preferably minimal) set of supplementary hypotheses on F that, together with the projection assumption above, imply n-complete mixability of F.
status_search_result: The problem is listed as an open problem in a survey on complete mixability published in Probability Surveys (2015). No subsequent resolution providing such sufficient extra conditions for general multivariate distributions appears in the literature based on available search results.

paper_title: Current Open Questions in Complete Mixability
original_question: Suppose a distribution F satisfies a known sufficient condition for n-complete mixability, such as one of the conditions listed earlier in Section 2.2. Can one write down an explicit copula for an n-complete mix with margins F, or more generally for a joint mix with prescribed margins?
self_contained_problem:
Let $n\ge 2$ be an integer and let $F$ be a univariate cumulative distribution function on $\mathbb{R}$. A random vector $(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ is called an $n$-complete mix with margins $F$ if each $X_i$ has distribution $F$ and the sum $X_1+\cdots+X_n$ is almost surely constant; in this case $F$ is said to be $n$-completely mixable ($n$-CM). More generally, given marginal distributions $F_1,\dots,F_n$, a joint mix with these margins is a random vector $(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ with $X_i\sim F_i$ and $X_1+\cdots+X_n$ almost surely constant. By Sklar's theorem, the joint distribution of any such vector with continuous margins is determined by a copula $C:[0,1]^n\to[0,1]$.

Assume that $F$ satisfies a known sufficient condition for $n$-complete mixability (for example, $F$ has a unimodal-symmetric density, or $F$ has a decreasing density on a bounded support with mean satisfying the standard mean condition for $n$-CM).

Problem: Provide an explicit closed-form expression for a copula $C$ of an $n$-complete mix with margins $F$. More generally, given marginals $F_1,\dots,F_n$ for which a joint mix exists, give an explicit copula realizing such a joint mix.
status_search_result: No explicit closed-form copula construction for general n-complete mixes or joint mixes appears in the literature. Standard existence proofs rely on combinatorial discretization arguments rather than producing explicit copulas, and full characterization of joint-mix sets for n≥3 remains open. Subsequent work (e.g., on elliptical families and detection procedures) addresses existence/detection but not explicit copula formulas in general.

original_question: For n > 3, can one fully characterize the set J_n(K) of n-tuples of distributions that are jointly mixable with joint center K, or equivalently the set M_n(μ) of distributions on ℝ that are n-completely mixable with center μ?

Let n ≥ 3 be an integer. A distribution function F on ℝ is called n-completely mixable with center μ ∈ ℝ if there exist random variables X_1, …, X_n, each with distribution F, such that
   X_1 + X_2 + ⋯ + X_n = nμ   almost surely.
Denote by M_n(μ) the set of all distribution functions on ℝ that are n-completely mixable with center μ.

More generally, an n-tuple (F_1, …, F_n) of one-dimensional distribution functions is called jointly mixable with joint center K ∈ ℝ if there exist random variables X_1, …, X_n with X_i ∼ F_i for each i such that
   X_1 + X_2 + ⋯ + X_n = K   almost surely.
Denote by J_n(K) the set of all such n-tuples.

For n = 1 the sets are trivial (only point masses), and for n = 2 the set M_2(μ) consists exactly of the distributions symmetric about μ, with a corresponding characterization of J_2(K).

Problem: For each integer n ≥ 3, give a complete characterization of the set M_n(μ) of one-dimensional distributions that are n-completely mixable with center μ, and equivalently of the set J_n(K) of n-tuples of one-dimensional distributions that are jointly mixable with joint center K.

Sufficient conditions (e.g., symmetric unimodal densities, concave densities, monotone densities under moment conditions) and detection algorithms have been developed, but no complete characterization is known. Recent works (e.g., on centers of probability measures and detection of mixability) extend partial results without resolving the general characterization.

paper_title: Current Open Questions in Complete Mixability
original_question: For a unimodal distribution supported on a bounded interval, what additional conditions are sufficient to guarantee n-complete mixability?
self_contained_problem:
A probability distribution F on the real line is called n-completely mixable (n-CM), where n ≥ 2 is an integer, if there exist random variables X_1, X_2, …, X_n, each with distribution F, such that the sum X_1 + X_2 + ⋯ + X_n is almost surely constant. A distribution F on a bounded interval [a, b] is called unimodal if it admits a density f on [a, b] such that f is non-decreasing on [a, m] and non-increasing on [m, b] for some m ∈ [a, b].

Determine additional conditions on a unimodal distribution F supported on a bounded interval [a, b] (e.g., conditions on its density, mean, mode, or support length) which are sufficient to guarantee that F is n-completely mixable for a given integer n ≥ 2. More precisely, identify and prove a useful set of sufficient conditions, beyond unimodality and bounded support, ensuring n-complete mixability.
status_search_result: Several partial sufficient conditions are known: continuous distributions with monotone density on a bounded interval (under a mean/length condition) and symmetric unimodal distributions with concave density are n-CM for all n ≥ 2; further sufficient conditions involve the density being bounded below by an explicit constant on a neighborhood of the mean. However, a complete characterization of which extra conditions on a unimodal bounded-support distribution guarantee n-complete mixability remains open.

paper_title: Settling Some Open Problems on 2-Player Symmetric Nash Equilibria
context_brief: symmetric fixed-rank games of rank 2 through 5
original_question: For each k in {2, 3, 4, 5}, what is the computational complexity of finding a symmetric Nash equilibrium in a two-player symmetric bimatrix game (A, A^T) whose rank is k, that is, for which rank(A + A^T) = k?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. A two-player bimatrix game is specified by a pair of real m×n payoff matrices (A,B): if the row player plays a mixed strategy x ∈ Δ_m and the column player plays y ∈ Δ_n (where Δ_k denotes the simplex of probability vectors in R^k), the row player's expected payoff is x^T A y and the column player's is x^T B y. A Nash equilibrium (NE) is a pair (x,y) such that no player can strictly improve by unilateral deviation.

A bimatrix game (A,B) is symmetric if m = n and B = A^T. For a symmetric game, a symmetric Nash equilibrium is a NE of the form (x,x); every symmetric bimatrix game admits at least one symmetric NE.

The rank of a bimatrix game (A,B) is defined as rank(A+B). Thus a symmetric game (A,A^T) has rank k when rank(A+A^T) = k.

Problem. For each k ∈ {2, 3, 4, 5}, determine the computational complexity of the following problem: given a symmetric bimatrix game (A,A^T) with integer (or rational) entries satisfying rank(A+A^T) = k, compute a symmetric Nash equilibrium of (A,A^T).

In particular, for each such k, decide whether this problem is solvable in polynomial time, is PPAD-complete, or has some intermediate complexity.
category_tag: Complexity of Nash equilibria in fixed-rank games
status_search_result: Available sources indicate that polynomial-time algorithms exist for symmetric Nash equilibria in symmetric games of rank 0 and 1, while the problem is PPAD-hard for symmetric games of rank ≥ 6 (and for general bimatrix games of rank ≥ 3). The complexity of computing a symmetric Nash equilibrium of a symmetric game of rank 2, 3, 4, or 5 is reported as still unresolved in the literature, with no algorithm or hardness result located that closes the gap.
