original_question: For the same production-step assignment problem, let T^* = min_{σ_1,…,σ_n∈ S_m} max_{i=1,…,m} ∑_{j=1}^n a_{σ_j(i),j}. Under what conditions does T^* equal the average value (1/m)∑_{i=1}^m∑_{j=1}^n a_{i,j}, and how can T^* be computed?
self_contained_problem:
Let m, n be positive integers and let A = (a_{i,j}) be an m×n matrix of nonnegative real numbers. Let S_m denote the symmetric group on {1,…,m}. For permutations σ_1,…,σ_n ∈ S_m, form the m×n matrix whose (i,j) entry is a_{σ_j(i),j}, and consider the maximum row sum

  M(σ_1,…,σ_n) = max_{1 ≤ i ≤ m} ∑_{j=1}^n a_{σ_j(i), j}.

Define
  T^*(A) = min_{σ_1,…,σ_n ∈ S_m} M(σ_1,…,σ_n).

Since rearranging the columns leaves the total sum invariant, one always has
  T^*(A) ≥ (1/m) ∑_{i=1}^m ∑_{j=1}^n a_{i,j}.

(a) Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the matrix A under which the equality
  T^*(A) = (1/m) ∑_{i=1}^m ∑_{j=1}^n a_{i,j}
holds (i.e., the average lower bound is attained).

(b) Provide an effective method (algorithm or closed-form characterization) to compute T^*(A) for an arbitrary nonnegative matrix A.
status_search_result: No targeted results were found establishing necessary-and-sufficient conditions for T^* to equal the average lower bound, nor a general algorithm for computing T^*. The question is posed as an open problem connected to complete mixability and appears not to have a published full resolution.

paper_title: Current Open Questions in Complete Mixability
original_question: If one prescribes fixed bivariate or higher-dimensional marginal distributions, when does there exist a joint mix compatible with those marginals, and how can one develop algorithms to determine this numerically?
self_contained_problem:
Let $d\geq 3$ and let $\mathcal{F}$ be a prescribed family of multivariate marginal distributions on subsets of coordinates of $(X_1,\dots,X_d)$. Specifically, fix an integer $k\in\{2,\dots,d-1\}$ and a collection $\{F_S : S\in\mathcal{S}\}$ where $\mathcal{S}$ is a family of $k$-element subsets of $\{1,\dots,d\}$ and each $F_S$ is a probability distribution on $\mathbb{R}^k$. A random vector $(X_1,\dots,X_d)$ is called a joint mix if there exists a constant $c\in\mathbb{R}$ such that $X_1+\cdots+X_d=c$ almost surely. Say that the family $\{F_S\}$ admits a joint mix compatible with the prescribed higher-dimensional marginals if there exists a joint distribution of $(X_1,\dots,X_d)$ such that for every $S\in\mathcal{S}$ the marginal distribution of $(X_i)_{i\in S}$ equals $F_S$ and $X_1+\cdots+X_d$ is almost surely constant.

(a) Provide necessary and sufficient conditions on the family $\{F_S\}$ under which such a compatible joint mix exists.

(b) Provide a numerical/algorithmic procedure that, given $\{F_S\}$ as input, decides (or detects up to prescribed accuracy) whether a compatible joint mix exists, and constructs one when it does.
status_search_result: Recent literature on joint and complete mixability (e.g., detection algorithms via the MDP method, and joint mixability with negative dependence) addresses the univariate-marginal case, while the problem of characterizing existence of a joint mix under prescribed bivariate or higher-dimensional marginal constraints, together with corresponding numerical algorithms, does not appear to have been resolved in general. No source explicitly resolving this question was found.

paper_title: Recent advances and open questions in neutrino-induced quasi-elastic scattering and single photon production
original_question: How can the scaling analyses and short-range correlation information obtained from inclusive electron quasielastic scattering be made usable in neutrino-nucleus CCQE analyses, given that neutrino experiments generally do not know the incident neutrino energy event by event and therefore cannot directly establish the transferred momentum q and transferred energy ω?
self_contained_problem:
In inclusive quasi-elastic (QE) electron-nucleus scattering, the four-momentum transfer to the nucleus is fully determined event by event from the measured momentum of the scattered electron, giving the three-momentum transfer q and the energy transfer ω. Using these variables, scaling analyses (first-kind and second-kind scaling, the scaling function f(ψ′) of the SuperScaling Approach, and Rosenbluth-separated longitudinal and transverse responses R_L(q,ω), R_T(q,ω)) have been extracted, and the role of short-range nucleon-nucleon correlations — high-momentum pairs involving roughly 20% of the nucleons, responsible for the well-known enhancement of the transverse response — has been quantified.

In charged-current quasi-elastic (CCQE) neutrino-nucleus scattering ν_ℓ + A → ℓ^- + X (and the antineutrino analogue), the incident neutrino energy E_ν is not known on an event-by-event basis: only the outgoing charged lepton's momentum and angle are directly measured, while E_ν is distributed according to a broad flux Φ(E_ν). Consequently, the values of q and ω cannot be reconstructed event by event without an additional model assumption.

Problem. Develop a framework that allows the scaling functions, Rosenbluth-separated nuclear responses, and short-range correlation information extracted from inclusive electron QE data to be used quantitatively to predict the flux-folded inclusive CCQE double differential cross section

  d²σ/(dT_ℓ d cos θ_ℓ) = ∫ dE_ν Φ(E_ν) · d²σ(E_ν, T_ℓ, cos θ_ℓ)/(dT_ℓ d cos θ_ℓ),

in a way that does not require event-by-event knowledge of (q, ω). Specifically, construct an explicit prescription that (i) maps the electron-scattering scaling function and transverse-enhancement contribution into the five weak nuclear response functions entering CCQE, (ii) properly incorporates the broad neutrino flux through integration over E_ν with the kinematically allowed (q, ω) consistent with the measured lepton kinematics, and (iii) yields predictions that simultaneously reproduce existing electron QE scaling data and CCQE neutrino and antineutrino cross sections on nuclear targets such as ¹²C, ⁴⁰Ar, and ⁵⁶Fe.
status_search_result: The question of transferring electron-scattering scaling and short-range-correlation information into neutrino CCQE analyses has been the subject of extensive ongoing work (SuSA, SuSAv2, SuSAv2-MEC, and related approaches), with significant progress in incorporating 2p2h/MEC contributions and transverse enhancement, but no fully agreed-upon, model-independent solution that bypasses the unknown incident neutrino energy. The problem is generally regarded as still open in the neutrino-physics literature.

paper_title: Recent advances and open questions in neutrino-induced quasi-elastic scattering and single photon production
original_question: Why do the Martini and IFIC/Nieves RPA-based calculations for carbon neutrino CCQE-like scattering integrated over the MiniBooNE flux give a two-particle–two-hole (2p–2h) contribution that differs by about a factor of two, and is the unresolved axial-response enhancement responsible for this difference?
self_contained_problem:
Consider charged-current quasi-elastic-like (CCQE-like) scattering of muon neutrinos on a carbon (¹²C) target, with the incoming neutrino flux corresponding to that of the MiniBooNE experiment. Two independent nuclear-physics calculations of this process — both based on the Random Phase Approximation (RPA) applied to a relativistic Fermi gas / local Fermi gas description of the nucleus, supplemented with a two-particle–two-hole (2p–2h) contribution arising from meson-exchange currents and short-range correlations — are performed: 

(i) the Martini et al. RPA + 2p–2h calculation, and 
(ii) the IFIC/Nieves et al. RPA + 2p–2h calculation. 

When their predicted flux-integrated double-differential and total CCQE-like cross sections are compared, the genuine one-body (1p–1h) RPA contributions agree reasonably well, but the 2p–2h contributions differ by approximately a factor of two.

Problem. Identify and quantitatively account for the origin of this factor-of-two discrepancy between the two RPA-based 2p–2h predictions for ν_μ–¹²C CCQE-like scattering integrated over the MiniBooNE flux. In particular, determine whether an unresolved enhancement of the axial nuclear response in the 2p–2h channel — beyond the vector and axial-vector meson-exchange-current contributions explicitly included — is responsible for this difference, by isolating the contributions of (a) the longitudinal/transverse axial response, (b) the meson-exchange-current diagrams retained or omitted in each calculation, (c) short-range correlation contributions, and (d) the treatment of Δ-resonance propagation and in-medium width.
status_search_result: Subsequent literature confirms that both Martini et al. and Nieves et al. RPA-based calculations describe MiniBooNE CCQE-like data with a standard axial mass once 2p–2h is included, but their 2p–2h strengths still differ by roughly a factor of two. Several follow-up studies (e.g., generator comparisons in NEUT, and reviews of MEC-induced two-nucleon emission) discuss possible origins (axial MEC, Δ in-medium width, short-range correlation treatment), but to date no single calculation has been shown to fully reconcile the two approaches; the role of an unresolved axial enhancement remains under investigation.

original_question: For a two-player symmetric bimatrix game (A, A^T) of rank 1, meaning rank(A + A^T) = 1, can one compute a symmetric Nash equilibrium (x, x) in polynomial time?

Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ be a payoff matrix such that the bimatrix game $(A, A^{T})$ has rank one in the sense that $\operatorname{rank}(A + A^{T}) = 1$. A pair of mixed strategies $(x, y)$, with $x, y$ in the simplex $\Delta_n = \{z \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^n : \sum_i z_i = 1\}$, is a Nash equilibrium of $(A, A^{T})$ if $x^{T} A y \geq (x')^{T} A y$ for all $x' \in \Delta_n$ and $x^{T} A y \geq x^{T} A y'$ for all $y' \in \Delta_n$. A Nash equilibrium $(x, y)$ is called symmetric if $x = y$. 

Question: Is there an algorithm that, given such a matrix $A$ with rational entries (so that $\operatorname{rank}(A+A^T)=1$), computes a symmetric Nash equilibrium $(x,x)$ of the symmetric bimatrix game $(A, A^{T})$ in time polynomial in the input size?

paper_title: Recent advances and open questions in neutrino-induced quasi-elastic scattering and single photon production
original_question: How should models and analyses of neutrino charged-current quasi-elastic (CCQE) scattering on carbon explain the apparent tension between MiniBooNE, which measured larger CCQE-like cross sections around 1 GeV, and NOMAD, which measured axial-mass values closer to deuterium at energies above 3 GeV? In particular, determine whether multinucleon (np-nh or two-particle–two-hole) effects are energy dependent and smaller at NOMAD energies, and whether NOMAD’s topological and kinematic event selections removed events whose kinematics or proton multiplicity were distorted by multinucleon dynamics.
self_contained_problem:
Consider neutrino charged-current quasi-elastic (CCQE) scattering on a carbon target, in which an incoming muon neutrino interacts with a bound nucleon via W-boson exchange producing a muon and a recoiling nucleon. The hadronic vertex is parameterized (within the dipole ansatz) by an axial form factor with a single free parameter, the axial mass M_A, which fixes the Q^2-dependence and overall normalization of the elementary cross section. Two classes of measurements yield apparently inconsistent extractions of M_A from CCQE-like event samples on carbon:

(i) At mean neutrino energies near 1 GeV, an analysis of CCQE-like absolute differential cross sections per nucleon on carbon is well described only by an effective axial mass M_A^{eff} ≈ 1.35 GeV, both in shape (Q^2 distribution) and in absolute rate.

(ii) At neutrino energies above 3 GeV, an analysis of CCQE events on carbon yields M_A ≈ 1.06 ± 0.06 GeV, consistent with extractions from light-target (deuterium) data.

A candidate explanation is that, in addition to genuine 1p1h quasi-elastic scattering, multinucleon (np-nh, in particular 2p2h or two-particle–two-hole meson-exchange-current) processes contribute to the CCQE-like sample at the lower energy and inflate the apparent M_A.

Provide a quantitative theoretical and experimental account that simultaneously reproduces both data sets, by addressing the following:

(a) Determine, within a controlled nuclear-model framework valid across the full range from ≈ 0.5 GeV to ≈ 10 GeV neutrino energy (e.g., RPA-based or equivalent treatments of nuclear correlations together with explicit 2p2h contributions), the energy dependence of the multinucleon contribution to the inclusive CCQE-like cross section on carbon, and decide whether this contribution is significantly smaller (relative to the genuine 1p1h CCQE rate) at neutrino energies above 3 GeV than at energies near 1 GeV.

(b) Determine whether the topological selection (constraints on observed charged-track multiplicity, including proton multiplicity) and kinematic selection (cuts on transverse momentum imbalance and missing energy) used in the high-energy CCQE measurement preferentially remove events in which 2p2h dynamics distort the muon kinematics or produce additional ejected protons, and quantify the resulting bias on the extracted axial mass.

(c) Combining (a) and (b), establish whether a single value of the nucleon axial mass M_A close to the deuterium value (≈ 1.03 GeV) together with multinucleon dynamics can simultaneously reproduce the absolute CCQE-like cross section at ≈ 1 GeV on carbon and the high-energy (>3 GeV) extraction of M_A on carbon.
status_search_result: The tension is widely attributed to multinucleon (2p2h) contributions enhancing the low-energy carbon cross section while leaving the deuterium-based axial mass near 1.03 GeV. RPA + 2p2h calculations (Nieves et al., Martini et al.) and SuSAv2-MEC approaches reproduce both MiniBooNE and (approximately) NOMAD cross sections, but quantitative agreement on the energy dependence of 2p2h and on the impact of NOMAD's selection cuts remains incomplete; combined NCE+CCQE analyses do not fully support multinucleon contributions large enough to remove the normalization tension. The question is therefore partially resolved.

paper_title: Recent advances and open questions in neutrino-induced quasi-elastic scattering and single photon production
original_question: What remaining neutral-current single-photon production mechanisms, especially anomalous ωZγ contributions with large theoretical uncertainties, and what direct measurements by MicroBooNE, MINERvA, ND280/T2K, or similar detectors are needed to make this background sufficiently controlled for electron-neutrino appearance studies?
self_contained_problem:
Consider neutrino–nucleus scattering at energies relevant to accelerator-based oscillation experiments (roughly 0.2–10 GeV), and focus on neutral-current (NC) processes whose final state contains a single photon and no charged leptons. Such NC γ events constitute an irreducible background to electron-neutrino appearance searches because a single photon shower is experimentally hard to distinguish from an electron shower.

Standard contributions to NC single-photon production include:
(i) NC excitation of baryon resonances (most importantly the Δ(1232)) followed by radiative decay,
(ii) non-resonant nucleon Born terms,
(iii) coherent single-photon production on nuclei,
(iv) anomaly-mediated contributions arising from the Wess–Zumino–Witten term, in particular the ωZγ vertex coupling the ω vector meson to the Z boson and a photon, whose strength is fixed by the chiral anomaly but whose hadronic form factors and off-shell behavior carry large theoretical uncertainty.

Problem. Determine, both theoretically and experimentally, the size and kinematic distributions of the remaining NC single-photon production mechanisms—especially the anomalous ωZγ contribution—on nuclear targets used in current and near-future oscillation experiments (argon, carbon, hydrocarbon, water/CH). Specifically:

(a) Provide a theoretically robust calculation of the anomalous ωZγ contribution to the NC 1γ cross section differential in photon energy and angle on the nucleon and on nuclei, with controlled uncertainties on the vector-meson form factors, off-shell extrapolations, and nuclear effects.

(b) Identify direct experimental measurements—using liquid-argon time projection chambers such as MicroBooNE, the MINERνA detector, and the ND280 near detector of T2K, or comparable detectors—of the NC 1γ inclusive and exclusive cross sections (including coherent and incoherent channels) that are sufficient to constrain these mechanisms to a level adequate for νe appearance analyses.

(c) Combine (a) and (b) to demonstrate that the NC single-photon background to νe appearance is controlled with quantified, sub-dominant systematic uncertainty.

These provide direct LAr-TPC measurements of the targeted backgrounds. However, a fully robust calculation of the anomalous ωZγ contribution with reduced theoretical uncertainty, and corresponding measurements at MINERνA and ND280/T2K of comparable precision, are not yet complete, so the overall program is partially solved.

paper_title: Recent advances and open questions in neutrino-induced quasi-elastic scattering and single photon production
original_question: What measurements, beam-line monitoring, and common simulation practices are needed for accelerator neutrino experiments to reduce absolute neutrino flux uncertainties below 5%, including uncertainties from secondary and tertiary hadron interactions, proton-beam optics, beam-line alignment, and the approximately 20% differences among NuMI-based flux predictions?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an accelerator-based neutrino experiment in which a primary proton beam impinges on a fixed target, producing secondary hadrons (predominantly pions and kaons) that decay in a magnetic-focused decay pipe to yield a neutrino beam (e.g., a NuMI-style configuration). The absolute neutrino flux Φ(E_ν) at the near and far detectors is predicted by a Monte Carlo simulation that convolves: (i) the primary proton beam optics and targeting, (ii) the alignment and geometry of the focusing horns and decay volume, (iii) hadron production cross sections from the primary p+target interaction, and (iv) secondary and tertiary re-interactions of hadrons in target, horn, and surrounding materials. Empirically, different simulation chains based on the same external hadron production data sets produce absolute flux predictions that disagree by up to roughly 20%.

Determine a concrete program — specifying (a) the set of dedicated hadron-production measurements (kinematic coverage in (x_F, p_T), target materials and thicknesses, including thin- and thick-target data sufficient to constrain secondary and tertiary interactions), (b) the in situ beam-line instrumentation and monitoring required (proton beam position, profile, intensity; horn current and alignment; target alignment; muon monitor responses), and (c) the common simulation conventions (interaction models, re-weighting prescriptions, error propagation methods, treatment of correlations) — such that the absolute neutrino flux uncertainty σ(Φ)/Φ at the relevant experimental energies can be demonstrably reduced below 5%. In particular, identify which of the listed sources (primary hadron production, secondary/tertiary interactions, proton beam optics, beam-line alignment) becomes the dominant systematic once primary hadron production is precisely measured, and quantify how the ~20% spread among existing predictions can be reconciled.
status_search_result: Reaching sub-5% absolute flux uncertainty in accelerator neutrino beams remains an active and open challenge. Modern long-baseline experiments (T2K, NOvA, MINERvA) currently report absolute flux uncertainties at the ~5–10% level, with ongoing efforts (e.g., NA61/SHINE replica-target measurements, EMPHATIC, and PPFX for NuMI) aimed at further reductions. No published result demonstrates a sub-5% absolute flux uncertainty across the full energy range with a unified treatment of hadron production, beam optics, and alignment.

original_question: How should neutrino experiments report CCQE measurements with precise definitions of the event selection, observables, and the meaning of “CCQE,” while providing model-independent quantities and flux information that theorists can calculate directly, so that comparisons with neutrino and electron-scattering theory are unambiguous?
self_contained_problem:
Consider charged-current quasi-elastic (CCQE) neutrino–nucleus scattering experiments, in which a neutrino scatters off a nuclear target producing a charged lepton and (nominally) a single nucleon, but where the actual experimental signature is defined by detector-level observables (e.g., presence of a charged lepton, hadronic activity cuts, and reconstructed kinematics) rather than by the underlying interaction process. Different theoretical and experimental communities (neutrino physics, electron-scattering physics) use the terms "quasi-elastic" and "final state interactions" in inequivalent ways, so the mapping between measured cross sections and theoretically calculable quantities is ambiguous.

Formulate a standardized reporting prescription for CCQE measurements that achieves all of the following:

1. A precise, detector-level definition of the event selection (signal definition) specified purely in terms of observable final-state particles, kinematic thresholds, and acceptance, without reference to any particular interaction model.

2. A precise specification of the reported observables (e.g., differential cross sections in chosen kinematic variables) together with their bin definitions, kinematic ranges, and acceptance corrections, such that the reported quantities are model-independent in the sense that any theoretical model can compute them directly from first principles given the incoming neutrino flux.

3. A complete, quantitative description of the incoming neutrino flux (central value plus correlated uncertainties) sufficient for a theorist to fold any predicted cross section against the flux without further assumptions.

4. A clear translation table or operational definition relating the experimentally reported "CCQE" signal to the terminology used in the electron-scattering community and in nuclear theory, so that comparisons across neutrino theory, electron-scattering theory, and experimental data are unambiguous.

Provide such a prescription, and demonstrate that any two experiments adhering to it produce results that can be directly and unambiguously compared to each other and to theoretical predictions.
status_search_result: This is a methodological/community-standards question rather than a closed mathematical problem. Subsequent neutrino-scattering reviews and NuSTEC white papers have advocated and partially implemented model-independent reporting (flux-folded differential cross sections, detector-level signal definitions), but a fully standardized, universally adopted prescription remains an ongoing community effort, so the question is best characterized as still open.

paper_title: Recent advances and open questions in neutrino-induced quasi-elastic scattering and single photon production
original_question: In Random Phase Approximation (RPA) models of neutrino-nucleus scattering that reproduce MiniBooNE CCQE-like data, what theoretically justified treatment should be used for the transverse magnetic and axial responses, conservation of the vector current, and non-plane-wave hadronic final states, instead of assuming that the transverse magnetic and axial responses are identical and representing all hadronic states as plane waves?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a Random Phase Approximation (RPA) framework for modeling charged-current quasi-elastic (CCQE) neutrino–nucleus scattering on a nuclear target. In such a framework, the inclusive nuclear response is decomposed into longitudinal and transverse pieces of the vector (in particular, the transverse magnetic) response and of the axial response, and the leptonic probe couples to a hadronic current acting on nuclear states. A widely used simplification proceeds under the following two assumptions:

(A) The transverse magnetic response R_T^{(V)} and the transverse axial response R_T^{(A)} are taken to be identical, motivated only by the formal similarity of the non-relativistic reductions of their associated one-body operators, both proportional to (σ × q̂) τ_±.

(B) The nuclear current is taken as a purely one-body operator, and all hadronic final states (including those arising in two-particle–two-hole excitations) are represented as plane waves, which forces a regularization of otherwise divergent two-body phase-space integrals.

The problem is: formulate a theoretically justified replacement for assumptions (A) and (B) within an RPA-based calculation of the CCQE-like cross section that
  (i) treats the transverse magnetic response and the transverse axial response as genuinely distinct, accounting for the known differences between pion-exchange (meson-exchange current) corrections on the vector and axial-vector currents;
  (ii) ensures exact conservation of the vector current (CVC) at the level of the many-body matrix elements actually used (i.e., is consistent under the addition of two-body currents required by current conservation when the one-body current alone fails to be conserved); and
  (iii) replaces the plane-wave description of the hadronic final states by distorted/interacting final states (e.g., final-state interactions or properly antisymmetrized correlated states) so that the two-body integrals entering the response are finite without ad hoc cutoffs,
while still reproducing the inclusive CCQE-like cross-section data on a nuclear target such as ^{12}C in the kinematic regime of the MiniBooNE experiment.
category_tag: Nuclear response functions in neutrino scattering
status_search_result: Subsequent literature on RPA-based neutrino–nucleus models (Martini et al., Nieves et al., and follow-ups through 2020s) continues to discuss the equality of transverse magnetic and axial responses, CVC implementation with one-body currents, and the plane-wave treatment of final hadronic states as approximations still under refinement; no fully theoretically justified replacement satisfying all three criteria simultaneously has been established in the literature accessible by web search.

paper_title: New Open Problems Related to Old Conjectures by Helleseth
context_brief: Avoid elliptic-curve proof for the q−2 case
original_question: Take p ∈ {2, 3} and let L be a finite field of characteristic p and order q. For the exponent s = q − 2, which satisfies s ≡ 1 (mod p − 1) exactly in these two characteristics, can one prove the Helleseth Vanishing Conjecture for this case without using the theory of elliptic curves? In other words, can one show by a different method that there exists a nonzero a ∈ L such that W_{L,q−2}(a) = 0?
self_contained_problem:
Let $p\in\{2,3\}$ be a prime, and let $L$ be a finite field of characteristic $p$ and cardinality $q$. Fix a nontrivial additive character $\psi:L\to\mathbb{C}^\times$ (e.g. $\psi(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,\mathrm{Tr}_{L/\mathbb{F}_p}(x)/p)$), and for an integer $s$ with $\gcd(s,q-1)=1$ define the Walsh/Weil-type exponential sum
$$W_{L,s}(a)=\sum_{x\in L}\psi(x^s+ax),\qquad a\in L.$$
Take the exponent $s=q-2$ (which is coprime to $q-1$ and satisfies $s\equiv 1\pmod{p-1}$ precisely when $p\in\{2,3\}$). The Helleseth Vanishing Conjecture in this case asserts that there exists a nonzero $a\in L$ with $W_{L,q-2}(a)=0$.

Problem: Give a proof of this statement for $p\in\{2,3\}$ and $s=q-2$ that does not invoke the theory of elliptic curves.
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not surface any published work providing an elliptic-curve-free proof of the Helleseth Vanishing Conjecture for $p\in\{2,3\}$ and $s=q-2$. No authoritative source was found confirming a resolution, so the current status is unclear.

paper_title: Recent advances and open questions in neutrino-induced quasi-elastic scattering and single photon production
original_question: What is the physical origin, magnitude, and model dependence of the axial transverse response enhancement from two-body currents in neutrino-nucleus quasielastic scattering, and how should theoretical frameworks such as RPA, Relativistic Mean Field (RMF), and superscaling (SuSA) state and test their assumptions about vector and axial transverse enhancements when predicting CCQE cross sections?
self_contained_problem:
In neutrino-nucleus charged-current and neutral-current quasielastic scattering on light/medium nuclei (e.g., carbon), the inclusive nuclear response can be decomposed into vector, axial, and vector-axial pieces, and further into longitudinal and transverse components with respect to the three-momentum transfer q. When two-body meson-exchange (and related) currents are added to the one-body current, the transverse vector response is known to be enhanced. The question concerns the corresponding axial transverse response.

Provide:

(a) A clear identification of the physical mechanism(s) (e.g., Δ-isobar excitation, pion-in-flight and contact terms, short-range correlations dressing one-body currents, interference between one-body and two-body amplitudes in the 1p1h sector, genuine 2p2h contributions) that produce an enhancement of the purely axial transverse response function R_T^{AA}(q,ω) and of the axial-vector interference response R_T^{VA}(q,ω) in CCQE and NCQE scattering on a nucleus such as ^{12}C.

(b) Quantitative estimates, as functions of the three-momentum transfer |q| and energy transfer ω across the kinematic regime relevant for accelerator neutrino experiments (|q| up to ~1 GeV), of the size of this axial transverse enhancement relative to the impulse-approximation (one-body) result, including its sign and its model dependence.

(c) For each of the principal theoretical frameworks used to predict CCQE/NCQE cross sections — Random Phase Approximation (RPA), Relativistic Mean Field (RMF), and SuperScaling Approach (SuSA/SuSAv2) — an explicit statement of which assumptions about vector and axial transverse enhancements are built into the framework, together with quantitative tests against ab initio calculations (e.g., Green's Function Monte Carlo on light nuclei) demonstrating whether or not those assumptions reproduce the axial transverse enhancement.

Determine the origin, magnitude (as a function of q and ω), and inter-model variability of the axial transverse response enhancement from two-body currents, and state precise criteria under which RPA, RMF, and SuSA predictions for CCQE on carbon are consistent with the underlying enhancement.
status_search_result: Subsequent work has made substantial progress but no full consensus exists. Recent calculations attribute much of the transverse (including axial) enhancement to interference between meson-exchange currents and short-range correlations acting on high-momentum nucleon pairs, while pure relativistic Fermi-gas treatments without SRC can yield a reduction. Different frameworks (RPA, RMF/SuSAv2, GFMC, factorized 2p2h) still disagree quantitatively on the axial transverse enhancement magnitude, so the question is partially solved.

paper_title: New Open Problems Related to Old Conjectures by Helleseth
context_brief: Characterize spectrum invariance under output scaling
original_question: Let L be a finite field and let f : L → L be a map, or more specifically a permutation. Determine necessary and sufficient conditions under which scalar multiplication of the output by any nonzero field element preserves the spectrum: for every b ∈ L×, the map bf defined by (bf)(x) = b f(x) has exactly the same Fourier spectrum as f. Which maps or permutations have this spectrum-invariance property for all nonzero scalars b?
self_contained_problem:
Let $L = \mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field of order $q$, regarded as an additive group, and let $\psi : L \to \mathbb{C}^\times$ be a fixed nontrivial additive character of $L$. For a map $f : L \to L$, define its Fourier (Walsh) transform at $(a,b) \in L \times L$ by
$$\widehat{f}(a,b) = \sum_{x \in L} \psi\bigl(a\,f(x) - b\,x\bigr),$$
and define the spectrum of $f$ to be the multiset
$$\mathrm{Spec}(f) = \{\!\{\,\widehat{f}(a,b) : (a,b) \in L^\times \times L\,\}\!\}.$$
For each $b \in L^\times$, let $bf : L \to L$ denote the map $x \mapsto b\,f(x)$.

Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on $f$ (respectively, on a permutation $f$ of $L$) such that
$$\mathrm{Spec}(bf) = \mathrm{Spec}(f) \qquad \text{for every } b \in L^\times.$$
Equivalently, characterize all maps (and all permutations) of a finite field whose Fourier spectrum is invariant under arbitrary nonzero scaling of the output.
category_tag: Fourier spectra of finite field maps
status_search_result: The problem appears as an explicitly stated open problem in a 2014 list of open problems related to Helleseth's conjectures. A web search did not surface a complete characterization (necessary and sufficient conditions) of maps or permutations of a finite field whose Fourier spectrum is invariant under all nonzero output scalings; the literature continues to study spectra of specific families (power maps, binomials, etc.) but no general resolution was found.

paper_title: Recent advances and open questions in neutrino-induced quasi-elastic scattering and single photon production
original_question: How should Relativistic Mean Field (RMF) and Relativistic Green’s Function (RGF) approaches be constrained so that the many-body physics apparently captured through final-state interactions and relativistic optical potentials is understood, the choice of optical potential is no longer ambiguous, and the enhancement of CCQE cross sections can be reconciled with multinucleon emission and other non-nucleonic contributions?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the description of charged-current quasi-elastic (CCQE) neutrino-nucleus scattering on nuclear targets within two relativistic many-body frameworks:

1. The Relativistic Mean Field (RMF) approach, in which the bound and outgoing nucleons are treated as solutions of a Dirac equation with strong scalar and vector mean-field potentials, and final-state interactions of the knocked-out nucleon are encoded by the same (real) RMF potential used for the bound state.

2. The Relativistic Green's Function (RGF) approach, in which the inclusive cross section is expressed via the single-particle Green's function with a complex relativistic optical potential (e.g. EDAI, EDAD1, EDAD2 parametrizations fitted to elastic proton-nucleus scattering); the imaginary part, which would represent loss of flux to inelastic channels in exclusive processes, is reinstated in the inclusive sum so as to redistribute strength among all open channels.

Develop a theoretical framework that achieves all of the following simultaneously:

(a) Identify, from an underlying microscopic many-body theory (such as Green's Function Monte Carlo or a comparable ab initio nuclear structure calculation), the precise dynamical content that an effective RMF final-state interaction must encode, and derive constraints that uniquely fix the appropriate RMF potential to be used for inclusive CCQE observables, removing the present latitude in its choice.

(b) Construct, or characterize, a phenomenological relativistic optical potential that satisfies the dispersion relations linking its real and imaginary parts over the full energy range relevant to accelerator-based neutrino experiments, so that the RGF prediction for inclusive CCQE cross sections is determined unambiguously from elastic nucleon-nucleus phenomenology rather than depending on the choice among inequivalent fits.

(c) Quantitatively decompose the enhancement of the inclusive CCQE cross section produced by the RGF model relative to impulse-approximation (IA) models into contributions from genuine single-nucleon final-state interaction effects, two- and multi-nucleon emission (meson-exchange currents and short-range correlations), and non-nucleonic channels (e.g. pion production followed by absorption), and reconcile this decomposition with independent calculations of those individual mechanisms.

State and prove (or otherwise rigorously establish) the conditions under which (a)–(c) hold consistently within a single relativistic many-body description of inclusive lepton-nucleus scattering.
status_search_result: The question concerns long-standing theoretical ambiguities in modeling inclusive CCQE neutrino-nucleus scattering with RMF and RGF approaches. Subsequent literature (Meucci, Giusti, and collaborators; Gonzalez-Jimenez et al.) continues to compare RMF/RGF with different optical potentials (EDAI, EDAD) against MiniBooNE/T2K/MINERvA data, and ab initio (GFMC, spectral function, SuSAv2) calculations have refined but not eliminated the ambiguity in the choice of RMF/optical potential or fully decomposed the RGF enhancement into 2p2h and non-nucleonic contributions. The problem remains an open program in the neutrino-nucleus interaction community.

paper_title: New Open Problems Related to Old Conjectures by Helleseth
context_brief: Four-valued analogue of Katz’s three-valued theorem
original_question: Suppose x ↦ x^s is a power permutation of a finite field and its spectrum takes exactly four distinct values. Is there an analogue of Theorem 3.5, the theorem that in the three-valued case forces singularity, integrality, and the congruence s ≡ 1 (mod p − 1)? More concretely, what structural restrictions must hold for four-valued exponents, parallel to the ones known for three-valued exponents?
self_contained_problem:
Let p be a prime, let q be a power of p, and let F = F_q be the finite field with q elements. Fix an integer s with gcd(s, q-1) = 1, so that the map x ↦ x^s is a permutation of F (a "power permutation"). For a nontrivial additive character ψ of F, define the Weil sum (spectrum value at a ∈ F^*) by

   W(a) = Σ_{x ∈ F} ψ(x^s + a x).

Call s singular if 0 lies in the spectrum {W(a) : a ∈ F^*}. The exponent s is called n-valued if the multiset {W(a) : a ∈ F^*} attains exactly n distinct values.

It is known (three-valued case) that if x ↦ x^s is a three-valued power permutation, then s is singular, the spectrum {0, A, B} consists of rational integers, and s ≡ 1 (mod p − 1).

Problem. Establish an analogue of this result in the four-valued case: namely, determine the structural restrictions (singularity, integrality of the spectrum, congruence conditions on s modulo p − 1, or other arithmetic constraints) that must necessarily hold for every exponent s such that the power permutation x ↦ x^s on F has spectrum taking exactly four distinct values.
status_search_result: D. J. Katz and A. E. Wong (2023/2024, "Rationality of four-valued families of Weil sums of binomials," J. Number Theory) prove that if the Weil spectrum of a power permutation x ↦ x^s takes exactly four values, then all four values are rational integers, with a single exceptional case (K = F_5 with s ≡ 3 (mod 4)). This establishes the integrality portion of the desired analogue, but a complete four-valued analogue of the three-valued theorem (covering singularity and the full congruence condition s ≡ 1 (mod p−1)) does not yet appear to be fully established, so the problem is partially solved.

paper_title: Recent advances and open questions in neutrino-induced quasi-elastic scattering and single photon production
original_question: What useful and reliable treatment of final-state interactions (FSI)—the propagation of hadrons created at the electroweak vertex through the nuclear medium—can be incorporated into neutrino event generators for exclusive CCQE final states, given that a fully formal treatment would require many unknown form factors and current generator implementations show shortcomings in proton-emission observables?
self_contained_problem:
Consider charged-current quasi-elastic (CCQE) neutrino-nucleus scattering, in which an incoming neutrino interacts with a bound nucleon inside a target nucleus via the exchange of a W boson, producing a charged lepton and a struck nucleon. After the primary electroweak interaction, the outgoing hadrons must propagate through the residual nuclear medium, where they may rescatter, be absorbed, charge-exchange, or produce additional hadrons; these processes are collectively called final-state interactions (FSI) and reshape the exclusive hadronic final state (in particular proton multiplicities, momenta, and angular distributions) actually observed in fine-grained tracking detectors and liquid-argon time-projection chambers.

A formally complete quantum-mechanical treatment of FSI in the exclusive CCQE channel would require introducing a large number of presently unknown nuclear transition form factors, which is not feasible in practice. Existing implementations in neutrino Monte Carlo event generators (e.g. intranuclear cascade models) reproduce inclusive observables reasonably well but exhibit documented shortcomings when confronted with proton-emission observables.

Problem: Devise a tractable, theoretically well-founded, and experimentally reliable prescription for FSI that
(i) can be implemented inside neutrino event generators on an event-by-event basis to produce exclusive hadronic final states for CCQE interactions on nuclear targets,
(ii) avoids the need to introduce an intractable number of unknown form factors,
(iii) is consistent with constraints from electron-nucleus scattering data on the same nuclei, and
(iv) reproduces measured proton kinematic distributions (multiplicities, momenta, angles, and transverse-kinematic-imbalance variables) in CCQE-like neutrino-nucleus events to within experimental uncertainties.
status_search_result: The problem of providing a reliable, tractable FSI treatment for exclusive CCQE final states in neutrino event generators remains an active area of research. Recent developments (2022–2025) include a dedicated GiBUU-based Monte Carlo neutrino generator, implementation of relativistic distorted-wave impulse approximation models in NEUT, and ongoing comparisons of transverse-kinematic-imbalance observables across generators, but the PDG 2024/2025 review of MC neutrino generators and recent workshops continue to list FSI modeling as an unresolved challenge requiring further input from electron scattering. No consensus solution has been established.

paper_title: New Open Problems Related to Old Conjectures by Helleseth
context_brief: Classify all nice exponents beyond the known families
original_question: Let s be an invertible exponent over a finite field of odd characteristic, and write s ≉ 1 to mean that s is not equivalent to 1 under the equivalence generated by s′ ≡ p^j s (mod q − 1) and inversion. Call s nice when the number N(1, v) of solutions to x + y = 1 and x^s + y^s = v takes at most three values as v ranges over the field. The authors found by computation that all nice exponents s ≉ 1 over prime fields of characteristic p < 5000 come from the paradigmatic families in Propositions 6.5 and 6.6. Does every nice exponent s ≉ 1 arise from those paradigmatic examples?
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be an odd prime and let $L=\mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field of odd characteristic $p$, with $q$ a power of $p$. An exponent $s\in\mathbb{Z}/(q-1)\mathbb{Z}$ is called invertible if $\gcd(s,q-1)=1$. Define an equivalence relation on invertible exponents generated by
\[ s\sim p^{j}s\pmod{q-1}\quad\text{and}\quad s\sim s^{-1}\pmod{q-1}.\]
For an invertible exponent $s$ and $v\in L$, let
\[ N(1,v)=\#\{(x,y)\in L^{2}:\ x+y=1,\ x^{s}+y^{s}=v\}.\]
Call $s$ a nice exponent over $L$ if the multiset $\{N(1,v):v\in L\}$ takes at most three distinct values.

Two paradigmatic families of nice exponents are known:
(P1) Exponents $s$ such that $x\mapsto x^{s}$ is a planar function (equivalently, the Dembowski–Ostrom type exponents giving planarity over $L$);
(P2) Exponents $s$ such that $s\equiv p^{k}+1$-type "almost-planar" examples coming from the standard known constructions giving at most three values of $N(1,v)$.
(More precisely, take "paradigmatic" to mean the two explicit families guaranteed to yield nice exponents by direct character-sum computation — namely planar monomials and their close relatives obtained via the standard Niho/Welch type constructions.)

Question: Prove or disprove that every nice exponent $s$ with $s\not\sim 1$ over any prime field $\mathbb{F}_p$ (or more generally any finite field of odd characteristic) arises from one of these two paradigmatic families.
status_search_result: A targeted search did not return any work claiming a complete classification of nice exponents over odd-characteristic finite fields beyond the two paradigmatic families. Related literature on Niho exponents, planar functions and three-valued cross-correlations exists, but no resolution of this specific classification problem was located, so it appears to remain open.

paper_title: Recent advances and open questions in neutrino-induced quasi-elastic scattering and single photon production
original_question: How can computationally sophisticated neutrino-nucleus calculations, including RPA differential cross-section tables, precomputed hadronic tensors, and possibly Green’s Function Monte Carlo results, be delivered to neutrino event generators together with uncertainty estimates and exclusive-final-state guidance so experiments can confront the predictions with data?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the problem of transferring sophisticated neutrino–nucleus scattering calculations into Monte Carlo neutrino event generators used to simulate experimental data. Such calculations include: (i) differential cross-section tables computed in the Random Phase Approximation (RPA) for charged-current quasi-elastic (CCQE) and related processes; (ii) precomputed hadronic tensors W^{μν}(q,ω) tabulated as functions of energy transfer ω and momentum transfer q, from which inclusive cross sections may be reconstructed by contraction with the leptonic tensor; and (iii) ab initio nuclear-structure outputs such as Green's Function Monte Carlo (GFMC) response functions, which are too computationally expensive to evaluate inside a generator at run time.

Develop a general framework that addresses the following questions:

1. Specify a standardized data format and interpolation scheme by which precomputed hadronic tensors and RPA differential cross-section tables on (E_ν, q, ω) (or equivalent kinematic) grids can be ingested by a neutrino event generator so as to reproduce the underlying inclusive predictions to a prescribed numerical accuracy.

2. Provide a method for propagating theoretical uncertainties (e.g. those arising from nuclear form factors, two-body current contributions, RPA correlation parameters, and nuclear-model variants) through the tabulated input into event-by-event reweighting factors usable in experimental analyses.

3. Prescribe how to supplement an inclusive calculation, which yields only the lepton kinematics, with a model for the exclusive hadronic final state (nucleon multiplicities, momenta, and intrinsic excitations) consistent with energy–momentum conservation and the underlying nuclear response, including for calculations such as GFMC where only inclusive responses are computed.

State precise consistency conditions the framework must satisfy and demonstrate, by mathematical construction or by a worked example for one such calculation, that all three requirements can be met simultaneously.
status_search_result: The challenge of interfacing advanced nuclear-theory calculations (RPA, hadronic tensors, GFMC) with neutrino event generators with full uncertainty propagation and exclusive final-state modeling remains an active, only partially solved area. RPA tables and spectral functions have been incorporated into generators such as GENIE, NuWro, and NEUT, and hadronic-tensor approaches have been demonstrated, but unified standards, complete uncertainty quantification, and consistent exclusive-state predictions (especially for GFMC-based inclusive responses) are still under development as of 2024–2026 NuSTEC and generator-development efforts.

paper_title: New Open Problems Related to Old Conjectures by Helleseth
original_question: Let s be an invertible exponent over a finite field of odd characteristic, and assume s ≉ 1. Must 2 always occur as a differential multiplicity of s? That is, for every such invertible exponent, does there always exist some v for which the number N(1, v) of solutions to x + y = 1 and x^s + y^s = v equals 2?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field of odd characteristic, with $q$ elements. For an integer $s$ with $\gcd(s,q-1)=1$ (so the map $x\mapsto x^s$ is a permutation of $\mathbb{F}_q$), and $s\not\equiv 1\pmod{q-1}$, define for each $v\in\mathbb{F}_q$
$$N(1,v) = \#\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{F}_q\times\mathbb{F}_q : x+y=1,\ x^s+y^s=v\}.$$
A value $m\geq 0$ is called a differential multiplicity of $s$ if there exists some $v\in\mathbb{F}_q$ with $N(1,v)=m$.

Prove or disprove: for every finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ of odd characteristic and every exponent $s$ with $\gcd(s,q-1)=1$ and $s\not\equiv 1\pmod{q-1}$, the value $2$ occurs as a differential multiplicity of $s$; that is, there exists $v\in\mathbb{F}_q$ with $N(1,v)=2$.
category_tag: Differential spectra of power mappings over finite fields
status_search_result: Web search did not surface a resolution of this specific "optimist" conjecture about 2 always being a differential multiplicity for invertible exponents in odd characteristic. Related research on differential spectra of power mappings and Helleseth's other conjectures remains active, but no source found confirms the conjecture has been proved or disproved.

paper_title: New Open Problems Related to Old Conjectures by Helleseth
context_brief: Helleseth vanishing conjecture for Weil sums
original_question: Let L be a finite field of characteristic p and order q, and let s be an integer coprime to q − 1 so that the power map x ↦ x^s is a permutation of L. Define the Weil sum W_{L,s}(a) = Σ_{x∈L} μ(x^s − ax), where μ is the canonical additive character of L. Call the exponent s singular if there exists a nonzero a ∈ L such that W_{L,s}(a) = 0. If |L| > 2 and s ≡ 1 (mod p − 1), must s always be singular? Equivalently, must there always exist some a ∈ L× for which the corresponding Weil sum vanishes?
self_contained_problem:
Let $L$ be a finite field of characteristic $p$ and cardinality $q$, and let $\mu\colon L\to\mathbb{C}^\times$ be the canonical additive character of $L$ (i.e., $\mu(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,\mathrm{Tr}_{L/\mathbb{F}_p}(x)/p)$). Let $s$ be a positive integer with $\gcd(s,q-1)=1$, so that $x\mapsto x^s$ is a permutation of $L$. For $a\in L$ define the Weil sum
$$W_{L,s}(a)=\sum_{x\in L}\mu(x^s-ax).$$
The exponent $s$ is called singular (over $L$) if there exists $a\in L^\times$ with $W_{L,s}(a)=0$.

Prove or disprove: whenever $q>2$ and $s\equiv 1\pmod{p-1}$, the exponent $s$ is singular; equivalently, the matrix $\bigl[\mu((x-y)^s)\bigr]_{x,y\in L}$ has rank less than $q-1$.
status_search_result: The Helleseth vanishing conjecture (1976) remains open in general. Partial results are known: it has been verified in various special cases, including for Niho exponents, but no proof for all exponents $s\equiv 1\pmod{p-1}$ coprime to $q-1$ has appeared.

paper_title: Algorithmic Information Theory: Open Problems
original_question: How often is an interesting or natural mathematical question independent of the usual axioms of mathematics?
self_contained_problem: Let ZFC denote the standard Zermelo–Fraenkel axioms of set theory together with the Axiom of Choice, and assume ZFC is consistent. Call a mathematical statement $\varphi$ (formulated in the language of set theory, or interpretable in it) "independent of ZFC" if neither $\varphi$ nor $\neg\varphi$ is provable from ZFC. Develop a meaningful, well-defined notion of "natural" or "mathematically interesting" statement, and within that framework, quantify how frequently such natural statements are independent of ZFC. Concretely: propose a precise measure or asymptotic density on a class $\mathcal{N}$ of "natural" mathematical statements (for instance, statements arising in number theory, analysis, combinatorics, or topology, possibly stratified by logical complexity such as $\Pi_1^0$, $\Sigma_1^1$, etc.), and determine the proportion or density of statements in $\mathcal{N}$ that are independent of ZFC. Is this proportion zero, positive, or one? Does the answer depend on the chosen stratification by logical complexity?
status_search_result: The question is a well-known philosophical/foundational meta-problem about how prevalent independence from ZFC is among naturally arising mathematical statements. It has been discussed by Gödel, Cohen, Friedman, Woodin and others, but it has no agreed-upon precise formulation, let alone a resolution. There is no known formal answer; it remains an open meta-mathematical problem.

paper_title: New Open Problems Related to Old Conjectures by Helleseth
original_question: Let L be a finite field of characteristic p such that the extension degree [L : F_p] is a power of two, and let s be an invertible exponent, meaning gcd(s, |L| − 1) = 1. Is it true that the reduced Fourier spectrum of the power map x ↦ x^s can never take exactly three distinct values? Equivalently, whenever [L : F_p] is a power of two, must every invertible exponent fail to be three-valued?
self_contained_problem:
Let p be a prime and let L be a finite field of characteristic p such that the extension degree [L : F_p] is a power of two. Let s be a positive integer with gcd(s, |L| − 1) = 1, so that the map x ↦ x^s is a permutation of L (an invertible exponent). For a ∈ L^*, define the Weil sum
  W_{L,s}(a) = ∑_{x ∈ L} ψ(x^s + a x),
where ψ is a fixed nontrivial additive character of L (e.g. ψ(y) = exp(2πi Tr_{L/F_p}(y)/p)). The reduced Fourier (Weil) spectrum of x ↦ x^s is the set of distinct values
  { W_{L,s}(a) : a ∈ L^* }.
Prove or disprove: whenever [L : F_p] is a power of two and gcd(s, |L| − 1) = 1, the reduced Fourier spectrum of x ↦ x^s contains at most two, or at least four, distinct values; equivalently, it never takes exactly three distinct values.
status_search_result: The Helleseth three-valued conjecture has been proved for characteristic p = 2 and p = 3 by D. J. Katz, but it remains open for primes p > 3. Recent work by Katz, Nguyen, and others continues to address related cases (Niho exponents, special families) but the general conjecture is not fully resolved.

paper_title: Algorithmic Information Theory: Open Problems
original_question: Let β(n)+iγ(n) denote the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function. If for every positive z != 1 the sequence ((log z)/(2π))γ(n), n >= 0, is uniformly distributed modulo 1, do the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function form a random sequence?
self_contained_problem:
Let the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function ζ(s) be enumerated as ρ_n = β(n) + iγ(n), n ≥ 0, with γ(n) > 0 listed in non-decreasing order. Recall that a sequence (x_n) of real numbers is said to be uniformly distributed modulo 1 if for every 0 ≤ a < b ≤ 1,
   lim_{N→∞} (1/N) #{ n < N : {x_n} ∈ [a,b) } = b − a,
where {x} denotes the fractional part of x.

Recall further that an infinite binary sequence is called (Martin-Löf) random if it passes every recursively enumerable statistical test of randomness; an arbitrary sequence of real numbers is said to form a random sequence if a natural binary encoding of it (e.g., the binary expansions of its terms) yields a Martin-Löf random sequence.

Suppose that for every positive real number z ≠ 1 the sequence
   ( (log z)/(2π) · γ(n) )_{n ≥ 0}
is uniformly distributed modulo 1. Does it follow that the sequence (γ(n))_{n ≥ 0} of imaginary parts of the non-trivial zeros of ζ(s) forms a random sequence in the sense of algorithmic randomness?
status_search_result: A technical report by Calude, Salomaa, and Roblot ("Zeros of Riemann's Zeta Function Are Uniformly Distributed, But Not Random") argues that, although the imaginary parts of the non-trivial zeros of ζ are conjecturally uniformly distributed modulo 1 in the stated sense, this sequence is not algorithmically random; the zeros are computable (e.g., to arbitrary precision by known algorithms), so the sequence cannot be Martin-Löf random. Thus the implication asked about fails: uniform distribution does not entail algorithmic randomness for these zeros.

paper_title: New Open Problems Related to Old Conjectures by Helleseth
context_brief: Divisibility of Fourier coefficients by primes ℓ ≠ p
original_question: Let L be a finite field of order q > 2, and let f be a power permutation of L with exponent s satisfying s ≡ 1 (mod p − 1), where p is the characteristic. Aubry and Langevin proved that there exists a nonzero a ∈ L such that the Fourier coefficient f̂(a) is divisible by 3. Can one prove an analogous divisibility theorem involving some other prime ℓ different from the characteristic p?
self_contained_problem:
Let $L$ be a finite field of order $q>2$ and characteristic $p$. For a function $f:L\to L$, define its Fourier (Walsh) coefficients by
$$\widehat{f}(a) \;=\; \sum_{x\in L} \chi\!\bigl(a\,f(x)\bigr), \qquad a\in L,$$
where $\chi:L\to\mathbb{C}^\times$ is a fixed nontrivial additive character of $L$ (so $\widehat{f}(a)$ is an algebraic integer in the cyclotomic field $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$). A power permutation of $L$ is a map of the form $f(x)=x^s$ that is a bijection of $L$, where $s$ is an integer exponent.

It is known that if $f(x)=x^s$ is a power permutation of $L$ with $s\equiv 1\pmod{p-1}$, then there exists $a\in L^\times$ such that $\widehat{f}(a)\equiv 0\pmod{3}$ in the ring of integers of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$.

Problem: Determine whether there exists a prime $\ell\neq p$, different from $3$ (or more generally, any prime $\ell\neq p$), and a nontrivial class of power permutations $f(x)=x^s$ of $L$ for which one can guarantee the existence of $a\in L^\times$ with $\widehat{f}(a)\equiv 0\pmod{\ell}$. In other words, prove or disprove an analogous divisibility theorem for the Fourier spectrum of power permutations involving a prime $\ell$ different from the characteristic.

paper_title: Algorithmic Information Theory: Open Problems
original_question: Is mathematics quasi-empirical, in the sense that mathematical research should be carried out more like physics?
self_contained_problem:
A discipline is called quasi-empirical if its methodology resembles that of the empirical sciences (such as physics): conjectures are tested against examples and computational evidence, hypotheses may be adopted on the basis of their explanatory or predictive power rather than from formal proof alone, and theories are subject to revision in light of new evidence. By contrast, the classical view holds that mathematics proceeds purely deductively, with theorems established only by rigorous proof from accepted axioms.

Question: Is mathematics quasi-empirical? That is, taking into account phenomena such as the incompleteness theorems, algorithmic randomness, the practical role of computer experimentation and probabilistic reasoning in mathematical discovery, and the existence of plausible but unproved hypotheses (e.g., axioms adopted for their consequences), should mathematical research be conducted in a manner more like physics — accepting and using mathematical statements on the basis of empirical/heuristic evidence rather than insisting exclusively on formal proof?
status_search_result: This is a philosophical/methodological question about the nature of mathematical practice rather than a formal mathematical problem with a definite answer. It has been discussed at length by Lakatos, Pólya, Putnam, Chaitin, and others, but no consensus resolution exists; its status is best described as unknown/unresolved as a matter of philosophical debate.

paper_title: New Open Problems Related to Old Conjectures by Helleseth
context_brief: Divisibility of product of nonzero spectral values
original_question: Let F(x) = μ(x^s) for a power map on a finite field, and let A_1, …, A_n denote the nonzero values in the spectrum of F. For which exponents s is the product of the nonzero spectral values, ∏_{i=1}^n A_i, divisible by q, the size of the field?
self_contained_problem:
Let $q = p^m$ be a prime power and let $\mathbb{F}_q$ denote the finite field with $q$ elements. Fix a nontrivial additive character $\mu \colon \mathbb{F}_q \to \mathbb{C}^\times$ (for example, $\mu(x) = \exp(2\pi i \, \mathrm{Tr}_{\mathbb{F}_q/\mathbb{F}_p}(x)/p)$). For a positive integer $s$ with $\gcd(s, q-1) = 1$, define the Weil-type sum
$$F(a) = \sum_{x \in \mathbb{F}_q} \mu(a \, x^s), \qquad a \in \mathbb{F}_q^*.$$
The (Walsh) spectrum of $F$ is the multiset of values $\{F(a) : a \in \mathbb{F}_q^*\}$. Let $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_n$ be the distinct nonzero values appearing in this spectrum (counted without multiplicity, or with multiplicity — fix one convention).

Determine all exponents $s$ (with $\gcd(s, q-1) = 1$) for which the product
$$\prod_{i=1}^{n} A_i$$
is divisible by $q$ in the ring of algebraic integers.

Recent work (e.g., on Weil sums, Niho exponents, and Helleseth's conjectures through 2021 and later) continues to address divisibility of values in such spectra, but no general characterization of exponents $s$ for which the product of nonzero spectral values is divisible by $q$ appears to be known. No source found resolves the divisibility-of-the-product question in full generality.

paper_title: Algorithmic Information Theory: Open Problems
original_question: Extend Chaitin complexity from finite strings to infinite strings, either by using non-terminating programs that run forever and generate infinite strings over infinite time, or by using computational models that process infinite strings in finite time, such as cellular automata or functions on reals.
self_contained_problem:
Background. The (prefix-free) Chaitin–Kolmogorov complexity H(x) of a finite binary string x is defined as the length of a shortest input p to a fixed universal prefix-free Turing machine U such that U(p) halts and outputs x; equivalently H(x) = min{|p| : U(p) = x}. This quantity is defined only for finite strings, since it relies on the universal machine halting after finitely many steps.

Problem. Develop a satisfactory notion of algorithmic complexity H(α) for infinite binary sequences α ∈ {0,1}^ω that extends the finite-string theory and shares its principal invariance, coding, and information-theoretic properties (e.g., machine-independence up to additive constants, a counting/Kraft inequality, a coherent relation to randomness of α, and consistent behavior under prefixes so that H(α) governs H(α↾n) as n → ∞). Two approaches are to be investigated and compared:

(a) Non-terminating computations: define H(α) using programs for the universal prefix-free machine that never halt but, while running forever, produce α as their (monotone) output, possibly via a transfinite or limit notion of program length and convergence.

(b) Infinite-time computational models: define H(α) using computational devices that consume and produce infinite strings in finite "physical" time, such as cellular automata acting on Z, real-valued computable functions in the BSS or computable-analysis sense, or infinite-time Turing machines, and use the size/description of such devices to measure complexity.

Determine, for at least one such formalization in each of (a) and (b), whether the resulting H(·) is well-defined up to an additive constant, prove its basic properties, characterize the sequences α with H(α) "small" or "maximal," and clarify the precise relationship between the two approaches and existing notions (plain, prefix, monotone, a-priori, and process complexity of finite prefixes; Martin-Löf and Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness).

original_question: Let s be an exponent over a finite field of odd characteristic, assume s ≉ 1, and suppose s is nice in the sense that the differential multiplicity counts N(1, v) take at most three values as v varies. Must 2 always occur as one of the differential multiplicities of s?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field of odd characteristic with $q$ elements, and let $s$ be a positive integer (an "exponent") considered modulo $q-1$, defining the power map $x \mapsto x^s$ on $\mathbb{F}_q$. For $a, b \in \mathbb{F}_q$ with $a \neq 0$, define the differential multiplicity
$$N(a,b) = \#\{x \in \mathbb{F}_q : (x+a)^s - x^s = b\}.$$
By a standard substitution one reduces to studying $N(1,v)$ as $v$ ranges over $\mathbb{F}_q$. The differential spectrum of $s$ is the multiset of values taken by $N(1,v)$. Call $s$ "nice" if the set of values $\{N(1,v) : v \in \mathbb{F}_q\}$ has cardinality at most $3$ (i.e. $N(1,v)$ takes at most three distinct values). Assume further that $s \not\equiv 1 \pmod{q-1}$.

Prove or disprove: if $s$ is nice, then $2$ is one of the values attained by $N(1,v)$, i.e. $2$ is a differential multiplicity of $s$.

paper_title: Algorithmic Information Theory: Open Problems
original_question: Study the transformations that preserve random strings and random sequences.
self_contained_problem:
Background. Fix the binary alphabet {0,1}. For a finite binary string x of length n, the (plain) Kolmogorov complexity C(x) is the length of a shortest input to a fixed universal Turing machine that outputs x. A finite string x of length n is called Kolmogorov random (with deficiency d) if C(x) ≥ n − d. For infinite binary sequences, write 2^ω for Cantor space with the uniform (fair-coin) measure. An infinite sequence X ∈ 2^ω is Martin-Löf random if it passes every Martin-Löf test, i.e. for every uniformly computably enumerable sequence (U_n) of open subsets of 2^ω with μ(U_n) ≤ 2^{−n}, one has X ∉ ⋂_n U_n.

A (partial) computable map F : 2^ω → 2^ω (defined on a set of full uniform measure) is said to preserve randomness if F(X) is Martin-Löf random whenever X is Martin-Löf random. Analogously, a computable function f mapping finite strings to finite strings is said to preserve Kolmogorov randomness if there is a constant c such that C(f(x)) ≥ |f(x)| − c whenever C(x) ≥ |x| − O(1).

Problem. Characterize the transformations that preserve randomness in each of the following senses, and clarify the relationship between the two notions:
(a) Describe necessary and sufficient conditions on a (partial) computable function F : 2^ω → 2^ω under which F(X) is Martin-Löf random for every Martin-Löf random X.
(b) Describe necessary and sufficient conditions on a computable function f on finite binary strings under which f preserves Kolmogorov randomness in the sense above.
(c) Determine the structural and measure-theoretic properties (e.g. measure preservation, almost-everywhere computability, layerwise computability) that characterize these classes of transformations, and determine to what extent the finite and infinite versions correspond.
status_search_result: The general study of randomness-preserving transformations has produced several substantive results — for example, Shen's theorem that almost-everywhere computable measure-preserving maps preserve Martin-Löf randomness (and in fact every ML-random point has an ML-random preimage), as well as work on layerwise computability and on continuous transformations of 2-random sequences. However, no complete characterization of all transformations preserving randomness (in either the finite Kolmogorov-complexity sense or the infinite Martin-Löf sense) appears to be established, so the problem as a whole is best regarded as partially solved.

paper_title: Braking index of isolated pulsars: open questions and ways forward
context_brief: Mismatch between observed and canonical pulsar braking indices
original_question: What physical spin-down model can explain isolated pulsars whose braking index, defined observationally from angular velocity Ω and its first and second time derivatives as n = ΩΩ̈/Ω̇², is measured in the range about 1 < n < 2.8, even though the standard magnetic-dipole-radiation model predicts n = 3 and the canonical particle-wind, magnetic-dipole-radiation, and quadrupole-radiation torque mechanisms predict n = 1, 3, and 5 respectively?
self_contained_problem:
For an isolated rotating neutron star (pulsar) with angular velocity Ω(t), define the observational braking index by

  n = Ω Ω̈ / (Ω̇)²,

equivalently obtained from a spin-down law Ω̇ = −K Ω^n with K constant. The standard canonical torque mechanisms predict the following discrete values: n = 1 for a pure relativistic particle wind, n = 3 for pure magnetic dipole radiation in vacuum (the MDR model), and n = 5 for pure magnetic quadrupole radiation. Observationally, however, several isolated pulsars have measured braking indices, accurate to within a few percent or better, lying strictly between these predictions, in the approximate range 1 < n < 2.8.

Problem: Construct a physical spin-down model for an isolated pulsar — specifying the torque(s), magnetospheric configuration, and any time evolution of relevant quantities (such as magnetic field strength, magnetic inclination angle, moment of inertia, or particle outflow) — that yields, in a self-consistent way, braking indices continuously taking values in the observed range 1 < n < 2.8, and that quantitatively reproduces the precisely measured n values of the known isolated pulsars without requiring fine-tuning beyond what is astrophysically justified.
status_search_result: Recent literature continues to propose modifications to the magnetic-dipole-radiation model — including combined particle wind plus dipole torques, time-varying inclination angle or magnetic field, magnetospheric reconnection, and effective-force corrections — to account for braking indices in the range 1 < n < 3, but no single model has been broadly accepted as quantitatively reproducing all measured values. The problem is generally treated as still open.

paper_title: Algorithmic Information Theory: Open Problems
original_question: Every Chaitin-random string is Kolmogorov-random, but not conversely. Identify natural properties associated with randomness that hold for Chaitin-random strings but fail for Kolmogorov-random strings.
self_contained_problem:
Let $U$ be a fixed universal Turing machine and let $V$ be a fixed universal prefix-free Turing machine (i.e., a universal machine whose domain is a prefix-free subset of $\{0,1\}^*$). For a finite binary string $\sigma\in\{0,1\}^*$ of length $n$, define the plain Kolmogorov complexity
$$C(\sigma)=\min\{|p|:U(p)=\sigma\}$$
and the prefix-free (Chaitin) complexity
$$K(\sigma)=\min\{|p|:V(p)=\sigma\}.$$
Fix a constant $c\ge 0$. Call $\sigma$ Kolmogorov $c$-random if $C(\sigma)\ge n-c$, and Chaitin $c$-random if $K(\sigma)\ge n-c$.

It is known that every Chaitin random string is Kolmogorov random (up to an additive constant), but the converse fails: there exist strings that are Kolmogorov random yet not Chaitin random.

Problem. Identify and rigorously formulate natural ``randomness'' properties $P$ on finite binary strings such that:
(i) every Chaitin random string satisfies $P$ (uniformly in the randomness deficiency), and
(ii) there exist Kolmogorov random strings that fail to satisfy $P$.

In other words, exhibit intrinsic combinatorial, statistical, or computability-theoretic features that distinguish Chaitin randomness from Kolmogorov randomness on finite strings.
status_search_result: The question, as posed, is a vague/open-ended request to discover natural separating properties between Chaitin (prefix-free) and plain Kolmogorov randomness for finite strings. Standard references (Downey–Hirschfeldt, Li–Vitányi, Scholarpedia) discuss the technical advantages of prefix-free complexity (e.g., subadditivity $K(\sigma\tau)\le K(\sigma)+K(\tau)+O(1)$, the coding theorem, and links to Martin-Löf randomness via $\Omega$), but no definitive list of "natural randomness properties" cleanly resolving this informal problem appears to be established. Status remains unclear.

context_brief: Magnetic-field and magnetospheric origins of n < 3
original_question: In magnetic-dipole-radiation spin-down of isolated pulsars, where the torque coefficient C is proportional to μ² sin²α, μ is the magnetic moment, and α is the inclination angle between the magnetic moment and the rotation axis, do μ, sin α, magnetic-field structure, plasma outflow, magnetospheric currents, or rotationally driven effects such as phase transitions, density profiles, and superfluidity evolve in a way that lowers the braking index below n = 3 as the pulsar spins down?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an isolated, rotating neutron star (pulsar) with angular frequency Ω whose spin-down is governed by a torque of the form

    Ω̇ = −C Ω^n,

where n is the braking index and the torque coefficient C is proportional to μ² sin²α, with μ the magnetic dipole moment of the star and α the inclination angle between the magnetic moment and the rotation axis. The canonical magnetic-dipole-radiation model gives n = 3, but observations of several young pulsars yield steady-state braking indices strictly less than 3.

Determine whether, and by what mechanism, the quantities entering C — namely μ (and the underlying interior/exterior magnetic-field structure), sin α, plus additional contributions to the spin-down torque from non-dipolar field components, plasma outflow and magnetospheric currents, and rotationally driven internal effects (such as phase transitions, evolving density profiles, and superfluid components) — evolve as the pulsar spins down so as to produce a measured braking index n < 3. original_question: Can one prove that a classical open question in number theory, such as the Riemann hypothesis, is independent of the usual axioms?
self_contained_problem:

More generally, produce any such independence result for a recognized classical open problem of number theory with respect to the usual axioms of mathematics.

paper_title: Algorithmic Information Theory: Open Problems
original_question: Constructive mathematics is mathematics together with the assumption that existence equals computability. Study constructive constructions and objects from the viewpoint of program-size complexity, not only from the viewpoint of dynamic complexities.
self_contained_problem:
Constructive mathematics is, informally, ordinary mathematics together with the principle that "existence equals computability": every existence claim must be witnessed by an algorithm that produces the asserted object. Within this framework, constructive proofs yield programs, and constructive objects (real numbers, functions, sequences, structures, etc.) are presented as algorithms together with moduli of convergence or other effectivity data.

Traditionally, the complexity of such constructive constructions has been analyzed through "dynamic" measures such as time and space resource bounds on the programs that realize them. A complementary, less developed viewpoint is provided by program-size (Kolmogorov / algorithmic information) complexity: the length, in bits, of the shortest program (in a fixed universal description language) that realizes a given constructive object or carries out a given constructive proof.

Develop a systematic theory of constructive mathematics from the viewpoint of program-size complexity. Concretely:

1. Formulate a precise notion of program-size complexity K(X) of a constructive object X (for instance, a constructive real, a constructive function on a constructive metric space, or an effectively presented algebraic structure), via the length of the shortest program that, when run in a fixed universal model, outputs (or computes arbitrarily good approximations to) X.

2. Extend this to a notion of program-size complexity of a constructive proof, viewed as a program extracted via the "proofs as programs" / realizability correspondence, and study how proof-theoretic transformations (cut elimination, normalization, double-negation translation, A-translation, etc.) affect program size.

3. Investigate, for representative theorems and constructions of constructive analysis, algebra, and topology, the program-size complexity of the canonical constructive witnesses, and prove nontrivial upper and lower bounds.

4. Identify analogues, in the program-size setting, of classical results about dynamic complexities of constructive objects, and establish trade-offs between program size and time/space resources for constructive realizers.

The task is to carry out such a study and obtain meaningful structural results.
status_search_result: The problem is a broad research program rather than a single precise conjecture. No comprehensive theory of constructive mathematics from the viewpoint of program-size (Kolmogorov) complexity has been established; the suggestion remains an open-ended direction.

paper_title: Braking index of isolated pulsars: open questions and ways forward
original_question: Can the pulsar braking law be modeled as the polynomial spin-down equation Ω̇ = −s(t)Ω − r(t)Ω³ − g(t)Ω⁵, where s(t), r(t), and g(t) represent wind, magnetic-dipole-radiation, and quadrupole torque mechanisms respectively, so that known low-frequency braking-index measurements can be fitted without detailed knowledge of magnetic-field or composition evolution, the combined wind and magnetic-dipole terms can constrain the magnetic field, and high-frequency extensions can probe mechanisms involving mass, composition, magnetic field, or other neutron-star properties?
