paper_title: Multi-D magnetohydrodynamic modelling of pulsar wind nebulae: recent progress and open questions
original_question: Where within the Crab Nebula are the gamma-ray flares produced, and can stochastic magnetic reconnection in thin current sheets near the termination shock or at the jet base accelerate particles to PeV energies on the observed hour-to-day timescales?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the Crab Nebula, a pulsar wind nebula powered by a young rotating neutron star, in which sporadic gamma-ray flares with photon energies extending above ~100 MeV have been observed on timescales of hours to days. Within ideal relativistic magnetohydrodynamics (MHD), the electric field magnitude is bounded by the magnetic field magnitude (E ≤ B), and synchrotron emission from particles accelerated under this constraint cuts off at approximately 200 MeV; the observed flare photons therefore require acceleration in regions where the ideal-MHD bound is violated, with a candidate mechanism being stochastic magnetic reconnection in thin current sheets where a non-ideal (reconnection) electric field can accelerate particles to PeV energies. Determine:

(a) the precise spatial location(s) within the Crab Nebula at which the gamma-ray flares are produced — in particular, whether they originate in the termination-shock region, at the base of the polar jet, or elsewhere; and

(b) whether stochastic magnetic reconnection in thin current sheets at such locations can self-consistently accelerate electrons (and/or positrons) to PeV energies, and produce the corresponding synchrotron gamma-ray emission, on the observed flare rise/decay timescales of hours to days, given the inferred local magnetic field strengths and plasma parameters of the nebula.
category_tag: Relativistic MHD and particle acceleration in pulsar wind nebulae
status_search_result: The exact location of the Crab gamma-ray flare emission and the detailed mechanism by which particles are accelerated to PeV energies on hour-to-day timescales remain unresolved. No optical/X-ray counterpart has been identified, and while relativistic magnetic reconnection (in the termination-shock region or jet base) is the leading candidate and has been shown via PIC and MHD simulations to plausibly produce the required acceleration, current models cannot yet pinpoint the location or fully reproduce flare statistics. Recent reviews continue to list the flare origin as an open question.

paper_title: Some Open Problems Concerning Orthogonal Polynomials on Fractals and Related Questions
original_question: Let K be a regular non-polar compact subset of the real line, let α be the leftmost endpoint of K, and suppose that for every c in R \ K the equilibrium measure satisfies μ_K([α, c]) ∈ Q. What structural consequences does this rationality condition force on K? In particular, must K be a polynomial generalized Julia set? Does it imply the existence of a sequence of admissible polynomials (f_n)_{n=1}^∞ such that the sets F_n^{-1}([-1,1]) form a decreasing sequence with K = ⋂_{n=1}^∞ F_n^{-1}([-1,1])?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. For a compact set $K\subset\mathbb{R}$ of positive logarithmic capacity (i.e. non-polar), let $\mu_K$ denote its (logarithmic) equilibrium measure, that is, the unique Borel probability measure on $K$ minimizing the logarithmic energy $I(\mu)=\iint\log\frac{1}{|x-y|}\,d\mu(x)\,d\mu(y)$. The set $K$ is called regular if its associated Green function (with pole at infinity) is continuous on $\mathbb{C}$. A polynomial $f(z)=a_d z^d+\cdots$ of degree $d\ge 2$ is called admissible (in the real generalized-Julia-set sense) if $f^{-1}([-1,1])\subset\mathbb{R}$ and the preimage consists of $d$ disjoint closed intervals. Given a sequence of admissible polynomials $(f_n)_{n\ge 1}$, set $F_n=f_n\circ f_{n-1}\circ\cdots\circ f_1$. Then $K=\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} F_n^{-1}([-1,1])$ (when this intersection is non-empty and the sets are nested decreasingly) is called a (real) polynomial generalized Julia set.
\medskip

Problem. Let $K\subset\mathbb{R}$ be a regular non-polar compact set, and let $\alpha=\min K$ be its leftmost endpoint. Suppose that
$$\mu_K\bigl([\alpha,c]\bigr)\in\mathbb{Q}\qquad\text{for every }c\in\mathbb{R}\setminus K.$$
What structural properties must $K$ possess? In particular:

(i) Must $K$ be a polynomial generalized Julia set?

(ii) Must there exist a sequence of admissible polynomials $(f_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}$ such that the sets $F_n^{-1}([-1,1])$ form a decreasing sequence with
$$K=\bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} F_n^{-1}([-1,1])?$$
category_tag: Potential theory and orthogonal polynomials on Julia sets
status_search_result: A web search did not surface any published resolution of this rationality-of-equilibrium-mass characterization problem. Related work by Goncharov, Alpan and others on weakly equilibrium Cantor-type sets and orthogonal polynomials on generalized Julia sets continues to develop, but no source identified establishes or disproves that the rationality condition on $\mu_K([\alpha,c])$ forces $K$ to be a polynomial generalized Julia set.

Setup. Let $(f_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be a sequence of polynomials $f_n(z)=a_{n,d_n}z^{d_n}+\cdots+a_{n,0}$ with complex coefficients and $\deg f_n=d_n\ge 2$. For $n\ge 1$ set $F_n:=f_n\circ f_{n-1}\circ\cdots\circ f_1$, and define the (generalized) filled-in Julia set and Julia set of the sequence by
$$K(f_n):=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:(F_n(z))_{n\ge 1}\text{ is bounded}\},\qquad J(f_n):=\partial K(f_n).$$
The sequence $(f_n)$ is called a regular polynomial sequence if there exist constants $A_n,\widetilde{A}_n>0$ and $L\ge 0$ with $\sup_n\widetilde{A}_n<\infty$ such that
$$|a_{n,d_n}|\,|z|^{d_n}\bigl(1-A_n|z|^{-1}\bigr)\le |f_n(z)|\le |a_{n,d_n}|\,|z|^{d_n}\bigl(1+\widetilde A_n|z|^{-1}\bigr)\quad(|z|\ge L\widetilde A_n),$$
together with the standard non-degeneracy conditions ensuring that $K(f_n)$ is a non-polar compact set. Under these conditions $K(f_n)$ admits a unique equilibrium measure (i.e., the measure of minimal logarithmic energy) $\mu_{J(f_n)}$, supported on $J(f_n)$.

$$\dim_H\bigl(\mu_{J(f_n)}\bigr):=\inf\{\dim_H(E):E\text{ Borel},\ \mu_{J(f_n)}(E)=\mu_{J(f_n)}(\mathbb{C})\}$$
of the equilibrium measure of the generalized Julia set $J(f_n)$ associated with an arbitrary regular polynomial sequence $(f_n)$.

paper_title: Crystal Nucleation in Liquids: Open Questions and Future Challenges in Molecular Dynamics Simulations
original_question: How can heterogeneous crystal nucleation be simulated atomistically for increasingly realistic interfaces, including the interfacial detail needed for reliable force fields, while still extracting general trends that are not tied to a single material system?
self_contained_problem:
Heterogeneous crystal nucleation refers to the formation of a crystalline phase from a metastable liquid (or supersaturated/supercooled fluid) in the presence of a foreign interface (e.g., a substrate, impurity, container wall, or another solid surface), where the interface lowers the nucleation barrier compared to homogeneous nucleation in the bulk. In molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, the system is described by a set of atomic positions evolving under classical equations of motion governed by an interatomic potential (force field) U(r_1,...,r_N), and rare-event sampling techniques (e.g., metadynamics, forward-flux sampling, seeding, transition path sampling) are used to estimate nucleation rates J and free-energy barriers ΔG* as functions of thermodynamic conditions (temperature T, pressure p, supersaturation Δμ) and of properties of the foreign interface (chemistry, lattice mismatch, roughness, wettability/contact angle θ, curvature).

Develop a quantitative atomistic simulation framework that simultaneously achieves the following:

(i) Realistic interfaces: prescribe a methodology for performing MD simulations of heterogeneous nucleation in which the substrate/interface is modeled with sufficient atomistic detail (chemical composition, surface termination, defect structure, finite temperature reconstruction, and electrostatic/polarization response) that the resulting nucleation rates and pathways are quantitatively reliable for the chosen force field, including a specification of the minimal interfacial features that the force field must reproduce in order to predict ΔG* and J within a target accuracy.

(ii) Transferable trends: from such simulations, extract general, possibly non-material-specific scaling laws or functional relationships of the form J = J(Δμ, T, X) and ΔG* = ΔG*(Δμ, T, X), where X is a small set of dimensionless interfacial descriptors (e.g., normalized lattice mismatch, contact angle, reduced curvature, interfacial stiffness ratio), such that the laws hold across distinct material systems within a quantified error.

State precisely the descriptors X, the class of force fields and interfaces for which the framework is valid, and prove or provide numerical evidence of the transferability of the resulting trends across at least two structurally and chemically different liquid–substrate systems.
status_search_result: Heterogeneous nucleation in atomistic MD remains an active research topic. Recent reviews and studies (2020–2025) continue to report progress on specific systems (ice on various substrates, metals, NaCl) but still emphasize the lack of transferable, material-independent trends and the difficulty of simulating sufficiently realistic interfaces with accurate force fields. No general framework satisfying both desiderata has been established.

paper_title: 1-Bend 3-D Orthogonal Box-Drawings: Two Open Problems Solved
original_question: For the complete graph K_n, does there exist a three-dimensional orthogonal cube-drawing in which each edge route has at most one bend and each vertex is represented by a cube whose surface area is O(n), equivalently a degree-restricted 1-bend cube-drawing for K_n?
self_contained_problem: A three-dimensional orthogonal box-drawing of a simple graph $G=(V,E)$ assigns to each vertex $v\in V$ an axis-aligned box (a rectangular parallelepiped with integer coordinates) in $\mathbb{R}^3$, with pairwise disjoint interiors, and to each edge $\{u,v\}\in E$ an axis-parallel polygonal route from a point on the surface of the box of $u$ to a point on the surface of the box of $v$. Distinct edge routes may share points only at common endpoints on box surfaces, and an edge route may not pass through the interior of any box. A drawing is called \emph{1-bend} if every edge route consists of at most two axis-parallel segments (i.e., has at most one bend). A drawing is called a \emph{cube-drawing} if every vertex box is a cube. A cube-drawing is called \emph{degree-restricted} if for every vertex $v$ the surface area of its cube is $O(\deg(v))$; equivalently, for the complete graph $K_n$ this means each vertex cube has surface area $O(n)$ (so side length $O(\sqrt{n})$).\n\nQuestion: Does there exist, for every $n$, a 1-bend degree-restricted three-dimensional orthogonal cube-drawing of the complete graph $K_n$?
status_search_result: The problem is reported as resolved in the negative: $K_n$ does not admit a 1-bend degree-restricted cube-drawing, so no such drawing exists for sufficiently large $n$.

paper_title: Crystal Nucleation in Liquids: Open Questions and Future Challenges in Molecular Dynamics Simulations
original_question: Can classical nucleation theory be improved into a universal theoretical framework for crystal nucleation in liquids, or do the system-specific behaviors of different supercooled liquids mean that progress will require different ad hoc variants of classical nucleation theory and different tailored enhanced-sampling methods for different classes of systems and conditions?
self_contained_problem:
Classical nucleation theory (CNT) models the rate of formation of a new (crystalline) phase from a metastable (supercooled liquid) parent phase by treating an emerging nucleus as a spherical cluster whose free energy of formation is written as the sum of a negative bulk term proportional to its volume (driven by the chemical potential difference Δμ between the two phases) and a positive surface term proportional to its area (governed by an effective interfacial free energy γ). The resulting free-energy barrier ΔG* and the steady-state nucleation rate J = A exp(−ΔG*/kBT) depend on Δμ, γ, the attachment kinetics, and a Zeldovich factor.

Different classes of supercooled liquids (e.g., simple atomic liquids, metallic alloys, network-forming liquids such as water and silica, colloidal suspensions, molecular liquids with complex polymorphism) exhibit qualitatively distinct nucleation behaviors, including non-classical multi-step pathways, pre-critical ordering, polymorph selection, and strongly non-spherical or diffuse interfaces, which are not captured by the standard CNT ansatz.

Question: Does there exist a single universal extension or refinement of classical nucleation theory — together with a corresponding universal enhanced-sampling computational framework — that quantitatively predicts crystal nucleation rates and pathways across all such classes of supercooled liquids and thermodynamic conditions; or is it instead the case that any quantitatively predictive theoretical and computational treatment must necessarily be system-specific, requiring different tailored variants of CNT and different tailored sampling techniques for different classes of systems?
status_search_result: The question is a broad, conceptual open problem in the theory of crystal nucleation. It is not a precisely formulated mathematical conjecture with a definitive resolution, and current literature continues to develop both system-specific extensions of CNT (e.g., two-step nucleation, non-classical pathways) and specialized enhanced-sampling methods, with no universal framework established. The status is therefore open in the sense that no universal theory has been demonstrated, while the meta-question of whether such universality is even achievable remains debated.

original_question: Given a modulus of continuity ω, find a compact set K such that the Green function g_{C\K} itself has two-sided pointwise bounds controlled by ω in terms of the distance to K. Specifically, for δ = dist(z, K) small enough, determine K so that there exist constants C1, C2 > 0 and δ0 > 0 with C1 ω(δ) ≤ g_{C\K}(z) ≤ C2 ω(δ) whenever δ ≤ δ0, uniformly in z.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\omega:[0,\infty)	o[0,\infty)$ be a modulus of continuity (i.e., $\omega$ is non-decreasing, continuous, subadditive, with $\omega(0)=0$). For a non-polar compact set $K\subset\mathbb{C}$, denote by $g_{\mathbb{C}\setminus K}(z)$ the Green function of the unbounded component of $\mathbb{C}\setminus K$ with logarithmic pole at infinity, extended by $0$ on $K$. For $z\in\mathbb{C}$, set $\delta:=\operatorname{dist}(z,K)$.

Problem: Construct a compact set $K=K(\omega)\subset\mathbb{C}$ and find constants $C_1,C_2>0$ and $\delta_0>0$ (independent of $z$) such that the two-sided pointwise estimate
$$ C_1\,\omega(\delta)\;\le\;g_{\mathbb{C}\setminus K}(z)\;\le\;C_2\,\omega(\delta) $$
holds for every $z$ with $0<\delta=\operatorname{dist}(z,K)\le\delta_0$.
status_search_result: Partial results are available: for specific moduli of continuity (notably the logarithmic modulus $\varphi(\delta)=1/\log(1/\delta)$ and certain Hölder-type moduli), Cantor-type sets with the desired two-sided pointwise Green function bounds have been constructed (e.g., via weakly equilibrium Cantor-type sets and rarefied Cantor sets). The general problem—prescribing an arbitrary modulus of continuity $\omega$ and producing a compact set giving the matched two-sided bound—does not appear to be settled in full generality.

original_question: Characterize which asymptotic growth rates of the Markov factors M_n(K) mark the boundary of the so-called zone of uncertainty for the extension property of a compact set K. In other words, determine the growth regimes of Markov's factors that separate cases where the extension property is forced from cases where it fails or is not determined by those growth rates.
self_contained_problem:
Let $K \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be an infinite compact set. For each integer $n \geq 1$, define the $n$-th Markov factor of $K$ by
$$M_n(K) = \sup\Big\{\frac{\|P'\|_K}{\|P\|_K} : P \in \mathbb{R}[x_1,\dots,x_d],\ \deg P \leq n,\ P|_K \not\equiv 0\Big\},$$
where $\|\cdot\|_K$ denotes the supremum norm on $K$ and $\|P'\|_K$ is taken to be the maximum of the supremum norms of the partial derivatives of $P$ on $K$.

Say that $K$ has the extension property if there exists a continuous linear operator $E : \mathcal{E}(K) \to C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d)$ that extends every Whitney jet on $K$ to a $C^\infty$-function on $\mathbb{R}^d$.

It is known that:
(i) if $M_n(K)$ grows at most polynomially in $n$ (i.e., $K$ has Markov's property), then $K$ has the extension property;
(ii) there exist compact sets $K$ with arbitrarily fast growth of $M_n(K)$ that nevertheless possess the extension property, and there exist compact sets without the extension property whose Markov factors grow rapidly.

Hence there is a "zone of uncertainty": a range of asymptotic growth rates of $M_n(K)$ within which the growth alone neither forces nor precludes the extension property.

Problem. Characterize the asymptotic growth rates of $M_n(K)$ that mark the boundaries of this zone of uncertainty for the extension property; that is, identify the growth regimes of $(M_n(K))_{n\geq 1}$ which separate the cases where the extension property is forced from the cases where it fails or where the growth alone does not determine it.
category_tag: Markov factors and Whitney extension property
status_search_result: Search results indicate the problem belongs to Goncharov's program on Mityagin's extension problem. It is established that the extension property cannot be characterized purely in terms of the growth of Markov factors (a compact set without Markov's property but with an extension operator exists). Characterizing the precise boundaries of the zone of uncertainty in terms of the growth rate of $M_n(K)$ does not appear to have been resolved; it remains an open problem in this circle of questions.

original_question: Let K be a non-polar compact subset of the real line, let μ_K denote its equilibrium measure, let P_n(·; μ_K) be the nth monic orthogonal polynomial for μ_K, let Z_n(μ_K) be the zero set of P_n(·; μ_K), and let U_n(μ_K) = inf{|x - x'| : x ≠ x' and x, x' ∈ Z_n(μ_K)} be the minimal spacing between distinct zeros. Is there a general relationship between this zero spacing and the smoothness of the Green function g_{C\K}? Is there also a general relationship between the zero spacing for μ_K and the Markov factors associated with K?
self_contained_problem:
Let $K \subset \mathbb{R}$ be a non-polar compact set, and let $\mu_K$ denote its logarithmic equilibrium measure (the unique Borel probability measure on $K$ minimizing the logarithmic energy $\iint \log\frac{1}{|x-y|}\,d\mu(x)d\mu(y)$). Let $g_{\mathbb{C}\setminus K}$ denote the Green function of the unbounded component of $\mathbb{C}\setminus K$ with pole at infinity, extended by $0$ to $K$. For each integer $n\ge 1$, let $P_n(\cdot;\mu_K)$ be the $n$th monic orthogonal polynomial with respect to $\mu_K$, let
$$Z_n(\mu_K) := \{x\in\mathbb{R} : P_n(x;\mu_K)=0\},$$
and define the minimal zero spacing
$$U_n(\mu_K) := \inf\{|x-x'| : x,x'\in Z_n(\mu_K),\ x\neq x'\}.$$
Recall that the $n$th Markov factor of $K$ is
$$M_n(K) := \sup_{\deg P \le n,\ P\not\equiv 0} \frac{\|P'\|_{L^\infty(K)}}{\|P\|_{L^\infty(K)}}.$$

(a) Establish a general quantitative relationship between the asymptotic behavior of $U_n(\mu_K)$ as $n\to\infty$ and the modulus of continuity / smoothness properties of the Green function $g_{\mathbb{C}\setminus K}$.

(b) Establish a general quantitative relationship between the asymptotic behavior of $U_n(\mu_K)$ and the Markov factors $M_n(K)$.
status_search_result: A targeted web search returned related work on equilibrium measures, Green-function smoothness, and Markov-type inequalities for compact subsets of the real line, but no source establishing a definitive general relationship of the type asked, nor a clear announcement that the problem has been resolved. The question appears to remain a guiding open problem in the area, but no conclusive solution was located.

paper_title: Some Open Problems Concerning Orthogonal Polynomials on Fractals and Related Questions
context_brief: Bounded Widom factors beyond Parreau-Widom sets
original_question: Does there exist a regular non-polar compact subset K of the real line that is not a Parreau-Widom set but nevertheless has bounded Widom factors (W_n(K))_{n=1}^∞? More specifically, if K has zero Lebesgue measure, must the sequence (W_n(K))_{n=1}^∞ be unbounded? The paper also asks the analogous pair of questions with the sequence (W_n^2(μ_K))_{n=1}^∞ in place of (W_n(K))_{n=1}^∞.
self_contained_problem:
Let K ⊂ ℝ be a non-polar compact set (i.e. of positive logarithmic capacity cap(K) > 0) that is regular for the Dirichlet problem in the unbounded component of ℂ ∖ K. Let G_K denote the Green function of this unbounded component with logarithmic pole at infinity, and let μ_K be the equilibrium measure of K.

For each n ≥ 1, let T_{n,K} be the n-th Chebyshev polynomial of K, that is, the unique monic polynomial of degree n that minimizes the sup-norm ‖P‖_{L^∞(K)} among all monic polynomials P of degree n. Define the (sup-norm) Widom factor
   W_n(K) := ‖T_{n,K}‖_{L^∞(K)} / cap(K)^n.

Similarly, for each n ≥ 1 let T_{n,μ_K}^{(2)} be the monic polynomial of degree n that minimizes ‖P‖_{L^2(μ_K)}, and define the L^2 Widom factor
   W_n^2(μ_K) := ‖T_{n,μ_K}^{(2)}‖_{L^2(μ_K)} / cap(K)^n.

Recall that K is called a Parreau–Widom set if Σ_j G_K(c_j) < ∞, where the sum is taken over all critical points c_j of G_K in ℂ ∖ K. (Every Parreau–Widom subset of ℝ has positive Lebesgue measure.)

Answer the following:

(a) Does there exist a regular non-polar compact set K ⊂ ℝ that is not a Parreau–Widom set but for which the sequence (W_n(K))_{n=1}^∞ is bounded?

(b) If K ⊂ ℝ is a regular non-polar compact set with Lebesgue measure zero, must (W_n(K))_{n=1}^∞ be unbounded?

(c) The same two questions with (W_n^2(μ_K))_{n=1}^∞ in place of (W_n(K))_{n=1}^∞.
category_tag: Widom factors and orthogonal polynomials on fractals
status_search_result: Recent work (e.g. constructions of zero-measure non-polar Cantor sets with prescribed unbounded growth of L^2 Widom factors, 2025) provides further examples of unbounded Widom factors on zero-measure sets but does not characterize all such sets, nor does it produce a non-Parreau–Widom regular compact set in ℝ with bounded Widom factors. The general questions appear to remain open.

paper_title: Some Open Problems Concerning Orthogonal Polynomials on Fractals and Related Questions
original_question: Let K be a non-polar compact subset of the real line such that its equilibrium measure μ_K coincides with a Hausdorff measure restricted to K. Must it follow that the Hausdorff dimension of K is equal to 0?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. For a compact set $K\subset\mathbb{R}$, the logarithmic capacity of $K$ is
$$\operatorname{cap}(K)=\exp\!\Big(-\inf_{\mu}\iint\log\tfrac{1}{|x-y|}\,d\mu(x)\,d\mu(y)\Big),$$
where the infimum is taken over all Borel probability measures $\mu$ supported on $K$. The set $K$ is called non-polar if $\operatorname{cap}(K)>0$, in which case the infimum above is attained by a unique probability measure $\mu_K$ supported on $K$, called the equilibrium measure of $K$.

For $s\ge 0$, the $s$-dimensional Hausdorff measure of a Borel set $E\subset\mathbb{R}$ is
$$\mathcal{H}^s(E)=\lim_{\delta\to 0^+}\inf\Big\{\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}(\operatorname{diam} U_i)^s:\ E\subset\bigcup_i U_i,\ \operatorname{diam} U_i\le\delta\Big\}.$$
More generally, given a non-decreasing continuous gauge function $h:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ with $h(0)=0$, the associated Hausdorff measure $\mathcal{H}^h$ is defined analogously with $(\operatorname{diam} U_i)^s$ replaced by $h(\operatorname{diam} U_i)$. The Hausdorff dimension of $K$ is $\dim_H(K)=\inf\{s\ge 0:\mathcal{H}^s(K)=0\}$.

Problem. Suppose $K\subset\mathbb{R}$ is a non-polar compact set whose equilibrium measure $\mu_K$ coincides (up to a positive multiplicative constant) with the restriction of some Hausdorff measure $\mathcal{H}^h$ to $K$. Must it then follow that $\dim_H(K)=0$?
status_search_result: Web searches surface related work by Alpan and Goncharov on equilibrium measures of Cantor-type sets, where in many cases the equilibrium measure is shown to be mutually singular with the Hausdorff measure of the set, but no source was found that resolves the question in full generality. The status appears to remain open, but no definitive recent confirmation was located.

original_question: Can finite-time blowup occur for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations Dt u + ∇p = νΔu + f with ∇·u = 0, in the sense that a solution loses regularity in finite time, and how should this mathematical blowup problem be understood in the temporal-limit study of closed-system turbulence?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on $\mathbb{R}^3$ (or on the torus $\mathbb{T}^3$) for a velocity field $u(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^3$ and pressure $p(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}$:
$$\partial_t u + (u\cdot
abla)u + 
abla p = 
u\,\Delta u + f, \qquad 
abla\cdot u = 0,$$
with viscosity $
u>0$, smooth divergence-free initial data $u_0$ of finite energy, and smooth (say, zero or smooth compactly supported / smooth periodic) external forcing $f$.

A smooth solution is said to exhibit finite-time blowup if there exists $T^*<\infty$ such that the solution $u$ is smooth on $[0,T^*)$ but $\limsup_{t	o T^{*-}}\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{H^s}=\infty$ for some $s$ large enough (equivalently, the solution loses regularity at $T^*$).

Question: Does there exist smooth, divergence-free initial data $u_0$ (with $f\equiv 0$, say) of finite energy such that the corresponding solution to the above equations develops finite-time blowup? Equivalently, prove or disprove that for every such initial datum the solution remains smooth for all $t\ge 0$.
status_search_result: The global regularity / finite-time blowup problem for the 3D incompressible Navier-Stokes equations is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems and remains open as of 2026. No proof of either global regularity or of finite-time blowup for smooth finite-energy data is known; recent work (e.g., on hypodissipative or generalized models, and Tao's averaged Navier-Stokes blowup result) has provided partial insight but not resolved the original problem.

paper_title: 1-Bend 3-D Orthogonal Box-Drawings: Two Open Problems Solved
original_question: For the complete graph K_n, must every three-dimensional orthogonal box-drawing in which each edge route has at most one bend have total volume Ω(n^3)?
self_contained_problem:
A three-dimensional orthogonal box-drawing of a simple graph G = (V, E) assigns to each vertex v ∈ V an axis-aligned box B_v ⊂ ℝ^3 with integer coordinates, such that the boxes have pairwise disjoint interiors. Each edge uv ∈ E is drawn as a polygonal curve made of axis-parallel segments whose endpoints lie on the surfaces of B_u and B_v respectively, with the interior of the curve disjoint from every box and from the other edge curves except at common endpoints. A bend of an edge route is an interior point of the curve where two segments of different axis directions meet. The drawing is called 1-bend if every edge route has at most one bend. The volume of the drawing is the volume of the smallest axis-aligned bounding box containing the union of all vertex boxes and edge routes (equivalently, the product of the side lengths of the integer bounding box).

Question: Let K_n be the complete graph on n vertices. Must every 1-bend three-dimensional orthogonal box-drawing of K_n have volume Ω(n^3)?
status_search_result: The problem is reported as solved: any 1-bend 3-D orthogonal box-drawing of K_n has volume Ω(n^3), obtained as a corollary of a more general lower bound for 1-bend drawings of dense bipartite-like graphs G_{n,n-1}.

paper_title: Two Open Problems in the Fixed Point Theory of Contractive Type Mappings on First-Countable Quasimetric Spaces
context_brief: Fixed points of contractions on complete F-symmetric spaces
original_question: Let (X, d) be a complete F-symmetric space. This means that d is a distance satisfying d(x, y) >= 0 for all x, y in X and d(x, y) + d(y, x) = 0 if and only if x = y, that d is symmetric in the sense that d(x, y) = d(y, x) for all x, y in X, and that d satisfies the F-condition: for every epsilon > 0 there exists delta = delta(epsilon) > 0 such that d(x, y) <= delta and d(y, z) <= delta imply d(x, z) <= epsilon. A sequence {x_n} is Cauchy if lim_{n,m->infinity} d(x_n, x_m) = 0, converges to x if lim_{n->infinity} d(x, x_n) = 0, and the space is complete if every Cauchy sequence converges in this sense. If g : X -> X is a contraction, meaning that there exists a constant lambda with 0 <= lambda < 1 such that d(g(x), g(y)) <= lambda d(x, y) for all x, y in X, must g have a fixed point?

paper_title: 1-Bend 3-D Orthogonal Box-Drawings: Two Open Problems Solved
original_question: Does every graph admit a three-dimensional orthogonal box-drawing in which each edge route has at most one bend and the total volume is O(Δ n^2), where n is the number of vertices and Δ is the maximum degree?
self_contained_problem:
Consider three-dimensional orthogonal box-drawings of simple graphs. In such a drawing, each vertex v of a graph G=(V,E) is represented by an axis-aligned rectangular box (with integer coordinates) in the 3D grid Z^3, the interiors of the boxes are pairwise disjoint, and each edge uv∈E is drawn as a polyline made of axis-parallel segments that starts on the surface of the box for u, ends on the surface of the box for v, has all interior points disjoint from every vertex box and from every other edge route, and uses only edges of the integer grid. A "bend" of an edge route is an interior point where two consecutive segments meet at a right angle. The "volume" of the drawing is the number of unit grid cells in the smallest axis-aligned bounding box containing the entire drawing.

Let n=|V| and let Δ denote the maximum degree of G. Determine whether the following holds: every (simple) graph G admits a three-dimensional orthogonal box-drawing in which every edge route has at most one bend and the total volume is O(Δ·n^2).

paper_title: THE DIFFUSE LIGHT OF THE UNIVERSE: On the microwave background before and after its discovery: open questions
context_brief: Distance and locality of the 3K radiation
original_question: At what distance, and with what spatial distribution of sources, is the observed 3 K microwave background actually produced? More specifically, is it only a very distant fossil background emitted in the early universe, or could it instead be a more universal radiation field produced partly or wholly locally and at long distances, given that its smooth blackbody spectrum does not itself provide a direct distance measurement?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an isotropic diffuse electromagnetic background that, when measured by an observer, exhibits a near-perfect Planck (blackbody) spectrum with characteristic temperature approximately 2.7 K (the so-called 3 K microwave background). Because a smooth blackbody spectrum carries no intrinsic distance information (no spectral lines, no parallax, no standard-candle structure), the spatial distribution of emitting sources along the line of sight cannot be inferred from the spectrum alone.

Determine, on the basis of independent physical arguments and observational constraints, the spatial origin of this radiation. Specifically:

(a) Is the observed 3 K background produced exclusively as a fossil relic emitted in the early universe at very large cosmological distances (i.e. on a last-scattering surface at high redshift), so that essentially none of the locally measured intensity originates from sources within the observable nearby universe?

(b) Or could a non-negligible fraction of the locally observed intensity be generated by sources distributed throughout space, including local and intermediate-distance regions, so that the 3 K background is a more universal radiation field filling space and produced both nearby and at large distances?

Provide quantitative bounds on the fraction of the observed 3 K intensity that may be attributed to local versus distant sources, using whatever constraints (anisotropy structure, polarization, Sunyaev–Zel'dovich distortions, spectral distortions, correlations with large-scale structure, etc.) can break the degeneracy left by the blackbody spectrum.

paper_title: Some Open Problems on Locally Finite or Locally Nilpotent Derivations and E-Derivations
original_question: Let R be a commutative ring, let A be an R-algebra, and let δ be either an R-derivation of A or an R-E-derivation of A, where an R-E-derivation means an R-linear map of the form I − φ for some R-algebra endomorphism φ of A. For an R-subspace V of A, write r(V) for the set of elements a in A such that a^m lies in V for all sufficiently large m; and say that V is a left, right, or two-sided Mathieu subspace when eventual membership of all powers a^m forces eventual membership of ba^m, a^mc, or ba^mc respectively. The LFNED problem asks for a description of r(δ(I)) for every left, right, or two-sided ideal I of A, asks which R-derivations and R-E-derivations of A have image Im δ = δ(A) that is a Mathieu subspace of the corresponding handedness, and asks which such maps send every left, right, or two-sided ideal I of A to a Mathieu subspace of the corresponding handedness.
self_contained_problem:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with identity and let $A$ be an associative (not necessarily commutative) $R$-algebra. An $R$-derivation of $A$ is an $R$-linear map $\delta:A	o A$ satisfying $\delta(xy)=\delta(x)y+x\delta(y)$ for all $x,y\in A$. An $R$-E-derivation of $A$ is an $R$-linear map of the form $\delta=\mathrm{Id}_A-\varphi$, where $\varphi:A	o A$ is an $R$-algebra endomorphism.

For an $R$-subspace $V\subseteq A$, define the radical of $V$ by
$$r(V)=\{a\in A : a^m\in V	ext{ for all sufficiently large }m\}.$$

Let $\vartheta\in\{	ext{left},	ext{right},	ext{two-sided}\}$. The $R$-subspace $V$ is called a $\vartheta$-Mathieu subspace of $A$ if, whenever $a\in A$ satisfies $a^m\in V$ for every integer $m\ge 1$, then for all $b,c\in A$:

(i) $ba^m\in V$ for all $m\gg 0$, when $\vartheta=	ext{left}$;
(ii) $a^mc\in V$ for all $m\gg 0$, when $\vartheta=	ext{right}$;
(iii) $ba^mc\in V$ for all $m\gg 0$, when $\vartheta=	ext{two-sided}$.

For every commutative ring $R$, every $R$-algebra $A$, and every $R$-derivation or $R$-E-derivation $\delta$ of $A$:

(A) Determine the radical $r(\delta(I))$ for every left, right, or two-sided ideal $I$ of $A$.

(B) Characterize those $\delta$ for which the image $\mathrm{Im}\,\delta=\delta(A)$ is a $\vartheta$-Mathieu subspace of $A$ (for each choice of $\vartheta$).

(C) Characterize those $\delta$ such that $\delta(I)$ is a $\vartheta$-Mathieu subspace of $A$ for every $\vartheta$-ideal $I$ of $A$ (for each choice of $\vartheta$).
status_search_result: The problem is a broad program with many cases; it remains open in general but several special cases have been settled. Affirmative answers are known, e.g., for rank-two locally nilpotent derivations of polynomial algebras, for rank-three homogeneous locally nilpotent derivations on three-variable polynomial rings, and for locally nilpotent derivations of bivariate polynomial algebras over one-dimensional UFDs. The full LFNED problem in its general formulation has not been resolved.

paper_title: 1-Bend 3-D Orthogonal Box-Drawings: Two Open Problems Solved
original_question: If every graph has a three-dimensional orthogonal 1-bend cube-drawing of volume O(Δ^3 n), does it follow that every graph has a three-dimensional orthogonal 1-bend drawing of volume O(Δ^2 m), where m is the number of edges and Δ is the maximum degree?
self_contained_problem:
A 3-dimensional orthogonal box-drawing of a simple graph $G=(V,E)$ assigns each vertex $v\in V$ to an axis-aligned box (a 3-dimensional rectangular parallelepiped with integer coordinates) so that distinct vertex-boxes have disjoint interiors, and assigns each edge $uv\in E$ to an axis-parallel polygonal curve whose endpoints lie on the boundaries of the boxes of $u$ and $v$, such that distinct edge-curves are pairwise interior-disjoint and the interior of each edge-curve avoids all vertex-boxes. The drawing is called a cube-drawing if every vertex-box is a cube. The drawing is called 1-bend if every edge-curve has at most one bend (i.e. consists of at most two axis-parallel segments). The volume of a drawing is the number of unit grid cells in the smallest axis-aligned bounding box that contains the entire drawing. Let $n=|V|$, $m=|E|$, and let $\Delta$ denote the maximum degree of $G$.

Assume the following hypothesis: every simple graph admits a 3-dimensional orthogonal 1-bend cube-drawing of volume $O(\Delta^{3} n)$.

Question: Does this hypothesis imply that every simple graph admits a 3-dimensional orthogonal 1-bend box-drawing of volume $O(\Delta^{2} m)$?

original_question: Let K be a field of characteristic zero, let A be a K-algebra, and let δ be either a locally nilpotent K-derivation of A or a locally nilpotent K-E-derivation of A, where locally nilpotent means that for every a in A there exists m ≥ 1 with δ^m(a) = 0. For each choice of handedness ϑ ∈ {left, right, two-sided}, if I is a ϑ-ideal of A, must the image δ(I) always be a ϑ-Mathieu subspace of A?
self_contained_problem:
Let $K$ be a field of characteristic zero and let $A$ be a $K$-algebra (not necessarily commutative or unital). 

A $K$-linear map $\delta : A \to A$ is called a $K$-derivation if $\delta(ab) = \delta(a)b + a\delta(b)$ for all $a,b \in A$, and a $K$-$\mathcal{E}$-derivation if $\delta = \mathrm{Id}_A - \phi$ for some $K$-algebra endomorphism $\phi$ of $A$. The map $\delta$ is locally nilpotent if for every $a \in A$ there exists an integer $m \geq 1$ (depending on $a$) such that $\delta^m(a) = 0$.

For $\vartheta \in \{\text{left}, \text{right}, \text{two-sided}\}$, a $K$-subspace $V \subseteq A$ is called a $\vartheta$-Mathieu subspace ($\vartheta$-MS) of $A$ if it satisfies the following property: for every $a \in A$ such that $a^m \in V$ for all sufficiently large $m \geq 1$, and for every $b \in A$, one has
- $ba^m \in V$ for all sufficiently large $m$, when $\vartheta = \text{left}$;
- $a^m b \in V$ for all sufficiently large $m$, when $\vartheta = \text{right}$;
- $ba^m c \in V$ for all $b,c \in A$ and all sufficiently large $m$, when $\vartheta = \text{two-sided}$.

A $\vartheta$-ideal of $A$ means a left ideal, right ideal, or two-sided ideal according to $\vartheta$.

Question: Let $\delta$ be either a locally nilpotent $K$-derivation or a locally nilpotent $K$-$\mathcal{E}$-derivation of $A$. For each $\vartheta \in \{\text{left}, \text{right}, \text{two-sided}\}$ and every $\vartheta$-ideal $I$ of $A$, must the image $\delta(I)$ be a $\vartheta$-Mathieu subspace of $A$?

paper_title: 1-Bend 3-D Orthogonal Box-Drawings: Two Open Problems Solved
original_question: For three-dimensional orthogonal graph drawings in which each edge route has at most three bends, what is the correct asymptotic lower bound on the required volume; specifically, for graphs of maximum degree Δ on n vertices, does every graph admit such a drawing of volume O(Δ n^1.5), which would match the known Ramanujan-graph lower bound Ω(Δ n^1.5)?
self_contained_problem:
A 3-dimensional orthogonal drawing of a simple graph G = (V, E) is an assignment of distinct grid points in Z^3 to the vertices of G together with, for each edge uv ∈ E, a polyline route from the point assigned to u to the point assigned to v whose segments are parallel to the coordinate axes, such that distinct edge routes are interior-disjoint and pass through no vertex point other than their endpoints. A bend of an edge route is an interior point at which two consecutive segments meet at a right angle. The volume of the drawing is the number of grid points in the smallest axis-aligned bounding box that contains all vertices and edge routes. A drawing is a k-bend drawing if every edge route has at most k bends.

It is known that for every n there exists an n-vertex Ramanujan graph of maximum degree Δ such that every 3-bend 3-dimensional orthogonal drawing has volume Ω(Δ · n^{3/2}).

Question: Does every graph G on n vertices with maximum degree Δ admit a 3-bend 3-dimensional orthogonal drawing of volume O(Δ · n^{3/2})? Equivalently, determine the correct asymptotic worst-case volume of 3-bend 3-dimensional orthogonal drawings of n-vertex graphs of maximum degree Δ.
status_search_result: Available literature on 3-dimensional orthogonal graph drawing reports an Ω(Δ n^{3/2}) lower bound from Ramanujan graphs and best known upper bounds of order n^3 (or n^{2.5} for K_n) for 3-bend drawings; no source found establishing an O(Δ n^{3/2}) upper bound for general graphs, so the matching question appears to remain open.

original_question: Let K be a field of characteristic zero, let A be a K-algebra, and let (Λ, ∗) be a monoid with unit element e. Suppose A has a K-algebra grading A = ⊕_{λ∈Λ} A_λ such that each A_λ is a K-subspace of A and A_λ A_μ ⊆ A_{λ∗μ} for all λ, μ in Λ. Must the K-subspace formed by all non-unit homogeneous pieces, namely ⊕_{e≠λ∈Λ} A_λ, always be a Mathieu subspace of A?
self_contained_problem:
Let $K$ be a field of characteristic zero (not necessarily algebraically closed), let $A$ be a $K$-algebra, and let $(\Lambda,*)$ be a monoid with unit element $e$. Assume $A$ admits a $K$-algebra grading by $\Lambda$, that is, a decomposition
$$A=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Lambda}A_\lambda$$
into $K$-subspaces $A_\lambda$ satisfying $A_\lambda A_\mu\subseteq A_{\lambda*\mu}$ for all $\lambda,\mu\in\Lambda$.

Recall that a $K$-subspace $M\subseteq A$ is called a Mathieu subspace (or Mathieu–Zhao space) of $A$ if for every $a\in A$ such that $a^m\in M$ for all $m\geq 1$, and for every $b\in A$, there exists $N\geq 1$ (depending on $a,b$) such that $b\,a^m\in M$ for all $m\geq N$.

Question: Must the $K$-subspace
$$\bigoplus_{e\neq\lambda\in\Lambda}A_\lambda$$
consisting of all homogeneous components of non-unit degree always be a Mathieu subspace of $A$?

Web searches did not surface any published resolution; the broader program around Mathieu–Zhao spaces (linked to the Jacobian Conjecture) remains active, and no source claims a proof or counterexample to this particular grading conjecture.

paper_title: Some open problems and research directions in the mathematical study of fluid dynamics.
original_question: Given either an arbitrary infinitely differentiable, incompressible, compactly supported initial velocity field in R^3, or an arbitrary three-dimensional divergence-free periodic real analytic initial velocity field, does the corresponding incompressible Navier-Stokes solution remain smooth for all time?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in three spatial dimensions:
\[ \partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u = \Delta u - \nabla p, \qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0, \]
where $u: [0,\infty)\times\Omega \to \mathbb{R}^3$ is the velocity field and $p:[0,\infty)\times\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ is the pressure, with unit kinematic viscosity. Address each of the following two cases:

(a) Whole space, smooth compactly supported data. Let $\Omega = \mathbb{R}^3$ and let $u_0 \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3;\mathbb{R}^3)$ be an arbitrary divergence-free, smooth, compactly supported initial velocity. Does there exist a unique solution $u \in C^\infty([0,\infty)\times\mathbb{R}^3;\mathbb{R}^3)$ with $u(0,\cdot) = u_0$ that remains smooth (and decaying suitably at infinity, with finite kinetic energy) for all time $t \geq 0$?

(b) Periodic, real analytic data. Let $\Omega = \mathbb{T}^3 = \mathbb{R}^3/\mathbb{Z}^3$ and let $u_0$ be an arbitrary divergence-free real-analytic vector field on $\mathbb{T}^3$. Does there exist a unique solution $u$ with $u(0,\cdot)=u_0$ that is smooth on $[0,\infty)\times\mathbb{T}^3$ for all time $t\geq 0$?

Determine, in each case, whether smoothness is preserved globally in time, or whether finite-time singularities (blow-up) can occur.
status_search_result: The global regularity of solutions to the three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations from smooth initial data (in either the whole-space Schwartz/compactly-supported setting or the periodic real-analytic setting) is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems and remains open as of 2026. No proof of global smoothness or of finite-time blow-up for these classical settings has been accepted.

paper_title: Some open problems and research directions in the mathematical study of fluid dynamics.
original_question: Can the Navier-Stokes regularity problem be reformulated and attacked by classifying time-dependent solution paths according to their qualitative properties, rather than by classifying initial data, and can such a path-based classification capture enough of the nonlinear part of the equation to address regularity?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on $\mathbb{R}^3$ (or on the periodic box $\mathbb{T}^3$) for the velocity field $u:[0,\infty)\times\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^3$ and pressure $p:[0,\infty)\times\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}$:
$$\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u - \nu\Delta u + \nabla p = 0,\qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0,\qquad u(0,\cdot)=u_0,$$
with viscosity $\nu>0$ and divergence-free, sufficiently smooth and decaying initial data $u_0$.

The global regularity problem asks whether, for every smooth divergence-free initial datum $u_0$, there exists a globally defined smooth solution $u$ on $[0,\infty)\times\mathbb{R}^3$ (with appropriate decay), or whether finite-time singularities can develop.

Rather than classifying admissible initial data $u_0$, consider the space $\mathcal{P}$ of all time-dependent solution paths $t\mapsto u(t,\cdot)$ (e.g., Leray-Hopf weak solutions, or suitable weak/mild solutions in a chosen function space). Define on $\mathcal{P}$ qualitative equivalence classes determined by path properties such as: long-time asymptotic behavior, scaling/self-similar structure, energy-dissipation profile, vorticity alignment, frequency cascade behavior, or topological/geometric features of the trajectory in phase space.

The problem: Does there exist such a classification of solution paths in $\mathcal{P}$ by qualitative properties of the trajectory (rather than by properties of the initial data) that
(i) is preserved or sufficiently controlled under the Navier-Stokes evolution,
(ii) captures enough information about the nonlinear term $(u\cdot\nabla)u$ to distinguish regular paths from potentially singular ones, and
(iii) can be used to establish or refute global regularity for the three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations?

Equivalently: can the global regularity question be reformulated and resolved through such a path-based qualitative classification scheme?
status_search_result: The three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes global regularity problem is one of the Clay Millennium Prize Problems and remains open as of 2026. No path-based qualitative classification scheme is known to resolve it; the question posed here is a research direction rather than a settled result.

paper_title: Some open problems and research directions in the mathematical study of fluid dynamics.
original_question: For incompressible Euler or Navier-Stokes flows, can one develop a useful Eulerian theory of mixed Eulerian-Lagrangian quantities, especially nonlinear commutator expressions involving second derivatives of the back-to-labels map A(x,t), where A is the inverse Lagrangian map assigning to a current position x at time t the initial label of the same fluid particle?
self_contained_problem:
Let $u(x,t)$ be a smooth, divergence-free velocity field on $\mathbb{R}^d$ (with $d=2$ or $d=3$) solving either the incompressible Euler equations
\[
\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u + \nabla p = 0, \qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0,
\]
or the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations
\[
\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u + \nabla p = \nu \Delta u, \qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0,
\]
with $\nu>0$. Let $X(a,t)$ denote the Lagrangian flow map defined by $\partial_t X(a,t)=u(X(a,t),t)$, $X(a,0)=a$, and let $A(x,t)$ be the back-to-labels (inverse Lagrangian) map, satisfying $A(X(a,t),t)=a$ and equivalently
\[
\partial_t A + (u\cdot\nabla)A = 0, \qquad A(x,0)=x.
\]
By incompressibility, $A(\cdot,t)$ is volume preserving and $\det(\nabla A)=1$.

Develop an Eulerian theory of mixed Eulerian-Lagrangian quantities built from $u$, $A$, and their derivatives. In particular, identify and analyze nonlinear commutator-type expressions involving the second derivatives $\partial_i\partial_j A^k(x,t)$ (for instance, expressions of schematic form
\[
C^{k}_{ij}[u,A](x,t) := \partial_i\partial_j A^k - (\nabla A)\text{-pullback of the corresponding Eulerian second-derivative object},
\]
and contractions thereof against $\nabla u$, $\nabla^2 u$, or curvature-like tensors of the map $A$) and determine whether such commutator quantities satisfy useful evolution equations, conservation or coercivity properties that can be exploited to obtain new a priori estimates, regularity criteria, or geometric information for the underlying Euler or Navier-Stokes flow.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research direction calling for the development of a new theory; no published work appears to settle it. Related Eulerian-Lagrangian formalisms (e.g. the Constantin formulation using the back-to-labels map) exist, but a systematic theory of nonlinear commutator quantities involving second derivatives of A does not appear to have been established.

original_question: For a mathematical turbulence theory based on Navier-Stokes solution paths, can one characterize the relevant function-space measures supported on those paths, including their existence, whether they are time-independent or time-dependent, whether they are unique, which symmetries they possess, how they depend on parameters, and how they behave under stability and bifurcation questions?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations on a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ ($d=2,3$), with viscosity $\nu>0$ and (possibly) a forcing $f$:
$$\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u - \nu\Delta u + \nabla p = f, \qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0,$$
together with appropriate boundary conditions (e.g.\ periodic on the torus $\mathbb{T}^d$, or no-slip on a bounded domain). Let $\mathcal{P}$ denote the space of weak (Leray–Hopf) solution paths $u:[0,\infty)\to H$, where $H$ is the standard divergence-free $L^2$ space.

Consider Borel probability measures $\mu$ on a suitable function space $\mathcal{X}$ (e.g.\ $C([0,\infty);H_w)$ or $L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$) that are supported on $\mathcal{P}$. One may regard such measures as candidates for describing statistical states of turbulent flow.

Provide a complete mathematical characterization of such measures, including:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Existence:} Construct measures $\mu$ supported on Navier–Stokes solution paths that are physically meaningful (e.g.\ invariant under the flow when applicable, or describing a stationary statistical equilibrium).
\item \textbf{Time dependence:} Determine for which regimes such measures can be chosen time-independent (statistically stationary) versus genuinely time-dependent.
\item \textbf{Uniqueness:} Determine whether, for given parameters $(\nu, f, \Omega, \text{boundary conditions})$, such a measure is unique within natural admissibility classes.
\item \textbf{Symmetries:} Identify which symmetries of the equations (translations, rotations, scaling, parity, etc.) are inherited by $\mu$, and whether spontaneous symmetry breaking can occur.
\item \textbf{Parameter dependence:} Describe the dependence of $\mu$ on $\nu$, on the forcing $f$, and on the geometry of $\Omega$, including limits such as $\nu\to 0$.
\item \textbf{Stability and bifurcations:} Analyze the stability of $\mu$ under perturbations and characterize bifurcations of the family $\{\mu_\lambda\}$ as parameters $\lambda$ vary.
\end{enumerate}

The problem is to give a rigorous mathematical theory answering all of the above.
status_search_result: A rigorous mathematical theory of turbulence based on function-space measures supported on Navier–Stokes solution paths remains open. Partial results exist (e.g., construction of stationary statistical solutions by Foias–Prodi, Vishik–Fursikov; invariant measures for stochastically forced Navier–Stokes by Hairer–Mattingly and Flandoli–Maslowski; recent non-uniqueness results stemming from convex integration), but a complete characterization addressing existence, uniqueness, symmetries, parameter dependence, and bifurcations in the deterministic 3D setting is not available, and is tied to the open Navier–Stokes regularity problem.

paper_title: Some open problems and research directions in the mathematical study of fluid dynamics.
original_question: For classical boundary-driven Navier-Stokes turbulence, can one obtain rigorous results for moments and structure functions of the Eulerian-Lagrangian back-to-labels map A(x,t), including averaged tensor products of A(x + y_j, t + s_j) - A(x,t), corresponding structure functions, their norms, and spatial derivatives?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations
\[ \partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u - \nu\Delta u + \nabla p = 0,\qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0, \]
in a bounded smooth domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ with no-slip boundary condition $u|_{\partial\Omega}=0$ and forcing or boundary data driving a statistically stationary turbulent regime. Associated to a smooth velocity field $u$ is the Eulerian–Lagrangian "back-to-labels" map $A(x,t)$, defined as the (diffusive) inverse of the Lagrangian trajectory map: in the inviscid case $A$ satisfies $\partial_t A + (u\cdot\nabla)A = 0$ with $A(x,0)=x$, and in the viscous case $A$ solves
\[ \partial_t A + (u\cdot\nabla) A - \nu\Delta A = 0,\qquad A(x,0)=x, \]
so that $A(x,t)$ records the (averaged) initial label of the fluid particle currently at position $x$ at time $t$.

Develop a rigorous theory for the statistics of $A$ in classical boundary-driven Navier–Stokes turbulence. Specifically, obtain rigorous quantitative results (bounds, scaling laws, or exact identities, in suitable averaged or ensemble sense) for:

1. The moments $\mathbb{E}\,|A(x,t)-x|^p$ for $p\ge 1$.
2. The averaged tensor products
\[ \mathbb{E}\,\bigotimes_{j=1}^{n}\bigl(A(x+y_j,t+s_j)-A(x,t)\bigr) \]
for arbitrary $n\ge 1$, spatial increments $y_j\in\mathbb{R}^3$ and temporal increments $s_j\in\mathbb{R}$.
3. The corresponding structure functions, their $L^p$ norms, and the statistics of the spatial derivatives $\nabla A$ (in particular moments of $\nabla A - I$).

Determine, in particular, scaling exponents in the inertial range and dependence on the viscosity $\nu$, with all estimates respecting the no-slip boundary condition.
status_search_result: Constantin's Eulerian–Lagrangian formulation introduces the back-to-labels map $A(x,t)$ for Navier–Stokes (CMP 216 (2001) 663–686; arXiv:math/0005116) and motivates studying statistics of $A$ in turbulence. Subsequent works study local well-posedness and Lagrangian-invariant diffusion, and numerical/Eulerian–Lagrangian analyses exist, but no rigorous quantitative results for moments, tensor-product structure functions, norms, and derivative statistics of $A$ in classical boundary-driven Navier–Stokes turbulence appear in the literature; the problem is widely regarded as open.

paper_title: A Few Results and Open Problems Regarding Incompressible Fluids
original_question: For the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations obtained by setting viscosity ν = 0 in the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, with zero body force and smooth rapidly decaying initial velocity, do smooth initial data guarantee smooth solutions for all time, or can finite-time blowup occur?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations on $\mathbb{R}^3$ for an ideal fluid with no body force:
$$\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u + \nabla p = 0,\qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0,\qquad u(0,x)=u_0(x),$$
where $u:[0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^3$ is the velocity field and $p:[0,T)\times\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}$ is the pressure. Assume the initial data $u_0$ is smooth (i.e., $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3;\mathbb{R}^3)$), divergence-free, and rapidly decaying (e.g., in the Schwartz class $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^3;\mathbb{R}^3)$).

Determine whether one of the following holds:

(a) For every such initial datum $u_0$, the corresponding solution $u(t,\cdot)$ exists and remains smooth for all $t\in[0,\infty)$; or

(b) There exists such an initial datum $u_0$ for which the solution develops a finite-time singularity, i.e., there is some $T^*<\infty$ such that $u(t,\cdot)$ cannot be continued as a smooth solution beyond $T^*$.
status_search_result: The blowup problem for the 3D incompressible Euler equations with smooth, rapidly decaying initial data on the whole space $\mathbb{R}^3$ remains open. Substantial recent progress includes Elgindi's finite-time singularity for $C^{1,\alpha}$ (non-smooth) axisymmetric data without swirl, and the Chen–Hou computer-assisted proof (2025, PNAS) of nearly self-similar finite-time blowup for the 3D axisymmetric Euler equations with smooth initial data in a bounded cylindrical domain with boundary. The case of smooth, finite-energy data in free space (no boundary) is still unresolved.

paper_title: Two Open Problems in the Fixed Point Theory of Contractive Type Mappings on First-Countable Quasimetric Spaces
context_brief: Fixed points of contractions on complete quasimetric spaces
original_question: Let (X, d) be a complete quasimetric space, where d is a distance satisfying d(x, y) >= 0 for all x, y in X, d(x, y) + d(y, x) = 0 if and only if x = y, and d(x, z) <= d(x, y) + d(y, z) for all x, y, z in X. Here a sequence {x_n} is Cauchy if lim_{n,m->infinity} d(x_n, x_m) = 0, converges to x if lim_{n->infinity} d(x, x_n) = 0, and the space is complete if every Cauchy sequence converges in this sense. If g : X -> X is a contraction, meaning that there exists a constant lambda with 0 <= lambda < 1 such that d(g(x), g(y)) <= lambda d(x, y) for all x, y in X, must g have a fixed point?
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be a nonempty set. A function $d: X \times X \to [0,\infty)$ is called a quasimetric on $X$ if it satisfies:
(a) $d(x,y) + d(y,x) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$;
(b) $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$ for all $x,y,z \in X$.
(Note that $d$ need not be symmetric and $d(x,x)$ need not be zero a priori, but (a) forces $d(x,x)=0$.)

For such a space, declare a sequence $\{x_n\} \subset X$ to be Cauchy if $\lim_{n,m\to\infty} d(x_n,x_m) = 0$, and to converge to $x \in X$ if $\lim_{n\to\infty} d(x,x_n) = 0$. Call $(X,d)$ complete if every Cauchy sequence in $X$ converges to some point of $X$.

A map $g: X \to X$ is called a contraction if there exists $\lambda \in [0,1)$ such that $d(g(x), g(y)) \le \lambda\, d(x,y)$ for all $x,y \in X$.

Question: Must every contraction $g$ on every complete quasimetric space $(X,d)$ have a fixed point?
category_tag: Fixed point theory on quasimetric spaces
status_search_result: The problem has been resolved in the negative: a contraction on a complete quasimetric space need not have a fixed point. A complete answer (with explicit counterexamples in the dislocated/quasimetric setting) was provided by Choban and Berinde, who exhibit a contractive self-map on a complete dislocated metric space (a quasimetric space in this sense) without any fixed point, and identify additional hypotheses under which a fixed point does exist.

paper_title: THE DIFFUSE LIGHT OF THE UNIVERSE: On the microwave background before and after its discovery: open questions
original_question: Is the cosmic microwave background necessarily of cosmological origin and inseparable from the big bang, or can the same sky-filling microwave radiation be explained within other cosmological theories or by other physical mechanisms? Here, the cosmological interpretation is the claim that the observed background is fossil light released in an early hot, dense universe; the competing possibility is that the observed microwave background could arise through non-big-bang mechanisms while still accounting for the measured diffuse radiation.
self_contained_problem: Consider the observed sky-filling diffuse microwave radiation, characterized to high precision by an almost perfect blackbody spectrum at temperature T ≈ 2.725 K together with small-amplitude angular anisotropies and polarization. The standard cosmological interpretation asserts that this radiation is fossil light decoupled from baryonic matter at recombination in an early hot, dense, expanding phase of the universe (the hot big bang scenario). Determine whether the cosmic microwave background must necessarily be of such cosmological origin and is inseparable from the hot big bang model, or whether the same observed diffuse microwave radiation (its blackbody spectrum, isotropy, anisotropy spectrum, and polarization properties) can be reproduced, in a quantitatively consistent manner with all current observational constraints, either within alternative cosmological frameworks (e.g., steady-state, quasi-steady-state, or other non-big-bang cosmologies) or by other physical mechanisms (such as thermalization by intergalactic dust or grains, integrated emission from unresolved sources, or other astrophysical processes) that do not require an early hot, dense phase.
status_search_result: The cosmological origin of the CMB is the consensus interpretation in mainstream cosmology, supported by COBE, WMAP, and Planck data. However, the underlying conceptual question — whether alternative mechanisms can in principle reproduce all CMB observables — remains debated by a minority of researchers (quasi-steady-state cosmology, plasma/thermalization models). No alternative model has been shown to reproduce the full set of CMB observations (blackbody spectrum, acoustic peaks, polarization) as successfully as ΛCDM, but no rigorous no-go result rules out all alternatives. The question is therefore best classified as open in the sense posed.

paper_title: THE DIFFUSE LIGHT OF THE UNIVERSE: On the microwave background before and after its discovery: open questions
original_question: Can observations decisively establish whether the 3 K microwave background comes from a very early epoch by directly verifying predicted signatures of a primordial origin, such as a higher background temperature at larger redshift or spectral distortions that reveal the production redshift near recombination around z≈1000? This remains open because current indirect temperature probes using CN, carbon, and CO excitation can be contaminated by other processes, and the proposed recombination-era spectral test may be too weak for present or near-future instruments.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the cosmic microwave background (CMB), an approximately isotropic blackbody radiation field with present-day temperature T_0 ≈ 2.725 K. Within the standard hot big bang cosmological model, the CMB originates from the epoch of last scattering at redshift z ≈ 1000–1100, and its blackbody temperature scales as T(z) = T_0 (1 + z). The model further predicts unavoidable spectral distortions imprinted during cosmological recombination (the cosmological recombination radiation, coming from bound–bound and free–bound transitions in primordial hydrogen and helium near z ≈ 1000–10000), as well as μ- and y-type distortions from earlier energy injections.

Devise an observational program that decisively establishes — independently of the indirect excitation-temperature method based on fine-structure or rotational lines of CN, neutral/ionized carbon, and CO seen in quasar absorption systems (which can be contaminated by local heating, collisional excitation, and radiative pumping) — that this 2.725 K background is of cosmological primordial origin. Specifically:

(a) Provide a measurement strategy that confirms the linear law T(z) = T_0 (1 + z) at large redshifts (e.g., z ≳ 6) with sufficient accuracy and freedom from astrophysical contamination to discriminate against alternative non-cosmological origin scenarios.

(b) Determine whether the predicted recombination-era spectral distortion signal near z ≈ 1000 can be detected with present or near-future instruments, and either exhibit such a detection or establish a quantitative lower bound on the instrumental sensitivity (in absolute spectral intensity) required to detect it.

A solution consists of either (i) reporting verified observational confirmations satisfying (a) and (b) together, or (ii) proving rigorous obstructions showing that one or both cannot be achieved with current technology.
status_search_result: Part (a) has substantial progress: T(z) measurements via the Sunyaev–Zel'dovich effect at z ≲ 1 and via molecular/atomic excitation in quasar absorbers extend to z ~ 3, and a 2021 Nature measurement using H2O absorption pushed a direct CMB temperature determination to z = 6.34, all consistent with T_0(1+z). However, contamination by local excitation processes is still acknowledged. Part (b) remains unresolved: the cosmological recombination line signal has not been detected; proposed missions (PIXIE, PRISTINE, BISOU, Voyage 2050 concepts) target the required ~nK-level sensitivity but no such instrument is yet in operation. Hence the overall question of a decisive primordial-origin verification through these specific signatures is partially solved.

paper_title: Some Open Problems on Locally Finite or Locally Nilpotent Derivations and E-Derivations
original_question: Let K be a field of characteristic zero and let A be a K-algebra. If δ is a locally finite K-derivation or a locally finite K-E-derivation of A, where locally finite means that for every a in A the K-submodule spanned by δ^i(a) for i ≥ 0 is finitely generated, must the image Im δ = δ(A) always be a two-sided Mathieu subspace of A?
self_contained_problem:
Let K be a field of characteristic zero and let A be a (not necessarily commutative or associative) K-algebra. A K-linear map δ: A → A is called a K-derivation if δ(ab) = δ(a)b + aδ(b) for all a,b ∈ A, and a K-E-derivation if δ = I − φ for some K-algebra endomorphism φ of A (where I is the identity map). The map δ is said to be locally finite if for every a ∈ A the K-linear span of {δ^i(a) : i ≥ 0} is a finite-dimensional K-subspace of A.

A K-subspace V ⊆ A is called a (two-sided) Mathieu subspace (or Mathieu–Zhao subspace) of A if it satisfies the following property: whenever a ∈ A is such that a^m ∈ V for every m ≥ 1, then for every b, c ∈ A there exists N = N(a,b,c) ≥ 1 such that b a^m c ∈ V for all m ≥ N.

Question: Is it true that for every K-algebra A over a field K of characteristic zero, and for every locally finite K-derivation or locally finite K-E-derivation δ of A, the image Im δ = δ(A) is a two-sided Mathieu subspace of A?
status_search_result: The LFED conjecture, due to Zhao, remains open in general. It has been verified in several special cases: locally finite derivations of K[x,y] (van den Essen–Wright–Zhao), locally finite E-derivations of bivariate polynomial algebras, linear derivations and linear E-derivations of K[x,y,z], and Laurent polynomial algebras in some cases. No counterexample or full proof for arbitrary K-algebras is known.

paper_title: Some Open Problems on Locally Finite or Locally Nilpotent Derivations and E-Derivations
original_question: Let K be a field of characteristic zero, let A be a K-algebra, and let δ be a K-derivation or K-E-derivation of A. If δ is locally finite, does every idempotent e in Im δ force the principal ideal (e) generated by e to lie inside Im δ? If δ is locally nilpotent, does every idempotent e in δ(I), for every left, right, or two-sided ideal I of A, force the corresponding left, right, or two-sided ideal generated by e to lie inside δ(I)?
self_contained_problem:
Let K be a field of characteristic zero and let A be a K-algebra (not necessarily commutative). A K-linear map δ: A → A is called a K-derivation if δ(ab) = δ(a)b + aδ(b) for all a,b ∈ A, and a K-E-derivation if there exists a K-algebra endomorphism φ of A such that δ = I − φ, where I is the identity map of A. The map δ is said to be locally finite (LF) if for every a ∈ A the K-linear span of {δ^n(a) : n ≥ 0} is finite-dimensional, and locally nilpotent (LN) if for every a ∈ A there exists n ≥ 1 with δ^n(a) = 0. Let Im δ denote the image of δ. For ϑ ∈ {left, right, two-sided}, a ϑ-ideal of A means a left, right, or two-sided ideal accordingly, and (e)_ϑ denotes the ϑ-ideal of A generated by e.

Decide whether each of the following statements holds:

(A) If δ is a locally finite K-derivation or a locally finite K-E-derivation of A, then for every idempotent e ∈ Im δ the principal (two-sided) ideal (e) generated by e is contained in Im δ.

(B) If δ is a locally nilpotent K-derivation or a locally nilpotent K-E-derivation of A, then for every ϑ ∈ {left, right, two-sided}, every ϑ-ideal I of A, and every idempotent e ∈ δ(I), the ϑ-ideal (e)_ϑ generated by e is contained in δ(I).
status_search_result: The Idempotent Conjecture for locally finite (LF) and locally nilpotent (LN) K-derivations and K-E-derivations was formulated by W. Zhao and remains open in general. Partial results exist: for instance, idempotents in the intersection of the kernel and the image of LF derivations/E-derivations have been studied (Zhao, Eur. J. Math. 2017, arXiv:1701.05993), and related image/LFED conjectures have been verified in special cases (polynomial, formal power series, and Laurent power series algebras). No source found establishing the full conjecture.

paper_title: Some Open Problems on Locally Finite or Locally Nilpotent Derivations and E-Derivations
original_question: Let K be a field of characteristic zero, let A be a K-algebra, and let z = (z_1, z_2, ..., z_n) be commutative or noncommutative free variables. In the Laurent polynomial algebra A[z^{-1}, z], let M be the K-subspace consisting of all Laurent polynomials whose constant term is zero. Must M always be a Mathieu subspace of A[z^{-1}, z]?
self_contained_problem:
Let $K$ be a field of characteristic zero and let $A$ be an associative (not necessarily commutative) $K$-algebra. Fix $n\ge 1$ and let $z=(z_1,\dots,z_n)$ be either commutative or noncommutative free variables, and form the Laurent polynomial algebra $R=A[z_1^{\pm 1},\dots,z_n^{\pm 1}]$ (in the noncommutative case, the free associative algebra generated by $z_1,\dots,z_n,z_1^{-1},\dots,z_n^{-1}$ subject only to $z_i z_i^{-1}=z_i^{-1}z_i=1$, with coefficients in $A$). Every element $f\in R$ has a well-defined "constant term" $f_0\in A$, namely the coefficient of the monomial $1$ (i.e. the term in which every $z_i$ appears with exponent $0$).

A $K$-subspace $M\subseteq R$ is called a Mathieu subspace of $R$ if it satisfies the following property: for every $a\in R$ such that $a^m\in M$ for all integers $m\ge 1$, and for every $b\in R$, there exists a positive integer $N=N(a,b)$ such that $b\,a^m\in M$ for all $m\ge N$.

Let $M\subseteq R$ be the $K$-subspace consisting of all Laurent polynomials whose constant term is zero, i.e. $M=\{f\in R : f_0=0\}$.

Question: Must $M$ be a Mathieu subspace of $R$?
category_tag: Mathieu subspaces of Laurent polynomial algebras
status_search_result: The conjecture is closely tied to the Duistermaat–van der Kallen theorem (which establishes the commutative case over $\mathbb{C}$ with $A=\mathbb{C}$) and to Mathieu's conjecture on compact Lie groups. While the classical commutative scalar case is known, the general version over arbitrary characteristic-zero $K$-algebras $A$ (and especially the noncommutative free-variable case) does not appear to have been resolved; recent work (e.g. on the SU(N) Mathieu conjecture, 2023–2025) continues to reduce or partially attack related conjectures, indicating the broader conjecture remains open.

paper_title: Two Open Problems in the Fixed Point Theory of Contractive Type Mappings on First-Countable Quasimetric Spaces
context_brief: Fixed points of contractions on complete quasimetric spaces
original_question: Let (X, d) be a complete quasimetric space, where d(x, z) ≤ d(x, y) + d(y, z) for all x, y, z in X and d(x, y) + d(y, x) = 0 holds only when x = y. If g : X → X is a contraction, meaning that there exists a constant λ with 0 ≤ λ < 1 such that d(g(x), g(y)) ≤ λ·d(x, y) for all x, y in X, must g have a fixed point?
self_contained_problem:
A quasimetric on a set X is a function d : X × X → [0, ∞) satisfying:
(i) d(x, z) ≤ d(x, y) + d(y, z) for all x, y, z ∈ X (triangle inequality);
(ii) d(x, y) + d(y, x) = 0 if and only if x = y (separation).
Note that d is not assumed to be symmetric. The pair (X, d) is called a quasimetric space. Topological notions such as convergence, Cauchy sequences and completeness can be defined using the forward topology generated by the forward balls B(x, r) = {y ∈ X : d(x, y) < r}; (X, d) is called complete if every (forward) Cauchy sequence converges.

A map g : X → X is called a contraction if there exists a constant λ ∈ [0, 1) such that
   d(g(x), g(y)) ≤ λ · d(x, y) for all x, y ∈ X.

Question: Must every contraction g : X → X on a complete quasimetric space (X, d) have a fixed point, i.e., a point x ∈ X with g(x) = x?
category_tag: fixed point theory on quasimetric spaces
status_search_result: The problem is resolved in the negative: there exist complete quasimetric spaces (X, d) and contractions g : X → X with empty fixed point set. Explicit counterexamples are constructed, showing that without additional hypotheses (such as d being an H-distance, or Smyth-completeness, or symmetry-type conditions), the Banach contraction principle fails on complete quasimetric spaces. Subsequent literature extends Banach's principle to quasimetric settings only under such extra conditions.

paper_title: Cyber-Physical Attacks on UAS Networks–Challenges and Open Research Problems
original_question: How should vulnerability-analysis frameworks for unmanned aerial system (UAS) networks model the interactions among communications, computation, sensors, and physical airframe components so that UAS are not treated merely as ordinary mobile ad hoc networks or isolated subsystems, and so that vulnerabilities created by interactions among heterogeneous UAV subsystems can be identified?
self_contained_problem:
Develop a vulnerability-analysis framework for unmanned aerial system (UAS) networks that explicitly models a UAS as a cyber-physical system composed of four heterogeneous subsystems: (i) the communications subsystem (radio links, networking protocols, ground-control links, swarm communications), (ii) the computation subsystem (onboard processors, flight-control software, autopilot logic), (iii) the sensing subsystem (GPS, IMU, cameras, lidar, environmental sensors), and (iv) the physical airframe subsystem (motors, actuators, power, aerodynamic structure). The framework should satisfy the following requirements:

1. It must represent the cross-couplings and feedback interactions among the four subsystems above, rather than treating the UAS as a standard mobile ad hoc network or as a collection of independent subsystems analyzed in isolation.

2. It must support the identification of vulnerabilities that arise specifically from interactions between heterogeneous subsystems (i.e., vulnerabilities that are not present in any single subsystem in isolation but emerge from their coupling).

3. It must be sufficiently general to apply across the heterogeneous space of UAV architectures and capabilities (varying airframes, sensor suites, autonomy levels, and mission profiles), while still permitting concrete instantiation for a given platform.

Formally describe such a framework, give a rigorous notion of an "interaction-induced vulnerability" within it, and provide an analysis methodology that, given a specific UAS instantiation, enumerates or characterizes the set of interaction-induced vulnerabilities. Demonstrate that the framework captures vulnerabilities that pure ad hoc network models or single-subsystem models provably miss.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open interdisciplinary research challenge. While various UAS/UAV security threat models and surveys have appeared since, no single widely-adopted formal framework that simultaneously models communications, computation, sensing, and physical airframe interactions and rigorously identifies interaction-induced vulnerabilities across heterogeneous UAV architectures has been established. The problem appears to remain open as a general research goal.
