original_question: Is it decidable whether or not an instance of PCP satisfies the property of unique equality continuation instances? References [1] Aberkane A., James Currie and Narad Rampersad, The number of ternary words avoiding abelian cubes grows exponentially, J. Integer Seq. 7.2 (2004), Art. 04.2.7. [2] Allouche J.-P., Shallit J., Automatic Sequences: Theory, Applications, Generalizations, Cambridge Univ. Press (2003). [3] Noga Alon, Joel H. Spencer, The Probabilistic Method, 4th ed., Wiley, NewYork, 2016. [4] Petr Ambrož, Štěpán Holub and Zuzana Masáková (Eds) WORDS 2011, Proceedings of the 8th International Conference on Words, Prague, Czech Republic, 12-16th September 2011, EPTCS 63, http://eptcs.web.cse.unsw.edu.au/content.cgi?WORDS2011. [5] Pierre Arnoux, Nicolas Bédaride and Julien Cassaigne (Eds) WORDS 2007, Proceedings of the 6th International Conference on Words, Marseille, France, September 17-21, 2007, Manuscript distribuated to the attendees of the conference. [6] Berthé V., Cassaigne J. and W. Steiner, Balance properties of Arnoux-Rauzy words, Intern. J. Algebra Comput. 23 (2013) 689– 703. [7] Baker K., McNulty G. and W. Taylor, Growth problems for avoidable words, Theoret. Comp. Sci. 69 (1989) 319–345.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ and $\Delta$ be finite alphabets and let $h,g:\Sigma^{*}\to\Delta^{*}$ be two morphisms. The pair $(h,g)$ is called an instance of the Post Correspondence Problem (PCP). A nonempty word $w\in\Sigma^{+}$ is called a solution if $h(w)=g(w)$.

For a word $w\in\Sigma^{*}$, the pair $(h(w),g(w))$ is called an equality pair if one of $h(w),g(w)$ is a prefix of the other; equivalently, there exist $z\in\Delta^{*}$ and $i\in\{1,2\}$ such that, writing $h_{1}=h$ and $h_{2}=g$, we have $h_{i}(w)=h_{3-i}(w)\,z$. Such a $w$ is said to admit an equality continuation if there exists $w'\in\Sigma^{*}$ with $h(ww')=g(ww')$.

The instance $(h,g)$ is said to satisfy the property of unique equality continuation instances if, for every $w\in\Sigma^{*}$ for which $(h(w),g(w))$ is an equality pair, there is at most one letter $a\in\Sigma$ such that $(h(wa),g(wa))$ is again an equality pair admitting an equality continuation; that is, the process of building up a solution letter by letter is deterministic at every step where extensions are still possible.

Question: Is the following problem decidable? Given an instance $(h,g)$ of PCP as input, determine whether $(h,g)$ satisfies the property of unique equality continuation instances.
status_search_result: Web searches indicate that classes of PCP instances satisfying various uniqueness/continuation conditions (marked instances, instances with unique blocks, instances with unique continuations) have been shown to belong to decidable classes by Halava, Harju, and collaborators, but no source located addresses the meta-question of deciding whether a given PCP instance possesses the unique equality continuation property itself. The status of this specific decision problem could not be verified from available sources.

paper_title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems
context_brief: Origin and distinctiveness of topological atoms
original_question: What mathematical principle explains the origin and distinctiveness of topological atoms in the quantum theory of atoms in molecules (QTAIM)? A topological atom is an atomic basin in real three-dimensional space obtained from the gradient vector field of the one-electron density: nuclei are (3,-3) attractors, gradient paths terminating at an attractor form its basin, and interatomic surfaces are zero-flux boundaries. Since other three-dimensional quantum divided basins can satisfy the net zero-flux equation without being these atomic basins, can QTAIM justify why topological atoms, rather than merely any net-zero-flux basins, are the physically natural quantum subsystems?
self_contained_problem:
Let $ho:\mathbb{R}^3	o\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ be the one-electron density of a molecular system in its ground (or a stationary) state, assumed smooth away from a finite set of nuclear positions $\{R_\alpha\}\subset\mathbb{R}^3$. Consider the gradient vector field $
ablaho$. A point $p$ is a critical point of rank 3 and signature $-3$ (a $(3,-3)$ attractor) if $
ablaho(p)=0$ and the Hessian of $ho$ at $p$ has three negative eigenvalues; in molecular systems these attractors coincide with the nuclear positions $R_\alpha$. The basin $\Omega_\alpha$ of an attractor $R_\alpha$ is the set of points whose gradient trajectory of $
ablaho$ terminates at $R_\alpha$. The boundary $\partial\Omega_\alpha$ is an interatomic surface satisfying the local zero-flux condition
$$
ablaho(r)\cdot n(r)=0\qquad	ext{for all }r\in\partial\Omega_\alpha,$$
where $n(r)$ is the outward unit normal. A region $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ whose boundary satisfies the same zero-flux equation is called a net-zero-flux basin. The collection of topological atoms $\{\Omega_\alpha\}$ is one such partition, but there exist many other net-zero-flux basins (called quantum divided basins) that are not topological atoms; in particular some such regions contain no nucleus.

Problem. Provide a mathematical principle, formulated intrinsically from the one-electron density and the framework of subsystem quantum mechanics, that singles out the topological atoms $\{\Omega_\alpha\}$ uniquely among all regions of $\mathbb{R}^3$ whose boundaries satisfy the zero-flux equation $
ablaho\cdot n=0$. Equivalently, identify an additional condition (or variational/topological characterization) that, together with the local zero-flux condition, has the topological atoms as its only solutions, and thereby explains why topological atoms—rather than arbitrary net-zero-flux basins—are the physically natural quantum subsystems in the quantum theory of atoms in molecules.
status_search_result: The question of providing a rigorous mathematical principle that uniquely characterizes topological (Bader) atoms among the infinite family of net-zero-flux basins (quantum divided basins) appears to remain open. Existing literature acknowledges that the local zero-flux equation admits many spurious solutions (some without nuclei) and that a rigorous definition of topological atoms requires supplementing it with an auxiliary condition; informal "naturalness" criteria (containing exactly one nucleus, simplest gradient-flow basins) are invoked, but no universally accepted derivation from first principles of subsystem quantum mechanics has been established.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: (due to I. Petrykiewicz): For any infinite ternary square-free word u, does an infinite ternary square-free word w exists such that u = u ▷β w for some infinite β?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A = \{0,1,2\}$ be a ternary alphabet. An infinite word $u \in A^{\mathbb{N}}$ is called square-free if it contains no nonempty factor of the form $xx$ (i.e., there is no nonempty finite word $x$ such that $xx$ appears as a contiguous block in $u$).

Given two infinite words $v, w \in A^{\mathbb{N}}$ and an infinite binary "control" sequence $\beta \in \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ in which both letters $0$ and $1$ occur infinitely often, define the shuffle $v \mathbin{\triangleleft_\beta} w \in A^{\mathbb{N}}$ to be the infinite word obtained by reading the letters of $v$ and $w$ in order, taking the next letter of $v$ whenever the corresponding entry of $\beta$ is $0$ and the next letter of $w$ whenever it is $1$.

Question: Is it true that for every infinite ternary square-free word $u \in A^{\mathbb{N}}$ there exist an infinite ternary square-free word $w \in A^{\mathbb{N}}$ and an infinite control sequence $\beta \in \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ (with both symbols occurring infinitely often) such that
$$u \;=\; u \mathbin{\triangleleft_\beta} w\,?$$

Equivalently, does every infinite ternary square-free word $u$ admit a partition of its positions into two infinite subsequences, one of which equals $u$ itself and the other of which spells out an infinite ternary square-free word?
status_search_result: Searches turned up related work on square-free shuffles (Currie–Saari, Harju–Müller, Guégan–Ochem on shuffled-square-free words over alphabets of size 7 and later 6) and on shuffled-square-free words generally, but no source explicitly resolves Petrykiewicz's specific question about whether every infinite ternary square-free word admits such a self-shuffle decomposition with another infinite ternary square-free word. The status appears to remain unresolved based on available evidence.

paper_title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems
context_brief: Coulombic origin of molecular density topology
original_question: How do Coulombic interactions between nuclei and electrons determine the topology of the molecular one-electron density so that topological atoms arise naturally? In particular, what mathematical mechanism makes nuclear attractors the usual attractors of the density-gradient field in Coulombic molecular systems, whereas replacing Coulomb interactions by harmonic interactions can produce a different density topology?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a non-relativistic molecular system consisting of $M$ fixed point-like nuclei with positive charges $\{Z_A\}_{A=1}^M$ at positions $\{\mathbf{R}_A\}_{A=1}^M$ and $N$ electrons, governed by the Hamiltonian
$$ H_{\mathrm{Coul}} = -\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^N \nabla_i^2 - \sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{A=1}^M \frac{Z_A}{|\mathbf{r}_i-\mathbf{R}_A|} + \sum_{i<j}\frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}_i-\mathbf{r}_j|}, $$
with associated ground-state wavefunction $\Psi$ and one-electron density
$$ \rho(\mathbf{r}) = N\int |\Psi(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}_2,\ldots,\mathbf{r}_N)|^2\, d\mathbf{r}_2\cdots d\mathbf{r}_N. $$
The gradient vector field $\nabla\rho$ partitions $\mathbb{R}^3$ into basins associated with its attractors (the asymptotic limits of integral curves of $\nabla\rho$). Empirically, for Coulombic molecular systems the attractors of $\nabla\rho$ coincide (with rare exceptions) with the nuclear positions $\{\mathbf{R}_A\}$, giving rise to the notion of a topological atom. By contrast, for a "Hookean" model in which the electron–nucleus Coulomb attractions $-Z_A/|\mathbf{r}_i-\mathbf{R}_A|$ are replaced by harmonic potentials $\tfrac{1}{2}k|\mathbf{r}_i-\mathbf{R}_A|^2$ (e.g., Hookean $\mathrm{H}_2^+$), the resulting density may possess a single attractor located between the nuclei rather than one attractor at each nucleus.

Provide a rigorous mathematical mechanism — for example, in terms of the Kato cusp condition, analytic structure of $\rho$ near the nuclei, or properties of the electron–nucleus interaction kernel — that explains why, for the Coulombic Hamiltonian $H_{\mathrm{Coul}}$, the nuclei are necessarily (or generically) the attractors of $\nabla\rho$, while the substitution of Coulomb attractions by harmonic attractions can destroy this property. Equivalently, characterize precisely how the singular $1/r$ form of the electron–nucleus interaction determines the critical-point structure and basin decomposition of the one-electron density so that the topological atom emerges naturally.
status_search_result: The question of why Coulombic electron–nucleus interactions force nuclei to be attractors of the one-electron density gradient field, and why replacing them with harmonic interactions changes the topology, remains a recognized open foundational question in quantum chemical topology. Studies of Hookean models confirm the topological discrepancy, and works on non-nuclear attractors and Hooke–Calogero models highlight that the link between potential form and density topology is not fully understood, but no rigorous derivation explaining the Coulombic case has been published.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: (Square conjecture, due to A. Fraenkel and J. Simpson): The number of different squares in a word of length n is bounded by n.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $w = w_1 w_2 \cdots w_n$ be a finite word over $\Sigma$ of length $n \ge 1$. A nonempty factor of $w$ of the form $uu$ (the concatenation of a nonempty word $u$ with itself) is called a square. Two squares are considered distinct if they are different as words (regardless of how many times or where they occur as factors of $w$). Let $S(w)$ denote the number of distinct squares occurring as factors of $w$.

Prove or disprove: for every finite word $w$ of length $n$,
$$S(w) \le n.$$
status_search_result: The Fraenkel–Simpson distinct squares conjecture (1998) appears to have been resolved by S. Brlek and S. Li in their 2022 preprint "On the number of squares in a finite word" (arXiv:2204.10204), where they prove the stronger bound S(w) ≤ |w| − |Alphabet(w)| + 1, confirming the conjecture. Earlier partial bounds included 2n (Fraenkel–Simpson), 2n − Θ(log n) (Ilie), and ⌊11n/6⌋ (Deza et al.), and a 1.5n bound was reported in 2020.

paper_title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems
context_brief: Extending density-topology conjectures beyond point nuclei
original_question: Can the critical-distance explanation of topological-atom naturalness be extended from point-charge Coulomb external potentials to larger classes of external potentials, such as finite-nucleus models or other marginal modifications, by proving that the topology of the one-electron density is independent of those marginal changes?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\rho:\mathbb{R}^3\to[0,\infty)$ denote the ground-state one-electron density of an $N$-electron molecular system with a fixed configuration of $M$ nuclei at positions $R_1,\dots,R_M\in\mathbb{R}^3$. For an external one-body potential $v:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}$, let $\rho_v$ denote the resulting ground-state one-electron density (assumed to exist and be sufficiently smooth so that its critical points and gradient flow are well defined). The topology of $\rho_v$ is the structure consisting of the set of critical points of $\rho_v$ classified by Morse index, together with the gradient-flow cell decomposition of $\mathbb{R}^3$ induced by $-\nabla\rho_v$ (i.e., the partition into "topological atoms" and the network of bond, ring, and cage critical points connecting them).

Consider the point-charge Coulomb external potential
$$v_{\text{pt}}(r) \;=\; -\sum_{A=1}^{M}\frac{Z_A}{|r-R_A|},$$
and let $\mathcal{V}$ be a class of "marginally modified" external potentials with the same nuclear positions $R_1,\dots,R_M$ and charges $Z_1,\dots,Z_M$, including in particular the finite-nucleus models in which each Coulomb singularity is replaced by a smooth potential generated by a finite nuclear charge distribution (e.g., Gaussian or uniform-ball nuclear models).

Problem. Prove or disprove: for every $v\in\mathcal{V}$, the topology of $\rho_v$ (in the sense above) is the same as the topology of $\rho_{v_{\text{pt}}}$. More precisely, establish a precise notion of "marginal modification" of the external potential under which the homeomorphism type of the gradient-flow cell decomposition of $\rho_v$, together with the number and Morse indices of its critical points, is invariant; and use this to extend the critical-distance explanation of the naturalness of topological atoms from the point-charge Coulomb case to this larger class of external potentials.
status_search_result: No published proof was located establishing topological invariance of the one-electron density under replacement of point-charge Coulomb potentials by finite-nucleus or other marginally modified external potentials. The statement is presented in the literature as a conjectural extension, and searches return only general references on finite-nucleus models and topological analysis of electron density without a resolution.

paper_title: Ten Conferences WORDS: Open Problems and Conjectures
original_question: (due to Kosciumaka, Radoszewski, Rytter, Waleń [23]): A word of length n contains O(n√n) inequivalent abelian-squares.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $w \in \Sigma^*$ be a finite word of length $n$. Two words $u, v \in \Sigma^*$ are said to be Abelian-equivalent, written $u \sim_a v$, if $|u|=|v|$ and for every letter $a \in \Sigma$ the number of occurrences of $a$ in $u$ equals the number of occurrences of $a$ in $v$. A factor $f$ of $w$ is called an Abelian square if $f = uv$ with $u \sim_a v$ (equivalently, $|u|=|v|$ and $u$ and $v$ have the same Parikh vector). Two Abelian squares $u_1 v_1$ and $u_2 v_2$ (with $u_i \sim_a v_i$) are said to be Abelian-equivalent (or "equivalent as Abelian squares") if $u_1 \sim_a u_2$ (which then forces $v_1 \sim_a v_2$ as well). Let $\mathrm{ASQ}(w)$ denote the number of pairwise Abelian-inequivalent Abelian squares occurring as factors of $w$.

Prove or disprove: there exists an absolute constant $C > 0$ such that for every finite alphabet $\Sigma$ and every word $w \in \Sigma^*$ of length $n \ge 1$,
$$\mathrm{ASQ}(w) \le C\, n\sqrt{n}.$$
status_search_result: The known lower bound for the maximum number of Abelian-inequivalent Abelian squares in a binary word of length n is Ω(n^{1.5}/log n), established by Kociumaka, Radoszewski, Rytter and Waleń (2014/2016). No matching upper bound of order O(n√n) has been published; the conjectured O(n^{1.5}) upper bound remains open according to surveys and follow-up work on nonstandard squares.

paper_title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems
original_question: How can one define an origin-independent energy for a topological atom when the molecular Hamiltonian contains non-Coulombic, inhomogeneous, or marginally modified potential-energy terms? The desired definition must work when the usual Coulombic homogeneity used in the subsystem virial theorem fails, including potentials that are sums of homogeneous terms of different degrees or are not finitely decomposable into homogeneous terms.
category_tag: Quantum theory of atoms in molecules
status_search_result: The question of defining an origin-independent topological atomic energy for non-Coulombic, inhomogeneous, or marginally modified potentials is posed as an open problem in the foundations of QTAIM. Subsequent literature on QTAIM (including extensions to relativistic, finite-nucleus, and magnetic-interaction settings) acknowledges that the subsystem virial theorem fails to deliver origin independence outside the strictly Coulombic case, and no general resolution satisfying all the standard requirements appears in the published literature; the problem is therefore considered open.

paper_title: A max-type recursive model: some properties and open questions
original_question: For a fixed integer m ≥ 2, let (X_n) be the max-type recursion X_{n+1} = max(X_n^{(1)} + ... + X_n^{(m)} - 1, 0), where X_n^{(1)}, ..., X_n^{(m)} are independent copies of X_n. Define the free energy F∞ = lim_{n→∞} E[X_n] / m^n. In the parametric initial law P_{X_0} = (1-p)δ_0 + p P_{Y_0}, where Y_0 is positive and p ∈ [0,1], let p_c be the threshold such that F∞(p)=0 below p_c and F∞(p)>0 above p_c. If p_c > 0, possibly under additional integrability conditions on Y_0, is there a constant K ∈ (0,∞) such that F∞(p) = exp(-(K+o(1))/(p-p_c)^{1/2}) as p decreases to p_c?
self_contained_problem:
Fix an integer $m \geq 2$. Let $X_0 \geq 0$ be a non-negative, non-constant random variable, and define recursively
$$X_{n+1} = \big(X_n^{(1)} + X_n^{(2)} + \cdots + X_n^{(m)} - 1\big)_+, \qquad n \geq 0,$$
where $X_n^{(1)}, \dots, X_n^{(m)}$ are independent copies of $X_n$ and $x_+ := \max(x,0)$. Since $mE(X_n) - 1 \leq E(X_{n+1}) \leq mE(X_n)$, the limit
$$F_\infty := \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{E(X_n)}{m^n}$$
exists in $[0, \infty)$.

Consider the parametric family of initial laws
$$P_{X_0} = (1-p)\,\delta_0 + p\,P_{Y_0},$$
where $Y_0$ is a fixed positive random variable and $p \in [0,1]$ is a parameter. Write $F_\infty(p)$ for the resulting free energy. Since $p \mapsto F_\infty(p)$ is non-decreasing, there exists a critical threshold $p_c \in [0,1]$ such that $F_\infty(p) = 0$ for $p < p_c$ and $F_\infty(p) > 0$ for $p > p_c$.

Assume $p_c > 0$ (and possibly impose additional integrability conditions on $Y_0$). Determine whether there exists a constant $K \in (0, \infty)$ such that
$$F_\infty(p) = \exp\!\left(-\frac{K + o(1)}{(p - p_c)^{1/2}}\right) \qquad \text{as } p \downarrow p_c.$$
status_search_result: The conjecture was proved in 2019–2021 by Chen, Dagard, Derrida, Hu, Lifshits and Shi (Annals of Probability, 2021), under a suitable integrability assumption on the initial distribution: the free energy vanishes at the transition with the predicted essential singularity of exponent 1/2. This establishes the conjecture in the integrable regime; weaker/other behaviors arise when the integrability condition fails. A dual (subcritical) version has subsequently been studied (2023).

paper_title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems
context_brief: Explicit atomic density functionals and variational principles
original_question: Can explicit functionals of a topological atom’s one-electron density, or a successful variational principle based on that density or another atomic function, be constructed so that topological-atom properties can be computed rather than only formally asserted to exist?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\psi$ be the (normalized, antisymmetric) electronic wavefunction of an $N$-electron molecular system, and let $ho:\mathbb{R}^3	o[0,\infty)$ be its associated one-electron density,
$$ho(\mathbf{r})=N\int |\psi(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}_2,\dots,\mathbf{r}_N)|^2\,d\mathbf{r}_2\cdots d\mathbf{r}_N.$$
A topological atom $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ is defined as a basin of attraction of the gradient vector field $
ablaho$, equivalently a maximal open region whose boundary $\partial\Omega$ satisfies the zero-flux condition
$$
ablaho(\mathbf{r})\cdot \mathbf{n}(\mathbf{r})=0\quad	ext{for all }\mathbf{r}\in\partial\Omega,$$
where $\mathbf{n}$ is the outward unit normal. For a quantum mechanical observable represented by an operator $\hat{A}$ acting on $N$-electron wavefunctions, the corresponding atomic property is
$$M_\Omega[\psi]=\int_\Omega \langle\psi|\hat{A}|\psiangle_\Omega\,d\mathbf{r},$$
where $\langle\cdotangle_\Omega$ denotes the appropriate basin-restricted expectation density.

Question. Does there exist (i) an explicit functional $F_{\hat{A}}[ho|_\Omega]$ of the one-electron density restricted to a topological atom $\Omega$, or alternatively (ii) a well-posed variational principle with Euler–Lagrange equations whose stationary points yield $ho|_\Omega$ (or some other atomic function $f_\Omega$ from which atomic properties may be reconstructed), such that for every quantum observable $\hat{A}$ in a suitable class one has $M_\Omega[\psi]=F_{\hat{A}}[ho|_\Omega]$ (respectively, $M_\Omega[\psi]$ is computable from the variational solution)? Construct such a functional or variational principle, or prove that none exists.
category_tag: Density functional theory for topological atoms (QTAIM)
status_search_result: No explicit density functional for topological-atom properties or a fully successful basin-restricted variational principle appears to have been established. Subsequent QTAIM literature continues to treat atomic properties via integration of expectation densities rather than via closed-form density functionals, and proposed variational principles for proper open subsystems remain disputed or limited in scope.

$$X_{n+1} \;=\; \big(X_n^{(1)}+X_n^{(2)}+\cdots+X_n^{(m)}-1\big)_+, \qquad n\ge 0,$$
where $X_n^{(1)},\dots,X_n^{(m)}$ are independent copies of $X_n$ and $x_+=\max(x,0)$. Assume the criticality condition

paper_title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems
original_question: Do interatomic zero-flux surfaces act as holograms for topological atoms by encoding the right amount of information needed to deduce basin properties from boundary data, rather than requiring full three-dimensional property densities inside each atomic basin?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\rho:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ be the (sufficiently smooth) one-electron charge density of a stationary molecular state, and consider the gradient vector field $\nabla\rho$. A topological atom (atomic basin) $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ is a connected open region whose boundary $\partial\Omega$ consists of interatomic zero-flux surfaces, i.e. surfaces $S$ on which
$$\nabla\rho(\mathbf{r})\cdot\mathbf{n}(\mathbf{r}) = 0 \quad \text{for every } \mathbf{r}\in S,$$
where $\mathbf{n}(\mathbf{r})$ is the unit outward normal at $\mathbf{r}$. For a one-electron Hermitian operator $\hat{A}$, define the basin property
$$A(\Omega) = \int_{\Omega} \rho_A(\mathbf{r})\,d\mathbf{r},$$
where $\rho_A$ is the corresponding property density derived from the molecular wavefunction, and the associated current $\mathbf{j}_A$ on $\partial\Omega$ via the subsystem hypervirial relations.

Question. Do the interatomic zero-flux surfaces act as a "hologram" for topological atoms, in the precise sense that for a sufficiently broad class of one-electron observables $\hat{A}$ the basin property $A(\Omega)$ is determined entirely by the restriction of $\rho$ and of the relevant currents $\mathbf{j}_A$ to the boundary $\partial\Omega$ (without requiring knowledge of $\rho_A$ throughout the three-dimensional interior of $\Omega$)? Equivalently, characterize the class of operators and the boundary data on $\partial\Omega$ that suffice to reconstruct the corresponding bulk basin properties.
category_tag: QTAIM topological atoms and holographic boundary principles
status_search_result: The holographic interpretation of interatomic zero-flux surfaces in QTAIM is discussed as a conjectural principle motivated by the subsystem hypervirial theorem; a general proof characterizing which atomic basin properties can be recovered solely from boundary data is not established in the literature, with discussions framing it as an open conceptual/mathematical problem. Recent reviews of quantum chemical topology continue to treat the boundary-vs-bulk relationship as suggestive rather than fully proven.

original_question: For a fixed integer m ≥ 2, let X_0 be a nonconstant Z_+-valued random variable and define X_{n+1} = max(X_n^{(1)} + ... + X_n^{(m)} - 1, 0), where X_n^{(1)}, ..., X_n^{(m)} are independent copies of X_n. $$X_{n+1} = \max\!\left(X_n^{(1)} + X_n^{(2)} + \cdots + X_n^{(m)} - 1,\; 0\right),\qquad n \ge 0,$$
where $X_n^{(1)}, \dots, X_n^{(m)}$ are independent copies of $X_n$ (independent across both $n$ and the index $i$). Assume the criticality condition
$$(m-1)\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[X_0\, m^{X_0}\right] \;=\; \mathbb{E}\!\left[m^{X_0}\right] \;<\; \infty,$$
together with whatever additional integrability is needed (for example $\mathbb{E}[X_0^3 m^{X_0}] < \infty$) to ensure the conclusion below.

$$\mathbb{E}\!\left[s^{X_n}\right] - 1 \;\sim\; \frac{4m}{(m-1)^2}\cdot\frac{s-1}{m-s}\cdot\frac{1}{n^2}\qquad\text{as } n\to\infty.$$

paper_title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems
original_question: Can QTAIM be reformulated as a practical boundary-only theory in which calculations use only the two-dimensional interatomic surfaces and still yield the properties of the three-dimensional topological atoms, and what analytical differential geometry of interatomic surfaces is needed to make such a holographic formulation work?
self_contained_problem:
Background. The Quantum Theory of Atoms in Molecules (QTAIM) partitions a molecule's three-dimensional space using the gradient vector field of the (single-particle) electron density ρ(r). A topological atom Ω is a basin of attraction of ∇ρ associated with a nuclear critical point; distinct basins are separated by interatomic surfaces S, which are the two-dimensional separatrices of the gradient flow, characterized by the zero-flux condition

  ∇ρ(r) · n(r) = 0   for all r ∈ S,

where n(r) is the unit normal to S. For a quantum-mechanical observable with one-particle density operator Ô, its atomic property on Ω is defined by the volume integral

  A(Ω) = ∫_Ω ⟨Ô⟩(r) dr.

Problem. Develop a "boundary-only" (holographic) reformulation of QTAIM with the following precise requirements:

(a) Provide a constructive procedure that, given only the geometric data of the interatomic surface ∂Ω (its embedding in ℝ³, its induced metric, second fundamental form, and the restriction of ρ and its derivatives to ∂Ω), expresses every atomic property A(Ω) of interest (such as electronic population, kinetic energy, dipole and higher multipole moments, virial quantities) as an integral over ∂Ω alone, with no recourse to integration over the three-dimensional basin.

(b) Prove that the resulting surface functionals reproduce the standard three-dimensional QTAIM atomic properties for arbitrary molecular electron densities satisfying the zero-flux boundary condition, and identify the minimal differential-geometric data on ∂Ω (e.g., principal curvatures, mean and Gaussian curvatures, geodesics, intrinsic Laplacian) that suffice for this reduction.

(c) Characterize the analytical differential geometry of QTAIM interatomic surfaces (regularity, curvature bounds, topology, behavior at bond critical points and at infinity) needed to make the reduction in (a)–(b) rigorous and computationally practical.

Determine whether such a boundary-only formulation exists, and if so, exhibit it explicitly.
status_search_result: Web searches surface foundational work on the differential geometry of QTAIM interatomic surfaces (e.g., curvature-based bond characterizations and surface property/bond-energy correlations) and recent applications, but no source presents a complete "boundary-only" (holographic) reformulation of QTAIM that derives all 3D atomic properties solely from 2D interatomic surface data. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Additive Combinatorics: A Menu of Research Problems
context_brief: Maximum sumset size in finite abelian groups
original_question: For finite abelian groups written additively, and for an m-element subset A of a group G, determine the maximum possible cardinality of the standard sumset variants formed from A, including hA, [0,s]A, the signed variants h±A and [0,s]±A, the restricted variants ĥA and [0,s]Â, and the restricted signed variants ĥ±A and [0,s]̂±A. Equivalently, determine the values of the maximum-size functions ν(G,m,h), ν(G,m,[0,s]), ν±(G,m,h), ν±(G,m,[0,s]), ν̂(G,m,h), ν̂(G,m,[0,s]), ν̂±(G,m,h), and ν̂±(G,m,[0,s]), and characterize extremal subsets when possible.
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a finite abelian group, written additively, and let m and h be positive integers with m ≤ |G|, and let s be a nonnegative integer. For a subset A ⊆ G with |A| = m, define the following sumsets.

Unrestricted h-fold sumset:
  hA = { a_1 + a_2 + ⋯ + a_h : a_i ∈ A } (repetitions of elements allowed).

Unrestricted sumset up to s terms:
  [0,s]A = ⋃_{h=0}^{s} hA, where 0A = {0}.

Unrestricted signed h-fold sumset:
  h_±A = { ε_1 a_1 + ⋯ + ε_h a_h : a_i ∈ A, ε_i ∈ {+1,−1} },
  and [0,s]_±A = ⋃_{h=0}^{s} h_±A.

Restricted h-fold sumset:
  ĥA = { a_1 + ⋯ + a_h : a_i ∈ A pairwise distinct },
  and [0,s]̂A = ⋃_{h=0}^{s} ĥA.

Restricted signed h-fold sumset:
  ĥ_±A = { ε_1 a_{i_1} + ⋯ + ε_h a_{i_h} : 1 ≤ i_1 < ⋯ < i_h ≤ m, ε_j ∈ {+1,−1} },
  and [0,s]̂_±A = ⋃_{h=0}^{s} ĥ_±A.

Define the maximum-size functions
  ν(G,m,h)      = max{ |hA|       : A ⊆ G, |A| = m },
  ν(G,m,[0,s])  = max{ |[0,s]A|   : A ⊆ G, |A| = m },
  ν_±(G,m,h)    = max{ |h_±A|     : A ⊆ G, |A| = m },
  ν_±(G,m,[0,s])= max{ |[0,s]_±A| : A ⊆ G, |A| = m },
  ν̂(G,m,h)     = max{ |ĥA|       : A ⊆ G, |A| = m },
  ν̂(G,m,[0,s]) = max{ |[0,s]̂A|  : A ⊆ G, |A| = m },
  ν̂_±(G,m,h)   = max{ |ĥ_±A|     : A ⊆ G, |A| = m },
  ν̂_±(G,m,[0,s])= max{ |[0,s]̂_±A| : A ⊆ G, |A| = m }.

Determine the values of each of these eight functions for all finite abelian groups G and all relevant parameters m, h, s, and characterize, whenever possible, those subsets A ⊆ G of size m that attain the maximum.
category_tag: sumset size in finite abelian groups
status_search_result: This is a broad family of problems on maximum sumset sizes in finite abelian groups, posed as an ongoing research program. While many partial results are known for specific groups (cyclic groups, elementary abelian groups) and specific parameter ranges, complete formulas and extremal characterizations for all eight ν-functions across all finite abelian groups and parameters are not known and remain an active area of investigation.

paper_title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems
context_brief: Principles for quantum subsystem theories and QTAIM extensions
original_question: How should a quantum subsystem, or a division into system plus environment, be introduced when the principles of quantum mechanics do not provide a clear recipe, and how should QTAIM’s own subsystem principles and axioms be extended as part of an ongoing research programme rather than treated as a finalized theory?
self_contained_problem:
In standard quantum mechanics, a closed system is described by a Hilbert space H, a state (a unit vector or density operator on H), and observables (self-adjoint operators on H), with dynamics generated by a Hamiltonian. The notion of a "subsystem" — a proper part of a larger quantum system together with its complementary "environment" — is not uniquely specified by these axioms: there is no canonical prescription that, given an interacting many-electron system (e.g. a molecule with nuclear configuration fixed in the Born–Oppenheimer approximation, described by an antisymmetric N-electron wavefunction Ψ on R^{3N} together with the one-electron density ρ(r) and the one-body and pair densities derived from Ψ), singles out a decomposition of the total Hilbert space, or of physical space R^3, into a subsystem and its environment in a way that yields well-defined, additive subsystem observables (kinetic energy, potential energy, charge, etc.).

The Quantum Theory of Atoms in Molecules (QTAIM) supplies one such prescription: it partitions R^3 into disjoint open regions Ω (atomic basins) bounded by zero-flux surfaces of the gradient field of the electron density,
   ∇ρ(r) · n(r) = 0  for all r ∈ ∂Ω,
where n(r) is the outward unit normal to ∂Ω. On each such region one defines subsystem observables by integrating appropriate densities over Ω, and a subsystem variational principle (an analogue of Schwinger's principle of stationary action restricted to Ω) is postulated as an additional axiom on top of the axioms of quantum mechanics.

Formulate, within a precise mathematical framework, a set of principles and axioms governing the notion of a quantum subsystem of an interacting N-particle quantum system that
(a) reduces to the standard axioms of quantum mechanics when the subsystem is taken to be the whole system;
(b) selects, from the set of admissible spatial or Hilbert-space decompositions, those which carry well-defined additive observables and a self-consistent subsystem dynamics (or stationary-action principle);
(c) contains the QTAIM zero-flux partitioning and its associated subsystem variational principle as a special case, while admitting natural extensions (for example to open quantum systems, to time-dependent and relativistic settings, to alternative scalar fields replacing ρ, and to non-disjoint or fuzzy partitions).

Determine whether such a system of principles can be formulated, prove its internal consistency, and characterize the class of admissible subsystem decompositions it singles out.
status_search_result: The question is foundational and open-ended: it asks for principles governing quantum subsystems and an extension of QTAIM's axioms. Subsequent literature on QTAIM and on subsystem/embedding theories (e.g., density functional embedding, partition DFT, interacting quantum atoms) continues to propose competing prescriptions, but no canonical, universally accepted axiomatic foundation for "quantum subsystem" has been established. The problem therefore appears to remain open as a research programme.

paper_title: Additive Combinatorics: A Menu of Research Problems
context_brief: Sidon-type sets in finite abelian groups
original_question: For a finite abelian group G, determine the largest possible size of a subset A whose unrestricted, signed, restricted, or restricted signed sumsets have the collision-free sizes expected from the corresponding coefficient vectors. Equivalently, determine the Sidon-type functions σ(G,h), σ(G,[0,s]), σ±(G,h), σ±(G,[0,s]), σ̂(G,h), σ̂(G,[0,s]), σ̂(G,N0), σ̂±(G,h), σ̂±(G,[0,s]), and σ̂±(G,N0), and characterize extremal sets where possible.
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite abelian group and let $A \subseteq G$ be a subset of size $m=|A|$. For a positive integer $h$, define the following sumsets:

- Unrestricted sumset: $hA = \{a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_h : a_i \in A\}$, with maximum possible cardinality $\binom{m+h-1}{h}$ (the number of multisets of size $h$ from $m$ elements).
- Unrestricted signed sumset: $h_\pm A = \{\varepsilon_1 a_1 + \cdots + \varepsilon_h a_h : a_i \in A,\ \varepsilon_i \in \{+1,-1\}\}$, with maximum cardinality $c(h,m) := \sum_{k=0}^{h}\binom{m+k-1}{k}\cdot[\text{signed multiset count}]$ (the number of signed multisets of size $h$ from $m$ elements).
- Restricted sumset: $\hat{h}A = \{a_{i_1}+\cdots+a_{i_h} : 1\le i_1<\cdots<i_h\le m\}$, with maximum cardinality $\binom{m}{h}$.
- Restricted signed sumset: $\hat{h}_\pm A = \{\varepsilon_1 a_{i_1}+\cdots+\varepsilon_h a_{i_h} : 1\le i_1<\cdots<i_h\le m,\ \varepsilon_j\in\{\pm 1\}\}$, with maximum cardinality $\binom{m}{h}2^h$.

For $s\ge 0$ define the cumulative versions $[0,s]A=\bigcup_{h=0}^{s} hA$, $[0,s]_\pm A=\bigcup_{h=0}^{s} h_\pm A$, $[0,s]\hat{}A=\bigcup_{h=0}^{s}\hat{h}A$, $[0,s]\hat{}_\pm A=\bigcup_{h=0}^{s}\hat{h}_\pm A$, and the full subset-sum sets $\Sigma A=\bigcup_{h=0}^{m}\hat{h}A$ and $\Sigma_\pm A=\bigcup_{h=0}^{m}\hat{h}_\pm A$.

A set $A$ is called Sidon-type for the corresponding operation if its sumset attains the maximum possible cardinality listed above (so all formal sums are distinct in $G$). Define:

$$\sigma(G,h)=\max\{|A|:|hA|=\tbinom{m+h-1}{h}\},\quad \sigma(G,[0,s])=\max\{|A|:|[0,s]A|=\tbinom{m+s}{s}\},$$
$$\sigma_\pm(G,h)=\max\{|A|:|h_\pm A|=c(h,m)\},\quad \sigma_\pm(G,[0,s])=\max\{|A|:|[0,s]_\pm A|=\textstyle\sum_{h=0}^{s} c(h,m)\},$$
$$\hat\sigma(G,h)=\max\{|A|:|\hat h A|=\tbinom{m}{h}\},\quad \hat\sigma(G,[0,s])=\max\{|A|:|[0,s]\hat{}A|=\textstyle\sum_{h=0}^{s}\binom{m}{h}\},$$
$$\hat\sigma(G,\mathbb{N}_0)=\max\{|A|:|\Sigma A|=2^m\},$$
$$\hat\sigma_\pm(G,h)=\max\{|A|:|\hat h_\pm A|=\tbinom{m}{h}2^h\},\quad \hat\sigma_\pm(G,[0,s])=\max\{|A|:|[0,s]\hat{}_\pm A|=\textstyle\sum_{h=0}^{s}\binom{m}{h}2^h\},$$
$$\hat\sigma_\pm(G,\mathbb{N}_0)=\max\{|A|:|\Sigma_\pm A|=3^m\}.$$

Determine, as functions of the structure of $G$ and the parameters $h$ and $s$, the values of all ten Sidon-type quantities above, and characterize the extremal sets attaining these maxima.
status_search_result: The problem is presented as a family of open research problems on Sidon-type functions in finite abelian groups. While many partial results exist for classical Sidon sets ($h=2$, unrestricted) — notably for cyclic groups and elementary abelian groups — the full determination of all ten Sidon-type functions $\sigma, \sigma_\pm, \hat\sigma, \hat\sigma_\pm$ for arbitrary $h$, $s$, and arbitrary finite abelian $G$ remains broadly open. No comprehensive solution has been reported.

paper_title: Additive Combinatorics: A Menu of Research Problems
original_question: For a finite abelian group G, determine the smallest integer m such that every m-element subset A of G necessarily spans all of G under a specified sumset operation. This includes determining χ(G,h), χ(G,[0,s]), χ(G,N0), χ±(G,h), χ±(G,[0,s]), χ±(G,N0), χ̂(G,h), χ̂(G,[0,s]), χ̂(G,N0), χ̂±(G,h), χ̂±(G,[0,s]), and χ̂±(G,N0), where the corresponding condition is that every A of size m has hA = G, [0,s]A = G, ⟨A⟩ = G, or the analogous signed or restricted equality.
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a finite abelian group (written additively), and for a subset A ⊆ G define the following sumset operations:

• Unrestricted h-fold sumset (h ∈ ℕ): hA = {a₁ + a₂ + ⋯ + aₕ : aᵢ ∈ A}.
• Unrestricted sumset over an interval [0,s] (s ∈ ℕ₀): [0,s]A = ⋃_{h=0}^{s} hA, with 0A = {0}.
• Subgroup generated: ⟨A⟩ = ⋃_{h≥0} hA.
• Restricted h-fold sumset: ĥA = {a₁ + ⋯ + aₕ : aᵢ ∈ A, all aᵢ distinct}.
• Restricted sumset over [0,s]: [0,s]̂A = ⋃_{h=0}^{s} ĥA.
• Subset sums: ΣA = {∑_{a ∈ S} a : S ⊆ A}.
• Signed (unrestricted) h-fold sumset: h±A = {ε₁a₁ + ⋯ + εₕaₕ : aᵢ ∈ A, εᵢ ∈ {+1,−1}}.
• Signed sumset over [0,s]: [0,s]±A = ⋃_{h=0}^{s} h±A.
• Restricted signed h-fold sumset: ĥ±A = {ε₁a₁ + ⋯ + εₕaₕ : aᵢ ∈ A pairwise distinct, εᵢ ∈ {+1,−1}}.
• Restricted signed sumset over [0,s]: [0,s]̂±A.
• Σ̂±A = {∑_{a ∈ S} ε(a) a : S ⊆ A, ε : S → {+1,−1}}.

For each such sumset operation ★, the corresponding critical number is defined as
   χ★(G) = min { m ∈ ℕ : every A ⊆ G with |A| = m satisfies ★A = G }.

Specifically, determine, for every finite abelian group G, the critical numbers
   χ(G,h),   χ(G,[0,s]),   χ(G,ℕ₀),
   χ±(G,h),  χ±(G,[0,s]),  χ±(G,ℕ₀),
   χ̂(G,h),  χ̂(G,[0,s]),  χ̂(G,ℕ₀),
   χ̂±(G,h), χ̂±(G,[0,s]), χ̂±(G,ℕ₀),
where the defining condition for each is that every m-element subset A ⊆ G forces, respectively, hA = G, [0,s]A = G, ⟨A⟩ = G, h±A = G, [0,s]±A = G, ⟨A⟩ = G (signed unrestricted), ĥA = G, [0,s]̂A = G, ΣA = G, ĥ±A = G, [0,s]̂±A = G, and Σ̂±A = G.
status_search_result: The classical critical number χ̂(G,ℕ₀) (subset-sum spanning) for finite abelian groups was settled in a series of works culminating around 2007–2009 (Gao–Hamidoune, Freeze–Gao–Geroldinger, and others). However, the full family of twelve critical-number variants (covering unrestricted/restricted, signed/unsigned, and h-fold, [0,s]-fold, and ℕ₀ sums) is not completely known; many of the signed and restricted-signed variants, and exact values for general G with arbitrary h or s, remain open. No source indicates a complete resolution of the entire family.

paper_title: Additive Combinatorics: A Menu of Research Problems
original_question: For a finite abelian group G, determine the maximum size of a subset A whose specified sumsets are pairwise disjoint in the sum-free sense. This includes determining μ(G,{k,l}), μ(G,[0,s]), μ±(G,{k,l}), μ±(G,[0,s]), μ̂(G,{k,l}), μ̂(G,[0,s]), μ̂(G,N0), μ̂±(G,{k,l}), μ̂±(G,[0,s]), and μ̂±(G,N0), where the defining conditions require kA and lA, or the corresponding signed or restricted variants, to be disjoint for prescribed k and l or for all 0 ≤ l < k in a range.
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a finite abelian group, written additively, and let A ⊆ G. For a positive integer k, define the following sumsets of A:

• kA = { a_1 + a_2 + ⋯ + a_k : a_i ∈ A } (the unrestricted k-fold sumset);
• k_±A = { ε_1 a_1 + ⋯ + ε_k a_k : a_i ∈ A, ε_i ∈ {+1,−1} } (the unrestricted signed k-fold sumset);
• k^A = { a_1 + ⋯ + a_k : a_i ∈ A, all a_i distinct } (the restricted k-fold sumset);
• k^±A = { ε_1 a_1 + ⋯ + ε_k a_k : a_i ∈ A pairwise distinct, ε_i ∈ {+1,−1} } (the restricted signed k-fold sumset);
with the conventions 0A = 0_±A = 0^A = 0^±A = {0}, 1A = 1^A = A, 1_±A = 1^±A = A ∪ (−A).

For nonnegative integers k > l ≥ 0 and a positive integer s, define the following extremal quantities:

μ(G,{k,l}) = max{ |A| : A ⊆ G, kA ∩ lA = ∅ },
μ(G,[0,s]) = max{ |A| : A ⊆ G, kA ∩ lA = ∅ for all 0 ≤ l < k ≤ s },
μ_±(G,{k,l}) = max{ |A| : A ⊆ G, k_±A ∩ l_±A = ∅ },
μ_±(G,[0,s]) = max{ |A| : A ⊆ G, k_±A ∩ l_±A = ∅ for all 0 ≤ l < k ≤ s },
μ̂(G,{k,l}) = max{ |A| : A ⊆ G, k^A ∩ l^A = ∅ },
μ̂(G,[0,s]) = max{ |A| : A ⊆ G, k^A ∩ l^A = ∅ for all 0 ≤ l < k ≤ s },
μ̂(G,ℕ_0) = max{ |A| : A ⊆ G, k^A ∩ l^A = ∅ for all 0 ≤ l < k },
μ̂_±(G,{k,l}) = max{ |A| : A ⊆ G, k^±A ∩ l^±A = ∅ },
μ̂_±(G,[0,s]) = max{ |A| : A ⊆ G, k^±A ∩ l^±A = ∅ for all 0 ≤ l < k ≤ s },
μ̂_±(G,ℕ_0) = max{ |A| : A ⊆ G, k^±A ∩ l^±A = ∅ for all 0 ≤ l < k }.

Determine, as functions of the finite abelian group G and the parameters k, l, s, exact formulas (or tight bounds) for each of these ten quantities.
status_search_result: These extremal quantities for sum-free–type sets in finite abelian groups (in particular the restricted, signed, and interval/ℕ_0 variants) are known only in special cases (e.g., classical sum-free sets corresponding to μ(G,{1,1}) settled by Diananda–Yap and Green–Ruzsa, and partial results for cyclic and elementary abelian groups). General exact formulas for arbitrary G and all parameters remain open.

paper_title: Open questions on the impact of an inflated ball
original_question: How should the regulated inflation pressure of a sports ball be chosen so that the ball's impact mechanics produce a game that is fast and entertaining while still limiting single-impact or repetitive-impact injury risk? The question requires relating inflation pressure to ball impact behavior before deciding whether the observed sport-specific pressure ranges reflect a fun-versus-risk trade-off.
self_contained_problem:
Model an inflated spherical ball as a thin elastic membrane of radius $R$, wall thickness $h$, Young's modulus $E$, and Poisson ratio $
u$, enclosing a gas at regulated absolute internal pressure $P$ (gauge pressure $P - P_{	ext{atm}}$). The ball, of total mass $m$, impacts a rigid planar surface (or is struck by a rigid implement) with normal incoming speed $v_0$.

During impact, model the contact mechanics so that the contact force $F(t)$, the contact duration $	au$, the maximum deformation $\delta_{\max}$, the coefficient of restitution $e$, and the peak deceleration $a_{\max}$ can each be expressed as functions of $(P, R, h, E, 
u, m, v_0)$.

Define two functionals on the regulated pressure $P$ (with all other parameters fixed by the sport):

1. A "playability" functional $\mathcal{F}(P)$ that increases with the speed and liveliness of the rebound, e.g.
$$\mathcal{F}(P) = e(P) \cdot v_{\text{rebound}}(P) / \tau(P),$$
or any monotone surrogate measuring how fast and dynamic the resulting game is.

2. An "injury risk" functional $\mathcal{R}(P)$ that increases with the impulsive load delivered to a target (a head, a hand, etc.) per impact and accumulates over repetitive impacts, e.g.
$$\mathcal{R}(P) = \big(\max_t F(t;P)\big)^{\alpha} \cdot \big(a_{\max}(P)\big)^{\beta}$$
for suitable exponents $\alpha, \beta > 0$ derived from a chosen biomechanical injury criterion.

The problem is:

for a Lagrange multiplier $\lambda > 0$ encoding the fun-versus-risk trade-off, and characterize how $P^*$ scales with $(R, h, E, m, v_0)$.

paper_title: Open questions on the impact of an inflated ball
original_question: Can the transfer of kinetic energy into shell or membrane vibrations explain the observed energy loss in impacts of hollow balls and inflated sports balls? A satisfactory answer should distinguish shell-dominated balls with storage number St much greater than 1, such as table-tennis balls, from gas-dominated inflated balls with storage number St much less than 1, such as basketballs, and should determine whether the relevant vibration amplitudes and frequencies are large enough to account for the measured dissipated energy.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the normal impact of a hollow or inflated spherical ball with a rigid surface. Define the dimensionless storage number St as the ratio of elastic energy stored in the shell to that stored in the enclosed gas during deformation, so that St ≫ 1 corresponds to a shell-dominated ball (e.g. a table-tennis ball, where the shell elasticity stores essentially all the deformation energy) and St ≪ 1 corresponds to a gas-dominated inflated ball (e.g. a basketball, where the gas pressure stores essentially all the deformation energy and the shell behaves as an inertial membrane). Let A denote the characteristic amplitude and f the characteristic frequency of post-impact vibrations of the shell/membrane, and let M denote the ball mass. Model the kinetic energy carried by such vibrations as E_{d,vib} ≈ (1/2) M (2π f A)^2 (or an appropriate modal generalization), and compare it with the kinetic energy lost in the collision (the difference between incoming and rebound translational kinetic energies).

Question: Can the transfer of translational kinetic energy into shell vibrations (St ≫ 1) or into inflated-membrane vibrations (St ≪ 1) quantitatively account for the measured energy dissipation in such impacts? Specifically:
(a) Derive, for each regime, the expected relations between A, f, the geometric and material parameters of the ball (radius, shell thickness, Young's modulus, surface density, internal gas pressure), and the impact velocity.
(b) Determine whether the resulting amplitudes and frequencies are large enough so that E_{d,vib} matches the experimentally observed dissipated energy, and identify in which of the two regimes (shell-elastic vs. gas-elastic membrane) vibrational losses can or cannot be the dominant dissipation mechanism.
status_search_result: The question of whether shell or inflated-membrane vibrations can quantitatively account for energy loss in hollow/inflated ball impacts is posed as one of several open questions on the impact of inflated balls. No subsequent work conclusively resolving the vibrational dissipation balance for both St ≫ 1 and St ≪ 1 regimes was identified; the proposed accelerometer/optical measurements are stated as future experiments.

paper_title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems
context_brief: Monotonicity and single attractor of free-atom density
original_question: Can one prove from the quantum theory of a free atom that the ground-state one-electron density has a single attractor, a (3,-3) critical point, at the nucleus and decays monotonically away from the nucleus, rather than treating this density topology as a computationally observed but unproved conjecture?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a non-relativistic free atom with N electrons and a single nucleus of charge Z>0 located at the origin in R^3, governed by the standard many-electron Schrödinger Hamiltonian
  H = -∑_{i=1}^N (1/2)Δ_i  - ∑_{i=1}^N Z/|r_i| + ∑_{1≤i<j≤N} 1/|r_i - r_j|,
acting on the antisymmetric subspace of L^2((R^3×{↑,↓})^N). Let Ψ_0 be a (normalized) ground-state wavefunction of H, and define the one-electron density
  ρ(r) = N ∑_{σ_1,...,σ_N} ∫_{R^{3(N-1)}} |Ψ_0(r,σ_1; r_2,σ_2; ... ; r_N,σ_N)|^2 dr_2 ... dr_N.

Prove (or disprove) the following two statements about ρ:

(a) The function ρ has exactly one attractor (i.e. local maximum) on R^3, located at the position of the nucleus r=0, and this critical point is non-degenerate of Morse type (3,−3) (the Hessian of ρ at 0 has three negative eigenvalues).

(b) The density ρ is radially monotonically decreasing away from the nucleus: along every ray emanating from the origin, ρ is a strictly decreasing function of the distance |r|. Equivalently, the spherically averaged density ρ̄(r) = (4π)^{-1} ∫_{S^2} ρ(rω) dω satisfies dρ̄/dr < 0 for r>0, and moreover ρ itself decreases on every radial direction.

Establish (a) and (b) as theorems derived from the underlying many-body quantum mechanics, rather than as numerically observed regularities.
status_search_result: The conjecture that the ground-state one-electron density of a free atom is monotonically decreasing along every ray from the nucleus (and has its unique maximum, of (3,−3) type, at the nucleus) is a long-standing open problem. Rigorous results are known only in special cases: it holds rigorously for hydrogen and for one-electron systems whose external potential increases monotonically from the nucleus, and partial/sufficient conditions have been derived for two-electron and many-electron systems (e.g. Ayers 2003, Angulo–Dehesa 1991). The general many-electron case remains unproven.

paper_title: Open questions on the impact of an inflated ball
original_question: Does the gas inside an inflated ball dissipate a significant fraction of impact energy through irreversible compression, viscous friction within the gas, or non-reversible transformations involving gas components such as water vapour? This should be tested by measuring whether the gas temperature after impact is higher than its initial equilibrium temperature and by varying the gas composition, for example from water-vapour-saturated air to dry air, nitrogen gas N2, and helium.
self_contained_problem:
Consider an inflated elastic ball (a thin membrane enclosing a gas at pressure above atmospheric) that is dropped onto a rigid horizontal surface and bounces. During impact, a portion of the kinetic energy is dissipated, and one candidate mechanism is dissipation inside the gas itself, namely:

(i) irreversible compression of the gas,
(ii) viscous friction within the gas flow generated by the deformation of the ball, and
(iii) non-reversible thermodynamic transformations of gas components such as condensation/evaporation of water vapour.

Formulate and answer the following question quantitatively. Let T_0 denote the equilibrium gas temperature inside the ball before the impact and T_eq the equilibrium gas temperature after the ball has come to rest following the bounce (after pressure equilibration but before significant thermal exchange with the surroundings). Let E_kin be the kinetic energy lost by the ball during the impact (difference between kinetic energies just before and just after the bounce).

(a) Is the fraction of E_kin dissipated by irreversible processes inside the enclosed gas a significant (non-negligible) part of the total impact dissipation?

(b) Does T_eq exceed T_0, and if so by how much, as a function of the impact velocity, ball geometry, internal pressure, and gas composition?

(c) How does this dissipated fraction depend on the gas filling the ball, when the gas is varied among water-vapour-saturated air, dry air, pure diatomic nitrogen N_2, and monoatomic helium He?

Provide a model (for example, computing the internal gas flow during deformation and the work of viscous stresses, together with the thermodynamic cycle followed by the gas) that predicts (a)–(c), and compare its predictions with the corresponding measurements (e.g. fast-response thermocouple recordings of the internal temperature evolution).
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open experimental/theoretical problem about whether gas-internal irreversible processes (viscous dissipation, irreversible compression, water-vapour transformations) account for a significant share of impact dissipation in inflated balls. No subsequent work resolving this with the proposed gas-variation experiments and thermocouple measurements was located in the search; the status appears to remain open.

paper_title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems
original_question: For a Coulombic molecular system with N electrons and q clamped nuclei, is there always a critical internuclear distance for each pair of nuclei such that, whenever all internuclear distances are larger than their critical values, the gradient of the molecular one-electron density has exactly q nuclear (3,-3) critical points and no non-nuclear attractors; and can the statement that most molecules have equilibrium internuclear distances larger than these critical distances be made mathematically precise and proved?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a non-relativistic Coulombic molecular system with N electrons and q clamped nuclei located at positions R_1,...,R_q in R^3, with nuclear charges Z_1,...,Z_q > 0. The electronic Hamiltonian (in atomic units) is

  H = -1/2 sum_{i=1}^N Δ_{r_i} - sum_{i=1}^N sum_{A=1}^q Z_A/|r_i - R_A| + sum_{1<=i<j<=N} 1/|r_i - r_j| + sum_{1<=A<B<=q} Z_A Z_B/|R_A - R_B|.

Let Ψ be a normalized ground-state wavefunction of H (with the nuclear positions fixed as parameters), and let

  ρ(r; R_1,...,R_q) = N ∫ |Ψ(r, r_2,...,r_N)|^2 ds dr_2 ... dr_N

be the associated one-electron density on R^3, where the spin coordinate s and the electron coordinates r_2,...,r_N are integrated out. A point r* ∈ R^3 is called a critical point of ρ if ∇ρ(r*) = 0; it is of type (3,-3) (a local maximum / "attractor") if the Hessian of ρ at r* is negative definite. A nuclear (3,-3) critical point is one located at some R_A; any other (3,-3) critical point is called a non-nuclear attractor.

Question: Prove or disprove the following conjecture.

(a) For every pair of nuclei (A,B) there exists a critical internuclear distance d^c_{AB} > 0 such that, whenever |R_A - R_B| > d^c_{AB} for all 1 <= A < B <= q, the gradient field of ρ has exactly q critical points of type (3,-3), and these are precisely the nuclear positions R_1,...,R_q (in particular, ρ has no non-nuclear attractors).

(b) Formulate in mathematically precise terms, and prove, the statement that for "most" molecules the equilibrium internuclear distances (the local minimizers of the Born–Oppenheimer total energy as a function of (R_1,...,R_q)) exceed the corresponding critical distances d^c_{AB}.
status_search_result: The conjecture concerns when the molecular one-electron density admits only nuclear (3,-3) attractors and no non-nuclear attractors. Non-nuclear attractors are documented in real molecules (e.g., Li_2, Na_3) at certain geometries, and existence/distribution results are mostly numerical or heuristic. No general mathematical proof of the existence of universal critical internuclear distances or of a precise "most molecules" statement appears in the literature; the problem remains an open mathematical conjecture in the quantum theory of atoms in molecules.

paper_title: Open questions on the impact of an inflated ball
context_brief: Design and strategic effects of controlled bounce
original_question: Can the mass, inflation pressure, inner-gas properties, and shell mechanical characteristics of sports balls be chosen to produce prescribed bouncing behavior, including faster but still controllable and safe play and nearly constant bouncing characteristics across altitude, field conditions, and weather? Relatedly, within a sport's allowed inflation-pressure range, can pressure selection advantage a fast team against a more technical team?
self_contained_problem:
Model a sports ball as a thin elastic spherical shell of mass $m$, radius $R$, thickness $h$, Young's modulus $E$, and Poisson ratio $\nu$, enclosing a gas of pressure $p$ (above ambient), molar mass $M_g$, and adiabatic index $\gamma$, in an external atmosphere of pressure $p_{\mathrm{atm}}$, temperature $T$, and humidity $\eta$, bouncing on a surface of stiffness $K$ and friction characteristics $\mu$. Let the bounce response be characterized by the coefficient of restitution $e(v;\theta)$, the contact time $\tau(v;\theta)$, and the rebound angle for an oblique impact at incoming speed $v$ and angle $\theta$, where $\theta$ collectively denotes environmental parameters $(p_{\mathrm{atm}},T,\eta,K,\mu)$.

(a) Determine whether the design parameters $(m,R,h,E,\nu,p,M_g,\gamma)$ can be chosen so that, simultaneously,
   (i) the rebound speed $e(v;\theta)\,v$ exceeds a prescribed threshold $v_{\min}^{\mathrm{out}}$ over a target range of incoming speeds (a "faster" ball),
   (ii) the contact time $\tau(v;\theta)$ stays in a prescribed interval ensuring controllability,
   (iii) the peak contact force remains below a prescribed safety bound, and
   (iv) the variation of $(e,\tau)$ with respect to the environmental parameters $\theta$ is uniformly small: $\sup_\theta \|(e,\tau)(v;\theta)-(e,\tau)(v;\theta_0)\|<\varepsilon$ for a chosen reference $\theta_0$ and tolerance $\varepsilon$.

(b) Within an allowed inflation-pressure interval $[p_{\min},p_{\max}]$, characterize the dependence of $(e,\tau,\text{rebound angle})$ on $p$, and decide whether there exist values $p\in[p_{\min},p_{\max}]$ that systematically favor impact regimes associated with high-speed play (large $e$, short $\tau$) versus regimes associated with technical control (intermediate $e$, longer $\tau$, predictable rebound angles).

Provide either explicit constructions or rigorous obstructions for (a) and (b).
status_search_result: The question concerns the design and tuning of inflated sports balls to achieve prescribed bouncing behavior across environmental conditions and pressure ranges. It is posed as an open research direction in the impact mechanics of inflated balls; no comprehensive solution covering all listed design and environmental criteria appears in the literature, and the question of whether allowed pressure ranges can systematically advantage one playing style remains a stated open problem.

paper_title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems
original_question: Can the literature and formalism of open quantum systems be used to redefine or improve the efficient state description of a topological atom, treating an atom in a molecule as an open subsystem whose properties must be inferred from an appropriate state specification?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a molecule modeled in the Born–Oppenheimer approximation as a quantum system of N electrons in the field of fixed nuclei, with associated electronic state described by a density operator ρ on the antisymmetric Fock/Hilbert space, and with one-electron density ρ(r) = N ∫|Ψ|² dτ' that is partitioned in real space according to the Quantum Theory of Atoms in Molecules (QTAIM): each topological atom Ω is the basin of attraction in the gradient vector field ∇ρ(r) of a nuclear maximum, with interatomic surfaces S(Ω) satisfying the zero-flux condition ∇ρ(r)·n(r) = 0 for all r ∈ S(Ω).

Adopt the framework of open quantum systems, in which a subsystem A coupled to an environment E is described by a reduced density operator ρ_A = Tr_E ρ_{AE} obtained by partial trace, together with an associated dynamical map (e.g., a completely positive trace-preserving evolution or a Lindblad-type master equation) governing its effective dynamics.

Problem. Develop a rigorous formalism in which a topological atom Ω ⊂ ℝ³ (an open spatial subsystem with permeable, zero-flux boundary, exchanging electrons and energy with its complement Ω' in the molecule) is treated as an open quantum subsystem, and use this formalism to give an efficient state specification of the topological atom. Specifically:

(a) Define an appropriate reduced state ρ_Ω that encodes the quantum state of the electrons confined to (or associated with) the basin Ω, obtained by an analogue of the partial trace over the degrees of freedom in Ω', and show that it reproduces the standard QTAIM observables (atomic populations, kinetic and potential energy contributions, atomic multipole moments) as expectation values Tr(ρ_Ω O_Ω) of suitable operators O_Ω restricted to Ω.

(b) Derive the effective (possibly non-unitary) dynamical equation governing ρ_Ω that accounts for the exchange of electrons and energy across the interatomic surface S(Ω), and identify the conditions under which this evolution admits a Markovian (Lindblad) form.

(c) Determine whether such an open-system description provides a more efficient and physically faithful state specification of the topological atom than the standard QTAIM characterization, and, in particular, whether it resolves the issue of inferring atomic properties from a well-defined subsystem state rather than from spatially restricted integrals over the total molecular wavefunction.

This constitutes substantial progress on parts (a)–(b) of the program, though a fully general dynamical (e.g., Lindblad-type) formulation and the question of whether such a description is genuinely "more efficient" than standard QTAIM remain active research topics. The problem is therefore best classified as partially solved.

paper_title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems
context_brief: General Gauss-like theorem for all atomic properties
original_question: Can one derive a general Gauss-like theorem for topological atoms that goes beyond the subsystem hypervirial theorem and covers all conceivable topological-atom properties, including properties such as atomic energy and electron localization or delocalization indices that are not evidently obtained from known property currents on interatomic surfaces?
self_contained_problem:
Setting. Let ρ : ℝ³ → ℝ_{≥0} be the (one-electron) electron density of a molecular system, viewed as a smooth scalar field with isolated nuclear maxima. The Quantum Theory of Atoms in Molecules (QTAIM) partitions ℝ³ into disjoint open "topological atoms" Ω_A, where each Ω_A is the basin of attraction (under the gradient flow of ρ) of a nuclear critical point. Each basin is bounded by an interatomic surface S_A consisting of points where the gradient ∇ρ is tangent to the surface, i.e. ∇ρ · n = 0, with n the outward unit normal (the zero-flux boundary condition).

For a quantum-mechanical observable represented by an operator O, the average value over the topological atom Ω_A is ⟨O⟩_A = ∫_{Ω_A} ρ_O(r) dr for an appropriate density ρ_O derived from the system's wavefunction. The subsystem hypervirial theorem states that for a wide class of observables, ⟨O⟩_A can be reconstructed from a "property current" J_O on S_A via a Gauss-like identity of the form
   ⟨O⟩_A = ∮_{S_A} J_O · n dS,
i.e. the basin property is recoverable purely from boundary data (a "holographic" relation).

However, certain properties of topological atoms are not known to admit such a representation. Two important examples are:
 (i) the atomic energy E(Ω_A), defined via the kinetic energy density and an appropriate share of the potential energy of Ω_A;
 (ii) the (de)localization indices λ(Ω_A) and δ(Ω_A, Ω_B), defined for a state with one- and two-electron density matrices ρ₁, ρ₂ by
   δ(Ω_A, Ω_B) = -2 ∫_{Ω_A} ∫_{Ω_B} [ρ₂(r₁,r₂) - ρ(r₁)ρ(r₂)] dr₁ dr₂,
   λ(Ω_A) = δ(Ω_A, Ω_A)/2,
which measure electron sharing between basins.

Problem. Establish (or disprove) a general Gauss-like theorem for topological atoms that strictly extends the subsystem hypervirial theorem and applies to every conceivable property ⟨O⟩_A of a topological atom Ω_A. More precisely: for any reasonable atomic property functional F[ρ, ρ₁, ρ₂, …](Ω_A) — including in particular the atomic energy E(Ω_A), the localization index λ(Ω_A), and the delocalization indices δ(Ω_A, Ω_B) — exhibit a vector (or tensor) field J_F constructible from the wavefunction, defined on (a neighborhood of) S_A, such that
   F(Ω_A) = ∮_{S_A} J_F · n dS,
thereby realizing a fully holographic principle in which all properties of a topological atom are determined by data on its interatomic surface; or else prove that no such universal boundary representation can exist.
status_search_result: Subsequent literature on Quantum Chemical Topology and QTAIM (e.g. reviews on non-covalent interactions and topological coordination numbers from 2022–2025) continues to discuss the subsystem hypervirial theorem and the holographic viewpoint without reporting a general Gauss-like theorem covering atomic energy and (de)localization indices. No proof or counterexample establishing such a universal boundary theorem appears in the available sources, so the problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems
context_brief: Non-trivial duals of QTAIM and topological atoms
original_question: Does QTAIM, or do topological atoms themselves, have non-trivial dual formulations? Candidate duals include viewing a topological atom’s density in three-dimensional Euclidean space as equivalent to a free-atom density in non-Euclidean space, and viewing property currents of a topological atom as flows on the boundaries of a stationary but non-equilibrium thermodynamic open system.
self_contained_problem:
Setup. In the Quantum Theory of Atoms in Molecules (QTAIM), a molecular system is described by a smooth, everywhere-positive electron density ρ : ℝ³ → ℝ_{>0} obtained from the underlying many-electron wavefunction. A topological atom Ω ⊂ ℝ³ is defined as a basin of the gradient vector field ∇ρ: namely, Ω is a maximal open subset of ℝ³ such that every integral curve of ∇ρ starting in Ω terminates at the same nuclear critical point (a local maximum of ρ). Equivalently, Ω is bounded by a zero-flux surface S = ∂Ω satisfying ∇ρ(r) · n(r) = 0 for every r ∈ S, where n is the outward unit normal. To each one-electron property A is associated a property current j_A on ℝ³, derived from the wavefunction, whose integral fluxes through ∂Ω determine the atomic contribution of Ω to A.

Problem. Determine whether QTAIM, viewed either as a theory of the pair (ρ, {j_A}) or as a theory of its topological atoms Ω, admits a non-trivial dual formulation. In particular, decide each of the following:

(a) Does there exist a non-Euclidean Riemannian (or more general) manifold (M, g), depending functorially on (ℝ³, ρ), and a density ρ̃ on M corresponding to a free (non-interacting) atom, such that the topological atom (Ω, ρ|_Ω) in Euclidean three-space is isomorphic — under a precisely specified equivalence of densities, currents, and basin/zero-flux structures — to (M, ρ̃)? Construct such a duality, or prove that no such non-trivial correspondence exists.

(b) Does there exist a stationary non-equilibrium thermodynamic open system, with a well-defined boundary geometry and boundary flows, such that the property currents {j_A} of a topological atom Ω are equivalent (as vector fields with associated conserved fluxes) to the boundary flows of this thermodynamic system, in a way that recovers all QTAIM atomic observables? Either exhibit such a correspondence or prove its impossibility.

A non-trivial dual is required to give a bijection on observables that is not merely a tautological relabeling.

No subsequent literature establishing such a non-trivial duality (either to free-atom densities on non-Euclidean spaces or to boundary flows of stationary non-equilibrium thermodynamic systems) was located, and the problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems
context_brief: Liquid model and mechanics of charge density
original_question: Can one develop a liquid model of charge density in atoms-in-molecules theory in which a principal parameter is the viscosity experienced by migrating critical points, and can the currently incomplete mechanics of charge density be extended into new models that answer old problems?
self_contained_problem:
In the quantum theory of atoms in molecules, a molecular system is described by its (scalar) one-electron charge density ρ: ℝ³ → ℝ_{≥0}, a smooth function whose critical points (where ∇ρ = 0) are classified by the signature of the Hessian into nuclear attractors (3,−3), bond critical points (3,−1), ring critical points (3,+1), and cage critical points (3,+3). Atomic basins are defined as the connected regions of the gradient field ∇ρ bounded by zero-flux surfaces (surfaces S satisfying ∇ρ(r)·n(r)=0 for all r ∈ S). As nuclear coordinates evolve along a reaction path R(t), the critical points of ρ(·;R(t)) migrate continuously in ℝ³ (away from catastrophe events).

The problem is to formulate a "liquid (continuum) model" for the dynamics of the charge density ρ in which:

1. The migrating critical points {x_k(t)} of ρ(·;R(t)) are treated as transported by an effective velocity field on a viscous medium, governed by a constitutive law of the form
   η(ρ,∇ρ,…) · ẋ_k(t) = F_k[ρ, R, Ṙ],
   where η is a scalar (or tensorial) viscosity functional taken as the principal parameter of the model and F_k is a force functional derivable from the energetic and topological structure of ρ.

2. The model reproduces, in appropriate limits, the established mechanics of the charge density (continuity equation for ρ, atomic-basin force and virial theorems, and stationarity of zero-flux surfaces), and yields a closed evolution equation for ρ along nuclear motion compatible with the catastrophe set of QTAIM.

Construct such a model with a precisely defined viscosity functional η, derive the corresponding equations of motion for ρ and for its critical points, and use it to address at least one of the following standing problems: (a) prediction of bifurcation thresholds at which bond/ring/cage critical points coalesce or annihilate, (b) quantitative characterization of "structural stability" of molecular graphs under nuclear displacement, and (c) extension of the mechanics of the charge density to a complete dynamical theory consistent with the underlying quantum stress-tensor field.

Determine whether such a viscosity-based liquid model of the charge density exists with the above properties, and exhibit it explicitly, or prove that no such consistent model can be formulated within the QTAIM framework.
status_search_result: The question is a programmatic open problem about formulating a new "liquid/viscous" continuum model for the QTAIM charge density. No subsequent work appears to have constructed such a model with viscosity as principal parameter; the broader program of completing the mechanics of the charge density remains open in the QTAIM literature.

paper_title: Revisiting the Arcade Learning Environment: Evaluation Protocols and Open Problems for General Agents
context_brief: Planning and learned models in ALE
original_question: How can one learn and use a model of Atari 2600 games in the Arcade Learning Environment that stays accurate over long rollouts, is fast enough to be useful for planning rather than slower than the emulator itself, and still supports effective planning when the learned model is imperfect and errors compound over time?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the Arcade Learning Environment (ALE), a reinforcement-learning benchmark in which an agent interacts with Atari 2600 games through a deterministic simulator (the emulator) that, at each discrete time step t, takes the current RAM/screen state s_t and an action a_t from a finite action set A and returns the next state s_{t+1}, a reward r_t, and a terminal flag. A learned model of an ALE game is a function M (typically parameterized by a neural network or other learned representation) that, given a state representation and an action, predicts the next state representation and reward, and which can be iterated to produce rollouts of length H by feeding its own predictions back as input.

Design and analyze a learned model M of Atari 2600 games in the ALE satisfying simultaneously the following three properties:

1. (Long-horizon accuracy.) The expected prediction error of M over rollouts of horizon H grows sufficiently slowly with H that compounding errors do not render the model useless for planning at horizons relevant to control on representative ALE titles.

2. (Computational efficiency.) The wall-clock cost per simulated step of M is no larger than that of the Stella emulator itself, so that using M for planning yields a strict speed advantage over planning directly with the emulator.

3. (Robust planning under model error.) Provide a planning algorithm that, when paired with such an imperfect M, achieves performance on a broad suite of ALE games that is competitive with, or better than, planning algorithms that have access to the exact emulator under matched compute budgets, despite errors in M that compound over time.

Equivalently: exhibit a learned model and an associated planning procedure for the ALE that is fast (faster than the emulator), accurate over long rollouts, and effective for planning even when the model is imperfect; or prove that no such combination can exist under stated computational/statistical assumptions.
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made since the problem was posed. SimPLe (Kaiser et al., ICLR 2020) demonstrated successful planning with a learned video model in the ALE, mitigating compounding error via short rollouts. MuZero (Schrittwieser et al., 2019/2020) achieved state-of-the-art Atari performance by planning with a learned latent model, and DreamerV2/V3 (Hafner et al., 2020/2023) attained human-level Atari performance using learned world models. These works address long-horizon accuracy and planning under imperfect models, though achieving a learned model that is simultaneously faster than the Stella emulator, accurate over long rollouts, and robust for planning across all ALE titles remains not fully resolved; hence partially solved.

paper_title: Open questions on the impact of an inflated ball
original_question: During the normal impact of an inflated ball on a rigid surface, what amount of energy is carried away by sound or a shock wave generated by the rapidly moving ball-ground-air contact line, and are these sound-radiated losses negligible compared with the total energy lost in the impact?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the normal impact of an inflated elastic ball (e.g. a sports ball, modeled as a thin pressurized spherical shell of radius R filled with gas at internal pressure p, mass m) striking a flat rigid surface at vertical velocity V. As the ball deforms against the surface, a circular contact patch forms whose radius l(t) grows in time; from the geometry of a sphere indented by a depth x = Vt, one has l(t) ≈ √(2Rx) so that the lateral expansion velocity of the ball–ground–air contact line is

  dl/dt ≈ V √(R/(2x)),

which diverges as x → 0+. While dl/dt exceeds the speed of sound c_s in the surrounding air, a shock wave is emitted from the contact line, and once dl/dt < c_s ordinary acoustic radiation continues.

Problem. Derive a quantitative estimate of the total energy E_sound radiated as sound and shock waves into the surrounding air during a single normal impact, expressed in terms of the impact parameters (V, R, m, ambient air density ρ_air and sound speed c_s, and any relevant material/pressure parameters). In particular:

(a) determine the contribution from the supersonic regime dl/dt > c_s, where shock-wave dissipation occurs along the moving contact line, and the contribution from the subsonic acoustic radiation regime;

(b) compare E_sound with the typical total kinetic energy lost in such an impact (of order ΔE ∼ (1/2) m V² with restitution losses on the order of tens of joules for a standard sports ball), and decide whether sound/shock-wave radiation is a negligible contribution to the overall energy budget of the impact.

Provide the scaling laws, the explicit estimate, and the criterion under which the inequality E_sound ≪ ΔE holds.
status_search_result: Web searches return the original problem listing and general references on shock-wave dissipation and droplet-impact contact-line shocks, but no subsequent work providing a confirmed quantitative estimate of sound/shock energy radiated by an inflated-ball impact or experimental verification that such losses are negligible. The question appears to remain open.
