paper_title: Light Chemical Elements in Stars: Mysteries and Unsolved Problems
original_question: Why is the primordial lithium abundance inferred from old FGK dwarf stars in the Galactic halo, with log ε(7Li) ≈ 2.2 on the Spite plateau, lower by about 0.5 dex than the Standard Model of the Big Bang prediction of about 2.7, even though the same model agrees well with observed primordial abundances of deuterium, 3He, and 4He?
self_contained_problem:
Standard Big Bang nucleosynthesis (SMBB), with the baryon-to-photon ratio fixed by cosmic microwave background measurements, predicts primordial abundances of the light isotopes D, 3He, 4He, and 7Li produced in the first minutes after the Big Bang. For 7Li the predicted primordial abundance, expressed as log ε(7Li) = log10[N(7Li)/N(H)] + 12, is approximately 2.7. Spectroscopic determinations of the photospheric lithium abundance in old, metal-poor FGK dwarf stars in the Galactic halo (whose surface composition is taken to reflect the gas from which they formed) yield a nearly flat "Spite plateau" with log ε(7Li) ≈ 2.2, i.e. about 0.5 dex below the SMBB prediction. By contrast, the SMBB predictions for D, 3He, and 4He agree with their observationally inferred primordial values.

Provide a quantitatively consistent explanation of this 0.5 dex deficit. Specifically, identify a mechanism (whether stellar — e.g. atomic diffusion, turbulent mixing, rotation-induced transport, pre-main-sequence depletion — cosmological, particle-physical, or otherwise) that:
(i) reduces the surface 7Li abundance of old halo dwarfs from ≈ 2.7 to the observed ≈ 2.2 plateau value,
(ii) reproduces the small dispersion and weak dependence of the plateau on effective temperature and metallicity, and
(iii) does not spoil the agreement between SMBB and the observed primordial abundances of D, 3He, and 4He.
category_tag: Big Bang nucleosynthesis / primordial lithium problem
status_search_result: As of 2025, the cosmological lithium problem remains a recognized open question in astrophysics. Recent reviews and a 2025 A&A article still discuss the factor-of-3 (≈0.5 dex) discrepancy between the SMBB prediction and the Spite-plateau abundance in halo dwarfs, with no single mechanism (stellar depletion via diffusion/turbulence/rotation, modified BBN, or new physics) accepted as a complete solution. Some recent works argue stellar-physics effects can largely account for the gap, while others contest this, so the problem is best characterized as still open / partially addressed.

paper_title: Light Chemical Elements in Stars: Mysteries and Unsolved Problems
original_question: What physical mechanism can explain the observed helium enrichment of early B-type main-sequence stellar atmospheres, especially for stars of about 12–19 solar masses where He/H increases by more than a factor of two toward the end of the main-sequence stage, even though most such stars have relatively low rotation velocities and current rotating-star models predict much smaller helium enhancement?
self_contained_problem:
Observations of early B-type main-sequence stars show that the surface helium-to-hydrogen number ratio He/H increases significantly during the main-sequence (MS) lifetime. In particular, for stars with masses in the range 12–19 solar masses, the surface He/H ratio is observed to increase by more than a factor of two between the zero-age main sequence and the terminal-age main sequence. Most of these stars are observed to rotate with relatively low projected equatorial velocities, and standard stellar evolution models that include rotationally induced mixing (meridional circulation, shear-induced turbulent diffusion, etc.) predict only a small surface helium enhancement for such rotation rates—much smaller than what is observed.

Identify and justify a physical mechanism (or combination of mechanisms) capable of transporting helium, the main product of CNO-cycle hydrogen burning, from the convective core to the radiative envelope and atmosphere of an early B-type MS star at a rate sufficient to reproduce the observed factor-of-two-or-more enhancement of He/H by the end of the main-sequence stage, while remaining consistent with the observed (low) surface rotational velocities and with other observed surface abundance patterns (e.g., CNO ratios) for stars in the 12–19 solar-mass range.
category_tag: Stellar astrophysics / mixing in massive stars
status_search_result: The problem of explaining the observed helium surface enrichment in early B-type main-sequence stars of ~12–19 solar masses remains an active research topic. Rotationally induced mixing alone (with initial velocities of 250–400 km/s) has been proposed as a partial explanation, and recent work (e.g., a 2020 MNRAS study and a 2024 IAC announcement) suggests that mass accretion from a binary companion or interplay between metallicity and rotation may also contribute. No single mechanism has been established as fully reconciling theory with observation for slow rotators in this mass range.

original_question: Why are three different kinds of B-type main-sequence stars found in the same effective-temperature range of about 17000–25000 K—He-strong stars with enhanced helium, He-weak stars with depleted helium, and chemically normal B-type stars—and what mechanism determines which helium-abundance class a given star occupies?

status_search_result: The coexistence of He-strong, He-weak, and normal B-type main-sequence stars in the 17000–25000 K range remains an open problem in stellar astrophysics. Models combining atomic diffusion with stellar winds and magnetic fields qualitatively reproduce some helium-line behavior in He-peculiar stars, but they fail to fully account for the observed strengths and the class assignment of individual stars. Recent work (e.g., on helium diffusion in magnetic atmospheres of early B-type stars, A&A 2021) explicitly states that diffusion alone is insufficient and that additional mechanisms must be explored.

paper_title: Some open problems on holomorphic foliation theory
original_question: Let F be a holomorphic foliation in the unit polydisc D^k in C^k whose leaves have dimension d > 1. Suppose the leaves are tangent to k-d holomorphic (1,0)-forms alpha_j on C^k, linearly independent at a generic point of D^k, and satisfying the Frobenius condition. Can F always be approximated by foliations in C^k or P^k? More precisely, can the forms alpha_j be uniformly approximated on compact subsets of D^k by entire forms, respectively polynomial forms, alpha_{j,n} that still satisfy the Frobenius condition?
self_contained_problem:
Let $k\ge 2$ and let $\mathbb{D}^k\subset\mathbb{C}^k$ denote the open unit polydisc. Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a holomorphic foliation on $\mathbb{D}^k$ whose leaves have complex dimension $d$ with $1<d<k$. Suppose that $\mathcal{F}$ is defined by $k-d$ holomorphic $(1,0)$-forms $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_{k-d}$ on $\mathbb{D}^k$ (so the tangent distribution to $\mathcal{F}$ at a point $p$ is the joint kernel of $\alpha_1(p),\dots,\alpha_{k-d}(p)$), which are linearly independent at a generic point of $\mathbb{D}^k$ and satisfy the Frobenius integrability condition
$$d\alpha_j\wedge\alpha_1\wedge\dots\wedge\alpha_{k-d}=0\qquad(j=1,\dots,k-d).$$

Question: Does there always exist a sequence of $(k-d)$-tuples of $(1,0)$-forms $(\alpha_{1,n},\dots,\alpha_{k-d,n})$, defined on $\mathbb{C}^k$ (respectively, with polynomial coefficients, viewed as forms on $\mathbb{P}^k$), each tuple satisfying the Frobenius integrability condition, such that for every $j$ the forms $\alpha_{j,n}$ converge to $\alpha_j$ uniformly on every compact subset of $\mathbb{D}^k$ as $n\to\infty$?

In other words, can every higher-dimensional holomorphic foliation on the polydisc be approximated, in the sense above, by holomorphic foliations on $\mathbb{C}^k$ (respectively algebraic foliations on $\mathbb{P}^k$)?
status_search_result: No published resolution was found. The question of Runge-type approximation of higher-dimensional holomorphic foliations on the polydisc by entire or polynomial integrable forms appears to remain open; related results exist for codimension-one foliations and for approximation in Stein/Runge settings, but the higher-dimensional Frobenius-preserving case in the form posed is not reported as solved.

paper_title: Light Chemical Elements in Stars: Mysteries and Unsolved Problems
original_question: What theoretical mechanism can reproduce, for FGK dwarf stars in old clusters such as the Hyades, both the overall decrease of lithium, beryllium, and boron abundances with falling effective temperature and the pronounced abundance dip near Teff ≈ 6600 K, including the different dip depths observed for Li, Be, and B?
self_contained_problem:
Consider FGK main-sequence dwarf stars in old open clusters (for example, of Hyades-like age, ~600–800 Myr) and their photospheric abundances of the light elements lithium, beryllium, and boron. Observations show two coupled features as functions of effective temperature T_eff:

(i) a global decrease of the surface abundances A(Li), A(Be), and A(B) with decreasing T_eff across the FGK range; and

(ii) a sharp localized depletion ("dip") centered near T_eff ≈ 6600 K, whose depth differs strongly among the three elements: roughly more than 2 dex for Li, about 1 dex for Be, and about 0.4 dex for B.

Develop a self-consistent stellar-physics model — incorporating mechanisms such as microscopic diffusion, rotationally induced mixing, internal gravity waves, meridional circulation, magnetic effects, mass loss, or any combination thereof — that quantitatively reproduces simultaneously, for a single coeval population at solar-like metallicity:

(a) the observed monotonic trend of A(Li), A(Be), and A(B) versus T_eff for FGK dwarfs, and

(b) the location, width, and the differential depths of the Li, Be, and B abundance dips near T_eff ≈ 6600 K, matching the relative ordering depth(Li) ≫ depth(Be) > depth(B).
status_search_result: Recent observational and theoretical literature on the Hyades Li–Be–B dip (e.g., Boesgaard et al. 2016 on boron abundances across the Li–Be dip, and reviews on light-element depletion in FGK dwarfs) confirms that no current stellar-evolution model simultaneously reproduces the global T_eff trend and the differential depths of the Li, Be, and B dips at ~6600 K. The problem is generally treated as still unresolved.

original_question: Over RCA0, are the following four statements equivalent: (A) the Halpern-Lauchli Theorem for any finite number of trees; (B) Milliken's Ramsey theorem for strong trees on one finitely branching infinite tree with no terminal nodes; (C) the canonical partition theorem for colorings of a fixed finite graph inside the Rado graph; and (D) the statement that for every k >= 2, the Rado graph has the rainbow Ramsey property for k-bounded colorings?
self_contained_problem:
Work in the subsystem $\mathsf{RCA}_0$ of second-order arithmetic. Consider the following four combinatorial principles.

(A) Halpern–Läuchli theorem (finite product version): For every $d \ge 1$, every sequence $T_1,\dots,T_d$ of finitely branching infinite trees with no terminal nodes, every $k \ge 2$, and every coloring $c:\prod_{i=1}^d T_i \to k$ of the level-product, there exist a color $j<k$ and strong subtrees $S_i \subseteq T_i$ of common height $\omega$ such that $c$ is constantly $j$ on $\prod_i S_i$ at matched levels.

(B) Milliken's Ramsey theorem for strong subtrees: For every finitely branching infinite tree $T$ with no terminal nodes, every $n \ge 1$, every $k \ge 2$, and every coloring of the strong subtrees of $T$ of height $n$ with $k$ colors, there is an infinite strong subtree $S \subseteq T$ all of whose strong subtrees of height $n$ receive the same color.

(C) Canonical partition theorem for the Rado graph: For every finite graph $H$, there is a finite list of "canonical" equivalence relations on the set $\binom{R}{H}$ of induced copies of $H$ in the Rado graph $R$ such that, for every coloring of $\binom{R}{H}$, there is an isomorphic copy $R' \subseteq R$ of the Rado graph on which the coloring is constant on the equivalence classes of one of the canonical relations.

(D) Rainbow Ramsey for the Rado graph: For every $k \ge 2$ and every coloring of the vertices (equivalently, of induced copies of a fixed finite graph) of the Rado graph $R$ in which each color class has size at most $k$, there is an isomorphic copy $R' \subseteq R$ of the Rado graph on which the coloring is injective.

Question: Are any two of (A), (B), (C), (D) equivalent over $\mathsf{RCA}_0$? In particular, is $(A) \Leftrightarrow (B) \Leftrightarrow (C) \Leftrightarrow (D)$ provable in $\mathsf{RCA}_0$, given that the implications $(A) \Rightarrow (B) \Rightarrow (C) \Rightarrow (D)$ are theorems of $\mathsf{ZF}$?
status_search_result: A subsequent work by Anglès d'Auriac, Cholak, Dzhafarov, Monin, and Patey, "Milliken's tree theorem and its applications: a computability-theoretic perspective" (arXiv:2007.09739), provides a comprehensive computability-theoretic and reverse-mathematical classification of Milliken's tree theorem and several of its consequences, including the Halpern–Läuchli theorem and partition theorems for the Rado graph. The analysis yields equivalences and separations among parameter-stratified versions of these principles, but the literature does not appear to give a definitive single statement asserting that all four principles (A)–(D), in the unrestricted forms above, are equivalent over $\mathsf{RCA}_0$. The question is therefore at least partially resolved.

paper_title: Light Chemical Elements in Stars: Mysteries and Unsolved Problems
original_question: Why do the cold supergiants HR 461 and HR 8313, which are more massive than about 6 solar masses, still show detectable lithium even though stellar-evolution calculations predict that stars in this mass range should have destroyed essentially all atmospheric lithium before reaching the red-giant or supergiant phase?
self_contained_problem:
Standard stellar-evolution theory predicts that in single stars with initial masses greater than approximately 6 solar masses, essentially all atmospheric lithium (⁷Li) should be destroyed by proton-capture reactions (the p,α reaction on ⁷Li, active at temperatures above ~2.5×10⁶ K) through convective mixing of surface material into hotter interior layers, so that by the time such a star evolves onto the red-giant or supergiant branch its photospheric lithium abundance should be far below detection limits. Nevertheless, the cool supergiants HR 461 (spectral type K0 Ia) and HR 8313 (spectral type G5 Ib), both with inferred initial masses exceeding 6 solar masses, exhibit clearly detectable photospheric lithium with abundance log ε(Li) ≈ 1.5 (on the standard scale where log ε(H) = 12).

Provide a quantitative astrophysical mechanism that explains how supergiants of initial mass M ≳ 6 M_⊙ in the post–main-sequence cool phase can retain, or freshly produce, photospheric lithium at the level log ε(Li) ≈ 1.5. The proposed mechanism should be consistent with the stars' observed effective temperatures, luminosities, surface gravities, and other surface abundances, and should specify whether the lithium is a survival of pre-main-sequence material, the result of in situ synthesis (for example via the Cameron–Fowler ⁷Be-transport mechanism or analogous processes), or a consequence of external enrichment, together with the conditions under which the prediction reproduces the observed abundance.
status_search_result: The discrepancy between the observed lithium in massive cool supergiants such as HR 461 and HR 8313 and the predictions of standard stellar-evolution theory remains an open puzzle. Reviews of lithium in stellar atmospheres and recent studies of strong lithium lines in red supergiants describe these stars as outliers and suggest that the lithium may have been recently synthesized (e.g. via Cameron–Fowler-type processes), but no fully accepted quantitative mechanism has been established.

context_brief: Triples of naturals versus three-vertex graphs
original_question: Fix any graph G with three vertices and any k >= 2. Assuming over RCA0 the rainbow Ramsey theorem for k-bounded colorings of triples of natural numbers, does it follow that every coloring of copies of G in the Rado graph into countably many colors, with each color used at most k times, has a subgraph isomorphic to the Rado graph in which no two copies of G receive the same color?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions.

(a) The Rado graph R is the unique (up to isomorphism) countable graph satisfying the extension property: for every pair of disjoint finite sets of vertices A, B there exists a vertex v adjacent to every vertex of A and to no vertex of B. A subgraph R' of R is called a copy of the Rado graph if R' (with the induced edge relation) is isomorphic to R.

(b) For a finite graph G, a copy of G in R is an induced subgraph of R isomorphic to G. Given a positive integer k, a coloring c of the copies of G in R using countably many colors is called k-bounded if for every color class, at most k copies of G receive that color.

(c) The rainbow Ramsey theorem RRT(G, k) for the Rado graph asserts: for every k-bounded coloring c of the copies of G in R into countably many colors, there exists a subgraph R' of R that is itself a copy of the Rado graph such that no two distinct copies of G inside R' receive the same c-color.

(d) For natural numbers, the rainbow Ramsey theorem RRT^3_k for triples states: for every k-bounded coloring of the 3-element subsets of N into countably many colors, there exists an infinite set H ⊆ N such that no two 3-element subsets of H receive the same color.

(e) RCA_0 denotes the standard base subsystem of second-order arithmetic (recursive comprehension with Σ^0_1 induction).

Question. Let G be any graph on three vertices and let k ≥ 2 be an integer. Working over RCA_0, does RRT^3_k (the rainbow Ramsey theorem for k-bounded colorings of triples of natural numbers) imply RRT(G, k) (the rainbow Ramsey theorem for k-bounded colorings of copies of G in the Rado graph)?
category_tag: Rainbow Ramsey theory in reverse mathematics
status_search_result: Web search located related literature on the reverse mathematics of rainbow Ramsey theorems (notably the result that RRT for triples is strictly weaker than ACA_0) and on rainbow Ramsey statements in homogeneous structures such as the Rado graph, but no source was found that resolves the specific implication from RRT^3_k to the rainbow Ramsey theorem for k-bounded colorings of three-vertex subgraphs in the Rado graph over RCA_0. The status appears unresolved in the accessible literature.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: If f (z) is meromorphic of finite order ρ and δ(a, f ) = 2, it is conjectured that ρ = n/2, where n is an integer and n ≥ 2, and all the deficiencies are rational. F. Nevanlinna [596] has proved this result on the condition that f (z) has no multiple values, so that n(r, a) = n(r, a) for every a (see also R. Nevanlinna [597]).
self_contained_problem:
Let $f$ be a meromorphic function on the complex plane of finite order $\rho$, where the order is defined by $\rho = \limsup_{r\to\infty} \frac{\log T(r,f)}{\log r}$ and $T(r,f)$ is the Nevanlinna characteristic. For $a \in \mathbb{C}\cup\{\infty\}$, define the Nevanlinna deficiency $$\delta(a,f) = \liminf_{r\to\infty} \frac{m(r,a)}{T(r,f)} = 1 - \limsup_{r\to\infty}\frac{N(r,a)}{T(r,f)},$$ where $m(r,a)$ and $N(r,a)$ are the usual Nevanlinna proximity and counting functions (with $N(r,\infty)$ counting poles, etc.). The First Fundamental Theorem implies $\sum_{a} \delta(a,f) \le 2$.

Suppose $f$ is an extremal case in the sense that $\sum_{a} \delta(a,f) = 2$. Prove that:
(i) the order $\rho$ must be of the form $\rho = n/2$ for some integer $n \ge 2$;
(ii) every deficiency $\delta(a,f)$ is a rational number.
status_search_result: The conjecture (often called the deficiency conjecture for the extremal case $\sum \delta(a,f)=2$) was completely proved by D. Drasin. Earlier partial results include F. Nevanlinna's proof under the assumption that $f$ has no multiple values, and Weitsman's bound that the number of deficiencies is at most $2\rho$ in this setting.

original_question: For each d, is the reverse-mathematical strength of the strong-tree version of the Halpern-Lauchli Theorem for d trees strictly stronger than the reverse-mathematical strength of the somewhere dense matrix form for d trees?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. For a positive integer d, let T_1, ..., T_d be finitely branching trees of height ω, each with no terminal nodes. For n ∈ ω, write T_i(n) for the n-th level of T_i, and let ⊗_{i=1}^{d} T_i(n) denote the "level product" {(t_1, ..., t_d) : t_i ∈ T_i(n)}. Set ⊗T := ⋃_{n∈ω} ⊗_{i=1}^{d} T_i(n).

(a) Strong-tree version (SS_d) of the Halpern–Läuchli theorem: For every finite coloring c : ⊗T → k, there exist strong subtrees S_i ⊆ T_i (i = 1, ..., d), each of height ω and sharing a common level set L ⊆ ω (so that S_i ∩ T_i(ℓ) is nonempty exactly for ℓ ∈ L, and at each such ℓ every node of S_i at lower levels of L has the same number of immediate successors in S_i at the next level of L), such that c is constant on ⋃_{ℓ∈L} ⊗_{i=1}^{d} (S_i ∩ T_i(ℓ)).

(b) Somewhere-dense matrix form (SD_d): For every finite coloring c : ⊗T → k, there exist a level n ∈ ω, a node t_i ∈ T_i for each i, and finite "matrices" A_i ⊆ T_i above t_i, all sharing a common level set, such that the union of level products ⊗_{i=1}^{d} A_i is monochromatic and somewhere dense in the sense that the A_i densely populate some block of levels above the t_i.

Both SS_d and SD_d can be formulated as Π^1_2 statements in the language of second-order arithmetic and so admit reverse-mathematical analysis over RCA_0 (or a suitable base theory).

Question. For each d ≥ 2, is the reverse-mathematical strength of SS_d strictly greater than the reverse-mathematical strength of SD_d? That is, does SS_d prove SD_d over the base theory while SD_d fails to prove SS_d?
status_search_result: A web search for reverse-mathematical comparisons of the strong-tree and somewhere-dense-matrix forms of the Halpern–Läuchli theorem returns work on the theorem at large cardinals and partition principles, but no source verifying that SS_d is strictly stronger than SD_d (or that they are equivalent) over a weak base system. The status thus appears unresolved in the publicly available literature.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Under what conditions can δ(a, P f ) be nearly 2 for an entire function of finite order ρ? Pfluger [633] proved that if δ(a, f ) = 2, then (see Hayman [395, p.115]) ρ is a positive integer q, the lower order λ is such that λ = ρ and all the deficiencies are integral multiplicities of 1/q. If further X δ(a, f ) > 2 − ε(λ), where ε(λ) is a positive quantity depending on λ, then Edrei and Fuchs ([216], [217]) proved that these results remain true ‘nearly’, in the sense that there exist ‘large’ deficiencies which are nearly positive integral multiplicities of 1/q, and whose sum of deficiencies is ‘nearly’ 2. Can there be a finite or infinite number of small deficiences as well in this case?
self_contained_problem:
Let $f$ be an entire function of finite order $\rho$ and lower order $\lambda$. For $a\in\mathbb{C}\cup\{\infty\}$ define the Nevanlinna deficiency
$$\delta(a,f)=1-\limsup_{r\to\infty}\frac{N(r,a,f)}{T(r,f)},$$
where $T(r,f)$ is the Nevanlinna characteristic and $N(r,a,f)$ is the integrated counting function of $a$-points of $f$. A classical theorem of Pfluger asserts that if $\sum_a \delta(a,f)=2$ for an entire function of finite order, then $\rho$ is a positive integer $q$, $\lambda=\rho$, and every deficiency $\delta(a,f)$ is an integer multiple of $1/q$. Edrei and Fuchs proved a near-extremal version: there exists a positive function $\varepsilon(\lambda)>0$ such that, whenever
$$\sum_a \delta(a,f) > 2-\varepsilon(\lambda),$$
there exist "large" deficiencies which are approximately positive integer multiples of $1/q$ and whose sum is close to $2$.

Question: In this near-extremal setting (i.e., for entire functions of finite order satisfying $\sum_a\delta(a,f)>2-\varepsilon(\lambda)$), can there in addition exist a finite or infinite collection of further "small" deficient values $a$ with $0<\delta(a,f)$ small? Determine whether such small deficiencies are possible, and if so, characterize the conditions under which they may occur.
status_search_result: The problem appears in Hayman's collection of research problems in function theory and remains unresolved; no published resolution was located. Hayman conjectures the answer is negative (no small additional deficiencies should occur), but no proof or counterexample has been recorded.

original_question: Does the reverse-mathematical strength of Milliken's theorem depend on the height of the finite strong trees being colored?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. Let T be an infinite, finitely branching tree with no terminal nodes (e.g., a subtree of ω^{<ω}). For a node x ∈ T, write |x| for its level (length). A subtree S ⊆ T is called a strong subtree of T if:
(i) S has a single root and is closed under meets in T;
(ii) there is a strictly increasing "level sequence" ℓ_0 < ℓ_1 < … such that every node of S at internal depth i has level exactly ℓ_i in T;
(iii) every non-terminal node of S has, as its immediate successors in S, exactly one extension in T at level ℓ_{i+1} for every immediate successor (in T) of the corresponding node — i.e., S branches in T in the canonical "strong" way.

For n ≥ 1, let S_n(T) denote the set of strong subtrees of T of height n. Milliken's tree theorem (MT) asserts: for every infinite finitely branching tree T with no terminal nodes, every n ≥ 1, and every finite coloring f : S_n(T) → k, there exists an infinite strong subtree T' ⊆ T such that f is constant on S_n(T').

For each fixed n ≥ 1, let MTT_n denote the restriction of MT to colorings of strong subtrees of height n.

Question. context_brief: Strength of the Rado rainbow Ramsey property
original_question: What is the reverse-mathematical strength of the following statement: for every finite graph G and every k >= 2, every coloring of all copies of G in the Rado graph into countably many colors, with each color used at most k times, has a subgraph isomorphic to the Rado graph in which no two copies of G receive the same color?
self_contained_problem:
Let R denote the Rado graph: the unique (up to isomorphism) countable graph satisfying the extension property that for every pair of disjoint finite sets of vertices A, B there exists a vertex adjacent to every vertex in A and to no vertex in B. For a finite graph G, a "copy of G in R" means an induced subgraph of R isomorphic to G. A subgraph R' of R is called a Rado subgraph if R' is itself isomorphic to the Rado graph.

Consider the following statement (D):

For every finite graph G and every integer k ≥ 2, and for every coloring c of the set of all copies of G in R using countably many colors such that each color is used on at most k copies of G, there exists a Rado subgraph R' ⊆ R such that the restriction of c to the copies of G contained in R' is injective (no two copies of G in R' receive the same color).

Determine the precise reverse-mathematical strength of statement (D): identify, over the base system RCA₀, a subsystem of second-order arithmetic to which (D) is equivalent (or otherwise classify its strength among standard subsystems such as RCA₀, WKL₀, ACA₀, ATR₀, Π¹₁-CA₀, and known Ramsey-theoretic principles).
status_search_result: The question is one of an explicitly posed list of open problems on the reverse mathematics of Ramsey theory on the Rado graph. Related work exists on the reverse mathematics of the rainbow Ramsey theorem for n-tuples on ω, and on Ramsey-theoretic properties of the Rado graph, but I found no published determination of the reverse-mathematical strength of the Rado-graph rainbow Ramsey statement (D). It thus appears to remain open.

context_brief: Rainbow theorem versus canonical partition theorem
original_question: Does the reverse-mathematical strength of the rainbow Ramsey theorem for the Rado graph coincide with the reverse-mathematical strength of Sauer's canonical partition theorem for colorings of a fixed finite graph inside the Rado graph?
self_contained_problem:
Let R denote the Rado graph, i.e., the unique countable graph that is universal and ultrahomogeneous for finite graphs (equivalently, the up-to-isomorphism unique countable graph satisfying the extension property: for every pair of disjoint finite vertex sets U, V there is a vertex adjacent to every vertex of U and to no vertex of V).

For a countably infinite graph G and a finite graph F, write Emb(F, G) for the set of induced copies of F in G. A coloring c : Emb(F, G) → ω is called rainbow-injective if every color is used at most finitely many times (or, in the standard formulation, c is injective on the relevant family). The rainbow Ramsey theorem for the Rado graph (RR(R)) is the statement: for every finite graph F and every coloring c : Emb(F, R) → ω that uses each color at most finitely often, there exists an induced copy R' of R inside R such that c restricted to Emb(F, R') is injective (a "rainbow" copy).

Sauer's canonical partition theorem for the Rado graph (CPT(R)) is the statement: for every finite graph F there is a finite list of "canonical" equivalence relations on Emb(F, R) such that for every coloring c : Emb(F, R) → ω there exists an induced copy R' of R inside R on which c is constant on the classes of one of the canonical equivalence relations. (This implies that the Rado graph has finite big Ramsey degrees.)

Working over the base system RCA₀ of second-order arithmetic, formalize RR(R) and CPT(R) in the standard way.

Question: Are RR(R) and CPT(R) equivalent over RCA₀? Equivalently, do the rainbow Ramsey theorem for the Rado graph and Sauer's canonical partition theorem for finite graphs inside the Rado graph have the same reverse-mathematical strength?
status_search_result: A web search did not turn up a published reverse-mathematical equivalence or separation between the rainbow Ramsey theorem for the Rado graph and Sauer's canonical partition theorem for finite graphs inside the Rado graph. Related work addresses the strength of the rainbow Ramsey theorem for pairs (strictly weaker than RT² over RCA₀) and structural Ramsey results of Laflamme–Sauer–Vuksanović for homogeneous binary structures, but none directly settles the equivalence in question. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: If f (z) is an entire function of finite order ρ and lower order λ with real zeros, find the best possible bound B = B(ρ, λ) such that δ(0, f ) ≥ B. From Edrei, Fuchs and Hellerstein [220] it is known that B > 0 if 2 < ρ < ∞, and it is conjectured that B → 1 as ρ → +∞.
self_contained_problem:
Let $f(z)$ be a transcendental entire function whose zeros are all real. Recall that the order and lower order of $f$ are
$$\rho = \limsup_{r\to\infty}\frac{\log\log M(r,f)}{\log r},\qquad \lambda = \liminf_{r\to\infty}\frac{\log\log M(r,f)}{\log r},$$
where $M(r,f)=\max_{|z|=r}|f(z)|$, and that the Nevanlinna deficiency of $0$ is
$$\delta(0,f) = 1 - \limsup_{r\to\infty}\frac{N(r,1/f)}{T(r,f)},$$
with $T(r,f)$ the Nevanlinna characteristic and $N(r,1/f)$ the integrated counting function of zeros of $f$.

Assume $0\le \lambda \le \rho < \infty$. Determine the best possible (largest) constant $B=B(\rho,\lambda)$, depending only on $\rho$ and $\lambda$, such that
$$\delta(0,f)\ge B(\rho,\lambda)$$
holds for every entire function $f$ of order $\rho$ and lower order $\lambda$ all of whose zeros are real. In particular, decide whether $B(\rho,\lambda)\to 1$ as $\rho\to+\infty$.
status_search_result: The qualitative version (whether $B(\rho,\lambda)>0$ for $2<\rho<\infty$) was established by Edrei, Fuchs and Hellerstein, and the exact value of the bound depending only on the lower order, $B(\lambda)$, was determined by Hellerstein and Shea, settling an important case of the problem. The full two-parameter best-possible bound $B(\rho,\lambda)$ does not appear to be completely determined, so the problem is regarded as partially solved.

original_question: Let M be a compact two-dimensional manifold, let X^r be the space of C^r vector fields on M, let Sigma^r be the subset of C^r-structurally stable vector fields, and let X_1^r = X^r \ Sigma^r with the induced C^r topology. Characterize the subset Sigma_1^r of vector fields in X_1^r that are structurally stable with respect to arbitrarily small perturbations that remain inside X_1^r.
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a compact two-dimensional manifold (without boundary), and for an integer $r \geq 1$ let $\mathfrak{X}^r(M)$ denote the Banach space of $C^r$ vector fields on $M$ endowed with the $C^r$ topology. A vector field $X \in \mathfrak{X}^r(M)$ is called $C^r$-structurally stable if there exists a neighborhood $\mathcal{U}$ of $X$ in $\mathfrak{X}^r(M)$ such that for every $Y \in \mathcal{U}$ there is a homeomorphism of $M$ mapping the oriented orbits of $X$ onto the oriented orbits of $Y$. Let $\Sigma^r \subset \mathfrak{X}^r(M)$ denote the (open) set of $C^r$-structurally stable vector fields, and set
$$\mathfrak{X}_1^r := \mathfrak{X}^r(M) \setminus \Sigma^r,$$
endowed with the topology induced from $\mathfrak{X}^r(M)$.

Define a vector field $X \in \mathfrak{X}_1^r$ to be first-order structurally stable if there is a neighborhood $\mathcal{V}$ of $X$ in $\mathfrak{X}_1^r$ (i.e., a set of the form $\mathcal{U} \cap \mathfrak{X}_1^r$ with $\mathcal{U}$ open in $\mathfrak{X}^r(M)$) such that for every $Y \in \mathcal{V}$ there exists a homeomorphism of $M$ carrying the oriented orbits of $X$ onto those of $Y$. Let $\Sigma_1^r \subset \mathfrak{X}_1^r$ denote the set of all such first-order structurally stable vector fields.

Give an intrinsic characterization of the set $\Sigma_1^r$ in terms of the qualitative dynamical properties of its elements (singularities, periodic orbits, and saddle connections), and determine whether $\Sigma_1^r$ is open and dense in $\mathfrak{X}_1^r$.

Let $f$ be a function meromorphic in the complex plane. For $r>0$ and $a\in\mathbb{C}\cup\{\infty\}$, let $T(r,f)$ denote the Nevanlinna characteristic of $f$, and define the Nevanlinna deficiency
$$\delta(a,f) = \liminf_{r\to\infty} \frac{m(r,a,f)}{T(r,f)},$$
where $m(r,a,f)$ is the usual proximity function (with $m(r,\infty,f) = m(r,f)$). The lower order of $f$ is
$$\lambda = \liminf_{r\to\infty} \frac{\log T(r,f)}{\log r}.$$
For $\varepsilon>0$, $a\in\mathbb{C}$, and $r>0$, define the angular set on which $f$ is close to $a$ by
$$E(r,a,\varepsilon) = \{\theta\in[-\pi,\pi] : \log^+\tfrac{1}{|f(re^{i\theta})-a|} > \varepsilon\, T(r,f)\},$$
with the analogous definition $E(r,\infty,\varepsilon) = \{\theta : \log^+|f(re^{i\theta})| > \varepsilon T(r,f)\}$ when $a=\infty$.

$$\mathrm{meas}\, E(r_\nu,a,\varepsilon_\nu) \;\geq\; \min\!\left(2\pi,\; \frac{4}{\lambda}\sin^{-1}\!\sqrt{\frac{\delta(a,f)}{2}}\right) + o(1)\qquad (\nu\to\infty).$$

original_question: Do there exist invariant perfect sets, meaning nonempty compact invariant sets that are transversally totally discontinuous, for differential equations of class C^2 on orientable two-dimensional manifolds?
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be an orientable two-dimensional differentiable manifold, and let $X$ be a vector field of class $C^2$ on $M$ generating a flow $\{\varphi_t\}_{t\in\mathbb{R}}$. A set $K\subset M$ is called invariant if $\varphi_t(K)=K$ for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$. Call $K$ an invariant perfect set (or nontrivial minimal set) if $K$ is nonempty, compact, invariant, and is transversally totally disconnected, meaning that for every point $p\in K$ there exists a local transversal section $\Sigma$ to $X$ at $p$ such that $K\cap\Sigma$ is a totally disconnected set containing $p$ as a non-isolated point (so in particular $K$ is neither a single periodic orbit nor a single equilibrium point).

Determine whether such an invariant perfect set can exist: that is, does there exist a $C^2$ vector field on some orientable two-dimensional manifold admitting a nonempty compact invariant set that is transversally totally disconnected and is not reduced to a fixed point or a periodic orbit?
status_search_result: This is the classical question resolved negatively by A. J. Schwartz (1963): a $C^2$ flow on an orientable 2-manifold has no nontrivial minimal sets; every minimal set is either a fixed point, a periodic orbit, or the whole manifold (when it is the 2-torus). The result is known as Schwartz's theorem and is a strengthening of Denjoy's theorem.

original_question: Let M be a compact n-dimensional manifold. If a C^r vector field on M has a nontrivial recurrent orbit through a point p in M, can that vector field be approximated arbitrarily closely in the C^s topology, with s <= r, by another vector field that has a periodic orbit through p?
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a compact $n$-dimensional smooth manifold and let $r \ge 1$ be an integer. Let $X$ be a $C^r$ vector field on $M$, and suppose $p \in M$ is a point whose orbit under the flow of $X$ is nontrivially recurrent (i.e., $p$ is a non-periodic point that lies in its own $\omega$-limit or $\alpha$-limit set under the flow generated by $X$).

Question: For every integer $s$ with $1 \le s \le r$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$, does there exist a $C^r$ vector field $Y$ on $M$ such that:
(i) $\|Y - X\|_{C^s} < \varepsilon$ (i.e., $Y$ is $\varepsilon$-close to $X$ in the $C^s$ topology), and
(ii) the point $p$ lies on a periodic orbit of $Y$?

Equivalently, can every $C^r$ vector field on a compact $n$-manifold possessing a nontrivial recurrent orbit through $p$ be approximated arbitrarily closely in the $C^s$ topology ($s \le r$) by a vector field having a periodic orbit through $p$?
status_search_result: The C^1 closing lemma was established by Pugh (and Pugh–Robinson for flows). The general C^r closing lemma for r ≥ 2 remains open and is listed among Smale's problems for the 21st century. Partial results exist: e.g., C^∞ closing lemmas for area-preserving/Hamiltonian surface diffeomorphisms (Asaoka–Irie and Cristofaro-Gardiner–Humilière–Seyfaddini), C^r closing lemmas for partially hyperbolic diffeomorphisms with one-dimensional center bundle, and progress for piecewise smooth planar vector fields. The case of dimension 2, s > 1, remains open on most non-orientable surfaces. The general statement is unresolved.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: If f (z) is non-constant and meromorphic in the plane, and n = 3 or 4, prove that φ(z) = f ′ (z) − f (z)n assumes all finite complex values. This is known to be true if f (z) is an entire function, or if n ≥ 5 in the case where f (z) is meromorphic, see Hayman [392]. In connection to this, it would be most interesting to have general conditions under which a polynomial in f (z) and its derivatives, can fail to take some complex value. When f (z) is a meromorphic rather than an entire function, rather little is known, see however Clunie ([159], [161]) and Hayman [395, Chp. 3].
self_contained_problem:
Let $f$ be a non-constant meromorphic function on the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$, and fix an integer $n \in \{3, 4\}$. Define
$$\varphi(z) = f'(z) - f(z)^n.$$
Prove that $\varphi$ assumes every finite complex value; that is, for every $c \in \mathbb{C}$ the equation $\varphi(z) = c$ has at least one solution $z \in \mathbb{C}$.

(For comparison, the analogous statement is known to hold when $f$ is entire and arbitrary $n \ge 1$, and when $f$ is meromorphic with $n \ge 5$.)
status_search_result: The conjecture as stated is false: E. Mues proved that for n = 3 or 4 there exist non-constant meromorphic functions f for which f' − f^n omits a finite non-zero value, providing a counterexample to the proposed statement. Thus the original problem is resolved in the negative.

paper_title: Light Chemical Elements in Stars: Mysteries and Unsolved Problems
original_question: Why do a significant fraction of old FGK dwarf stars in the Galactic halo have lithium abundances substantially below the Spite plateau at log ε(Li) ≈ 2.2, rather than clustering near that plateau value?
self_contained_problem: In Galactic halo FGK main-sequence dwarf stars (old, metal-poor stars with effective temperatures roughly 5000–6500 K and metallicities [Fe/H] ≲ −1.5), the surface lithium abundance, expressed as A(Li) = log ε(Li) = log10(N_Li/N_H) + 12, is observed to cluster around a nearly constant value A(Li) ≈ 2.2 known as the Spite plateau. However, a significant fraction of such halo dwarfs are observed to have lithium abundances substantially below this plateau value (so-called "sub-plateau" or "Li-poor" halo dwarfs) rather than scattering tightly around 2.2. Identify and quantitatively justify the physical mechanism (or combination of mechanisms — e.g., atomic diffusion and gravitational settling, turbulent mixing, convective overshoot, rotationally induced mixing, mass loss, magnetic effects, pre-main-sequence depletion, accretion or pollution history) responsible for producing this sub-plateau population, in a way consistent with the observed dependence of Li depletion on effective temperature, metallicity, and evolutionary status, and consistent with the inferred primordial lithium abundance from standard Big Bang nucleosynthesis (A(Li) ≈ 2.7).
status_search_result: The origin of sub-Spite-plateau lithium abundances in halo dwarfs is still debated. Proposed mechanisms include atomic diffusion plus turbulent mixing, convective overshoot dependent on mass and evolutionary stage, rotationally induced mixing, and mass loss, but no single model is universally accepted, and recent literature continues to describe the underlying lithium problem (including the sub-plateau population) as unresolved.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Under what circumstances does f (z0 + z) have the same deficiencies as f (z)? It was shown by Dugué [202] that this need not be the case for meromorphic functions, and by Hayman [387] that it is not necessarily true for entire functions of infinite order. The case of functions of finite order remains open. Valiron [765] notes that a sufficient condition is T (r + 1, f ) → 1, as r → ∞, T (r, f ) and this is the case in particular if ρ − λ < 1. Since for entire functions of lower order λ, λ ≤ 12 there are no deficiencies anyway, it follows that the result is true at any rate, for entire functions of order ρ < 23 and, since λ ≥ 0 always, for meromorphic functions of order less than one.
self_contained_problem:
Let f be a meromorphic function on the complex plane of finite order. For a∈ℂ∪{∞}, define the Nevanlinna deficiency of f at a by
   δ(a,f) = liminf_{r→∞} m(r,a,f)/T(r,f),
where T(r,f) is the Nevanlinna characteristic and m(r,a,f) is the proximity function (with m(r,∞,f)=m(r,f)). A value a is called deficient (for f) if δ(a,f) > 0.

For z₀ ∈ ℂ, let f_{z₀}(z) := f(z₀+z). Determine necessary and/or sufficient conditions on f under which the set of deficient values, together with the corresponding deficiencies, of f_{z₀} coincides with that of f for every z₀ ∈ ℂ.

Known partial information:
 • A sufficient condition is T(r+1,f)/T(r,f) → 1 as r→∞; in particular this holds whenever ρ − λ < 1, where ρ and λ denote the order and lower order of f.
 • For entire functions, λ ≤ 1/2 implies that f has no finite deficient values, so the conclusion holds for entire f of order ρ < 3/2.
 • For meromorphic functions of order less than 1 the conclusion likewise holds.
 • Examples are known showing that the conclusion can fail for meromorphic functions in general, and for entire functions of infinite order.

Resolve the case of arbitrary meromorphic (and in particular entire) functions of finite order: do f and f(z₀+·) always have the same deficiencies?
status_search_result: Searches turned up no resolution of the finite-order case. Standard references on Nevanlinna theory note that T(r,f(z+η))∼T(r,f) for finite-order meromorphic functions, and counterexamples are known only in the meromorphic (Dugué) and infinite-order entire (Hayman) settings. The finite-order case appears to remain open.

paper_title: Light Chemical Elements in Stars: Mysteries and Unsolved Problems
original_question: Why do early B- and O-type stars that are components of close binary systems retain their original low helium abundance through roughly the first half of the main-sequence stage and then undergo a sharp increase in He/H by about a factor of two over the short interval t/tMS ≈ 0.5–0.7, and how should stellar mixing models incorporate both rotation and tidal interaction effects to reproduce this behavior?
self_contained_problem:
Consider early B-type and O-type stars that are components of close binary systems, evolving on the main sequence. Let t denote the elapsed main-sequence time and t_MS the total main-sequence lifetime, so τ = t/t_MS ∈ [0,1] is the fractional main-sequence age. Let He/H denote the photospheric helium-to-hydrogen number-density ratio.

Empirically, such close-binary components exhibit the following pattern (in contrast to isolated hot stars, in which He/H rises gradually and monotonically with τ):

1. For 0 ≤ τ ≲ 0.5, He/H remains essentially equal to the original (initial) value with no detectable enhancement.
2. Over the short interval 0.5 ≲ τ ≲ 0.7, He/H rises sharply by approximately a factor of two.
3. For 0.7 ≲ τ ≤ 1, He/H stays at this enhanced level until the end of the main-sequence stage.

The problem is: provide a physical and quantitative explanation of this delayed, abrupt mid-main-sequence helium enrichment. Specifically, construct a stellar interior mixing model for the components of close binary systems that simultaneously incorporates

(a) rotational mixing (meridional circulation, shear-induced turbulence, etc.), and
(b) tidal interaction between the binary components (including tidal spin–orbit coupling, tidally driven internal flows, and tidally enhanced/suppressed differential rotation),

and that reproduces the observed three-phase behavior of He/H(τ) above — namely the suppression of surface helium enhancement during the first half of the main-sequence evolution, the sharp factor-of-two jump in He/H over τ ∈ [0.5, 0.7], and the subsequent plateau until τ = 1.
category_tag: stellar evolution and mixing in binaries
status_search_result: Recent work (e.g., 2026 A&A study on chemical evolution of close massive binaries with tidally enhanced/suppressed mixing) continues to investigate rotation+tide mixing models, finding complex, partially decoupled He vs N enhancement patterns and strong shear from tidal torques, but no model has been shown to reproduce the observed flat He/H below τ≈0.5 followed by an abrupt factor-of-two jump on the short interval τ∈[0.5,0.7] and a subsequent plateau. The phenomenon remains characterized as a mystery for current mixing theory.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Can one establish an upper bound on the number of finite asymptotic values of a meromorphic function f (z) in C, taking into account both the order of f , and the angular measure of its tracts? (W. Al-Katifi)
self_contained_problem:
Let $f$ be a meromorphic function on $\mathbb{C}$ of order $\rho(f)$, where
$$\rho(f) = \limsup_{r\to\infty} \frac{\log T(r,f)}{\log r}$$
and $T(r,f)$ denotes the Nevanlinna characteristic. A finite asymptotic value of $f$ is a value $a \in \mathbb{C}$ for which there exists a continuous path $\gamma:[0,1)\to\mathbb{C}$ with $\gamma(t)\to\infty$ as $t\to 1^-$ and $f(\gamma(t))\to a$. Associated with each finite asymptotic value $a$ one has a tract: a connected unbounded component of $\{z\in\mathbb{C}: |f(z)-a|<\varepsilon\}$ for some $\varepsilon>0$, and one may measure the angular size of such a tract by
$$\theta(r) = \operatorname{meas}\{\phi\in[0,2\pi): re^{i\phi}\in T\},$$
giving an angular measure function $\theta(r)$ for each tract $T$.

Establish an upper bound for the number of finite asymptotic values of $f$ that depends both on the order $\rho(f)$ and on the angular measures $\theta_k(r)$ of the corresponding tracts $T_k$. More precisely, find an explicit function $N(\rho(f), \{\theta_k\})$ such that the number of finite asymptotic values of $f$ is at most $N$.
status_search_result: Classical Denjoy–Carleman–Ahlfors-type bounds give that an entire function of order $\rho$ has at most $2\rho$ finite asymptotic values, and Al-Katifi's 1966 work in the Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society gives lower bounds of the form: if $f$ has $n$ distinct finite asymptotic values attained in tracts of total angular measure at most $\pi\alpha$, then the order is at least $n/\alpha$. However, a complete sharp upper bound for meromorphic functions taking into account both order and the angular measure of tracts does not appear to have been definitively established; the search did not produce a conclusive resolution of the problem as posed.

paper_title: Light Chemical Elements in Stars: Mysteries and Unsolved Problems
original_question: Can a quantitative diffusion-based model for chemically peculiar main-sequence stars simultaneously explain the helium and lithium anomalies together with the broader abundance pattern, including the tendency for element excesses to grow with atomic number, the surface spot distribution of different elements, and the depth-dependent stratification of abundances within a single star?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a chemically peculiar (CP) main-sequence star, modeled as a self-gravitating, radiating plasma in hydrostatic equilibrium with a stratified atmosphere and (in the magnetic case) a large-scale magnetic field. Assume that the observed surface and near-surface abundance anomalies of chemical elements are governed by atomic diffusion, in which each element migrates under the competing action of gravitational settling, radiative acceleration arising from selective absorption of photons in spectral lines, and (where present) magnetic forces, while thermonuclear processing in the deep interior is assumed not to alter the surface composition.

Formally, let n_i(r,θ,φ,t) denote the number density of chemical species i with atomic number Z_i in the stellar envelope, evolving according to a coupled system of continuity equations

  ∂n_i/∂t + ∇·(n_i v_i) = 0,

where the diffusion velocity v_i is determined by the balance of gravity g, radiative acceleration g_rad,i (computed from the local radiation field and atomic line opacities of species i), pressure gradients, thermal diffusion, and Lorentz forces from the magnetic field B(r,θ,φ). Couple this transport system to the equations of stellar structure and to a radiative transfer treatment yielding g_rad,i.

Problem. Construct a quantitative diffusion-based model of this form for an individual CP star that simultaneously reproduces all of the following observed features:
  (a) the helium underabundance/overabundance and the lithium abundance anomalies;
  (b) the systematic tendency for the surface excess of heavy elements to increase with atomic number Z;
  (c) the observed two-dimensional surface distribution of abundance "spots" of different elements over the stellar surface; and
  (d) the vertical (depth-dependent) stratification profiles n_i(r) of the various elements in the atmosphere of the same star.

Does such a self-consistent diffusion model exist for at least one specific CP star, and if so, exhibit it; otherwise, identify which of (a)–(d) cannot be reconciled within the diffusion framework above.
status_search_result: Searches in the stellar astrophysics literature indicate that while diffusion theory remains the standard explanation for CP-star abundance anomalies and substantial progress has been made on individual aspects (e.g., vertical stratification in HgMn and Ap stars, radiative acceleration calculations, and magnetically-controlled spot models), no published model simultaneously reproduces helium and lithium anomalies together with the Z-trend, surface spot maps, and full vertical stratification for any single CP star. The problem appears still open.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let n1 (r, a, f ) denote the number of simple zeros of f (z)−a in {|z| ≤ r}. Selberg [703] has shown that if: (a) f is a meromorphic function of finite order ρ, and (b) n1 (r, a, f ) = O(1), as r → ∞ for four distinct values of a, then ρ is an integral multiple of 12 or 13 . Does this conclusion remain true if (b) is replaced by: (c) n1 (r, a, f ) = o(T (r, f )), as r → ∞, for four distinct values of a? Gol’dberg [313] has constucted an entire function of arbitrary prescribed order which satisfies the condition (c) for two distinct values of a. (A. Eremenko)
self_contained_problem:
Let $f$ be a meromorphic function in the complex plane. For $a \in \mathbb{C} \cup \{\infty\}$ and $r > 0$, let $n_1(r,a,f)$ denote the number of simple zeros of $f(z) - a$ (with the usual convention for $a = \infty$, namely simple poles of $f$) in the disk $\{|z| \le r\}$, and let $T(r,f)$ denote the Nevanlinna characteristic function of $f$. Recall that the order of $f$ is $\rho = \limsup_{r \to \infty} \frac{\log T(r,f)}{\log r}$.

It is known that if $f$ has finite order $\rho$ and there exist four distinct values $a_1, a_2, a_3, a_4 \in \mathbb{C} \cup \{\infty\}$ such that
$$n_1(r, a_j, f) = O(1) \quad \text{as } r \to \infty, \quad j = 1, 2, 3, 4,$$
then $\rho$ is an integral multiple of $\tfrac12$ or $\tfrac13$.

Question: Suppose instead that $f$ is a meromorphic function of finite order $\rho$ and there exist four distinct values $a_1, a_2, a_3, a_4$ such that
$$n_1(r, a_j, f) = o(T(r,f)) \quad \text{as } r \to \infty, \quad j = 1, 2, 3, 4.$$
Must $\rho$ then be an integral multiple of $\tfrac12$ or $\tfrac13$?
status_search_result: The problem has been resolved in the negative: Künzi showed that under the relaxed condition the order $\rho$ may be any value with $1 < \rho < \infty$, and Gol'dberg constructed counterexamples of arbitrary positive order, so the conclusion does not remain true.

Künzi has shown that ρ can be arbitrary, subject to 1 < ρ < ∞, and Gol'dberg has a counter-example for arbitrary positive ρ.", "claim": "Counterexamples by Künzi and Gol'dberg show the conclusion fails under condition (c)."}]

paper_title: Light Chemical Elements in Stars: Mysteries and Unsolved Problems
original_question: How are lithium-rich and super-lithium-rich FGK giants and supergiants produced when many of these stars cannot be explained by standard stellar-evolution theory, some have already passed through deep convective mixing that should have destroyed their surface lithium, and candidate mechanisms such as post-mixing lithium synthesis through the Cameron–Fowler process, extra mixing, or engulfment of a giant planet do not yet provide a complete explanation?
self_contained_problem:
Consider FGK-type giant and supergiant stars whose photospheric lithium abundance, expressed as A(Li) = log(N(Li)/N(H)) + 12, exceeds the standard post–first-dredge-up prediction. Call a star lithium-rich if A(Li) ≥ 1.5 and super-lithium-rich if A(Li) ≥ 3.3 (i.e. above the meteoritic/primordial benchmark). Many such stars lie evolutionarily beyond the luminosity bump or red clump, so according to standard (non-rotating, single-star) stellar-evolution theory their surface lithium should already have been diluted and/or destroyed by deep convective mixing (DCM) during the first dredge-up. Two principal physical scenarios have been proposed to account for the anomalous Li enhancement:

(i) In situ post-mixing synthesis through the Cameron–Fowler mechanism, in which ⁷Be produced by ³He(α,γ)⁷Be in hot interior layers is transported on a timescale shorter than its electron-capture lifetime to cooler regions where it decays to ⁷Li, possibly aided by an extra-mixing process (e.g. thermohaline mixing, rotational mixing, or magnetic buoyancy) that connects the convective envelope to the hydrogen-burning shell.

(ii) External enrichment via the engulfment of a substellar companion of mass ≳ 1 M_Jup, whose lithium-rich envelope material is dissolved into the stellar convective envelope.

Problem. Construct a quantitative stellar-evolution model that, starting from standard initial conditions on the main sequence and evolving through the red giant branch (and, where applicable, the asymptotic giant branch or red supergiant phase), reproduces the observed distribution of surface lithium abundances A(Li) of FGK giants and supergiants — including both the lithium-rich (A(Li) ≥ 1.5) and super-lithium-rich (A(Li) ≥ 3.3) populations and their joint distribution with luminosity, effective temperature, mass, metallicity, rotation rate, and evolutionary phase — by specifying which combination of mechanism(s) (Cameron–Fowler synthesis with a prescribed extra-mixing law, planet engulfment with a prescribed engulfment rate and mass spectrum, or another physically motivated process) operates, and prove that the resulting model is consistent with all of: (a) the fraction of giants observed to be Li-rich at each evolutionary phase, (b) the existence of super-Li-rich giants with A(Li) up to ≈ 4–5, (c) the lifetime of the Li-rich phase as inferred from population statistics, and (d) the absence of a unique observational signature (e.g. enhanced ⁹Be, infrared excess, rapid rotation, or close companion) that would single out one mechanism.
status_search_result: The origin of lithium-rich and super-lithium-rich FGK giants remains an active open problem. Recent (2024–2025) studies continue to debate competing scenarios — Cameron–Fowler synthesis with extra mixing, planet engulfment, binary interaction with differential rotation, and mass-loss-driven scenarios — without consensus. A 2024 radial-velocity study of 1400 giants (Castro-Tapia et al.) finds no binary-nature evidence for red-clump Li-rich giants, while new mass-loss and binary-architecture proposals (2024–2025) are still being tested, indicating no complete and accepted explanation yet.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let F be a polynomial in two variables, and let y be a meromorphic solution of the algebraic ordinary differential equation F (y (n) , y) = 0. Is it true that y must be an elliptic function, or a rational function of exponentials, or a rational function? This is known in the following cases: (a) n = 1: a classical result, probably due to Abel; (b) n = 2: an old result of Picard [634], and independently, Bank and Kaufman [52]; (c) n is odd and y has at least one pole, Eremenko [235]; and (d) the genus of the curve F (x1 , x2 ) = 0 is at least equal to one, Eremenko [235]. (A. Eremenko)
self_contained_problem:
Let $F \in \mathbb{C}[x_1, x_2]$ be a nonconstant polynomial in two complex variables, and let $n \geq 1$ be an integer. Suppose that $y$ is a function meromorphic in the entire complex plane $\mathbb{C}$ that satisfies the algebraic ordinary differential equation
$$F\bigl(y^{(n)}(z),\, y(z)\bigr) = 0 \qquad \text{for all } z \in \mathbb{C},$$
where $y^{(n)}$ denotes the $n$-th derivative of $y$. Prove or disprove: $y$ must be one of the following three types of functions:
(i) an elliptic function (i.e., a doubly periodic meromorphic function on $\mathbb{C}$);
(ii) a rational function of $\exp(az)$ for some constant $a \in \mathbb{C} \setminus \{0\}$, i.e., $y(z) = R(\exp(az))$ for some rational function $R$;
(iii) a rational function of $z$.

It is known that the answer is affirmative in each of the following cases: (a) $n=1$; (b) $n=2$; (c) $n$ is odd and $y$ has at least one pole; (d) the algebraic curve $\{(x_1,x_2) \in \mathbb{C}^2 : F(x_1,x_2)=0\}$ has genus at least one. The general case remains.
status_search_result: The problem appears to be still open in general. Known affirmative cases include $n=1$ (classical), $n=2$ (Picard; Bank–Kaufman), $n$ odd with at least one pole and the case of curve genus $\geq 1$ (Eremenko). Recent work by Liao–Ng–Eremenko and Yanchenko has produced further partial progress on Briot–Bouquet type equations, but the full conjecture for all $n$ has not been resolved.

original_question: Let f (z) be an entire function of finite order ρ, and let n1 (r, a) denote the number of simple zeros of the equation f (z) = a. $$\Theta(a) \;=\; 1 - \limsup_{r\to\infty}\frac{\overline{N}(r,a)}{T(r,f)},$$
where $\overline{N}(r,a)$ is the integrated counting function of distinct $a$-points of $f$ and $T(r,f)$ is the Nevanlinna characteristic.

$$n_1(r,a)=O(r^c) \quad\text{and}\quad n_1(r,b)=O(r^c) \qquad (r\to\infty).$$

where M(r,f) = max_{|z|=r} |f(z)|.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Suppose that f (z) is a meromorphic function in the plane, and that for some θ, 0 ≤ θ < 2π, f (z) assumes every value infinitely often, with at most two exceptions, in every angle θ − ε < arg z < θ + ε, when ε > 0. Then the ray arg z = θ is called a Julia line. Lehto [508] has shown that if f (z) is an entire function, or if f (z) is meromorphic and T (r, f ) lim sup = +∞, r→∞ (log r)2 (but not necessarily otherwise), at least one direction of Julia exists. What can we say about the exceptional values at different Julia lines? In particular, can an entire function f (z) have one exceptional (finite) value a at one Julia line Γa , and a different exceptional value b at a different Julia line Γb ? (C. Rényi)
self_contained_problem:
Let f be a non-constant entire function on the complex plane. For θ ∈ [0, 2π), the ray arg z = θ is called a Julia line of f if, for every ε > 0, the function f assumes every complex value, with at most two exceptions, infinitely often in the angular sector {z ∈ ℂ : θ − ε < arg z < θ + ε}. A finite complex number a is called an exceptional value at the Julia line Γ_θ = {arg z = θ} if there exists ε > 0 such that f attains the value a only finitely often in the sector θ − ε < arg z < θ + ε.

Question: Can there exist a (transcendental) entire function f together with two distinct Julia lines Γ_a and Γ_b of f such that some finite value a is exceptional at Γ_a, some finite value b is exceptional at Γ_b, and a ≠ b? More generally, what relations must hold between the sets of exceptional values associated with different Julia lines of an entire function?

original_question: If f (z) is an entire function of finite order ρ which has a finite deficient value, find the best possible lower bound for the lower order λ of f (z). (Edrei and Fuchs [217] showed that λ > 0.) Gol’dberg [309] showed that for every ρ > 1, λ ≥ 1 is possible.

Let f be a transcendental entire function of finite order
   ρ = limsup_{r→∞} log log M(r,f) / log r,

   λ = liminf_{r→∞} log log M(r,f) / log r
denote the lower order of f. Recall that, in the sense of Nevanlinna theory, a value a ∈ ℂ is called a deficient value of f if
   δ(a,f) = liminf_{r→∞} m(r, 1/(f−a)) / T(r,f) > 0,
where T(r,f) is the Nevanlinna characteristic and m(r, 1/(f−a)) is the proximity function. Suppose f has a finite deficient value (so there exists a ∈ ℂ with δ(a,f) > 0).

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: If f (z) of finite order, can anything be asserted about the length of Γ∞ , which is the path on which f (z) tends to ∞, or the part of it in |z| ≤ r?
self_contained_problem:
Let $f$ be a transcendental entire function of finite order, i.e.
$$\rho(f) := \limsup_{r\to\infty} \frac{\log\log M(r,f)}{\log r} < \infty, \qquad M(r,f) := \max_{|z|=r}|f(z)|.$$
By a classical theorem of Iversen, there exists at least one continuous unbounded curve $\Gamma_\infty:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{C}$ with $|\Gamma_\infty(t)|\to\infty$ as $t\to\infty$ such that $f(\Gamma_\infty(t))\to\infty$ as $t\to\infty$; such a curve is called an asymptotic path of $f$ for the value $\infty$.

Assume that such a path $\Gamma_\infty$ can be chosen to be rectifiable, and for $r>0$ let
$$\ell(r) := \text{length}\bigl(\Gamma_\infty \cap \{z : |z|\le r\}\bigr).$$

Establish nontrivial bounds, in terms of $\rho(f)$ (or more generally in terms of $M(r,f)$), on $\ell(r)$ as $r\to\infty$ for the best possible choice of such an asymptotic path $\Gamma_\infty$. In particular, determine the slowest possible growth of $\ell(r)$ that can always be achieved for an entire function of finite order, and decide whether one can always choose $\Gamma_\infty$ so that $\ell(r) = O(r)$.
status_search_result: The question is a classical Hayman-style problem on asymptotic paths of entire functions of finite order. Partial results are known: Hayman and Piranian showed that if $\log M(r,f) = O(\log^2 r)$ then one may take $\Gamma_\infty$ to be a ray through the origin (so $\ell(r)=r$). Eremenko and others have obtained results bounding the length of asymptotic curves in terms of $M(r,f)$, and related problems on asymptotic functions have been studied recently (e.g. arXiv:2102.11332). However, no complete characterization for all entire functions of finite order appears to be available, so the problem is partially solved.

Blumenthal's conjecture asks: if f_1 and f_2 are entire functions satisfying

   M(r, f_1) = M(r, f_2)   for all 0 < r < infinity,

must f_1 and f_2 be equivalent in the sense above?

The analogous question for polynomials of degree higher than about 6 is also part of the problem. Note that the equality M(r, f_1) = M(r, f_2) is required only globally on (0, infinity); examples such as (1-z)e^z and e^{z^2/2} (which agree in maximum modulus on 0 < r < 2) and e^{z - z^2} versus e^{z^2 + 1/2} (which agree for r >= 1/4) show that local agreement on subintervals is not enough to force equivalence.

Prove or disprove the conjecture, and resolve the corresponding problem for polynomials of arbitrary degree.
status_search_result: The conjecture remains open in general. Hayman, Tyler and White established Blumenthal's conjecture for polynomials with at most four non-zero terms, in particular all quadratics and cubics, but the polynomial case for general (high) degree and the entire-function case are not known to be settled.

original_question: Are there upper bounds of any kind on the set of asymptotic values of a meromorphic function of finite order? (D. Drasin and A. Weitsman)
self_contained_problem:
Let f be a meromorphic function on the complex plane C of finite order, where the order of f is

  ρ(f) = limsup_{r→∞} log T(r,f) / log r,

with T(r,f) the Nevanlinna characteristic. A value a ∈ Ĉ = C ∪ {∞} is called an asymptotic value of f if there exists a continuous path γ : [0,1) → C with |γ(t)| → ∞ as t → 1 such that f(γ(t)) → a. Let A(f) ⊂ Ĉ denote the set of asymptotic values of f.

Question: Does finiteness of the order of f impose any nontrivial upper bound (in terms of cardinality, capacity, Hausdorff dimension, measure, or any other set-theoretic or potential-theoretic restriction) on the set A(f)? In particular, can A(f) be all of Ĉ for some meromorphic function f of finite (including zero) order?
status_search_result: A. Eremenko answered the question negatively by constructing meromorphic functions of positive order, and also of order zero, whose set of asymptotic values is all of the closed complex plane Ĉ. Subsequently, Canton, Drasin and Granados showed that for every φ(r) → ∞ and every analytic (Suslin) set A ⊂ Ĉ, there is a meromorphic function f with T(r,f) = O(φ(r) log² r) whose set of asymptotic values is exactly A. Thus no nontrivial upper bound on the set of asymptotic values exists for meromorphic functions of finite order beyond the analytic-set restriction.

original_question: Determine the upper and lower estimates for the growth of entire and meromorphic solutions of algebraic ordinary differential equations (AODE). (This is a classical problem.) For AODEs of first order, it is known that the meromorphic solutions f must have finite order (see Gol’dberg [308]) and that (log r)2 = O(T (r, f )) (see Eremenko [234], [236]). (The latter two references contain a general account of first order AODEs, including modern proofs of some classical results.) The order of entire solutions of first order AODEs is an integral multiple of 21 (see Malmquist [552]). For AODEs of second order, it is known that the order of entire solutions is positive, see Zimogljad [817]. There is no upper estimate valid for all entire or meromorphic solutions of AODEs of order grreater than one, but there is an old conjecture that log |f (z)| ≤ expn (|z|) for entire solutions f of an AODE of order n. self_contained_problem:
Let $n\ge 1$ be a positive integer. An algebraic ordinary differential equation (AODE) of order $n$ is an equation of the form
$$P\bigl(z,f(z),f'(z),\ldots,f^{(n)}(z)\bigr)=0,$$
where $P$ is a polynomial in its $n+2$ arguments with complex coefficients. Define the iterated exponentials by $\exp_0(x)=x$ and $\exp_k(x)=\exp(\exp_{k-1}(x))$ for $k\ge 1$.

For a meromorphic function $f$ on $\mathbb{C}$, let $T(r,f)$ denote its Nevanlinna characteristic and let $\rho(f)$ denote its order of growth.

Establish optimal upper and lower estimates for the growth of entire and meromorphic solutions of AODEs. In particular, address the following:

(a) Prove or disprove: every entire solution $f$ of an AODE of order $n$ satisfies
$$\log|f(z)| \le \exp_n(|z|)$$

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: If Γ is a continuum that recedes to ∞, it is known (see Hayman [386]) that as z → ∞ on Γ, log |f (z)| lim sup ≥ −A, r→∞ log M (|z|) where A is an absolute constant. Is it true that A = 1? This is certainly the case if Γ is a ray through the origin, see Beurling [96]. If A > 1, is it possible to obtain a good numerical estimate for A?
self_contained_problem:
Let $f$ be a non-constant entire function, and let
$$M(r) = \max_{|z|=r} |f(z)|, \qquad r > 0.$$
Let $\Gamma \subset \mathbb{C}$ be a continuum (a connected closed set) that recedes to infinity, i.e., $\Gamma$ is unbounded. It is known that there exists an absolute constant $A > 0$ such that for every such $f$ and $\Gamma$,
$$\limsup_{\substack{z \to \infty \\ z \in \Gamma}} \frac{\log |f(z)|}{\log M(|z|)} \;\geq\; -A.$$
When $\Gamma$ is a ray emanating from the origin, the optimal value is $A = 1$.

(a) Determine whether $A = 1$ is admissible for every continuum $\Gamma$ receding to infinity; equivalently, decide whether the inequality above holds with $A = 1$ for all non-constant entire $f$ and all unbounded continua $\Gamma$.

(b) If the optimal absolute constant satisfies $A > 1$, obtain a sharp (or good) numerical estimate for $A$.
status_search_result: Hayman and Kjellberg ("On the minimum of a subharmonic function on a connected set", 1983) gave a positive answer: for any non-constant subharmonic function $u$ and any $A > 1$, the set $\{z : u(z) + A\,B(|z|) < 0\}$ (with $B(r) = \max_{|\zeta|=r} u(\zeta)$) has no unbounded component, which implies $A = 1$ is the correct constant. Thus the problem is solved.

original_question: Find criteria for and/or give explicit methods for the construction of meromorphic functions f in C with the following properties: (a) all poles of f are of odd multiplicity; (b) all zeros of f are of even multiplicity. (Here ‘explicit methods’ means that all computations must be practicable.) The background of this problem lies in the question of meromorphic solutions of the differential equation y ′′ + A(z)y = 0 in the whole plane. (J. Winkler)
self_contained_problem:
Find criteria for, and/or give explicit constructive methods (in the sense that all required computations are practicable) for, meromorphic functions $f$ on the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$ satisfying both of the following conditions:

(a) every pole of $f$ has odd multiplicity;
(b) every zero of $f$ has even multiplicity.

The motivation is the study of meromorphic solutions on $\mathbb{C}$ of the linear differential equation
$$y'' + A(z)\, y = 0,$$
where $A$ is a given function (entire or meromorphic) on $\mathbb{C}$: a non-trivial meromorphic solution $y$ of this equation with a meromorphic coefficient $A$ must have all zeros of even order at points where $A$ is holomorphic, and the local behavior at poles is similarly constrained, leading naturally to functions $f$ with the parity properties (a) and (b).

Provide either necessary and sufficient analytic/structural conditions characterizing such $f$, or an explicit construction scheme producing all such $f$.

If all the aj are constant, then the problem has also been solved by Steinmetz [732] using results from Frank and Hellerstein [275]. $$F(z) = f^{(k)}(z) + \sum_{j=0}^{k-2} a_j(z)\, f^{(j)}(z)$$
is non-constant, and that both $f$ and $F$ have no zeros in $\mathbb{C}$. Characterise all such functions $f$. In particular, prove or disprove the following: if $f$ has infinitely many poles, then $f$ must have the form
$$f = (H')^{2/(k-1)} H^{-l},$$

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Suppose that f (z) has finite order, and that Γ is a rectifiable path on which f (z) → ∞. Let ℓ(r) be the length of Γ in |z| < r. Find such a path for which ℓ(r) grows as slowly as possible, and estimate ℓ(r) in terms of M (r, f ). If f (z) has zero order, or more generally, finite order, can a path be found for which ℓ(r) = O(r) as r → ∞? If log M (r, f ) = O(log2 r) as r → ∞, but under no weaker growth condition, it is shown by Hayman [394] and Piranian [635] that we may choose a ray through the origin for Γ. If f (z) has a finite asymptotic value a, the corresponding question may be asked for paths on which f (z) → a. (P. Erdös)
self_contained_problem:
Let $f$ be an entire function of finite order, and let $M(r,f)=\max_{|z|=r}|f(z)|$. Suppose $\Gamma$ is a rectifiable path in the complex plane along which $f(z)\to\infty$, and let $\ell(r)$ denote the length of the portion of $\Gamma$ inside the disc $|z|<r$.

(a) Find a path $\Gamma$ for which $\ell(r)$ grows as slowly as possible, and obtain an estimate of $\ell(r)$ in terms of $M(r,f)$.

(b) If $f$ has order zero, or more generally finite order, determine whether one can always choose such a path $\Gamma$ with $\ell(r)=O(r)$ as $r\to\infty$.

(c) Formulate and answer the analogous questions when $f$ has a finite asymptotic value $a$ and $\Gamma$ is required to be a rectifiable path along which $f(z)\to a$.

It is known that if $\log M(r,f)=O(\log^2 r)$ as $r\to\infty$ (and under no weaker growth hypothesis), then $\Gamma$ may be chosen to be a ray through the origin.
status_search_result: Hayman showed that if $\log M(r,f)\ll(\log r)^2$ one may take $\ell(r)=O(r)$ along a ray. Gol'dberg and Eremenko disproved the corresponding conjecture for faster-growing functions: for any $\varphi(r)\to\infty$ there is an entire function with $\log M(r)\ll\varphi(r)(\log r)^2$ admitting no path with $f\to\infty$ and $\ell(r)\ll r$, and such examples exist of any prescribed finite order. Sharp estimates of $\ell(r)$ in terms of $M(r,f)$ and the asymptotic-value version remain only partially understood.

Let $f(z)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n z^{\lambda_n}$ be a non-constant entire function, where $(\lambda_n)$ is a strictly increasing sequence of non-negative integers. Assume that
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\lambda_n} < \infty.$$
For $r>0$, set
$$M(r,f)=\max_{|z|=r}|f(z)|, \qquad m_0(r,f)=\min_{|z|=r}|f(z)|.$$
A finite asymptotic value of $f$ is a complex number $a\in\mathbb{C}$ such that there exists a continuous path $\gamma:[0,1)\to\mathbb{C}$ with $|\gamma(t)|\to\infty$ as $t\to 1^-$ and $f(\gamma(t))\to a$.

Prove or disprove each of the following:

(a) Under the above hypothesis, $f$ has no finite asymptotic value.

(b) Under the above hypothesis,
$$\limsup_{r\to\infty} \frac{\log m_0(r,f)}{\log M(r,f)} = 1.$$

(It is known that (a) holds under the stronger gap condition $\lambda_n > n(\log n)^{1+\varepsilon}$ for some $\varepsilon>0$, and (b) holds under $\lambda_n > n(\log n)^2$. The question is whether the conclusions persist under the weaker hypothesis that $\sum 1/\lambda_n$ converges.)
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not yield definitive evidence that either part (a) or (b) has been resolved under the sole hypothesis $\sum 1/\lambda_n<\infty$. Known results establish the conclusions under stronger gap conditions (Kövári), and Macintyre showed that the convergence of $\sum 1/\lambda_n$ is sharp for the absence of finite radial asymptotic values, but the full questions appear to remain unresolved in the searched literature.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: If f (z) is a transcendental entire function, we define M = {z : |f (z)| = M (|z|, f )}. Tyler [762] has shown that M can have isolated points, and that, given any N , we can have ν(r) > N for infinitely many r, where ν(r) is the number of points in M ∩ {|z| = r}. Herzog and Piranian [440] have shown that lim supr→∞ ν(r) can be infinite; is it true that lim inf r→∞ ν(r) < ∞ for all entire f ? (J. G. Clunie)
self_contained_problem:
Let f be a transcendental entire function on the complex plane, and for r ≥ 0 let
  M(r, f) = max{ |f(z)| : |z| = r }.
Define the maximum modulus set
  𝓜(f) = { z ∈ ℂ : |f(z)| = M(|z|, f) }.
For r > 0, let
  ν(r) = #( 𝓜(f) ∩ { z : |z| = r } )
denote the number of points of 𝓜(f) on the circle of radius r (allowing the value +∞).

It is known that 𝓜(f) may contain isolated points, that for every N one can arrange ν(r) > N for infinitely many r, and that there exist transcendental entire functions f for which limsup_{r→∞} ν(r) = ∞.

Question: Is it true that for every transcendental entire function f,
  liminf_{r→∞} ν(r) < ∞ ?
category_tag: Maximum modulus set of entire functions
status_search_result: Recent literature (e.g., 2022 and 2026 arXiv works on Erdős' maximum modulus points problem and the Clunie–Hayman construction) indicates the question of whether ν(r) can tend to infinity (equivalently, whether liminf ν(r) is always finite) remains unresolved. Constructions giving entire functions with unbounded ν(r) are known (Herzog–Piranian), but no example with ν(r) → ∞ has been produced, nor has a proof that liminf ν(r) < ∞ always.
