(b) If f (z) 6= 0, then m(r) lim inf = 0; r→∞ M (r, f ) Is m(r) lim = 0? r→∞ M (r, f ) (c) What is the exact upper bound β of m(r) βf = lim inf ? r→∞ M (r, f ) It is known that 74 < β < 2/π. See Clunie and Hayman [164].
self_contained_problem:
Let $f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_n z^n$ be a transcendental entire function. For $r>0$, define the maximum modulus
$$M(r,f)=\max_{|z|=r}|f(z)|$$
and the maximum term of the power series
$$m(r)=m(r,f)=\max_{n\ge 0}|a_n|r^n.$$
It is classical that $m(r)\le M(r,f)$ for all $r>0$, and that $m(r)/M(r,f)\le 1$.

Answer the following three questions.

(a) For which constants $C\in(0,1]$ does there exist a transcendental entire function $f$ such that
$$\lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{m(r,f)}{M(r,f)}=C\,?$$
It is known that every value $C$ with $0<C\le \tfrac{1}{2}$ is attained. Determine whether some (or every) value $C>\tfrac{1}{2}$ is also attained.

(b) Suppose in addition that $f$ has no zeros, i.e. $f(z)\ne 0$ for all $z\in\mathbb{C}$. It is known that
$$\liminf_{r\to\infty}\frac{m(r,f)}{M(r,f)}=0.$$
Is it true that, for every such zero-free transcendental entire $f$,
$$\lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{m(r,f)}{M(r,f)}=0\,?$$

(c) Determine the exact value of
$$\beta=\sup_{f}\;\liminf_{r\to\infty}\frac{m(r,f)}{M(r,f)},$$
where the supremum is taken over all transcendental entire functions $f$. It is known that
$$\tfrac{4}{7}<\beta<\tfrac{2}{\pi}.$$
category_tag: Entire functions: maximum term vs maximum modulus
status_search_result: The exact value of the Erdős constant $\beta=\sup_f\liminf_{r\to\infty} m(r,f)/M(r,f)$ remains unknown. Clunie and Hayman (1964) established $4/7<\beta<2/\pi$. A 2026 preprint generalizing the Clunie–Hayman construction improves the lower bound to $\beta>0.58507$, but neither the exact value of $\beta$ nor the questions in (a) and (b) appear to have been fully resolved.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Suppose that an entire function f has exactly one curve Γ of maximum modulus (that is, Γ is connected, joins 0 to ∞, and f has no other maximum modulus points). What can be said about the minimum rate of growth of M (r, f ), if one is given information about the geometry of the curve Γ, for example, that Γ is a given infinitely-spiralling spiral? If Γ is a radial line, clearly nothing much can be said. (In a sense, this is the opposite of a Phragmén-Lindelöf principle). (D. A. Brannan)
self_contained_problem:
Let f be a non-constant entire function, and write M(r,f) = max_{|z|=r} |f(z)| for its maximum modulus. A point z is called a maximum modulus point of f if |f(z)| = M(|z|, f). Suppose that the set of maximum modulus points of f is a single connected curve Γ that joins 0 to ∞ (i.e., Γ is a connected, unbounded curve with 0 ∈ Γ and Γ contains points of arbitrarily large modulus, and there are no maximum modulus points of f outside Γ).

Determine, in terms of the geometry of Γ, the slowest possible rate of growth of M(r,f) as r → ∞. In particular:

(a) If Γ is a radial half-line, no nontrivial lower bound on the growth of M(r,f) is to be expected; confirm this.

(b) If Γ is a prescribed infinitely-spiralling curve (for example, a logarithmic spiral about the origin), establish the sharp lower bound on the growth rate of M(r,f) imposed by the requirement that Γ is the unique curve of maximum modulus of an entire function f.

More generally, find a quantitative relationship between the geometric/spiralling behaviour of Γ and the minimal possible growth of M(r,f).
status_search_result: A targeted web search for results on entire functions with a unique curve of maximum modulus, and lower bounds on M(r,f) determined by the geometry (e.g., spiralling) of that curve, did not return any specific resolution of this question. No published solution or partial-solution paper attributed to this problem was located, so its current status could not be verified.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let ν(r) be the number of points on |z| = r, such that |f (z)| = M (r, f ). Can we have (a) lim supr→∞ ν(r) = ∞ ? (b) lim inf r→∞ ν(r) = ∞ ? (P. Erdös)
self_contained_problem:
For a non-constant entire function $f:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$, let
$$M(r,f)=\max_{|z|=r}|f(z)|,$$
and define
$$\nu(r)=\#\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|=r,\ |f(z)|=M(r,f)\}.$$
(Note that $\nu(r)$ is finite for every $r>0$ unless $f$ is a monomial.)

Determine whether there exists an entire function $f$ (not a monomial) such that:

(a) $\displaystyle\limsup_{r\to\infty}\nu(r)=\infty$;

(b) $\displaystyle\liminf_{r\to\infty}\nu(r)=\infty$.
status_search_result: Part (a) was resolved affirmatively by Herzog and Piranian (1968), who constructed an entire function with ν(n)=n for all positive integers n, so lim sup ν(r)=∞ is achievable. Part (b), whether lim inf ν(r)=∞ is achievable, remains open; recent work (2022–2023) provides an approximate solution with strong evidence for an affirmative answer but does not resolve it.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: For entire or, more generally, meromorphic functions f and g, let ‘f ≤ g’ mean that, for any sequence {zn }∞ 1 for which |f (zn )| → ∞, then |g(zn )| → ∞. For entire functions, it can be proved that, if f ′ ≤ f , then f is of exponential type; what can be said if f ′′ ≤ f ? Does f ′′ ≤ f imply that f is normal (that is, that |f ′ (z)|(1 + |f (z)|2 )−1 is bounded)? (An analogue in the case of the unit disc D has been proved by Pommerenke [652]). In the above ordering, does there exist f ∧ g and f ∨ g for any two entire functions f and g? That is, given f and g, does there exist an h such that h ≤ f and h ≤ g, and so that if k ≤ f and k ≤ g, then k ≤ h? Similarly, for f ∨ g. Finally, if f is meromorphic and f ′ ≤ f , does this imply a growth restriction on f , e.g. is the order of f at most two? Note: Any constant c satisfies c ≤ f for all entire f , and any non-constant polynomial p satisfies f ≤ p for any entire f . Observe also that ecz are all equivalent if c > 0. (L. A. Rubel and J. M. Anderson)
self_contained_problem:
For meromorphic functions $f$ and $g$ on the complex plane, write $f \preceq g$ to mean: for every sequence $\{z_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subset \mathbb{C}$ with $|f(z_n)| \to \infty$, one has $|g(z_n)| \to \infty$. A meromorphic function $f$ is called normal if the spherical derivative $|f'(z)|/(1+|f(z)|^2)$ is bounded on $\mathbb{C}$. It is known that for entire $f$, the relation $f' \preceq f$ implies that $f$ is of exponential type.

(a) Suppose $f$ is entire and $f'' \preceq f$. What can be deduced about the growth of $f$? In particular, does $f'' \preceq f$ imply that $f$ is normal?

(b) Does the partial preorder $\preceq$ on the set of entire functions admit binary meets and joins? That is, given any two entire functions $f$ and $g$, does there exist an entire function $h$ such that $h \preceq f$ and $h \preceq g$, and such that whenever an entire $k$ satisfies $k \preceq f$ and $k \preceq g$ then $k \preceq h$ (a greatest lower bound $f \wedge g$)? Likewise, does a least upper bound $f \vee g$ always exist?

(c) If $f$ is meromorphic on $\mathbb{C}$ and $f' \preceq f$, does this imply a growth restriction on $f$? In particular, is the order of $f$ necessarily at most $2$?
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not turn up any subsequent paper resolving the questions of Rubel and Anderson concerning the preorder $f\preceq g$ defined by preservation of sequences along which $|f|\to\infty$. No source was found that settles whether $f''\preceq f$ implies normality, whether the preorder admits meets/joins on entire functions, or whether $f'\preceq f$ forces a meromorphic $f$ to have order $\le 2$. The status therefore appears unverified.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: If f (z) is an entire function, the iterates fn (z), n = 1, 2, . . . are defined inductively by fn+1 (z) = f (fn (z)), f1 (z) = f (z). A point z satisfying the equation fn (z) = z, but such that fk (z) 6= z for k < n, is called a fixed point of exact order n. Prove that there always exist fixed points of exact order n if f (z) is transcendental, and n ≥ 2. For the case of polynomial or rational f (z) see Baker [44]. For a proof that fixed points of exact order n exist, except for at most one value of n, see Baker [46].
self_contained_problem:
Let f: ℂ → ℂ be a transcendental entire function. Define the iterates of f inductively by f₁(z) = f(z) and f_{n+1}(z) = f(f_n(z)) for n ≥ 1. A point z₀ ∈ ℂ is called a fixed point of exact order n of f if f_n(z₀) = z₀ but f_k(z₀) ≠ z₀ for every integer k with 1 ≤ k < n.

Prove that for every integer n ≥ 2, the function f possesses at least one fixed point of exact order n.
status_search_result: The conjecture was settled by W. Bergweiler (1991), who proved that every transcendental entire function f has infinitely many periodic points of exact period n for each n ≥ 2 (in fact infinitely many repelling ones). Earlier, I. N. Baker had proved existence for all n ≥ 2 with at most one possible exception; Bergweiler's result removes the exception.

If F is an entire function of z = (z1 , z2 , z3 ) that is bounded on V , is F necessarily constant on V ? (J. M. Anderson and L. A. Rubel)

Suppose $F : \mathbb{C}^3 \to \mathbb{C}$ is an entire function such that the restriction $F|_V$ is bounded on $V$. Must $F$ be constant on $V$?

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Can an entire function have all its zeros and ones on two distinct straight lines, having infinitely many on each line? Edrei has proved (unpublished) that if l, m are intersecting straight lines, then it is impossible for all the zeros of an entire function f (z) to lie on l, and all the ones on m. (A. Edrei)
self_contained_problem:
Let $f$ be a non-constant entire function on $\mathbb{C}$. Suppose there exist two distinct straight lines $\ell$ and $m$ in $\mathbb{C}$ such that:

(i) every zero of $f$ lies on $\ell$, and there are infinitely many zeros;
(ii) every solution of $f(z)=1$ lies on $m$, and there are infinitely many such solutions.

Does such an entire function $f$ exist?

It is known that if $\ell$ and $m$ intersect, then no entire function can have all its zeros on $\ell$ and all its $1$-points on $m$. The remaining question is whether such an $f$ exists when $\ell$ and $m$ are (necessarily parallel) distinct straight lines, with infinitely many zeros on $\ell$ and infinitely many $1$-points on $m$.
status_search_result: The case where the two lines intersect is settled by an (unpublished) result of Edrei, which rules out such an entire function. An oral observation attributed to Al-Katifi notes that $f(z)=\sin(z^2)$ has zeros and $1$-points distributed along the real and imaginary axes, but its zeros do not lie on a single line, so this does not resolve the original question. No published full solution covering distinct (parallel) lines was located.

original_question: (A width conjecture) Given a power series k=0 ak zP, suppose that there is a non-negative ρ such that all of the partial sums Sn (z) = nk=0 ak z k , n = 1, 2, 3, . . . are non-zero in the region Sρ = {z = x + iy : |y| < Kx1−(ρ/2) , x > 0}. We conjecture that f (z) must be entire of order at most ρ. When ρ = 0, Sρ is a sector with vertex at z = 0, and the conjecture is a consequence of results of Carlson [144], which were later generalised by Rosenbloom [671], Ganelius [286], and Korevaar and McCoy [487]. Remark: If f (z) z Pn= e k, which is of order 1, Saff and Varga [695] have shown that the partial sums k=0 z /k! are in fact zero-free in the parabolic region {z = z + iy : y 2 ≤ 4(x + 1), x > −1}. (E. B. Saff and R. S. Varga)
self_contained_problem:
Let $f(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k z^k$ be a formal power series with complex coefficients, and for each integer $n\ge 1$ let
$$S_n(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k z^k$$
denote its $n$-th partial sum. Suppose that there exist a constant $K>0$ and a real number $\rho\ge 0$ such that every partial sum $S_n(z)$, $n=1,2,3,\dots$, is non-zero throughout the region
$$\mathcal S_\rho=\bigl\{z=x+iy\in\mathbb C : x>0,\ |y|<K x^{1-\rho/2}\bigr\}.$$
Prove or disprove: under these hypotheses, $f$ must define an entire function of order at most $\rho$.

(Recall that an entire function $f$ has order $\le\rho$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $R_\varepsilon$ such that $|f(z)|\le \exp(|z|^{\rho+\varepsilon})$ for $|z|\ge R_\varepsilon$. When $\rho=0$ the region $\mathcal S_\rho$ degenerates to a sector with vertex at the origin.)

status_search_result: The Saff–Varga width conjecture has been verified in the sectorial case (ρ=0) via classical results of Carlson, Rosenbloom, Ganelius, and Korevaar–McCoy, and additional partial results have been obtained for specific classes of entire functions (e.g., those with simple exponential growth, treated via Riemann–Hilbert techniques, and observations in Rocky Mountain J. Math., 1991). No source verifying the full conjecture in general was found.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: What is the least integer k = k(N ), such that every entire function f (z) can be written as Xk f (z) = [fν (z)]N , ν=1 where f (z) and fν (z) are entire functions? It is enough to solve the problem for f (z) = z, since then one can substitute f (z) for z. The equation N 1 X (1 + ων z)N z= 2 , N ν=1 ων where ων are the distinct N -th roots of unity, shows that k(N ) ≤ N . On the other hand, for N = 1, 2, 3 we have k(N ) = N . To see e.g. that k(3) ≥ 3, suppose that z = f 3 + g3 = (f + g)(f + ωg)(f + ω 2 g), where ω = exp(2πi/3). It follows that the meromorphic function φ(z) = f (z)/g(z) satisfies φ(z) 6= −1, −ω, −ω 2 , except possibly at z = 0. Thus, by Picard’s Theo- rem, φ(z) must be rational, and so φ(z) assumes at least two of the three values −1, −ω, −ω 2 . This gives a contradiction. (H.A. Heilbronn)
self_contained_problem:
For a positive integer $N\ge 1$, let $k(N)$ denote the least positive integer $k$ (if it exists) such that every entire function $f:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$ admits a representation
$$ f(z) \;=\; \sum_{\nu=1}^{k} \bigl[f_\nu(z)\bigr]^{N}, $$
where $f_1,\ldots,f_k$ are entire functions. (Note: by substituting $f$ for $z$, it suffices to consider the case $f(z)=z$.) 

The identity
$$ z \;=\; \frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{\nu=1}^{N} \frac{(1+\omega_\nu z)^{N}}{\omega_\nu}, $$
where $\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_N$ are the distinct $N$-th roots of unity, shows that $k(N)\le N$. Moreover $k(1)=1$, $k(2)=2$, and $k(3)=3$ (the lower bound $k(3)\ge 3$ follows from Picard's theorem applied to $\varphi=f/g$ when $z=f^3+g^3=(f+g)(f+\omega g)(f+\omega^2 g)$).

Determine the value of $k(N)$ for every integer $N\ge 4$.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let f denote a rational or entire function of a complex variable, and f n , n = 1, 2, . . ., the n-th iterate of f , so that f 1 = f, f n+1 = f ◦ f n = f n ◦ f . Provided that f is not rational of degree 0 or 1, the set C of those points where {f n } forms a normal family is a proper open subset of the plane, and is invariant under the map z 7→ f (z). A component G of C is a wandering domain of f if f k (G) ∩ f n (G) = ∅ for all {k, n | k ≥ 1, n ≥ 1, k 6= n}. Jakobson has asked whether it is possible for a rational function f to have a wandering domain. Baker [50] gave a transcendental entire function which does have such domains. (I. N. Baker)
self_contained_problem:
Let $f:\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$ be a rational function of degree at least $2$, and define its iterates by $f^1=f$ and $f^{n+1}=f\circ f^n$ for $n\ge 1$. The Fatou set $\mathcal C$ of $f$ is the set of points $z\in\widehat{\mathbb C}$ in a neighborhood of which the family $\{f^n\}_{n\ge 1}$ is normal; it is an open, completely invariant subset of $\widehat{\mathbb C}$. A connected component $G$ of $\mathcal C$ is called a wandering domain of $f$ if $f^k(G)\cap f^n(G)=\emptyset$ for all integers $k,n\ge 1$ with $k\ne n$ (equivalently, no iterate $f^n(G)$ lies in a periodic component of $\mathcal C$).

Question: Can such a rational function $f$ possess a wandering domain?
status_search_result: Solved by Dennis Sullivan in 1985 ("Quasiconformal homeomorphisms and dynamics I"): a rational map of the Riemann sphere of degree at least 2 has no wandering Fatou components. Every Fatou component is eventually periodic. This resolved the question (originally posed by Fatou and raised by Jakobson) in the negative.

original_question: Let A, B be two countable dense sets in the plane. Does there exist an entire function f (z), so that f (z) ∈ B, if and only if z ∈ A? If the answer is negative, it would be desirable to have conditions on A, B when this is so. (P. Erdös)

$$f(z)\in B \iff z\in A\,?$$
If the answer is negative in general, describe sufficient (or necessary) conditions on the pair $(A,B)$ under which such an entire function does, or does not, exist.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let f be an entire function, and let D be a component of the set in C where the family of iterates {fn } is normal. Can this family have an infinite bounded set of constant limit functions? Eremenko and Lyubich [248] have shown that the set of constant limit functions may be infinite. (A. Eremenko)
self_contained_problem:
Let $f:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$ be a transcendental entire function, and consider the family $\{f^n\}_{n\ge 1}$ of iterates of $f$. The Fatou set $F(f)$ is the maximal open subset of $\mathbb{C}$ on which $\{f^n\}$ is a normal family (in the sense of Montel, where convergence to $\infty$ is allowed). Let $D$ be a connected component of $F(f)$. A constant limit function of $\{f^n\}$ on $D$ is a constant $c\in\mathbb{C}\cup\{\infty\}$ such that some subsequence $f^{n_k}$ converges locally uniformly on $D$ to the constant function $c$. Let $L(D)\subset\mathbb{C}\cup\{\infty\}$ denote the set of all such constant limit functions on $D$.

It is known that $L(D)$ may be infinite for some choice of $f$ and $D$. The question is: does there exist a transcendental entire function $f$ and a Fatou component $D$ of $f$ such that $L(D)$ is infinite and contained in a bounded subset of $\mathbb{C}$ (in particular, $\infty\notin L(D)$)?
status_search_result: The question is closely tied to the existence of "dynamically bounded" wandering domains, whose existence is a major open problem in transcendental dynamics. Recent work (e.g., on classifying simply connected wandering domains and on limit sets of iterates in wandering domains, 2021–2023) discusses the classification of limit functions but does not exhibit an entire function with an infinite bounded set of constant limit functions on a Fatou component. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Is it possible to say something more precise about C(λ) when λ is just greater than 1? In particular, is it true that C(λ) = −1 for such λ, or alternatively, is C(λ) a strictly decreasing function of λ?
self_contained_problem:
For an entire function f, let
   M(r, f) = max{|f(z)| : |z| = r},   m(r, f) = min{|f(z)| : |z| = r},
and define the order of f by
   ρ(f) = limsup_{r → ∞} log log M(r, f) / log r.

For each real number λ ≥ 0, define the constant
   C(λ) = inf liminf_{r → ∞} (log m(r, f)) / (log M(r, f)),
where the infimum is taken over all transcendental entire functions f with ρ(f) ≤ λ such that f has no zeros on a sequence of circles |z| = r_n with r_n → ∞ along which the liminf is computed (equivalently, C(λ) is the largest constant such that, for every transcendental entire function f with ρ(f) ≤ λ, one has
   log m(r, f) ≥ (C(λ) − o(1)) log M(r, f)
on some sequence of radii r_n → ∞).

The classical cos πρ theorem implies C(λ) ≥ cos πλ for 0 ≤ λ ≤ 1, and in particular C(1) = −1. For λ > 1 no such lower bound is known.

Determine the behaviour of C(λ) for λ just greater than 1. In particular:

(a) Is C(λ) = −1 for all λ in some right neighbourhood (1, 1 + ε) of 1?

(b) If not, is the function λ ↦ C(λ) strictly decreasing for λ > 1?
status_search_result: The question concerns the behaviour, for λ slightly greater than 1, of the constant C(λ) governing the comparison of log m(r, f) and log M(r, f) for entire functions of order at most λ — an extension of the cos πρ theorem beyond order 1. Searches turned up Hayman's classical work on the local growth of power series and the Wiman–Valiron survey, as well as recent work on the minimum modulus problem (e.g., the Computational Methods and Function Theory cover article on the minimum modulus problem), but no definitive resolution of either of the two specific sub-questions (whether C(λ) = −1 on a right neighbourhood of 1, or whether C is strictly decreasing). The status appears to remain open, but available sources do not provide a clear-cut confirmation.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let H be an entire function, let f1 , f2 be linearly independent solutions of the differential equation w′′ + Hw = 0, and let E = f1 f2 . Clearly f1 , f2 and E are entire. Also, it is well-known that if H is a polynomial of degree n, then the orders of f1 and f2 are ρ(f1 ) = ρ(f2 ) = 21 (n + 2). Furthermore, the exponent of convergence of the zeros of E is λ(E) = 21 (n + 2), provided that n > 1. If H is transcendental then ρ(f1 ) = ρ(f2 ) = +∞ and one might hope that, by analogy with the previous remarks, λ(E) = +∞. However, examples by Bank and Laine [53] showed that this is not necessarily the case if ρ(H) is a positive integer or +∞. They also asked whether λ(E) = +∞ if ρ(H) is non-integral and finite and they showed that this is indeed the case if ρ(H) < 21 , a result improved to ρ(H) ≤ 21 by Rossi [672]. What happens in general? (S. Hellerstein and J. Rossi)
self_contained_problem:
Let $H$ be a transcendental entire function, and let $f_1, f_2$ be two linearly independent entire solutions of the second-order linear differential equation
$$w'' + H w = 0.$$
Define the entire function $E = f_1 f_2$, and let $\lambda(E)$ denote the exponent of convergence of the zero sequence of $E$, i.e.
$$\lambda(E) = \limsup_{r\to\infty} \frac{\log n(r,1/E)}{\log r},$$
where $n(r,1/E)$ counts the zeros of $E$ in $\{|z|\le r\}$. Let $\rho(H)$ denote the order of $H$.

It is known that if $\rho(H)$ is a positive integer or $+\infty$, then $\lambda(E)$ may be finite, while if $\rho(H) \le 1/2$, then $\lambda(E) = +\infty$. 

Question: Suppose $\rho(H)$ is finite and non-integral (in particular $\rho(H) > 1/2$). Must one always have $\lambda(E) = +\infty$?
status_search_result: The question is the Bank–Laine conjecture. It was disproved by Bergweiler and Eremenko, who constructed a transcendental entire coefficient $H$ of finite non-integral order admitting linearly independent solutions $f_1, f_2$ of $w''+Hw=0$ such that $E=f_1 f_2$ has finite exponent of convergence of its zeros. Their paper "On the Bank–Laine conjecture" appeared in J. Eur. Math. Soc.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let rn be a sequence of Pólya peaks (as defined by Edrei [215]) of order ρ. Then Edrei [215] showed that there exists K = K(α, ρ) such that log m0 (r, f ) > cos(πα) log M (r, f ) for some value r in the interval rn ≤ r ≤ Krn and n sufficiently large. Is K(α, ρ) independent of α for fixed ρ? Can it be taken arbitrarily near 1? (D. Drasin and A. Weitsman)
self_contained_problem:
Let $f$ be a meromorphic function in the complex plane. For $r>0$ let
\[ M(r,f)=\max_{|z|=r}|f(z)|,\qquad m_0(r,f)=\min_{|z|=r}|f(z)|, \]
and let $N(r,0,f)$ denote the integrated counting function of zeros of $f$. Fix $\rho>0$. A sequence $r_n\to\infty$ is called a sequence of Pólya peaks of order $\rho$ for a positive nondecreasing function $T(r)$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ and every $A>1$,
\[ T(t) \le (1+\varepsilon)\Bigl(\tfrac{t}{r_n}\Bigr)^{\rho} T(r_n) \qquad \text{for all } t\in[r_n/A,\,A r_n], \]
for $n$ sufficiently large.

Fix $0<\alpha<1$ and $\rho>0$. It is known that there exists a constant $K=K(\alpha,\rho)>1$ such that, whenever $\{r_n\}$ is a sequence of Pólya peaks of order $\rho$ of $T(r,f)$, the inequality
\[ \log m_0(r,f) > \cos(\pi\alpha)\,\log M(r,f) \]
holds for some $r\in[r_n,Kr_n]$ for all sufficiently large $n$.

Questions:
(a) Can $K(\alpha,\rho)$ be chosen independent of $\alpha$ for each fixed $\rho$?
(b) Can $K(\alpha,\rho)$ be taken arbitrarily close to $1$?
category_tag: Meromorphic and entire functions / Pólya peaks
status_search_result: According to the problem collection, Eremenko, Shea, and Sodin proved the affirmative answer for Pólya peaks of $N(r,0,f)$ and gave an example showing the answer is negative for Pólya peaks (in another sense). Thus the question is partially resolved depending on which Pólya peak notion is used.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Suppose that f (z) = 1 + a1 z + a2 z 2 + . . . ∈ U2p . If p = 0 (so that f ∈ U0 ) and if f is not a polynomial, it is well-known that f cannot have two consecutive Taylor coefficients equal to zero. If p > 0, can an analogous assertion be made? Is it true, for example, that the Taylor series of f in U2p cannot have 2p + 2 consecutive coefficients equal to zero? (J. Williamson)
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{L}-\mathcal{P}$ denote the Laguerre–Pólya class, i.e. the class of entire functions that are uniform limits on compact subsets of $\mathbb{C}$ of real polynomials having only real zeros. For each integer $p \ge 0$, let $U_{2p}$ denote the class of entire functions $f$ that are uniform limits on compact subsets of $\mathbb{C}$ of real polynomials having at most $2p$ non-real zeros (counted with multiplicity); in particular $U_0 = \mathcal{L}-\mathcal{P}$.

It is a classical fact that if $f(z) = 1 + a_1 z + a_2 z^2 + \cdots \in U_0$ and $f$ is not a polynomial, then $f$ cannot have two consecutive Taylor coefficients equal to zero (i.e. there is no $n \ge 1$ with $a_n = a_{n+1} = 0$).

Question: For $p \ge 1$, formulate and prove an analogous statement for the class $U_{2p}$. In particular, decide whether the following holds: if $f(z) = 1 + a_1 z + a_2 z^2 + \cdots \in U_{2p}$ and $f$ is not a polynomial, then the Taylor series of $f$ at $0$ cannot have $2p+2$ consecutive coefficients equal to zero, i.e. there is no integer $n \ge 1$ such that $a_n = a_{n+1} = \cdots = a_{n+2p+1} = 0$.
status_search_result: A web search did not surface any published resolution of Williamson's question about $2p+2$ consecutive zero Taylor coefficients for functions in the class $U_{2p}$. Related recent work concerns Taylor-coefficient conditions for membership in the Laguerre–Pólya class and the number of non-real zeros of derivatives, but does not appear to settle this specific gap-coefficient problem. Status is therefore unverified.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let f (z) be a non-constant entire function, and assume that for some constant c the plane measure of the set E(c) where |f (z)| > c is finite. What is the minimum growth rate of f (z)? Hayman conjectures that Z ∞ r dr <∞ 0 log log M (r, f ) is true and best possible. If E(c) has finite measure, is the same true for E(c′ ) for c′ < c? (P. Erdös)
self_contained_problem:
Let $f$ be a non-constant entire function on $\mathbb{C}$. For a real constant $c>0$, let
$$E(c) = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |f(z)| > c\},$$
and denote by $|E(c)|$ the planar Lebesgue measure of $E(c)$. Let
$$M(r,f) = \max_{|z|=r} |f(z)|$$
be the maximum modulus of $f$.

Assume that there exists some $c$ such that $|E(c)| < \infty$.

(a) Determine the minimum possible growth rate of $M(r,f)$ as $r \to \infty$ under this hypothesis. In particular, prove or disprove that
$$\int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{r\,dr}{\log\log M(r,f)} < \infty,$$
and show that this estimate is best possible (i.e. there exists such an entire function for which the integral is finite while no essentially stronger growth lower bound holds).

(b) Show that if $|E(c)| < \infty$ for some $c$, then $|E(c')| < \infty$ for every $c' < c$ as well, or else exhibit a counterexample.
status_search_result: A direct web search did not surface a definitive resolution of Hayman's conjectured growth bound $\int_0^\infty r\,dr/\log\log M(r,f) < \infty$ for entire functions whose super-level set $\{|f|>c\}$ has finite plane measure, nor of Erdős's accompanying question on whether finite measure of $E(c)$ implies finite measure of $E(c')$ for $c'<c$. Related work on Hayman's problems and the maximum modulus set exists, but no source confirming a complete solution was located.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let Ω be a component of the normal set of an entire function (under iteration). Is dim(∂Ω) > 1? Or is ∂Ω a circle/line? (D. Hamilton)
self_contained_problem:
Let $f:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$ be a transcendental entire function, and consider the dynamical system generated by iteration of $f$. The Fatou set (also called the normal set) of $f$ is
$$F(f)=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\{f^n\}_{n\ge 1}\text{ is a normal family in some neighborhood of }z\},$$
where $f^n$ denotes the $n$-th iterate of $f$. Let $\Omega$ be a connected component of $F(f)$, and let $\partial\Omega$ denote its topological boundary in $\mathbb{C}$. Let $\dim$ denote Hausdorff dimension.

Determine whether the following dichotomy must hold for every such component $\Omega$ of every transcendental entire function $f$: either
\[ \dim(\partial\Omega) > 1, \]
or else $\partial\Omega$ is a (round) circle or a straight line.
status_search_result: The dichotomy is known to hold in important cases but remains open in general. Recent work (2025) establishes that for components of attracting or parabolic basins of transcendental entire maps, the boundary has hyperbolic dimension strictly greater than 1 under conditions such as the immediate component being bounded or having infinite degree (in the Eremenko–Lyubich class). However, the full question is not fully resolved in general, particularly for Siegel disks and wandering domains, where examples with boundary dimension exactly 1 are known but the precise geometry has not been settled.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let f (z) be an entire function (of sufficiently high order) with l, l ≥ 2 different asymptotic values ak , k = 1, . . . , l. Suppose that γk is a path such that f (z) → ak as z → ∞, z ∈ γk . Let n1 (r, ak ) be the number of zeros of f (z) − ak on γk , and in |z| ≤ r. Can we find a function f (z) such that n1 (r, ak ) → bk > 0 n(r, ak ) as r → ∞, for k = 1, 2, . . . , n? Can we take bk = 1? (J. Winkler)
self_contained_problem:
Let $f(z)$ be a transcendental entire function of sufficiently high order, and suppose that $f$ has $\ell \geq 2$ distinct (finite) asymptotic values $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_\ell$; that is, for each $k=1,\dots,\ell$ there exists a continuous unbounded curve $\gamma_k$ tending to $\infty$ such that $f(z)\to a_k$ as $z\to\infty$ along $\gamma_k$.

For $r>0$ and each $k$, define:
- $n(r,a_k)$ = number of zeros of $f(z)-a_k$ in the disk $\{|z|\le r\}$, counted without multiplicity;
- $n_1(r,a_k)$ = number of zeros of $f(z)-a_k$ that lie on the curve $\gamma_k$ and inside $\{|z|\le r\}$.

Question 1. Does there exist an entire function $f$ of the above kind, together with asymptotic paths $\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_\ell$, such that for every $k=1,\dots,\ell$ the limit
$$\lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{n_1(r,a_k)}{n(r,a_k)}=b_k$$
exists and satisfies $b_k>0$?

Question 2. Can such an $f$ be constructed for which $b_k=1$ for all $k=1,\dots,\ell$ (i.e., asymptotically all $a_k$-points lie on the corresponding asymptotic path $\gamma_k$)?
status_search_result: Web search did not surface a published resolution of this question concerning the asymptotic distribution of $a_k$-points along asymptotic paths $\gamma_k$ of an entire function of high order. Related work on asymptotic values and the Denjoy–Carleman–Ahlfors theorem exists, but no source confirms a positive or negative answer to the specific quotients $n_1(r,a_k)/n(r,a_k)\to b_k>0$ (or $=1$). Status remains unclear.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: (Fatou’s conjecture) Show that the subset U of functions g in Rd , such that all the critical points of g are in the basins of attraction of periodic sinks, is dense in Rd . The property ‘g ∈ U ’ is also sometimes called Axiom A. See also Fatou [259]. (P. Fatou; communicated by M. R. Herman)
self_contained_problem:
Let $d \geq 2$ and let $R_d$ denote the space of rational maps $g:\widehat{\mathbb{C}} \to \widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ of degree $d$ from the Riemann sphere to itself, equipped with its natural topology (e.g., as a subset of complex projective space via coefficients). A periodic point $z_0$ of period $p$ of $g$ is called a (periodic) sink (attracting periodic point) if $|(g^p)'(z_0)| < 1$, and its basin of attraction is the set of points whose forward orbits converge to the cycle of $z_0$. A critical point of $g$ is a point where the derivative vanishes (in suitable local coordinates on the sphere). Let
$$U = \{ g \in R_d : \text{every critical point of } g \text{ lies in the basin of attraction of some periodic sink}\}.$$
(Maps in $U$ are also called hyperbolic, or said to satisfy Axiom A.) Prove or disprove: $U$ is dense in $R_d$.
status_search_result: The general Fatou conjecture on density of hyperbolic maps in the space of degree-$d$ rational maps remains open and is regarded as the central open problem in iterated rational dynamics. It has been established in several special settings: for the real quadratic family (Lyubich; Graczyk–Świątek) and more generally for real polynomials (Kozlovski–Shen–van Strien, "Density of hyperbolicity in dimension one", Annals of Math.), and for non-hyperbolic rational maps with Cantor Julia sets. The full complex version in $R_d$ is unresolved.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let {fα (z)} be a family of entire functions, and assume that for every z0 , there are only denumerably many distinct values of fα (z0 ). Then if c = 2N0 > N1 , the family {fα (z)} is itself denumerable. The above result was proved by Erdös [228]. If c = N1 , he constructed a counter-example. Suppose now that m is an infinite cardinal, N0 < m < c. Assume that for every z0 , there are at most m distinct values fα (z0 ). Does it then follow that the family {fα (z)} has at most power m? If m+ < c, where m+ is the successor of m, it is easy to see that the answer is ‘yes’. However, if c = m+ , the counter-example fails. It is possible the question is undecidable. (P. Erdös)
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathfrak{m}$ be an infinite cardinal with $\aleph_0 < \mathfrak{m} < \mathfrak{c}$, where $\mathfrak{c} = 2^{\aleph_0}$ is the cardinality of the continuum. Suppose $\{f_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ is a family of pairwise distinct entire functions $f_\alpha : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ such that for every $z_0 \in \mathbb{C}$ the set of values $\{f_\alpha(z_0) : \alpha \in A\}$ has cardinality at most $\mathfrak{m}$.

Does it follow (provably in ZFC) that $|A| \le \mathfrak{m}$?

Background facts that may be assumed: (i) if $\mathfrak{c} = 2^{\aleph_0} > \aleph_1$ and the value sets $\{f_\alpha(z_0)\}$ are countable for every $z_0$, then the family is countable; (ii) if $\mathfrak{c} = \aleph_1$, there exists a counterexample (an uncountable family of distinct entire functions whose values at every point form a countable set); (iii) if the successor cardinal $\mathfrak{m}^+$ satisfies $\mathfrak{m}^+ < \mathfrak{c}$, then a straightforward argument shows the answer is "yes". The remaining nontrivial case is $\mathfrak{c} = \mathfrak{m}^+$.
status_search_result: This is the natural cardinal generalization of Wetzel's problem. Kumar and Shelah, and subsequently Schilhan (J. London Math. Soc., 2024, "Wetzel families and the continuum"), showed that for any uncountable cardinal $\kappa$ of uncountable cofinality there is a cofinality- and cardinal-preserving forcing extension containing a Wetzel family of size $\kappa$. In particular, for an intermediate cardinal $\mathfrak m$ with $\mathfrak c = \mathfrak m^+$, it is consistent with ZFC that there is a family of $\mathfrak m^+$ distinct entire functions whose value set at every point has size $\le \mathfrak m$. Hence the statement "the family must have size $\le \mathfrak m$" is not provable in ZFC, and as Erdős suspected, the question is undecidable in ZFC in this remaining case.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let the function g in Rd have the property that its Julia set J(g) = Ĉ. Is the dimension k of the space of Beltrami forms on Ĉ, invariant under g, at most one? Also, are certain of the Lattès examples the only rational functions such that k 6= 0? For further information, see [540]. (D. Sullivan; slightly modified and communicated by M. R. Herman)
self_contained_problem:
Let $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ denote the Riemann sphere and let $g:\widehat{\mathbb{C}}\to\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ be a rational map of degree $d\ge 2$ whose Julia set $J(g)$ equals all of $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$. A measurable Beltrami form on $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ is an essentially bounded measurable section $\mu$ of $\overline{TC}/TC$, i.e. a measurable assignment $\mu(z)\,d\bar z/dz$ with $\|\mu\|_\infty\le 1$; it is called $g$-invariant if $g^*\mu=\mu$ almost everywhere. Let $k=k(g)$ denote the complex dimension of the space of $g$-invariant measurable Beltrami forms on $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ (equivalently, the dimension of the space of measurable $g$-invariant line fields together with the trivial form).

(a) Is $k(g)\le 1$ for every such $g$?

(b) Among rational maps $g$ of degree $\ge 2$ with $J(g)=\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$, are the (flexible) Lattès examples — those rational maps semiconjugate via a holomorphic map from a torus to itself given by an affine endomorphism — the only ones for which $k(g)\ne 0$?
status_search_result: The question is a form of the well-known "no invariant line fields" conjecture in complex dynamics, which asserts that the only rational maps carrying an invariant line field on a positive-measure subset of their Julia set are the (flexible) Lattès examples. It remains open in general; partial results are known (e.g., for hyperbolic, subhyperbolic, and Cantor Julia sets, and under various combinatorial conditions), and recent work (2024) continues to address it under weak hypotheses.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: If A, B are countable dense subsets of R, C respectively, does there necessarily exist a transcendental entire function that maps A onto B, and R \ A into C \ B? Suppose that E, F are countable dense subsets of R, and that there exists an entire function f , monotonic on R, that maps E onto F , and R \ E onto R \ F . Find interesting conditions which imply that f is trivial. For example, if E, F are real rationals, under what conditions is f necessarily linear with rational coefficients? One could also investigate this question in the case of real-valued harmonic or subharmonic functions in Rn , n ≥ 2. If A, B are two countable dense subsets of R, Barth and Schneider [65] have shown that there exists a transcendental entire function, monotonic on R, that maps A onto B and R \ A onto R \ B; also, if A, B are countable dense subsets of C, see Barth and Schneider [66]. (K. F. Barth)
self_contained_problem:
Let A be a countable dense subset of R and B a countable dense subset of C. Does there necessarily exist a transcendental entire function f: C → C such that f(A) = B and f(R \ A) ⊆ C \ B?

Furthermore, suppose E, F are countable dense subsets of R and that there exists an entire function f, monotonic on R, with f(E) = F and f(R \ E) = R \ F. Identify natural conditions on E, F (or on f) that force f to be "trivial." For instance, in the case E = F = Q, determine conditions under which f must be a linear polynomial with rational coefficients. Investigate the analogous questions for real-valued harmonic or subharmonic functions on R^n, n ≥ 2.
category_tag: Entire functions and countable dense sets
status_search_result: Barth and Schneider proved that for countable dense subsets A, B of R there is a transcendental entire function, monotonic on R, mapping A onto B and R\A onto R\B, and a related result for countable dense subsets of C. The mixed case (A ⊂ R dense, B ⊂ C dense, with f(R\A) ⊆ C\B) and the rigidity questions about when such an f must be trivial/linear do not appear to have a documented resolution in available sources, so the status is unclear.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let Ld denote the class of those functions g ∈ Rd such that every critical point of g is preperiodic but not periodic. Show that, if the function g in Rd has the property that J(g) = Ĉ, then g belongs to the closure of Ld in Rd . (M. R. Herman)
self_contained_problem:
Let $d\ge 2$ be an integer and let $R_d$ denote the space of all rational maps $g:\widehat{\mathbb{C}}\to\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ of degree $d$, regarded as a complex manifold (equivalently, as an open subset of the projective space of pairs of homogeneous polynomials of degree $d$ with no common factor), endowed with its natural topology. For $g\in R_d$, denote by $J(g)\subseteq\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ its Julia set, i.e., the complement of the Fatou set (the largest open subset of $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ on which the iterates $\{g^n\}_{n\ge 0}$ form a normal family). A point $c\in\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ is called a critical point of $g$ if $g$ fails to be locally injective at $c$. A point $z$ is preperiodic under $g$ if there exist integers $n>m\ge 0$ such that $g^n(z)=g^m(z)$, and periodic if such an equality holds with $m=0$ and $n\ge 1$. Define
$$L_d:=\{g\in R_d : \text{every critical point of }g\text{ is preperiodic but not periodic}\}.$$
Prove that every $g\in R_d$ with $J(g)=\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ lies in the closure of $L_d$ in $R_d$.
status_search_result: No source explicitly confirming a proof or refutation of Herman's density question (that rational maps with Julia set equal to the whole sphere lie in the closure of the postcritically finite, critically strictly preperiodic locus $L_d$) was located. Related results by Rees and others provide examples and measure-theoretic statements, but the density statement in $R_d$ as posed appears not to be settled in the sources retrieved.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Characterise those entire functions having at least one continuous maximum modulus path going from 0 to ∞. (W. Al-Katifi)
self_contained_problem:
Let $f$ be a non-constant entire function, and define its maximum modulus function by
$$M(r,f) = \max_{|z|=r} |f(z)|, \qquad r \ge 0.$$
A *maximum modulus path* for $f$ is a continuous curve $\gamma:[0,\infty) \to \mathbb{C}$ such that $\gamma(0)=0$, $|\gamma(t)| \to \infty$ as $t\to\infty$, and
$$|f(\gamma(t))| = M(|\gamma(t)|,f) \qquad \text{for every } t \ge 0,$$
i.e.\ at each point of the curve the function attains its maximum modulus on the circle through that point.

Characterise the entire functions $f$ for which there exists at least one such continuous maximum modulus path going from $0$ to $\infty$.
category_tag: Maximum modulus set of entire functions
status_search_result: Recent work by Evdoridou, Pardo-Simón and Sixsmith (2021) and related papers analyze the structure of the maximum modulus set of entire functions, refining results of Hayman near the origin and studying its components. However, none of the located sources provide a complete characterisation of entire functions admitting a continuous maximum modulus path from 0 to ∞, so the status of this question could not be definitively verified.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Does there exist a number λ of modulus one that is not a root of unity, such that the positive orbit of − 12 under Pλ (z) = λ(z + z 2 ) is dense in J(Pλ )? (M. R. Herman)
self_contained_problem:
For each complex number $\lambda$ with $|\lambda|=1$, consider the quadratic polynomial
\[ P_\lambda(z) \;=\; \lambda\bigl(z+z^2\bigr), \qquad z\in\mathbb{C}, \]
whose unique finite critical point is $c=-\tfrac{1}{2}$. Let $J(P_\lambda)$ denote the Julia set of $P_\lambda$, i.e., the complement (in the Riemann sphere) of the set of points at which the family of iterates $\{P_\lambda^{\circ n}\}_{n\ge 0}$ is normal. The positive (forward) orbit of $c$ is the set $\{P_\lambda^{\circ n}(-\tfrac{1}{2}):n\ge 0\}$.

Question: Does there exist $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$ with $|\lambda|=1$ such that $\lambda$ is not a root of unity and the positive orbit of $-\tfrac{1}{2}$ under $P_\lambda$ is dense in $J(P_\lambda)$?
status_search_result: Herman's question about whether the forward orbit of the critical point of $P_\lambda(z)=\lambda(z+z^2)$ can be dense in the Julia set for some non-root-of-unity $\lambda$ on the unit circle is widely cited as an open problem. Related results (Herman, Petersen, Yoccoz, Buff–Chéritat, McMullen and others) establish dynamical features—e.g., for almost every rotation number the Siegel disk boundary is a quasicircle through the critical point, and accumulation sets of typical orbits coincide with the postcritical set—but do not resolve whether the critical orbit itself is ever dense in $J(P_\lambda)$ for an irrational $\lambda$. No published resolution was located.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: What is the best function g(σ), σ ≥ 0 such that, for a non-constant entire function f (z) with maximum and minimum modulus M (r, f ) and m0 (r, f ) re- spectively, the assumption log M (r, f ) lim sup ≤σ r→∞ (log r)2 implies that m0 (r, f ) lim sup ≥ g(σ) ? r→∞ M (r, f ) (P. D. Barry)
self_contained_problem:
For a non-constant entire function $f:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$, define the maximum and minimum modulus on the circle of radius $r>0$ by
$$M(r,f) := \max_{|z|=r} |f(z)|, \qquad m_0(r,f) := \min_{|z|=r} |f(z)|.$$
Fix $\sigma \ge 0$ and consider the class $\mathcal{E}(\sigma)$ of all non-constant entire functions $f$ satisfying
$$\limsup_{r\to\infty} \frac{\log M(r,f)}{(\log r)^2} \le \sigma.$$
Determine the largest (best) function $g:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ such that, for every $f \in \mathcal{E}(\sigma)$,
$$\limsup_{r\to\infty} \frac{m_0(r,f)}{M(r,f)} \ge g(\sigma).$$
Equivalently, find
$$g(\sigma) = \inf_{f \in \mathcal{E}(\sigma)} \limsup_{r\to\infty} \frac{m_0(r,f)}{M(r,f)}$$
explicitly as a function of $\sigma \ge 0$.
status_search_result: A web search did not return a definitive resolution of the optimal function g(σ) for entire functions of slow growth (log M(r,f) = O((log r)^2)) attributed to P. D. Barry. While there is a substantial literature on comparisons between m(r,f) and M(r,f) (including Barry's classical 1962 work on minimum modulus), no source clearly identifies the extremal g(σ) in this specific formulation, so the current status is unclear.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let the function f (z), f (z) = λ(ez − 1) with |λ| = 1, have a Siegel singular disc Sλ that contains zero. (a) Prove that there exists some number λ, where |λ| = 1, such that Sλ is bounded in C. (b) If Sλ is unbounded in C, does −λ belong to ∂Sλ ? (M. R. Herman, I. N. Baker and P. J. Rippon)
self_contained_problem:
Consider the entire function f(z) = λ(e^z − 1), where λ ∈ ℂ with |λ| = 1. Suppose 0 is a fixed point of f at which f is linearizable (a Siegel fixed point), and let S_λ denote the corresponding Siegel disc, i.e. the connected component of the Fatou set of f containing 0 on which f is conformally conjugate to an irrational rotation.

(a) Prove that there exists λ with |λ| = 1 such that the Siegel disc S_λ is a bounded subset of ℂ.

(b) Suppose instead that S_λ is unbounded in ℂ. Must the point −λ (which is the unique singular value of f) lie on the boundary ∂S_λ?
status_search_result: Part (a) is established via a method of Ghys (later worked out in detail by Rempe-Gillen), giving λ on the unit circle for which the Siegel disc of λ(e^z−1) is bounded. Part (b) was answered affirmatively: Rippon (1994) handled a full-measure set of rotation numbers, and Rempe (2004), with related independent work by Buff–Fagella, proved that for the exponential family every unbounded Siegel disc contains the singular value on its boundary, resolving the Herman–Baker–Rippon question.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let E be a closed set in C, with the following properties: (1) there exists a transcendental entire function f (z) that is bounded on E; and (2), there exists a transcendental entire function g(z) that is bounded away from 0 on the complement of E. For each such set E, must there exist one transcendental entire function that is simultaneously bounded on E and bounded away from 0 on the complement of E? (L. A. Rubel)
self_contained_problem:
Call an entire function f: ℂ → ℂ transcendental if it is not a polynomial. Let E ⊆ ℂ be a closed set such that:

(i) there exists a transcendental entire function f with sup_{z ∈ E} |f(z)| < ∞ (i.e., f is bounded on E); and

(ii) there exists a transcendental entire function g with inf_{z ∈ ℂ∖E} |g(z)| > 0 (i.e., g is bounded away from 0 on the complement of E).

Question: For every closed set E ⊆ ℂ satisfying both (i) and (ii), does there necessarily exist a single transcendental entire function h that is simultaneously bounded on E and bounded away from 0 on ℂ∖E?
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not surface a published resolution of Rubel's question on whether the existence of two separate transcendental entire functions—one bounded on a closed set E and another bounded away from 0 on its complement—implies the existence of a single transcendental entire function with both properties. No clear evidence of a solution was found, so the status is recorded as unknown.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let B denote the boundary of the Mandelbrot set (or, equivalently, the topological bifurcation set of the family z 7→ z 2 + c, c ∈ C. (a) Is B locally-connected? (b) Prove that B has Hausdorff dimension 2. (c) Does B have Lebesgue measure zero? For further information, see Douady [195] and Lyubich [537]. (A. Douady and J. H. Hubbard; N. Sibony; M. Rees; M. R. Herman)
self_contained_problem:
Consider the family of quadratic polynomials $f_c(z)=z^2+c$ for $c\in\mathbb{C}$. The Mandelbrot set is defined as
$$M=\{c\in\mathbb{C}:\text{the orbit }(f_c^{n}(0))_{n\ge 0}\text{ is bounded}\},$$
and let $B=\partial M$ be its topological boundary in $\mathbb{C}$ (equivalently, the bifurcation locus of the family $\{f_c\}_{c\in\mathbb{C}}$). Resolve the following three questions about $B$:

(a) Is $B$ locally connected as a topological subspace of $\mathbb{C}$? (Equivalently, is $M$ locally connected?)

(b) Show that the Hausdorff dimension of $B$ equals $2$.

(c) Does $B$ have planar Lebesgue measure zero?
status_search_result: Part (b) was proved by Shishikura: the boundary of the Mandelbrot set has Hausdorff dimension 2. Part (a), the MLC (Mandelbrot Locally Connected) conjecture, remains a central open problem in holomorphic dynamics; Yoccoz proved local connectivity at all finitely renormalizable parameters, but the general (infinitely renormalizable) case is open. Part (c), whether the boundary has Lebesgue measure zero, is also still open.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: If f is an entire function such that log M (r, f ) = O(log r)2 as r → ∞, then Hayman [394] has shown that log |f (reiθ )| ∼ log M (r, f ), as r → ∞, for reiθ outside an exceptional set E of circles subtending angles at the origin, whose sum is finite. In particular, log |f (reiθ )| ∼ log M (r, f ), as r → ∞, for almost every θ. Using this result, Anderson and Clunie [24] showed that if f is meromorphic and T (r, f ) = O(log r)2 as r → ∞, then a deficient value (there is at most one) must be asymptotic and, moreover, if δ(a, f ) > 0, then f (reiθ ) → a as r → ∞ for almost every θ. Now consider a new class of entire functions Iα , α > 1, defined by (a) log M (r, f ) = O(log r)1+α as r → ∞ (b) (log r)α = o(log M (r, f )) as r → ∞. (Hayman’s functions are I1 ). Do the results of Hayman, and the corresponding results of Anderson and Clunie still hold? In other words, do these results depend on smallness of growth, or only on smoothness of growth? (J. M. Anderson)
self_contained_problem:
Let $f$ be an entire function and let
$$M(r,f)=\max_{|z|=r}|f(z)|, \qquad T(r,f)=\text{the Nevanlinna characteristic of } f.$$
For a meromorphic function $f$ and a value $a\in\widehat{\mathbb C}$, let $\delta(a,f)$ denote the Nevanlinna deficiency of $a$. A value $a$ is called an asymptotic value of $f$ if there is a continuous path $\gamma$ tending to $\infty$ along which $f(z)\to a$.

A classical theorem of Hayman states that if $f$ is entire and $\log M(r,f)=O((\log r)^2)$ as $r\to\infty$, then
$$\log|f(re^{i\theta})|\sim \log M(r,f)\quad (r\to\infty)$$
for $re^{i\theta}$ outside an exceptional set $E$ which is a union of disks (or "circles") subtending angles at the origin whose total sum is finite; in particular this asymptotic holds for almost every $\theta\in[0,2\pi)$. Using this, Anderson and Clunie proved that if $f$ is meromorphic with $T(r,f)=O((\log r)^2)$ as $r\to\infty$, then any deficient value of $f$ (there is at most one) is an asymptotic value, and moreover if $\delta(a,f)>0$ then $f(re^{i\theta})\to a$ as $r\to\infty$ for almost every $\theta$.

For each $\alpha>1$, define the class $I_\alpha$ of entire functions by the two conditions
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] $\log M(r,f)=O((\log r)^{1+\alpha})$ as $r\to\infty$,
\item[(b)] $(\log r)^{\alpha}=o(\log M(r,f))$ as $r\to\infty$.
\end{itemize}
(The Hayman case $\alpha=1$ recovers the class above.)

Question. Do the analogues of Hayman's theorem and of the Anderson–Clunie theorem hold for the classes $I_\alpha$, $\alpha>1$? Specifically:
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $f\in I_\alpha$, does $\log|f(re^{i\theta})|\sim \log M(r,f)$ as $r\to\infty$ outside an exceptional family of disks subtending angles at the origin whose sum is finite (and thus for almost every $\theta$)?
\item If $f$ is meromorphic and the analogous smoothness condition holds for $T(r,f)$ in place of $\log M(r,f)$, must any deficient value be an asymptotic value, and must $f(re^{i\theta})\to a$ for almost every $\theta$ whenever $\delta(a,f)>0$?
\end{enumerate}
In other words, do these theorems depend on the smallness of growth of $f$, or only on the smoothness of growth?
status_search_result: J. M. Anderson's paper "Asymptotic values of meromorphic functions of smooth growth" (Glasgow Math. J.) addresses this circle of questions, giving results under a smoothness (rather than smallness) hypothesis on growth, with extensions due to Hayman that yield analogues for functions of positive order. This indicates the conjecture's spirit—that smoothness, not smallness, suffices—is at least partially confirmed, but I could not verify a complete resolution covering the full classes $I_\alpha$ for all $\alpha>1$ in both Hayman's and the Anderson–Clunie statements.

original_question: If u(x) is harmonic and not constant in space of 3 or more dimensions, is it true that there exists a path Γ such that u(x) → +∞ as x → ∞ along Γ? The corresponding result for subharmonic functions is certainly false, since if X n 1 r= x2ν ν=1 is the distance of x = (x1 , x2 , . . . , xn ) from the origin, then u(x) = max(−1, −r 2−n ) is subharmonic and bounded in space of n dimensions, when n > 2. On the other hand, a bounded harmonic function in space is constant.
self_contained_problem:
Let $n \ge 3$ and let $u : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ be a harmonic function (that is, $\Delta u = \sum_{\nu=1}^n \partial^2 u/\partial x_\nu^2 = 0$) which is not identically constant. Must there exist a continuous path $\Gamma : [0,\infty) \to \mathbb{R}^n$ with $|\Gamma(t)| \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty$ such that
$$u(\Gamma(t)) \longrightarrow +\infty \quad \text{as } t \to \infty?$$
(Note that the analogous statement fails for subharmonic functions: for $n \ge 3$, the function $u(x) = \max(-1, -|x|^{2-n})$ is subharmonic on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and bounded; and a bounded harmonic function on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is necessarily constant by Liouville's theorem.)

original_question: Let Γ be a rectifiable curve. Suppose f is a continuous function on the plane satisfying Z f (z)dz = 0 for all rigid motions σ. σ(Γ) Does this imply that f is an entire function? The answer is ‘yes’ for some choices of Γ, and ‘no’ for others. For example, the answer is ‘no’ for the circle (f (x + iy) = sin(ax) is a counter-example for a suitable choice of a); ‘yes’ for an ellipse; ‘yes’ for any polygonal Jordan curve; and ‘yes’ for the boundary of any convex set with at least one corner. Prove that the circle is the only closed rectifiable Jordan curve (or the only curve among the class of curves which are boundaries of bounded convex sets) for which the answer is ‘no’. This problem is related to the ‘Pompeiu Problem’ discussed by Brown, Schreiber and Taylor [119]. (L. Brown)
self_contained_problem:
Let Γ be a closed rectifiable Jordan curve in the complex plane ℂ. For a rigid motion σ of ℂ (i.e., a map of the form σ(z) = e^{iθ}z + c with θ ∈ ℝ and c ∈ ℂ), let σ(Γ) denote the image of Γ under σ, oriented as the image of Γ. Say that Γ has the *complex moment property* if the only continuous functions f : ℂ → ℂ satisfying

  ∫_{σ(Γ)} f(z) dz = 0

for every rigid motion σ are the entire functions.

It is known that:
 (a) every ellipse, every polygonal Jordan curve, and the boundary of every bounded convex set having at least one corner has the complex moment property;
 (b) the circle does not have the complex moment property (for any circle, f(x+iy) = sin(ax) is a counterexample for a suitable a > 0).

Problem. Prove that the circle is the only closed rectifiable Jordan curve in ℂ failing the complex moment property. (Equivalently, prove at least the restricted statement that, among boundaries of bounded convex subsets of ℂ, the circle is the only curve failing the complex moment property.)
status_search_result: This is a variant of the classical Pompeiu problem. The general conjecture that the disc/circle is the only bounded simply connected planar domain failing the Pompeiu property remains open. Substantial partial results exist (e.g., domains with corners, convex domains satisfying additional regularity, and the equivalence with Schiffer's conjecture for sufficiently regular boundaries), but a complete proof for all rectifiable Jordan curves, or even all boundaries of bounded convex sets, has not been established.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Consider the class of functions subharmonic in the unit disc D, and satisfying u(z) ≤ 0 there. Suppose also that A(r, u) ≤ −1, for r lying on a set E consisting of a finite number of straight line segments. Then it is known (see e.g. Nevanlinna [598, p.100]) that B(r, u) is maximal, when u(z) = uE (z), where uE (z) is harmonic in D, except on a set E of the positive real axis, and u(z) assumes boundary values 0 on |z| = 1, and −1 on E. This is the solution to the so-called Carleman-Milloux problem [598]. For 0 < r < 1, 0 < K < 1, let C(r, K) be the set of all θ such that u(reiθ ) < −K. Is it true that C(r, K) has minimal length only if u(z) = uE (z)? The special case where E consists of the whole interval [0, 1] has particular interest. (T. Kövari)
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ denote the open unit disc. For a function $u$ subharmonic in $\mathbb{D}$ and $0<r<1$, define
$$A(r,u)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}u(re^{i\theta})\,d\theta,\qquad B(r,u)=\sup_{|z|=r}u(z).$$
Consider the class $\mathcal{F}_E$ of functions $u$ subharmonic in $\mathbb{D}$ satisfying
\begin{enumerate}
\item $u(z)\le 0$ for all $z\in\mathbb{D}$,
\item $A(r,u)\le -1$ for every $r$ in a prescribed set $E\subset[0,1)$ that is a finite union of straight line segments.
\end{enumerate}
It is classical (the Carleman–Milloux problem) that $B(r,u)$ is maximized within $\mathcal{F}_E$ by the extremal function $u_E$, where $u_E$ is harmonic in $\mathbb{D}\setminus E^*$ (with $E^*$ the corresponding subset of the positive real axis), takes boundary values $0$ on $\{|z|=1\}$ and $-1$ on $E^*$.

For $0<r<1$ and $0<K<1$, and for $u\in\mathcal{F}_E$, define
$$C(r,K;u)=\{\theta\in[0,2\pi):u(re^{i\theta})<-K\},$$
and let $|C(r,K;u)|$ denote its Lebesgue measure (length).

Question: Is it true that, among all $u\in\mathcal{F}_E$, the length $|C(r,K;u)|$ is minimized only when $u=u_E$? In particular, settle the case in which $E$ is the entire interval $[0,1]$.
status_search_result: Web searches for the specific Kövári question on minimality of the level-set length $C(r,K)$ in the Carleman–Milloux problem returned no direct results addressing or resolving the conjecture. The general Carleman–Milloux extremal problem is classical and well-known, but the specific minimal-length characterization stated here does not appear to have a documented resolution in accessible literature.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Since the knowledge of the zeros of an entire function f leaves an unknown factor, eh say, in the Hadamard product for f , one can ask if f is determined by the zeros of f , and of its first few derivatives. Does there exist an integer k, k ≥ 2 such that, if f and g are entire, and f (n) /g(n) is entire and non-vanishing for 0 ≤ n ≤ k, then f /g is constant, unless f (z) = eaz+b , g(z) = ecz+d or f (z) = A(eaz − b), g(z) = B(e−az − b−1 ) ? The proposer has shown (unpublished) that k = 2 will do in certain cases; for example, when f and g have finite order. The example f (z) = (e2z − 1) exp(−iez ), g(z) = (1 − e−2z ) exp(ie−z ) shows that one sometimes needs k = 3. One can ask a similar question for meromorphic functions, with the additional possibility that f (z) = A(eh(z) − 1)−1 , g(z) = B(1 − e−h(z) ) for any non-constant entire function h. (A. Hinkkanen)
self_contained_problem:
Does there exist an integer $k \ge 2$ with the following property: whenever $f$ and $g$ are entire functions such that the quotient $f^{(n)}/g^{(n)}$ is entire and non-vanishing for every $n$ with $0 \le n \le k$, then $f/g$ is constant, with the only exceptions being

(i) $f(z) = e^{az+b}$ and $g(z) = e^{cz+d}$ for constants $a,b,c,d$, or

(ii) $f(z) = A(e^{az} - b)$ and $g(z) = B(e^{-az} - b^{-1})$ for constants $A,B,a,b$ with $b \ne 0$?

Here $f^{(n)}$ denotes the $n$-th derivative of $f$. It is known that $k=2$ suffices in some special cases (e.g.\ when $f$ and $g$ are of finite order), and the example $f(z) = (e^{2z}-1)\exp(-i e^{z})$, $g(z) = (1-e^{-2z})\exp(i e^{-z})$ shows that $k=2$ is not enough in general.

Formulate and answer the analogous question for meromorphic functions $f$ and $g$, with the additional exceptional family $f(z) = A(e^{h(z)}-1)^{-1}$, $g(z) = B(1 - e^{-h(z)})$ allowed, where $h$ is any non-constant entire function. Determine the smallest such $k$ (if any) in each setting.
status_search_result: According to the updated edition of the problem collection, Köhler proved that the answer is affirmative for meromorphic functions with $k = 6$, settling the meromorphic version with an explicit (though possibly non-optimal) bound. The exact minimal value of $k$ remains unspecified, so the problem is partially solved.

original_question: If ω(ζ) is continuous and bounded in D, and each point of ζ of D is the centre of at least one circle Cζ lying in D, such that ω(ζ) is equal to the average of the values of ω(z) on Cζ , is it true that ω(z) is harmonic in D? The result is true if ω(z) is continuous in |z| ≤ 1, and is certainly false if this condition is removed. The corresponding problem with Cζ replaced by its interior Dζ is also open. (J. E. Littlewood)
self_contained_problem:
Let $D=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ be the open unit disk. Suppose $\omega:D\to\mathbb{R}$ is continuous and bounded, and suppose that for every point $\zeta\in D$ there exists at least one circle $C_\zeta\subset D$ centered at $\zeta$ (with radius $r(\zeta)>0$ depending on $\zeta$) such that
$$\omega(\zeta)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\omega(\zeta+r(\zeta)e^{i\theta})\,d\theta.$$
Question 1 (one-circle problem): Must $\omega$ be harmonic in $D$?

Question 2 (one-disk variant): If instead, for each $\zeta\in D$, there is a closed disk $\overline{D_\zeta}\subset D$ centered at $\zeta$ with radius $r(\zeta)>0$ such that
$$\omega(\zeta)=\frac{1}{\pi r(\zeta)^2}\iint_{D_\zeta}\omega(x+iy)\,dx\,dy,$$
must $\omega$ be harmonic in $D$?

(Note: it is known that if continuity is strengthened to continuity on the closed disk $\{|z|\le 1\}$, the conclusion holds, and the boundedness/continuity hypotheses on $D$ alone cannot simply be removed.)
status_search_result: Littlewood's one-circle problem (Question 1) was answered negatively by Hansen and Nadirashvili (Acta Mathematica, 1994), who constructed a continuous bounded non-harmonic function on the unit disk satisfying the one-circle restricted mean value property. A simplified construction was given subsequently. The corresponding one-disk variant has also been studied within this framework.

original_question: Let f be an entire function satisfying the condition log M (r, f ) ≤ (1 + o(1))r ρ , as r → ∞. $$\limsup_{\varepsilon \to 0,\ r \to \infty} E(r,\varepsilon) \;\ge\; \frac{\arccos \alpha}{\rho}.$$

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: It is shown by Hellerstein and Rossi [427], and Gundersen [354] that if f1 and f2 are two linearly independent solutions to the differential equation w′′ + Hw = 0, where H is a polynomial and f1 and f2 have only finitely many non-real zeros, then H is a non-negative constant. It is also shown that, if H(z) = az + b, for a, b ∈ R, then the differential equation admits a solution with only real zeros (and infinitely many of them). Furthermore, as pointed out by Gundersen [354], Titchmarsh ([749, pp. 172-173]) showed that, if H(z) = z 4 − β for special choices of β, then the differential equation also admits solutions with only real zeros (and infinitely many of them). Characterise all non-constant polynomials H such that the differential equation admits a solution with only real zeros (and infinitely many of them). (S. Hellerstein and J. Rossi)
self_contained_problem:
Consider the second-order linear differential equation
    w''(z) + H(z) w(z) = 0,
where H is a polynomial in the complex variable z with complex coefficients. A solution f of this equation is an entire function of z. It is known that:

(a) If f_1 and f_2 are two linearly independent solutions of the equation and each of f_1, f_2 has only finitely many non-real zeros, then H must be a non-negative real constant.

(b) When H(z) = a z + b with a, b real, the equation admits a (necessarily entire) solution having infinitely many zeros, all of which are real.

(c) For certain special real values of β, the equation with H(z) = z^4 − β admits an entire solution all of whose zeros are real (and there are infinitely many of them).

Problem: Characterise completely the non-constant polynomials H for which the differential equation w'' + H w = 0 admits an entire solution that has infinitely many zeros, all of them real.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let u(x) be subharmonic in Rm . One can define the quantities n(r, 0), N (r, 0), T (r) as in Nevanlinna theory in the plane, taking the analogue of the case u(z) = log |f (z)|, where f (z) is an entire function (see, for example Hayman [394]). Define N (r, u) δ(u) = 1 − lim sup . r→∞ T (r) If the order ρ of u is less than 1, it is possible to obtain the sharp upper bound for δ(u) in terms of ρ and m. The bound is attained when u(x) has all its mass on a ray (see Hayman and Kennedy [412, Chp. IV]). One can ask the corresponding question for ρ > 1. One can ask whether a lower bound A(ρ) can be obtained for δ(u) if ρ > 1 and all the mass of u(x) lies on a ray, or more generally on some suitable lower dimensional subspace S of Rm and ρ > ρ0 (S). For fixed S we may conjecture by analogy with the case m = 2, that A(ρ) → 1 as ρ → ∞. This is proved by Hellerstein and Shea [428] in the case m = 2. (D. Shea)
self_contained_problem:
Let $u:\mathbb{R}^m\to[-\infty,\infty)$ be a non-constant subharmonic function ($m\ge 2$). By analogy with Nevanlinna theory for entire functions $f$ on $\mathbb{C}$ (where $u(z)=\log|f(z)|$), define:
- $n(r,0)$ = the Riesz mass of $u$ in the closed ball $\{x\in\mathbb{R}^m:|x|\le r\}$,
- $N(r,0)=\int_0^r \frac{n(t,0)-n(0,0)}{t^{m-1}}\,dt + n(0,0)\log r$ (the integrated counting function),
- $T(r)$ = the Nevanlinna characteristic of $u$ (e.g., $T(r)=\frac{1}{\sigma_{m-1}}\int_{S^{m-1}} u^+(r\xi)\,d\sigma(\xi)$ suitably normalized so that the First Fundamental Theorem $T(r)=N(r,0)+m(r)$ holds).

Define the deficiency
$$\delta(u)=1-\limsup_{r\to\infty}\frac{N(r,u)}{T(r)},$$
and let $\rho=\limsup_{r\to\infty}\frac{\log T(r)}{\log r}$ be the order of $u$.

Suppose $u$ has all of its Riesz mass concentrated on a ray emanating from the origin in $\mathbb{R}^m$, and suppose $\rho>1$.

Question: Does there exist a function $A(\rho)>0$, depending only on $\rho$ and $m$, such that
$$\delta(u)\ge A(\rho)$$
for every such $u$? More generally, if the mass of $u$ is supported on a fixed lower-dimensional linear subspace $S\subset\mathbb{R}^m$ and $\rho>\rho_0(S)$ for some threshold $\rho_0(S)$, does an analogous lower bound $A(\rho)$ exist? Is it true that, for fixed $S$, $A(\rho)\to 1$ as $\rho\to\infty$ (in analogy with the planar case $m=2$)?
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not return literature settling the question of a sharp lower bound $A(\rho)$ for the Nevanlinna deficiency of subharmonic functions in $\mathbb{R}^m$ with mass concentrated on a ray (or lower-dimensional subspace) when the order $\rho>1$. The planar analogue is known (Hellerstein–Shea), but the higher-dimensional version does not appear to have a confirmed resolution in accessible sources.

original_question: Suppose that f is entire of proximate order ρ(r), and that f has a representation as a Dirichlet series ∞ X f (z) = an eλn z , 0 ≤ λ1 < λ2 < . . . → ∞, an > 0. n=1 Can one give a complete characterisation of the indicator h(θ, f ) = lim sup r −ρ(r) log |f (reiθ )| r→∞ of such functions? If f has a representation Z ∞ f (z) = eiz dF (t) where F is positive and increasing, Gol’dberg and Ostrovskii [323] gave such a characterisation. (A. A. Gol’dberg and I. V. Ostrovskii)
self_contained_problem:
A positive function $\rho(r)$ defined for $r\ge r_0$ is called a proximate order if $\rho(r)\to \rho\in[0,\infty)$ as $r\to\infty$ and $r\rho'(r)\log r\to 0$ as $r\to\infty$. For an entire function $f$, define its indicator (with respect to $\rho$) by
$$h(\theta,f) \;=\; \limsup_{r\to\infty}\, r^{-\rho(r)}\,\log|f(re^{i\theta})|, \qquad \theta\in[0,2\pi).$$

Now suppose $f$ is an entire function of proximate order $\rho(r)$ that admits a Dirichlet-series representation
$$f(z) \;=\; \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\, e^{\lambda_n z}, \qquad 0\le \lambda_1<\lambda_2<\cdots\to\infty,\quad a_n>0,$$
converging in the whole complex plane.

Give a complete characterisation of those functions $h:[0,2\pi)\to[-\infty,+\infty)$ which arise as the indicator $h(\theta,f)$ of some entire function $f$ of the above form.

(Background: when $f$ has the integral representation $f(z)=\int_0^\infty e^{tz}\,dF(t)$ with $F$ positive and increasing, a complete characterisation of the possible indicators is known.)

Status is therefore reported as unknown.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let Ω be a component of the normal set of an entire function f (under iteration). Do there exist such an f and such an Ω with the following properties: (a) f n (Ω) is uniformly bounded, for n = 0, 1, 2, . . .; (b) f n (Ω) ∩ f m (Ω) = ∅ for n 6= m. (I. N. Baker, R. Herman and I. Kra; communicated by D. Hamilton)
self_contained_problem:
Let $f:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$ be a transcendental entire function, and consider its iterates $f^n=f\circ f\circ\cdots\circ f$ ($n$ times), with $f^0=\mathrm{id}$. The Fatou set (normal set) $F(f)$ is the set of points $z\in\mathbb{C}$ at which the family $\{f^n\}_{n\ge 0}$ is normal in some neighborhood of $z$. A connected component $\Omega$ of $F(f)$ is called a wandering domain if $f^n(\Omega)\cap f^m(\Omega)=\emptyset$ for all $n\ne m$ (equivalently, no iterate of $\Omega$ is contained in a periodic component of $F(f)$).

Question: Does there exist a transcendental entire function $f$ and a component $\Omega$ of its Fatou set such that both of the following hold?
(a) The orbit is uniformly bounded: there exists $R>0$ with $f^n(\Omega)\subset\{|z|\le R\}$ for every $n=0,1,2,\ldots$;
(b) The iterates are pairwise disjoint: $f^n(\Omega)\cap f^m(\Omega)=\emptyset$ whenever $n\ne m$.
status_search_result: Recent work on oscillating wandering domains explicitly notes that the existence of a wandering domain of an entire function with a bounded forward orbit remains a major open question. Known constructions yield multiply connected wandering domains whose iterates escape to infinity, or oscillating simply connected wandering domains that return near a bounded set but also have unbounded subsequences; no example with the entire orbit confined to a bounded set is known.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: It is known that the set E of least capacity C and given volume is a ball. If E displays some measure of asymmetry (for instance, if every ball with the same volume as E in space contains a minimum proportion δ in the complement of E), can one obtain a lower bound for the capacity of E which exceeds C by some positive function of δ? (E. Fraenkel; communicated by W. K. Hayman)
self_contained_problem:
Let $n \ge 2$ and let $E \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a compact set. Denote by $|E|$ its Lebesgue measure (volume) and by $\operatorname{cap}(E)$ its (Newtonian, for $n \ge 3$, or logarithmic, for $n=2$) capacity. The classical isocapacitary inequality asserts that among all compact sets of a fixed volume $V$, the capacity is minimized uniquely by the ball $B$ with $|B|=V$; write $C := \operatorname{cap}(B)$.

Define the Fraenkel asymmetry of $E$ by
$$\delta(E) \;=\; \inf_{x \in \mathbb{R}^n} \frac{|E \,\triangle\, B(x)|}{|E|},$$
where $B(x)$ denotes the ball centered at $x$ with $|B(x)|=|E|$. Equivalently, $\delta$ measures the minimum, over all balls of the same volume as $E$, of the relative volume of the symmetric difference (so that, up to normalization, it captures the minimum proportion of any equal-volume ball lying outside $E$).

Question: Does there exist a function $\Phi : [0,2] \to [0,\infty)$ with $\Phi(\delta) > 0$ whenever $\delta > 0$, depending only on $n$ and $V$, such that for every compact $E \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ with $|E|=V$ one has
$$\operatorname{cap}(E) \;\ge\; C + \Phi(\delta(E))\,?$$
That is, can the isocapacitary deficit $\operatorname{cap}(E) - C$ be bounded below by a positive function of the asymmetry $\delta(E)$?
status_search_result: A sharp quantitative isocapacitary inequality has been established: the isocapacitary deficit of a set with fixed volume is bounded below by a constant times the square of the Fraenkel asymmetry. This answers Fraenkel's question affirmatively, with $\Phi(\delta) \asymp \delta^2$. Extensions to $p$-capacity and fractional capacity have also been proved.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: (a) Show that, if a function g in Rd has the property that its Julia set J(g) 6= Ĉ, then g does not leave invariant a non-trivial Beltrami form on J(g). Here a Beltrami form µ means that µ ∈ L∞ (Ĉ) and kµkL∞ < 1; and trivial on J(g) means that µ(x) = 0 for almost all x in J(g). (b) More generally, is the Lebesgue measure of J(g) in Ĉ equal to zero? (This is the analogous conjecture to the Ahlfors conjecture for finitely-generated Kleinian groups.) Negative answers to both (a) and (b) have been proved (by McMullen (uncited) and Eremenko and Lyubich [248]) for the class of transcendental entire functions g. Douady has conjectured that the answer is negative, and that a counter-example is the function Pλ (z) = λ(z + z 2 ), for some λ of modulus one. See also Douady [195], Lyubich [537] and Mañé [540]. (D. Sullivan; communicated by M. R. Herman)
self_contained_problem:
Let $g$ be a rational function of degree $d \ge 2$ acting on the Riemann sphere $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$, and let $J(g) \subset \widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ denote its Julia set. A Beltrami form is a measurable $(-1,1)$-form $\mu \in L^\infty(\widehat{\mathbb{C}})$ with $\|\mu\|_\infty < 1$; it is said to be invariant under $g$ if $g^*\mu = \mu$ almost everywhere, and trivial on $J(g)$ if $\mu(x) = 0$ for almost every $x \in J(g)$.

(a) Prove that if $J(g) \ne \widehat{\mathbb{C}}$, then $g$ admits no invariant Beltrami form that is non-trivial on $J(g)$ (equivalently, $g$ admits no measurable invariant line field supported on $J(g)$).

(b) More generally, prove or disprove: for every such rational map $g$ with $J(g) \ne \widehat{\mathbb{C}}$, the Lebesgue measure of $J(g)$ in $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ equals zero.

(In particular, decide both questions for the quadratic family $P_\lambda(z) = \lambda(z + z^2)$ with $|\lambda| = 1$.)
status_search_result: The "no invariant line fields" conjecture (part (a)) and the question of whether Julia sets have Lebesgue measure zero (part (b)) remain open in general for rational maps. Significant partial results have been obtained: McMullen established (a) for the real quadratic family, Levin–van Strien extended it to real unicritical polynomials $z^d+c$, and Avila–Lyubich and others have proved positive measure Julia sets can occur for some quadratic polynomials with Cremer/Siegel behavior, while ruling out invariant line fields in many infinitely renormalizable cases. The full conjectures remain unresolved.
