original_question: Nelson--Nguyen conjecture: Subspace embedding properties of sparse random matrices: Prove or disprove the Nelson--Nguyen conjecture: A SparseStack embedding with parameters $ = O(( r) / epsilon)$ and $k = O(r / epsilon^2)$ is an oblivious subspace embedding with parameters $alpha = 1 - epsilon$ and $beta = 1+epsilon$.
self_contained_problem:
Setup. For integers $n \geq m \geq 1$, an $m \times n$ random matrix $S$ is called an oblivious subspace embedding (OSE) with parameters $(\alpha, \beta)$, distortion, and rank $r$, if for every fixed $r$-dimensional linear subspace $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, with high probability one has
$$\alpha \, \|x\|_2 \;\leq\; \|S x\|_2 \;\leq\; \beta \, \|x\|_2 \qquad \text{for all } x \in V.$$

The SparseStack construction with parameters $(k, \zeta)$, where $k$ is the number of rows and $\zeta$ is the column sparsity, is the random $k \times n$ matrix obtained as follows. Partition the $k$ rows into $\zeta$ equal blocks of size $k/\zeta$. In each block, every column is zero except in one row chosen independently and uniformly at random, where the entry is an independent $\pm 1/\sqrt{\zeta}$ Rademacher random variable. The full SparseStack matrix is the vertical stack of these $\zeta$ independent block matrices.

Problem (Nelson–Nguyen conjecture). Let $r \geq 1$ be an integer and $\varepsilon \in (0, 1)$. Prove or disprove: there exist absolute constants such that the SparseStack embedding with column sparsity 
$$\zeta = O\!\left(\frac{\log r}{\varepsilon}\right) \quad\text{and number of rows}\quad k = O\!\left(\frac{r}{\varepsilon^2}\right)$$
is an oblivious subspace embedding for $r$-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with parameters $\alpha = 1 - \varepsilon$ and $\beta = 1 + \varepsilon$.
status_search_result: The Nelson–Nguyen conjecture has seen substantial recent progress but is not fully resolved at the exact target parameters. Chenakkod, Dereziński, Dong, and Rudelson (arXiv:2311.10680, 2023) established optimal embedding dimension m = O(d/ε²) with sparsity O(log⁴ d) per column. Dereziński, Yang and collaborators (arXiv:2411.08773, 2024) achieved optimal dimension with near-optimal sparsity Õ(1/ε). A 2025 work (arXiv:2508.14234) is titled "Resolving Nelson–Nguyen Conjecture Up to Sub-Polylogarithmic Factors," indicating the conjecture is settled up to sub-polylogarithmic factors but not at the precise O((log r)/ε), O(r/ε²) bounds.

original_question: Rerandomized subsampled trigonometric transforms: Assume that $n = Omega( r)$. Prove or disprove: The rerandomized SRHT of dimension $k = O(r/epsilon^2)$ is an oblivious subspace embedding with $alpha = 1-epsilon$ and $beta = 1+epsilon$.
self_contained_problem:
Let $H_n \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ denote the (normalized) Walsh–Hadamard matrix on $n$ points (assume $n$ is a power of two), so that $H_n^\top H_n = I_n$. For a positive integer $k \le n$ define the subsampled randomized Hadamard transform (SRHT) by
$$ S \;=\; \sqrt{n/k}\, P\, H_n\, D, $$
where $D \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is a random diagonal sign matrix whose diagonal entries are i.i.d. uniform on $\{\pm 1\}$, and $P \in \{0,1\}^{k \times n}$ is a uniformly random row-subsampling matrix that selects $k$ rows of $H_n D$ (with or without replacement).

A rerandomized SRHT of dimension $k$ is the random linear map obtained by drawing an independent fresh copy $(D, P)$ of the SRHT for each input vector (equivalently, the sketch is allowed to be redrawn for each query rather than fixed once and applied to all of a subspace simultaneously).

For parameters $0 < \varepsilon < 1$, a positive integer $r$, and constants $0 < \alpha \le \beta$, a random matrix $S \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times n}$ is called an oblivious subspace embedding for $r$-dimensional subspaces with distortion $(\alpha, \beta)$ if, for every fixed $r$-dimensional linear subspace $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$,
$$ \Pr\!\Big[\, \alpha \|x\|_2 \le \|Sx\|_2 \le \beta \|x\|_2 \ \text{for all } x \in V \,\Big] \;\ge\; 1 - \delta, $$
for some absolute constant $\delta \in (0,1)$ (e.g. $\delta = 1/3$).

Assume $n = \Omega(\log r)$. Prove or disprove the following statement: there exists an absolute constant $C > 0$ such that for every $r$-dimensional subspace and every $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, the rerandomized SRHT with embedding dimension
$$ k \;=\; C\, r / \varepsilon^2 $$
is an oblivious subspace embedding with $\alpha = 1 - \varepsilon$ and $\beta = 1 + \varepsilon$.
category_tag: randomized numerical linear algebra / subspace embeddings
status_search_result: Recent work (2023–2025) establishes that sparse oblivious subspace embeddings can attain the optimal embedding dimension $m = \Theta(r/\varepsilon^2)$ (resolving the Nelson–Nguyen conjecture up to sub-polylogarithmic factors), and standard SRHT analyses give $k = \tilde O(r/\varepsilon^2)$ with extra $\log$ factors. However, no source directly confirms that the specifically rerandomized SRHT achieves the clean optimal $k = O(r/\varepsilon^2)$ bound under the stated assumption $n = \Omega(\log r)$. The status of this exact statement could not be verified.

original_question: What is the asymptotic error $epsilon_m*$ as a function of $m$ and $delta$?
self_contained_problem:
For a parameter $\delta\in(0,1)$ and an integer $m\ge 1$, let $\mathcal{P}_m$ denote the set of real polynomials of degree at most $m$, and define the best uniform approximation error to the sign function on the symmetric two-interval set $[-1,-\delta]\cup[\delta,1]$ by
$$\epsilon_m^*(\delta)\;=\;\inf_{p\in\mathcal{P}_m}\;\sup_{x\in[-1,-\delta]\cup[\delta,1]}\bigl|\operatorname{sgn}(x)-p(x)\bigr|,$$
where $\operatorname{sgn}(x)=1$ for $x>0$ and $\operatorname{sgn}(x)=-1$ for $x<0$. Determine the precise asymptotic behavior of $\epsilon_m^*(\delta)$ as $m\to\infty$, as an explicit function of $m$ and $\delta$.
status_search_result: The exact asymptotic of the best uniform polynomial approximation error to $\operatorname{sgn}(x)$ on $[-1,-\delta]\cup[\delta,1]$ is known. Eremenko and Yuditskii established that $\epsilon_m^*(\delta)\sim \tfrac{1-\delta}{\sqrt{\pi\delta}}\cdot\tfrac{2}{\sqrt{m-1}}\bigl(\tfrac{1-\delta}{1+\delta}\bigr)^{(m-1)/2}$ as $m\to\infty$, with extremal polynomials described via conformal maps onto comb-like domains. The problem is therefore solved in the asymptotic sense.

paper_title: Pulsars and Millisecond Pulsars I: Advancements, Open Questions and finding Gaps via statistical insights
original_question: How do different binary-system configurations affect the spin-up of neutron stars into pulsars or millisecond pulsars? In particular, how do structural properties of the neutron star, such as its spin and magnetic field, together with orbital parameters such as semi-major axis and eccentricity, change the efficiency and outcome of the accretion-driven transfer of angular momentum that accelerates the neutron star's rotation?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a binary system consisting of a neutron star of mass $M_{\mathrm{NS}}$, radius $R_{\mathrm{NS}}$, moment of inertia $I$, surface dipolar magnetic field strength $B$, and initial spin angular frequency $\Omega_0$, in orbit with a companion star of mass $M_c$ on a Keplerian orbit characterized by semi-major axis $a$ and eccentricity $e$. Suppose mass transfer occurs via either Roche-lobe overflow or stellar-wind accretion at a rate $\dot{M}(t)$, and that accreted matter forms (where applicable) a Keplerian disk truncated at the magnetospheric (Alfvén) radius
$$r_m \;=\; \left(\frac{B^2 R_{\mathrm{NS}}^6}{\dot{M}\sqrt{2 G M_{\mathrm{NS}}}}\right)^{2/7},$$
with corotation radius $r_{\mathrm{co}} = (G M_{\mathrm{NS}}/\Omega^2)^{1/3}$. The angular momentum evolution of the neutron star is governed by
$$I\,\dot{\Omega} \;=\; \dot{M}\,\sqrt{G M_{\mathrm{NS}} r_m}\;-\;N_{\mathrm{mag}}(\Omega,B,r_m,r_{\mathrm{co}}),$$
where $N_{\mathrm{mag}}$ is the magnetic propeller/braking torque, which depends on the fastness parameter $\omega_s = (r_m/r_{\mathrm{co}})^{3/2}$.

Determine, as a function of the parameters $(B, \Omega_0, a, e, M_c, \dot{M})$:
(i) the conditions under which the neutron star is spun up to the millisecond regime (final spin period $P_{\mathrm{spin}} \lesssim 10$ ms);
(ii) the total accreted mass $\Delta M$ and timescale $\tau_{\mathrm{rec}}$ required for recycling to that regime;
(iii) the dependence of the spin-up efficiency $\eta = \Delta\Omega/\Delta M$ on orbital eccentricity $e$ and semi-major axis $a$, including the role of periastron-enhanced accretion in eccentric orbits;
(iv) the threshold magnetic field above which the propeller effect prevents spin-up entirely.

Provide quantitative criteria and asymptotic regimes characterizing the outcome (isolated recycled pulsar versus millisecond pulsar versus spin-down) in terms of the listed parameters.
status_search_result: The recycling scenario for millisecond pulsar formation is broadly accepted, but the detailed dependence of spin-up efficiency on binary structural and orbital parameters (especially eccentricity, magnetic-field decay during accretion, and the propeller/accretion transition) remains an active area of research with no closed-form quantitative solution; this is generally treated as an open modeling problem in pulsar astrophysics.

original_question: How can pulsar timing arrays (PTAs), which detect low-frequency gravitational waves by monitoring the timing of millisecond pulsars with very high precision, be optimized so that they become more sensitive and can detect gravitational-wave signals from weaker or more distant cosmic sources, including events such as supermassive black hole mergers?
self_contained_problem:
A pulsar timing array (PTA) is a collection of millisecond pulsars whose pulse times-of-arrival (TOAs) are monitored over many years. Let the residuals of the i-th pulsar at observation time t_{i,k} be modeled as r_i(t_{i,k}) = h_i(t_{i,k}; \theta) + n_i(t_{i,k}), where h_i denotes the timing perturbation induced by a stochastic or deterministic gravitational-wave (GW) signal of parameters \theta (e.g. from a supermassive black hole binary merger or a stochastic GW background), and n_i is a noise process consisting of (a) white measurement noise of variance \sigma_{i,k}^2, (b) intrinsic red spin noise, (c) frequency-dependent dispersion-measure noise from the interstellar medium, and (d) pulsar jitter. Cross-pulsar correlations of the GW-induced residuals follow the Hellings–Downs curve as a function of angular separation.

Develop a quantitative optimization framework that determines, jointly:

1. The optimal allocation of total observing time T across N_p pulsars (cadence schedule c_i and per-observation integration time \tau_i, subject to \sum_i c_i \tau_i \le T),
2. The optimal selection and expansion of the pulsar set (which new millisecond pulsars to add, weighted by their timing precision \sigma_i and sky position),
3. The optimal multi-frequency observing strategy that minimizes interstellar-medium-induced TOA variance,
4. The optimal data-analysis pipeline (timing model, noise model, and Bayesian/frequentist detection statistic),

so as to maximize the detection sensitivity—quantified by the signal-to-noise ratio or the Bayes factor—of the array to weak GW signals at frequencies f \in [10^{-9}, 10^{-7}] Hz, including individually resolvable supermassive black hole binary mergers and faint stochastic backgrounds.

Specifically, derive the configuration that maximizes the expected detection probability for a GW source of fixed strain amplitude h_c and quantify how the achievable strain sensitivity h_{\min}(f) scales with N_p, T, \sigma_i, and observing cadence under realistic noise models.
status_search_result: This is a broad, ongoing research direction in gravitational-wave astrophysics. Active PTA collaborations (NANOGrav, EPTA, PPTA, IPTA, MeerKAT/MPTA, CPTA) continue to publish improvements in sensitivity, noise modeling, and array optimization. While partial results exist (e.g., the 2023 evidence for a stochastic GW background and ongoing optimization studies of cadence and pulsar selection), the overall question of how to optimize PTAs to detect weaker/more distant sources remains an open and actively pursued problem.

original_question: How do pulsars influence cosmic evolution and stellar dynamics, and how does that role change between globular clusters, where stellar encounters and binary interactions are common, and the Galactic field, where pulsars evolve in more isolated conditions? The question asks both what pulsars contribute to the evolution of their environments and how those contributions depend on environment.
status_search_result: This is a broad open-ended astrophysical research question rather than a single well-defined mathematical conjecture. The relative role of pulsars in globular clusters versus the Galactic field remains an active area of research, with ongoing discoveries of new millisecond pulsars in clusters and continued modeling of dynamical formation channels; no single definitive answer exists.

original_question: Let N be a smooth convex curve in R^2, and consider the Minkowski billiard in the unit ball of the norm N, defined by the generating function L(s0, s1) = N(gamma(s1) - gamma(s0)) with gamma parameterized by N-arc length. If this Minkowski billiard is totally integrable, must the norm N be Euclidean?
self_contained_problem:
Let $N:\mathbb{R}^2\to[0,\infty)$ be a (not necessarily symmetric) Minkowski norm whose unit ball $K=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^2:N(x)\le 1\}$ is a smooth strictly convex body, and let $\gamma:\mathbb{R}/L\mathbb{Z}\to\partial K$ be a smooth parametrization of $\partial K$ by $N$-arc length, i.e. $N(\dot\gamma(s))=1$ for all $s$.

Define the Minkowski billiard map inside $K$ as the twist map associated with the discrete variational principle
$$\mathcal{L}(\{s_n\})=\sum_n L(s_n,s_{n+1}),\qquad L(s_0,s_1)=N(\gamma(s_1)-\gamma(s_0)),$$
so that orbits are sequences $(s_n)$ critical for $\mathcal{L}$.

The billiard is said to be totally integrable if the phase space (an open annulus) is foliated by invariant curves on which the billiard map is conjugate to a rotation, except for the boundary fixed points.

Question: If the Minkowski billiard in the unit ball of $N$ is totally integrable in this sense, must $N$ be a Euclidean norm (i.e., must $K$ be an ellipse centered at some point)?

original_question: Consider the elliptic equation Delta u = -V'_u(u, x1, ..., xn), where V is 1-periodic in u, x1, ..., xn. Suppose that for every rotation vector alpha in R^n there exists a foliation of T^(n+1) by graphs of minimal solutions of slope alpha. Does it follow that V does not depend on u?
self_contained_problem:
Let $n\ge 1$ and let $V:\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$, $(u,x_1,\dots,x_n)\mapsto V(u,x_1,\dots,x_n)$, be a smooth function that is $1$-periodic in each of its $n+1$ arguments. Consider the elliptic Euler–Lagrange equation
$$\Delta u(x) \;=\; -\,\partial_u V\bigl(u(x),x_1,\dots,x_n\bigr), \qquad x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n,$$
associated to the variational integrand $\tfrac12|\nabla u|^2 - V(u,x_1,\dots,x_n)$. A function $u:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ is called a minimal solution if it is a smooth solution of the equation and minimizes the action on every compact set among compactly supported variations. Such a $u$ is said to have rotation vector (slope) $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^n$ if $u(x)-\alpha\cdot x$ is bounded on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Identify $\mathbb{T}^{n+1}=\mathbb{R}^{n+1}/\mathbb{Z}^{n+1}$ in coordinates $(u,x_1,\dots,x_n)$.

Assume that for every rotation vector $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^n$ there exists a foliation of $\mathbb{T}^{n+1}$ whose leaves are the graphs (projected to $\mathbb{T}^{n+1}$) of minimal solutions of slope $\alpha$.

Question: Does it follow that $V$ is independent of $u$, i.e. $\partial_u V\equiv 0$?
status_search_result: A web search located the foundational works of Moser and Bangert on minimal foliations on tori and follow-up developments (Rabinowitz–Stredulinsky, de la Llave and others) and an example of nonexistence of minimal foliations, but no source was found that explicitly resolves the rigidity question of whether existence of a minimal foliation for every rotation vector forces the potential to be independent of $u$. The status appears unresolved in the literature accessible by search.

original_question: If N is a closed hyperbolic surface and Omega_i are embedded simply connected billiard tables in N, does there exist a sequence Omega_i for which the length of the shortest closed billiard trajectory Omega_i-sys tends to infinity as i tends to infinity?
self_contained_problem:
Let $N$ be a closed hyperbolic surface, i.e., a closed orientable Riemannian 2-manifold of constant curvature $-1$. By an embedded billiard table in $N$ we mean a compact, embedded, simply connected smooth domain $\Omega \subset N$ with smooth boundary $\partial\Omega$. A closed billiard trajectory in $\Omega$ is a piecewise geodesic curve in $\Omega$ whose interior segments are geodesic arcs in $N$ and which reflects elastically (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection) at each boundary impact, returning to its starting point and direction after finitely many reflections. Denote by $\Omega\text{-sys}$ the infimum of the lengths of all closed billiard trajectories in $\Omega$ (the billiard systole).

Question: Does there exist a sequence $\{\Omega_i\}_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ of embedded simply connected billiard tables in $N$ such that 
$$\Omega_i\text{-sys} \longrightarrow \infty \quad \text{as } i \to \infty?$$
status_search_result: No published resolution was found. The question is posed as an open problem in the context of quantitative symplectic geometry and billiards, and a positive answer would reportedly yield novel examples in the field. Available literature on systoles of hyperbolic surfaces and on billiards in hyperbolic settings does not appear to settle this specific question.

original_question: Does the quadratic lower bound lim inf_{T -> +infinity} log P(T) / log T >= 2 hold for every Hamiltonian diffeomorphism on a standard symplectic torus? More generally, does it hold on every aspherical closed symplectic manifold?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,\omega)$ be a closed symplectically aspherical symplectic manifold; that is, $\omega|_{\pi_2(M)}=0$ and $c_1(TM)|_{\pi_2(M)}=0$. For a Hamiltonian diffeomorphism $\varphi\colon M\to M$, let $P(T)$ denote the number of (geometrically distinct) periodic points of $\varphi$ of period at most $T$, i.e. the number of distinct fixed points of the iterates $\varphi^k$ for $1\le k\le T$, counted as orbits.

(a) Is it true that for every Hamiltonian diffeomorphism $\varphi$ of the standard symplectic torus $(\mathbb{T}^{2n},\omega_0)$ one has
$$\liminf_{T\to+\infty}\frac{\log P(T)}{\log T}\ge 2\,?$$

(b) More generally, does the same quadratic lower bound hold for every Hamiltonian diffeomorphism of every closed symplectically aspherical symplectic manifold?
status_search_result: The Conley conjecture (existence of infinitely many periodic points) is established for symplectically aspherical closed manifolds, and generic lower bounds of order k/log k on the number of periodic orbits are known. However, a uniform quadratic lower bound liminf log P(T)/log T ≥ 2 for every Hamiltonian diffeomorphism on the standard torus, or on arbitrary aspherical closed symplectic manifolds, does not appear to be established in the literature, and the question is posed as an open problem.

original_question: Construct a continuous theory for particles with positive and negative mass, or equivalently for billiards in pseudo-Euclidean metrics, and determine whether the resulting Euler-like equations for a fluid of negative density exhibit interesting phenomena.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a system of point particles in $\mathbb{R}^n$ in which each particle is assigned a mass $m_i \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$ that may be positive or negative, with pairwise elastic interactions governed by conservation of momentum $\sum_i m_i v_i$ and kinetic energy $\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_i m_i \|v_i\|^2$. Equivalently, regard such a system as a billiard in a pseudo-Euclidean space whose metric is the indefinite quadratic form $Q(v)=\sum_i m_i\|v_i\|^2$ on the configuration space, with reflections at the walls $\{x_i=x_j\}$ governed by $Q$.

(a) Develop a continuum (hydrodynamic) limit of this discrete system: derive Euler-type equations governing a compressible fluid whose density field $\rho:\mathbb{R}^n\times \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is allowed to take negative values, together with a velocity field $u:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^n$ and pressure $p$, in such a way that the equations reduce, in the discrete (atomic) limit, to the elastic dynamics of mixed positive- and negative-mass particles described above.

(b) Analyze the resulting "negative-density Euler equations." In particular, determine whether they exhibit qualitatively new phenomena absent in the classical (positive-density) Euler equations — for example, instabilities at the zero-density interface $\{\rho=0\}$, runaway/self-acceleration solutions, formation of singularities, well-posedness or ill-posedness of the Cauchy problem, conserved quantities arising from the indefinite metric, or analogues of shocks and rarefaction waves with negative density.
status_search_result: No evidence was found of a worked-out continuum theory of fluids of negative density derived from pseudo-Euclidean billiards, nor of a systematic analysis of the corresponding Euler-like equations. The question appears to remain an open research direction.

original_question: Characterize which C^0-Hamiltonian self-maps of a fiber-wise convex domain W in T^*S^n arise as billiard maps of convex billiard tables.
self_contained_problem:
Let $n\geq 1$ and let $S^n$ denote the standard $n$-sphere. Consider the cotangent bundle $T^*S^n$ with its canonical symplectic structure, and let $W\subset T^*S^n$ be a fiber-wise convex domain (i.e., for each $q\in S^n$ the fiber $W\cap T^*_qS^n$ is a convex set containing the origin). A homeomorphism $f:W\to W$ is called a $C^0$-Hamiltonian self-map of $W$ if it is the $C^0$-limit (uniform limit) of time-one maps of compactly supported smooth Hamiltonian isotopies of $W$.

A convex billiard table is a smooth, strictly convex bounded domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ (with smooth boundary $\partial\Omega$). Its associated billiard map $B_\Omega$ acts on the set of unit tangent vectors based on $\partial\Omega$ pointing inward, sending an inward unit vector $(q,v)$ to $(q',v')$ where $q'$ is the next intersection of the trajectory $q+tv$ with $\partial\Omega$ and $v'$ is the reflection of $v$ across $T_{q'}\partial\Omega$. After identification (via the Gauss map and the Legendre/Lagrangian correspondence) the billiard map can be viewed as a $C^0$-Hamiltonian self-map of a fiber-wise convex domain in $T^*S^n$.

Problem: Give an intrinsic characterization of those $C^0$-Hamiltonian self-maps $f:W\to W$ of a fiber-wise convex domain $W\subset T^*S^n$ which arise (under the above identification) as billiard maps of convex billiard tables in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. Resolve this in particular in the case $n=1$.
status_search_result: The problem is stated as open by its proposer, who notes that even the case $n=1$ is open. No published characterization of billiard maps among $C^0$-Hamiltonian self-maps of fiber-wise convex domains in $T^*S^n$ appears to be known.

original_question: Within the class of tiling billiards in periodic tilings, is there a finite list of generic archetypal behaviors? In particular, does a general dichotomy hold in which typical trajectories are either dense in open sets or integrable in the sense of being periodic or linearly escaping?
self_contained_problem:
A tiling billiard is a dynamical system defined as follows. Fix a locally finite tiling $\mathcal{T}$ of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ by polygons (the "tiles"), and assume $\mathcal{T}$ is invariant under a rank-2 lattice of translations (a periodic tiling). A point particle moves along straight segments inside each tile; when it crosses an edge separating two adjacent tiles, its direction is updated by Snell's law of refraction with refraction coefficient $-1$, i.e. the outgoing trajectory is the reflection of the incoming trajectory across the crossed edge (rather than across the normal to that edge). A trajectory is called periodic if it closes up after finitely many edge crossings, drift-periodic if it is invariant under a non-trivial translation of the tiling, linearly escaping if its distance from its starting point grows asymptotically linearly in time without being drift-periodic, and dense in an open set $U \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ if its closure contains $U$.

(a) Does there exist a finite list of "archetypal" behaviors such that, for every periodic tiling $\mathcal{T}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$, the typical (in the sense of Lebesgue-almost-every initial condition in phase space) trajectory of the associated tiling billiard exhibits one of the behaviors on this list?

(b) More specifically, does the following dichotomy hold for every periodic tiling $\mathcal{T}$: for Lebesgue-almost every initial condition, the trajectory is either
  (i) dense in some open subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$, or
  (ii) integrable, in the sense of being periodic or linearly escaping?
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem in surveys of tiling billiards. Recent research (e.g., results on triangle tiling billiards and the Rauzy gasket, the trihexagonal tiling, brick tilings, and deviations for generalized tiling billiards in cyclic polygons) has confirmed the proposed dichotomy in additional specific families of tilings, but no general classification or proof of the dichotomy across all periodic tilings has been established.

original_question: Provide examples of real-world systems from areas such as physics, mechanics, biology, or economics that can be modeled as locally conformal symplectic flows or maps.
self_contained_problem:
A locally conformal symplectic (l.c.s.) manifold is a smooth manifold $M^{2n}$ equipped with a non-degenerate 2-form $\omega$ and a closed 1-form $\eta$ (the Lee form) such that $d\omega = \eta \wedge \omega$. Equivalently, around each point of $M$ there is an open neighborhood $U$ and a smooth function $f_U : U \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $e^{-f_U}\omega$ is a symplectic form on $U$, with $\eta|_U = df_U$. A diffeomorphism $\varphi : M \to M$ is called a locally conformal symplectic map if $\varphi^*\omega = e^{g}\omega$ for some smooth function $g$ on $M$; a vector field $X$ on $M$ generates a locally conformal symplectic flow if its flow consists of such maps. When $\eta \equiv 0$ this recovers ordinary symplectic / Hamiltonian dynamics; when $\eta$ is exact (globally $\eta = df$) one obtains globally conformal symplectic dynamics, which model uniformly dissipative systems. The genuinely locally conformal (non-globally-conformal) case allows non-uniform, spatially dependent dissipation.

Problem. Exhibit concrete examples of real-world dynamical systems—drawn from physics, mechanics, biology, economics, or related applied domains—whose phase-space dynamics is naturally modeled by a locally conformal symplectic flow or by a locally conformal symplectic map on some l.c.s. manifold $(M,\omega,\eta)$ with non-exact Lee form $\eta$. For each example, specify the underlying manifold, the l.c.s. structure $(\omega,\eta)$, the generating vector field or map, and explain why the model genuinely requires the locally conformal (rather than merely conformal or symplectic) framework.
status_search_result: This is an open-ended modeling/discovery problem rather than a precise theorem-style conjecture. The literature on locally conformal symplectic (l.c.s.) dynamics emphasizes the formalism's potential for non-conservative mechanics with spatially dependent dissipation, but explicit, genuinely locally (non-globally) conformal real-world examples remain scarce. No comprehensive resolution is reported as of the search date.

original_question: Assume eta_p_bar = 0 so that eta is pulled back from the base manifold, and assume H is a Tonelli Hamiltonian so that the equations become dot x = partial_p H and dot p = -partial_x H + f p - L(x, dot x) eta_x_bar. What physical interpretation, if any, should be assigned to the term -L(x, dot x) eta_x_bar?
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and let $\pi : T^*M 	o M$ denote the cotangent bundle projection, with canonical coordinates $(x,p)$. Let $H : T^*M 	o \mathbb{R}$ be a Tonelli Hamiltonian (i.e. $H$ is $C^2$, fiberwise strictly convex, and superlinear in $p$), and let $L : TM 	o \mathbb{R}$ be its associated Lagrangian, defined by the Legendre transform
$$L(x,\dot x) = p\cdot \dot x - H(x,p), \qquad \dot x = \partial_p H(x,p).$$
Let $f : T^*M 	o \mathbb{R}$ be a smooth function (a friction/forcing coefficient), and let $\eta$ be a closed $1$-form on $T^*M$. Decompose $\eta =  ar\eta_x \cdot dx +  ar\eta_p \cdot dp$ in canonical coordinates, and assume $ ar\eta_p = 0$, so that $\eta = \pi^* ar\eta$ is the pullback of a closed $1$-form $ ar\eta =  ar\eta_x \cdot dx$ on $M$. Consider the forced Hamiltonian system
$$\dot x = \partial_p H(x,p), \qquad \dot p = -\partial_x H(x,p) + f\,p - L(x,\dot x)\, ar\eta_x.$$
The term $f\,p$ admits the standard physical interpretation of a momentum-dependent dissipation or repulsion. 

Problem: Determine whether the additional forcing term $-L(x,\dot x)\, ar\eta_x$ admits a physical interpretation, and if so identify it.

original_question: Given a closed immersed submanifold M of Euclidean space, estimate from below the number of generalized n-periodic billiard trajectories, meaning inscribed n-gons with vertices on M that have extremal perimeter, in terms of the topology of M and the immersion.
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a closed smooth manifold and let $\iota : M \to \mathbb{R}^d$ be a smooth immersion of $M$ into Euclidean space. For an integer $n \geq 2$, consider ordered $n$-tuples $(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \in M^n$ (with $x_i \neq x_{i+1}$ in a suitable sense) and the perimeter functional
$$P(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \|\iota(x_{i+1}) - \iota(x_i)\|, \qquad x_{n+1} := x_1,$$
where $\|\cdot\|$ is the Euclidean norm. A *generalized $n$-periodic billiard trajectory* on the immersed submanifold $\iota(M)$ is, by definition, a critical point of $P$ on the configuration space of cyclic $n$-tuples on $M$ (modulo the natural cyclic and dihedral symmetries); equivalently, it is an inscribed $n$-gon with vertices on $\iota(M)$ whose perimeter is extremal.

Problem: Find a lower bound, in terms of topological invariants of $M$ (such as its Betti numbers, Lusternik–Schnirelmann category, or cup-length) and invariants of the immersion $\iota$, for the number of distinct generalized $n$-periodic billiard trajectories on $\iota(M)$.
status_search_result: Lower bounds are known in several specialized settings: for prime $r \geq 3$, the number of $r$-periodic Finsler billiard trajectories on a smooth closed hypersurface in $\mathbb{R}^d$ is at least $(r-1)(d-2)+1$ (Harutyunyan–Tabachnikov), and for odd $n \geq 3$ the number of $n$-periodic billiard trajectories inscribed in a smooth closed hypersurface $M^{m-1} \subset \mathbb{R}^m$ is at least $(n-1)(m-1)$ (Farber–Tabachnikov and others). The general problem for arbitrary closed immersed submanifolds of arbitrary codimension, with bounds expressed in terms of the topology of $M$ and the immersion, does not appear to have a complete published answer and remains partially solved.

original_question: Do there exist chaotic symplectic billiards in convex C^1-smooth domains?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a strictly convex bounded domain whose boundary $\partial\Omega$ is of class $C^1$. The symplectic billiard map $T: \partial\Omega \times \partial\Omega \to \partial\Omega \times \partial\Omega$ is defined as follows: a pair $(x, y)$ with $x \neq y$ in $\partial\Omega$ is mapped to $(y, z)$, where $z \in \partial\Omega$ is the unique point (other than $y$) such that the tangent line to $\partial\Omega$ at $y$ is parallel to the chord $xz$. This map preserves the symplectic (area) form $\omega = dx \wedge dy$ on $\partial\Omega \times \partial\Omega$ away from the diagonal.

Question: Does there exist a strictly convex domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ with $C^1$-smooth boundary such that the associated symplectic billiard map $T$ is chaotic, i.e., is ergodic with positive metric entropy (equivalently, has nonzero Lyapunov exponents almost everywhere) with respect to its invariant measure?

A natural candidate is the stadium domain (the convex hull of two disjoint disks of equal radius), for which numerical evidence suggests chaotic behavior of the symplectic billiard.

original_question: In a domain with smooth boundary in Euclidean space, fix a generic interior point P and consider the time-t front consisting of light rays emitted from P in all directions, reflected specularly at the boundary, and evolved for time t. Does this time-t front become dense as t tends to infinity?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ (with $n \geq 2$) be a bounded domain with smooth boundary $\partial\Omega$. Fix a point $P$ in the interior of $\Omega$, chosen generically. Consider the billiard flow inside $\Omega$: a "photon" emitted from $P$ in some unit direction $v \in S^{n-1}$ travels along a straight line at unit speed, and upon hitting $\partial\Omega$ undergoes specular (optical) reflection (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection); thereafter it continues, reflecting again at every subsequent boundary encounter. For each $t > 0$, define the time-$t$ wave front $F_t(P) \subset \overline{\Omega}$ as the set of all positions reached at time exactly $t$ by such trajectories, taken over all initial unit directions $v \in S^{n-1}$.

Question: Does $F_t(P)$ become dense in $\overline{\Omega}$ as $t \to \infty$? That is, is it true that for every nonempty open set $U \subset \Omega$ there exists $T > 0$ such that $F_t(P) \cap U \neq \emptyset$ for all $t \geq T$ (equivalently, $\bigcup_{t \geq T} F_t(P)$ is dense, or the appropriate density formulation)?
status_search_result: Recent work (2025) establishes density of wave fronts in special cases: on the flat torus, square billiards, the flat Klein bottle, and the cube surface. The general case for arbitrary smooth bounded Euclidean domains does not appear to be resolved; the problem remains open in that generality, with affirmative results known only in particular geometries.

original_question: When a smooth convex closed curve is approximated by n-gons and the quality of approximation is measured by the area of the symmetric difference, is the resulting function of n related to some billiard-like dynamical system?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\gamma$ be a smooth strictly convex closed curve in the plane (an oval), bounding a convex region $K$. For each integer $n \geq 3$, define
$$f(n) = \min_{P} \operatorname{area}(K \triangle P),$$
where the minimum is taken over all convex $n$-gons $P$ (one may consider separately the inscribed case $P \subset K$, the circumscribed case $K \subset P$, or the unrestricted case), and $K \triangle P = (K \setminus P) \cup (P \setminus K)$ denotes the symmetric difference.

paper_title: Anomalous transport in the Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou model: a review and open problems
original_question: In the symmetric Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou-β chain, what is the correct universality class governing anomalous heat transport and the associated interface dynamics? More specifically, how should one characterize the large-scale scaling behavior of this model when the observed dynamics disagrees with both Kardar-Parisi-Zhang scaling and the Edwards-Wilkinson analogy predicted by fluctuating hydrodynamics, yet numerical evidence still indicates a transport exponent consistent with kinetic-theory predictions?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the symmetric Fermi–Pasta–Ulam–Tsingou-β (FPUT-β) chain: a one-dimensional lattice of N classical particles with positions q_i and momenta p_i (i = 1, …, N), governed by the Hamiltonian
  H = Σ_i [ p_i^2 / 2 + (1/2)(q_{i+1} − q_i)^2 + (β/4)(q_{i+1} − q_i)^4 ],
with β > 0 and (for definiteness) periodic boundary conditions. Because the on-site potential is even in the relative displacement, the only nonlinearity is quartic (no cubic asymmetry).

It is well documented numerically that the equilibrium energy current correlations exhibit anomalous (super-diffusive) decay, so that the finite-size thermal conductivity κ(N) diverges as κ(N) ∼ N^{α} with an exponent α consistent with the kinetic-theory / mode-coupling prediction (often quoted as α = 2/5 for the symmetric case). One may also study the associated stochastic interface obtained by integrating the local energy fluctuations in space, and ask which kinetic roughening universality class (characterized by growth, roughness, and dynamical exponents) this interface belongs to.

Empirically, the large-scale fluctuations of this interface match neither the Kardar–Parisi–Zhang (KPZ) class (with dynamical exponent z = 3/2 and the standard Tracy–Widom / Baik–Rains height statistics) nor the linear Edwards–Wilkinson (EW) class (with z = 2 and Gaussian height fluctuations) predicted by nonlinear fluctuating hydrodynamics for momentum-conserving anharmonic chains, even though the heat-transport exponent agrees with mode-coupling / kinetic-theory predictions.

Problem. Identify and rigorously characterize the universality class governing the large-scale scaling behavior of heat transport and the associated interface dynamics in the symmetric FPUT-β chain. In particular:
(a) Determine the correct dynamical, growth, and roughness exponents of the energy-fluctuation interface.
(b) Provide the limiting scaling functions (analogous to the KPZ or EW scaling functions) describing space–time correlations of the energy current and the height statistics of the interface.
(c) Reconcile this universality class with the observed transport exponent α (compatible with kinetic theory) while explaining why both KPZ and EW predictions fail.
category_tag: Anomalous heat transport in anharmonic chains
status_search_result: Recent reviews and numerical studies on anomalous heat transport in 1D Hamiltonian chains continue to report that the symmetric FPUT-β model does not match KPZ (z = 3/2) nor Edwards–Wilkinson (z = 2) predictions, and is variously associated with a Lévy-type heat mode and an exponent δ ≈ 2/5, while the asymmetric FPUT-αβ model belongs to the KPZ class. No identification of a definitive universality class for the symmetric FPUT-β interface dynamics has been established; the question remains open.

paper_title: Anomalous transport in the Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou model: a review and open problems
original_question: When conservative stochastic momentum-exchange noise is added to a nonlinear Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou chain, why can the observed finite-size scaling appear to move toward different effective exponents even though the asymptotic universality class is argued to remain unchanged? Equivalently, what mechanism lets conservative noise alter convergence rates and effective thermal resistance without changing the long-distance hydrodynamic universality class?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a one-dimensional anharmonic oscillator chain of N sites with Hamiltonian
  H = Σ_i [ p_i^2/(2m) + V(q_{i+1} - q_i) ],
where V is a nonlinear nearest-neighbor interaction potential (for instance the Fermi–Pasta–Ulam–Tsingou potential V(r) = (1/2)r^2 + (α/3)r^3 + (β/4)r^4, with α ≥ 0 and β > 0). The chain is coupled at its two ends to Langevin heat baths at temperatures T_L and T_R, and after a long time it reaches a nonequilibrium stationary state with a heat current J(N) and an effective finite-size thermal conductivity
  κ(N) = J(N) N / (T_L − T_R).
For nonintegrable potentials, κ(N) is expected to diverge as κ(N) ∼ N^δ for large N, with the exponent δ determined by a hydrodynamic universality class (δ = 1/3 for asymmetric potentials in the KPZ class, δ = 1/2 for symmetric potentials).

Now superimpose on the deterministic Hamiltonian dynamics a "conservative" stochastic noise that, at independent random times, exchanges the momenta of randomly chosen neighboring particles (or, more generally, applies random rotations to neighboring momentum pairs). This noise preserves total momentum and total kinetic energy at every event, and in the limit where it dominates one obtains a stochastic system whose hydrodynamic universality class for energy transport is rigorously known and is argued to coincide with that of the purely deterministic chain.

Problem. Provide a quantitative explanation of the following empirical observation. When the conservative momentum-exchange noise is added to the FPUT chain, the apparent finite-size exponent δ_eff(N) extracted from κ(N) ∼ N^{δ_eff(N)} on accessible system sizes can shift toward values different from (and in particular larger than) the deterministic one, even though the asymptotic universality class is unchanged. Specifically:

(a) Identify the mechanism by which adding a conservative noise — which on physical grounds should reduce the conductivity by introducing additional momentum scrambling — instead accelerates the apparent convergence of κ(N) and modifies its effective growth exponent at finite N.

(b) Derive (or characterize) how the crossover length N* separating the preasymptotic regime from the true asymptotic anomalous regime depends on the noise rate γ, and explain why N* can decrease with γ even when the long-wavelength hydrodynamic exponent δ does not depend on γ.

(c) Reconcile (a) and (b) with the statement that the conservative noise leaves the long-distance hydrodynamic universality class invariant.
status_search_result: The question of why a conservative momentum-exchange noise accelerates finite-size scaling and shifts the apparent conductivity exponent in FPUT chains, while not changing the asymptotic hydrodynamic universality class, is highlighted as an unresolved issue in the recent review on anomalous transport in FPUT and remains discussed in the literature without a generally accepted quantitative explanation. Related work has clarified universality classes (KPZ δ=1/3 vs. symmetric δ=1/2) and the role of finite-size crossovers, but no source verified here provides a definitive resolution of the mechanism.

paper_title: Anomalous transport in the Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou model: a review and open problems
original_question: What qualitatively new nonequilibrium heat-transport phenomena arise in Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou dynamics when the model is extended to include long-range interactions whose coupling decays as an inverse power of distance, or when disorder and nonlinearity act together in the same system?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a one-dimensional chain of N classical particles with displacements q_i and momenta p_i (i = 1, ..., N) governed by the Hamiltonian

  H = Σ_i p_i^2/(2 m_i) + (1/2) Σ_{i ≠ j} K_{ij} V(q_i - q_j) + Σ_i U(q_i),

where V is a nonlinear pair potential of Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou type, e.g. V(x) = x^2/2 + α x^3/3 + β x^4/4. Consider two extensions of the standard nearest-neighbor, homogeneous case:

(a) Long-range couplings: K_{ij} = |i - j|^{-s} for some exponent s > 0 (with appropriate Kac-type rescaling for s ≤ 1), and otherwise homogeneous masses m_i = m, no on-site potential (U = 0).

(b) Disorder plus nonlinearity: nearest-neighbor couplings only, but with random masses m_i (or random on-site potentials U(q_i) = ε_i q_i^2/2) drawn i.i.d. from a non-degenerate distribution, together with α ≠ 0 or β ≠ 0.

Place the chain in a non-equilibrium steady state by coupling the boundary particles to Langevin thermostats at unequal temperatures T_L and T_R, and let J_N denote the time-averaged heat current and κ(N) = J_N N/(T_L - T_R) the finite-size thermal conductivity.

Determine the qualitatively new nonequilibrium heat-transport phenomena that arise in cases (a) and (b) compared with the clean, short-range FPUT chain. Specifically:

1. In case (a), characterize the asymptotic scaling κ(N) ~ N^δ as a function of the decay exponent s, identify the value(s) of s at which transitions between normal (δ = 0), anomalous (0 < δ < 1), and ballistic (δ = 1) transport occur, and describe the structure of the temperature profile and the nonequilibrium current correlations.

2. In case (b), determine whether the combination of disorder and nonlinearity produces normal Fourier conduction (κ(N) tending to a finite limit) for arbitrarily small nonlinearity, or whether anomalous/insulating behavior persists; identify the dependence of κ(N) on the nonlinearity strength and on temperature, and clarify the role of nonlinearity in destroying Anderson localization for energy transport.
category_tag: Anomalous heat transport in FPUT chains
status_search_result: Recent reviews on anomalous heat transport in low-dimensional systems (2020-2024) discuss long-range FPUT and disorder+nonlinearity as active research directions with no complete picture. Partial results exist (e.g., for long-range harmonic chains with conservative noise, and numerical evidence of size-dependent conductivity in long-range FPUT), but a full classification of regimes and a rigorous understanding of the disorder-nonlinearity interplay for heat transport remain open.

paper_title: A short tour of operator learning theory: Convergence rates, statistical limits, and open questions
original_question: For empirical risk minimization in operator learning under statistical noise, Theorem 1 gives a nonparametric rate that is at best n^{-1/2}. Is this rate merely an artifact of the proof technique used in the statistical-learning analysis, or does it reflect a genuine minimax barrier for the noisy operator-learning problem?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$ be separable Hilbert spaces, and let $\mathcal{F}$ be a class of (e.g., Lipschitz or higher-regularity) operators $F:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$. Suppose we observe i.i.d. noisy input–output pairs
$$ (X_i, Y_i)_{i=1}^n, \qquad Y_i = F^\star(X_i) + \xi_i, $$
where $F^\star\in\mathcal{F}$ is the unknown target operator, $X_i$ is drawn from some probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal{X}$, and $\xi_i$ is centered noise on $\mathcal{Y}$ (e.g., Gaussian with bounded covariance) independent of $X_i$. For an estimator $\widehat{F}_n$ depending only on the data, define the squared $L^2(\mu)$-risk
$$ \mathcal{R}(\widehat{F}_n, F^\star) = \mathbb{E}\,\|\widehat{F}_n - F^\star\|_{L^2(\mu;\mathcal{Y})}^2. $$
Standard statistical-learning analyses of empirical risk minimization over $\mathcal{F}$ produce upper bounds on $\sup_{F^\star\in\mathcal{F}} \mathcal{R}(\widehat{F}_n, F^\star)$ that decay no faster than $n^{-1/2}$, even when the complexity of $\mathcal{F}$ would otherwise allow a faster nonparametric rate in the noiseless setting.

Question: Determine whether the rate $n^{-1/2}$ is a genuine minimax barrier for noisy operator learning, i.e., whether
$$ \inf_{\widehat{F}_n}\;\sup_{F^\star\in\mathcal{F}}\;\mathcal{R}(\widehat{F}_n, F^\star) \;\gtrsim\; n^{-1/2} $$
holds for natural infinite-dimensional regularity classes $\mathcal{F}$, or whether this $n^{-1/2}$ ceiling is merely an artifact of the proof technique used in the statistical-learning upper-bound analysis and can be improved by a different estimator or analysis.
status_search_result: Recent work (arXiv:2512.17805, "Towards Sharp Minimax Risk Bounds for Operator Learning") makes substantial progress: it establishes a curse of sample complexity for Lipschitz/Hölder operator classes, showing that for generic finite-regularity operator classes the minimax risk cannot decay at algebraic rates, while for more restrictive holomorphic classes ERM achieves rates faster than $n^{-1/2}$ such as $n^{-(1/p - 1/2)}$. This indicates that the $n^{-1/2}$ wall is not universal but depends sharply on the class; a complete resolution of whether $n^{-1/2}$ is a genuine minimax floor in all natural noisy settings has not been fully settled.

paper_title: A short tour of operator learning theory: Convergence rates, statistical limits, and open questions
original_question: Which classes of operators arising in scientific applications are both practically relevant and mathematically structured enough to admit algebraic minimax sample-complexity rates for operator learning?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$ be separable Hilbert spaces (for instance, $L^2$ spaces over compact domains in $\mathbb{R}^d$), and let $\mathcal{F}$ be a class of (possibly nonlinear) operators $F:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$. Given $n$ i.i.d. input–output pairs $(X_i, Y_i)_{i=1}^n$ where $X_i$ is drawn from a probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal{X}$ and $Y_i = F^\star(X_i) + \varepsilon_i$ for some unknown $F^\star\in\mathcal{F}$ and centered noise $\varepsilon_i$, define the minimax risk
$$ R_n(\mathcal{F}) \;=\; \inf_{\widehat{F}_n}\;\sup_{F^\star\in\mathcal{F}}\; \mathbb{E}\,\bigl\|\widehat{F}_n - F^\star\bigr\|_{L^2(\mu;\mathcal{Y})}^2, $$
where the infimum is over all measurable estimators $\widehat{F}_n$ based on the sample.

A class $\mathcal{F}$ is said to admit an algebraic minimax sample-complexity rate if there exist constants $c,C>0$ and an exponent $\alpha>0$ such that
$$ c\, n^{-\alpha} \;\le\; R_n(\mathcal{F}) \;\le\; C\, n^{-\alpha} \qquad \text{for all sufficiently large } n. $$
Many natural function-space classes (e.g.\ general Lipschitz operators between infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces) suffer from infinite-dimensional curse-of-dimensionality phenomena and only admit logarithmic rates in $n$.

Problem. Identify classes $\mathcal{F}$ of operators arising in scientific applications—such as solution operators of parametric partial differential equations, Hamiltonian flow maps, homogenization operators, or parameter-to-observable maps in inverse problems—that are
(i) practically relevant to scientific computing, and
(ii) sufficiently structured (through smoothness, low effective dimension, holomorphic parameter dependence, multiscale structure, etc.) that the minimax risk $R_n(\mathcal{F})$ obeys an algebraic decay $n^{-\alpha}$ with explicit exponent $\alpha>0$ independent of any ambient infinite dimension.

Provide such a class, together with matching upper and lower bounds establishing the algebraic rate.
status_search_result: This is posed as an open research direction in operator learning theory. Recent works establish algebraic minimax rates for specific structured classes (e.g., linear/Hilbert–Schmidt operators, holomorphic operators with summable Taylor coefficients, Lipschitz operators with low-dimensional latent structure), but a comprehensive identification of practically relevant scientific-computing operator classes admitting algebraic rates remains an active and open research program.

paper_title: A short tour of operator learning theory: Convergence rates, statistical limits, and open questions
original_question: Is empirical risk minimization minimax-optimal, in the sense of the noiseless sampling-width formulation, for operator classes beyond holomorphic ones? Examples singled out by the paper include infinitely Fréchet-differentiable operator classes and classes generated by specific parametric PDE problems.
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be (real or complex) separable Banach spaces and let $K \subset X$ be a compact subset (for example, the unit ball of a compactly embedded subspace). Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a class of continuous operators $F : K \to Y$. Given $n \in \mathbb{N}$ "sampling points" $x_1,\dots,x_n \in K$ chosen by the learner (adaptively or non-adaptively), the learner observes the noiseless data $\{(x_i, F(x_i))\}_{i=1}^n$ and produces an estimator $\widehat{F}_n : K \to Y$. Define the sampling (worst-case) width
$$ s_n(\mathcal{F}) \;=\; \inf_{\widehat{F}_n}\; \sup_{F\in\mathcal{F}}\; \sup_{x\in K}\, \|F(x)-\widehat{F}_n(x)\|_Y, $$
where the infimum runs over all measurable reconstruction maps based on $n$ point evaluations. An algorithm is called minimax-optimal in this noiseless sampling-width formulation if the rate of its worst-case error over $\mathcal{F}$ matches $s_n(\mathcal{F})$ as $n\to\infty$ up to constants (or up to logarithmic factors).

Empirical risk minimization (ERM) refers to estimators of the form
$$ \widehat{F}_n \;\in\; \arg\min_{G\in\mathcal{H}_n}\; \sum_{i=1}^n \|G(x_i)-F(x_i)\|_Y^2, $$
where $\{\mathcal{H}_n\}$ is a suitable sequence of hypothesis classes (e.g., neural-network or polynomial surrogate model classes) chosen to approximate $\mathcal{F}$.

It is known that for certain classes of holomorphic operators on infinite-dimensional Banach spaces, ERM-based reconstructions achieve the minimax sampling-width rate. The question is:

Determine whether ERM is minimax-optimal, in the sense of the sampling width $s_n(\mathcal{F})$ above, for operator classes $\mathcal{F}$ beyond holomorphic ones. In particular, settle this for:

(i) classes of infinitely Fréchet-differentiable ($C^\infty$) operators $F : K \to Y$ with prescribed bounds on all Fréchet derivatives;

(ii) classes of solution operators arising from specific parametric PDE problems, namely operators $F$ mapping a coefficient/parameter $a \in K$ to the solution $u(a) \in Y$ of a parametric elliptic, parabolic, or hyperbolic PDE under standard well-posedness assumptions.

In each case, identify the minimax sampling-width rate and prove matching upper bounds achieved (or not achieved) by ERM with an appropriate hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}_n$.
status_search_result: This is posed as an explicit open question in the operator learning theory literature concerning the minimax optimality of ERM beyond holomorphic operator classes. No published resolution for general $C^\infty$ operator classes or for general parametric-PDE solution operator classes was found; results currently exist for specific holomorphic and (Gevrey/analytic) parametric-PDE settings, leaving the broader question open.

Other sets of interest could include C∞ operators or those arising from specific parametric PDE problems.", "claim": "The question is explicitly listed as an open problem in operator learning theory."}]

paper_title: A short tour of operator learning theory: Convergence rates, statistical limits, and open questions
original_question: Consider the class K_FNO^α of operators that can be approximated efficiently at rate α by Fourier neural operators, and let β★ denote the optimal algebraic minimax-rate exponent for learning that class in L^2_ϱ. The paper proves bounds showing β★ is at most 1/2 and approaches 1/2 as α grows. Is the exponent 1/2 actually sharp for these FNO-based operator classes, or can the true optimal exponent exceed the currently known upper-bound heuristic?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $\varrho$ be a Borel probability measure on a separable Hilbert space $\mathcal{X}$ and let $\mathcal{Y}$ be a separable Hilbert space. Consider learning an unknown operator $G:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$ from $n$ i.i.d. noisy input–output samples $(x_i,y_i)$, $x_i\sim\varrho$, $y_i=G(x_i)+\eta_i$, with the loss measured in $L^2_\varrho(\mathcal{X};\mathcal{Y})$.

For a parameter $\alpha>0$, define the Fourier-neural-operator approximation class $\mathcal{K}^\alpha_{\mathrm{FNO}}$ as the set of operators $G$ such that there exists a sequence $\{G_M\}_{M\in\mathbb{N}}$ of Fourier neural operators of complexity (number of parameters / Fourier modes) at most $M$ with
$$\|G-G_M\|_{L^2_\varrho}\;\le\; C\, M^{-\alpha}.$$

For an estimator $\widehat G_n$ based on $n$ samples, define the minimax risk
$$R_n(\alpha)\;=\;\inf_{\widehat G_n}\sup_{G\in\mathcal{K}^\alpha_{\mathrm{FNO}}}\mathbb{E}\,\|\widehat G_n-G\|^2_{L^2_\varrho},$$
and let the optimal algebraic minimax-rate exponent be
$$\beta^\star(\alpha)\;=\;\sup\{\beta\ge 0:\, R_n(\alpha)=O(n^{-\beta})\}.$$

It is known that $\beta^\star(\alpha)\le 1/2$ for all $\alpha$, and that $\beta^\star(\alpha)\to 1/2$ as $\alpha\to\infty$, while existing lower bounds (proved via empirical risk minimization arguments) leave a gap at finite $\alpha$.

Question. Determine whether the upper bound $\beta^\star(\alpha)=1/2$ is sharp for finite $\alpha>0$. Equivalently, does there exist a finite $\alpha$ and an estimator achieving an algebraic rate exponent strictly larger than the currently established lower-bound exponent, possibly attaining $1/2$, or can one prove a strict separation $\beta^\star(\alpha)<1/2$ for finite $\alpha$?
status_search_result: Recent work on sharp minimax risk bounds for operator learning (e.g., arXiv:2512.17805, Dec 2025) develops information-theoretic lower bounds and upper bounds for Lipschitz operator classes between Hilbert spaces, but does not resolve whether the exponent 1/2 is sharp for finite-α FNO approximation classes. No source found that closes the gap between the upper and lower bounds for $\beta^\star(\alpha)$ at finite $\alpha$, so the question appears to remain open.

paper_title: A note on the convergence of RED algorithms under minimal hypotheses and open questions
original_question: Consider the inverse problem y = A x̂ + e, where x̂ belongs to a low-dimensional model set Σ, A is a linear measurement map, and e is noise. Let P_Σ be a generalized projection onto Σ with the restricted β-Lipschitz property: for every z, every x in Σ, and every u in P_Σ(z), ||u − x||₂ ≤ β ||z − x||₂. The modified RED iteration is z_n = (1 − λ)x_n + λP_Σ(x_n), followed by x_{n+1} = z_n − μAᵀ(Az_n − y). A convergence bound is known when Σ is proximinal and P_Σ is close to the orthogonal projection P_Σ^⊥, specifically ||P_Σ − P_Σ^⊥||₂ ≤ η. Can one prove convergence of this modified RED iteration to a stable solution when P_Σ is only a generic restricted-Lipschitz projection, without assuming orthogonality or approximate orthogonality of the projection, as in the generalized projected-gradient-descent setting?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $A:\mathbb{R}^N\to\mathbb{R}^M$ be a linear measurement operator and consider the inverse problem
$$y = A\hat x + e, \qquad \hat x \in \Sigma \subset \mathbb{R}^N,$$
where $\Sigma$ is a (low-dimensional) proximinal model set and $e\in\mathbb{R}^M$ is noise.

Generalized projection. A (possibly set-valued) map $P_\Sigma:\mathbb{R}^N\rightrightarrows \Sigma$ is called a generalized projection onto $\Sigma$. It is said to have the restricted $\beta$-Lipschitz property with respect to $\Sigma$ if
$$\forall z\in\mathbb{R}^N,\ \forall x\in\Sigma,\ \forall u\in P_\Sigma(z): \quad \|u-x\|_2 \le \beta \,\|z-x\|_2.$$
Let $P_\Sigma^{\perp}$ denote an orthogonal projection onto $\Sigma$ (a selection minimizing $\|z-\cdot\|_2$ over $\Sigma$).

Modified RED iteration. For step sizes $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\mu>0$, and an initial point $x_0\in\mathbb{R}^N$, define
$$z_n = (1-\lambda)x_n + \lambda P_\Sigma(x_n), \qquad x_{n+1} = z_n - \mu A^\top(Az_n - y).$$

Known result. Let $\beta = \beta_\Sigma(P_\Sigma)$ be the restricted Lipschitz constant and let $\delta=\delta_\Sigma(\mu A^\top A)$ be a restricted contraction constant of $I-\mu A^\top A$ on $\Sigma$. Assume $\|P_\Sigma - P_\Sigma^{\perp}\|_2 \le \eta$ in the sense that any selection of $P_\Sigma$ stays within distance $\eta$ of $P_\Sigma^{\perp}$. If
$$r := \delta\beta + |1-\lambda|\,\|I-\mu A^\top A\|_{op} < 1,$$
then
$$\|x_n-\hat x\|_2 \le r^n \|x_0-\hat x\|_2 + \frac{1}{1-r}\bigl(|1-\lambda|\,\|I-\mu A^\top A\|_{op}\,\eta + \mu\,\|A^\top e\|_2\bigr).$$

Question. Drop the closeness-to-orthogonality assumption $\|P_\Sigma - P_\Sigma^\perp\|_2 \le \eta$. Does the modified RED iteration above still converge to a stable solution of the inverse problem under only the assumption that $P_\Sigma$ is a generic restricted-$\beta$-Lipschitz generalized projection onto the proximinal set $\Sigma$ (i.e., in the same generality as the generalized projected-gradient-descent setting), and if so, under what conditions on $\lambda,\mu,\beta,A,\Sigma$ can one obtain a quantitative error bound analogous to the one above but without the $\eta$ term?
status_search_result: The question is explicitly posed as an open problem about extending the convergence analysis of the modified RED iteration to generic restricted-Lipschitz generalized projections, parallel to known results for generalized projected gradient descent. Web searches did not surface a published resolution of this specific question.

paper_title: A note on the convergence of RED algorithms under minimal hypotheses and open questions
context_brief: When RED is theoretically preferable to GPGD
original_question: For inverse problems y = A x̂ + e with x̂ in a low-dimensional model set Σ, generalized projected gradient descent (GPGD) uses x_{n+1} = P_Σ(x_n) − μAᵀ(AP_Σ(x_n) − y) and can stably recover x̂ with a linear rate under restricted-isometry and restricted-Lipschitz hypotheses. Modified RED reduces to GPGD when λ = 1, while other admissible λ values are described as giving slower convergence and less identifiability; the classical RED convergence route also appears to require restrictive conditions. Under what theoretical setup would the use of a classical or modified RED scheme be warranted instead of GPGD, given that RED has worse convergence-rate and identifiability properties in the analyzed setting?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let A : R^N → R^m be a linear measurement operator and consider the inverse problem y = A x̂ + e, where x̂ belongs to a (possibly nonconvex) low-dimensional model set Σ ⊂ R^N and e ∈ R^m is a noise vector. Let P_Σ : R^N → Σ denote a (not necessarily orthogonal) projection onto Σ, i.e., P_Σ(x) ∈ argmin_{z∈Σ} ‖x − z‖.

Generalized projected gradient descent (GPGD) for this problem is defined by the iteration
  x_{n+1} = P_Σ(x_n) − μ A^T(A P_Σ(x_n) − y),
where μ > 0 is a step size. Assume A satisfies a restricted isometry property on Σ − Σ and that P_Σ satisfies a restricted Lipschitz property, so that under these hypotheses the GPGD iterates converge linearly to a neighborhood of x̂ whose radius is controlled by ‖e‖ (stable recovery with linear rate).

Define a denoiser f : R^N → R^N by f(x) = P_Σ(x). The classical Regularization by Denoising (RED) iteration with parameter λ ≥ 0 is
  x_{n+1} = x_n − μ [ A^T(A x_n − y) + λ (x_n − f(x_n)) ],
and a modified RED iteration (in which the data-fidelity gradient is evaluated at the denoised point) is
  x_{n+1} = x_n − μ [ A^T(A f(x_n) − y) + λ (x_n − f(x_n)) ].
When λ = 1, modified RED coincides with GPGD; admissible values λ ≠ 1 yield strictly slower linear convergence rates and weaker identifiability guarantees in this analysis, and analogous convergence results for classical RED require still more restrictive hypotheses.

Problem. Identify a theoretical regime — i.e., a class of measurement operators A, model sets Σ, denoisers f, and parameters λ — in which using either the classical RED iteration or the modified RED iteration with some λ ≠ 1 is provably preferable to running GPGD (λ = 1). More precisely, exhibit hypotheses under which a (classical or modified) RED scheme attains a strictly better convergence rate, a strictly better stability/identifiability constant, or recovery guarantees that GPGD provably cannot achieve; or alternatively prove that no such regime exists, so that GPGD always dominates RED under the present hypotheses.
status_search_result: The question is explicitly posed as an open problem at the end of the source note, asking for a theoretical justification of RED-type schemes over GPGD. No published resolution was located; the problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Multiparty Quantum Key Agreement: Architectures, State-of-the-art, and Open Problems
original_question: Can a circle, ring, tree, star, or other O(N)-channel topology for multiparty quantum key agreement achieve information-theoretic fairness against arbitrary coalitions of N−1 dishonest parties, meaning that no proper subset can force or predict a predetermined final key with more than negligible advantage, without relying on hidden trust assumptions or incurring unacceptable key-rate loss? If not, what information-theoretic lower bounds, hybrid classical–quantum mechanisms, or approximate-fairness frameworks characterize the achievable security–efficiency frontier?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Consider an N-party quantum key agreement (MQKA) protocol involving parties P_1,...,P_N (N ≥ 3). Each party P_i contributes a private input bit-string x_i and the protocol uses a quantum communication network whose underlying interaction graph is one of the following sparse topologies, each having O(N) quantum channels: a ring (cycle), a chain, a tree, or a star. After execution of the protocol, every honest party outputs the same final key K ∈ {0,1}^ℓ.

Security definitions.
(i) Correctness: when all parties are honest, all outputs equal a common key K which is uniformly distributed and statistically close to uniform from the viewpoint of any external eavesdropper.
(ii) Information-theoretic fairness against (N−1)-collusions: for every proper subset S ⊊ {P_1,...,P_N} with |S| = N−1, and for every (computationally unbounded) joint strategy of the parties in S, including any adaptive choice of inputs and any allowed quantum operations on the channels they touch, the probability that the coalition can either (a) force the honest party's output to equal a value K* chosen in advance by the coalition, or (b) predict the honest party's output K with advantage greater than a negligible function of the security parameter, is itself negligible. The fairness must not depend on any hidden trust assumption (e.g., a third party assumed honest beyond the protocol's stated model).
(iii) Efficiency / key rate: the asymptotic key length per quantum-channel-use should remain bounded below by a positive constant independent of N (no superpolynomial degradation in N).

Problem. Determine whether there exists an MQKA protocol whose communication graph is one of the topologies above (ring, chain, tree, or star), or any other topology with O(N) quantum channels, that simultaneously achieves correctness (i), information-theoretic fairness against arbitrary (N−1)-coalitions (ii), and the constant-rate efficiency property (iii). 

If no such protocol exists, prove an information-theoretic impossibility result that quantifies the tradeoff: identify a lower bound demonstrating that for graphs with O(N) edges, any protocol satisfying (i) and (ii) must incur a key-rate loss that grows unboundedly with N, or equivalently must rely on an unverifiable trust assumption. If a relaxed notion of approximate fairness (allowing the coalition's predictive/forcing advantage to be bounded by some explicit function ε(N)) is the best one can attain, characterize the optimal achievable ε(N) as a function of N for each of the listed topologies.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an explicit open question in a 2026 survey on multiparty quantum key agreement. No published work was found that establishes either the existence of an O(N)-channel MQKA protocol with information-theoretic fairness against (N−1)-collusions, or a matching impossibility theorem; the question appears to remain open.

paper_title: Multiparty Quantum Key Agreement: Architectures, State-of-the-art, and Open Problems
original_question: Can Dicke states |D^n_k>, the symmetric n-qubit states with k excitations distributed among n qubits, be made first-class resources for multiparty quantum key agreement by designing protocols that use them as the fundamental entangled resource and by proving security and fairness comparable to GHZ- and Bell-based schemes? In particular, how do the Dicke-state parameters (n,k) affect strong fairness under collusion, qubit efficiency, realistic key rates, noise and loss thresholds, and performance across star, tree, and hybrid architectures under device-dependent, measurement-device-independent, and semi-device-independent security models?
self_contained_problem:
Let n ≥ 2 and 1 ≤ k ≤ n−1 be integers. The Dicke state |D^n_k⟩ is the symmetric n-qubit pure state defined by

  |D^n_k⟩ = C(n,k)^{−1/2} · Σ_{x ∈ {0,1}^n, |x|=k} |x⟩,

where the sum is over all binary strings of length n with Hamming weight exactly k. A multiparty quantum key agreement (MQKA) protocol among n parties is a protocol producing a common shared classical key K such that:
 (i) Correctness: all honest parties output the same K;
 (ii) Security: any external eavesdropper learns negligible information about K;
 (iii) Strong fairness under collusion: for every proper subset S ⊊ {1,…,n} of dishonest participants (possibly all but one honest party), the colluding set S cannot bias, predetermine, or determine K alone, and every honest party contributes equally to K;
 (iv) The protocol may be analyzed in three security models: device-dependent (DD), measurement-device-independent (MDI), and semi-device-independent (SDI);
 (v) The protocol may be deployed on different network architectures: star (one central node connected to n−1 leaves), tree (general rooted tree topology), and hybrid (combinations thereof, possibly client–server).

Open problem: Construct an MQKA protocol in which the fundamental entangled resource consumed in each round is a Dicke state |D^n_k⟩ (rather than GHZ or Bell states), and rigorously prove that it satisfies correctness, security, and strong fairness against any collusion of up to n−1 participants, with security and fairness guarantees comparable to existing GHZ-based and Bell-based MQKA protocols. Furthermore, characterize quantitatively, as functions of (n,k), the protocol's:
 (a) qubit efficiency (key bits per transmitted qubit),
 (b) asymptotic and finite-size key rates under realistic channel noise and loss,
 (c) noise and loss tolerance thresholds,
 (d) resilience to collusion of size up to n−1,
 (e) performance trade-offs across the star, tree, and hybrid architectures, and
 (f) achievable security guarantees in each of the DD, MDI, and SDI models.
status_search_result: Web search reveals an active literature on multiparty quantum key agreement and on fair MQKA protocols resistant to collusive attacks, but these protocols are based on GHZ states, Bell pairs, single qubits, or post-selected GHZ states (in the MDI variant). No published protocol uses Dicke states |D^n_k⟩ as the fundamental entangled resource together with proofs of strong fairness, security, and architecture/security-model characterization. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Multiparty Quantum Key Agreement: Architectures, State-of-the-art, and Open Problems
original_question: Can fully device-independent multiparty quantum key agreement be realized in a way that guarantees both secrecy and fairness solely from observed multipartite nonlocal correlations, despite untrusted devices, insider coalitions, and practical constraints such as loophole-free multipartite Bell tests; and what semi-device-independent or measurement-device-independent pathways provide experimentally realistic approximations to that goal?
self_contained_problem:
Setting. Consider $n \geq 3$ mutually distrustful parties $P_1, \ldots, P_n$ who wish to agree on a common secret bit string $K \in \{0,1\}^\ell$ via a quantum protocol. Each party holds an untrusted measurement device (a black box accepting classical inputs and returning classical outputs) and access to quantum states distributed by an untrusted source over an authenticated classical broadcast channel. Let $P(a_1,\ldots,a_n \mid x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ denote the joint conditional distribution of outputs $a_i$ given inputs $x_i$ realized by the devices in a given run.

A multiparty quantum key agreement (MQKA) protocol is fully device-independent (DI) if its security and correctness guarantees are derived solely from statistical features of $P$ (e.g., violations of multipartite Bell-type inequalities), without any assumption on the Hilbert-space dimension, the internal state preparation, or the form of measurements implemented by the devices. The protocol must satisfy:

(i) Correctness: with probability at least $1-\varepsilon_c$, all honest parties output the same key $K$.

(ii) Secrecy (against an eavesdropper Eve and against any coalition $C \subsetneq \{P_1,\ldots,P_n\}$ of dishonest insiders, possibly controlling the source and devices of $C$): the trace distance between the joint state of $K$ and the side information held by Eve $\cup\, C$, conditioned on the protocol not aborting, is at most $\varepsilon_s$.

(iii) Fairness: no proper subset of parties (honest or dishonest) can bias the final key toward a value of their choice; formally, for every proper coalition $C$, the conditional distribution of $K$ given $C$'s view is $\varepsilon_f$-close to uniform on $\{0,1\}^\ell$, and every honest party contributes equally to $K$ in a sense made precise by a chosen fairness functional.

Question. Does there exist an $n$-party protocol $(n \geq 3)$ in this fully device-independent model that, given only the observed $n$-partite nonlocal correlations $P$, simultaneously achieves correctness, secrecy, and fairness with $\varepsilon_c, \varepsilon_s, \varepsilon_f \to 0$ in the asymptotic limit, while remaining robust to (a) loophole-free multipartite Bell-test constraints (finite detection efficiency, finite statistics, no signaling), (b) arbitrary insider coalitions $C$ of size up to $n-1$, and (c) bounded quantum and classical resources? In particular, exhibit such a protocol together with a positive secret-key rate as a function of the observed Bell-inequality violation, or prove an impossibility result.

Subproblem. Identify semi-device-independent variants—e.g., where sources are trusted but measurements are untrusted (measurement-device-independent MQKA), or where the Hilbert-space dimension is bounded—under which the above three guarantees can be provably achieved with experimentally realistic parameters, and quantify the trade-off between the strength of the relaxed device assumptions and the achievable key rate.
status_search_result: Recent literature treats fully device-independent multiparty quantum key agreement (DI-MQKA) as an active, unresolved research frontier. Device-independent conference key agreement protocols using GHZ states and generalized CHSH-type inequalities have been proposed, and measurement-device-independent and semi-DI MQKA schemes exist, but no protocol simultaneously establishes secrecy, fairness against arbitrary insider coalitions, and loophole-free experimental feasibility. Surveys identify DI-MQKA among the principal open challenges for future quantum-internet key agreement.

paper_title: Multiparty Quantum Key Agreement: Architectures, State-of-the-art, and Open Problems
original_question: Can cluster-state or graph-state multiparty quantum key agreement protocols be characterized quantitatively enough to predict key rate, loss tolerance, and error thresholds as functions of the underlying graph topology and hardware-specific noise model, so that graph-structured entanglement can be used reliably for routing, error mitigation, and measurement-based key-agreement primitives?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let G = (V, E) be a finite simple graph with |V| = n vertices, each vertex assigned to one of n parties. The associated graph (cluster) state is the n-qubit pure state

  |G⟩ = (∏_{(u,v)∈E} CZ_{u,v}) |+⟩^{⊗n},

where |+⟩ = (|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2 and CZ_{u,v} is the controlled-Z gate acting on qubits u and v. A multiparty quantum key agreement (MQKA) protocol based on |G⟩ is a procedure in which the n parties each hold one qubit of (possibly many copies of) |G⟩, perform local measurements (single-qubit Pauli or adaptive measurements as in measurement-based quantum computation), and through classical post-processing (sifting, parameter estimation, error correction, privacy amplification) produce an identical bit-string of length ℓ that is secret from any eavesdropper, including dishonest insiders.

Noise model. Fix a hardware noise model N consisting of: (i) an independent photon-loss / qubit-erasure rate η ∈ [0,1] per qubit; (ii) a depolarizing or Pauli error channel with rate p ∈ [0,1/2] applied per qubit before measurement; and (iii) measurement error rate q ∈ [0,1/2]. Let R(G, N) denote the asymptotic secret-key rate per copy of |G⟩ achievable by the optimal cluster-state MQKA protocol against general coherent attacks (composable security), let η*(G) denote the maximum loss rate η for which R(G, N) > 0 holds (with p = q = 0), and let p*(G) denote the maximum Pauli error rate p for which R(G, N) > 0 (with η = q = 0).

Problem. Provide closed-form or efficiently computable expressions, or matching upper and lower bounds, for the three functionals

  R(G, N),  η*(G),  p*(G),

as functions of the graph topology of G (e.g. degree sequence, girth, vertex connectivity, expansion, or local-Clifford equivalence class) and of the parameters (η, p, q) of the noise model N. In particular, determine whether for natural graph families (paths, stars, complete graphs, 2D and 3D lattices) one can rigorously establish:

(a) an explicit secret-key-rate formula R(G, N) achievable by an explicit protocol;
(b) loss-tolerance thresholds η*(G) and error thresholds p*(G) that scale favorably with n for at least one infinite family of graphs;
(c) a topological criterion on G that is necessary and sufficient for the resulting MQKA protocol to support measurement-based routing (i.e. distillation of an n-party GHZ-type secret-sharing primitive between any chosen subset of parties) under the noise model N.
category_tag: Multiparty quantum key agreement with graph states
status_search_result: No comprehensive characterization of cluster-state MQKA key rates, loss tolerances, and error thresholds as functions of graph topology and hardware-specific noise is available in the literature; existing work treats specific small graphs or specific noise channels and leaves the general quantitative characterization unresolved. The question is identified as a direction requiring further work and is not known to be solved.
